# Assumptions, checks and notes register

Generated by `node build-manifest.js` on 2026-11-08 from every calculator's calc.js (schema.assumptions, schema.notes,
schema.sources, the runtime warnings and validation errors in the code) and tests.js (the self-tests). Edit the calculator,
then regenerate — do not edit this file by hand. The assumptions and sources are also shown on each calculator page and
everything here is carried in manifest.json for programmatic access. The long-form discussion lives in each content.md.

## Admiralty coefficient and speed–power scaling

<a id="admiralty-coefficient"></a>

Folder `admiralty-coefficient/` · Maritime · Admiralty and fuel coefficients from a known point; power or speed at a new displacement and speed (cube or chosen exponent), with fuel per day and per mile.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The Admiralty coefficient A_c = Δ^(2/3) V³ / P is a similarity rule: it holds between conditions of the SAME ship (or closely similar ships) at similar speed–length ratios, in calm water, with the same hull and propeller condition and the same propulsive efficiency.
- Power scales with displacement to the power 2/3 (wetted surface scaling) — this ignores the change of trim, draft-dependent wave resistance and propeller immersion that accompany a real displacement change.
- The speed exponent n is 3 by default (the cube law); real exponents are 3.2–3.5 for container ships and ferries and rise steeply near the hull speed, so the result is reliable only for speed changes of ±15–20 % around the known point.
- Fuel per day is proportional to power at constant specific fuel consumption; SFOC rises by 5–10 % below about 50 % engine load, which is not modelled.
- Fuel per nautical mile uses the same speed for both conditions' distance (fuel/day ÷ 24 V), so with n = 3 it scales with V² at constant displacement.
- Weather, fouling and shallow water are excluded; the known point should be a calm-water, clean-hull reference (sea trials or a verified noon report).
- The fuel coefficient Δ^(2/3) V³ / (fuel per day) is a legacy comparison figure and depends on SFOC and fuel calorific value.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the default point (47 232 t, 14 kn, 8 000 kW) gives A_c = 447.7, inside the 350–600 range quoted for cargo ships; power at 12 kn (5 038 kW), speed at 6 000 kW (12.72 kn), displacement scaling to 40 000 t (7 161 kW) and the fuel-per-mile change (−26.5 %) were checked by hand.
- Design decision: the speed exponent is an input (default 3) because the cube law is a teaching idealisation; MAN quotes 3.2–3.5 for faster hull forms.
- Design decision: the fuel outputs reuse the SFOC definition of the fuel-voyage-cost calculator (P × SFOC × 24 / 10⁶ t/day) so the two agree.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Speed change beyond ±20 % of the known point: the fixed speed exponent is unreliable (resistance curves bend); use a nearer reference point.
- Displacement change beyond ±30 %: trim, draft and propeller-immersion effects are not captured by the 2/3 power.
- New power below 50 % of the known point: SFOC rises at low engine load, so the fuel figures understate consumption.
- Admiralty coefficient outside 250–800: check the units of the known point (power in kW at the shaft, speed in knots, displacement in tonnes).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Admiralty coefficient of the default point: 47 232^(2/3) × 14³ / 8 000 = 1 306.6 × 2 744 / 8 000 = 448.2 (cargo ships 350–600)
  - Source: Rawson & Tupper, Basic Ship Theory, ch. 10: A_c = Δ^(2/3) V³ / P; typical range quoted by Taylor, Introduction to Marine Engineering
- Cube law at constant displacement: 8 000 kW at 14 kn → 5 038 kW at 12 kn; back-solving gives 12 kn
  - Source: P ∝ V³ (Admiralty coefficient held constant), Barrass ch. "Admiralty coefficient"
- Speed at 6 000 kW: 14 × (6000/8000)^(1/3) = 12.72 kn
  - Source: Inverse of the cube law
- Displacement scaling: 40 000 t at 14 kn needs 8 000 × (40 000/47 232)^(2/3) = 7 161 kW
  - Source: Wetted-surface scaling Δ^(2/3) in the Admiralty coefficient (Rawson & Tupper ch. 10)
- Speed exponent 3.5: 12 kn needs 8 000 × (12/14)^3.5 = 4 665 kW instead of 5 038 kW
  - Source: MAN Energy Solutions, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion (2018): P ∝ V^n with n = 3.2–3.5 for faster ships
- Fuel: 33.6 t/day at 14 kn → 21.16 t/day at 12 kn; fuel per mile falls from 100.0 to 73.5 kg/nmi (−26.5 % = 1 − (12/14)²)
  - Source: Fuel per day = P × SFOC × 24 / 10⁶ (ISO 3046-1 SFOC definition); per mile ∝ V² under the cube law
- Warnings: a 30 % speed cut and a 40 % displacement change are flagged; implausible A_c (power in W) is flagged
  - Source: Validity limits of the similarity rule (Rawson & Tupper; MAN 2018)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero speed, zero power, unknown mode
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 448, 106 700, 5 038 kW, 33.6 t/day, 21.2 t/day, 100 kg/nmi, 73.5 kg/nmi to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Rawson & Tupper, Basic Ship Theory, 5th ed. (2001), ch. 10 "Powering of ships" (Admiralty coefficient)
- D.A. Taylor, Introduction to Marine Engineering, 2nd ed. (1996), "Admiralty coefficient" and "fuel coefficient"
- C.B. Barrass, Ship Design and Performance for Masters and Mates (2004), ch. "Admiralty coefficient and fuel coefficient"
- MAN Energy Solutions, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion (2018), "Power and speed relationship" (speed exponent 3 to 4 by ship type)

## Air changes per hour (ACH) and CFM calculator

<a id="air-changes"></a>

Folder `air-changes/` · HVAC · Air changes per hour from a room’s airflow, or the CFM, m³/h and L/s for a target ACH, plus the ASHRAE 62.2 whole-house ventilation rate.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The room volume is length × width × ceiling height; furniture is ignored. ACH counts the outdoor or supply air delivered, assuming it mixes through the room.
- Recommended air changes depend on the use and the code in force: ventilation codes (ASHRAE 62.1 and 62.2, EN 16798-1) set rates per person and per floor area, which this page converts to ACH, rather than a single ACH figure.
- ASHRAE 62.2 gives the total mechanical ventilation for a whole dwelling from its conditioned floor area and number of bedrooms; infiltration credits and local exhaust requirements are not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 12 × 15 × 8 ft room (1 440 ft³) at 6 ACH needs 144 cfm (245 m³/h, 68 L/s); a 2 000 ft² three-bedroom house needs 90 cfm under ASHRAE 62.2. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Below 0.35 ACH, the old ASHRAE 62 minimum for homes: stale air and moisture can build up.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 12 × 15 × 8 ft room (1 440 ft³) at 6 ACH: 144 cfm = 244.7 m³/h = 67.96 L/s, one change every 10 minutes
  - Source: CFM = ACH × ft³ / 60 (ASHRAE Fundamentals, Ch. 16)
- Reverse: 100 cfm into the same room is 4.17 ACH; metric 300 m³/h into a 5 × 4 × 2.5 m room is 6 ACH
  - Source: ACH = 60 × CFM / ft³ = (m³/h) / m³
- ASHRAE 62.2: 2 000 ft², 3 bedrooms needs 0.03 × 2 000 + 7.5 × 4 = 90 cfm (0.34 ACH with 8 ft ceilings)
  - Source: ANSI/ASHRAE 62.2-2022, 4.1.1, Q_tot = 0.03 A_floor + 7.5 (N_br + 1)
- ASHRAE 62.2 in metric: 100 m² with 2 bedrooms is 25.9 L/s, within 2 % of the rounded SI form 0.15 × 100 + 3.5 × 3 = 25.5 L/s
  - Source: ASHRAE 62.2 SI form: Q = 0.15 A + 3.5 (N_br + 1) L/s
- A very low airflow warns; zero sizes and negative bedrooms are rejected
  - Source: ASHRAE 62-1989 residential minimum 0.35 ACH; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1 440 ft³, 144 cfm, 245 m³/h, 68.0 L/s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ANSI/ASHRAE Standard 62.2-2022, Ventilation and Acceptable Indoor Air Quality in Residential Buildings, 4.1.1 (Q_tot = 0.03 A_floor + 7.5 (N_br + 1))
- ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals, Chapter 16 Ventilation and Infiltration (air change rate definition)

## Air density calculator

<a id="air-density"></a>

Folder `air-density/` · HVAC · Density of dry or humid air from temperature, humidity and altitude or pressure, with specific volume, the ratio to standard air and the density altitude.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Moist air is an ideal-gas mixture of dry air and water vapour (ASHRAE Fundamentals Chapter 1); the error is below 0.5 % at normal pressures.
- Altitude converts to pressure with the standard atmosphere; on a given day the station pressure can differ by a few percent, so enter it directly when known.
- The density altitude is the height in the ISA standard atmosphere that has the same density; it is used for engine, fan and aircraft performance.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: dry air at 15 °C and 101.325 kPa is 1.2250 kg/m³, the ISA sea-level value; 30 °C at 60 % is 1.153 kg/m³.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- (none — all conditions are hard errors or silent)

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Dry air at 15 °C and sea level is 1.2250 kg/m³ (ISA), ratio 100 %, density altitude 0
  - Source: ISO 2533 Standard Atmosphere: ρ0 = 1.225 kg/m³ at 15 °C and 101.325 kPa
- 30 °C at 60 % and sea level: 1.153 kg/m³ humid against 1.164 kg/m³ dry; humid air is lighter
  - Source: ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 1 eq. (26): v = 287.042 T (1 + 1.607858 W)/p, ρ = (1 + W)/v
- Dry air agrees with the ideal gas law ρ = p / (287.05 T) at 0 °C and 100 kPa: 1.2754 kg/m³
  - Source: Ideal gas, R_dry air = 287.05 J/(kg·K)
- Denver, 1 609 m: standard pressure 83.4 kPa; dry 15 °C air at that pressure is 1.008 kg/m³, density altitude equals the altitude when the air is standard
  - Source: ASHRAE eq. (3); ISA troposphere ρ/ρ0 = (1 − 2.25577e−5 h)^4.2559
- Out-of-range humidity and altitude are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.153 kg/m³, 1.164 kg/m³, 94.2 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals (SI), Chapter 1 Psychrometrics, eqs. (3), (20) and (26)
- ISO 2533:1975 Standard Atmosphere (sea-level density 1.225 kg/m³, troposphere lapse rate 6.5 K/km)

## Air draft and bridge clearance

<a id="air-draft"></a>

Folder `air-draft/` · Maritime · Clearance under a bridge or power cable from the charted clearance, tide, the ship's air draft at its actual draft and trim, and the allowances.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The charted vertical clearance is measured from its own datum (HAT on recent British Admiralty charts, MHWS on older ones, MHW on US charts); the height of that datum above chart datum comes from the tide tables, and the predicted height of tide is above chart datum. Clearance above the water = charted clearance + datum above chart datum − height of tide.
- The ship's air draft is the height of its highest fixed point above the keel minus the draft at the longitudinal position of that point, interpolated linearly between the forward and aft drafts (perpendiculars); masts, antennas and cranes must be lowered or stowed as they will be during the passage.
- Squat lowers the ship and so increases the clearance, but it is taken as a credit only when entered explicitly; ship motions (pitch, heave, roll of a mast off the centreline) and the uncertainty of the tide are covered by one allowance; negative surges and storm surges are not predicted by the tide tables.
- For overhead power cables an additional electrical safety distance is kept clear of the conductor (flash-over); it depends on the line voltage and is set by the cable owner or the port, and sag increases with temperature and load so the charted figure can be optimistic in hot weather.
- The required margin is the clearance the master, the pilot or the port requires above the allowances; the highest permissible tide gives the window: the passage is safe while the tide is below it.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: a 45 m charted clearance above HAT with HAT 5.6 m above chart datum and a 2.5 m tide leaves 48.1 m over the water; a 56 m highest point above the keel at 150 m from the aft perpendicular of a 280 m ship trimmed 11.5 m forward and 12.5 m aft sits at a draft of 11.96 m, so the air draft is 44.04 m and the gross clearance 4.06 m.
- Design decision: squat is not credited by default; taking it reduces the safety margin exactly when the ship is moving fastest, so the page warns whenever a credit is entered.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Credit taken for squat: it disappears if the ship slows down or stops under the structure — confirm with the pilot.
- For an overhead power cable add the electrical safety distance required by the cable owner or the port; cables sag more in hot weather.
- The tide is above the clearance datum: the clearance is LESS than charted.
- Check the datum of the charted clearance (HAT, MHWS or MHW) on the chart in use; storm surges and river flow can raise the water above the prediction.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The draft at the highest point is not below it: check the height above the keel and the drafts

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Clearance at a 2.5 m tide: 45 m above HAT with HAT 5.6 m above chart datum gives 48.1 m over the water; a 56 m mast at 150 m from the AP of a 280 m ship trimmed 11.5/12.5 m sits at 11.96 m draft, air draft 44.04 m, gross clearance 4.06 m
  - Source: Datum arithmetic (IHO S-4 B-302: clearances above HAT, tides above chart datum)
- Trim: the draft at the aft perpendicular is the aft draft, at the forward perpendicular the forward draft, and halfway the mean draft
  - Source: Linear draft between the perpendiculars (rigid hull)
- Tide window: at the reported highest permissible tide the net margin equals the required margin exactly; the largest permissible air draft does the same at the present tide
  - Source: Inverse of the clearance equation
- Squat credit of 0.5 m raises the gross clearance by 0.5 m and triggers a warning; without the credit no squat is applied
  - Source: Squat lowers the hull (Barrass); credit is a deliberate choice
- Failing passages: at a 6 m tide only 0.06 m net margin remains (below the 2 m required); at 8 m the mast would hit the structure
  - Source: Clearance equation with a rising tide
- Invalid inputs fail fast: a highest point beyond the length, a draft above the highest point, a negative allowance
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 48.1 m, 11.96 m, 44.04 m, 4.06 m, 3.56 m, 4.06 m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IHO Publication S-4, Regulations for International (INT) Charts and Chart Specifications of the IHO, B-302 and B-380 (vertical datums for heights and clearances)
- UKHO NP 100 The Mariner's Handbook — heights, clearances and their datums on Admiralty charts
- UKHO Admiralty Tide Tables (NP 201) — HAT, MHWS and predicted heights above chart datum
- PIANC Report 121 (2014) Harbour Approach Channels — Design Guidelines, air draft allowances

## Alternative fuel tank volume

<a id="alternative-fuel-tanks"></a>

Folder `alternative-fuel-tanks/` · Maritime · Mass, volume and tank capacity of LNG, methanol, ammonia, hydrogen, LPG or biofuels carrying the same energy as a quantity of oil fuel.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Same energy on board: E = m_ref × LCV_ref; the alternative fuel mass is E / (η_rel × LCV), where η_rel is the efficiency of the machinery on the alternative fuel relative to the reference (1 = same energy per kWh delivered).
- Lower calorific values: FuelEU Maritime Annex II defaults (HFO 40.5, LFO 41.0, MGO 42.7, LNG 49.1, LPG 46.0, hydrogen 120, ammonia 18.6, methanol 19.9 MJ/kg) and the RED Annex III values used in the EC FuelEU guidance for biofuels (ethanol 27, FAME 37, HVO 44 MJ/kg).
- Densities of the pure substances from NIST (SRD 69) at the storage condition named: saturated liquid at 1 atm for refrigerated liquids, saturated liquid at 15 °C for pressurised LPG and ammonia, 15 °C for compressed hydrogen. LNG is taken as methane (422 kg/m³); real LNG with ethane and heavier components is denser, so enter the delivered density as a custom fuel. HVO and FAME use values inside the EN 15940 (765–800) and EN 14214 (860–900 kg/m³) ranges.
- Tank capacity = fuel volume / (filling limit − unpumpable volume). For liquefied gas fuels the IGF Code limits filling to 98 % at the reference temperature and the loading limit is lower (LL = FL ρR/ρL), and a heel may be kept to hold the tank cold.
- Not included: the space of the tank system around the tank (insulation, cylindrical type C tanks in a prismatic hold, cofferdams, tank connection spaces, vent masts), pilot fuel, boil-off, and the mass of the tanks themselves.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 1000 t of MGO (42 700 GJ) equals 2145.7 t of methanol, 2696.6 m³ at 795.7 kg/m³, 2.32 times the MGO volume at 860 kg/m³; with a 98 % filling limit and 2 % unpumpable the tank capacity is 2809.0 m³. NIST densities read 2026-10-31: methanol 795.69 (15 °C), NH3 681.8 (1 atm) and 617.7 (15 °C), H2 70.85 (1 atm), 23.995 (350 bar) and 40.172 (700 bar), propane 580.90 (1 atm) and 507.63 (15 °C), methane 422.36 kg/m³ (1 atm).
- Design decision: the reference fuel density is an input, since bunker densities vary across the ISO 8217 grades; the alternative fuels use fixed property values, and any other fuel or condition can be entered as a custom fuel.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Gas fuels: the IGF Code loading limit, the tank type and the space around cylindrical or insulated tanks add to the space needed beyond the capacity shown.
- LNG is taken as pure methane (422 kg/m³); delivered LNG is denser, which reduces the volume — enter its density as a custom fuel.
- Compressed hydrogen: the volume is the gas inside the cylinders only; the cylinders and their spacing take a multiple of it.
- The alternative fuel needs … times the reference energy for the same work.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The unpumpable volume must be smaller than the filling limit

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 1000 t of MGO (42.7 MJ/kg) carry 42 700 GJ, the energy of 2145.73 t of methanol (19.9 MJ/kg), 2696.7 m³ at 795.7 kg/m³
  - Source: FuelEU Maritime Annex II LCVs (EC guidance Table 4.2); NIST SRD 69 methanol density at 15 °C
- Liquid hydrogen needs 4.32 times the volume of MGO at 860 kg/m³ but only 0.356 times the mass
  - Source: LCV 120 MJ/kg (FuelEU Annex II); saturated liquid H₂ at 1 atm 70.85 kg/m³ (NIST SRD 69)
- Tank capacity is the fuel volume over the usable fraction: 98 % filling limit less 2 % unpumpable gives V / 0.96
  - Source: IGF Code 6.8 filling limit; usable volume = filling limit − unpumpable
- A machinery efficiency 5 % lower on the alternative fuel raises its mass and volume by 1/0.95
  - Source: Same work: m = E / (η_rel × LCV)
- Every row of the comparison carries the same energy, and its energy density is LCV × ρ
  - Source: E = m × LCV for each fuel
- A custom fuel with the properties of a listed fuel gives the same result
  - Source: Consistency of the custom path
- Invalid inputs are rejected: an unpumpable volume above the filling limit, an unknown fuel, zero quantity
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 42 700 GJ, 2145.7 t, 2696.7 m³, 2809.0 m³, 1162.8 m³, 2.32 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- European Commission, Guidance on the FuelEU Maritime Regulation (2025), Table 4.2 (reproduction of Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 Annex II) and Table 4.9 (biofuel LCVs from Directive (EU) 2018/2001 Annex III)
- NIST Chemistry WebBook, SRD 69: Thermophysical properties of fluid systems (E. W. Lemmon et al.) — densities of methanol, ammonia, hydrogen, propane and methane
- IMO, IGF Code (MSC.391(95)), 6.8 — maximum filling limit of liquefied gas fuel tanks
- ISO 8217:2017 (marine fuel density limits), EN 15940:2016+A1 (paraffinic diesel 765–800 kg/m³), EN 14214:2012+A2 (FAME 860–900 kg/m³)
- CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics — density of ethanol 789.3 kg/m³ at 20 °C

## Amps to kW

<a id="amps-to-kw"></a>

Folder `amps-to-kw/` · Electrical · Real power in kW from current and voltage for three-phase, single-phase and DC circuits, with kVA and kvar at the power factor.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The current is the RMS line current, measured or rated; for three-phase the load is balanced and the voltage is line-to-line. With unbalanced phases, use the average of the three line currents as an estimate.
- The power factor is the displacement power factor at that load; a clamp meter reading current alone cannot tell the kW without it.
- Harmonic currents from drives and rectifiers add to the RMS current without adding real power, so for those loads this overstates the kW.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 100 A at 400 V three-phase and 0.8 power factor is 55.4 kW, 69.3 kVA and 41.6 kvar. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- (none — all conditions are hard errors or silent)

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 100 A at 400 V three-phase, 0.8: P = 55.43 kW, S = 69.28 kVA, Q = 41.57 kvar
  - Source: Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, ch. "Three-phase systems": P = √3 V I cos φ; Q = √3 V I sin φ
- The power triangle holds: S² = P² + Q² for several power factors
  - Source: IEEE Std 1459-2010 (sinusoidal power quantities)
- Single-phase 10 A at 230 V and 0.9 is 2.07 kW; DC 50 A at 24 V is 1.2 kW
  - Source: P = V I cos φ; P = V I
- A 480 V, 60 A three-phase feeder at 0.9 carries 44.9 kW
  - Source: P = √3 × 480 × 60 × 0.9
- Zero current and a power factor above 1 are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 55.4 kW, 69.3 kVA, 41.6 kvar to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, 12th ed., ch. "Three-phase systems" (P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ, Q = √3 V_L I_L sin φ)
- IEEE Std 1459-2010 Definitions for the measurement of electric power quantities (apparent, real, reactive power)

## Amps to watts

<a id="amps-to-watts"></a>

Folder `amps-to-watts/` · Electrical · Watts from amps and voltage for DC, single-phase and three-phase circuits, with the power factor: what a circuit, fuse or socket can supply.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The current is the RMS current in each line; for three-phase the voltage is the line-to-line voltage and the load is balanced.
- For AC the real power is the volt-amperes times the power factor; with a power factor of 1 the watts equal the volt-amperes.
- A circuit's rated current gives the most it can supply; continuous loads are usually limited to 80 % of a breaker's rating in North American practice.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 13 A socket at 230 V supplies 2 990 W; a 15 A circuit at 120 V 1 800 W; 32 A three-phase at 400 V and 0.9 power factor 19.95 kW. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- (none — all conditions are hard errors or silent)

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- A 13 A socket at 230 V supplies 2 990 W; a 15 A circuit at 120 V supplies 1 800 W
  - Source: Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, ch. 2: P = V I; BS 1363 13 A outlets
- DC: 10 A at 24 V is 240 W
  - Source: P = V I
- Three-phase: 32 A at 400 V and 0.9 power factor is 19.95 kW and 22.17 kVA
  - Source: Hughes, ch. "Three-phase systems": P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ
- Round trip with the inverse relation I = P / (k V cos φ) for every supply and a power factor of 0.8
  - Source: Inverse relations
- Zero current is rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2 990 W to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, 12th ed., ch. 2 (P = V I) and ch. "Three-phase systems" (P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ)
- BS 1363 (13 A plugs and sockets) and IEC 60038 standard voltages

## Anchor cable catenary and scope

<a id="anchor-catenary"></a>

Folder `anchor-catenary/` · Maritime · Anchor cable catenary: chain on the bottom, uplift at the anchor, hawse tension, maximum force before the anchor lifts, wind force, holding and swinging radius.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The cable is an ideal inextensible catenary of uniform submerged weight in still water; the seabed is flat and horizontal and the chain lying on it is straight along the line of pull. Soil friction on the grounded chain is not counted as holding.
- Depth D is measured from the seabed to the hawse pipe (water depth + height of the hawse above the waterline at the current draft and tide).
- The horizontal environmental force is wind drag 0.5 ρ_air C_d A V² on the entered windage area plus any other force you give (current, waves, yawing); C_d ≈ 1.0 is a mid-range value for ships head to wind, and OCIMF coefficients should replace it for a specific ship.
- Chain mass per metre follows the ISO 1704 stud-link approximation 0.0219 d² kg/m (d in mm) unless entered directly; submerged weight uses steel 7 850 and sea water 1 025 kg/m³.
- Holding capacity = anchor mass × g × holding coefficient; coefficients are crude (ordinary stockless 3–4, high-holding-power 6–10 in sand, less in soft mud) and depend on burial, soil and the fluke angle, so the margin is indicative only.
- The anchor holds best with the cable horizontal at the shank; an uplift angle reduces the holding and the calculator reports the angle rather than quantifying the loss.
- Dynamic loads from pitching, yawing and snatching in a seaway are not included; they can double the static tension.
- Swinging radius = horizontal distance from hawse to anchor + ship length, measured from the anchor position.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the catenary identity (a + D)² = a² + s² and the inversion for the maximum force (a = (L² − D²)/(2D)) were checked by substitution; the 76 mm chain mass (126.5 kg/m) agrees with class/ISO tables (≈ 127 kg/m) within 1 %.
- Design decision: when the cable is too short to lie on the bottom, the catenary is solved for the uplift angle by bisection on the virtual arc length below the anchor (y² = a² + s² parametrisation), which converges for any L > D.
- Design decision: the shackle is 27.5 m (ISO 1704); the older 15-fathom shackle is 27.43 m and the Admiralty 12.5-fathom shackle 22.86 m — the unit menu offers the ISO value.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The cable lifts off the bottom at the anchor (uplift …°): the anchor's holding power is reduced and it may drag — pay out more cable.
- Less than 10 % of the cable is on the bottom: little reserve before the anchor lifts in a gust or yaw.
- Estimated holding capacity is below the horizontal force: dragging is likely regardless of scope.
- Holding margin below 1.5: marginal in a rising wind or with yawing.
- Scope below 4 × depth is short for anything but a brief stop in calm weather; 6–8 is usual, 10 in heavy weather.
- Static catenary only: snatching and yawing in a seaway can double the tension; holding coefficients are indicative.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Cable paid out (… m) must exceed the depth to the hawse pipe (… m)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Stud-link chain mass: 76 mm → 126.5 kg/m (tables ≈ 127), 50 mm → 54.8 kg/m; submerged weight is 86.9 % of the air weight
  - Source: ISO 1704:2008 / class equipment tables: mass ≈ 0.0219 d² kg/m; buoyancy factor 1 − 1025/7850
- Catenary with H = 200 kN, 76 mm chain, D = 30 m: a = 185.4 m, cable needed for a horizontal pull 109.7 m, horizontal reach 104.1 m, hawse tension 232.4 kN
  - Source: Catenary relations s² = D² + 2 a D, x = a asinh(s/a), T = H + w D (Danton, Theory and Practice of Seamanship; Admiralty Manual of Seamanship)
- Five shackles (137.5 m) leave 27.8 m on the bottom at 200 kN; the maximum force without uplift is 323.7 kN, at which the suspended length equals the cable
  - Source: Inversion L² = D² + 2 a D → a = (L² − D²)/(2D), H = w a
- Cable too short to lie on the bottom (80 m at 200 kN): the catenary is fully suspended with an uplift angle at the anchor and satisfies the rise equation
  - Source: General catenary y² = a² + s² solved for the virtual arc below the anchor (bisection)
- Wind force: 30 kn on 1 500 m² with C_d 1.0 = 0.5 × 1.225 × 1500 × 15.43² = 218.8 kN
  - Source: Drag equation F = ½ ρ C_d A V² with ρ_air = 1.225 kg/m³ (OCIMF MEG4 wind force formulation)
- Holding: 7 800 kg HHP anchor × 7 = 535 kN against 219 kN → margin 2.45, OK; coefficient 2 gives 153 kN and a dragging warning
  - Source: Holding capacity = anchor weight × holding coefficient (IACS UR A1: HHP ≥ 2 × ordinary; typical coefficients 3–4 ordinary, 6–10 HHP in sand)
- Default case: 5 shackles in 30 m with 219 kN → scope 4.58, swing radius = horizontal distance + 190 m; cable rules text lists 1.5 √D = 8.2 shackles
  - Source: Admiralty Manual of Seamanship rules of thumb (1.5 √D shackles; scope 6–10 × depth)
- Zero horizontal force: the cable hangs vertically, L − D lies on the bottom and the hawse tension is w D
  - Source: Limiting case of the catenary (a → ∞)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: cable shorter than the depth, zero chain diameter, unknown basis
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 126.5 kg/m, 219 kN, 203 m, 114 m, 23 m, 132 m, 251 kN, 324 kN to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Admiralty Manual of Seamanship, Vol. 1 (BR 67), ch. "Anchoring" (scope, catenary, rules for cable length)
- G. Danton, The Theory and Practice of Seamanship, 11th ed., ch. "Anchor work" (catenary of the cable)
- ISO 1704:2008, Ships and marine technology — Stud-link anchor chains (mass ≈ 0.0219 d² kg/m, 27.5 m shackles)
- IACS UR A1 / DNV Rules Pt.3 Ch.11, Anchoring equipment (equipment number, HHP anchors with twice the holding power of ordinary anchors)
- OCIMF, Mooring Equipment Guidelines (MEG4, 2018), wind and current force coefficients

## Anchor holding power calculator

<a id="anchor-holding"></a>

Folder `anchor-holding/` · Maritime · Holding capacity of an anchor from its mass and type (efficiency by anchor class) and the anchor mass needed to hold a design force.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Holding capacity = efficiency × anchor weight in air. The efficiency ranges by anchor class are those of the Vryhof Anchor Manual, quoted for a 10 t anchor fully embedded in good holding ground with the line horizontal at the seabed.
- The low end of the range is used by default. Holding is highest in sand and stiff clay and lower in very soft clay (mud), where the fluke angle must be set to about 50°; it can be close to nothing on rock, weed or a fouled anchor.
- Vryhof's holding-capacity charts follow UHC = A W^0.92, so efficiency falls slowly as anchors get bigger. The size-scaled option applies that law from the 10 t reference size; the linear option keeps the efficiency constant, which is conservative for anchors smaller than 10 t.
- Any uplift of the line at the anchor shank reduces the holding sharply: check the scope with the anchor catenary calculator. Dynamic loads from yawing and snatching in a seaway come on top of the static force.
- The safety factor divides the holding capacity. API RP 2SK uses 1.5 for drag anchors of permanent moorings in the intact condition with a dynamic analysis; ship anchoring relies on paying out cable and on the engine instead.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 6 t stockless anchor (Class F, η 4) holds 4 × 6 t = 24 t, 235 kN, and 157 kN with a safety factor of 1.5; holding 300 kN with that factor needs 300 × 1.5 / (4 × 9.81) = 11.5 t of stockless anchor, or 5.7 t of a Class D anchor at η 8 (3.1 t at η 15). Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The Vryhof size law is drawn from anchors of about 1 to 65 t; outside that range it is an extrapolation.
- Small anchors: the class efficiencies are quoted for 10 t offshore anchors. Small boat anchors in good sand often hold more per kilogram, and much less in weed, rock or soft mud.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 6 t stockless anchor (Class F, η 4): holding 24 tf = 235.4 kN, allowable 156.9 kN at a safety factor of 1.5
  - Source: Vryhof Anchor Manual (2000), Class F efficiency 4–6; hand calculation
- Class ranges: a 10 t Class A anchor holds 33 to 55 times its weight; Class D middle is 11.5
  - Source: Vryhof Anchor Manual (2000), "Characteristics of anchor types" (efficiency for a 10 t anchor)
- Required mass: 300 kN with SF 1.5 needs 450 / (4 × 9.80665) = 11.47 t of Class F, 5.74 t of Class D at η 8
  - Source: W = F SF / (η g); hand calculation
- Vryhof size law UHC ∝ W^0.92: equal to the linear rule at 10 t; a 20 t anchor holds 2^0.92 = 1.892 times a 10 t one; inverse round trip
  - Source: Vryhof Anchor Manual (2000), UHC = A W^0.92 charts; consistency check
- Small anchors warn; a safety factor below 1 and a zero mass are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 235 kN, 157 kN to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Vryhof Anchors, Anchor Manual 2000 (Krimpen a/d IJssel), "Characteristics of anchor types" (classes A–G, efficiency for a 10 t anchor) and the UHC = A W^0.92 holding-capacity charts
- API RP 2SK, Design and Analysis of Stationkeeping Systems for Floating Structures, 3rd ed. (2005): factors of safety for drag anchor holding capacity
- IACS UR A1, Anchoring equipment: high holding power anchors with at least twice the holding power of an ordinary stockless anchor of the same mass

## Polygon area from coordinates (shoelace method)

<a id="area-coordinates"></a>

Folder `area-coordinates/` · Civil · Area, perimeter and centroid of a lot or any polygon from its corner coordinates by the shoelace method, in m², ft², acres and hectares.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The corners are listed in order around the boundary, either clockwise or counter-clockwise, and the edges are straight lines that do not cross.
- Coordinates are plane (grid) coordinates. On a map projection such as UTM or a state plane grid, the area is a grid area; divide it by the square of the combined scale factor for the ground area.
- Curved boundaries must be broken into short chords or have their segment areas added separately.
- An acre is 43 560 international square feet (4 046.856 m²). The US survey foot, 1200/3937 m, can be chosen for older US state plane coordinates.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: the default four corners (the adjusted traverse of the traverse calculator, in feet) give 211 322 ft², 4.851 acres, 1.963 ha, perimeter 1 901.20 ft and centroid E 5 351.03, N 5 009.28. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Two edges of the polygon cross each other: the corners are probably out of order, and the area is not the area of the lot.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Points, line …: write two coordinates such as "1250.40, 860.15".
- Points, line …: "…" holds something that is not a number; use a decimal point, not a comma.
- Points: a polygon needs at least three different corners.
- Points: the corners lie on one line, so the polygon has no area.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- A square of 208.7103 ft sides is 43 560 ft² = 1 acre = 0.404686 ha; a 100 m square is 1 ha = 2.471054 acres
  - Source: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C: 1 acre = 43 560 ft² = 4 046.856 422 4 m²; 1 ha = 10 000 m²
- Triangle (0,0), (6,0), (0,3): area 9, centroid (2, 1); L-shape 0–4 × 0–1 plus 0–1 × 1–4: area 7, centroid (1.5, 1.5)
  - Source: Geometry: triangle area ½ b h and centroid at the mean of the corners; composite centroid by moments (4 × (2, 0.5) + 3 × (0.5, 2.5)) / 7
- Default lot (the adjusted traverse): shoelace sum −422 643.8 ft², so 211 322 ft², 4.851 acres, clockwise; the same in northing-easting order and with a closing repeat of the first point
  - Source: Hand calculation with the origin moved to the first corner: cross products 0, −162 725.27, −259 918.55, 0
- US survey foot: a 1 000 × 1 000 survey-ft square is 92 903.41 m², 4 ppm more than in international feet (92 903.04 m²)
  - Source: NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C: US survey foot = 1200/3937 m; international foot = 0.3048 m
- A bow-tie (crossing edges) warns; collinear corners, two points, a decimal comma and a lone number are refused; names before the coordinates are read
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 211 322 ft², 4.851, 1.963, 1 901.20 ft, 5 351.03 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Ghilani, C.D. and Wolf, P.R., Elementary Surveying: An Introduction to Geomatics, 13th ed., Pearson, ch. 12 Area (area by coordinates)
- Bourke, P. (1988), Calculating the area and centroid of a polygon (signed area and centroid formulas)
- NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C (1959 international foot 0.3048 m, US survey foot 1200/3937 m, acre 43 560 ft²)

## Asphalt calculator: tons of hot mix

<a id="asphalt"></a>

Folder `asphalt/` · Civil · Tons of hot-mix asphalt for a driveway, parking area or patch from area and compacted thickness, with density, waste allowance and cost per ton.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The paved area is a rectangle, or an area you enter, paved to a uniform compacted thickness; for an irregular shape add the areas of simple pieces.
- Tonnage uses the compacted density of the mix in place, 145 lb/ft³ (2.32 t/m³) by default; dense-graded mixes weigh 144 to 160 lb/ft³, so use the density on your plant's mix design when you have it.
- The waste allowance covers uneven base, edges and material left in the truck and paver; 5 to 10 % is usual.
- The thickness is the compacted thickness; the loose mat behind the paver is thicker and the rollers compact it down.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 12 × 50 ft driveway with 3 in compacted is 150 ft³ = 5.56 yd³; at 145 lb/ft³ that is 21 750 lb = 10.88 short ton, 11.42 short ton with 5 % waste, $1 142 at $100 per ton. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Compacted thickness under 1.5 in (38 mm): only suitable for a thin overlay or patch on a sound base; a new driveway needs a thicker course on a compacted aggregate base.
- Density outside 135 to 165 lb/ft³ (2.16 to 2.64 t/m³): unusual for dense-graded hot mix; check the mix design.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 12 × 50 ft driveway, 3 in compacted at 145 lb/ft³: 150 ft³, 10.88 short ton, 11.42 with 5 % waste, $1 142 at $100 per ton
  - Source: Hand calculation: 600 ft² × 0.25 ft = 150 ft³ × 145 lb/ft³ = 21 750 lb = 10.875 short ton; × 1.05 = 11.419
- Spread rate: 145 lb/ft³ is 108.75 lb per yd² per inch; the 110 lb rule corresponds to 146.7 lb/ft³
  - Source: NAPA/Penn State checklist booklet: 108 to 120 lb/yd²/in for 144 to 160 lb/ft³; 145 × 9 / 12 = 108.75
- Rule of thumb check: 100 yd² at 2 in with 110 lb/yd²/in is 11 short ton
  - Source: tons = yd² × in × 110 / 2 000 = 100 × 2 × 110 / 2 000 = 11
- Metric patch: 10 m² at 50 mm and 2 400 kg/m³ is 1.2 t, 1.32 t with 10 % waste, 132 at 100 per tonne
  - Source: Hand calculation: 10 × 0.05 × 2 400 = 1 200 kg
- A 1 in course warns; no price gives no cost; zero thickness and a density of 1 000 kg/m³ are rejected
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract

## AWG wire gauge chart and converter

<a id="awg-wire-gauge"></a>

Folder `awg-wire-gauge/` · Electrical · Diameter, mm², circular mils, resistance and weight of every AWG size from 4/0 to 40, or the gauge of a measured wire, with the matching metric size.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Diameters and areas follow the ASTM B258 formula for solid round wire. A stranded conductor of the same gauge has the same metal area but a larger overall diameter.
- Resistance is ρ/A at the chosen temperature, with the ASTM B8 increment of 2 % for stranded conductors; tinned or coated wire is a few percent higher.
- The metric size shown is the smallest IEC 60228 nominal cross-section at least as large as the AWG area, the usual safe substitution; IEC conductors are specified by maximum resistance, so check the resistance too.
- Current-carrying capacity is not given: it depends on insulation, installation and ambient temperature and is set by the wiring code (NEC Table 310.16, IEC 60364-5-52).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 12 AWG is 2.053 mm, 3.309 mm² and 6 530 cmil (ASTM B258 Table 1); 5.21 Ω/km solid copper at 20 °C. At 75 °C the shared module matches NEC Chapter 9 Table 8 (see shared/awg.js).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- This size is outside the AWG range (4/0 to 40); larger conductors are sized in kcmil (250 kcmil and up).
- The size falls between gauges (exact gauge …); … is the next larger.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 12 AWG solid copper at 20 °C: 2.053 mm, 3.309 mm², 6 530 cmil, 5.211 Ω/km, 1.588 Ω/1000 ft, next IEC size 4 mm²
  - Source: ASTM B258-18 Table 1 (0.0808 in, 6 530 cmil); IEC 60028 ρ = 1.7241 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m
- 4/0 is 0.4600 in and 211.6 kcmil; 1/0 is 105.5 kcmil; 40 AWG is 0.0031 in
  - Source: ASTM B258-18 Table 1
- Stranded 10 AWG copper at 75 °C is 1.24 Ω/1000 ft; aluminium is 1.639 times copper at 20 °C

## Ballast water exchange time

<a id="ballast-exchange"></a>

Folder `ballast-exchange/` · Maritime · D-1 ballast exchange: sequential, flow-through and dilution times and distance, the 3-volume / 95 % rule from perfect mixing, and the location criteria.

### Assumptions and caveats

- BWM Convention Regulation D-1: ballast water exchange must achieve at least 95 % volumetric exchange; for the pumping-through (flow-through and dilution) methods, pumping three times the volume of each tank is deemed to meet the standard (Reg. D-1.2). The sequential method empties each tank to the stripping limit and refills it; the residual that cannot be stripped stays on board and is entered as a percentage.
- Times assume the pumps deliver the rated capacity continuously (Q = pumps in use × rated capacity), shared equally between the tanks exchanged at the same time, so the total time is N × 2V(1 + s)/Q for the sequential method (s the stripping time allowance as a fraction of the pumping time) and N × nV/Q for pumping-through with n volumes; valve operations, line-up and the reduced head during flow-through overflow are inside the allowance entered.
- Exchange efficiency of pumping-through: with perfect mixing in the tank the fraction of original water remaining after n volumes is e^(−n), so 3 volumes give 95.0 % exchange — the physical origin of the D-1 three-volume rule; real tanks mix imperfectly (short-circuiting lowers, plug flow raises the efficiency), which is why the Convention fixes the volume rather than requiring a measurement.
- Location (Reg. B-4): exchange at least 200 nautical miles from the nearest land in water at least 200 m deep; where that is not possible, as far from land as practicable and at least 50 nmi off in 200 m depth, or in an area designated by the port State; the distance the ship covers during the exchange at the speed entered shows how much sea room the operation needs.
- Since 8 September 2024 all ships must meet the D-2 performance standard with an approved treatment system (Reg. B-3 as amended by MEPC.297(72)); D-1 exchange remains relevant as a contingency measure (BWM.2/Circ.62) when the system is inoperable, for exemptions, and for exchange-plus-treatment in low-salinity or challenging water quality. Stability, shear force and bending moment, sloshing and overpressure during flow-through must be checked against the ship's Ballast Water Management Plan — not evaluated here.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 1 − e^(−3) = 0.9502, the 95 % of D-1; ten 1 500 m³ tanks with two 1 000 m³/h pumps: flow-through 45 h (3 × 15 000/2 000), sequential with 10 % stripping allowance 16.5 h — the ratio 2.7 explains why sequential exchange is faster but needs the stability check between tanks.
- Design decision: the 2024 D-2 deadline is stated in the assumptions so the page is not read as current routine practice; the exchange calculation remains needed for contingency operations and for the many plans still carrying D-1 as a fallback.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Sequential exchange empties tanks: check stability, shear forces, bending moments, propeller immersion and slamming for every intermediate condition in the Ballast Water Management Plan.
- Flow-through overflows ballast on deck through vents or manholes: check the venting capacity against the pumping rate to avoid over-pressurising the tank, and the deck arrangements for ice and freezing.
- Exchange location does not meet the preferred 200 nmi / 200 m criterion: record the reason in the Ballast Water Record Book.
- Exchange takes … h: plan the sea room (… nmi at … kn) and the weather window; exchange may be deferred for safety (Reg. B-4.4).
- Since 8 September 2024 the D-2 standard (treatment system) applies to all ships; exchange is a contingency or exemption measure, not routine compliance.
- Pump capacity assumed constant at the rated value; flow-through at reduced head and valve line-up time are inside the allowance only for the sequential method.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Perfect-mixing efficiency: 1 − e^(−3) = 95.02 % (the D-1 three-volume rule), 1 volume 63.2 %, 2 volumes 86.5 %; 99 % needs 4.61 volumes
  - Source: BWM Convention Reg. D-1.2 (three volumes deemed 95 %); continuously stirred tank dilution e^(−n)
- Flow-through timing: 10 × 1 500 m³ with 2 × 1 000 m³/h → 45 000 m³ pumped in 22.5 h, 2.25 h per tank, 270 nmi run at 12 kn
  - Source: t = N n V / Q
- Sequential timing and residual: 2 × 15 000 × 1.10 = 33 000 m³ pumped in 16.5 h; 2 % residual → 98 % exchange meets D-1; 6 % residual fails it
  - Source: t = N × 2V (1 + s)/Q; D-1 95 % criterion
- Volumes below three fail D-1 (2 volumes → 86.5 %); dilution uses the same pumping-through arithmetic as flow-through
  - Source: Reg. D-1.2; method definitions (G6)
- Location rule: 220 nmi / 1 500 m meets B-4.1.1; 80 nmi / 500 m only the 50-nmi fallback; 30 nmi or 150 m depth fails; long exchanges (> 48 h) are flagged with the sea room
  - Source: BWM Convention Reg. B-4.1 and B-4.4
- Validation: fractional tank count, zero pump rate and an unknown method are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2 000 m³/h, 45 000 m³, 2.25 h, 22.5 h, 270 nmi, 95.0 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IMO International Convention for the Control and Management of Ships' Ballast Water and Sediments (BWM Convention, 2004), Regulations B-4, D-1, D-2; amendments MEPC.297(72) (D-2 schedule)
- IMO Resolution MEPC.124(53), Guidelines for ballast water exchange (G6) — sequential, flow-through and dilution methods, safety
- IMO BWM.2/Circ.62 (2017) Guidance on contingency measures under the BWM Convention
- ABS Guide for Ballast Water Exchange (2010) — pumping-through efficiency, overflow arrangements

## Column base plate calculator (AISC Design Guide 1)

<a id="base-plate"></a>

Folder `base-plate/` · Structural · Size a steel column base plate for a concentric axial load by AISC Design Guide 1 (LRFD): bearing area, plate N × B, cantilevers and required thickness.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The column is a wide-flange (I-shaped) section carrying a concentric axial compression only; moments, uplift, shear and anchor rods need the other cases of Design Guide 1.
- LRFD with φc = 0.65 for bearing on concrete (AISC 360-16 J8) and φ = 0.90 for plate bending; the factored load Pu comes from the LRFD load combinations.
- The support area A2 is the largest area of the pedestal or footing that is geometrically similar to and concentric with the plate; √(A2/A1) is limited to 2.
- The plate is sized with Design Guide 1's near-optimum rule N ≈ √A1 + Δ and rounded up to whole inches or 10 mm, then checked again for bearing. Grout, the pedestal reinforcement and the column-to-plate weld are not designed here.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: AISC Design Guide 1 (2nd ed.) Example 4.1, a W12×96 (d 12.7 in, bf 12.2 in) with Pu = 700 kips on f'c = 3 ksi concrete with A2 = A1 and an A36 plate: A1 required 422 in², plate 22 × 20 in, φcPp = 729 kips, n = 5.12 in governs and t = 1.60 in, as in the Guide. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Pu exceeds the design bearing strength: the plate or the support area is too small.
- The plate is thicker than 100 mm (4 in): consider a larger plate, stiffeners or a stronger concrete.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Plate length N: the plate must be at least as large as the column (N ≥ d and B ≥ bf).
- Pedestal length N2: the plate does not fit on the pedestal; enlarge the pedestal.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Design Guide 1 Example 4.1: W12×96, Pu 700 kips, f'c 3 ksi, A2 = A1, A36: A1 = 422 in², plate 22 × 20 in, φcPp = 729 kips, n = 5.12 in governs, t = 1.60 in
  - Source: AISC Design Guide 1, 2nd ed. (2006), Example 4.1 Base plate for concentric axial compressive load (no concrete confinement), LRFD
- Bearing on concrete: √(A2/A1) = 1.5 raises φcPp by 50 %, A2 = 4 A1 doubles it, and the factor stops at 2 (1.7 f'c)
  - Source: AISC 360-16 J8: φc Pp = 0.65 × 0.85 f'c A1 √(A2/A1) ≤ 0.65 × 1.7 f'c A1
- Thornton λ: X = 0.5 gives λ = 2√0.5/(1 + √0.5) = 0.828; X ≥ 1 gives λ = 1; λn' = λ √(d bf)/4
  - Source: AISC Design Guide 1, section 3.1.2: λ = 2√X / (1 + √(1 − X)) ≤ 1 (Thornton 1990)
- Given 24 × 24 in plate for the Example 4.1 column: m = 5.97 in, n = 7.12 in governs, t = 7.12 √(2 × 700/(0.9 × 36 × 576)) = 1.95 in
  - Source: Hand calculation with Design Guide 1 eq. t_min = l √(2 Pu / (0.9 Fy B N))
- A large footing (A2 ≥ 4 A1) halves the required area to 211 in²; a pedestal sizes a plate that passes bearing; plates smaller than the column or the pedestal are refused
  - Source: AISC Design Guide 1 section 3.1.1 (A1 = Pu / (2 φc 0.85 f'c) when A2 ≥ 4 A1); validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 422 in², 22.00 in, 20.00 in, 729 kip, 1.60 in to the digits printed

## Battery charge time

<a id="battery-charge-time"></a>

Folder `battery-charge-time/` · Electrical · Time to charge a battery from any state of charge with a given charger, allowing for the chemistry's charge efficiency, with the charge rate in C.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The charger delivers its rated current for the whole charge; in practice lithium batteries switch to constant voltage near full and lead-acid batteries need a long absorption stage, which the warning shows.
- The charge efficiency is the typical share of the charge put in that the battery stores; it falls when a battery is hot, old or charged fast.
- The state of charge is the share of the rated capacity; a battery that has aged holds less than its rating, which shortens the charge.
- The charger's own losses and any load running from the battery while it charges are not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 100 Ah flooded lead-acid battery from 50 % to 100 % at 10 A needs 50 Ah / (10 × 0.85) = 5.88 h at 0.10 C. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A charge rate of … C is above the usual … C for this chemistry; it shortens the battery's life or trips the battery's protection.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Charge to must be above the state of charge now (… % is not above … %)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 100 Ah flooded lead-acid from 50 % to 100 % at 10 A: 50 Ah back, 58.8 Ah from the charger, 5.88 h at 0.10 C, with an absorption warning
  - Source: Linden's Handbook of Batteries, ch. 16: charge input = capacity × ΔSoC / charge efficiency
- A 5 Ah Li-ion pack from 20 % to 80 % at 2.5 A (0.5 C): 3 Ah back in 1.26 h at 95 %, no warnings
  - Source: Linden, ch. 26: lithium-ion charge efficiency about 95 %; constant-current phase below 80 %
- Charging a 100 Ah AGM battery at 40 A (0.4 C) warns about the rate
  - Source: Typical AGM maximum charge current 0.2–0.3 C (battery makers' data)
- Doubling the charger current halves the time; a custom efficiency of 100 % gives the ideal time
  - Source: t ∝ 1 / I; t = ΔQ / I at η = 1
- A target at or below the present charge and a zero current are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 5.88 h, 50 Ah, 0.10 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Linden's Handbook of Batteries, 4th ed., ch. 16 (lead-acid charging and efficiency), ch. 26 (lithium-ion charging, CC-CV)
- IEC 61427-1:2013 Secondary cells and batteries for renewable energy storage (charge efficiency in cycling)

## Battery capacity and runtime

<a id="battery-runtime"></a>

Folder `battery-runtime/` · Electrical · Runtime of a battery bank under a constant load with Peukert correction, or the capacity for a target runtime; C-rate, usable energy, recharge Ah and time.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Constant-current discharge: the load is converted to a constant DC current at the nominal battery voltage (AC loads through the inverter efficiency); real loads at falling voltage draw rising current, and intermittent loads recover some Peukert loss, so the result is a planning figure.
- Peukert's law t = H (C/(I H))^k with the capacity rated at the H-hour rate (20 h for most lead-acid, 10 h in IEC 60896 and for many marine batteries, 1 h or 0.5 h for lithium); the exponent is a battery-specific fit (flooded lead-acid 1.2–1.3, AGM 1.1–1.15, LiFePO4 1.02–1.05) and the law overestimates capacity at currents well below the rated rate and is unreliable above about 1 C.
- Depth of discharge is a cycle-life choice, not a physical limit: 50 % for lead-acid (longer life) and 80 % for lithium are typical; the runtime is the time to reach that DoD, not to full discharge.
- Temperature and age derate the capacity (lead-acid loses roughly 1 % per °C below 25 °C and is considered end-of-life at 80 % of rated capacity); the derating factor is a single multiplier entered by the user.
- Recharge Ah = discharged Ah ÷ charge efficiency, and the recharge time assumes the charger current is accepted for the whole period — lead-acid absorption tapering can double the real time.
- Series/parallel wiring is not modelled: enter the bank capacity in Ah at the bank voltage.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the textbook Peukert case (100 Ah at the 20 h rate, k = 1.3, discharged at 10 A) gives 8.12 h and 81.2 Ah; at the rated 5 A exactly 20 h; the required-capacity inversion returns the input capacity for the same load and runtime.
- Design decision: chemistry presets carry k, DoD and charge efficiency together, because users rarely know their Peukert exponent but do know the battery type; all three can be overridden with the custom option.
- Design decision: runtime is reported to the chosen depth of discharge rather than to 100 %, and both figures are shown.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Discharge above 1 C: Peukert's law is unreliable at high rates and lead-acid voltage collapses early — use the manufacturer's discharge curves.
- Discharge well below the rated rate: Peukert's law overestimates the capacity gain; self-discharge and the real cut-off voltage dominate.
- Lead-acid above 50 % depth of discharge shortens cycle life markedly.
- No derating: cold batteries and aged batteries deliver less (lead-acid ≈ −1 % per °C below 25 °C; end-of-life 80 %).
- Inverter efficiency 1.0 assumed: typical inverters are 85–95 % at full load and worse at light load.
- Constant-current planning figure; voltage sag, intermittent loads and charger tapering change the real runtime and recharge time.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Load must be greater than zero to compute a runtime

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Peukert textbook case: 100 Ah (C20), k = 1.3, discharged at 10 A → 8.12 h and 81.2 Ah; at the rated 5 A exactly 20 h and 100 Ah
  - Source: Peukert (1897) t = H (C/(I H))^k; Doerffel & Sharkh (2006) worked illustration (k = 1.3 flooded lead-acid)
- k = 1 removes the effect (10 A → 10 h, 100 Ah); at 1 A with k = 1.3 the law predicts 162 Ah, which is why it warns at low rates
  - Source: Limits of Peukert's law (Doerffel & Sharkh 2006)
- Default AGM bank 24 V 200 Ah with a 1 kW AC load at 90 % inverter efficiency: 46.3 A, k 1.12, time to empty 3.59 h, runtime 1.80 h at 50 % DoD, 83.2 Ah removed
  - Source: Load current = P / (η V); Peukert k 1.12 for AGM (Linden & Reddy ch. 23 typical values); DoD 50 % for lead-acid cycle life
- Recharge: 83.2 Ah removed at 90 % charge efficiency needs 92.4 Ah back, 2.31 h at 40 A bulk charging
  - Source: Ah efficiency of lead-acid charging 85–90 % (Linden & Reddy); bulk-phase time = Ah / I
- Required capacity: for a 10 h runtime at 50 % DoD (20 h to empty) at 46.3 A the inversion gives I × H = 926 Ah; the inversion is exact for the default bank
  - Source: Inverse Peukert C = I H (t/H)^(1/k) — at t = H the capacity is I H regardless of k
- Derating 0.8 (end of life) scales the effective capacity and runtime by 0.8 and raises the required capacity by 1/0.8
  - Source: IEEE Std 485 aging factor 1.25 (= 1/0.8) and temperature correction
- LiFePO4 preset: k 1.03, DoD 80 %, charge efficiency 97 % → nearly rate-independent capacity and a longer runtime than AGM for the same bank
  - Source: Lithium iron phosphate Peukert exponents 1.02–1.05 (Doerffel & Sharkh 2006); typical DoD 80 %
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero load, Peukert exponent below 1, unknown chemistry
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 46.3 A, 10 A, 1.12, 166, 17 %, 3.59 h, 1.80 h, 4.8 kWh to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- W. Peukert, "Über die Abhängigkeit der Kapazität von der Entladestromstärke bei Bleiakkumulatoren", Elektrotechnische Zeitschrift 20 (1897)
- D. Doerffel & S. A. Sharkh, "A critical review of using the Peukert equation for determining the remaining capacity of lead-acid and lithium-ion batteries", J. Power Sources 155 (2006)
- Linden & Reddy, Handbook of Batteries, 4th ed. (depth of discharge, charge efficiency, temperature effects)
- IEC 60896-11 / IEC 60896-21 (stationary lead-acid batteries, capacity rating at the 10 h rate); IEEE Std 485 (sizing lead-acid batteries for stationary applications)

## Beam deflection and bending stress

<a id="beam-deflection"></a>

Folder `beam-deflection/` · Structural · Maximum bending moment, bending stress, deflection and reactions for simply supported, cantilever and fixed beams with standard sections.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Euler–Bernoulli beam theory: plane sections remain plane and shear deflection is neglected; accurate for span-to-depth ratios above about 10, and it understates deflection for deep or short beams.
- Linear elastic material and small deflections (deflection well below span/100); results are invalid once the extreme fibre yields.
- Prismatic beam with the load in the plane of symmetry: no torsion, and no check of lateral-torsional buckling, web crippling or local flange buckling — those need the relevant design code.
- Bending stress only (σ = M c / I); shear stress, stress concentrations at holes or welds and fatigue are not evaluated.
- Supports are ideal: frictionless pins/rollers or perfectly fixed ends. Real connections are between the two, so simply supported deflections are an upper bound and fixed-end moments an upper bound.
- Self-weight is not added automatically; include it in the distributed load if it matters.
- I-section properties use the thin-walled rectangle formula without root fillets, which gives about 5 % less I than the rolled-section tables (IPE 200: 1846 vs 1943 cm⁴); enter the tabulated I as a custom section for exact values.
- Utilisation compares the elastic bending stress with the yield strength only; design codes add partial factors and may allow plastic section moduli.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the IPE 200 fillet-free formula gives 1 846 cm⁴ against the tabulated 1 943 cm⁴ (−5 %), so the self-tests use the tabulated I as a custom section and the page warns when the I-section formula is used.
- Verification: the off-centre point-load case reduces to P L³/48 EI at a = L/2 and the fixed-end cases are exactly ¼ and ⅕ of the simply supported deflections, as in Roark.
- Design decision: eight load cases only, all with closed-form solutions; superposition is left to the user and explained in content.md.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Bending stress exceeds the yield strength: the elastic formulas no longer apply and the beam would yield.
- Span-to-depth ratio below 10: shear deflection (neglected here) adds roughly 10 % or more to the deflection.
- Deflection exceeds span/100: the small-deflection assumption is strained and serviceability limits (typically span/250 to span/360) are exceeded.
- I-section I ignores root fillets and is about 5 % below rolled-section tables; use a custom I for a tabulated profile.
- Lateral-torsional buckling of the compression flange is not checked; verify it for unrestrained spans per the design code.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Unknown section "…"
- Unknown load case "…"

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Simply supported, 10 kN at midspan of 4 m on IPE 200: M = 10 kN·m, σ = 51.5 MPa, δ = P L³ / 48 EI = 3.27 mm
  - Source: Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials, 8th ed., Appendix G Table G-2 case 4; W_el,y of IPE 200 = 194.3 cm³ (ArcelorMittal tables) gives 10 kN·m / 194.3 cm³ = 51.5 MPa
- Simply supported UDL 5 kN/m over 4 m: M = w L²/8 = 10 kN·m, δ = 5 w L⁴ / 384 EI = 4.08 mm
  - Source: Gere & Goodno, Appendix G Table G-2 case 1; Roark 8th ed. Table 8.1 case 2e
- Cantilever 2 m: end load 10 kN → M = 20 kN·m, δ = P L³ / 3 EI = 6.54 mm; UDL 5 kN/m → M = 10 kN·m, δ = w L⁴ / 8 EI = 2.45 mm
  - Source: Gere & Goodno, Appendix G Table G-1 cases 1 and 4; Hibbeler Appendix C
- Fixed both ends: central 10 kN → M = P L / 8 = 5 kN·m, δ = P L³ / 192 EI (¼ of simply supported); UDL → M = w L² / 12, δ = w L⁴ / 384 EI (⅕)
  - Source: Roark 8th ed. Table 8.1 cases 1d and 2d (both ends fixed); Gere Appendix G
- Off-centre point load a = 1 m on 4 m span: R_A = 7.5 kN, M = P a b / L = 7.5 kN·m, δmax = 2.284 mm at 1.764 m from the left; a = L/2 reproduces the midspan case
  - Source: Gere & Goodno, Appendix G Table G-2 case 5: δmax = P b (L² − b²)^{3/2} / (9√3 E I L) at x = √((L² − b²)/3)
- Cantilever with the load 1.5 m from the fixed end of 2 m: M = P a = 15 kN·m, δ_end = P a² (3L − a) / 6 EI = 4.14 mm
  - Source: Gere & Goodno, Appendix G Table G-1 case 5
- Section properties: circle Ø100 I = 490.9 cm⁴, Z = 98.2 cm³; rectangle 100×200 I = 6 667 cm⁴; tube Ø100×5 I = 168.8 cm⁴; IPE 200 by formula 1 846 cm⁴ (tables 1 943, fillets)
  - Source: Standard section formulas (Gere Appendix E); ArcelorMittal / EN 10365 IPE 200: h 200, b 100, t_w 5.6, t_f 8.5, I_y 1943 cm⁴, A 28.5 cm²
- Utilisation and safety: σ 51.5 MPa against S235 → 21.9 %, factor 4.57; yielding case raises a warning
  - Source: Utilisation = σ / f_y with f_y = 235 MPa (EN 10025-2 S235)
- Unit layer: 1 in⁴ = 41.623 cm⁴, 1 kip·ft = 1.3558 kN·m, 1 ksi = 6.8948 MPa
  - Source: NIST SP 811 Appendix B (exact inch and pound definitions)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero span, load position beyond the span, wall thicker than half the tube
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Shear, moment and deflection diagrams agree with the closed-form maxima for all eight cases; fixed ends carry −PL/8 and −wL²/12
  - Source: Gere and Goodno, Mechanics of Materials, Appendix G (beam deflections and slopes); equilibrium of the free body
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 5 kN, 10 kN·m, 194.3 cm³, 51.5 MPa, 21.9 %, 4.57, 3.27 mm, 1224 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Gere & Goodno, Mechanics of Materials, 8th ed., Appendix G (deflections and slopes of beams)
- Young, Budynas & Sadegh, Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain, 8th ed., Table 8.1
- Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, 10th ed., Appendix C (slopes and deflections of beams)
- ArcelorMittal, Sections and Merchant Bars / EN 10365 (IPE 200 properties)

## Rolling bearing L10 life (ISO 281)

<a id="bearing-life"></a>

Folder `bearing-life/` · Mechanical · Basic rating life in revolutions and hours from dynamic load rating, equivalent load and speed, with reliability and lubrication factors.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Basic rating life L10 = (C/P)^p million revolutions (ISO 281:2007 §5), the life 90 % of a population of identical bearings reaches under constant load and speed with adequate lubrication and no contamination, with p = 3 for ball and 10/3 for roller bearings; C is the catalogue basic dynamic load rating (for 10⁶ revolutions) and P the dynamic equivalent load.
- Dynamic equivalent load P = X F_r + Y F_a with the catalogue factors X and Y for the bearing type and the ratio F_a/(F_r) relative to the limiting value e — the user enters X, Y and e (defaults 0.56 / 1.55 / 0.28, a deep-groove ball bearing at F_a/C0 ≈ 0.08, for which 0.56 + Y e ≈ 1 so P is continuous at e); when F_a/F_r ≤ e the radial load alone applies (X = 1, Y = 0). Shock, vibration and misalignment are not included in P unless the user adds an application factor.
- Reliability: Lnm = a1 L10 with a1 from ISO 281:2007 Table 1 (90 % 1.00, 95 % 0.64, 96 % 0.55, 97 % 0.47, 98 % 0.37, 99 % 0.25, down to 99.95 % 0.077; three-parameter Weibull). The 1990 edition tabulated 0.62/0.53/0.44/0.33/0.21.
- Life modification factor a_ISO (lubricant film, contamination, fatigue load limit) is an input: 1 for the basic life; manufacturers' diagrams give 0.1–50 depending on the viscosity ratio κ and the contamination factor η_c — the calculator does not reproduce them.
- Static safety s0 = C0/P0 uses the static load rating C0 and the static equivalent load, approximated here by the dynamic equivalent load unless entered; ISO 76 recommends s0 ≥ 1–2 for smooth running, more for shock or quiet running.
- Constant load and speed: variable duty cycles need the cubic-mean (Miner) combination of loads and the time-weighted speed before using this page.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the catalogue illustration C/P = 4 at 1 500 rpm gives L10 = 64 million revolutions and 711 hours (ball), 101.6 million and 1 129 hours (roller); a1 values transcribed from ISO 281:2007 Table 1 (99 % → 0.25, confirmed against the 1990 value 0.21 in the Accendo comparison); P = 0.56 × 4 + 1.55 × 1.5 = 4.565 kN for the default deep-groove case (F_a/F_r 0.375 > e 0.28); P never falls below F_r.
- Design decision: X and Y are inputs with deep-groove defaults because they vary with bearing series and F_a/C0; the register records this.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- P above 0.5 C: outside the normal range of the rating-life formula (ISO 281 limits P to 0.5 C for ball bearings).
- Static safety s0 below 1: permanent indentation of raceways under the static or shock load (ISO 76 recommends ≥ 1–2).
- a_ISO = 1 (basic life): with good lubrication and clean conditions the modified life can be several times longer; with contamination or thin films, shorter — see the manufacturer\'s a_ISO diagram.
- Default X 0.56 / Y 1.55 / e 0.28 (deep-groove ball bearing at F_a/C0 ≈ 0.08): Y and e depend on F_a/C0 and the series — take the catalogue values.
- High speed: check the bearing\'s limiting speed and lubrication; the rating life formula ignores centrifugal and thermal effects.
- Constant load and speed assumed; combine duty cycles with the cubic-mean load before entering P.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Enter a radial or axial load

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Catalogue illustration: C/P = 4 at 1 500 rpm → ball bearing L10 = 4³ = 64 million revolutions = 711 h; roller bearing 4^(10/3) = 101.6 million = 1 129 h
  - Source: ISO 281:2007 §5.1 L10 = (C/P)^p, p = 3 (ball) and 10/3 (roller); L10h = 10⁶ L10/(60 n)
- Reliability factors (ISO 281:2007 Table 1): 90 % 1.00, 95 % 0.64, 96 % 0.55, 97 % 0.47, 98 % 0.37, 99 % 0.25, 99.9 % 0.093, 99.95 % 0.077; 99 % life = 0.25 × 711 = 178 h
  - Source: ISO 281:2007 Table 1 (three-parameter Weibull); 1990 edition 0.62/0.53/0.44/0.33/0.21 recorded in the register
- Equivalent load: F_r 4 kN, F_a 1.5 kN, e 0.28 → F_a/F_r 0.375 > e → P = 0.56 × 4 + 1.55 × 1.5 = 4.565 kN; with F_a 1 kN (ratio 0.25 ≤ e) P = F_r = 4 kN; P never drops below F_r; application factor 1.3 multiplies P
  - Source: ISO 281 §4.1 P = X F_r + Y F_a with the limiting ratio e (deep-groove ball bearing X 0.56, Y 1.55 at e 0.28)
- Required rating: for 20 000 h at 1 500 rpm (1 800 million revolutions) with P 8.75 kN a ball bearing needs C = 8.75 × 1800^(1/3) = 106.4 kN; the default 35 kN is SHORT; a_ISO 3 cuts the requirement by 3^(1/3)
  - Source: Inversion of Lnm = a1 a_ISO (C/P)^p for C
- Static safety s0 = C0/P = 20/8.75 = 2.29; years = Lnmh / hours per year; P share of C 25 %
  - Source: ISO 76 static safety factor; arithmetic
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero loads in X/Y mode, unknown reliability, zero speed
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.375, 4.57 kN, 7.67, 450, 5 000 h, 450, 5 000 h, 55.5 kN to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 281:2007 Rolling bearings — Dynamic load ratings and rating life (§5 basic rating life, Table 1 reliability factor a1, §9 modified rating life)
- ISO 76:2006 Rolling bearings — Static load ratings (static safety factor s0)
- ISO/TR 1281-2:2008 Rolling bearings — Explanatory notes on ISO 281 — Part 2: Modified rating life calculation (three-parameter Weibull a1)
- SKF Rolling Bearings catalogue (bearing selection, X/Y factors, a_SKF diagrams) and Schaeffler/FAG technical pocket guide

## Beaufort, wind speed and sea state converter

<a id="beaufort-sea-state"></a>

Folder `beaufort-sea-state/` · Maritime · Convert between Beaufort force, wind speed, probable wave height and Douglas sea state using the WMO tables.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Beaufort force is classified on the official knot bounds of WMO code table 1100 after rounding the wind speed to the nearest knot; the WMO m/s column is a rounded equivalent and differs slightly at some boundaries.
- Wind speed means the 10-minute mean true wind at 10 m height; gusts (1.3–1.5 × mean) must not be used to pick the force.
- Wave heights against Beaufort force are WMO/Met Office guidance for a fully developed open sea with no swell; fetch, duration and swell change the real height by up to a factor of two.
- Going from wave height or sea state back to wind picks the Beaufort row with the nearest probable height (mid-range height for a sea-state code); it is a plausibility check, not a measurement.
- Douglas sea state is defined on significant wave height H_s (WMO code table 3700); individual waves reach about 1.9 × H_s and the "maximum" column is guidance, not a statistical extreme.
- The "typical" wind speed of a force is the WMO empirical relation v = 0.836 × B^1.5 m/s, not the midpoint of the knot band.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Provenance: knot bounds, descriptions and probable/maximum wave heights were transcribed from WMO code table 1100 and the UK Met Office Beaufort table; Douglas sea-state bounds from WMO code table 3700.
- Design decision: classification uses the knot bounds (the original definition) after rounding to the nearest knot, because the WMO m/s column is a rounded derivative and the two disagree at some boundaries.
- Design decision: the "typical" wind speed is the WMO empirical 0.836 B^1.5 m/s rather than the band midpoint, so that force 12 has a finite value.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Wind from wave height assumes a fully developed open sea with no swell; actual wind may differ by one or two forces.
- Wind from sea state uses the mid-range wave height of the Douglas code and the fully developed sea assumption.
- Storm force and above: the wave heights are indicative only; actual seas depend on fetch, duration and swell.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Beaufort 6 is "Strong breeze", 22–27 kn, probable wave 3.0 m, maximum 4.0 m, sea state 5 "Rough"
  - Source: WMO Manual on Codes, WMO-No. 306, code table 1100 (Beaufort) and code table 3700 (Douglas sea state); UK Met Office Beaufort scale table
- Full table spot checks: force 0 calm <1 kn, force 8 gale 34–40 kn, force 12 hurricane ≥ 64 kn
  - Source: WMO-No. 306 code table 1100
- Wind 24 kn (12.35 m/s) → force 6; 10 m/s (19.4 kn) → force 5; 70 kn → force 12
  - Source: WMO-No. 306 code table 1100 knot bounds; 1 kn = 1852/3600 m/s
- WMO empirical speed 0.836 × B^1.5: force 6 → 12.29 m/s (23.9 kn), force 12 → 34.75 m/s
  - Source: WMO Guide to Meteorological Instruments and Methods of Observation (WMO-No. 8), Beaufort equivalent speeds; relation v = 0.836 B^(3/2)
- Wave 7 m → sea state 7 "High" (6–9 m) and nearest Beaufort 9; 0.3 m → sea state 2 "Smooth"
  - Source: WMO-No. 306 code table 3700 (state of the sea)
- Sea state 4 "Moderate" is 1.25–2.5 m; table has 10 codes with contiguous bounds
  - Source: WMO-No. 306 code table 3700
- Force 12 has no upper wind bound and no maximum wave height (reported as null)
  - Source: WMO-No. 306 code table 1100: force 12 is open-ended
- Invalid inputs fail fast: Beaufort 13, sea state 10, fractional Beaufort, negative wind
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 12.3 m/s, 4.0 m, 4.0 m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)
