## Belt and pulley calculator (ratio, rpm, belt length)

<a id="belt-pulley"></a>

Folder `belt-pulley/` · Mechanical · Pulley ratio, driven rpm, belt speed, exact open or crossed belt length and wrap angle from the two pulley diameters and the centre distance.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Diameters are the effective (pitch) diameters on which the belt runs: the outside diameter plus the belt thickness for a flat belt, the pitch diameter for V-belts and timing belts.
- The belt length uses the exact geometry of two circles joined by straight spans (Shigley eq. 17-1); belt sag, stretch and installation allowance are not included.
- The driven speed is n₁ d₁/d₂ reduced by the slip entered; flat and V-belts typically creep 1 to 2 %, timing belts do not slip.
- A wrap angle on the small pulley below about 120° limits the torque a friction belt can transmit; the calculator warns below 120°.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: open belt, d = 100 mm at 1 450 rpm, D = 250 mm, C = 600 mm: ratio 2.5, 580 rpm, 7.59 m/s, wrap 165.6° on the small pulley, belt length 1 190.6 + 549.8 + 18.8 = 1 759 mm. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Wrap angle on the small pulley below 120°: a friction belt may slip; increase the centre distance or add an idler.
- Speed ratio beyond 8 : 1 in one belt stage: the wrap on the small pulley is short; consider two stages.
- Belt speed above 30 m/s: check the belt maker\'s speed limit and the maximum rim speed of the pulleys.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Centre distance: it must be more than the sum of the two pulley radii, or the pulleys overlap.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Open belt 100/250 mm on 600 mm centres at 1 450 rpm: ratio 2.5, 580 rpm, 7.592 m/s, wrap 165.64°, L = 1 759.17 mm
  - Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., eq. 17-1 (hand calculation)
- Crossed belt, same pulleys: wrap 213.92° on both, L = √(1.44 − 0.1225) + 0.175 × 3.7335 = 1 801.19 mm
  - Source: Shigley eq. 17-1, crossed belt (hand calculation)
- Equal pulleys: open length is 2C + π d and both wraps are 180°
  - Source: Limiting case of eq. 17-1 with D = d
- Slip: 2 % slip lowers 580 rpm to 568.4 rpm; swapping driver and driven gives the inverse ratio and the same belt length
  - Source: n₂ = n₁ d₁/d₂ (1 − s); the belt geometry is symmetric in the two pulleys
- A short centre distance warns of low wrap (100/400 mm on 280 mm: 115°); overlapping pulleys and zero speed are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2.500, 580 rpm, 7.59 m/s, 1 759 mm to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §17-2 Flat and round belts, eq. 17-1 (open and crossed belt geometry)
- Oberg et al., Machinery's Handbook, 31st ed., Belts and pulleys: pulley speeds and belt length formulas

## Bend allowance calculator (sheet metal flat length)

<a id="bend-allowance"></a>

Folder `bend-allowance/` · Manufacturing · Sheet metal bend allowance, bend deduction, outside setback and flat length for one or many bends, from thickness, radius, angle and K-factor.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The neutral axis lies at K × T from the inside surface and keeps its length through the bend; the K-factor depends on material, tooling and R/T, so a test bend gives the best value.
- The suggested K-factor uses the DIN 6935 correction factor k = 0.65 + 0.5 log10(R/T) for R/T below 5 and k = 1 above, with K = k/2: 0.325 at R = T and 0.5 from R = 5T.
- Leg lengths are outside dimensions measured to the intersection of the outside surfaces (the mould lines); the flat length is their sum minus one bend deduction per bend.
- The bend angle is the angle the sheet turns through (90° for an L), not the included angle between the legs; angles from just above 0° to just below 180° are allowed.
- Thinning in the bend, springback and the press brake's actual inside radius are not modelled; in air bending the radius follows the die opening rather than the punch.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 2 mm sheet bent 90° over a 2 mm inside radius has K = 0.325 by DIN 6935, BA = π/2 × (2 + 0.65) = 4.16 mm, OSSB = 4 mm and BD = 3.84 mm; a 30/50/30 mm channel needs a 102.33 mm blank. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Inside radius below the thickness: the K-factor of such tight bends scatters; make a test bend.
- A leg is shorter than the outside setback: the flange is too short to bend; check the leg lengths and their units.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Legs, line …: write "length" or "length; angle of the next bend".
- Legs, line …: the length "…" must be a number above zero.
- Legs, line …: the bend angle "…" must be between 0 and 180 degrees.
- Legs: enter at least two legs (one bend between them).
- Bend angle: it must be below 180° (a 180° hem has no finite setback).
- Inside bend radius R: below 0.1 × T the DIN 6935 formula does not apply; enter your own K-factor.
- Legs: the bend deductions exceed the leg lengths; check the leg units and the thickness.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- DIN 6935: K = 0.325 at R = T, 0.400 at R = 2T, 0.4997 just below R = 5T and 0.5 from 5T
  - Source: DIN 6935: k = 0.65 + 0.5 log10(R/T), K = k/2
- 2 mm sheet, R 2 mm, 90°, K 0.325: BA = 4.1626 mm, OSSB = 4 mm, BD = 3.8374 mm; channel 30/50/30 mm has a 102.33 mm blank
  - Source: BA = θ(R + KT), OSSB = tan(θ/2)(R + T), BD = 2 OSSB − BA (hand calculation)
- Consistency: the flat length equals the inside flat portions plus the bend allowances (L-bracket 2 × 1 in, 0.06 in sheet, R 0.06 in, K 0.44)
  - Source: Flat = Σ(leg − setbacks) + Σ BA, the same blank measured two ways
- Per-bend angles: a 45° bend has OSSB = tan 22.5° (R + T) and a smaller deduction than 90°; a 1° bend deducts under 1 % of a 90° bend
  - Source: Bend geometry; limiting case θ → 0
- A 180° bend, a single leg, a bad number, a radius below 0.1 T with the DIN K-factor and a too-short leg are caught
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.325, 4.16 mm, 3.84 mm, 102.33 mm to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- DIN 6935:2011 Cold bending of flat rolled steel products, correction factor k and neutral fibre position
- Benson, S. D., Press Brake Technology: A Guide to Precision Sheet Metal Bending (SME, 1997): bend allowance, outside setback and bend deduction with the K-factor

## Bernoulli's equation and venturi

<a id="bernoulli"></a>

Folder `bernoulli/` · Thermal and fluids · Pressure at a second point from Bernoulli's equation, with velocity from the bores (venturi, reducer, nozzle), height change and head loss.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Steady, incompressible flow along a streamline; for liquids, and for gases only where the pressure changes by less than about 10 %.
- Without a head loss the flow is frictionless; real flows lose energy, which is entered as a head loss (from the pipe flow calculator or a fitting's K value).
- Both pressures use the same reference, both gauge or both absolute; the cavitation check needs absolute pressures.
- Velocities are mean velocities, and the bores at the two points set them through continuity; the kinetic-energy correction factor of a non-uniform profile is taken as 1.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: water at 1 m/s through a 100 to 50 mm venturi at 200 kPa reaches 4 m/s and 192.5 kPa (a 7.49 kPa drop); a 10 m rise at constant velocity loses 97.9 kPa. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The pressure at point 2 comes out below absolute zero: the flow cannot do this; it would cavitate or separate long before.
- The absolute pressure at point 2 is below the vapour pressure of water at 20 °C (2.34 kPa): expect cavitation.
- For air, Bernoulli holds only while the pressure changes by less than about 10 %.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Pressure at point 1 must be above zero when pressures are absolute (got …)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Venturi 100 to 50 mm, water at 1 m/s and 200 kPa: V₂ = 4 m/s, p₂ = 192.51 kPa, drop 7.487 kPa
  - Source: White, Fluid Mechanics, ch. 3.5: p₁ + ½ρV₁² = p₂ + ½ρV₂²; continuity V₂ = V₁ (D₁/D₂)²
- Rising 10 m at constant velocity loses ρ g Δz = 97.9 kPa of water pressure
  - Source: Hydrostatic term of Bernoulli's equation (Çengel and Cimbala, ch. 5)
- A 3 m head loss lowers p₂ by ρ g × 3; total head is conserved without loss
  - Source: Energy equation with head loss (White, ch. 3.6)
- A fast nozzle from 50 kPa gauge drives point 2 below the vapour pressure: cavitation warning
  - Source: Vapour pressure of water at 20 °C = 2.339 kPa (IAPWS)
- Equal bores and heights with no loss leave the pressure unchanged
  - Source: Bernoulli with V₁ = V₂ and z₁ = z₂
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 4 m/s, 192.5 kPa, 7.49 kPa to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- White, F. M., Fluid Mechanics, 7th ed., ch. 3.5 (Bernoulli equation) and ch. 3.6 (energy equation with head loss)
- Çengel and Cimbala, Fluid Mechanics: Fundamentals and Applications, 4th ed., ch. 5 (Bernoulli and energy equations, venturi meter)

## Berthing energy and fender selection

<a id="berthing-energy"></a>

Folder `berthing-energy/` · Maritime · PIANC berthing energy from displacement, approach velocity and the mass, eccentricity, configuration and softness factors; fender energy and reaction.

### Assumptions and caveats

- PIANC WG33 (2002) kinetic method: E_N = ½ M_D v_B² C_M C_E C_C C_S with the displacement at berthing (not necessarily fully laden) and the velocity component perpendicular to the berthing line; PIANC WG211 (2024) has since dropped C_C and C_S and revised the velocities — this page implements the 2002 method, which BS 6349-4, EAU 2004 and most existing specifications still use.
- Added mass: PIANC 2002 combines added mass and under-keel clearance — C_M = 1.8 for K_C/D ≤ 0.1, 1.5 for K_C/D ≥ 0.5, 1.875 − 0.75 K_C/D between, and then C_C = 1.0; the Vasco Costa (1 + 2D/B) and Shigeru Ueda (1 + πD/(2 C_B B)) alternatives are offered with the separate berth-configuration factor.
- Eccentricity C_E = (K² + R² cos²γ)/(K² + R²) with the radius of gyration K = (0.19 C_B + 0.11) L_BP, R the distance from the centre of mass to the contact point (R² = (L/2 − x)² + (B/2)²) and γ = 90° − α − asin(B/(2R)); the formula assumes the velocity vector is perpendicular to the berth within the berthing angle α and that the hull contact is at the parallel body — the special case γ = 90° should be used with care.
- Berth configuration C_C (when not already inside the PIANC C_M): solid quay 0.8 (K_C/D ≤ 0.5) or 0.9 (K_C/D > 0.5) for α ≤ 5°, partly closed 0.9/1.0, open piles 1.0, and 1.0 whenever α > 5°; softness C_S = 0.9 for hard fenders (deflection ≤ 150 mm), 1.0 otherwise.
- Design velocities from the Brolsma curves (BS 6349-4:2014 Fig. 9) tabulated against displacement for conditions a–e, interpolated log-linearly; they assume conventional ships berthing with tug assistance and values below 0.08 m/s are not recommended (floored); without tugs EAU 2004 / ROM 2.0-11 give 1.3–3 times higher speeds. Measured velocities at the berth are always preferable.
- The abnormal energy E_A = E_N × factor uses PIANC 2002 Table 4.2.5 (tankers/bulk 1.25 large to 1.75 small, container 1.5–2.0, general cargo 1.75, RoRo/ferries/cruise/tugs 2.0); PIANC stresses that "the designers' judgement should be paramount". The fender must absorb E_A at its rated performance, reduced by manufacturing tolerance, angle, temperature and velocity factors (not applied here).
- Hull pressure = fender reaction / panel contact area, compared with PIANC guidance (tankers and bulk carriers 150–300 kPa, container ships 200–400 kPa, general cargo 400–700 kPa, RoRo usually belted) — enter the allowable for the actual ship class.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the fender manual's 100 000 DWT tanker (M_D 125 000 t, L_BP 236 m, B 43 m, D 15.1 m, third-point contact at 5°) reproduces C_B 0.796, K 61.7 m, R 44.8 m, γ 56.3° and C_E 0.761; Brolsma table and coefficient values transcribed from the ShibataFenderTeam design manual (2021) which reproduces PIANC 2002 and BS 6349-4:2014.
- Design decision: the 2002 method (with C_C and C_S) rather than the 2024 WG211 method, because existing berth specifications and BS 6349-4 use it; the register records that WG211 supersedes it.
- Design decision: velocities are read from the tabulated Brolsma values with log-linear interpolation in displacement, floored at 0.08 m/s where the table shows no value.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Brolsma design velocity … m/s for condition … assumes tug assistance; without tugs speeds can be 1.3–3 times higher.
- PIANC notes that curves d and e may be high and should be used with caution.
- Velocity floored at 0.08 m/s: design speeds below this are not recommended.
- γ is small (contact nearly in line with the velocity vector): the eccentricity formula is sensitive here; PIANC says the special case γ = 90° should be used with care and small γ gives C_E ≈ 1.
- Berthing angle above 10°: the first contact is near the bow or stern and the ship is likely to hit a single fender — check the fender spacing and the hull belting.
- PIANC 2002 added mass includes the under-keel clearance effect, so C_C = 1.0 regardless of the structure.
- PIANC WG33 (2002) method; the 2024 WG211 guidelines supersede it with revised velocities and without C_C and C_S — use them for new specifications that cite WG211.
- Fender rated energy must be reduced by manufacturing tolerance, compression angle, temperature and velocity factors before comparing with E_A (not applied here).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Block coefficient … is not plausible: check displacement, L_BP, B and D

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Manual example: 125 000 t tanker, L 236 m, B 43 m, D 15.1 m → C_B 0.796, K = (0.19·0.796 + 0.11)·236 = 61.65 m (manual prints 61.7), third-point R = 44.8 m, γ = 90 − 5 − asin(43/89.6) = 56.3°, C_E = 0.761
  - Source: ShibataFenderTeam Fender Design Manual (2021) p. 19 worked example of the PIANC 2002 eccentricity coefficient
- Eccentricity presets: midships contact gives C_E = 1 (γ = 90° − α − asin(B/2R) with R = B/2 → γ = −α… formula gives 1.0 at α 0); quarter point ≈ 0.5 and fifth point ≈ 0.45 as the manual's rules of thumb for a typical hull
  - Source: Fender manual p. 19 common approximations (fifth 0.45, quarter 0.50, third 0.70, midships 1.00)
- Added mass: PIANC K_C/D 0.199 → C_M = 1.875 − 0.75·0.199 = 1.726; K_C/D 0.05 → 1.8; K_C/D 0.6 → 1.5; Vasco Costa 1 + 2·15.1/43 = 1.702; Ueda 1 + π·15.1/(2·0.796·43) = 1.693
  - Source: PIANC 2002 §4.2.3 (as reproduced in the fender manual p. 18); Vasco Costa (1964); Ueda (1981)
- Berth configuration and softness: PIANC C_M → C_C = 1; Vasco Costa with solid quay and K_C/D 0.2 at 5° → 0.8, at 8° → 1.0, with K_C/D 0.6 → 0.9; partly closed 0.9; hard fender C_S 0.9
  - Source: PIANC 2002 §4.2.4–4.2.5 (fender manual p. 20)
- Brolsma velocities: 10 000 t condition c = 0.287 m/s, 100 000 t condition b = 0.083, 500 000 t e = 0.115; 12 500 t condition c interpolates between 0.287 and 0.252; below-table values floor at 0.08 m/s (300 000 t condition a)
  - Source: BS 6349-4:2014 Figure 9 / PIANC 2002 Brolsma curves as tabulated in the fender manual p. 21
- Energies: tanker at 0.15 m/s → ½·125 000·0.15² = 1 406 kJ kinetic, E_N = 1 406 × 1.726 × 0.761 = 1 847 kJ, factor 1.25 → E_A = 2 309 kJ; fender 2 500 kJ OK; 2 200 kN on 12 m² = 183 kPa ≤ 200 kPa
  - Source: PIANC 2002 E_N = ½ M v² C_M C_E C_C C_S, Table 4.2.5 factor 1.25 for large tankers, hull pressure guidance
- Safety factors follow PIANC Table 4.2.5: small tankers 1.75, large container 1.5, small container 2.0, general cargo 1.75, RoRo 2.0; custom factor honoured
  - Source: PIANC 2002 Table 4.2.5 as interpreted by the fender manual p. 22
- Invalid inputs fail fast: implausible block coefficient, berthing angle above 45°, unknown vessel class
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.796, 0.12 m/s, 1.726, 44.8 m, 1.25, 183 kPa to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- PIANC MarCom WG33, Guidelines for the Design of Fender Systems: 2002 (kinetic energy method, Table 4.2.5 safety factors, hull pressure guidance) — superseded by PIANC WG211 (2024)
- BS 6349-4:2014, Maritime works — Code of practice for design of fendering and mooring systems (Brolsma berthing velocities, Figure 9)
- ShibataFenderTeam, Fender Design Manual (2021 edition), pp. 18–22 and 33 — reproduction of the PIANC coefficients, velocity table and worked example
- F. Vasco Costa, "The Berthing Ship" (1964); S. Ueda (1981) added-mass method; EAU 2004 Recommendations of the Committee for Waterfront Structures

## Bilged compartment (lost buoyancy)

<a id="bilged-compartment"></a>

Folder `bilged-compartment/` · Maritime · Sinkage, end drafts, trim, freeboard and the new GM of a box-shaped vessel after a compartment is bilged, by the lost buoyancy method.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Lost buoyancy (constant displacement) method: the flooded compartment no longer provides buoyancy, displacement and KG are unchanged, and the ship sinks until the intact volume replaces the lost volume v = μ·l·b·d; the added water is not treated as a weight. Both methods give the same final waterline; this one is the standard for bilging and avoids recomputing KG.
- Box-shaped vessel (rectangular sections, constant waterplane) with a compartment of length l and breadth b centred on the centreline, open from the keel to above the final waterline; the permeability μ is the fraction of the compartment volume that floods (SOLAS typical values: 0.95 accommodation and voids, 0.85 machinery, 0.60 stores, cargo 0.60–0.95 by type).
- Small trims: the vessel trims about the centre of flotation of the intact waterplane by tan τ = moment / I_L' with the longitudinal inertia about that centre; drafts at the ends are reckoned from the length L. A wing compartment (off the centreline), which also causes list, is not covered.
- GM after bilging uses the transverse inertia of the intact waterplane (the lost part has no waterplane) and the new KB; it is the initial GM only — damage stability rules (SOLAS II-1, ICLL) assess the whole GZ curve and the intermediate stages of flooding.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: a box 75 m × 10 m at 6 m draft with KG 4 m and a 15 m midship compartment bilged (μ = 1) sinks 1.5 m to 7.5 m; KB rises to 3.75 m, BM falls to 1.111 m and GM rises from 0.389 m to 0.861 m (the classic result: bilging a midship compartment of a box increases GM). A 10 m end compartment of a 100 m × 10 m box at 5 m draft gives tan τ = 0.04115 and drafts of 7.82 m forward and 3.70 m aft, matching the trimmed-box geometry.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Large trim (…°): the small-trim assumption loses accuracy and the deck edge may immerse.
- One end lifts out of the water: the box formulas no longer hold.
- Initial GM of a box-shaped vessel only; real damage stability needs the hull form, the whole GZ curve and the intermediate stages of flooding.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Box 75 m × 10 m at 6 m draft, KG 4 m, 15 m midship compartment bilged: sinkage 15 × 6/60 = 1.5 m, KB 3.75 m, BM (60 × 10³/12)/4500 = 1.111 m, GM rises from 0.389 m to 0.861 m
  - Source: Barrass & Derrett, "Bilging and permeability": lost buoyancy method for a box-shaped vessel
- Permeability 0.5 halves the flooded volume: sinkage 0.5 × 15 × 10 × 6 / (750 − 75) = 0.667 m
  - Source: Lost volume μ l b d over the intact waterplane L B − μ l b
- End compartment: 10 m at the bow of a 100 m × 10 m box at 5 m draft gives tan τ = 0.04115 and drafts 7.82 m forward, 3.70 m aft — the same as trimming the intact 90 m box until its buoyancy is under G
  - Source: Lost buoyancy moment v(x − x_F)/I_L'; independent check by the trimmed-box geometry (LCB shift = t L'/(12 T_m))
- Part-breadth compartment: a 6 m wide centre compartment keeps more waterplane inertia: I = 75 × 10³/12 − 15 × 6³/12 = 5980 m⁴, BM = 1.329 m
  - Source: Transverse inertia of the intact waterplane (centred lost area)
- Sinking: a 60 m compartment in a 100 m box at 6 m draft with 8 m depth floods over the deck and is reported
  - Source: Final draft ≥ depth means loss of the vessel
- Invalid inputs fail fast: a compartment longer than the vessel, a position beyond the end, permeability above 1
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 900 m³, 600 m², 1.5 m, 7.5 m, 0.389 m, 3.75 m, 1.111 m, 0.861 m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- C. B. Barrass, D. R. Derrett, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed. — "Bilging and permeability" (lost buoyancy method, box-shaped vessels)
- Rawson & Tupper, Basic Ship Theory, 5th ed., ch. 5 (flooding and damaged stability: lost buoyancy and added weight methods)
- SOLAS 1974 Chapter II-1 Part B-1, Regulation 7-3 (permeability)

## Blending ratio calculator (two liquids to a target property)

<a id="blending-ratio"></a>

Folder `blending-ratio/` · Process · Fractions and volumes of two liquids to blend to a target concentration, density, sulphur content or viscosity (Refutas), by mass or by volume.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Mass-based properties (concentration in % w/w, sulphur in % m/m, ash, water by mass) blend linearly by mass fraction; volume-based properties (density, % v/v, often the octane number as an approximation) blend linearly by volume fraction.
- Viscosity blends by the Refutas method: the viscosity blending number VBN = 14.534 ln(ln(ν + 0.8)) + 10.975 is linear in mass fraction, with both viscosities at the same temperature; it is accurate to a few per cent for miscible petroleum oils.
- Volumes are taken as additive (no shrinkage on mixing), which is close for similar hydrocarbons but not for alcohol and water, whose mix shrinks by up to about 4 %.
- Compatibility and stability are not predicted: some residual and distillate fuels precipitate asphaltenes when blended; test before blending fuels of different types.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: ISO VG 100 (VBN 33.196) and ISO VG 32 (VBN 29.143) blend to VG 68 (VBN 31.940) at 69.0 % VG 100 by mass; with densities 880 and 860 kg/m³ that is 68.5 % by volume, 685 L and 315 L of 1 000 L. Checked by hand.
- Refutas check: 10 cSt and 100 cSt blend 50/50 by mass to 26.7 cSt, as in the fuel-blend-heating calculator.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The densities differ by more than 30 %: check that the liquids mix, and expect volumes not to add exactly.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Property of liquid B: it equals that of liquid A, so no blend can change it.
- Target property: it must lie between the values of liquid A and liquid B.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- ISO VG 100 and VG 32 to VG 68: VBN 33.196, 29.143 and 31.940; 69.0 % VG 100 by mass, 68.5 % by volume, 685 L of 1 000 L
  - Source: Refutas VBN = 14.534 ln(ln(ν + 0.8)) + 10.975 (Maples; ASTM D7152 family), hand calculation; ISO 3448 grade midpoints
- Refutas: VBN(10 cSt) = 23.57 and VBN(100 cSt) = 33.20; a 50/50 mass blend is 26.7 cSt, not the 55 cSt average
  - Source: Refutas method as verified in the fuel-blend-heating calculator (VBI 23.58 and 33.20, blend 26.7 cSt)
- Sulphur by mass: 3.5 % and 0.1 % fuels blend to 0.5 % S at 11.76 % of the high-sulphur fuel by mass, 10.37 % by volume (991 and 860 kg/m³)
  - Source: Linear blending by mass (Maples), hand calculation: w = (0.5 − 0.1) / (3.5 − 0.1)
- Density by volume: 991 and 860 kg/m³ blend to 900 kg/m³ at 30.53 % by volume; the blend density is the target
  - Source: Linear blending by volume with additive volumes, hand calculation: φ = 40 / 131
- Limits: a target equal to A gives 100 % A; VBN inverts exactly; a target outside A and B and equal properties are rejected
  - Source: Limiting cases and validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 33.196, 29.143, 31.940, 69.0 %, 68.5 %, 685 L, 315 L to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASTM D7152, Standard Practice for Calculating Viscosity of a Blend of Petroleum Products (blending-index methods)
- Maples, R.E., Petroleum Refinery Process Economics, 2nd ed., PennWell, 2000 (Refutas viscosity blending index; linear blending of sulphur by weight and gravity by volume)
- ISO 3448:1992 Industrial liquid lubricants — ISO viscosity classification (VG 32, 68, 100 midpoints at 40 °C)

## Block coefficient and hull form coefficients

<a id="block-coefficient"></a>

Folder `block-coefficient/` · Maritime · Block, midship, prismatic and waterplane coefficients of a hull from its dimensions, and the displacement Δ = C_B L B T ρ in salt or fresh water.

### Assumptions and caveats

- L, B and T are the length, breadth and draught at the waterline of the condition considered (for ships usually L_PP, moulded breadth and moulded draught). Coefficients from different length definitions are not comparable.
- The coefficients describe the underwater hull at that draught; they fall as the draught decreases, so design values do not apply at ballast draught.
- The displacement volume ∇ is moulded (inside the shell plating, without appendages). The displacement of the shell plating and appendages (rudder, propeller, bilge keels) comes on top.
- Salt water is taken as 1.025 t/m³ and fresh water as 1.000 t/m³, the values of the load line rules; other densities can be entered.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a hull 100 m × 16 m × 6 m with ∇ = 7 200 m³, A_M = 92 m² and A_WP = 1 300 m² has C_B = 0.750, C_M = 0.958, C_P = 0.783, C_WP = 0.813, C_VP = 0.923 and displaces 7 380 t in salt water and 7 200 t in fresh water. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- C_P is above 1: the volume exceeds the midship section × length. Check A_M and ∇.
- C_VP is above 1 (C_B larger than C_WP): no normal hull has this. Check A_WP and ∇.
- C_B below 0.3 is unusually fine even for a planing hull: check the units of the volume and dimensions.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Displacement volume: it is larger than L × B × T, so the block coefficient would exceed 1. Check the dimensions and the volume.
- Midship section area: it is larger than B × T, which no hull section can be.
- Waterplane area: it is larger than L × B, which no waterplane can be.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 100 × 16 × 6 m, ∇ 7 200 m³, A_M 92 m², A_WP 1 300 m²: C_B 0.750, C_M 0.958, C_P 0.783, C_WP 0.813, C_VP 0.923
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, ch. 2 (definitions); hand calculation
- Displacement: 7 200 m³ is 7 380 t in salt water (1.025) and 7 200 t in fresh water; TPC = 1 300 × 1.025 / 100 = 13.33 t/cm
  - Source: Δ = ∇ ρ; TPC = A_WP ρ / 100 (Derrett & Barrass ch. 9)
- From mass: 1 800 t in salt water on 64 × 10 × 4 m gives C_B = 1 800 / (1.025 × 2 560) = 0.686
  - Source: C_B = Δ / (ρ L B T); hand calculation in the form of Derrett & Barrass ch. 2 exercises
- A box barge has every coefficient equal to 1; from C_B, Δ = C_B L B T ρ
  - Source: Limiting case of the definitions
- A volume larger than L B T and a midship area larger than B T are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.750, 0.958, 0.783, 0.813, 0.923, 7 380 t, 7 200 t to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Derrett, D.R. and Barrass, C.B., Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed. (Butterworth-Heinemann, 2012), ch. 2: form coefficients C_B, C_M, C_P, C_W
- Lewis, E.V. (ed.), Principles of Naval Architecture, 2nd rev. (SNAME, 1988), Vol. I ch. 1: hull form coefficients
- International Convention on Load Lines 1966, Annex I: sea water density 1.025 t/m³ for the fresh water allowance
- MAN Energy Solutions, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion (2018): examples of block coefficients by ship type

## Boat fuel consumption calculator

<a id="boat-fuel"></a>

Folder `boat-fuel/` · Maritime · Boat fuel burn in litres and gallons per hour from engine power and load, with range and endurance on a tank, fuel per mile and cost per hour.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Fuel flow is power × specific fuel consumption ÷ fuel density. The default SFC is 225 g/kWh for diesel (Volvo Penta D4 series, 220–232 g/kWh at rated power) and 300 g/kWh for four-stroke petrol engines, a little above the 270 g/kWh Heywood gives as a typical best value.
- SFC rises at light load: below about a third of rated power a diesel can burn 10 to 30 % more per kWh than at its best point. Use the engine maker's fuel curve or a measured flow where you have one.
- With the load given as a share of rated rpm, the power follows the propeller law P ∝ n³ (MAN, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion). Planing boats depart from it, especially around the hump speed.
- Range and endurance use the usable fuel after the reserve, at constant speed and load, in calm water with a clean hull. Wind, sea, current and fouling all cut the range.
- Prices are per litre in any single currency; for a price per US gallon divide by 3.785.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 200 hp diesel at 70 % power (104.4 kW) burns 104.4 × 225 = 23.5 kg/h, 27.96 L/h or 7.39 US gal/h; 400 L with 20 % reserve lasts 11.4 h, 229 nmi at 20 kn; at 1.80 per litre 50.3 per hour. Checked by hand.
- Design decision: fuel flow is shown in L/h and US gal/h as plain numbers because the unit library has no L/h or gal/h volume-flow units.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Below about 30 % of rated power the specific fuel consumption rises: the fuel flow shown is probably low. Check the engine maker\'s curve.
- More than rated power: engines are not run continuously above their rating.
- Boat speed is zero: range and fuel per mile are not defined.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 200 hp diesel at 70 % power: 104.4 kW × 225 g/kWh = 23.49 kg/h = 27.96 L/h = 7.39 US gal/h
  - Source: Fuel flow = P × SFC / ρ (Heywood §2.9); SFC 225 g/kWh within the Volvo Penta D4 data (220–232 g/kWh); hand calculation
- Range: 400 L with 20 % reserve at 27.96 L/h lasts 11.44 h, 228.9 nmi at 20 kn; 1.80 per litre costs 50.33 per hour
  - Source: Endurance = usable fuel / flow, range = endurance × speed; hand calculation
- Propeller law: 80 % of rated rpm is 0.8³ = 51.2 % of rated power
  - Source: MAN, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion: P = c n³
- Petrol: 150 hp at full power, 300 g/kWh and 0.745 kg/L burns 45.04 L/h (11.90 US gal/h); a 40 nmi trip at 35 kn uses 51.5 L
  - Source: Fuel flow = P × SFC / ρ; hand calculation
- Measured flow of 25 L/h at 8 kn: 3.125 L/nmi; with a 200 L tank and no reserve, 8 h and 64 nmi
  - Source: Hand calculation
- Light load warns; zero speed gives no range; zero power and an SFC out of range are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 104.4 kW, 27.96, 7.39, 11.4 h, 229 nmi, 50.33 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- J.B. Heywood, Internal Combustion Engine Fundamentals (McGraw-Hill, 1988), §2.9: specific fuel consumption (typical best values about 270 g/kWh for spark-ignition and 200 g/kWh for diesel engines)
- Volvo Penta D4 series marine diesel data (D4-180 to D4-300): specific fuel consumption 220–232 g/kWh at rated power
- MAN Energy Solutions, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion (2018): the propeller law, power proportional to the cube of the speed
- EN 590:2022 (diesel) and EN 228:2012+A1:2017 (petrol): density limits at 15 °C

## Boiler efficiency calculator (direct and indirect method)

<a id="boiler-efficiency"></a>

Folder `boiler-efficiency/` · Thermal and fluids · Steam boiler efficiency by the direct method, steam heat over fuel input on HHV and LHV basis, or the indirect method with Siegert flue gas loss.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Steam and feedwater enthalpies come from IAPWS-IF97 at the boiler pressure (atmospheric pressure 1.01325 bar added to the gauge pressure); the feedwater is compressed liquid at that pressure.
- The direct method counts only the heat in the steam as output, so blowdown, flue gas and casing losses all appear as losses. Fuel heating values are the GREET values (ORNL Biomass Energy Data Book); enter measured values from a fuel analysis where available, especially for coal and wood.
- The Siegert formula gives the sensible flue gas loss on the lower heating value basis for oil and gas firing (1. BImSchV); it assumes complete combustion and a flue gas above its dew point, and does not include unburnt fuel (CO) losses.
- Efficiency on the HHV basis is the LHV efficiency times LHV/HHV: the latent heat of the water vapour in the flue gas is then a loss. US practice and ASME PTC 4 use HHV; European practice and EN 12952-15 often use LHV.
- The radiation and convection loss is entered as a percentage of the fuel input at full load: about 0.5 to 2 %, higher at part load. Blowdown leaves as saturated water at the boiler pressure.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: BEE direct-method example, 8 t/h of saturated steam at 10 kg/cm² g, feedwater 85 °C, 1.6 t/h of coal with GCV 4 000 kcal/kg: h_s = 2 780 kJ/kg, h_fw = 356.7 kJ/kg, heat to steam 5 385 kW, fuel input 7 443 kW, efficiency 72.3 % (BEE prints 72.5 % with 665 kcal/kg steam). Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Efficiency below 40 %: check the steam and fuel flow measurements before trusting this result.
- Flue gas below 60 °C: the water vapour condenses and the Siegert formula no longer applies; a condensing boiler needs the latent heat recovered added to its efficiency.
- Oxygen above 8 %: a lot of excess air; tuning the burner would reduce the flue gas loss.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Steam temperature: superheated steam must be above the saturation temperature, … °C at this pressure.
- Steam temperature: this state is near the critical point (IAPWS-IF97 region 3), outside the range covered.
- Feedwater temperature: it must be below the saturation temperature, … °C at this pressure.
- Lower heating value: it cannot exceed the higher heating value.
- Fuel flow: the steam carries more heat than the fuel supplies on the gross basis; check the flows and units.
- Siegert constants: the 1. BImSchV gives them only for heating oil, natural gas and LPG; choose "Enter A2 and B" for this fuel.
- Flue gas temperature: it must be above the combustion air temperature.
- Lower heating value: the Siegert flue gas loss is on the LHV basis; enter the lower heating value of the fuel.
- Flue gas temperature: the flue gas and radiation losses exceed 100 %; check the readings.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- BEE example: 8 t/h steam at 10 kg/cm² g, feedwater 85 °C, 1.6 t/h coal of GCV 4 000 kcal/kg gives 72.5 %
  - Source: Bureau of Energy Efficiency, Book 4 Ch. 1 Boilers, direct method example (72.5 % with h_s = 665 kcal/kg)
- Steam at 10 bar absolute: dry saturated h_g = 2 777.1 kJ/kg, wet x = 0.9 gives h_f + 0.9 h_fg = 2 575.7 kJ/kg; 250 °C superheated 2 943.1 kJ/kg
  - Source: IAPWS-IF97 steam tables (saturation at 1 MPa: h_f 762.7, h_g 2 777.1 kJ/kg; 1 MPa, 250 °C: 2 943.1 kJ/kg; Çengel & Boles Tables A-5 and A-6)
- Siegert: natural gas, flue 180 °C, air 20 °C, 3 % O2 gives 7.31 % loss; heating oil 200 °C, 4 % O2 gives 8.46 %
  - Source: 1. BImSchV Anlage 2 Nr. 3.4: q_A = (t_A − t_L)(A2/(21 − O2) + B), gas 0.66/0.009, oil 0.68/0.007; hand calculation
- Indirect without blowdown: η_LHV = 1 − q_A − q_rad and η_HHV = η_LHV × LHV/HHV (natural gas 47.141 / 52.225 MJ/kg)
  - Source: Loss balance; GREET heating values (ORNL Biomass Energy Data Book, Appendix A)
- Blowdown share: 5 % blowdown at 10 bar g, feedwater 80 °C takes (0.05/0.95)(h_f − h_fw) of the heat absorbed
  - Source: Energy balance of the boiler water (blowdown leaves as saturated liquid); hand calculation
- Invalid input: Siegert table for coal, feedwater above saturation, superheat below saturation and LHV above HHV are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2 780 kJ/kg, 356.7 kJ/kg, 5 385 kW, 7 443 kW, 72.3 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Bureau of Energy Efficiency (India), Energy Performance Assessment for Equipment and Utility Systems, Book 4 Ch. 1 Boilers: direct and indirect methods (worked direct-method example)
- IAPWS R7-97(2012) Revised Release on the IAPWS Industrial Formulation 1997 (regions 1, 2 and 4) for steam and feedwater enthalpy
- Erste Verordnung zur Durchführung des Bundes-Immissionsschutzgesetzes (1. BImSchV, 2010), Anlage 2 Nr. 3.4: Siegert formula q_A = (t_A − t_L)(A2/(21 − O2) + B) with A2 and B for heating oil, natural gas and LPG
- ORNL Biomass Energy Data Book (2011), Appendix A: Lower and Higher Heating Values of Gas, Liquid and Solid Fuels (GREET 1.8d.1, Argonne National Laboratory)

## Bollard pull for a tow

<a id="bollard-pull"></a>

Folder `bollard-pull/` · Maritime · Towing force to hold a tow in wind, waves and current (DNV method: wind, current and wave-drift forces) and the tug bollard pull required with tug efficiency.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Static (zero-speed) holding condition with wind, waves and current co-linear and head-on to the tow, as the DNV marine-operations rules require: ocean tows must hold station in 20 m/s wind, 5 m significant wave height and 0.5–1 m/s current (DNVGL-ST-N001 / ND-0030 use 0.5 m/s, the 1996 DNV Rules for Marine Operations 1 m/s); benign-weather tows 15 m/s, 2 m, 0.5 m/s; coastal tows must make 2 knots over the ground, which adds 2 knots to the current speed.
- Wind force ½ ρ_air C_s C_h A V² with the DNV-OS-C301 shape coefficient (1.0 flat hull side, 1.1 clustered deckhouses, 1.25–1.5 isolated structures) and height coefficient (1.0 below 15.3 m, 1.1 to 30.5 m, 1.2 to 46 m, 1.3 to 61 m, 1.37 to 76 m) applied to the whole transverse windage area; a real calculation sums several area bands — enter Σ C_s C_h A as the area with coefficients 1.0 if you have it.
- Current/hull force: for barges and blunt tows ½ ρ_w C_d A_frontal V² with C_d 0.5 (raked or square bow), 0.35 or 0.20 (DNV-OS-C301 / RP-H103 §3.2.4); for ship-shaped hulls the ITTC-1957 friction on the wetted surface with a form factor and an optional fouling allowance ΔC_F — a Holtrop–Mennen calm-water resistance at the current speed is the more complete alternative.
- Wave drift force on the towed object ⅛ ρ_w g R² B H_s² with the DNV-RP-H103 §7.2.6.4 reflection coefficients (ship bow 0.45, spoon-bow barge 0.55, raked barge 0.67, vertical cylinder 0.88, Condeep 0.97, square face 1.0): a mean second-order force in irregular head seas, valid for the object much longer than the waves; wave-frequency towline snatch loads are a separate dynamic matter.
- Tug efficiency η = effective pull in the weather ÷ certified continuous static bollard pull: 0.75 is the classic DNV value for ocean tows; DNVGL-ST-N001 Table 11-2 gives values by tug size and weather (roughly 0.70 for small tugs up to 0.80 for large tugs in moderate seas) — enter the value agreed with the marine warranty surveyor. Certified BP is at 100 % MCR averaged over 10 minutes; the 110 % maximum must not be used.
- No allowance is made for the towline catenary weight, propeller-race interaction at short towlines (ST-N001 §11.12.2.14), shallow water or the tug's own resistance when making way; the "towing speed" shown is a simple linear estimate of the free-running pull reduction.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the Global Maritime technical note for the Haewene Brim FPSO tow (L 252 m, B 42 m, T 7 m; 20 m/s, 5 m, 1 m/s; Σ C_s C_h A = 2 113 m², bow area 292.7 m² with C_d 0.5, R 0.45, η 0.75) is reproduced: wave drift 27.2 t, wind 52.6 t, current 7.65 t, required 116.7 t; the 2-knot case (2.03 m/s relative) gives 148.5 t — against 165 t available.
- Design decision: forces are reported in kN and tonnes-force because towing contracts and bollard pull certificates quote tonnes.
- Design decision: the DNV reflection-coefficient table is offered as a select with a custom value, and both the frontal-drag and friction hull methods are available because barges and ships are treated differently in practice.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Coastal condition: 2 knots over the ground added to the current for the hull force (wind and waves unchanged), per the DNV marine-operations rules.
- Shape and height coefficients 1.0: either the windage area already includes Σ C_s C_h A, or deckhouses and tall structures are being under-counted (C_s up to 1.5, C_h up to 1.37).
- Frontal-drag hull force is a barge simplification subject to warranty-surveyor acceptance; use the friction method or Holtrop–Mennen for a ship-shaped tow.
- Margin below 10 %: warranty surveyors usually expect some reserve over the calculated requirement.
- Tug efficiency … converts the towline pull to certified bollard pull; confirm the value with the marine warranty surveyor (DNVGL-ST-N001 Table 11-2).
- Static holding calculation with co-linear head weather; towline dynamics, catenary weight and short-towline propeller-race losses are not included.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- No environmental force: enter a wind speed, wave height or current

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Haewene Brim, zero speed: wind 52.6 t, current 7.65 t, wave drift 27.24 t, total 87.5 t, required bollard pull 116.7 t (÷ 0.75); 165 t tug OK
  - Source: Global Maritime TN_24138_1 (2013) spreadsheet results (wind 52.64 t, current 7.65 t, wave 27.24 t, total 87.53 t, required 116.71 t) — their g = 9.81 and ρ_air 0.00122 t/m³
- Haewene Brim, 2 knots over the ground: relative speed 2.03 m/s, current force 31.5 t, total 111.4 t, required 148.5 t
  - Source: Global Maritime TN_24138_1 case 2 (current 31.47 t, total 111.36 t, required 148.48 t)
- Component formulas: wind ½·1.22·2113.06·400 = 515.6 kN; current ½·1025·0.5·292.74·1 = 75.0 kN; wave drift ⅛·1025·g·0.45²·42·25 = 267.2 kN
  - Source: DNV-OS-C301 wind/current forms; DNV-RP-H103 §7.2.6.4 wave drift force with R 0.45 (ship bow)
- Reflection table (DNV-RP-H103): square 1.00, Condeep 0.97, cylinder 0.88, raked barge 0.67, spoon barge 0.55, ship bow 0.45; a raked barge sees (0.67/0.45)² = 2.2 × the ship-bow drift force
  - Source: DNV-RP-H103 (2011) §7.2.6.4 reflection coefficients
- Ship-shaped hull by ITTC friction: S 12 000 m², L 252 m at 1 m/s → Rn 2.12·10⁸, C_F 0.001874, (1+k) 1.25 + ΔC_F 0.0004 → 16.9 kN; the design conditions scale forces with V²
  - Source: ITTC-1957 friction line; DNV-RP-H103 recommends a calm-water resistance method for ship-shaped tows
- Benign-weather tow (15 m/s, 2 m, 0.5 m/s): wave drift falls by (2/5)² and the requirement to about 48 t (wind 290 kN, current 19 kN, wave 43 kN); tug efficiency 0.80 lowers the requirement by 6.25 %
  - Source: ND-0030 / DNVGL-ST-N001 benign criteria; η definition
- Tug adequacy and towing speed: 165 t tug holds the Brim with 41 % margin and makes ≈ 2–4 knots in the design weather; a 100 t tug is INSUFFICIENT with zero speed
  - Source: Linear pull-reduction estimate (thenavalarch part II) — indicative only
- Invalid inputs fail fast: no environment at all, tug efficiency above 1, unknown bow type
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 516 kN, 75 kN, 267 kN, 87.5 t, 41 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- DNVGL-ST-N001 Marine operations and marine warranty (2016, amended 2020), Sec. 11.12 tug selection and bollard pull requirements; DNV Rules for Planning and Execution of Marine Operations (1996/2000) Pt. 2 Ch. 2 §3.3 towing resistance and tug efficiency 0.75
- DNV-RP-H103 Modelling and analysis of marine operations (2011), §7.2.6 wave drift force on towed objects and reflection coefficients, §3.2.4 current force
- DNV-OS-C301 Stability and watertight integrity (2011), Tables B1–B2 wind shape and height coefficients
- Global Maritime, Technical Note TN_24138_1 "Haewene Brim bollard pull calculation" (2013) — worked example used for verification; Noble Denton ND-0030 Guidelines for marine transportations (design environments 20 m/s, 5 m, 0.5 m/s)

## Bolt torque and preload

<a id="bolt-torque"></a>

Folder `bolt-torque/` · Mechanical · Preload and tightening torque for ISO metric bolts by the VDI 2230 method, with property class, friction, proof load and preload scatter.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Torque–preload relation per VDI 2230: M_A = F_M (0.16 P + 0.58 d₂ μ_G + D_Km μ_K / 2); the coefficients 0.16 ≈ 1/(2π) and 0.58 ≈ 1/(2 cos 30°) are the standard approximations for 60° ISO threads.
- The 90 %-of-yield preload follows VDI 2230 eq. R8/1 with the plastic torsion section modulus (π d_s³/12) and d_s = (d₂ + d₃)/2, which is why it reproduces the VDI/Bossard tables (M12 8.8, μ = 0.14: 41.9 kN, 93 N·m).
- Friction coefficients dominate the result (a change from 0.10 to 0.20 nearly doubles the torque for the same preload) and are only known to the VDI class range; the presets are mid-class values.
- Under-head bearing diameter D_Km is taken as the mean of the ISO 4014/4017 hex-head minimum bearing diameter and an ISO 273 medium clearance hole; flange bolts, washers, socket heads and nuts change it.
- Material strengths are ISO 898-1 minimum values (8.8 uses 660/600 MPa above M16); stainless classes use R_p0.2 as proof stress and are valid up to M24.
- Torque-controlled tightening scatters: the minimum preload is F_M divided by the tightening factor α_A (1.4–1.6 torque wrench with measured friction, 1.6–2.0 standard torque wrench, 2.5–4 impact wrench).
- No joint analysis: clamp-load loss from embedding and relaxation, external load sharing, thread stripping, fatigue and gasket requirements need the full VDI 2230 procedure.
- Coarse-pitch ISO 261 threads only; fine threads have smaller pitch and larger stress area and are not tabulated here.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the VDI 2230 / Bossard table value for M12 8.8 at μ = 0.14 (41.9 kN, 93 N·m) is reproduced only when the plastic torsion modulus π d_s³/12 and the exact thread-torque form are used; a purely elastic von Mises check gives about 38.3 kN. Bossard F-047 values were confirmed online the same day.
- Verification: ISO 898-1 proof loads (M12 8.8 48.9 kN, M20 10.9 203 kN, M20 8.8 147 kN) and stress areas are reproduced from the ISO 724 geometry to 0.3 %.
- Design decision: the tightening torque uses the rounded VDI R8/4 coefficients (0.16 P + 0.58 d₂ μ_G) as published, while the stress check uses the exact form, so that both the torque table and the 90 % utilisation are reproduced.
- Design decision: the under-head bearing diameter defaults to the ISO 4014/4017 head on an ISO 273 medium hole (D_Km = 15.07 mm for M12) because that is what the VDI tables assume.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Preload exceeds the ISO 898-1 proof load: permanent set is likely. Reduce the target or use a higher property class.
- Reduced stress exceeds the yield strength: the bolt yields during tightening (acceptable only for angle-controlled tightening into the plastic range).
- Thread and under-head friction differ by more than 0.1 — unusual unless only one surface is lubricated.
- Stainless property classes A2-70/A4-80 are specified up to M24 in ISO 3506-1; larger sizes have lower guaranteed strength.
- Torque tightening gives a preload scatter of roughly ±… % for α_A = …; the minimum preload is what the joint design may rely on.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- ISO thread geometry: stress areas M10 58.0, M12 84.3, M16 157, M20 245 mm²; M12 d₂ = 10.863 mm, d₃ = 9.853 mm
  - Source: ISO 898-1:2013 Table 4 (nominal stress areas, coarse thread); ISO 724 basic dimensions (d₂ = d − 0.6495 P, d₃ = d − 1.2269 P)
- Proof loads: M12 8.8 = 48.9 kN, M20 10.9 = 203 kN, M20 8.8 = 147 kN (600 MPa above M16)
  - Source: ISO 898-1:2013 Table 7 (proof loads, coarse thread): 48 900 N, 203 000 N, 147 000 N
- VDI 2230 Table A1 / Bossard: M12 8.8 at μ_G = μ_K = 0.14, 90 % yield → F_M = 41.9 kN, M_A = 93 N·m
  - Source: VDI 2230 Part 1 (2015) Table A1; Bossard technical resource F-047 (M12/0.14, class 8.8: F_M max 41.9 kN, M_A max 93 N·m)
- Shigley: the nut factor K comes out ≈ 0.20 when thread and collar friction are both 0.15
  - Source: Budynas & Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §8-8 eq. 8-27 (K ≈ 0.20 for μ = μ_c = 0.15)
- Percent-of-proof mode: 75 % of 48.9 kN = 36.7 kN, torque at μ = 0.14 = 81.2 N·m; 90 % permanent = 44.0 kN
  - Source: Shigley 10th ed. §8-7: F_i = 0.75 F_p reusable, 0.90 F_p permanent; torque per VDI formula with D_Km 15.065 mm
- Given preload 30 kN on M12 with μ = 0.10: M_G = 18.9 N·m, head torque 22.6 N·m, M_A = 49.9 N·m vs 72 N·m from the K = 0.2 rule
  - Source: VDI 2230 eq. R8/4 M_A = F_M (0.16 P + 0.58 d₂ μ_G + D_Km μ_K / 2); hand calculation
- VDI preload formula: M12 8.8 allows 45.2 kN at μ_G 0.08 but 38.5 kN at μ_G 0.20 (more torsion); tightening factor 1.7 gives F_min = F_M / 1.7
  - Source: VDI 2230 Part 1 (2015) eq. R8/1 evaluated by hand (bracket 0.226 → √1.153; bracket 0.444 → √1.591) and Table A8 (tightening factor α_A)
- Warnings: a given preload above the proof load and a reduced stress above yield are flagged
  - Source: ISO 898-1 proof load definition; VDI 2230 yield criterion
- Unit layer: 93 N·m = 68.6 lbf·ft; 41.9 kN = 9 420 lbf
  - Source: NIST SP 811 Appendix B: 1 lbf·ft = 1.355818 N·m, 1 lbf = 4.448222 N
- Invalid inputs fail fast: unknown size, unknown class, zero given preload
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 10.863 mm, 9.853 mm, 84.3 mm², 640 MPa, 48.9 kN, 42.0 kN, 24.7 kN, 48.8 N·m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

- VDI 2230 Part 1 (2015), Systematic calculation of highly stressed bolted joints — eq. R8/1 (assembly preload), R8/4 (tightening torque), Table A1 (preloads and torques), Table A5 (friction classes)
- ISO 898-1:2013, Mechanical properties of fasteners — Table 3 (property classes), Table 7 (proof loads)

- ISO 4014 / ISO 4017 (hex head bolts, bearing diameter d_w), ISO 273 (clearance holes)
