- Bossard, Technical resources F-047 (VDI 2230 preload and torque tables)

## Breaker size calculator

<a id="breaker-size"></a>

Folder `breaker-size/` · Electrical · Breaker size for a load in amps or watts, by the NEC 125 % continuous-load rule or IEC Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, with the standard rating and a wire check.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The breaker protects a feeder or branch circuit for general loads. Motor circuits follow other rules (NEC 430.52 allows up to 250 % of the motor current for inverse-time breakers; IEC uses motor-protection breakers or fuses chosen for the starting current).
- NEC: a continuous load runs for 3 hours or more, and the breaker must be rated at least 125 % of it (210.20(A), 215.3), the same as loading a standard breaker to 80 %. 100 %-rated breakers in listed assemblies are not covered.
- IEC: the rated current must be at least the design current, Ib ≤ In, and at most the current-carrying capacity of the cable, In ≤ Iz (IEC 60364-4-43, 433.1). For MCBs and most circuit breakers the conventional tripping current is 1.45 In or less, so the second condition of 433.1 is then met as well.
- The power factor applies only to AC; the current from power uses P = V I (DC), V I cos φ (single-phase) or √3 V I cos φ (three-phase).
- The wire is not sized here because its ampacity depends on insulation, installation and ambient temperature; enter it from the code table to check the pair. NEC 240.4(D) limits 14, 12 and 10 AWG copper to 15, 20 and 30 A.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 7.2 kW EV charger at 240 V draws 30 A; as a continuous load it needs 37.5 A, so a 40 A breaker (NEC 625.41 and 210.20(A)). Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above the largest standard rating (… A): split the load or use parallel feeders.
- The wire is too small for the breaker.
- The wire ampacity (… A) is below the minimum rating needed for the load (… A).
- Most fixed loads that can run 3 hours or more, such as heaters, EV chargers and lighting, count as continuous under the NEC.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- NEC: a 7.2 kW EV charger at 240 V draws 30 A; continuous, it needs 37.5 A, so a 40 A breaker loaded to 75 %
  - Source: NFPA 70 (2023) 625.41 and 210.20(A): 125 % of the continuous load; 240.6(A) standard ratings
- NEC: 16 A continuous needs a 20 A breaker (the 80 % rule) and allows 12 AWG copper; 40 A non-continuous takes a 40 A breaker
  - Source: NFPA 70 (2023) 210.20(A); 240.4(D)(5): 12 AWG copper 20 A
- IEC: a 3.5 kW load at 230 V draws 15.2 A, so a 16 A MCB; 11 kW three-phase at 400 V and 0.9 draws 17.6 A, so 20 A, OK on a 24 A cable
  - Source: IEC 60364-4-43, 433.1: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz; IEC 60898-1 preferred ratings 16, 20 A
- Wire checks: 52 A on a 55 A wire takes 60 A, allowed only by NEC 240.4(B); 50 A continuous needs 70 A and fails on 55 A wire; IEC never rounds up past Iz
  - Source: NFPA 70 (2023) 240.4(B) (next higher standard rating up to 800 A); IEC 60364-4-43 433.1
- Rating lists are increasing; beyond the largest rating the outputs are empty with a warning; bad inputs are rejected
  - Source: NEC 240.6(A); IEC 60898-1 and IEC 60059; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 30.0 A, 37.5 A, 40 A, 75 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- NFPA 70, National Electrical Code (2023): 210.20(A), 215.3 (125 % of continuous load), 240.4(B) and 240.4(D) (conductor protection), 240.6(A) (standard ratings), 625.41 (EV charging, 125 %)
- IEC 60364-4-43:2023, 433.1 (coordination between conductors and overload protective devices: Ib ≤ In ≤ Iz, I2 ≤ 1.45 Iz)
- IEC 60898-1:2015 (preferred rated currents of circuit-breakers for household installations) and IEC 60059:1999 (IEC standard current ratings, R10 series)

## Brick calculator: bricks and mortar for a wall

<a id="brick-count"></a>

Folder `brick-count/` · Civil · Number of bricks for a wall from its area less openings, for modular, standard, metric or custom bricks, one or two wythes, with waste and mortar.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Running or stack bond with every joint the same thickness. Each brick takes up its face plus one bed joint and one head joint; patterns with header courses use more bricks, by BIA TN 10 Table 6.
- Mortar is the theoretical volume of full bed and head joints through the brick width, the method behind BIA TN 10 Table 4, with no waste; a double wythe adds a solid collar joint of the same thickness.
- Mortar bags use the QUIKRETE Mortar Mix rate of 37 standard bricks per 80 lb bag, scaled by the joint mortar of the chosen brick; this rate includes the droppings and waste of normal laying.
- The waste allowance on bricks covers cutting and breakage; 5 % is common for plain walls, more with many openings and corners.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 20 × 8 ft wall less a 12 ft² window in modular brick with ⅜ in joints is 148 ft² × 6.857 = 1 015 bricks, 1 066 with 5 % waste; mortar 8.18 ft³ (8.06 ft³ per 1 000 bricks, BIA TN 10 Table 4: 8.1); 27 bags of 80 lb. Checked by hand.
- BIA TN 10 lists 675 modular bricks per 100 ft² because three modular courses fill 8 in; with joints of exactly ⅜ in the count is 686. Its non-modular mortar column is 1.73 times the geometric volume, apparently in³ per brick; the geometric method is used here.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Joint thickness outside ¼ to ½ in (6 to 13 mm): unusual for brickwork; check the specification.
- Zero joint thickness: the count is for dry-laid units and gives no mortar.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Area of doors and windows: the openings (… m²) must be smaller than the wall (… m²)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- BIA TN 10 Table 4, modular brick: mortar 8.1 ft³ per 1 000 bricks with ⅜ in joints and 10.3 with ½ in joints
  - Source: Brick Industry Association TN 10 (2009), Table 4: modular 4 × 2⅔ × 8 nominal, ⅜ in 8.1 and ½ in 10.3 ft³ per 1 000 brick
- BIA TN 10 Table 4 counts: standard brick 655 per 100 ft² and king 455 per 100 ft² with ⅜ in joints
  - Source: Brick Industry Association TN 10, Table 4 (non-modular sizes); 144 / (8⅜ × 2⅝) = 6.55 per ft²
- 20 × 8 ft wall less a 12 ft² window, modular, ⅜ in joints: 1 015 bricks, 1 066 with 5 % waste, 8.18 ft³ of mortar, 27 bags
  - Source: Hand calculation: 148 ft² × 144 / (8 × 2.625) = 1 014.9; mortar (21 − 7.625 × 2.25) × 3.625 = 13.93 in³ per brick
- Double wythe adds the collar joint of BIA TN 10 Table 5: 3.13 ft³ per 100 ft² for a ⅜ in joint
  - Source: Brick Industry Association TN 10, Table 5 (mortar in collar joints): ⅜ in, 3.13 ft³ per 100 ft²
- UK bricks 215 × 65 mm with 10 mm joints: 59.3 per m²; zero joint warns; openings larger than the wall are rejected
  - Source: Hand calculation: 1 / (0.225 × 0.075) = 59.26 per m²; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 6.857, 1 015, 1 066, 8.18 ft³, 8.06 ft³, 27 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Brick Industry Association, Technical Note 10, Dimensioning and Estimating Brick Masonry (2009), Table 4 (bricks and mortar per 100 ft²) and Table 5 (collar joints)
- Brick Development Association, The BDA Guide to Successful Brickwork, 3rd ed. (2005): UK brick format 215 × 102.5 × 65 mm laid with 10 mm joints
- QUIKRETE Mortar Mix No. 1102 data sheet (an 80 lb bag lays up to 37 standard bricks)

## BTU calculator: AC size for a room

<a id="btu-ac-size"></a>

Folder `btu-ac-size/` · HVAC · Air conditioner size in BTU, kW and tons for a room from its floor area, with the ENERGY STAR adjustments for sun, people and kitchens.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Capacities follow the ENERGY STAR room air conditioner sizing chart for rooms of 100 to 2 500 ft² (9 to 232 m²) with ceilings of about 8 ft (2.4 m) in a typical climate; taller ceilings, large windows, poor insulation or a very hot climate need more.
- ENERGY STAR adjustments: reduce 10 % for a heavily shaded room, add 10 % for a very sunny one, add 600 Btu/h for each regular occupant beyond two, and add 4 000 Btu/h for a kitchen.
- This sizes a room or window unit or a single mini-split head. A whole house with central air needs a room-by-room load calculation such as ACCA Manual J.
- An oversized unit cools the air quickly but removes little moisture and cycles often; buy the size the chart gives rather than the next one up.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 14 × 20 ft room (280 ft²) is 7 000 Btu/h on the chart; very sunny with three people gives 7 700 + 600 = 8 300 Btu/h, 2.43 kW, 0.69 ton.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Below 100 ft² (9 m²): the smallest room units, 5 000 Btu/h, are already enough.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Room length and width: the area is above 2 500 ft² (232 m²), beyond the room air conditioner chart; a central system needs a Manual J load calculation.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 14 × 20 ft very sunny room with 3 people: chart 7 000, ×1.1 = 7 700, +600 = 8 300 Btu/h = 2.43 kW = 0.69 ton
  - Source: ENERGY STAR room air conditioner sizing: 250–300 ft² → 7 000 Btu/h; +10 % very sunny; +600 Btu/h per person beyond two
- Chart rows: 100 → 5 000, 150 → 6 000, 450 → 12 000, 700 → 18 000, 1 500 → 30 000, 2 500 → 34 000 Btu/h; under 100 ft² takes 5 000
  - Source: ENERGY STAR room air conditioner sizing chart (each row from its lower area up to the next)
- A 300 ft² room entered in feet lands on the 8 000 Btu/h row, not 7 000; shaded removes 10 %; a kitchen adds 4 000
  - Source: ENERGY STAR: 300–350 ft² → 8 000 Btu/h; −10 % heavily shaded; +4 000 Btu/h kitchen
- Metric room 4 × 5 m = 20 m² = 215 ft²: 6 000 Btu/h (1.76 kW) with two people and normal sun; rule of thumb 4 306 Btu/h
  - Source: ENERGY STAR chart 150–250 ft²; rule of thumb 20 Btu/h per ft²
- Above 2 500 ft² is rejected with a pointer to Manual J; zero size and negative people are rejected
  - Source: Chart range; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 280 ft², 7 000 Btu/h, 8 300 Btu/h, 2.43 kW to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ENERGY STAR, Room Air Conditioner sizing chart and adjustments (U.S. EPA and DOE), energystar.gov
- ACCA Manual J, Residential Load Calculation, 8th edition (whole-house loads; named for scope only)

## Bunker quantity and density correction

<a id="bunker-quantity"></a>

Folder `bunker-quantity/` · Maritime · Bunker mass in vacuo and in air from sounded volume, temperature and density at 15 °C (Table 54B VCF), with energy content, cost and BDN comparison.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The volume correction factor uses the 1980 Table 54B generating equation VCF = exp(−α ΔT (1 + 0.8 α ΔT)) with α = K0/ρ15² + K1/ρ15 by product group; the printed tables round VCF to four decimals and the 2004 edition (ASTM D1250-04) differs from 1980 by up to about ±0.0002 for fuel oils.
- Product group is selected automatically from the density at 15 °C: gasolines, transition zone, jet fuels, fuel oils (838.3–1163.5 kg/m³ covers MGO, MDO and all residual grades). Densities outside 610.6–1163.5 kg/m³ are rejected.
- Density at 15 °C must be the value in vacuo as stated on the bunker delivery note; if the figure is in air, select that basis and 1.1 kg/m³ is added. Mass in air (the commercial quantity) = volume at 15 °C × (ρ15 − 1.1 kg/m³).
- The observed volume is taken as given from the tank tables after trim and heel correction; this calculator does not convert soundings or ullages and does not deduct free water or sediment.
- Temperature is the representative bulk temperature of the parcel; a 1 °C error changes the mass of HFO by about 0.07 %, so average the readings across the tank.
- Energy uses the entered lower calorific value (ISO 8217 does not specify LCV; typical HFO 40.2–40.8 MJ/kg, MGO 42.5–42.8 MJ/kg); the reference-fuel equivalent converts to the 42.7 MJ/kg basis used for SFOC and consumption curves.
- Cost is price × mass in air in a single currency; no exchange rate, no fuel-quality adjustments.
- The BDN comparison is a simple difference; typical measurement uncertainty of a sounding-based quantity is ±0.5 %, and larger shortfalls are the usual trigger for a letter of protest.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Defect caught before release 2026-10-30: the Table 54B coefficients first recalled (K0 = 103.8720, K1 = 0.2701 for fuel oils) are the Fahrenheit set of Table 6B; the Celsius set is 1.8 × larger (186.9696, 0.4862) and gives the field-known VCF of 0.976 for HFO at 50 °C instead of 0.987.
- Verification 2026-10-30: VCF 0.9760 (991 kg/m³ at 50 °C) and 0.9875 (850 kg/m³ at 30 °C) agree with the printed Table 54B values; the temperature sensitivity of 0.07 % per °C for HFO matches the field rule.
- Design decision: the product group is chosen from the density automatically, with a warning when a "fuel oil" turns out to fall in another group, which usually means a unit error in the density.
- Design decision: the commercial figure is mass in air with the fixed ISO 91 buoyancy correction of 1.1 kg/m³; density stated in air on a BDN is converted to in vacuo before use.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Density places this product in the "…" group, not the fuel-oil group — check that the density is in kg/m³ at 15 °C in vacuo.
- Density above 991 kg/m³: exceeds the ISO 8217 RMG limit (RMK grades allow 1010); check the grade on the BDN.
- Density above 1010 kg/m³ exceeds every ISO 8217 residual grade — verify the figure.
- Residual fuel below 30 °C is near or below typical pour points; the sounding may be unreliable and the parcel non-homogeneous.
- Measured quantity differs from the BDN by … %, beyond the usual ±0.5 % measurement tolerance — document temperatures, densities and soundings and consider a letter of protest.
- VCF from the 1980 Table 54B relation; the 2004 tables differ by up to ±0.0002. Free water and sediment are not deducted.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Density … kg/m³ is outside the Table 54B range 610.6–1163.5 kg/m³
- Density … kg/m³ in vacuo is outside the Table 54B range 610.6–1163.5 kg/m³

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- VCF is exactly 1 at 15 °C for any density; product groups cover 610.6–1163.5 kg/m³ contiguously
  - Source: ASTM D1250-80 Table 54B: reference temperature 15 °C; group boundaries 770.352, 787.5195, 838.3127 kg/m³
- HFO 991 kg/m³ at 50 °C: α = 186.9696/991² + 0.4862/991 = 6.810 × 10⁻⁴ /°C, VCF = 0.9760 (density falls to 967 kg/m³)
  - Source: Table 54B fuel-oil coefficients K0 = 186.9696, K1 = 0.4862 (API MPMS 11.1-1980, °C form); printed Table 54B value 0.9760; field rule 0.00068 kg/L per °C
- MGO 850 kg/m³ at 30 °C: VCF = 0.9875; at 0 °C the factor exceeds 1 (contraction)
  - Source: Table 54B generating equation; printed value 0.9875 for 850 kg/m³ at 30 °C
- Default parcel: 500 m³ at 45 °C, 985 kg/m³ → VCF 0.9796, 489.8 m³ at 15 °C, 482.4 t in vacuo, 481.9 t in air (ρ − 1.1)
  - Source: Table 54B relation; ISO 91 / ASTM Table 56 air-buoyancy convention of 1.1 kg/m³; hand calculation
- Density stated in air: 985 in air = 986.1 in vacuo, and the mass in air is then based on 985 again
  - Source: ISO 91: ρ_air = ρ_vacuo − 1.1 kg/m³
- Energy and reference fuel: 481.9 t × 40.5 MJ/kg = 19 517 GJ = 457.1 t of 42.7 MJ/kg reference fuel; cost 481.9 × 550 $
  - Source: Energy = mass × LCV; reference LCV 42 700 kJ/kg (ISO 3046-1 / ISO 15550)
- BDN comparison: BDN 500 t vs measured 481.9 t = −18.1 t = −3.6 % and a protest warning; 0 disables the comparison
  - Source: Bunker-dispute practice: ±0.5 % measurement tolerance (industry guidance, e.g. IBIA best practice)
- Temperature sensitivity: for HFO a 1 °C error moves the mass by about 0.07 %
  - Source: d(VCF)/dT ≈ −α ≈ −6.8 × 10⁻⁴ per °C for residual fuel
- Unit layer: 1 MJ/kg = 1000 kJ/kg = 429.9 Btu/lb; 1 US gal = 0.003785 m³
  - Source: NIST SP 811: 1 Btu/lb = 2326 J/kg exactly
- Invalid inputs fail fast: density outside Table 54B, temperature above 150 °C, negative volume
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.9793, 964.6 kg/m³, 482.3 t, 481.8 t, 265 000 $ to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASTM D1250-80 / API MPMS Chapter 11.1 (1980) / ISO 91-1:1992 — Petroleum measurement tables, Table 54B generating equations and product-group coefficients
- ISO 91:2017 — Petroleum and related products: temperature and pressure volume correction factors; air-buoyancy convention 1.1 kg/m³ (ASTM Table 56 weight conversion)
- ISO 8217:2017 — Fuel standard for marine distillate and residual fuels (density limits, e.g. RMG 380 ≤ 991 kg/m³, DMA ≤ 890 kg/m³)
- ISO 3046-1 / ISO 15550 — reference fuel lower calorific value 42 700 kJ/kg for SFOC
- IMO MEPC.1/Circ.875 and MARPOL Annex VI reg. 18 — bunker delivery note content

## Buoyancy calculator (Archimedes)

<a id="buoyancy"></a>

Folder `buoyancy/` · Maritime · Buoyant force, net force and whether an object floats, the draft of a floating box or cylinder, and the load a pontoon or raft can carry.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Archimedes' principle: the upward force equals the weight of the water displaced, ρ g V. The body is rigid and watertight, and the water is still.
- Sea water is taken as 1 025 kg/m³ and fresh water as 1 000 kg/m³; brackish dock water lies in between and can be entered as another density.
- The floating body floats upright and level, with its weight shared equally by the floats. Stability against capsizing is not checked: a tall narrow float can be buoyant enough and still roll over.
- For a horizontal cylinder the end caps are ignored: the submerged volume is the segment area × length. Rounded or conical ends of real pontoons add a little volume.
- The payload is what the floats can support down to the required freeboard; a working margin is still needed for people moving about, waves and water shipped on deck.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: two horizontal pontoon tubes 0.6 m in diameter and 6 m long (3.39 m³) carrying 1 500 kg in fresh water need 0.125 m² of submerged section each and float at 0.273 m draught; at 0.15 m freeboard (0.45 m immersion, segment 0.2275 m²) they carry 2 730 kg, 1 230 kg more. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The freeboard is below the value you asked for: the floats are overloaded for that margin.
- The mass is more than the water the body can displace: it sinks unless more buoyancy is added.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Freeboard to keep: it must be less than the height (or diameter) of the float.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- A 0.2 m³ body of 150 kg in sea water: buoyancy 1 025 × 9.80665 × 0.2 = 2 010.4 N, net +539.4 N, floats 73.2 % immersed
  - Source: Archimedes' principle (White, Fluid Mechanics §2.8); hand calculation
- Box 6 × 2 × 1 m carrying 2 000 kg in sea water floats at 2 000 / (1 025 × 12) = 0.163 m
  - Source: T = m / (ρ L B) (Derrett & Barrass, box-shaped vessels); hand calculation
- Horizontal cylinder: half immersed carries half its volume; two 0.6 m × 6 m tubes with 1 500 kg float at 0.273 m
  - Source: Circular segment area r² acos((r − h)/r) − (r − h)√(2rh − h²); hand calculation
- Upright drum 0.57 m diameter: 100 kg in fresh water sinks 100 / (1 000 × 0.2552) = 0.392 m
  - Source: T = m / (ρ π D²/4); hand calculation
- Too heavy sinks with a warning; a freeboard taller than the float and a fractional count are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 3.39 m³, 0.273 m, 2 730 kg, 1 230 kg to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Archimedes' principle as stated in F.M. White, Fluid Mechanics, 8th ed. (McGraw-Hill, 2016), §2.8 Buoyancy and stability
- Derrett, D.R. and Barrass, C.B., Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed. (2012), ch. 1–2: displacement, density and the draught of box-shaped vessels
- ITTC Recommended Procedure 7.5-02-01-03, Fresh water and seawater properties (2011): standard sea water of 35 g/kg is 1 026 kg/m³ at 15 °C and 1 025 kg/m³ at about 19 °C

## Cable short-circuit withstand

<a id="cable-sc-withstand"></a>

Folder `cable-sc-withstand/` · Electrical · Adiabatic short-circuit check of a cable and its protective conductor, with the earth-fault loop impedance, fault current and disconnection time.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Adiabatic heating for faults up to 5 s: the energy let through, I²t, must not exceed k²S² for each conductor (IEC 60364-4-43 434.5.2); for current-limiting devices and times below about 0.1 s the let-through energy from the device data is used instead of I²t.
- k = K √ln((θf + β)/(θi + β)) with K = 226 and β = 234.5 °C for copper, 148 and 228 °C for aluminium (IEC 60949, IEC 60364-5-54 Annex A); θi is the maximum operating temperature and θf the short-circuit limit of the insulation: PVC 70/160 °C (140 °C above 300 mm²), XLPE or EPR 90/250 °C, 60 °C rubber 60/200 °C. These give the tabulated k of 115, 103, 143 and 141 for copper and 76 and 94 for aluminium.
- The protective conductor is a core of the same cable, at the same temperatures as the line conductor; a separate or bare protective conductor has other k values.
- Loop impedance Zs = Ze + R1 + R2 with the conductor resistances at the maximum operating temperature, R(θ) = R20 (β + θ)/(β + 20); R20 from the cable data (IEC 60228) or, when not entered, ρ20/S, which underestimates stranded conductors by a few per cent. Reactance is neglected, which suits cross-sections up to about 35 mm².
- Minimum earth-fault current If = c U0/Zs with c = 0.95 for low-voltage systems (IEC 60909-0 Table 1, c_min); the device must disconnect within the permitted time, for example 0.4 s for 230 V final circuits up to 32 A and 5 s for distribution circuits in TN systems (IEC 60364-4-41).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: K reproduces the tabulated k: copper 70 → 160 °C 115.0, 70 → 140 °C 102.8, 90 → 250 °C 143.1, 60 → 200 °C 140.9; aluminium 70 → 160 °C 76.0, 90 → 250 °C 94.5. K itself is √(Q_c (β + 20)/ρ20) with Q_c = 3.45 J/(K·cm³) for copper (225.7) and 2.5 J/(K·cm³) for aluminium (148.1).
- Design decision: the device operating time at the fault current is an input read from its time–current curve, so any fuse or breaker can be checked.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The line conductor does not withstand the fault energy: use a larger cable or a faster device.
- The protective conductor needs at least … mm² for this fault energy.
- The device takes … s, longer than the permitted … s: reduce the loop impedance or choose a device that trips faster at … A.
- Resistance from ρ/S: stranded conductors have a few per cent more (IEC 60228 maximum values); enter the data-sheet resistance for an exact loop impedance.
- Above about 35 mm² the cable reactance becomes significant and the loop impedance shown is too low.
- Below 0.1 s use the let-through energy from the device data rather than I² t.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The final temperature must be above the initial temperature

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- k from IEC 60949 reproduces the tabulated values: copper 115 (PVC), 103 (PVC > 300 mm²), 143 (XLPE), 141 (rubber 60 °C); aluminium 76 (PVC), 94 (XLPE)
  - Source: IEC 60949 constants; IEC 60364-4-43 Table 43A / IEC 60364-5-54 Annex A
- Loop impedance and fault current: 16 mm² copper at 90 °C over 50 m and Ze = 0.35 Ω give Zs = 0.4874 Ω and If = 0.95 × 230/Zs = 448.3 A
  - Source: R(θ) = R20 (β + θ)/(β + 20); If = c U0/Zs (IEC 60909-0 c_min = 0.95)
- Adiabatic limits: the 16 mm² protective conductor withstands the 448 A fault for (k S/I)² = 26.1 s; the smallest conductor for 0.1 s is I √t / k = 0.99 mm²
  - Source: IEC 60364-4-43 434.5.2: t = (k S/I)²
- A 2.5 mm² cable 5 m from the board (Ze 0.02 Ω) for 0.2 s lets through 8.2 × 10⁵ A²s against 1.28 × 10⁵: both conductors fail and 6.3 mm² is needed
  - Source: I²t ≤ k²S² (IEC 60364-4-43 434.5.2)
- The device let-through energy, when entered, replaces I² t; a device slower than the permitted time is flagged
  - Source: IEC 60364-4-43 434.5.2 (current-limiting devices); IEC 60364-4-41 disconnection times
- A data-sheet resistance of 1.15 Ω/km at 20 °C is corrected to 90 °C by (234.5 + 90)/(234.5 + 20)
  - Source: Temperature correction with β = 234.5 °C for copper (IEC 60949, IEC 60228)
- Invalid inputs are rejected: a custom final temperature below the initial one, zero length
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 143.1, 143.1, 0.487 Ω, 448 A, 26 s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IEC 60949:1988 Calculation of thermally permissible short-circuit currents — adiabatic constants K, β, ρ20
- IEC 60364-4-43 (434.5.2) and IEC 60364-5-54 Annex A — adiabatic equation and k factors, as reproduced in myCableEngineering, The adiabatic equation
- IEC 60909-0:2016 Table 1 — voltage factor c_min = 0.95 for low voltage
- IEC 60364-4-41 — automatic disconnection times in TN systems

## Cable sizing and voltage drop

<a id="cable-sizing"></a>

Folder `cable-sizing/` · Electrical · Voltage drop, power loss and the minimum IEC conductor size for DC, single-phase and three-phase circuits from current, length, material and allowed drop.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Conductor resistance uses the IEC 60228 class 2 maximum DC values at 20 °C (copper 1.5–500 mm², aluminium 16–500 mm²) scaled with the temperature coefficient to the conductor temperature; real cables are up to 5–7 % better, so the drop is slightly conservative. Custom sizes use the theoretical ρ/A.
- The conductor is assumed at its rated temperature (PVC 70 °C, XLPE/EPR 90 °C) as in IEC 60364-5-52 Annex G; at partial load the conductor is cooler and the real drop smaller.
- The default reactance 0.08 Ω/km (IEC 60364-5-52 Annex G) applies to multicore and touching single-core LV cables; widely spaced single cores have higher reactance, and DC circuits have none.
- Balanced sinusoidal load with the entered power factor; harmonics (skin effect, neutral current) and unbalance are not covered.
- Length is the one-way route length of the circuit; the formula includes the return conductor (factor 2) or the three-phase factor √3.
- Voltage drop is referred to the nominal system voltage (line-to-line for three-phase, phase-to-neutral for single-phase, DC voltage) and compared with the allowed percentage: IEC 60364-5-52 suggests 3 % lighting / 5 % other, IEC 60092-201 allows 6 % on ships.
- Current-carrying capacity is NOT calculated — it depends on installation method, grouping, ambient temperature and insulation; enter the derated rating from the cable standard (IEC 60092-352, IEC 60364-5-52) or catalogue to see the utilisation. Short-circuit withstand and protective-device coordination are also outside this calculator.
- The recommended size is the smallest standard IEC 60228 size that meets the voltage-drop limit; it may still be too small for ampacity or too small for mechanical minimums (IEC 60092 requires ≥ 1.0 mm² power circuits).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Defect found and fixed 2026-10-30: JavaScript orders integer-like object keys before "1.5" and "2.5", so the smallest-size search started at 4 mm²; the sizes are now sorted numerically (test: 2.5 mm² at 4.63 % is the correct answer for the single-phase case).
- Verification 2026-10-30: theoretical ρ/A lies 4–11 % below the IEC 60228 maxima for every copper size (the 50 mm² conductor is the extreme at 11 %), consistent with stranding and tolerance allowances.
- Design decision: resistances come from the IEC 60228 table (conservative, what designers quote) with theoretical ρ/A only for custom sizes; the conductor is assumed at its rated temperature as in IEC 60364-5-52 Annex G.
- Design decision: ampacity is deliberately not computed — it depends on installation method, grouping and ambient — and is only checked against a derated rating the user enters.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Aluminium conductors below 16 mm² are not standard (IEC 60228 class 2 starts at 16 mm²); the theoretical resistance is used.
- Low power factor: the reactive part of the drop is significant; use the actual cable reactance rather than the 0.08 Ω/km default.
- Load current exceeds the cable rating: the cable is undersized for ampacity regardless of voltage drop.
- No single standard conductor up to 500 mm² meets the allowed drop — use parallel conductors, a higher voltage or a shorter route.
- Voltage drop … % exceeds the … % limit; … mm² would give … %.
- Ampacity, short-circuit withstand and protection coordination are not checked here.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Unknown conductor size "…"

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- IEC 60228 class 2 copper at 20 °C: 1.5 mm² 12.1, 2.5 mm² 7.41, 16 mm² 1.15, 95 mm² 0.193 Ω/km; aluminium 16 mm² 1.91 Ω/km
  - Source: IEC 60228:2004 Table 2
- Theoretical ρ/A (IACS copper 1.7241 µΩ·cm) lies 4–11 % below the IEC 60228 maximum for every standard copper size (stranding allowance)
  - Source: IEC 60028 (ρ_Cu = 1.7241 µΩ·cm at 20 °C); IEC 60228 values include stranding and tolerance (largest gap 50 mm²: 0.345 vs 0.387 Ω/km)
- Temperature correction: copper 16 mm² at 70 °C = 1.15 × (1 + 0.00393 × 50) = 1.376 Ω/km; aluminium α = 0.00403
  - Source: IEC 60287-1-1 Table 1 (α₂₀: copper 3.93 × 10⁻³, aluminium 4.03 × 10⁻³ per K)
- Three-phase 400 V, 50 A, 50 m, 16 mm² Cu at 70 °C, pf 0.85, X 0.08 Ω/km: ΔU = √3 I (R cos φ + X sin φ) = 5.25 V = 1.31 %; loss 516 W
  - Source: IEC 60364-5-52:2009 Annex G voltage-drop method; hand calculation
- Single-phase 230 V, 20 A, 30 m, 2.5 mm² Cu at 70 °C, pf 1: ΔU = 2 I R = 10.64 V = 4.63 % (within 5 %)
  - Source: IEC 60364-5-52 Annex G (b = 2 for single-phase); hand calculation 7.41 × 1.1965 × 0.03 × 2 × 20
- DC 24 V, 10 A, 10 m on 2.5 mm² at 20 °C: ΔU = 1.48 V = 6.2 % — exceeds 5 %; recommended 4 mm² (3.84 %)
  - Source: Ohm's law for the loop 2 L; IEC 60228 2.5 mm² 7.41 Ω/km, 4 mm² 4.61 Ω/km
- Reactance matters at low power factor: with pf 0.5 the X term adds √3 I X sin φ; DC ignores reactance; pf 1 removes it
  - Source: IEC 60364-5-52 Annex G formula structure
- Cable rating utilisation: 50 A on a 63 A derated cable = 79.4 %; 80 A on 63 A raises the ampacity warning
  - Source: Utilisation = I / I_z (IEC 60364-5-52 §523)
- Unit layer: 1 Ω/km = 1 mΩ/m = 0.3048 Ω/1000 ft; 16 mm² = 0.0248 in²
  - Source: SI definitions; 1 ft = 0.3048 m
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero voltage, unknown size, negative current
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.15 Ω/km, 1.376 Ω/km, 0.0688 Ω, 5.25 V, 1.31 %, 394.8 V, 516 W, 3.4 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IEC 60287-1-1, Electric cables — current rating equations — Table 1 (temperature coefficients of resistance)
- IEC 60364-5-52:2009, Annex G (voltage drop in consumers' installations; λ = 0.08 mΩ/m; 3 % / 5 % limits)

## Series and parallel capacitors

<a id="capacitors-series-parallel"></a>

Folder `capacitors-series-parallel/` · Electrical · Equivalent capacitance of capacitors in series or parallel, with the charge, the stored energy and the voltage across each capacitor in a series stack.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The capacitors are ideal: no leakage, no equivalent series resistance and their nominal capacitance; electrolytic capacitors are often −20 % / +80 % of nominal.
- In series, every capacitor holds the same charge, so the voltage splits in inverse proportion to capacitance; in practice leakage currents decide the long-term DC sharing, which is why series stacks need balancing resistors.
- The applied voltage is DC, or the peak of an AC voltage for the stored energy; each capacitor's voltage rating must exceed its own share.
- Values are typed as marked: plain numbers are microfarads, and the prefixes p, n, u (µ) and m give pico-, nano-, micro- and millifarads.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 10, 22 and 47 µF in series give 6.00 µF; at 12 V the charge is 72.0 µC, the energy 0.432 mJ, and the voltages 7.20, 3.27 and 1.53 V add up to 12 V. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- In a series stack the smallest capacitor takes the largest voltage; check every capacitor\'s voltage rating, and fit balancing resistors across electrolytics.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Values: enter at least one capacitor
- Values: capacitor … must be greater than zero (got …)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 10, 22 and 47 µF in series at 12 V: 5.998 µF, 71.97 µC, 0.432 mJ; voltages 7.20, 3.27 and 1.53 V add to 12 V
  - Source: Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, ch. 5: 1/C = Σ1/Cᵢ, Q = C V, Vᵢ = Q/Cᵢ, W = ½ C V²
- In parallel the same three give 79 µF; at 12 V each sees 12 V and the charge is 948 µC
  - Source: Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, ch. 10: C = ΣCᵢ in parallel
- Two equal capacitors: series halves (2 × 100 nF = 50 nF), parallel doubles (200 nF); marked values 100n, 4u7 and 22p read correctly
  - Source: Equal capacitors; IEC 60062 letter and digit code
- Energy: a 1000 µF capacitor at 50 V stores 1.25 J
  - Source: W = ½ C V² (Hughes, ch. 5)
- Series stacks warn about voltage sharing; an empty list and a zero value are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract; series voltage sharing by leakage (Hughes, ch. 5)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 6.00 µF, 72.0, 0.432 mJ, 7.20 V to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, 12th ed., ch. 5 (capacitors in series and parallel, Q = C V, W = ½ C V²)
- Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, 13th ed., ch. 10 (capacitors)
- IEC 60062:2016 clause 5, letter and digit code for capacitance values (4n7, 4u7)

## Carbon equivalent calculator (CE, Pcm, CET) and preheat

<a id="carbon-equivalent"></a>

Folder `carbon-equivalent/` · Mechanical · Weldability of steel from its composition: IIW carbon equivalent, AWS CE with silicon, Pcm and CET, with the EN 1011-2 minimum preheat temperature.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Element contents are mass per cent from the mill certificate (heat or product analysis). Elements left at zero are taken as absent, which can understate the carbon equivalent if they are present.
- CE(IIW) suits carbon and carbon-manganese steels; AWS D1.1 adds Si/6 to it. Pcm (Ito and Bessyo) was derived for low-carbon low-alloy steels, where CE(IIW) is less suitable. CET is the carbon equivalent of EN 1011-2 method B.
- The preheat temperature uses the formula of EN 1011-2 Annex C method B and is given only within its validity range: CET 0.20 to 0.50 %, thickness 10 to 90 mm, diffusible hydrogen 1 to 20 ml/100 g, heat input 0.5 to 4.0 kJ/mm, and the composition limits of that annex. Outside it the calculator refuses rather than extrapolates.
- The preheat is the minimum to avoid hydrogen cold cracking in the heat-affected zone of a butt weld; restraint, hardness limits, the welding procedure and the governing code may require more. Heat input Q here is the effective value (arc energy × thermal efficiency).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: C 0.18, Mn 1.40, Si 0.30, Cr 0.05, Mo 0.02, V 0.01, Ni 0.05, Cu 0.10: CE(IIW) 0.439, CE(AWS) 0.489, Pcm 0.271, CET 0.331; EN 1011-2 preheat for 30 mm, HD 5 ml/100 g, Q 1.0 kJ/mm = 108 °C. Checked by hand.
- Formula provenance: the CET, Pcm and IIW expressions, the preheat equation and its validity ranges were checked against the Dillinger welding tool documentation of EN 1011-2 method B; the Si/6 term of AWS D1.1 against the TWI FAQ on carbon equivalent formulae.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Carbon above 0.5 %: a high-carbon steel, beyond the range the carbon-equivalent formulas were derived for; welding needs a specific procedure.
- Carbon below 0.18 %: for such low-carbon steels Pcm or CET describes cold-cracking risk better than CE(IIW).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Composition: the alloying elements add up to more than 30 %; carbon equivalents apply to carbon and low-alloy steels.
- Composition: outside the range of the EN 1011-2 method B preheat formula: …. Choose "carbon equivalents only".
- Composition: CET = … %, outside 0.20 to 0.50 % where the EN 1011-2 preheat formula is valid.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- C-Mn steel C 0.18, Mn 1.40, Si 0.30, Cr 0.05, Mo 0.02, V 0.01, Ni 0.05, Cu 0.10: CE 0.4393, CE(AWS) 0.4893, Pcm 0.2707, CET 0.3308
  - Source: EN 1011-2 Annex C (CE, CET); AWS D1.1 Annex B (CE + Si/6); Ito–Bessyo Pcm (hand calculation)
- Plain carbon steel C 0.20, Mn 0.60: CE = 0.20 + 0.10 = 0.30, Pcm = 0.20 + 0.03 = 0.23, CET = 0.20 + 0.06 = 0.26
  - Source: Formulas of EN 1011-2 Annex C and Ito–Bessyo (hand calculation)
- EN 1011-2 C.3 preheat: CET 0.35 %, d 20 mm, HD 2, Q 1.5 kJ/mm gives 57.4 °C; the example gives 108.1 °C
  - Source: T_p = 697 CET + 160 tanh(d/35) + 62 HD^0.35 + (53 CET − 32) Q − 328 (EN 1011-2 Annex C, method B; hand calculation)
- Preheat trends: thicker plate and more hydrogen need more preheat, a higher heat input needs less
  - Source: EN 1011-2 Annex C: the effects of d, HD and Q on the minimum preheat
- Each element enters with its coefficient: 0.5 % Ni adds 0.0333 to CE, 0.0083 to Pcm and 0.0125 to CET; 0.002 % B adds 0.01 to Pcm only
  - Source: Coefficients of CE(IIW), Pcm and CET
- Outside EN 1011-2 method B: Mn 0.3 %, C 0.40 %, 5 mm plate, HD 30 and Q 5 kJ/mm are refused; CE alone still calculates
  - Source: EN 1011-2 Annex C validity range (C 0.05–0.32, Mn 0.5–1.9 %, d 10–90 mm, HD 1–20, Q 0.5–4.0)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.439, 0.489, 0.271, 0.331, 108 °C to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- EN 1011-2:2001, Welding — Recommendations for welding of metallic materials — Part 2: Arc welding of ferritic steels, Annex C (method A, CE; method B, CET and preheat equation C.3)
- AWS D1.1/D1.1M:2025, Structural Welding Code — Steel, Annex B (alternative methods for determining preheat; CE with Si/6 and Pcm)

- TWI, FAQ: What is the difference between the various carbon equivalent formulae used in relation to hydrogen cracking?

## Cargo securing (CSS Code Annex 13)

<a id="cargo-securing"></a>

Folder `cargo-securing/` · Maritime · Design accelerations, forces and the sliding and tipping balance of a lashed cargo unit by the CSS Code Annex 13 advanced calculation method.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Advanced calculation method of CSS Code Annex 13: basic accelerations of Table 2 for a 100 m ship at 15 kn with B/GM ≥ 13 in unrestricted service all year (25-day voyage), interpolated linearly along the ship (x/L from aft, held at the ends below 0.1 and above 0.9); corrected by Table 3 for length and speed (bilinear interpolation) and, for B/GM < 13, the transverse acceleration by Table 4. The transverse figures include the gravity component of roll.
- External forces F = m·a + wind + sea sloshing, with 1 kN/m² of wind on the exposed side and front of a unit on deck and 1 kN/m² of sloshing up to 2 m above the deck (not applied below deck; may be neglected in restricted areas); the vertical force is used only to reduce friction in the longitudinal balance, as the Code's formulas prescribe.
- Securing devices count with their calculated strength CS = MSL/1.5; the MSL of a lashing is the smallest MSL of its components (Table 1, for example 50 % of the breaking strength for mild-steel shackles, rings, deck eyes and turnbuckles, 80 % for single-use wire rope, 30 % for re-usable wire rope, 50 % for chains — take the value from the Cargo Securing Manual). The efficiency factor f = μ sin α + cos α depends on the vertical lashing angle α (Table 5); lashings steeper than 60° and those deviating more than 30° from the transverse direction should be disregarded for sliding.
- Transverse sliding: F_y ≤ μ m g + Σ CS f for the lashings on the side that holds the unit; transverse tipping: F_y a ≤ b m g + Σ CS c, with a the height of the centre of gravity above the tipping edge, b the lever of stableness and c the lever of each lashing about the tipping edge; longitudinal sliding: F_x ≤ μ (m g − F_z) + Σ CS f for longitudinal lashings, taking the longitudinal components of transverse lashings as no more than 0.5 CS.
- The figures may be exceeded in marked roll resonance (amplitudes over 30°), when running before large stern or quartering seas with marginal stability, and with slamming in head seas; the Code requires the master to avoid these by course and speed. Containers on containerships and standardized cargo follow their own rules (Annex 14, the Cargo Securing Manual).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: the worked example of Annex 13 — a 62 t unit stowed low on deck at x/L 0.7 of a 120 m ship at 15 kn, 6 m × 4 m × 4 m, lashings with an MSL of 90 kN (CS 60 kN) — gives F_x = 2.9 × 0.89 × 62 + 16 + 8 = 184 kN, F_y = 6.3 × 0.89 × 62 + 24 + 12 = 384 kN and F_z = 342 kN; four starboard lashings at 40° hold 0.3 × 62 × 9.81 + 4 × 60 × 0.959 = 412 kN, the port arrangement 422 kN, as printed in the Code. Tables 2–4 were read from the published Annex 13 text (MSC/Circ.664).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Lashings on line … are steeper than 60°: not counted against sliding (they still count against tipping).
- No longitudinal lashings entered: the longitudinal balance relies on friction alone; longitudinal components of transverse lashings may be counted up to 0.5 CS if their geometry is known.
- B/GM = … is below the smallest Table 4 entry (7): the ship is very stiff and transverse accelerations may exceed the table; the factor is held at 7.
- Length or speed outside Table 3 (50–200 m, 9–24 kn): the nearest table value is used.
- Steel on wet steel: no friction at all — every newton must be taken by the lashings.
- Accelerations may be exceeded in roll resonance, in following or quartering seas with marginal stability, and with slamming; avoid these by course and speed (Annex 13 caution).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- …: side must be S, P, F or A
- …: the number of lashings must be a whole number of at least 1
- …: MSL must be greater than zero
- …: vertical angle must be between 0 and 90°
- …: lever c must not be negative

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Annex 13 worked example, forces: 62 t low on deck at x/L 0.7, 120 m ship at 15 kn → F_x = 2.9 × 0.89 × 62 + 16 + 8 = 184 kN, F_y = 6.3 × 0.89 × 62 + 24 + 12 = 384 kN, F_z = 6.2 × 0.89 × 62 = 342 kN
  - Source: CSS Code Annex 13 (MSC/Circ.664), example of the advanced calculation method
- Annex 13 worked example, balance: starboard 0.3 × 62 × 9.81 + 4 × 60 × 0.96 ≈ 412 kN and port 0.3 × 62 × 9.81 + 2 × 60 × 0.96 + 2 × 60 × 1.04 ≈ 422 kN, both above F_y = 384 kN
  - Source: CSS Code Annex 13 example (CS = 90/1.5 = 60 kN, f from Table 5)
- Table 5: f = μ sin α + cos α gives 0.96 at 40°, 1.04 at 10° and 0.72 at −30° for μ 0.3; 0.83 at 40° for μ 0.1
  - Source: CSS Code Annex 13 Table 5 (f-values)
- Tables 3 and 4: 100 m at 15 kn is 1.00, 200 m at 24 kn 0.85, 50 m at 9 kn 1.20, 110 m at 16.5 kn interpolates between 1.10/1.00/0.98/0.89; B/GM 10 on deck high multiplies a_y by 1.19
  - Source: CSS Code Annex 13 Tables 3 and 4 (linear interpolation)
- Longitudinal sliding with friction reduced by F_z: μ (m g − F_z) = 0.3 (608.2 − 342.1) = 79.8 kN without longitudinal lashings, too little for F_x = 184 kN; below deck no wind or sloshing is added
  - Source: CSS Code Annex 13 §7.2.3 longitudinal sliding
- Invalid inputs fail fast: an unknown side letter, a fractional number of lashings, a vertical angle over 90°, zero mass
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 184 kN, 384 kN, 342 kN to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IMO Code of Safe Practice for Cargo Stowage and Securing (CSS Code), Annex 13 "Methods to assess the efficiency of securing arrangements for non-standardized cargo" (MSC/Circ.664, as amended), Tables 1–5 and the worked example
- IMO MSC.1/Circ.1353/Rev.2 Revised guidelines for the preparation of the Cargo Securing Manual
- IMO/ILO/UNECE Code of Practice for Packing of Cargo Transport Units (CTU Code), Annex 7 — friction and securing principles

## Cargo tank heating time and steam

<a id="cargo-tank-heating"></a>

Folder `cargo-tank-heating/` · Thermal and fluids · Heat-up energy, heat losses through deck, shell and bulkheads, heating power or time, steam consumption and heating coil area for a cargo or fuel tank.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Lumped (well-mixed) cargo: the whole mass is at one temperature that rises linearly from the initial to the target value, so the sensible heat is m c_p ΔT and the losses during heating are evaluated at the mean cargo temperature; stratification (cold bottom layers in unagitated heavy oils) makes the real heat-up slower and the coil surface temperature-limited.
- Heat loss through three surface groups — deck to air, shell to sea water, bulkheads to adjacent spaces — as U × A × ΔT with the overall coefficients entered: typical values for uninsulated steel are 6–8 W/(m²·K) from the shell to sea water, 5–7 from the deck to air at moderate wind (higher in strong wind), 2–4 to adjacent empty or ballast tanks, and 0 to adjacent heated cargo tanks; insulated surfaces 0.5–1.5. The coefficients, not the arithmetic, dominate the uncertainty (±30 %).
- Steam heating with saturated steam fully condensed at the coil pressure and no sub-cooling of the condensate: steam rate = heat / latent heat (h_fg at the saturation pressure selected, IAPWS-IF97 values); flashing and heat recovered from condensate are not credited; a thermal-oil system is treated by entering the equivalent power.
- Coil area from the overall coil coefficient (steam to cargo) and the mean temperature difference between the saturation temperature and the mean cargo temperature; U_coil 100–150 W/(m²·K) for crude and light products, 60–90 for heavy fuel oil and bitumen (viscosity), lower when the coil is fouled; the coil area is a sizing indication, the maintained-at-temperature case needs much less.
- No phase change, no cargo circulation or heat exchanger (deck heater) losses, no solar gain, constant ambient temperatures; heating above the flash-point-related or cargo-specification limits (e.g. 65 °C for most heavy fuel oil storage, carriage temperatures of the charter party) is the user's check.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 5 000 t of heavy fuel oil (c_p 1.9 kJ/kg·K) from 30 to 55 °C in 48 h with 400 m² deck (U 6, air 15 °C), 600 m² shell (U 6, sea 18 °C) and 500 m² bulkheads (U 3, 30 °C): sensible heat 237.5 GJ (1 374 kW), mean losses 173 kW → 1 547 kW, 2 720 kg/h of 7 bar g steam (65 t/day, 131 t in total), coil area 121 m² at U 100; maintaining 55 °C needs 267 kW = 469 kg/h — numbers consistent with tanker heating-coil design practice (1–2 m² of coil per 100 m³ of heavy cargo).
- Design decision: three surface groups with editable U values rather than a wind-speed model, because the overall coefficients in cargo-heating practice are tabulated by the classification societies and oil majors, and the user knows which apply.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Steam temperature less than 30 K above the target: the coil area becomes very large — use higher-pressure steam.
- Target above 65 °C: check the cargo specification, flash point margin and the tank coating temperature limit.
- Heating rate … K per day: above the usual 10–15 K/day for heavy cargoes — thermal stress on the structure and coil surface temperatures may limit it.
- Negative heat loss: the surroundings are warmer than the cargo and heat flows in.
- More than half of the heating power is lost to the surroundings: consider insulation or heating only before discharge.
- Overall heat transfer coefficients (U) dominate the result (±30 %); use the values from the heating system design or measured heating curves where available.
- Well-mixed cargo assumed: heavy oils stratify, so the real heat-up is slower and a cold bottom layer may remain.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Target temperature must be above the initial temperature
- Available power does not exceed the heat loss: the cargo cannot be heated to the target

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Sensible heat and losses: 5 000 t × 1.9 kJ/kg·K × 25 K = 237.5 GJ; losses at the 42.5 °C mean: deck 400 × 6 × 27.5 = 66.0 kW, shell 600 × 6 × 24.5 = 88.2 kW, bulkheads 500 × 3 × 12.5 = 18.75 kW → 172.95 kW; at 55 °C 266.7 kW
  - Source: Lumped energy balance; U A ΔT losses
- Power and steam: 237.5 GJ / 48 h = 1 374 kW + 173 kW = 1 547 kW; 7 bar g steam (h_fg 2 047 kJ/kg) → 2 721 kg/h, 130.6 t over 48 h; maintaining 55 °C: 469 kg/h; heating rate 12.5 K/day
  - Source: ṁ = P/h_fg; IAPWS-IF97 saturated steam at 8 bar abs
- Coil area: 1 547 kW / (100 W/m²K × (170.4 − 42.5) K) = 121.0 m² for the heat-up, 23.1 m² to maintain; the heat lost during heat-up is 11.2 % of the total 267.4 GJ
  - Source: A = P/(U ΔT_mean); energy accounting
- Power mode: with 1 547.2 kW available the time comes back as 48 h; with 1 000 kW it takes 79.8 h; power below the losses is rejected
  - Source: t = E/(P − Q_loss)
- Steam pressure and warnings: 16 bar g steam (h_fg 1 919) needs 6.7 % more mass flow per kW than 7 bar g but a smaller coil; a 90 °C target is flagged for the cargo limit and the steam margin; target below initial is rejected
  - Source: IAPWS-IF97 latent heat trend; behaviour specification
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 237.5 GJ, 173 kW, 267 kW, 1 547 kW, 12.5, 2 721 kg/h, 131 t, 469 kg/h to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISGOTT (International Safety Guide for Oil Tankers and Terminals), 6th ed., 2020 — cargo heating practice and temperature limits
- Lloyd's Register / OCIMF guidance on cargo heating systems; typical overall heat transfer coefficients for uninsulated steel to sea and air (Intertanko "Guide to the Vetting Process" cargo heating section)
- IAPWS-IF97 steam tables — saturation temperature and latent heat at 6, 8, 11 and 17 bar abs
- F. P. Incropera, D. P. DeWitt, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, 7th ed. — lumped capacitance and overall heat transfer coefficients

## Cargo ventilation and dew point

<a id="cargo-ventilation-dewpoint"></a>

Folder `cargo-ventilation-dewpoint/` · Maritime · Dew point and humidity from dry and wet bulb, ventilate-or-not decision by the three-degree and dew-point rules, condensation risk.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Saturation vapour pressure over water by the Magnus formula with the Alduchov & Eskridge (1996) coefficients e_s = 6.1094 exp(17.625 T/(T + 243.04)) hPa, accurate to about 0.4 % between −40 and +50 °C; no ice-bulb correction below 0 °C.
- Wet-bulb to vapour pressure by the psychrometric (Sprung) equation e = e_s(T_w) − A p (T − T_w) with A = 6.62·10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ for an aspirated or whirling psychrometer (ISO 4677-1, WMO-No. 8) and 8.0·10⁻⁴ K⁻¹ for a non-ventilated screen or hand-held instrument; a wet bulb that is not wetted or ventilated reads high and understates the humidity.
- Dew point rule: ventilate when the outside dew point is below the dew point of the air in the hold headspace — the universal rule; three-degree rule (hygroscopic cargoes such as grain, rice, cocoa, coffee, timber): ventilate when the outside dry-bulb temperature is at least 3 °C below the average cargo temperature at loading. The rules are compared with margins the user can see; the P&I guidance treats them as decision aids, not laws.
- Sweat: ship sweat (condensation on steel) forms when the hold dew point exceeds the hull/steel temperature, approximated by the sea or deck temperature entered; cargo sweat forms when air with a dew point above the cargo temperature is admitted — the calculator flags both with the entered temperatures.
- Humidity ratio W = 622 e/(p − e) g/kg dry air and the absolute humidity assume ideal gas behaviour at the station pressure (default 1013.25 hPa).
- Records: P&I clubs expect ventilation decisions and the outside/hold readings to be logged every watch; this page gives the numbers, not the log.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: Magnus e_s(20 °C) = 23.33 hPa (reference 23.39, 0.3 %); 20 °C at 50 % RH gives a dew point of 9.3 °C (psychrometric tables 9.3); dry bulb 25 / wet bulb 20 °C at 1013 hPa gives RH 63 % and dew point 17.5 °C, matching the ASHRAE chart (63 %, 17.5 °C).
- Design decision: both the dew-point and three-degree rules are evaluated every time with an explicit margin, and the overall advice follows the dew-point rule for non-hygroscopic cargo and requires both rules for hygroscopic cargo, as the club guidance does.
- Design decision: the hold air may be entered as dry/wet bulb or as dry bulb and RH, because many ships have hygrometers rather than psychrometers in the holds.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Non-ventilated psychrometer coefficient used (8.0·10⁻⁴ /K): readings from hand-held or screen instruments are less reliable than a whirling or aspirated psychrometer.
- Outside wet-bulb depression under 0.5 K: the air is nearly saturated; small reading errors change the dew point by several tenths of a degree.
- Hold humidity from a hygrometer: check its calibration — electronic sensors drift in dusty holds.
- Below 0 °C the wet bulb may be iced; the Magnus formula over water and the water-bulb coefficient are used regardless.
- The rules are decision aids from P&I guidance; the master decides with the cargo, voyage and weather in mind, and the readings and decisions should be logged every watch.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Outside wet bulb … °C cannot exceed the dry bulb … °C
- Outside wet-bulb depression is too large for the pressure: check the readings
- Hold wet bulb … °C cannot exceed the dry bulb … °C
- Hold wet-bulb depression is too large: check the readings

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Magnus (Alduchov–Eskridge): e_s(0 °C) = 6.109 hPa, e_s(20 °C) = 23.33 hPa (reference 23.39), e_s(30 °C) = 42.4 hPa (reference 42.47); dew point of 20 °C / 50 % RH = 9.3 °C
  - Source: Alduchov & Eskridge (1996) coefficients 17.625 / 243.04 / 6.1094; WMO/Buck reference saturation pressures; psychrometric tables
- Psychrometer: dry 25 °C, wet 20 °C, 1013.25 hPa, aspirated → e = 23.33 − 0.000662 × 1013.25 × 5 = 19.98 hPa, RH 63 %, dew point 17.5 °C, humidity ratio 12.5 g/kg (ASHRAE chart 63 %, 17.5 °C, 12.5 g/kg)
  - Source: Sprung psychrometric equation (ISO 4677-1, A = 6.62·10⁻⁴ K⁻¹); ASHRAE Fundamentals psychrometric chart
- Hold air 22 / 20 °C: RH 83 %, dew point 19.0 °C; given instead as 22 °C and 80 % RH the dew point is 18.4 °C; screen psychrometer coefficient lowers the computed humidity
  - Source: Same psychrometric relations; e = RH × e_s(T)
- Dew-point rule: outside 17.5 °C vs hold 19.0 °C → VENTILATE (margin 1.5 K); outside 27/25 °C (dew point 24 °C) → DO NOT VENTILATE; equal dew points → MARGINAL
  - Source: Britannia P&I / Gard: ventilate only when the outside dew point is lower than the hold dew point
- Three-degree rule: cargo 18 °C, outside 25 °C → DO NOT (margin −7 K); outside 14 °C → VENTILATE (margin 4 K); hygroscopic advice needs both rules, non-hygroscopic follows the dew point only
  - Source: Britannia P&I / Steamship Mutual: ventilate hygroscopic cargo when the outside dry bulb is at least 3 °C below the cargo temperature at loading
- Sweat: hold dew point 19 °C above steel 16 °C → ship sweat RISK; outside dew point 17.5 °C below cargo 18 °C → no cargo sweat; cargo at 10 °C → cargo sweat RISK; steel at 22 °C → no ship sweat
  - Source: Steamship Mutual "The problem of sweat": ship sweat when the hold dew point exceeds the steel temperature, cargo sweat when admitted air's dew point exceeds the cargo temperature
- Pressure dependence: at 950 hPa the same readings give a slightly higher vapour pressure and humidity ratio; the Sprung term scales with p
  - Source: Psychrometric equation e = e_s(T_w) − A p (T − T_w); W = 622 e/(p − e)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: wet bulb above dry bulb, unknown cargo type, implausible wet-bulb depression
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 20.0 hPa, 63 %, 17.5 °C, 12.5 g/kg, 22.0 hPa, 83 %, 19.0 °C, 1.5 K to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- O. A. Alduchov & R. E. Eskridge, "Improved Magnus form approximation of saturation vapor pressure", J. Appl. Meteor. 35 (1996) 601–609
- ISO 4677-1:1985 Atmospheres for conditioning and testing — Determination of relative humidity — Part 1: Aspirated psychrometer method (Sprung constant 6.6·10⁻⁴ K⁻¹); WMO-No. 8 Guide to Instruments and Methods of Observation, ch. 4
- Britannia P&I, "Cargo ventilation logs — three degree rule and when to ventilate the hold"; Steamship Mutual, "The problem of sweat"; West P&I loss prevention bulletin "Cargo ventilation and precautions to minimise sweat"
- ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals, ch. 1 Psychrometrics (humidity ratio, dew point, chart check values)

## Carnot efficiency and COP calculator

<a id="carnot-cop"></a>

Folder `carnot-cop/` · Thermal and fluids · Carnot efficiency of a heat engine and the ideal COP of a heat pump or refrigerator between two temperatures, with a realistic estimate and the heat or power.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Temperatures are those of the hot and cold reservoirs in kelvin (°C + 273.15). For a heat pump use the temperature delivered (flow temperature) and the source temperature (outdoor air or ground); the refrigerant runs a few kelvin beyond both, so a real machine sees a wider lift.
- The Carnot value is the theoretical maximum of any machine between the two temperatures. Real machines reach a fraction of it, the second-law efficiency: typically 40–55 % for heat pumps and chillers, 30–60 % for heat engines.
- The power figures assume steady operation at the given temperatures; seasonal performance (SCOP, SEER) averages over changing conditions, defrost and part load.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a heat pump delivering 35 °C from 0 °C outdoor air has a Carnot COP of 308.15/35 = 8.80; at 50 % of Carnot, COP 4.40, so 2 kW of electricity gives 8.8 kW of heat. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A lift under 5 K gives a very high theoretical COP that real machines cannot reach; fans, pumps and heat-exchanger temperature differences dominate.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Cold side temperature: it must be above absolute zero.
- Hot side temperature: it must be above the cold side temperature.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Heat pump 35 °C from 0 °C: Carnot COP 308.15/35 = 8.804; at 50 %, 4.40; 2 kW in gives 8.80 kW of heat, 6.80 kW from outdoors
  - Source: Çengel and Boles, Thermodynamics, eq. 6-21: COP_HP,rev = T_H/(T_H − T_L)
- Refrigerator 5 °C inside, 35 °C outside: Carnot COP 278.15/30 = 9.27; COP_heating − COP_cooling = 1 for the same temperatures
  - Source: Çengel and Boles, eq. 6-20: COP_R,rev = T_L/(T_H − T_L)
- Steam plant 550 °C to 30 °C: Carnot efficiency 1 − 303.15/823.15 = 63.2 %; 100 MW of heat at 60 % of Carnot gives 37.9 MW of work
  - Source: Çengel and Boles, eq. 6-18: η_th,rev = 1 − T_L/T_H
- A colder source lowers the heat pump COP: −10 °C gives a Carnot COP of 6.80 at 35 °C flow
  - Source: COP = 308.15/45
- Hot side not above the cold side and a fraction above 1 are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 8.804, 4.40, 8.80 kW to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Çengel, Y.A. and Boles, M.A., Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, 9th ed., ch. 6 (Carnot efficiency and COP, eqs. 6-18, 6-20, 6-21)
- EN 14511-2:2018 (rating conditions of air-to-water heat pumps, e.g. A7/W35), for the typical fraction of Carnot

## Cathodic protection anodes

<a id="cathodic-protection"></a>

Folder `cathodic-protection/` · Maritime · Sacrificial anode mass, number and life for a hull or tank from surface area, coating breakdown and current density (DNV-RP-B401).

### Assumptions and caveats

- Galvanic (sacrificial) anode design following DNV-RP-B401 (2021): the mean current demand I_cm = A i_cm f_cm sets the anode mass through the charge capacity, M = I_cm t_f 8760/(u ε); the initial and final demands I_ci = A i_ci f_ci and I_cf = A i_cf f_cf must be met by the total anode current output N (E_c − E_a)/R_a, where E_c = −0.80 V is the protective potential, E_a the closed-circuit anode potential and R_a the anode resistance from the Table 8-7 formulas.
- Design current densities are the RP-B401 Tables 8-1 and 8-2 values for bare steel by climatic region and depth band (open sea, uncoated, average flow); coating breakdown f_c = a + b t uses the Table 8-4 constants for categories I–IV with mean f_cm = a + b t_f/2 and final f_cf = a + b t_f (capped at 1); the initial breakdown is f_ci = a.
- Ship-hull mode replaces the offshore tables by user current densities per area — coated hull 10–20 mA/m² (+5 mA/m² for dockings beyond 30 months or high coating wear, as class guidance recommends), propeller ≈ 500 mA/m² when bonded, uncoated appendages 100–150 mA/m² — and takes initial = mean = final; the design life is the docking interval. Class rules (DNV-CG-0288, ABS) and ICCP interaction are not reproduced.
- Anode material data from Table 8-6 for seawater ≤ 30 °C: Al-Zn-In 2 000 Ah/kg at −1.05 V, zinc 780 Ah/kg at −1.03 V; capacities fall at higher temperature and in sediments (Al 1 500 Ah/kg in sediments), and zinc above 50 °C needs qualification. Utilisation factors from Table 8-8 by anode type.
- Anode resistance: long slender stand-off R_a = ρ/(2πL)(ln(4L/r) − 1) with r the equivalent radius from the cross-section periphery; short stand-off and flush/bracelet formulas as in Table 8-7; seawater resistivity is an input (about 0.20 Ω·m tropical, 0.30 Ω·m temperate). The final current output is estimated with the same resistance (RP-B401 asks for the consumed anode dimensions), so the final check is approximate.
- Current drain to other structures (chains, wells, reinforcing steel), stray currents, electrical continuity and anode distribution are outside the calculation; the result is the required inventory, not a layout.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: table values transcribed from the DNV-RP-B401 May 2021 PDF (Tables 8-1, 8-2, 8-4, 8-6, 8-7, 8-8); temperate 0–30 m category II at 25 years gives f_cm 0.3625, f_cf 0.675, I_cm 36.25 A for 1 000 m² and 4 410 kg of Al anodes at u 0.90; a 2 m × r 0.1 m stand-off anode in 0.30 Ω·m water has R_a 0.0807 Ω and 3.10 A initial output.
- Design decision: two modes (offshore structure with the RP-B401 tables; ship hull with per-area densities) because class hull tables are not public and hull practice works in mA/m² per area.
- Design decision: the final current check is reported with the warning that RP-B401 requires the resistance of the consumed anode; typical practice uses the utilisation-reduced length and mass.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Coating breakdown reaches 100 % before the end of the design life: the mean factor is computed with f_c capped at 1 (RP-B401 §3.4.8 — recalculate the mean when f_cf > 1).
- 5 mA/m² added to the coated-hull current density for a docking interval beyond 30 months (class guidance).
- Mass is sufficient but the anodes cannot deliver the peak current: the number is governed by current output, not by mass — increase the count or choose a slender stand-off shape.
- Propeller protected through the shaft earthing: the 500 mA/m² drain assumes a bonded (slip-ring) propeller; without bonding the propeller is unprotected and the drain vanishes.
- L < 4r: the long slender stand-off formula is outside its range; choose the short stand-off type.
- Zinc at depth/low temperature: check the anode potential and capacity for the ambient conditions (Table 8-6 notes).
- Final current output is estimated with the new-anode resistance; RP-B401 requires the resistance of the anode consumed to its utilisation factor for the final check.
- Inventory only: anode distribution, current drain to other structures, ICCP interaction and class-specific hull tables (DNV-CG-0288, ABS) are not covered.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- RP-B401 tables: temperate 0–30 m bare steel 0.200/0.100/0.130 A/m² (initial/mean/final), tropical > 300 m 0.180/0.090/0.130; category II a 0.05, b 0.025 (0–30 m) and 0.015 (> 30 m); Al 2 000 Ah/kg −1.05 V, Zn 780 Ah/kg −1.03 V; u 0.90/0.85/0.85/0.80
  - Source: DNV-RP-B401 (May 2021) Tables 8-1, 8-2, 8-4, 8-6, 8-8
- Offshore example: 1 000 m² temperate 0–30 m, category II, 25 years → f_ci 0.05, f_cm 0.3625, f_cf 0.675; I_ci 10 A, I_cm 36.25 A, I_cf 87.75 A; charge 7.94 MAh; Al anodes u 0.9 → 4 410 kg → 15 × 300 kg
  - Source: DNV-RP-B401 §3.4 (f_c = a + b t), §4.4 (I_c = A i_c f_c), eq. 4.5 (M = I_cm t_f 8760/(u ε))
- Anode resistance (Table 8-7): long slender stand-off L 2 m, periphery 0.628 m (r 0.1 m), ρ 0.3 Ω·m → R_a = 0.3/(4π)(ln 80 − 1) = 0.0807 Ω, output (−0.80 + 1.05)/0.0807 = 3.10 A; bracelet 0.315 ρ/√A
  - Source: DNV-RP-B401 Table 8-7 (Dwight formula), protective potential −0.80 V, Al closed-circuit potential −1.05 V
- Output check: 15 Al stand-off anodes give 46.5 A — above the 10 A initial demand but below the 87.75 A final demand → INSUFFICIENT with the count governed by output (29 anodes)
  - Source: RP-B401 §4.8: total anode current output must meet the initial and final demands
- Ship hull: 6 000 m² at 15 mA/m² + 40 m² propeller at 500 + 50 m² bare at 120 → 116 A; 2.5 years → 2.54 MAh; zinc, u 0.80 → 4 070 kg → 204 × 20 kg; life 2.51 years; 3.4 anodes per 100 m²
  - Source: Hull practice (DNV-CG-0288 / Cathwell: coated hull 10–20 mA/m², propeller 500 mA/m²); RP-B401 mass formula
- 30-month rule: design life 3 years adds 5 mA/m² automatically (20 mA/m²); "no" suppresses it, "yes" forces it at 2 years
  - Source: Class guidance: increase the design current density by 5 mA/m² for operation beyond 30 months
- Aluminium instead of zinc on the hull needs 780/2000 = 39 % of the mass; bare steel coating category gives f_c = 1 and the full bare-steel demand
  - Source: Table 8-6 capacities; f_c = 1 for uncoated steel
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero area, negative design life, unknown region
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 116 A, 116 A, 116 A, 4 070 kg, 204, 0.26 Ω, 0.88 A, 179 A to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- DNV-RP-B401, Cathodic protection design, edition May 2021, Sec. 3 (design parameters), Sec. 4 (calculation procedures) and Sec. 8 Tables 8-1 to 8-8
- ISO 12473:2017 General principles of cathodic protection in seawater; ISO 15589-2 (offshore pipelines)
- DNV-CG-0288 Corrosion protection of ships (2021) and Cathwell design notes — hull current density practice (+5 mA/m² beyond 30 months, 500 mA/m² for propellers)
- NACE SP0176 / Peabody's Control of Pipeline Corrosion — Dwight anode resistance formula

## Chain and sprocket calculator (roller chain length)

<a id="chain-sprocket"></a>

Folder `chain-sprocket/` · Mechanical · Roller chain drive: ratio, output rpm, chain speed, chain length in pitches (even), actual centre distance and sprocket pitch diameters.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Standard roller chain of pitch p on two sprockets in one plane; ANSI chain numbers give the pitch in eighths of an inch (No. 40 = 1/2 in). ISO 606 B-series chains of the same pitch use the same geometry.
- The chain length in pitches follows Shigley eq. 17-27 and is rounded up to the next even number, so that no offset (cranked) link is needed; the actual centre distance for that length follows eq. 17-28.
- The centre distance is nominal with the chain just taut; provide adjustment or an idler for wear elongation and sag.
- The chordal speed variation is the change in chain speed as each link seats on the small sprocket; it falls quickly as the tooth count rises.
- Power capacity, lubrication and the number of strands are not checked here; use the ANSI or ISO power-rating tables of the chain maker.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: No. 40 chain (12.7 mm), 17 and 51 teeth, 900 rpm, 500 mm centres: L/p = 78.74 + 34 + 0.744 = 113.48, rounded to 114 pitches; actual C = 503.3 mm; pitch diameters 69.12 and 206.30 mm; 300 rpm out; chain speed 3.24 m/s. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Small sprocket with fewer than 17 teeth: the chordal speed variation exceeds 1.7 %, with more noise, vibration and wear; use more teeth if the speed is high.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Desired centre distance: it must be more than the sum of the two sprocket pitch radii, or the sprockets overlap.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 2 : 1 drive, 17 and 34 teeth, C = 25 pitches: L/p = 50 + 25.5 + 0.293 = 75.79 → 76 pitches; actual C = 25.104 pitches
  - Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., eqs. 17-27 and 17-28 (hand calculation with the data of the §17-5 design example)
- Pitch diameter D = p / sin(180°/N): 1/2 in chain, 17 teeth = 2.721 in; 51 teeth = 8.122 in
  - Source: Shigley eq. 17-25 (hand calculation)
- No. 40, 17/51 teeth, 900 rpm, 500 mm: 300 rpm, 3.2385 m/s, 113.48 → 114 pitches (1 447.8 mm), C = 503.31 mm
  - Source: Shigley eqs. 17-25 to 17-28 (hand calculation)
- Equal sprockets: L/p = 2C/p + N exactly, and the centre distance inverts it; an exact even length keeps C
  - Source: Limiting case N₁ = N₂ of eqs. 17-27 and 17-28
- Chordal speed variation: 1 − cos(180°/N) over N sin(180°/N)/π; 17 teeth 1.71 %, 25 teeth 0.79 %
  - Source: Shigley §17-5, chordal speed variation of a roller chain (derived from V_max = rω, V_min = rω cos(180°/N))
- Small sprockets warn; overlapping sprockets, fractional tooth counts and unknown chain sizes are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 113.48, 114, 503.3 mm, 69.12 mm, 206.30 mm, 3.24 m/s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §17-5 Roller chain, eqs. 17-25 to 17-28 (pitch diameter, chain velocity, length in pitches, centre distance)
- ASME B29.100, Precision power transmission, double-pitch power transmission, and double-pitch conveyor roller chains, attachments and sprockets (standard chain numbers and pitches)
- Renold, Roller chain design guide: chain length and centre distance calculation

## Charter party performance claim

<a id="charter-party-claim"></a>

Folder `charter-party-claim/` · Maritime · Time lost and over-consumption against the warranted speed and consumption by the good-weather method, with the "about" allowances and the claim value.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Good-weather method of English law: the performance on the good-weather periods of the passage (as the charter party defines them, typically up to Beaufort 4 and Douglas sea state 3) is taken as the ship's capability and extrapolated to the whole passage, as if all of it were sailed in good weather (The Didymi [1988] 2 Lloyd's Rep 108 CA; The Gas Enterprise [1993] 2 Lloyd's Rep 352 CA; The Ocean Virgo [2015] EWHC 3405 (Comm)).
- Basic formula (Kasi, 4-5 Gray's Inn Square): time lost = passage time at the good-weather speed − passage time at the allowed speed; over-consumption = good-weather daily consumption × passage days at the good-weather speed − allowed daily consumption × passage days at the allowed speed, so the fuel burned in the time lost is included. Other formulas have been advocated (London Arbitration 12/14).
- "About" gives the owners 0.5 knot on speed and 5 % on consumption, both applied under a double "about" (The Al Bida [1987] 1 Lloyd's Rep 124 CA; London Arbitration 15/07); the margin is for the tribunal and is an input here, set to zero for "without about" or an average-speed warranty.
- Offset: gains to the charterers are set off against their losses in a damages claim (The Ioanna [1985] 2 Lloyd's Rep 164); fuel saved is measured from the lower end of the "about" range over the passage time at the allowed speed (The Gaz Energy (No 2) [2012] EWHC 1686 (Comm); London Arbitration 20/07 for the time base), and time gained, by the same principle, from the upper end of the speed range. A net gain gives no claim either way (The Al Bida).
- Current: the mean current component along the track in the good-weather periods (+ with the ship) is subtracted from the speed over the ground; whether currents are corrected when the charter party is silent is unsettled, the better view being that they are (London Arbitrations 21/04 and 15/05).
- Claim values are the time lost × daily hire and the over-consumption × bunker price; excluded periods (extreme weather, speed reduced on the charterers' orders), off-hire, interest and the evidence (deck logs against weather routing reports) are matters for the charter party and the tribunal.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: the basic example of Kasi (warranted 15 kn on 30 t/day, good-weather performance 14 kn on 31 t/day, 15 000 nmi) gives 71.43 h lost and 133.93 t over-consumed, as published; the London Arbitration 20/07 example (about 12.5 kn on about 30 t/day, 288 nmi at 10 kn burning 29 t) gives 4.8 h lost and a 1 t credit when the consumption is taken without margin.
- Design decision: the hire and bunker price are applied to the time and fuel heads only; damages beyond those heads and the choice of good-weather periods are left to the user.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Less than 24 h of good weather: shorter periods may be used if they are a representative sample (The Ocean Virgo), but the extrapolation is less certain.
- The good-weather distance exceeds the total distance of the passage: check the inputs.
- The credits exceed the losses: there is no claim, and the owners cannot recover the net gain (The Al Bida).
- The ship did better than the warranty on one head; that gain is not credited with the option chosen.
- Good weather, the speed basis (over the ground or through the water), current corrections and the allowances are defined by the charter party, which governs.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The speed allowance must be smaller than the warranted speed
- The current exceeds the speed over the ground: the good-weather speed through the water must be greater than zero

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Kasi basic example: warranted 15 kn on 30 t/day, good-weather performance 14 kn on 31 t/day over 15 000 nmi give 71.43 h lost and 133.93 t over-consumed
  - Source: A. Kasi, Performance claims under NYPE 1946 and 1993: establishing and extrapolating (4-5 Gray's Inn Square), worked example
- London Arbitration 20/07: about 12.5 kn, 288 nmi at 10 kn burning 29 t against 30 t without margin: 4.8 h lost, 1 t saved and credited
  - Source: A. Kasi, The "about" margin in speed-consumption warranty (4-5 Gray's Inn Square), example of London Arbitration 20/07
- The Gaz Energy (No 2): with a 5 % margin the saving is measured from 28.5 t/day, so 29 t is no saving and the claim is the time head alone
  - Source: Hyundai Merchant Marine v Trafigura (The Gaz Energy No 2) [2012] EWHC 1686 (Comm), as summarised in the West P&I defence guide
- Default passage: 13.33 kn on 32 t/day against 13.5 kn on 31.5 t/day over 5000 nmi: 4.630 h lost, 13.889 t over-consumed, claim 11 226.85
  - Source: Basic formula: 375 h − 370.37 h; 32 × 375/24 − 31.5 × 370.37/24
- A favourable current of 0.3 kn lowers the good-weather speed to 13.033 kn and raises the time lost to 13.26 h
  - Source: Current correction of the speed over the ground (London Arbitration 15/05; West P&I defence guide)
- A ship inside the "about" range has no claim either way; gains are credited only with the offset, and a net gain never becomes a claim against the charterers
  - Source: The Ioanna [1985] 2 Lloyd's Rep 164; The Al Bida [1987] 1 Lloyd's Rep 124
- Invalid inputs are rejected: an allowance as large as the warranted speed, a current larger than the speed, negative fuel
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 13.33 kn, 32.0 t/day, 13.5 kn, 31.5 t/day, 4.63 h, 13.89 t to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources
