- A. Kasi, Performance claims under NYPE 1946 and 1993 (time charter): establishing and extrapolating, 4-5 Gray's Inn Square — basic formula and worked example
- A. Kasi, The "about" margin in speed-consumption warranty, 4-5 Gray's Inn Square — 0.5 knot and 5 %, double about, offset and London Arbitration 20/07
- West P&I, Defence guide: speed and consumption claims — good-weather days, currents, The Ioanna and The Gaz Energy credits
- The Gaz Energy (No 2): Hyundai Merchant Marine Co Ltd v Trafigura Beheer BV [2012] EWHC 1686 (Comm) — over-consumption from the upper and under-consumption from the lower end of the "about" range
- T. Coghlin et al., Time Charters, 7th ed., Informa Law 2014 — speed and performance claims

## Chemical dosing calculator (feed rate, pump setting, chlorine dose)

<a id="chemical-dosing"></a>

Folder `chemical-dosing/` · Process · Chemical feed rate and dosing pump setting in L/h and gal/day from flow, dose in mg/L, product strength and density, with chlorine dose, demand and residual.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The dose is the mass of active chemical per litre of treated water (mg/L = g/m³), applied to the whole flow; 1 mg/L in 1 m³ is 1 g, and in 1 million US gallons 8.34 lb.
- Product strength is the active content of the delivered product: % w/w is per mass of product, % w/v is grams per 100 mL (as for trade-strength hypochlorite, where % w/v = % w/w × specific gravity).
- The pump setting is the product volume per hour while the water flows; the daily use is that rate times the dosing hours per day. Pump ratings in gal/day are the same rate over 24 hours.
- Chlorine dose equals chlorine demand plus the residual left after the contact time; the demand depends on the water and the contact time, so measure the residual and adjust.
- Sodium hypochlorite loses strength in storage, faster when warm; check the strength of the product on delivery and periodically.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 100 m³/h dosed at 5 mg/L needs 0.5 kg/h of active chemical, 12.0 kg a day; with 12.5 % w/v hypochlorite of density 1 200 kg/m³ the pump delivers 4.00 L/h (25.4 US gal/day), 115.2 kg of product a day. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A residual above 4 mg/L exceeds the US EPA maximum residual disinfectant level for chlorine in drinking water (4.0 mg/L as Cl₂).
- Pump setting below 0.05 L/h: few dosing pumps meter that accurately; dilute the product or use a smaller pump.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Chlorine residual: it cannot exceed the dose; the demand would be negative.
- Chlorine demand: it exceeds the dose, so no residual is left; raise the dose above the demand.
- Chlorine dose: it must be greater than zero to size a feed.
- Product strength: at this density the % w/v is more than 100 % by weight; check the strength and density.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 100 m³/h at 5 mg/L with 12.5 % w/v hypochlorite (1 200 kg/m³): 12.0 kg/day active, 4.00 L/h, 25.36 US gal/day, 115.2 kg/day
  - Source: Hand calculation: active = Q × dose; product volume = active / (125 g/L)
- Pounds formula: 1 MGD at 1 mg/L needs 8.34 lb/day; 2.5 MGD at 3 mg/L needs 62.6 lb/day of chlorine
  - Source: CSU Sacramento, Water Treatment Plant Operation Vol. I: lb/day = MGD × mg/L × 8.34
- Chlorine: demand 1.5 + residual 0.5 = dose 2.0 mg/L; a 3.0 mg/L dose with 0.6 mg/L residual has 2.4 mg/L demand
  - Source: Chlorine dose = demand + residual (CSU Sacramento; Metcalf & Eddy ch. 12)
- Calcium hypochlorite at 65 % w/w: 100 lb of chlorine needs 153.8 lb of product; the % w/w and % w/v routes agree
  - Source: CSU Sacramento: lb of hypochlorite = lb of chlorine / (% available chlorine / 100); consistency of the two bases
- Fewer dosing hours scale the daily use but not the pump rate; 1 L/h is 6.34 US gal/day
  - Source: Hand calculation (24 h / 3.785 L per gal)
- A residual above the dose, zero flow and an impossible strength are rejected; a high residual warns
  - Source: Validation contract; US EPA MRDL for chlorine 4.0 mg/L
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 12.0 kg, 4.00, 25.4, 115.2 kg to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Office of Water Programs, California State University, Sacramento: Water Treatment Plant Operation, Vol. I, chapter on disinfection (chlorine dose = demand + residual; pounds formula lb/day = MGD × mg/L × 8.34)
- AWWA B300, Standard for Hypochlorites (sodium and calcium hypochlorite supplied for water treatment)
- Metcalf & Eddy, Wastewater Engineering: Treatment and Resource Recovery, 5th ed., ch. 12 (chlorine dose, demand and residual)

## Chip load calculator with chip thinning

<a id="chip-load"></a>

Folder `chip-load/` · Manufacturing · Chip load per tooth from feed rate, rpm and flutes, or the feed rate for a target chip load, with the radial chip thinning factor for light cuts.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Chip load is the feed per tooth, f_z = feed rate / (teeth × rpm); every tooth is assumed to cut equally, with no runout.
- At a radial engagement of half the diameter or more, the maximum chip thickness equals the feed per tooth. Below that the chip thins, and the maximum chip thickness is f_z × √(1 − (1 − 2 a_e/D)²).
- The chip thinning factor applies to the side of a straight-flute or helical end mill with a square end; ball-nose and chamfer tools also thin the chip axially, which is not included.
- Raising the feed by the thinning factor restores the chip thickness, not the cutting force per tooth; check the machine, the holder and the tool maker's maximum feed.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 1/2 in four-flute end mill at 5 000 rpm and 0.05 in radial engagement (10 %) has RCTF = 1/√(1 − 0.8²) = 1.667; for a 0.002 in chip it needs 0.00333 in per tooth and 66.67 in/min instead of 40 in/min. Checked by hand.
- Dapra published adjustments: 35 % engagement 1.05 and 5 % engagement +130 % (2.29), both reproduced by the formula.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The chip thinning factor is above 3: such light cuts multiply the feed rate; check the tool maker\'s limit and the machine\'s feed.
- The feed per tooth is above 10 % of the cutter diameter: check the units of the feed rate.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Radial depth of cut a_e: it cannot exceed the cutter diameter.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Chip load: 40 in/min at 5 000 rpm with 4 flutes is 40 / (4 × 5 000) = 0.002 in per tooth; at half-diameter engagement the chip is not thinned
  - Source: Harvey Tool: IPM = RPM × IPT × T (rearranged)
- Dapra: 35 % radial engagement needs × 1.05; 5 % engagement allows 130 % more feed (factor 2.29)
  - Source: Dapra Corporation, Radial chip thinning (published adjustments)
- 10 % engagement: RCTF = 1/√(1 − 0.8²) = 1.667; a 0.002 in chip needs 0.00333 in per tooth, 66.67 in/min instead of 40
  - Source: RCTF = 1/√(1 − (1 − 2 a_e/D)²) (hand calculation)
- Metric round trip: 600 mm/min at 8 000 rpm, 3 flutes = 0.025 mm per tooth; with 1 mm of a 10 mm cutter the chip is 0.015 mm, and asking for 0.015 mm gives 600 mm/min back
  - Source: Consistency of the forward and inverse calculations
- Very light cuts warn; a cut wider than the cutter, zero stepover and a fractional flute count are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.667, 0.00333 in, 66.67 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Dapra Corporation, Radial chip thinning: radial engagement feed rate adjustment (35 % WOC × 1.05; 5 % WOC +130 %)
- Harvey Tool, General Machining Guidelines: IPM = RPM × IPT × T, chip load tables by cutter diameter

## CII rating estimator

<a id="cii-rating"></a>

Folder `cii-rating/` · Maritime · Attained and required operational CII with the A–E rating, from ship type, capacity, annual fuel or CO₂ and distance.

### Assumptions and caveats

- This is an estimate of the regulatory calculation; the verified rating is issued by the Administration or recognised organisation on the verified IMO DCS data.
- No voyage adjustments or correction factors (MEPC.355(78), G5: ice class, shuttle tankers, STS, electrical cargo consumers, excluded segments) are applied; they can only lower the attained CII, so the result is conservative for entitled ships.
- Capacity is DWT for cargo and gas/LNG ships and GT for ro-ro and passenger ships; the reference-line caps and floors (bulk carriers 279 000 DWT, LNG carriers below 65 000 DWT, vehicle carriers 57 700 GT) apply to the reference line only, never to the attained CII.
- Distance is the total distance over ground reported to the DCS, ballast legs included; time at anchor or in port adds CO₂ without distance.
- LNG carrier parameters are reproduced exactly as printed in MEPC.353(78): 14479E10 for 65 000–100 000 DWT and 14779E10 below 65 000 DWT, which makes the reference line discontinuous at 65 000 DWT.
- Reduction factors exist for 2023–2030 only (MEPC.338(76) for 2023–2026, MEPC.400(83) for 2027–2030); nothing is set beyond 2030.
- Ratings use strict comparisons, so a value exactly on a boundary falls in the better band.
- EEXI is deliberately out of scope: it is a one-off design certificate verified at the first survey after 1 January 2023 and does not change year to year.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: every reference-line parameter and dd vector was read from the MEPC.353(78) and MEPC.354(78) PDFs rather than from memory; a remembered combination-carrier line (40853 / 0.812) was wrong and was corrected to 5119 / 0.622 before coding.
- Verification 2026-10-30: the 2027–2030 reduction factors (13.625 / 16.25 / 18.875 / 21.5 %) were confirmed as MEPC.400(83), adopted 11 April 2025, via DNV, Lloyd's Register and Türk Loydu MEPC 83 summaries.
- Provenance: the IMO worked example in MEPC.354(78) (required 10 → boundaries 8.6/9.4/10.6/11.8, attained 9 = B) is used as a self-test.
- Design decision (Chris, 2026-10-30): EEXI is excluded — it is a one-off certificate every ship has already obtained; the calculator covers the annual CII only.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- No CO₂ entered — the rating is meaningless until fuel or CO₂ is given.
- D rating: three consecutive D years require a corrective action plan in SEEMP Part III (MARPOL Annex VI reg. 28.8).
- E rating: a corrective action plan must be included in SEEMP Part III and verified before the ship can keep trading (reg. 28.8).
- No voyage adjustments or correction factors (MEPC.355(78), G5) are applied; those can only improve the attained value.
- Distance below 10 000 nmi for a year is low for an ocean-going ship — check whether the figure is for a full calendar year.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- IMO worked example: required 10 for a bulk carrier → boundaries 8.6 / 9.4 / 10.6 / 11.8; attained 9 rates B
  - Source: MEPC.354(78), 2022 CII rating guidelines (G4), text following Table 1
- Reference line, bulk carrier 80 000 DWT: 4745 × 80 000^−0.622 = 4.2317 g/(DWT·nmi); DWT above 279 000 is capped
  - Source: MEPC.353(78), 2022 CII reference lines guidelines (G2), eq. (1) and Table 1; value computed by hand
- Reduction factors Z: 5/7/9/11 % for 2023–2026 and 13.625/16.25/18.875/21.5 % for 2027–2030
  - Source: MEPC.338(76) (G3, 2021) and MEPC.400(83) adopted 11 April 2025 (2027–2030, +2.625 %/year)
- Attained CII: 5 000 t HFO (15 570 t CO₂) over 60 000 nmi on 80 000 DWT = 3.2438 g/(DWT·nmi) → B in 2026; 4 800 t → A
  - Source: MEPC.352(78) (G1) eq. for attained CII; CF 3.114 from MEPC.364(79); boundaries from MEPC.354(78)
- GT-based type: cruise ship 100 000 GT reference 930 × 100 000^−0.383 = 11.31 g/(GT·nmi)
  - Source: MEPC.353(78) Table 1 (cruise passenger ship row); value computed by hand
- LNG carrier below 65 000 DWT uses capacity 65 000 and 14779E10 in the reference line (≈ 20.17); attained still uses the real DWT
  - Source: MEPC.353(78) Table 1, LNG carrier rows; MEPC.354(78) dd vector for LNG carriers below 100 000 DWT
- Gas-carrier dd vectors switch at 65 000 DWT (0.81… above, 0.85… below); every dd vector is increasing
  - Source: MEPC.354(78) Table 1
- CO₂ limit for C: 1.06 × 3.7662 × 80 000 × 60 000 / 10⁶ = 19 162 t; margin = limit − actual
  - Source: Rearranged attained-CII formula (MEPC.352(78)) with the C/D boundary (MEPC.354(78))
- Invalid inputs fail fast: year 2031, zero gross tonnage, unknown ship type, negative fuel
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 80 000, 11 %, 19 162 t to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IMO Resolution MEPC.352(78) — 2022 Guidelines on operational carbon intensity indicators and the calculation methods (G1)
- IMO Resolution MEPC.353(78) — 2022 Guidelines on the reference lines (G2), Table 1
- IMO Resolutions MEPC.338(76) and MEPC.400(83) — operational carbon intensity reduction factors (G3)
- IMO Resolution MEPC.354(78) — 2022 Guidelines on the operational carbon intensity rating (G4), Table 1 and example
- IMO Resolution MEPC.364(79) — 2022 EEDI calculation guidelines, Table 1 (CF factors)
- MARPOL Annex VI, regulation 28 (CII) and regulation 2 (ship-type definitions)

## Fixed CO₂ fire-extinguishing system

<a id="co2-fire-system"></a>

Folder `co2-fire-system/` · Maritime · Required CO₂ quantity, cylinders and minimum discharge rate for machinery, cargo, bulk and vehicle spaces under the FSS Code chapter 5.

### Assumptions and caveats

- FSS Code chapter 5, 2.2.1 (MSC.206(81) as amended by MSC.339(91)): machinery spaces need free gas of the larger of 40 % of the gross volume without the casing above the level where its horizontal area is 40 % or less of that of the space (taken midway between tank top and the lowest part of the casing), and 35 % of the gross volume including the casing; 35 % and 30 % for cargo ships under 2000 GT whose machinery spaces are not entirely separate; cargo spaces 30 %; vehicle and ro-ro spaces that are not special category spaces 45 % of the largest space that can be sealed.
- Free carbon dioxide is calculated at 0.56 m³/kg (FSS 2.2.1.5); the free air of the starting air receivers, V (p + p_atm)/p_atm, is added to the machinery space volume unless the receiver safety valves discharge to the open air (FSS 2.1.1.2).
- Discharge: 85 % of the gas within 2 min for machinery spaces; two thirds within 10 min for container and general cargo spaces and for vehicle and ro-ro spaces; two thirds within 20 min for solid bulk cargo spaces, whose controls also allow one third, two thirds or the entire quantity to suit the loading condition. The rate shown is the average rate those times require.
- Cylinders: the CO₂ in each cylinder may not exceed two thirds of a kilogram per litre of water capacity at 15 °C (MCA MSIS 12 chapter 7), so a cylinder needs at least 1.5 L per kg of charge. The number of cylinders is rounded up.
- The concentration shown is that after discharge with free efflux of the displaced atmosphere, 1 − e^(−v/V) (NFPA 12), for information. Only the largest protected space sets the quantity when one system serves several spaces (FSS 2.1.1.1).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: a 6000 m³ engine room (5000 m³ without the upper casing) with 2.5 m³ of receivers at 30 bar needs max(0.40 × 5076.5, 0.35 × 6076.5) = 2126.8 m³ of free gas, 3797.9 kg of CO₂, 85 cylinders of 45 kg, and 26.9 kg/s on average to discharge 85 % in 2 min.
- Design decision: the calculator gives the regulatory minimum quantity; the system flow calculation, nozzle layout, pre-discharge alarm and time delay remain with the system maker and the Administration.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The starting air receivers add … m³ of free air to the machinery space volume (FSS 2.1.1.2).
- The reduced percentages for small cargo ships apply to machinery spaces only.
- The controls must allow one third, two thirds or the entire quantity to be released to suit the loading condition of the hold.
- Carbon dioxide systems shall not protect special category spaces.
- CO₂ at these concentrations is lethal: release only after the space is evacuated and sealed; the pre-discharge alarm and time delay are part of the system (FSS 2.1.3).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The volume without the upper casing cannot exceed the gross volume

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Engine room of 6000 m³ (5000 m³ without the upper casing) and 2.5 m³ of receivers at 30 bar: max(0.40 × 5076.5, 0.35 × 6076.5) = 2126.8 m³, 3797.8 kg, 85 cylinders of 45 kg
  - Source: FSS Code ch. 5, 2.1.1.2, 2.2.1.2 and 2.2.1.4 (MSC.206(81)): 40 %/35 % criteria, receiver air, 0.56 m³/kg
- With the receiver safety valves led to the open air the engine room needs 0.35 × 6000 = 2100 m³, i.e. 3750 kg of CO₂
  - Source: FSS Code ch. 5, 2.1.1.2: alternatively a discharge pipe from the safety valves led to the open air
- A small upper casing makes the 40 % criterion govern: 0.40 × 5800 = 2320 m³ against 0.35 × 6000 = 2100 m³
  - Source: FSS Code ch. 5, 2.2.1.2.1 and 2.2.1.2.2: the larger of the two volumes
- Cargo ship under 2000 GT with machinery spaces not entirely separate: 35 % and 30 % instead of 40 % and 35 %
  - Source: FSS Code ch. 5, 2.2.1.3 (renumbered 2.2.1.4 by MSC.339(91))
- Cargo holds 30 %, vehicle spaces 45 %; two thirds within 10 min (cargo, vehicle) or 20 min (solid bulk), 85 % within 2 min for machinery
  - Source: FSS Code ch. 5, 2.2.1.1, 2.2.1.2 and 2.2.1.7 (MSC.339(91)); 2.2.1.5 (MSC.206(81))
- A 45 kg charge needs at least 67.5 L of cylinder water capacity at 2/3 kg/L; free efflux of 35 % free gas leaves 1 − e^(−0.35) = 29.5 % CO₂
  - Source: MCA MSIS 12 ch. 7, 7.3.1.1 (filling ratio); NFPA 12 free-efflux relation
- Invalid inputs are rejected: a volume without the casing larger than the gross volume, an unknown space, zero cylinder charge
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2126.8 m³, 3798 kg, 3825 kg, 26.9 kg/s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IMO, FSS Code chapter 5 as replaced by MSC.206(81) (2006): 2.1.1.1, 2.1.1.2, 2.2.1.1–2.2.1.5
- IMO, MSC.339(91) (2012): new FSS 2.2.1.2 (vehicle and ro-ro spaces, 45 %, two thirds in 10 min) and 2.2.1.7 (container, general cargo and solid bulk discharge times)
- MCA, MSIS 12 chapter 7, Fixed fire extinguishing installations, 7.3.1.1 — filling ratio of CO₂ cylinders
- NFPA 12, Standard on Carbon Dioxide Extinguishing Systems — free-efflux concentration 1 − e^(−v/V)

## Air-core coil inductance calculator

<a id="coil-inductance"></a>

Folder `coil-inductance/` · Electrical · Inductance of an air-core coil by Wheeler's single-layer and multilayer formulas or the long-solenoid formula, and the turns for a target inductance.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The coil has no core, or a core of a non-magnetic material such as plastic, wood or ceramic; a ferrite or iron core multiplies the inductance by its effective permeability.
- Wheeler's single-layer formula uses the diameter to the centre of the wire and the winding length; Wheeler gives it as accurate to about 1 % when the length is more than 0.4 times the diameter.
- Wheeler's multilayer formula uses the mean radius, the winding length and the radial depth of the winding; it is accurate to about 1 % when 6a, 9b and 10c are about equal, and less otherwise.
- The long-solenoid formula μ0 N² A / l ignores the field at the ends, so it overestimates a short coil; the current-sheet value with Nagaoka's coefficient is exact for a thin, evenly wound single layer and is shown for comparison.
- Self-capacitance, the wire's own inductance and the change of current distribution with frequency are ignored; they matter near the coil's self-resonant frequency.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 20 turns, 1 in diameter and 1 in long give 6.90 µH by Wheeler (400 / 58 = 6.897), 10.03 µH as a long solenoid and 6.90 µH with Nagaoka's coefficient 0.6884 for d/l = 1; 24.1 turns give 10 µH. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The coil is shorter than 0.4 times its diameter: Wheeler\'s single-layer formula loses its 1 % accuracy; the current-sheet value is the better estimate.
- The coil is not long compared with its diameter: the long-solenoid formula overestimates it; the current-sheet value with Nagaoka\'s coefficient is closer.
- The terms 6a, 9b and 10c differ widely: Wheeler\'s multilayer formula is less accurate than its usual 1 % for this shape.
- The winding pitch is under 0.05 mm: the turns will not fit in one layer at this length.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Winding depth: the depth must be less than the mean diameter (got … m for a mean diameter of … m)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Single layer, 1 in by 1 in, 20 turns: Wheeler 400/58 = 6.897 µH; current sheet 0.6884 × 10.03 = 6.903 µH (within 0.1 %)
  - Source: Wheeler, Proc. IRE 16 (1928) single-layer formula; Nagaoka (1909) coefficient for d/l = 1
- Nagaoka coefficients match the published tables: d/l = 0.5 → 0.8181, 1 → 0.6884, 2 → 0.5255, and → 1 for a very long coil
  - Source: Nagaoka (1909) and Grover, Inductance Calculations, tables of K
- Turns for 10 µH on the 1 in by 1 in former: N = √(10 × 58) = 24.08, and that N gives 10 µH back
  - Source: Wheeler single-layer formula solved for N
- Multilayer, mean radius 0.5 in, length 0.5 in, depth 0.45 in, 100 turns: 0.8 × 0.25 × 10⁴ / (3 + 4.5 + 4.5) = 166.7 µH
  - Source: Wheeler, Proc. IRE 16 (1928) multilayer formula, hand calculation
- Long solenoid, 1 000 turns, 10 mm diameter, 0.5 m long: μ0 N² A / l = 197.4 µH, within 1 % of the current sheet
  - Source: Physics long-solenoid formula L = μ0 N² A / l; Nagaoka K → 1 for l ≫ d
- Invalid entries are rejected: zero diameter, zero turns, a winding deeper than the mean diameter
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 6.90, 10.03, 6.90, 0.6884 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Wheeler, H. A., Simple Inductance Formulas for Radio Coils, Proceedings of the IRE, vol. 16, no. 10, 1928, pp. 1398–1400 (single-layer and multilayer formulas)
- Nagaoka, H., The Inductance Coefficients of Solenoids, Journal of the College of Science, Imperial University of Tokyo, vol. 27, art. 6, 1909 (coefficient K for d/l = 1: 0.6884)
- Grover, F. W., Inductance Calculations, Van Nostrand 1946 (Dover reprint), the chapter on single-layer coils and its tables of Nagaoka's coefficient

## Column buckling (Euler and Johnson)

<a id="column-buckling"></a>

Folder `column-buckling/` · Structural · Critical buckling load of a compression member by Euler or the Johnson parabola, with end-condition factors, slenderness, allowable load and utilisation.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Ideal elastic column: straight, homogeneous, concentrically loaded, with the effective length K L set by the end conditions; real columns have initial crookedness and load eccentricity, which design codes cover with buckling curves (EN 1993-1-1 §6.3, AISC E3) and a safety factor — the Euler/Johnson result is the theoretical capacity.
- Buckling occurs about the weak axis (minimum I) over the full unbraced length; if the weak axis is braced at intermediate points, enter the braced length or the strong-axis I as a custom section.
- The Johnson parabola is used for slenderness ratios below the transition (KL/r)₁ = π √(2E/σ_y), where the Euler stress would exceed half the yield stress; it is the classic machine-design treatment (Shigley) of inelastic buckling, not a code curve.
- Effective-length factors: the theoretical values assume perfectly rigid or perfectly free ends; the recommended design values (AISC Table C-A-7.1) allow for the fact that fixed ends are never fully fixed, and are the default.
- Local buckling of thin flanges or walls, torsional and flexural-torsional buckling of open sections, and lateral-torsional buckling are not checked; the I-section weak-axis I ignores root fillets.
- Allowable load = critical load ÷ the entered factor of safety; typical factors are 1.67–1.92 (AISC ASD) for structures and 2–3 for machine members with uncertain loads.
- Material presets are nominal values; timber uses the compressive strength parallel to the grain in place of yield.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: a 3 m pinned 50 mm steel rod gives the textbook Euler load π² × 200 GPa × 3.068 ×10⁻⁷ / 9 = 67.3 kN at KL/r = 240; the S235 transition slenderness 129.6 and the Johnson load at KL/r = 100 (σ_cr = 165 MPa, 324 kN) were checked by hand.
- Design decision: Euler and Johnson values are both reported and the governing one is named, so the user sees where the column sits relative to the transition.
- Design decision: section properties come from shared/sections.js (shared with beams and shafts) and the weak-axis I is used automatically.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Applied load exceeds the allowable load: the column is inadequate at this factor of safety.
- Slenderness above 200: most codes limit compression members to KL/r ≤ 200 (AISC) because small imperfections dominate.
- D/t above 90: thin-walled tube, check local (shell) buckling.
- Wall slenderness above 40: check local plate buckling of the walls.
- Weak-axis flexural buckling only; open sections can also fail by torsional or flexural-torsional buckling, and the fillet-free I is about 5 % low.
- Theoretical K assumes perfectly rigid fixity; design practice uses the recommended values.
- Theoretical capacity of a perfect column; codes reduce it for imperfections (buckling curves) — compare with EN 1993-1-1 §6.3 or AISC E3 for a design check.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Unknown section "…"

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Euler: 3 m pinned 50 mm steel rod, I = π d⁴/64 = 30.68 cm⁴, P_cr = π² × 200 GPa × I / 3² = 67.3 kN, σ_cr 34.3 MPa at KL/r = 240 (long column)
  - Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, ch. 13 eq. 13-5 P_cr = π² E I / (K L)²; Shigley §4-12
- Transition slenderness π √(2E/σ_y): A36 125.7, S235 132.8; at the transition the Euler and Johnson stresses both equal σ_y/2
  - Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., eq. 4-45 and Fig. 4-19 (Johnson parabola tangent to Euler at σ_y/2)
- Johnson: the same rod at 1.25 m (KL/r = 100) has σ_cr = 250 − (250²/4π²E) × 100² = 170.8 MPa and P_cr = 335 kN, below the Euler value (197.4 MPa)
  - Source: Shigley eq. 4-43 (J. B. Johnson parabola) for intermediate columns
- End conditions: fixed–free (K = 2) carries a quarter of the pinned Euler load, fixed–fixed theoretical (0.5) four times, recommended (0.65) 2.37 times
  - Source: Hibbeler Fig. 13-8 effective lengths; AISC Commentary Table C-A-7.1 recommended K values
- Default CHS 139.7 × 6: A 25.2 cm², I 564 cm⁴, i 47.3 mm (EN 10210 tables); 4 m pinned S235 → KL/r 84.5, Johnson 472 kN, Euler 731 kN, allowable 246 kN at FoS 1.92
  - Source: Section tables for hot-finished CHS 139.7 × 6 (A = 25.2 cm², I = 564 cm⁴, i = 4.73 cm); Johnson/Euler formulas as above
- Weak axis is used: a 100 × 200 rectangle has I_min = 200 × 100³/12 = 1 667 cm⁴ (not 6 667) and r_min = b/√12 = 28.9 mm; IPE 200 weak-axis I by formula 141.9 cm⁴ vs 142 in the tables
  - Source: Section properties (Gere Appendix E); ArcelorMittal / EN 10365 IPE 200: I_z = 142 cm⁴
- Custom section IPE 200 from the tables (A 28.5 cm², I_z 142 cm⁴), 4 m pinned S235: KL/r 179, Euler 184 kN, σ_cr 64.5 MPa; slenderness warning above 200 for 4.5 m
  - Source: Euler formula with tabulated properties; AISC KL/r ≤ 200 recommendation (E2 user note)
- Overloaded column is flagged: 300 kN applied on the default CHS exceeds the 246 kN allowable
  - Source: Behaviour specification
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero length, unknown end condition, zero custom area
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 25.2 cm², 564 cm⁴, 4.73 cm, 84.5, 132.8, 731 kN, 290 MPa, 472 kN to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Budynas & Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §4-12 to §4-14 (Euler columns, Johnson parabola, transition slenderness)
- Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, 10th ed., ch. 13 "Buckling of columns" (Euler load, effective length)
- AISC Steel Construction Manual, 15th ed., Commentary Table C-A-7.1 (approximate values of effective length factor K)
- EN 1993-1-1 §6.3 and EN 338 (material values for steel grades and timber C24)

## Compass error by amplitude or azimuth

<a id="compass-error"></a>

Folder `compass-error/` · Maritime · True bearing of the sun or another body by amplitude or time azimuth, then the compass error and deviation from the observed bearing.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Spherical astronomy on the celestial sphere: the azimuth of a body of declination Dec at true altitude h seen from latitude Lat follows cos Z = (sin Dec − sin Lat sin h)/(cos Lat cos h); at the moment of theoretical rising or setting (centre on the celestial horizon, h = 0) this is the amplitude formula sin A = sin Dec / cos Lat.
- Amplitude observations: the sun's centre is on the celestial horizon when its lower limb is about half a diameter above the visible horizon, the usual moment for the observation. With the centre on the visible horizon instead, the true altitude is −(dip + refraction), with dip 1.76′ √h for a height of eye h in metres and the horizontal refraction from Bennett's formula (about 34′ to 36′), and the bearing is computed at that altitude (the visible-horizon amplitude correction).
- Time azimuth: LHA = GHA + longitude (east positive) from the almanac GHA at the time of the bearing; the azimuth is exact at any altitude, but bearings of bodies higher than about 30° are hard to take accurately with an azimuth circle.
- Compass error is true minus compass bearing, easterly when positive ("compass least, error east"); deviation is the compass error minus the magnetic variation from the chart, both east positive. The variation must be for the year of observation.
- The declination and GHA are taken as entered for the moment of the bearing (the sun's declination changes by up to 0.4′ per hour); parallax and semi-diameter are irrelevant for the bearing of the centre.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: latitude 40° N, declination 20° N gives an amplitude of 26.5° and a rising bearing of 063.5°; at the equator the amplitude equals the declination; the time azimuth at the LHA of theoretical sunset equals the amplitude bearing; a true bearing of 063.5° read as 061.0° on the compass is an error of 2.5° E, which with 4° W variation is 6.5° E deviation.
- Design decision: a single altitude–azimuth formula serves both the celestial-horizon and the visible-horizon amplitude, so no amplitude-correction table is needed and the two cases agree by construction.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above 60° latitude the body rises and sets at a shallow angle: the moment of the observation is uncertain and so is the bearing.
- The body is …° below the horizon at this LHA: check the GHA, the longitude sign (east +) and the time.
- Altitude …°: bearings of high bodies are hard to take accurately with an azimuth circle.
- Compass error over 10°: check the observation, the time and the body before correcting the compass.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- At latitude …° a body of declination …° does not rise or set (it is circumpolar or never above the horizon)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Amplitude at latitude 40° N, declination 20° N: sin A = sin 20°/cos 40° → A = 26.5°, rising bearing 063.5° (E 26.5° N), setting 296.5°
  - Source: Bowditch, "Azimuths and Amplitudes": sin A = sin Dec / cos Lat
- Special cases: at the equator the amplitude equals the declination (23.44° → bearing 066.56°); a southern declination sets south of west (Lat 50° N, Dec 20° S → W 32.1° S, 237.8°)
  - Source: Amplitude formula with cos Lat = 1 and with negative declination
- Time azimuth: Lat 0°, Dec 0°, LHA 90° is due west (270°); on the meridian (LHA 0) at Lat 50° N the sun bears 180°; at the LHA of theoretical sunset the time azimuth equals the amplitude bearing
  - Source: Bowditch time-azimuth formula; cos LHA_set = −tan Lat tan Dec at altitude 0
- Compass error and deviation: true 063.5° read as 061.0° is 2.5° E error ("compass least, error east"); with variation 4° W the deviation is 6.5° E
  - Source: Error rules: error = true − compass, deviation = error − variation (east positive)
- Visible horizon: with a 16 m height of eye the dip is 1.76√16 = 7.04′ and the refraction about 36′, so the true altitude is about −43′ and the bearing is computed at that altitude; refraction at 0° is 34.5′ (Bennett)
  - Source: Nautical Almanac dip formula; Bennett (1982) refraction; Bowditch visible-horizon amplitude correction
- Invalid inputs fail fast: a body that never sets (Lat 80° N, Dec 20° N), a latitude of 90°, an unknown method
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions"); |sin Dec / cos Lat| > 1 has no amplitude
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 26.5°, 063.5°, 2.5°, 6.5° to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- The American Practical Navigator (Bowditch), NGA Pub. 9 — "Azimuths and Amplitudes" (amplitude formula, visible-horizon correction, time azimuth)
- The Nautical Almanac (HM Nautical Almanac Office / US Naval Observatory) — GHA and declination, dip = 1.76′ √h(m)
- G. G. Bennett, "The calculation of astronomical refraction in marine navigation", Journal of Navigation 35 (1982) 255–259
- A. Frost, The Principles and Practice of Navigation, Brown, Son & Ferguson — compass error by amplitude and azimuth

## Compressed air calculator: leaks, receiver, pipe drop and power

<a id="compressed-air"></a>

Folder `compressed-air/` · Mechanical · Compressed air leak flow and yearly cost, receiver tank size, air main pressure drop and compressor power, isothermal and adiabatic.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Air is an ideal gas with R = 287.05 J/(kg·K) and γ = 1.4. Flows are free air delivery (FAD): volume at the atmospheric pressure and air temperature entered, the way compressors are rated (ISO 1217).
- A leak is a round hole of diameter d with a coefficient of flow Cd; Cd = 1 reproduces the published leakage tables (104 cfm through 1/4 in at 100 psig), and the US DOE multiplies by 0.61 for sharp-edged holes. Above 13 psig the flow through a hole to the atmosphere is choked (sonic) and grows linearly with the absolute pressure.
- The leak cost uses a compressor specific power: about 18 kW per 100 cfm of free air for a typical plant (US DOE), 15 to 16 for an efficient one; the power is assumed to fall in proportion when the leaks are fixed, which needs good compressor control.
- The receiver size is the volume that supplies the demand minus any compressor or metered supply during the event while the pressure falls from the line pressure to the lowest acceptable pressure, at constant temperature.
- Pipe pressure drop is isothermal flow with the Darcy friction factor (Colebrook, roughness 0.046 mm for steel) and Sutherland viscosity; the Atlas Copco/BCAS empirical formula is shown for comparison. Fittings must be added as equivalent length.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 1/4 in hole at 100 psig, 14.7 psia and 68 °F leaks 104 cfm of free air (0.0591 kg/s), the published table value; at 18.4 kW per 100 cfm, 8 760 h and 0.10 per kWh it costs 16 764 a year, the CAGI fact sheet figure. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A pressure band under 0.2 bar (3 psi) needs a very large receiver: check whether the lowest acceptable pressure can be lower.
- Pressure drop above 0.1 bar (1.5 psi): Atlas Copco recommends no more than 0.1 bar from the compressor to the farthest user in a fixed network.
- Pressure drop above 10 % of the line pressure: the pipe is undersized and the empirical formula is no longer reliable.
- Pressure ratio above 11 in one stage: oil-free compressors need two stages; oil-injected screws handle up to about 13 bar.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Lowest acceptable pressure: it must be below the line pressure, or the receiver cannot release any air.
- Supply during the event: it covers the whole demand, so no storage is needed; enter a supply below the demand.
- Pipe inside diameter: the pipe is far too small for this flow; the pressure would fall to nothing (the flow chokes). Choose a larger pipe or a shorter run.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Leakage table at coefficient 1: 100 psig 1/16 in 6.49, 1/4 in 104, 3/8 in 234 cfm; 15 psig 1/4 in 26.9 cfm; 50 psig 1/64 in 0.229 cfm
  - Source: US DOE Compressed Air Tip Sheet #3 leakage table; "Discharge of air through an orifice" table (Burton Companies)
- Leak cost at 0.10 per kWh, constant operation: 1/16 in 1 046, 1/8 in 4 190, 1/4 in 16 764 a year (18.4 kW per 100 cfm)
  - Source: CAGI / Compressed Air Challenge Fact Sheet #7, "The cost of leaks" (rev. May 2026)
- Subsonic leak at 5 psig follows the isentropic nozzle equation and is below the choked value
  - Source: F. M. White, Fluid Mechanics, Ch. 9 (isentropic flow through a nozzle); hand calculation
- Receiver: 100 cfm for 1 min, 100 to 90 psig at 14.7 psia needs 147 ft³ = 1 099 US gal; with a 40 cfm metered supply 660 gal
  - Source: US DOE / ORNL MEASUR Receiver Tank Calculator, dedicated and metered storage methods; hand calculation
- Air main: 100 L/s free air, 59 m of 53 mm bore at 7 bar g gives 0.040 bar by the BCAS/Atlas Copco formula; Darcy within 10 %
  - Source: BCAS simplified equation PD = 1.6 × 10⁸ L Q^1.85 / (P d⁵) (pocketEngineer worked example data); Atlas Copco d⁵ = 450 qc^1.85 l/(Δp p)
- Compressor work for 100 cfm free air to 100 psig: isothermal 9.83 kW, one-stage adiabatic 13.37 kW, two stages 11.42 kW
  - Source: Çengel & Boles, Thermodynamics, Ch. 7: W = p1V1 ln r and n γ/(γ−1) p1V1 (r^((γ−1)/nγ) − 1); hand calculation
- Invalid input: a minimum pressure above the line pressure, a supply above the demand and a choked pipe are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 104.0 cfm, 19.1 kW, 167 700 kWh, 16 767 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- US DOE, Compressed Air Tip Sheet #3 "Minimize Compressed Air Leaks" (leakage table at coefficient 1, ×0.61 sharp-edged, 18 kW/100 cfm) and CAGI / Compressed Air Challenge Fact Sheet #7 "Compressed Air System Leaks" (rev. 2026)
- US DOE / ORNL MEASUR Tools Suite, Receiver Tank Calculator: dedicated and metered storage V = t (Q − Q_metered) p_atm / (p_in − p_out)
- Atlas Copco, Compressed Air Manual, 8th ed.: pipe dimensioning d⁵ = 450 qc^1.85 l / (Δp p) (BCAS form 1.6 × 10⁸ L Q^1.85 / (d⁵ p)) and the 0.1 bar network guideline
- F. M. White, Fluid Mechanics, 7th ed., Ch. 9 (choked flow through an orifice, isothermal flow with friction); Y. A. Çengel & M. A. Boles, Thermodynamics, Ch. 7 (isothermal, isentropic and multistage compressor work)

## Compression ratio calculator

<a id="compression-ratio"></a>

Folder `compression-ratio/` · Automotive · Static compression ratio from bore, stroke, chamber volume, head gasket, deck clearance and piston dome or dish, with swept and clearance volumes.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The static compression ratio is the cylinder volume at bottom dead centre divided by the volume at top dead centre, CR = (V_s + V_c) / V_c; it ignores valve timing, so the dynamic (effective) ratio with a late-closing intake valve is lower.
- The head gasket is treated as a cylinder of its compressed thickness and its bore diameter; use the compressed thickness from the gasket maker, not the free thickness.
- The deck volume is a cylinder of the bore diameter and the deck clearance: positive when the piston crown stops below the block deck at top dead centre, negative when it rises above it.
- The piston volume is positive for a dish and valve reliefs (they add clearance volume) and negative for a dome (it fills the chamber); the small volume beside the top ring land is not included.
- Chamber and piston volumes are entered in cc (1 cc = 1 mL); measure them with a burette for an accurate ratio.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: bore 4.030 in, stroke 3.480 in, 64 cc chamber, 0.041 in gasket of 4.100 in bore, 0.025 in deck clearance and 5 cc of valve reliefs: swept 727.4 cc, gasket 8.87 cc, deck 5.23 cc, clearance 83.1 cc, CR 9.75:1, eight cylinders 355.1 in³. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The head gasket bore is smaller than the cylinder bore: the gasket would overhang the bore. Check both values.
- A static compression ratio above 14:1 is beyond what pump gasoline tolerates in a spark-ignition engine; it suits diesels, race fuel or methanol.
- A static compression ratio below 6:1 is unusually low; check the chamber and dish volumes.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Deck clearance: the piston would rise above the deck by more than the gasket thickness and hit the head.
- Piston dish or dome volume: the dome fills the whole clearance volume; check the dome volume and its sign (a dome is negative).

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 4.030 × 3.480 in, 64 cc chamber, 0.041 in gasket of 4.100 in, 0.025 in deck, 5 cc reliefs: 727.4 cc swept, 83.1 cc clearance, 9.75:1
  - Source: Hand calculation: π/4 b² s = 44.389 in³ = 727.41 cc; gasket π/4 × 4.1² × 0.041 = 0.5413 in³ = 8.870 cc; deck 0.3189 in³ = 5.226 cc
- Chevrolet 350: 4.000 in bore × 3.480 in stroke × 8 is 349.9 in³ (5.73 L)
  - Source: Published GM small-block 350 dimensions (4.00 in × 3.48 in, 350 cu in, 5.7 L)
- Chamber only (no gasket, deck or dish): 86 × 86 mm with 50 cc gives (499.6 + 50) / 50 = 10.99
  - Source: Limiting case of r_c = (V_d + V_c) / V_c (Heywood Section 2.2)
- A 5 cc dome instead of 5 cc of reliefs removes 10 cc of clearance and raises the ratio to 10.95
  - Source: Sign convention of the piston volume (dome negative); hand calculation (810.508 − 10) / 73.096
- Piston above the deck by more than the gasket, or a dome larger than the clearance, is rejected; a small gasket bore warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 727.4 mL, 8.87 mL, 5.23 mL, 83.1 mL, 9.75, 355.1 in³ to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- J.B. Heywood, Internal Combustion Engine Fundamentals, McGraw-Hill 1988, Section 2.2 Geometrical properties of reciprocating engines (V_d = π B² L / 4, r_c = (V_d + V_c) / V_c)
- W.W. Pulkrabek, Engineering Fundamentals of the Internal Combustion Engine, 2nd ed., Pearson Prentice Hall 2004, Chapter 2 Operating characteristics (engine geometry and compression ratio)

## Concrete bag calculator

<a id="concrete-bags"></a>

Folder `concrete-bags/` · Civil · How many 80, 60, 50 or 40 lb bags (or 20 to 30 kg) of premixed concrete you need for any volume, with the yield per bag, the weight to carry and the cost.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Premixed concrete yields 0.60 ft³ per 80 lb bag, 0.45 ft³ per 60 lb, 0.375 ft³ per 50 lb and 0.30 ft³ per 40 lb, the figures printed on US bags; metric bags use the same yield per kilogram (11.7 L per 25 kg).
- Mortar, high-strength, fast-setting and lightweight mixes yield different volumes; read the yield on the bag and compare.
- The weight to carry is the dry weight of the bags; the water added on site is not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: one cubic yard is 45 bags of 80 lb (3 600 lb of dry mix), 60 of 60 lb and 90 of 40 lb, as in premix yield charts.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- More than one cubic yard: ready-mix by truck is usually cheaper and faster than mixing this many bags.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- One cubic yard: 45 bags of 80 lb (3 600 lb), 0.600 ft³ per bag, 58.9 bags per m³
  - Source: US premix yield charts: 45 × 80 lb bags per cubic yard; 27 ft³ / 0.60 ft³ = 45
- One cubic yard in other sizes: 60 bags of 60 lb, 72 of 50 lb, 90 of 40 lb
  - Source: US premix yield charts (0.45, 0.375 and 0.30 ft³ per bag)
- 10 ft³ with 10 % waste: 11 ft³ = 18.33 bags of 80 lb, so 19 bags, $114 at $6 each
  - Source: 10 × 1.1 / 0.60 = 18.33
- Half a cubic metre in 25 kg bags: 42.7, so 43 bags, 1 075 kg to carry
  - Source: 25 kg yields 11.705 L (0.60 ft³ per 80 lb by mass); 0.5 / 0.011705 = 42.72
- Two cubic yards hints at ready-mix; zero volume and an unknown bag are rejected
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 45, 0.600 ft³, 58.9, 3 600 lb to the digits printed

### Sources

- QUIKRETE Concrete Mix (No. 1101) product data: 80 lb yields about 0.60 ft³, 60 lb about 0.45 ft³
- 1 yd³ = 27 ft³ = 0.764554857984 m³ (NIST Handbook 44, Appendix C)

## Concrete block calculator: CMU, mortar and grout

<a id="concrete-block"></a>

Folder `concrete-block/` · Civil · Concrete blocks for a wall (8 × 16 in or 440 × 215 mm), with openings and waste, bags of mortar and the grout volume to fill the cores.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Single-wythe wall laid in running bond. The count uses the face module of the unit plus one joint: 8 × 16 in (0.889 ft²) for US blocks and 225 × 450 mm (0.101 m²) for metric blocks. Corners, lintels and bond beams need their own special units.
- Mortar uses the NCMA estimate of 16 conventional blocks per 80 lb bag of preblended mortar with face-shell bedding, which includes nominal waste; the QUIKRETE Mortar Mix data sheet gives 13, so use that rate for inexperienced masons. Metric blocks are scaled by their longer joint length.
- Grout volumes are those of NCMA TEK 4-2A Table 3 for two-core hollow units, including 3 % waste; units with larger cells or bond beams take more. Grout is not estimated for metric blocks, which are often solid or have other cell shapes.
- The waste allowance on blocks covers breakage and cuts; NCMA uses about 5 %.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a wall 40 ft long and 8 ft high, 8-in units grouted at 48 in: 320 ft² / 0.889 = 360 blocks, 378 with 5 % waste; 22.5 so 23 bags of mortar; grout 320 × 6.1/100 = 19.5 ft³ = 0.723 yd³. Checked by hand.
- Grout table transcribed from NCMA (CMHA) TEK 4-2A Table 3 for unit widths 6 to 14 in and spacings 8 to 48 in.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The wall height is not a whole number of courses; adjust it to the 8 in (225 mm) module or allow for cut blocks.
- Hollow, unreinforced walls are suitable for low garden walls only; walls that retain soil or carry loads need reinforced, grouted cores to an engineer\'s design.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Area of doors and windows: the openings (… m²) must be smaller than the wall (… m²)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 40 × 8 ft wall of 8 in blocks grouted at 48 in: 360 blocks, 378 with 5 % waste, 23 bags, 19.5 ft³ = 0.723 yd³ of grout
  - Source: Hand calculation: 320 ft² / (16 × 8 / 144) = 360; 360 / 16 per bag = 22.5 → 23; TEK 4-2A Table 3: 6.1 ft³ per 100 ft²
- NCMA TEK 4-2A Table 3, solid grouted per 100 ft²: 6 in 25.6 ft³, 8 in 36.1, 10 in 47.0, 12 in 58.9; 12 in at 32 in o.c. 14.8
  - Source: NCMA (CMHA) TEK 4-2A, Estimating Concrete Masonry Materials, Table 3 (two-core units, 3 % waste)
- One block covers 0.889 ft², so 100 ft² takes 112.5 blocks (113); NCMA rate of 16 blocks per 80 lb bag gives 8 bags per 128 blocks
  - Source: NCMA TEK 4-2A: 8 × 16 in face = 8/9 ft² per unit; Table 2: one 80 lb bag of preblended mortar lays 16 conventional CMU
- Metric 440 × 215 mm blocks: 9.88 per m², 10 × 2.25 m wall = 223 blocks, no grout estimate; openings are deducted
  - Source: Hand calculation: 1 / (0.45 × 0.225) = 9.877 per m²; 22.5 × 9.877 = 222.2 → 223
- Openings as large as the wall, zero length and an unknown width are rejected; an off-module height warns
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 360, 378, 23, 19.5 ft³, 0.723 yd³ to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- NCMA (CMHA) TEK 4-2A, Estimating Concrete Masonry Materials: Table 2 (mortar, 16 units per 80 lb preblended bag) and Table 3 (grout volume per 100 ft² of wall)
- QUIKRETE Mortar Mix No. 1102 data sheet (an 80 lb bag lays up to 13 standard 8 × 8 × 16 in blocks)

## Concrete column and post hole calculator

<a id="concrete-column"></a>

Folder `concrete-column/` · Civil · Concrete for round columns, piers and tube forms, or for setting fence and deck posts, with premix bags per hole and in total, weight and cost.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Columns and holes are round with a uniform diameter; a bell or flared base at the bottom of a pier is not included.
- In a post hole, the post displaces concrete over the depth of the hole above the gravel; the post is assumed to stand on the gravel at the bottom.
- Rules of thumb in the article (hole about three times the post width, one third of the post in the ground) are common fencing practice; posts for decks and structures follow the local code and the drawings.
- Premix bags yield 0.60 ft³ per 80 lb; the weight uses 2 400 kg/m³ and counts only the concrete.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 12 in hole 36 in deep around a 4 × 4 post (3.5 in actual) holds 2.10 ft³, 3.5 bags of 80 lb; ten holes with 10 % waste need 39 bags. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The hole is narrower than about three times the post width, the usual rule for fence posts; the post may lean in soft ground.
- More than one cubic yard: ready-mix by truck is usually cheaper and faster than mixing bags.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Post width or diameter: the post does not fit in the hole; make the hole wider.
- Gravel at the bottom of the hole: the gravel fills the whole hole; it must be less than the depth.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Ten 12 in holes 36 in deep around 4 × 4 posts: 2.10 ft³ and 3.50 bags of 80 lb per hole, 23.1 ft³ and 39 bags with 10 % waste
  - Source: (π/4 × 1² − 3.5²/144) × 3 = (0.7854 − 0.0851) × 3 = 2.101 ft³; / 0.60 = 3.50; × 10 × 1.1 = 23.11 ft³; / 0.60 = 38.5 → 39
- Four 12 in tube forms 4 ft tall: π ft³ each = 5.24 bags of 80 lb, 0.465 yd³ in total, 21 bags
  - Source: π/4 × 1² × 4 = 3.1416 ft³; × 4 = 12.566 ft³ = 0.4654 yd³; / 0.60 = 20.9 → 21
- Metric: 300 mm hole 800 mm deep, 100 mm round post, 100 mm of gravel: 0.0440 m³, 3.76 bags of 25 kg, so 4 bags
  - Source: (π/4 × 0.3² − π/4 × 0.1²) × (0.8 − 0.1) = 0.06283 × 0.7 = 0.04398 m³; 25 kg yields 11.7 L
- A 6 in hole for a 4 × 4 post is narrow and warns; a 3.5 in post in a 4 in hole does not fit and is rejected
  - Source: Fencing rule of thumb: hole about three times the post width; a square post needs a hole wider than its diagonal
- Gravel deeper than the hole, zero diameter and an unknown type are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2.10 ft³, 3.50, 23.1 ft³, 39 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

- International Residential Code (2021), R507.3 (deck footings) and R403.1.4 (footing depth below frost)

## Concrete footing calculator

<a id="concrete-footing"></a>

Folder `concrete-footing/` · Civil · Concrete for strip footings under walls or square pad footings under posts, in cubic yards or m³ with waste, premix bags, weight and cost.

### Assumptions and caveats

- A strip footing is measured along its centreline, so the corners are counted once. Measuring the outside perimeter instead double-counts each corner.
- Footings are rectangular in section with a level base; stepped footings, stem walls and trench over-dig are not included. The waste allowance covers over-dig and spillage, 10 % or more when pouring against earth.
- The size of a footing comes from the load and the soil, and its depth from the local frost line; this page only estimates quantities. IRC R403.1.1 sets 12 in wide and 6 in thick as the minimum for light-frame buildings.
- Premix bags yield 0.60 ft³ per 80 lb; the weight uses 2 400 kg/m³.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Smaller than the IRC R403.1.1 minimum of 12 in wide and 6 in thick for footings of light-frame buildings.
- More than one cubic yard: ready-mix by truck is usually cheaper and faster than mixing bags.

## Concrete slab calculator

<a id="concrete-slab"></a>

Folder `concrete-slab/` · Civil · Cubic yards or m³ of concrete for a slab, patio, driveway or shed base, with waste, the number of 80, 60 or 40 lb bags, weight and cost.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The slab is rectangular with a uniform thickness; for an L-shape, add two rectangles. Thickened edges, beams under the slab and the gravel base are not included.
- The waste allowance covers spillage, an uneven sub-base and formwork that bows; 5 to 10 % is usual for slabs.
- Premix bags yield 0.60 ft³ per 80 lb; ready-mix is ordered by the cubic yard or cubic metre, usually in steps of a quarter or half.
- Thickness guidance in the article (4 in for patios and walkways, 5 to 6 in for driveways) is common residential practice; slabs that carry structural loads need an engineer's design.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 10 × 10 ft slab 4 in thick is 33.3 ft³ = 1.23 yd³, 1.36 yd³ with 10 % waste, 62 bags of 80 lb. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Slabs thinner than about 3.5 in (90 mm) crack easily; 4 in (100 mm) is the usual minimum for a patio or walkway.
- More than one cubic yard: ready-mix by truck is usually cheaper, faster and more uniform than mixing bags.

## Concrete volume and rebar weight

<a id="concrete-volume"></a>

Folder `concrete-volume/` · Civil · Concrete volume and mass for slabs, walls, footings and columns with waste, cement/sand/aggregate for nominal mixes, and rebar length, mass and steel ratio.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Volumes are the gross geometric volume of the element times the count; openings, chamfers and embedded items are not deducted, and the waste factor (5–10 % typical for in-situ work) covers over-excavation, spillage and formwork deflection.
- Concrete density 2 400 kg/m³ for the mass (EN 1991-1-1 Table A.1: 24 kN/m³ plain, 25 kN/m³ reinforced); the reinforcement mass computed separately can be added for the reinforced weight.
- Material quantities use the classic nominal-mix estimate: 1.54 m³ of loose dry materials per m³ of compacted concrete, split in the mix ratio by volume, with cement at a bulk density of 1 440 kg/m³ (one 50 kg bag ≈ 34.7 L). Designed mixes from a ready-mix supplier follow their mix design, not this rule.
- Reinforcement mass per metre = ρ_steel π d²/4 = 0.006165 d² kg/m with d in mm — the d²/162 rule — for plain or deformed bars of the same nominal diameter.
- Mesh layouts (slabs, walls): bars at the given spacing in both directions per layer, number of bars = floor(span/spacing) + 1 in each direction, each bar the full element dimension; cover, bends, hooks and chairs are covered only by the lap/waste percentage. Bar layouts (beams, columns): a given number of longitudinal bars over the element length plus links at a spacing with a perimeter from the cover.
- Steel ratios are reported in kg/m³ for comparison with typical ranges (slabs 80–120, beams 150–250, columns 150–300, foundations 60–100 kg/m³); they are an estimating check, not a structural design.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: a 10 × 5 × 0.2 m slab gives 10 m³ (11 m³ with 10 % waste) and 24 t; the 1 : 2 : 4 mix gives 6.3 bags of 50 kg per m³ (316.8 kg), the figure quoted in estimating handbooks; 12 mm bars at 200 mm both ways in two layers give 1 030 m and 1 006 kg with 10 % laps, i.e. 101 kg/m³, inside the typical slab range.
- Design decision: the d²/162 rule is used instead of a bar-mass table so any diameter works; the exact 0.006165 d² is used (d²/162 = 0.006173 d², 0.1 % apart).
- Design decision: reinforcement geometry is deliberately simple (full-length bars, perimeter links) because detailing varies by code; the lap/waste percentage is the user's allowance for that.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- No waste allowance: in-situ concrete orders normally carry 5–10 % for over-break, spillage and formwork deflection.
- Material split uses the nominal-mix estimate (1.54 dry-volume factor); a designed or ready-mixed concrete follows the supplier\'s mix design.
- Mesh quantities assume full-length bars at the spacing in both directions per layer; cover, hooks and chairs are inside the lap allowance.
- Quantities for estimating only; the structural design (bar sizes, spacing, cover) comes from the design code.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Unknown element "…"
- Cover is too large for the section — links would have no size

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Slab 10 × 5 × 0.2 m: 10 m³ net, 11 m³ to order with 10 % waste, 24.0 t at 2 400 kg/m³; three slabs triple everything
  - Source: Geometry; EN 1991-1-1 Table A.1 concrete density 24 kN/m³
- Nominal mix 1 : 2 : 4 with dry-volume factor 1.54: cement 316.8 kg/m³ = 6.3 bags of 50 kg, sand 0.44 m³, aggregate 0.88 m³ per m³ of concrete
  - Source: Standard estimating rule (IS 456 nominal mixes; 1.54 dry volume; cement 1 440 kg/m³ → 6.3 bags/m³ for 1:2:4)
- Bar mass per metre d²/162: 8 mm 0.395, 12 mm 0.888, 16 mm 1.578, 20 mm 2.466, 25 mm 3.853 kg/m
  - Source: ρ_steel π d²/4 with 7 850 kg/m³ (EN 1992-1-1 Annex C); d²/162 rule from detailing handbooks
- Mesh in the slab: 12 mm at 200 mm both ways, two layers → 26 bars × 10 m + 51 bars × 5 m per layer = 515 m, 1 030 m total, 1 133 m with 10 % laps, 1 006 kg, 101 kg/m³ (typical slab 80–120)
  - Source: Bar count = floor(span / spacing) + 1 per direction; typical steel ratios (Reynolds, Reinforced Concrete Designer's Handbook)
- Rectangular column 400 × 400 × 3 m with 8 × 20 mm bars and 8 mm ties at 200 mm, 40 mm cover: 0.48 m³, 59.2 kg main steel, 16 ties of 1.44 m, ≈ 142 kg/m³ with no lap allowance
  - Source: Bar layout arithmetic; tie length = 2 (a + b − 4c) + 20 d (perimeter inside cover plus hooks); typical column ratios 150–300 kg/m³
- Round column Ø400 × 3 m: 0.377 m³; wall 10 × 3 × 0.25 m: 7.5 m³; footing 2 × 2 × 0.6 m: 2.4 m³
  - Source: Geometry
- Plain concrete: no reinforcement outputs; zero waste raises a warning
  - Source: Behaviour specification
- Invalid inputs fail fast: fractional element count, cover larger than the section, unknown mix
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 10.0 m³, 11.0 m³, 24.0 t, 3 485 kg, 69.7, 4.84 m³, 9.68 m³, 1 133 m, 1 006 kg, 0.888 kg/m, 101 kg/m³, 25.0 t to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- EN 1991-1-1:2002, Table A.1 (densities of concrete 24–25 kN/m³) and EN 1992-1-1 (reinforcement steel density 7 850 kg/m³, Annex C)
- IS 456:2000 Table 9 (nominal mix proportions M10–M20) and standard estimating practice (dry-volume factor 1.54, cement 1 440 kg/m³)

## Conduit fill calculator (NEC)

<a id="conduit-fill"></a>

Folder `conduit-fill/` · Electrical · Percent fill and the smallest EMT or PVC conduit for THHN wires under NEC Chapter 9, with how many wires of one size fit in each trade size.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Conductors are THHN, THWN or THWN-2 copper building wire, with the areas of NEC Chapter 9 Table 5. Other insulations (XHHW, RHW, USE) and compact conductors have different areas.
- Conduit areas are the NEC Chapter 9 Table 4 values for EMT (Article 358) and PVC Schedule 40 (Article 352). Equipment grounding and bonding conductors count in the fill (Chapter 9 Note 3).
- The fill limit is 53 % for one conductor, 31 % for two and 40 % for three or more (Chapter 9 Table 1); a nipple of 24 in or less may be filled to 60 % (Note 4).
- The number of one wire size that fits uses Note 7: when the count has a decimal of 0.8 or more, the next whole number is allowed.
- Fill is one check among several: ampacity adjustment for more than three current-carrying conductors (310.15(C)(1)), pulling tension and jam ratio are not covered.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: the Steel Tube Institute worked example (3 × 12, 4 × 10 and 8 × 8 AWG THWN, 0.4171 in²) needs 1-1/4 in EMT, since the 40 % area of 1 in EMT is 0.346 in² and of 1-1/4 in is 0.598 in². Table 4 and 5 values cross-checked against published fill tables (1 in EMT 0.864 in², 1 in PVC 40 0.832 in², 1/0 THHN 0.1855 in², 300 kcmil 0.4608 in²).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- No trade size up to 4 in is large enough: split the conductors between two conduits or use larger conduit.
- More than three current-carrying conductors in one raceway: derate their ampacity per NEC 310.15(C)(1) (grounds and most neutrals are not counted).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Number of conductors: enter at least one conductor.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 3 × 12, 4 × 10 and 8 × 8 AWG THWN: 0.4171 in², too full for 1 in EMT (0.346 in² at 40 %), so 1-1/4 in EMT (0.598 in²)
  - Source: Steel Tube Institute, "NEC Conduit and EMT Fill Tables" worked example (NEC Chapter 9 Tables 1, 4 and 5)
- Same-size counts in EMT: 1/2 in holds 12 × 14, 9 × 12, 5 × 10 AWG; 3/4 in 22, 16, 10; 1 in 26 × 12 and 9 × 8 AWG
  - Source: NEC (2023) Annex C Table C.1 (EMT, THHN/THWN/THWN-2), which applies Chapter 9 Note 7
- Same-size counts in PVC Schedule 40: 1/2 in holds 8 × 12 AWG, 3/4 in 15, 1 in 25
  - Source: NEC (2023) Annex C Table C.11 (rigid PVC Schedule 40, THHN/THWN/THWN-2)
- Fill limits 53 %, 31 %, 40 % and 60 % for a nipple; table areas agree with π d²/4 of the listed diameters
  - Source: NEC Chapter 9 Table 1 and Note 4; Tables 4 and 5 (area and diameter columns)
- No conductors, a negative count and an unknown size are rejected; more than 3 conductors warns about derating
  - Source: Validation contract; NEC 310.15(C)(1)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 15, 0.4171 in², 48.3 %, 0.3456 in² to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

## Consolidation settlement calculator (clay layer)

<a id="consolidation-settlement"></a>

Folder `consolidation-settlement/` · Civil · Primary consolidation settlement of a normally or over-consolidated clay layer, and the time to reach a degree of consolidation by Terzaghi's theory.

### Assumptions and caveats

- One-dimensional consolidation: the clay is laterally confined, saturated and loaded over a wide area, and the stresses are those at the middle of the layer. Thick layers should be split into sublayers and the settlements added.
- Cc, Cr (also called Cs), e0 and the preconsolidation pressure come from an oedometer test (ASTM D2435) on undisturbed samples; the void ratio changes linearly with the logarithm of effective stress on each branch.
- The rate follows Terzaghi's theory with a constant c_v, an instantly applied load and a uniform initial excess pore pressure. Double drainage halves the drainage path.
- Immediate (elastic) settlement and secondary compression (creep) are not included; secondary compression can be significant in organic and soft clays.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 3 m clay layer with e0 0.9, Cc 0.30, Cr 0.05, σ'0 80 kPa, σ'p 120 kPa and Δσ 60 kPa settles 13.9 + 31.7 = 45.6 mm. With c_v 2 m²/year and double drainage, 90 % consolidation (T_v 0.848) takes 0.954 years. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A layer thicker than about 10 m should be divided into sublayers, each with its own mid-layer stresses, for an accurate settlement.
- The strain exceeds 20 %: small-strain consolidation theory overestimates the settlement; consider finite-strain methods.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Preconsolidation pressure: it is below the present effective stress, which would make the clay under-consolidated; enter σ\'p ≥ σ\'0 or choose normally consolidated.
- Recompression index Cr: it must not exceed the compression index Cc (Cr is usually 1/5 to 1/10 of Cc).

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Time factors: U 10 % → 0.008, 20 % → 0.031, 30 % → 0.071, 40 % → 0.126, 50 % → 0.197, 60 % → 0.287, 70 % → 0.403, 80 % → 0.567, 90 % → 0.848
  - Source: Das & Sobhan, Principles of Geotechnical Engineering, ch. 11: table of T_v against U from Terzaghi's solution
- Approximations: T_v = (π/4) U² below 60 % is exact to 1e-6 at U = 30 %; 1.781 − 0.933 log(100 − U%) is within 0.3 % at 90 %; the series inverts to itself
  - Source: Das & Sobhan, ch. 11 (approximations of Terzaghi's solution quoted there)
- Normally consolidated: 4 m, e0 1.1, Cc 0.36, 100 → 150 kPa: S = 0.36 × 4/2.1 × log 1.5 = 120.7 mm
  - Source: Hand calculation: S = Cc H/(1 + e0) log(σ'1/σ'0) (Das & Sobhan, ch. 11)
- Over-consolidated example: 3 m, e0 0.9, Cc 0.30, Cr 0.05, 80 → 140 kPa past σ'p 120 kPa: 13.90 + 31.71 = 45.6 mm; staying below σ'p uses Cr only
  - Source: Hand calculation: S = Cr H/(1 + e0) log(σ'p/σ'0) + Cc H/(1 + e0) log(σ'1/σ'p) (Das & Sobhan, ch. 11)
- Rate: c_v 2 m²/year, H_dr 1.5 m, t90 = 0.848 × 2.25/2 = 0.954 years; single drainage takes 4 times as long; 2 m²/year = 6.34 × 10⁻⁴ cm²/s
  - Source: T_v = c_v t / H_dr² (Terzaghi); unit conversion with the 365.25-day year
- σ'p below σ'0 and Cr above Cc are refused; a very thick layer warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 45.6 mm, 0.848, 0.954 year, 1.50 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Das, B.M. and Sobhan, K., Principles of Geotechnical Engineering, 9th ed., Cengage, ch. 11 Compressibility of Soil (settlement equations for normally and overconsolidated clay; Terzaghi time factor table and approximations)
- Terzaghi, K. (1925), Erdbaumechanik auf bodenphysikalischer Grundlage, Deuticke, Vienna (one-dimensional consolidation theory)
- ASTM D2435/D2435M, Standard Test Methods for One-Dimensional Consolidation Properties of Soils Using Incremental Loading

## Control valve Cv / Kv sizing

<a id="control-valve-cv"></a>

Folder `control-valve-cv/` · Thermal and fluids · Liquid control valve coefficient Kv and Cv to IEC 60534 with the choked-flow and cavitation check, valve opening and pipe velocity.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Turbulent, non-flashing liquid flow in a valve whose inlet and outlet pipes have the valve's nominal size (piping geometry factor F_P = 1 and no Reynolds correction F_R): Kv = Q √(ρ/ρ₀ / Δp) with Q in m³/h, Δp in bar and ρ₀ = 1 000 kg/m³ (IEC 60534-2-1 eq. 1), Cv = 1.156 Kv (US gpm and psi); reducers, laminar flow (viscous fluids, small valves) and two-phase flow need the full standard.
- Choked flow: above the limiting pressure drop Δp_max = F_L² (p₁ − F_F p_v) the flow no longer increases with Δp because the vena contracta pressure reaches the vapour pressure; the sizing pressure drop is the smaller of the actual Δp and Δp_max, with the liquid critical pressure ratio factor F_F = 0.96 − 0.28 √(p_v/p_c); F_L (liquid pressure recovery factor) is a valve-style property at full opening — typical values are offered, the manufacturer's value governs and it changes with opening.
- Cavitation (damage and noise) begins before choking; the page reports the ratio Δp/(p₁ − p_v) against F_L² and flags incipient cavitation when Δp exceeds about 70 % of the choked limit (the K_c / σ criteria of the manufacturers vary, 0.6–0.8 F_L²); the choked case is flagged separately because it also limits the flow.
- Valve opening is estimated as the ratio of the required to the rated coefficient, the usual rule being 60–80 % opening at maximum flow and not below 10–20 % at minimum flow; the inherent characteristic (linear, equal percentage) decides the actual stem position and is not modelled.
- Pipe velocity from the nominal pipe diameter entered, with the usual 3–4 m/s liquid limit at the valve outlet for noise and erosion; water properties at 20 °C by default (p_v 0.023 bar, p_c 221.2 bar).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 100 m³/h of water across 2 bar → Kv 70.7, Cv 81.7 (the textbook case); with p₁ 6 bar abs and F_L 0.9 the choked limit is 0.81 × (6 − 0.957 × 0.023) = 4.84 bar, so a 5.5 bar drop (p₂ 0.5 bar abs) is choked and the valve sizes to Kv 45.4 on Δp_max instead of 42.6 on the actual Δp — the direction of the correction manufacturers' sizing programs show.
- Design decision: the typical F_L table is offered because sizing starts before a valve is chosen; the page states that the manufacturer's F_L for the selected trim replaces it.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Choked flow: the pressure drop … bar exceeds Δp_max … bar — the flow cannot increase with a larger drop and the valve is sized on Δp_max; expect cavitation damage and noise unless anti-cavitation trim is used.
- Pressure drop above 70 % of the choked limit: incipient cavitation likely (σ margin small) — check the manufacturer's cavitation index for the trim.
- Pipe velocity … m/s above 4 m/s: erosion and noise risk at the valve outlet — consider a larger pipe.
- Density far from water: check that the fluid is a single-phase Newtonian liquid (viscous fluids need the Reynolds factor F_R).
- F_P = 1 (line-size valve) and turbulent flow assumed; reducers, viscous liquids, flashing (p₂ < p_v) and gas/steam service need the full IEC 60534-2-1 procedure.
- Typical F_L values: the manufacturer\'s value for the selected trim and opening governs the choked-flow limit.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Outlet pressure must be below the inlet pressure
- Vapour pressure at or above the inlet pressure: the liquid flashes at the inlet

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Basic sizing: 100 m³/h of water (ρ 998) across 2 bar → Kv = 100 √(0.998/2) = 70.64, Cv = 1.156 Kv = 81.7; opening 70.6 % of a Kv 100 valve → OK
  - Source: IEC 60534-2-1 eq. 1 (Kv = Q √(ρ/ρ₀/Δp)); Cv/Kv = 1.156
- Choked-flow limit: F_F = 0.96 − 0.28 √(0.023/221.2) = 0.9571; Δp_max = 0.9² × (6 − 0.9571 × 0.023) = 4.842 bar; the 2 bar drop is 41 % of it → non-cavitating
  - Source: IEC 60534-2-1 eqs. for F_F and Δp_max (choked flow)
- Choked case: p₂ 0.5 bar abs gives Δp 5.5 bar > 4.84 → sized on Δp_max: Kv = 100 √(0.998/4.842) = 45.4 (not 42.6 on the actual drop); maximum flow through a Kv 100 valve = 100 √(4.842/0.998) = 220 m³/h; warning
  - Source: IEC 60534-2-1 choked liquid flow; Fisher Control Valve Handbook ch. 5
- Valve styles and incipient cavitation: a butterfly at 90° (F_L 0.55) has Δp_max 0.55² × 5.978 = 1.81 bar, so the 2 bar drop is choked; a globe valve with p₂ 2.2 bar (Δp 3.8 = 78 % of Δp_max) is flagged as near cavitation
  - Source: Typical F_L values (Fisher handbook); 70 % incipient-cavitation rule
- Selection and velocity: a Kv 75 valve puts the duty at 94 % → UNDERSIZED; Kv 500 → 14 % OVERSIZED; no valve (0) gives guidance; 100 m³/h in a 100 mm pipe is 3.54 m/s, in 80 mm 5.5 m/s with a velocity warning
  - Source: Sizing practice (60–80 % at maximum flow); liquid velocity limits 3–4 m/s
- Validation: outlet pressure not below inlet, vapour pressure at the inlet pressure (flashing) and an unknown valve type are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract; flashing excluded
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.957, 4.84 bar, 70.6, 81.7, 71 %, 3.5 m/s, 220 m³/h to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IEC 60534-2-1:2011 Industrial-process control valves — Part 2-1: Flow capacity — Sizing equations for fluid flow under installed conditions (eqs. 1–7, F_F, F_L)
- ANSI/ISA-75.01.01-2012 Industrial-Process Control Valves — Part 2-1: Flow capacity — Sizing equations (identical to IEC 60534-2-1)
- Emerson Fisher, Control Valve Handbook, 5th ed., 2017 — ch. 5 liquid sizing, typical F_L values, cavitation
- IEC 60534-8-4 — prediction of noise generated by hydrodynamic flow (cavitation onset)

## Belt conveyor speed and capacity calculator

<a id="conveyor-belt"></a>

Folder `conveyor-belt/` · Manufacturing · Belt speed from pulley diameter and rpm, and the capacity in t/h of a flat or troughed belt from width, angles and bulk density (CEMA method).

### Assumptions and caveats

- Belt speed is the pulley circumference times its speed, measured at the pulley surface (include the lagging); belt slip and the belt thickness are neglected.
- The load lies on the belt width less the CEMA standard edge distance of 0.055 b + 0.9 in on each side, with a circular top surface meeting the belt edges at the surcharge angle, as in the CEMA standard cross-section.
- Troughed belts sit on three equal rolls; the gaps between the rolls are ignored. With the default centre roll of a third of the belt width the area is 2.5 to 3 % above the Precision Pulley & Idler table for 24 to 36 in belts at 20° surcharge (4.6 % at 0°); entering the real roll length (13 in for a 36 in belt) brings it within about 1 %.
- The surcharge angle is usually 5° to 15° less than the angle of repose of the material; capacity assumes the belt is evenly and fully loaded to that cross-section.
- Power is only the power to lift the load through the given height; belt, idler and skirt friction, accelerating the load and drive losses need the full CEMA or ISO 5048 method and are not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 36 in belt on 35° three-equal-roll idlers with 13 in rolls and a 20° surcharge carries 0.991 ft² (CEMA edge distance 2.88 in); at 100 fpm that is 5 946 ft³/h against 5 886 ft³/h in the Precision Pulley & Idler table (+1.0 %). Driven by a 24 in pulley at 100 rpm the belt runs 628.3 fpm and carries 1 694 t/h of 100 lb/ft³ material; lifting it 30 ft takes 42.2 kW. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The loaded width is no wider than the centre roll: the load sits on the centre roll only, as on a flat belt.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Centre roll length: it must be shorter than the belt width.
- Surcharge angle: a flat belt with no surcharge carries no load; enter the surcharge angle of the material.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 36 in belt, 35° three equal 13 in rolls, 20° surcharge: 5 946 ft³/h at 100 fpm against 5 886 in the PPI table (within 1.5 %); 0° surcharge 4 133 against 4 058
  - Source: Precision Pulley & Idler idler selection guide, Table 2 (35° troughed belt, 3 equal rolls, 100 fpm)
- Default rolls of b/3: 24 in 2 511 vs 2 438, 30 in 4 082 vs 3 975, 36 in 6 032 vs 5 886 ft³/h at 100 fpm (within 3.5 %, on the high side)
  - Source: Precision Pulley & Idler idler selection guide, Table 2
- CEMA edge distance 0.055 b + 0.9 in: 2.88 in for a 36 in belt (a published conveyor specifier sheet shows 2.9 in); a flat belt with 20° surcharge carries the circular segment only
  - Source: CEMA Belt Conveyors for Bulk Materials, standard edge distance; circular segment area R²(β − sin β cos β)
- Speed and capacity: a 24 in pulley at 100 rpm runs π × 2 ft × 100 = 628.3 fpm; 0.9909 ft² × 628.3 fpm × 100 lb/ft³ = 1 868 short tons/h; lifting 30 ft takes ṁ g H = 42.2 kW
  - Source: v = π D n; Q = A v ρ; P = Q g H (hand calculation)
- A flat belt with no surcharge, a centre roll as wide as the belt and zero pulley speed are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.991 ft², 628.3 ft/min, 1 694 t/h, 42.2 kW to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- CEMA, Belt Conveyors for Bulk Materials, 7th ed., Chapter 4 (standard edge distance 0.055 b + 0.9 in, standard cross-sectional area of the load on three equal roll idlers, eq. 4.15)
- Precision Pulley & Idler, Idler selection guide, Table 2: 35° troughed belt, 3 equal rolls, capacity at 100 fpm (36 in belt, 20° surcharge, 5 886 ft³/h); surcharge angle 5–15° below the angle of repose

## Course to steer with set and drift

<a id="course-to-steer"></a>

Folder `course-to-steer/` · Maritime · Course to steer, speed over ground and passage time to make good a track through a current of known set and drift, with leeway.

### Assumptions and caveats
