- Velocity triangle: the ground velocity is the vector sum of the ship's velocity through the water (speed S on the heading) and the current (drift D towards the set C); to make good the track T the heading is offset to windward of the current by δ with sin δ = D sin(C − T)/S, giving the course to steer CTS = T − δ and the speed over ground SOG = S cos δ + D cos(C − T); all directions true, set = direction the current flows TOWARDS (navigational convention, opposite to wind).
- The current is uniform along the leg and constant in time (a tidal stream is averaged over the passage or the leg is split); when the cross-track component of the current exceeds the ship speed the track cannot be made good and the page says so.
- Leeway is the angle the wind pushes the ship off its heading; it is applied after the current triangle by steering into the wind by the leeway angle entered (positive when the wind is on the starboard side, pushing the ship to port, so the correction adds to the course); 2–5° in strong beam winds for high-sided ships, under 1° for loaded tankers in moderate weather.
- Plane (flat-earth) triangle: exact for the leg lengths of coastal and tidal navigation (tens of miles); for ocean legs apply it to each great-circle or rhumb-line segment with its own current.
- The "if current ignored" result is the course and speed made good when the ship steers the track course without allowance — the classic set-and-drift problem in reverse.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: track 090° at 12 kn with a 2 kn current setting 180° (beam current from port) gives δ = asin(2/12) = 9.59°, course to steer 080.4°, SOG 11.83 kn and 10.14 h for 120 nmi; steering 090° without allowance makes good 099.5° at 12.17 kn; a head current (set 270°) gives SOG 10 kn with no heading change, a following one (set 090°) 14 kn — the textbook results.
- Design decision: set is the direction towards which the current flows, as on charts and in tidal atlases; the page states this in the label because wind directions follow the opposite convention and this is the usual source of error.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Cross current above half the ship speed: large heading offset and strong sensitivity to the current estimate — check the tidal data.
- Leeway above 5°: only light high-sided ships in strong beam winds; verify against the observed track.
- Leg longer than 100 nmi: the current is unlikely to be uniform; split the leg at the tidal-stream or current-chart boundaries.
- Set is the direction the current flows towards (chart convention); wind directions are the opposite — a common source of error.
- Uniform, steady current along the leg; tidal streams must be averaged over the hours of the passage.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Cross-track current … kn exceeds the ship speed … kn: the track cannot be made good
- Speed over ground is not positive: the current carries the ship backwards along the track

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Beam current: track 090° at 12 kn, current 2 kn setting 180° → cross 2 kn to starboard, δ = asin(2/12) = 9.59°, course to steer 080.4°, SOG 12 cos 9.59° = 11.83 kn, 120 nmi in 10.14 h
  - Source: Bowditch ch. 11, current triangle (course to steer and speed of advance)
- Head and following currents: set 270° (against the 090° track) gives SOG 10 kn with no heading change; set 090° gives 14 kn; a 45° quartering current from astern (set 045°) gives cross −1.414 kn and along +1.414 kn
  - Source: Vector addition along the track
- Without allowance: steering 090° at 12 kn in the 2 kn southerly current makes good 099.5° at 12.17 kn and ends 20 nmi off track after 120 nmi (10 h × 2 kn)
  - Source: Set-and-drift problem (Bowditch ch. 11)
- Leeway and wrap-around: +3° leeway adds to the course (080.4° → 083.4°); a track of 005° with a 2 kn current setting 090° (pushing to starboard) gives a course to steer of 355.4°, wrapped past north
  - Source: Leeway convention (steer into the wind); compass arithmetic
- Impossible and invalid cases: a 3 kn beam current against a 2 kn ship cannot make good the track; a head current faster than the ship gives no progress; zero distance is rejected
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 11.83 kn, 10.14 h, 12.17 kn, 20 nmi to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- The American Practical Navigator (Bowditch), NGA Pub. 9, 2019 edition, ch. 11 "Dead Reckoning" and ch. 10 — current triangle, set and drift, leeway
- Admiralty Manual of Navigation, BR 45, Vol. 1 — course to steer with tidal stream
- UK Hydrographic Office tidal stream atlases — set/rate conventions
- IMO Resolution A.893(21) Guidelines for voyage planning (allowance for currents and leeway)

## CPA and TCPA from radar plots

<a id="cpa-tcpa"></a>

Folder `cpa-tcpa/` · Maritime · Target course and speed, closest point of approach and its time, bow crossing, aspect and the alteration for a safe passing distance.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Relative-motion triangle: both ships hold course and speed between the plots and until the closest point of approach; the target's relative motion line is the straight line through the two plots, its true velocity is the relative velocity plus own ship's velocity, CPA is the perpendicular distance from own ship to that line and TCPA the time to reach the foot of the perpendicular.
- Bearings are true (gyro-stabilised, north-up plot) and own ship's course and speed are those used for the plot: course and speed through the water give the target's course and speed through the water, which is what the anti-collision rules and the target's aspect refer to; over the ground (GPS) they include the current. A radar plot taken over 3–6 minutes is the minimum; a single bearing and range give no motion at all.
- Bow crossing range is the distance ahead (+) or astern (−) of own ship at which the target crosses own ship's heading line; it is shown only when the crossing is still to come.
- The encounter type follows Rules 13–15 of COLREG for vessels in sight of one another and is indicative only: overtaking when coming up from more than 22.5° abaft the other vessel's beam, head-on for nearly reciprocal courses (within 6°) with the other vessel within 6° of the bow, crossing otherwise (target on the starboard side: own ship gives way). In restricted visibility Rule 19 applies instead and there is no stand-on vessel.
- The avoiding action is the smallest alteration of course to starboard at constant speed (0.5° steps up to 90°), or the smallest speed reduction at constant course (0.1 kn steps), that gives a CPA at least the chosen limit, assuming the target holds its course and speed and the change takes effect immediately; a real ship needs time and distance to turn or slow down, so act early and by a substantial, readily apparent change (Rules 8 and 16).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: a target plotted at 045° 8.0 nmi and six minutes later at 045° 7.0 nmi, with own ship on 000° at 12 kn, is on a collision course: relative motion 225° at 10 kn, CPA 0 in 42 minutes, target true course 304.9° at 8.62 kn; a stationary buoy dead ahead closing from 6.0 to 4.8 nmi in six minutes gives a target speed of zero.
- Design decision: the encounter type and avoiding action are aids for training and post-event analysis; the page says so in a runtime warning every time, because a plot from two noisy radar observations can be badly wrong in aspect.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The target is already inside the CPA limit (… nmi < … nmi): no alteration can restore it; take the action that best opens the range.
- No alteration to starboard of up to …° gives a CPA of … nmi at the present speed; combine a course change with a speed reduction.
- Even stopping does not give the CPA limit (the target itself is closing): alter course as well.
- CPA … nmi in … min — inside both limits: take early and substantial action (Rules 8 and 16).
- CPA … nmi is inside the … nmi limit, … min ahead: monitor and plan the avoiding action.
- Compass bearing not appreciably changing while the range closes: risk of collision exists (Rule 7(d)).
- Plot interval under 3 minutes: small bearing and range errors give large errors in the target\'s course and speed.
- The target crosses ahead at only … nmi.
- Indicative aid for training and analysis: the encounter type assumes vessels in sight of one another (Rules 13–17); in restricted visibility Rule 19 applies and there is no stand-on vessel.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Collision course: 045° 8.0 nmi then 045° 7.0 nmi six minutes later, own ship 000° at 12 kn → relative motion 225° at 10 kn, CPA 0 in 42 min, target 304.9° at 8.62 kn
  - Source: NGA Pub. 1310 relative-motion triangle: e·r·m with em = own velocity, rm = relative velocity, er = target velocity
- Stationary target: a buoy dead ahead closing from 6.0 to 4.8 nmi in 6 minutes at 12 kn has zero speed, CPA 0 and TCPA 24 minutes
  - Source: Relative motion of a fixed object equals the reciprocal of own ship's motion (Pub. 1310)
- Known course and speed give the same answer as the plots: target 304.88° at 8.619 kn from 045° 7 nmi; a passing case 10 nmi off on 050° with the target crossing at 270° 10 kn gives CPA = 10 sin 5° × √2 and TCPA from the projection
  - Source: Vector identity V_r = V_t − V_o; CPA = |P × V_r|/|V_r|, TCPA = −P·V_r/|V_r|²
- Encounter types: a faster target 2 nmi dead astern on the same course is overtaking (CPA 0 in 24 min at 5 kn closing); a reciprocal target dead ahead is head-on; a target on the port bow is a crossing where own ship stands on
  - Source: COLREG Rules 13, 14 and 15 (sector 22.5° abaft the beam = 112.5° from the bow)
- Avoiding action: from the collision course, the returned starboard alteration gives CPA ≥ 2 nmi while 0.5° less does not; the returned speed reduction does the same for speed
  - Source: Trial manoeuvre (IMO MSC.192(79) radar performance standard; Bole, Dineley & Wall ch. 8)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero range, negative speed, an unknown data mode and a zero plot interval
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 12 kn, 1.0 nmi to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Radar Navigation and Maneuvering Board Manual, NGA Pub. 1310, 9th ed. (2019) — relative motion, CPA and target true course and speed
- A. Bole, B. Dineley, A. Wall, Radar and ARPA Manual, 3rd ed., Butterworth-Heinemann 2013 — the plotting triangle, CPA/TCPA, aspect, trial manoeuvre
- Convention on the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972 (COLREG), Rules 7, 8, 13–17 and 19
- IMO Resolution MSC.192(79) Performance standards for radar equipment — CPA/TCPA limits and trial manoeuvre

## Culvert capacity and headwater calculator (HDS-5)

<a id="culvert-capacity"></a>

Folder `culvert-capacity/` · Civil · Headwater for a flow, or flow for an allowed headwater, in concrete pipe and box culverts by FHWA HDS-5 inlet and outlet control, with Manning full flow.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Single-barrel concrete culvert, circular pipe or rectangular box, with one of the HDS-5 inlet types listed; the inlet-control constants are those of HDS-5 Table A.1 for Form 1 and the entrance loss coefficients those of HDS-5 Table C.2.
- Inlet control uses the HDS-5 regression equations: unsubmerged up to Q/AD^0.5 = 3.5, submerged from 4.0 (ft and ft³/s), with straight-line interpolation between. Results are as good as the laboratory tests behind them, about ±10 %.
- Outlet control uses the HDS-5 full-barrel method with h_o = max(TW, (d_c + D)/2); it is accurate when the barrel flows full and approximate when it runs partly full. The higher of the two headwaters controls.
- Headwater is measured from the invert at the inlet. Approach velocity, debris blockage, skew and improved (tapered) inlets are not included.
- Manning's n for concrete culverts is 0.011 to 0.013 (Chow); 0.012 is a common design value. The full-flow Manning capacity is only a reference: a culvert's real capacity is set by the headwater.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 36 in concrete pipe with a square-edged headwall, 100 ft long on 1 %, n = 0.012, carrying 50 ft³/s with no tailwater: Q/AD^0.5 = 4.08, inlet control HW = 3 × (0.0398 × 4.08² + 0.67 − 0.005) = 3.99 ft; outlet control H = (1 + 0.5 + 0.612) × 0.778 = 1.64 ft, h_o = (2.30 + 3)/2 = 2.65 ft, HW = 1.64 + 2.65 − 1.00 = 3.29 ft; inlet control governs. Checked by hand.
- Check against the HDS-5 Chart 1 nomograph values tabulated by V. M. Ponce (SDSU online culvert tables): 36 in square edge, S = 0: HW/D 0.695 at 20 ft³/s, 1.12 at 40, 3.28 at 100; the equations agree within 2.5 % up to HW/D 3.3 and within 7 % at HW/D 3.9 (24 in, 40 ft³/s), where the nomograph is read off its scale.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Headwater more than three times the barrel height: far beyond usual design practice; check roadway overtopping and the embankment.
- Outlet control with headwater below 0.75 D: the barrel runs partly full and the HDS-5 approximation h_o = (d_c + D)/2 is rough; use a water-surface profile for a precise value.
- Barrel velocity above 15 ft/s (4.6 m/s): provide outlet protection against scour.
- Zero slope: no full-flow Manning capacity is given; inlet and outlet control headwaters are still valid.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Allowable headwater: … ft is below the headwater the culvert needs for even a trickle (tailwater … ft); raise it or lower the tailwater

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 36 in pipe, square edge with headwall, 50 ft³/s, S 1 %: Q/AD^0.5 = 4.084, submerged HW = 3 × (0.0398 × 4.084² + 0.67 − 0.005) = 3.99 ft
  - Source: HDS-5 Appendix A, eq. A.3 with Table A.1 constants c = 0.0398, Y = 0.67, Ks = −0.5 (hand calculation)
- Outlet control, same pipe: H = (1 + 0.5 + 29 × 0.012² × 100 / 0.75^1.33) V²/2g = 1.64 ft, h_o = (d_c + D)/2 = 2.65 ft, HW = 3.29 ft
  - Source: HDS-5 chapter 3 full-flow outlet control with ke = 0.5 (Table C.2, square-edged headwall) (hand calculation)
- HDS-5 Chart 1 (36 in, square edge, S 0): HW/D 0.695 at 20, 0.895 at 30, 1.12 at 40, 1.62 at 60, 2.33 at 80, 3.28 at 100 ft³/s, within 2.5 %
  - Source: FHWA HDS-5 Chart 1 nomograph values as tabulated by V. M. Ponce, SDSU online culvert tables (Table 1, square edge with headwall)
- Box critical depth d_c = (q²/g)^(1/3): 6 × 4 ft box at 200 ft³/s gives 3.26 ft; capacity mode inverts headwater mode
  - Source: Rectangular-section critical depth (Chow, ch. 3); consistency of the bisection
- A better inlet lowers the inlet-control headwater; high tailwater moves control to the outlet; impossible inputs are rejected
  - Source: HDS-5 Table A.1 (groove end c = 0.0292 < square edge 0.0398); behaviour specification; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 4.08, 3.99 ft, 3.29 ft, 7.07 ft/s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- FHWA, Hydraulic Design of Highway Culverts, HDS-5, 3rd ed. (FHWA-HIF-12-026, 2012), Appendix A: inlet control equations A.1 to A.3 and Table A.1 constants; Appendix C, Table C.2 entrance loss coefficients
- FHWA HDS-5, chapter 3: outlet control full-flow head loss H = [1 + ke + 29 n² L / R^1.33] V²/2g and the tailwater rule h_o = max(TW, (d_c + D)/2)
- V. T. Chow, Open-Channel Hydraulics (McGraw-Hill, 1959), Table 5-6: n for concrete culverts 0.010 to 0.013

## Decibel calculator (dB, dBm, dBV, dBu)

<a id="decibels"></a>

Folder `decibels/` · Electrical · Decibels from power or voltage ratios and back, dBm, dBW, dBV, dBµV and dBu converted to watts and volts, and the sum of several decibel levels.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Power ratios use 10 log10 and voltage or current ratios 20 log10; the 20 log form gives the power ratio only when both voltages act across the same impedance.
- Voltages are r.m.s. values. dBm and dBW are power levels; dBV, dBµV and dBu are voltage levels, converted to power with P = V² / R across the impedance entered (50 Ω for RF, 600 Ω for traditional audio lines, 75 Ω for video and cable TV).
- 0 dBu is 0.7746 V r.m.s., the voltage of 1 mW in 600 Ω; dBu is a voltage level and needs no 600 Ω load, so dBu equals dBm only across 600 Ω.
- Levels add as uncorrelated (incoherent) sources: their powers add, so two equal levels give 3 dB more. Coherent signals in phase add their voltages instead and can give up to 6 dB more.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 10 dBm is 10 mW, −20 dBW and 0.707 V in 50 Ω, which is −3.01 dBV, 117.0 dBµV and −0.79 dBu; 85, 82 and 79 dB add to 87.4 dB. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Only one level entered: the total is that level.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Levels, line …: "…" is not a number of decibels.
- Levels, line …: … dB is outside ±1 000 dB.
- Levels: enter at least one level in dB.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- A power ratio of 2 is 3.0103 dB, 10 is 10 dB; a voltage ratio of 2 is 6.0206 dB, 10 is 20 dB
  - Source: IEC 60027-3: L_P = 10 lg(P2/P1) dB, L_F = 20 lg(F2/F1) dB
- −6 dB is a power ratio of 0.2512 and a voltage ratio of 0.5012; 0 dB is 1
  - Source: Inverse of the definitions: 10^(dB/10), 10^(dB/20)
- 0 dBm in 50 Ω is 1 mW, −30 dBW, 0.2236 V, −13.01 dBV, 107.0 dBµV; 0 dBu in 600 Ω is 0.7746 V and 0 dBm
  - Source: ITU-R V.574-5 absolute levels; 0 dBu = √(1 mW × 600 Ω) = 0.7746 V
- Round trip: 1 V r.m.s. is 0 dBV and 120 dBµV, and 120 dBµV gives 1 V back
  - Source: dBV re 1 V, dBµV re 1 µV
- Incoherent sum: two equal levels add 3.01 dB, ten add 10 dB; 85 + 82 + 79 dB = 87.4 dB
  - Source: L = 10 lg Σ 10^(L_i/10) for uncorrelated sources
- Invalid entries are rejected: zero ratio, text in the levels, negative watts, zero impedance
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.0100 W, 0.707 V, −20.00, −3.01, 117.0, −0.79 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IEC 60027-3:2002 Letter symbols to be used in electrical technology, Part 3: Logarithmic and related quantities, and their units (power and root-power quantities, the decibel)
- ITU-R Recommendation V.574-5 (2015), Use of the decibel and the neper in telecommunications (absolute levels dBW, dBm, dB(µV))
- Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, 13th ed., ch. 21 (decibels: power gain 10 log, voltage gain 20 log, dBm referred to 1 mW in 600 Ω)

## Deflection limits calculator (L/360, L/240)

<a id="deflection-limits"></a>

Folder `deflection-limits/` · Structural · Allowable deflection of floors, roofs, walls and cantilevers (L/360, L/240, L/180) by IBC Table 1604.3 and Eurocode, checked against your deflection.

### Assumptions and caveats

- IBC Table 1604.3 limits apply to the deflection under each load named in its columns; the D + L column may use 0.5 D for dry wood (footnote d) and zero dead load for steel members (footnote g), and wind may be taken as 0.42 times the component and cladding loads (footnote f).
- For cantilevers the IBC uses l = twice the cantilever length (footnote i); the UK National Annex to EN 1993-1-1 gives length/180 directly, and EN 1995-1-1 has its own cantilever row.
- The UK National Annex limits for steel apply to characteristic variable actions only, without the permanent load. EN 1992-1-1 7.4.1 gives span/250 for the sag under quasi-permanent loads and span/500 for deflection after construction.
- EN 1995-1-1 Table 7.2 gives ranges; the national annex fixes the value. Choose the lenient or the strict end of each range.
- These are code serviceability limits. Vibration of floors, ponding of flat roofs and limits for glass or crane runways need separate checks.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 14 ft floor joist (IBC) may deflect 168/360 = 0.47 in under live load and 168/240 = 0.70 in under dead plus live; actual 0.35 in and 0.55 in use 75 % and 79 %. A 6 ft cantilever is checked over 12 ft. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- EN 1992-1-1 gives no separate cantilever rule; the span/250 and span/500 limits are applied to the cantilever length as entered.
- Horizontal limits: enter the column or storey height as the span and the sway as the deflection.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Cantilever?: the cantilever rule applies to roof and floor members; choose No for walls and partitions.
- Cantilever?: this member has no cantilever limit; choose No.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- IBC Table 1604.3: floor L/360 and D+L/240; roof with plaster ceiling 360/360/240, non-plaster 240/240/180, no ceiling 180/180/120; walls 360/240/120; farm 180, greenhouse 120
  - Source: IBC 2021 Table 1604.3 Deflection Limits
- Worked example: 14 ft floor joist, L/360 = 0.467 in and L/240 = 0.700 in; 0.35 in and 0.55 in use 75.0 % and 78.6 %, span/480
  - Source: Hand calculation: 14 × 12 = 168 in; 168/360, 168/240
- IBC cantilever: a 6 ft roof cantilever with no ceiling uses l = 12 ft, so L/180 = 0.80 in; walls cannot be cantilevers
  - Source: IBC Table 1604.3 footnote i: for cantilever members, l is twice the length of the cantilever
- UK NA steel: 8 m beam with brittle finish span/360 = 22.2 mm, other beam span/200 = 40 mm, 2 m cantilever length/180 = 11.1 mm
  - Source: NA to BS EN 1993-1-1, NA.2.23 (vertical deflections under variable actions)
- EN 1992: 6 m slab span/250 = 24 mm and span/500 = 12 mm; EN 1995: 4 m beam w_inst l/300 = 13.3 mm (lenient) or l/500 = 8 mm (strict), w_fin l/150 = 26.7 mm
  - Source: EN 1992-1-1 7.4.1(4), (5); EN 1995-1-1 Table 7.2
- A deflection over the limit fails; zero deflections are not checked; a negative deflection and an unknown member are refused
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.47 in, 0.70 in, 78.6 %, 480 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- International Building Code 2021, Table 1604.3 Deflection Limits and footnotes a to i (same values in IBC 2018)
- NA+A1:2014 to BS EN 1993-1-1:2005+A1:2014, clause NA.2.23 (vertical and horizontal deflection limits for buildings)
- EN 1992-1-1:2004, 7.4.1(4) and (5) (span/250 and span/500)
- EN 1995-1-1:2004+A1:2008, 7.2 and Table 7.2 (limiting values for deflections of beams)

## Density calculator (mass, volume and density)

<a id="density"></a>

Folder `density/` · Process · Density, mass or volume from the other two, with reference densities of water, solvents, fuels, gases, metals, timber, concrete and glass.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Density is mass divided by volume, ρ = m / V; the calculator solves for whichever of the three is missing.
- Library liquids are at 20 °C unless the label says otherwise, gases at 0 °C and 101.325 kPa; liquids lose about 0.02 % (water at 20 °C) to 0.1 % (solvents, fuels) of their density per kelvin of warming and gases change with pressure and temperature as in the ideal gas law.
- Fuel, timber and concrete densities are typical values within a range: petrol 720–775 and diesel 820–845 kg/m³ at 15 °C, timber at about 12 % moisture, concrete with normal aggregates; use a measured value for anything that matters.
- Specific gravity is the density divided by that of water at 4 °C (999.972 kg/m³).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 200 L of ethanol at 20 °C (789.3 kg/m³) has a mass of 157.9 kg and a specific gravity of 0.789; 1 m³ of carbon steel is 7 850 kg. Checked by hand.
- Library values checked against the CRC Handbook (organic liquids at 20 °C: ethanol 0.7893, methanol 0.7914, benzene 0.8765, toluene 0.8668, glycerol 1.2613 g/cm³; gas densities at 0 °C agree with M/22.414 L corrected for the second virial coefficient).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Gas densities are for 0 °C and 1 atm; at 20 °C they are 7 % lower, and they rise in proportion to the absolute pressure.
- The density is above that of osmium (22 590 kg/m³), the densest element: check the mass and volume units.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 200 L of ethanol at 20 °C (0.7893 g/cm³) has a mass of 157.86 kg and a specific gravity of 0.789
  - Source: CRC Handbook, density of ethanol at 20 °C; m = ρ V by hand
- Water at 4 °C is 62.43 lb/ft³ and at 20 °C 62.32 lb/ft³; carbon steel is 490 lb/ft³
  - Source: Standard US values (62.4 lb/ft³ for water, 490 lb/ft³ for steel, AISC Manual)
- Normal gas densities agree with M / 22.414 L/mol within the real-gas correction (under 0.7 %)
  - Source: Ideal molar volume 22.414 L/mol at 0 °C and 1 atm (CODATA); IUPAC 2021 molar masses
- Density from mass and volume: 7.85 kg in 1 L is 7 850 kg/m³; volume of 1 t of water at 20 °C is 1.0018 m³
  - Source: ρ = m / V and V = m / ρ by hand
- Gases warn about their reference state; zero volume, negative mass and an unknown material are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 157.9 kg, 0.789 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed., sections 3 (organic liquids), 4 (elements) and 6 (density of gases and of water)
- EN 1993-1-1:2005 §3.2.6 (steel 7 850 kg/m³); EN 10088-1:2014 (stainless steels); EN 338:2016 Tables 1 and 3 (timber mean densities)
- EN 228:2012 and EN 590:2013 (density limits of petrol and diesel at 15 °C); EN 572-1:2012 (soda-lime glass 2 500 kg/m³)

## Density altitude calculator

<a id="density-altitude"></a>

Folder `density-altitude/` · Automotive · Pressure altitude from field elevation and altimeter setting, and density altitude from temperature and dew point, with the ISA formula and the rule of thumb.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The atmosphere below the tropopause (36 089 ft, 11 km) follows the ICAO standard atmosphere: 15 °C and 1 013.25 hPa (29.92 inHg) at sea level, a lapse rate of 1.98 °C per 1 000 ft, dry-air gas constant 287.053 J/(kg·K).
- The altimeter setting is QNH: the station pressure reduced to sea level through the standard atmosphere, so the station pressure is recovered with the same relation; the small instrument-height correction of US weather stations is ignored.
- Pressure altitude is the standard-atmosphere height with the station pressure; density altitude is the standard-atmosphere height with the actual air density.
- Humidity lowers the density through the virtual temperature T_v = T / (1 − (e/p)(1 − 0.622)), with e the saturation vapour pressure at the dew point (Hyland–Wexler, as in ASHRAE).
- The rule of thumb DA ≈ PA + 120 ft × (OAT − ISA temperature) is shown for comparison; it ignores humidity and drifts from the exact value at high altitude and large temperature deviations.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: field 5 000 ft, altimeter 30.10 inHg, OAT 30 °C: station 25.04 inHg, pressure altitude 4 841 ft, ISA 5.4 °C, density altitude 7 608 ft dry; with a 15 °C dew point 7 855 ft; rule of thumb 7 792 ft. ICAO 10 000 ft: 696.8 hPa, −4.8 °C, σ 0.7385 reproduced. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Density altitude above 8 000 ft: expect much longer take-off runs and weak climb in normally aspirated aircraft; check the POH performance charts.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Dew point: it cannot be above the outside air temperature.
- Outside air temperature: the density altitude is above the tropopause (36 089 ft), beyond the troposphere formula.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Standard day at sea level (29.92 inHg, 15 °C): pressure and density altitude 0 ft, density 1.2250 kg/m³
  - Source: ICAO Doc 7488/3, sea-level values (101 325 Pa, 288.15 K, 1.2250 kg/m³)
- ISA at 10 000 ft: station pressure 696.82 hPa (20.58 inHg), σ = 0.73848, density altitude 10 000 ft
  - Source: ICAO Doc 7488/3 table at 3 048 m: 696.82 hPa, 268.34 K, σ 0.73848
- Field 1 165 ft, altimeter 30.10 inHg: pressure altitude 1 001 ft, matching the NWS formula (1 − (p/1013.25)^0.190284) × 145 366.45
  - Source: NOAA/NWS pressure altitude formula; FAA rule (29.92 − 30.10) × 1 000 + 1 165 = 985 ft for comparison
- Hot day: 5 000 ft, 30.10 inHg, 30 °C gives 7 608 ft; the 120 ft/°C rule gives 7 792 ft, within 3 %
  - Source: Hand calculation from the ISA relations; rule of thumb DA ≈ PA + 120 (OAT − ISA)
- A 15 °C dew point raises the virtual temperature to 32.3 °C and the density altitude to 7 855 ft
  - Source: T_v = T / (1 − (e/p)(1 − ε)), Wallace and Hobbs Section 3.1; e from Hyland–Wexler (shared psychrometrics)
- A dew point above the temperature and an altimeter setting of 25 inHg are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 25.04 inHg, 4 841 ft, 5.4 °C, 7 608 ft, 7 792 ft, 0.9746 kg/m³ to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ICAO Doc 7488/3, Manual of the ICAO Standard Atmosphere (extended to 80 km), 3rd ed. 1993 (troposphere relations and tables: 10 000 ft = 696.82 hPa, −4.81 °C, σ = 0.73848)
- FAA-P-8740-2, Density Altitude (FAA Aviation Safety Program, 2008): pressure altitude with the altimeter at 29.92 inHg; density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature
- J.M. Wallace and P.V. Hobbs, Atmospheric Science: An Introductory Survey, 2nd ed., Academic Press 2006, Section 3.1 (virtual temperature)

## Dew point calculator

<a id="dew-point"></a>

Folder `dew-point/` · HVAC · Dew point from temperature and relative humidity, or humidity from the dew point, with wet bulb, humidity ratio, absolute humidity and enthalpy.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Moist-air properties follow ASHRAE Fundamentals Chapter 1 with the Hyland–Wexler saturation pressure; below 0 °C the saturation is over ice, so the result is the frost point.
- Relative humidity is the ratio of the vapour pressure to the saturation pressure at the air temperature, as weather stations and hygrometers report it.
- The pressure sets the humidity ratio, wet bulb and density but not the dew point; enter the altitude or the local barometric pressure.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 20 °C at 50 % gives a dew point of 9.27 °C, wet bulb 13.8 °C and 7.26 g/kg at sea level, as read from the ASHRAE psychrometric chart.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The air is within 2.5 °C of its dew point: fog, condensation on cold surfaces and mould risk are likely.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Dew point: it cannot be above the air temperature (the air would be more than saturated).

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 20 °C and 50 % at sea level: dew point 9.27 °C, wet bulb 13.78 °C, 7.26 g/kg, 8.64 g/m³, 38.55 kJ/kg, 1.199 kg/m³
  - Source: ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals, Chapter 1 (psychrometric chart and eqs. 20, 26, 30, 33)
- Agrees with the Magnus formula (b = 17.625, c = 243.04 °C) within 0.1 °C at 30 °C / 70 % and 5 °C / 80 %
  - Source: Alduchov and Eskridge (1996), J. Appl. Meteor. 35, 601–609
- Reverse: 30 °C air with a 20 °C dew point is at 55.1 % relative humidity; a saturated sample has dew point = air temperature
  - Source: RH = p_ws(t_d) / p_ws(t), ASHRAE eq. (12) with (5)–(6)
- Altitude lowers the pressure: at 1 500 m the humidity ratio rises to 8.7 g/kg while the dew point stays 9.27 °C; below freezing the frost point is used
  - Source: ASHRAE eq. (3) standard pressure; eq. (5) over ice
- Comfort bands, near-saturation warning, and a dew point above the air temperature rejected
  - Source: US National Weather Service comfort levels; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 9.27 °C, 13.78 °C, 7.26 g/kg to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals (SI), Chapter 1 Psychrometrics
- US National Weather Service, "The Dew Point" (comfort levels by dew point), weather.gov
- Alduchov, O.A. and Eskridge, R.E. (1996), Improved Magnus form approximation of saturation vapor pressure, Journal of Applied Meteorology 35(4) (the common Magnus rule, used only in the article)

## Dilution calculator (C1V1 = C2V2 and serial dilution)

<a id="dilution"></a>

Folder `dilution/` · Process · Solve C1V1 = C2V2 for any one term, with the dilution factor, diluent volume and ratio, plus serial dilution steps and their concentrations.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The amount of solute is conserved: what is taken from the stock ends up in the final solution, so C1 V1 = C2 V2 in any consistent concentration unit (mol/L, mg/L, % w/v, cells/mL).
- V2 is the final volume after making up, not the volume of diluent added; the diluent is V2 − V1 when volumes are additive, which holds closely for dilute aqueous solutions but not for concentrated acids or alcohol and water.
- Mass-based concentrations (% w/w, mg/kg) dilute exactly by mass, not by volume; use masses in place of volumes for them, or convert with the densities.
- Serial dilution uses equal steps: each tube receives the transfer volume from the previous one and (f − 1) times that volume of diluent, mixed before the next transfer.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 500 mL of 1 M HCl from a 12 M stock needs 1 × 500 / 12 = 41.67 mL of stock and 458.3 mL of water, a dilution factor of 12 (1 : 11 stock to diluent). Checked by hand.
- Serial check: six 1 : 10 steps give a total factor of 10⁶; with 1 mL transfers each tube holds 1 mL of the previous one and 9 mL of diluent.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A dilution factor above 1 000 in one step needs a very small stock volume; a serial dilution is more accurate.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 500 mL of 1 M HCl from 12 M stock: 41.67 mL of stock, 458.3 mL of water, dilution factor 12 (1 : 11)
  - Source: Harris, Quantitative Chemical Analysis, ch. 1: M_conc V_conc = M_dil V_dil, by hand
- Each unknown in turn: 10 mL of 0.5 M made up to 250 mL is 0.02 M; 10 mL of 2 M to 0.1 M needs 200 mL; 0.02 M from 10 mL into 250 mL means 0.5 M stock
  - Source: C1V1 = C2V2 rearranged, by hand
- Serial: six 1 : 10 steps from 10⁸ cells/mL give a factor of 10⁶ and 100 cells/mL; 1 mL transfers need 9 mL of diluent per tube
  - Source: Serial dilution, DF_total = f^n (Skoog et al., ch. 4), by hand
- Two-fold series: 5 steps of 1 : 2 is a factor of 32; a one-step factor of 1 leaves the concentration unchanged with no diluent
  - Source: Limiting cases by hand
- A final concentration above the stock, a final volume below the stock volume and a fractional step count are rejected; a large one-step factor warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 41.67 mL, 458.3 mL, 12.0 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Harris, D.C., Quantitative Chemical Analysis, 9th ed., W.H. Freeman, ch. 1 (dilution formula M_conc V_conc = M_dil V_dil)
- Skoog, D.A., West, D.M., Holler, F.J. and Crouch, S.R., Fundamentals of Analytical Chemistry, 9th ed., ch. 4 (preparing solutions by dilution)

## Distillation stages calculator (Fenske–Underwood–Gilliland)

<a id="distillation-stages"></a>

Folder `distillation-stages/` · Process · Minimum stages (Fenske), minimum reflux (Underwood), theoretical stages at a reflux ratio (Gilliland, Molokanov) and feed stage (Kirkbride) of a binary column.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The mixture is binary with a constant relative volatility α of the light component to the heavy one; use the geometric mean of the top and bottom values. Constant molar overflow is assumed, so the method suits ideal and near-ideal mixtures and not azeotropes.
- Compositions are mole fractions of the light component: x_D in the distillate, x_B in the bottoms and z in the feed. The feed condition q is the fraction of the feed that is liquid: 1 for saturated liquid, 0 for saturated vapour, above 1 for subcooled liquid.
- Stage counts are theoretical (equilibrium) stages including a partial reboiler, with a total condenser not counted. Real trays = (N − 1) divided by the overall tray efficiency, rounded up.
- The Gilliland correlation (Molokanov form) is a fit to plate-to-plate results and is good for estimates: typically within about 7 % and occasionally 30 % (Wankat). Check the final design with a stage-by-stage or simulation calculation.
- The Kirkbride equation places the feed so that the rectifying and stripping sections have N_R and N_S stages; the feed stage is the first stage below N_R, counted from the top.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: α = 2.5, z = 0.5, x_D = 0.95, x_B = 0.05, saturated liquid feed, R = 1.3 R_min: N_min = 6.43, R_min = 1.10, R = 1.43, X = 0.136, Y = 0.518, N = 14.4 including the reboiler, N_R = N_S = 7.2, feed on stage 8. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- R/R_min below 1.05: the stage count rises steeply near minimum reflux and the Gilliland correlation is least reliable there.
- Relative volatility below 1.2: a very difficult separation; check α carefully, as N_min grows with 1/ln α.
- Feed condition q outside 0 to 1.5: a superheated vapour or strongly subcooled feed changes the internal flows; check the result with a stage-by-stage calculation.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Distillate mole fraction: the compositions must satisfy x_B < z < x_D for the light component.
- Feed condition q: with this feed condition the Underwood minimum reflux is not positive; check q and the compositions.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Fenske: benzene–toluene α = 2.4, x_D = 0.90, x_W = 0.10 needs n + 1 = 5.0 stages at total reflux
  - Source: Al-Mustaqbal University College, Mass transfer lecture (Fenske example: n + 1 = 5.0, 4 plates plus the reboiler)
- Underwood for a saturated liquid feed equals the constant-α closed form [x_D/z − α(1 − x_D)/(1 − z)]/(α − 1) = 1.10
  - Source: Seader, Henley & Roper, Ch. 9 (Underwood); McCabe–Thiele pinch at the feed composition for constant α
- Saturated vapour feed (q = 0): the pinch is at y = z, x = z/(α − (α − 1) z), so R_min = 2.10 for α = 2.5, z = 0.5, x_D = 0.95
  - Source: McCabe–Thiele construction with constant α (q-line horizontal through y = z); hand calculation
- Molokanov: Y = 0 at X = 1 (infinite reflux gives N = N_min), Y → 1 as X → 0; X = 0.1358 gives Y = 0.5185, N = 14.42
  - Source: Molokanov et al. (1972), Int. Chem. Eng. 12, 209; Seader, Henley & Roper Ch. 9; hand calculation
- Kirkbride: z = 0.4, x_D = 0.98, x_B = 0.02 gives B/D = 1.526 and N_R/N_S = (1.5 × 1 × 1.526)^0.206 = 1.186
  - Source: Kirkbride equation (Seader, Henley & Roper Ch. 9); hand calculation
- More reflux means fewer stages; real trays are (N − 1)/E rounded up; impossible compositions are rejected
  - Source: Gilliland correlation trend; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 6.43, 1.10, 1.43, 0.136, 0.518, 14.4, 7.2 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- J. D. Seader, E. J. Henley & D. K. Roper, Separation Process Principles, 3rd ed., Ch. 9 (Fenske eq., Underwood eqs., Gilliland correlation with the Molokanov equation, Kirkbride equation)
- P. C. Wankat, Separation Process Engineering, 5th ed., Ch. 7 Approximate shortcut methods for multicomponent distillation (Fenske, Underwood, Gilliland; accuracy of the Gilliland correlation)
- Y. K. Molokanov, T. P. Korablina, N. I. Mazurina & G. A. Nikiforov, An approximation method for calculating the basic parameters of multicomponent fractionation, Int. Chem. Eng. 12 (2), 209–212 (1972)

## Draft survey

<a id="draft-survey"></a>

Folder `draft-survey/` · Maritime · Six observed drafts to corrected drafts, quarter-mean draft, trim and density corrections, net displacement and cargo or constant from the hydrostatic tables.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Drafts are read at the marks and corrected to the perpendiculars with the apparent trim over the length between marks (LBM = LBP − distance of forward marks aft of FP − distance of aft marks forward of AP); the same ratio corrects midship marks that are not exactly at midships.
- The mean draft entered into the tables is the "mean of means" (quarter mean) (F + A + 6M)/8, which approximates the draft at the LCF including hog or sag; the hydrostatic values (displacement, TPC, LCF, MCTC) must be read from the ship's tables at that draft and entered by the user — the calculator has no tables of its own.
- First trim correction = trim(cm) × LCF(m) × TPC / LBP with LCF measured from midships, positive forward, and trim positive by the stern; the correction is positive when the LCF lies towards the deeper end.
- Second trim correction (Nemoto) = 50 × trim(m)² × (MCTC at +50 cm − MCTC at −50 cm) / LBP and is always added; it is small for trims below about 1 m.
- Density correction scales the displacement by the measured dock-water density over the table density (1.025 t/m³ unless the tables state otherwise); the hydrometer reading must be the true density in vacuo or in air as the tables assume, sampled at mid-draft on both sides.
- Deductibles (ballast, fresh water, fuel, diesel, lube oil, others) are entered as surveyed masses; the calculator does not sound tanks or apply free-surface or trim corrections to tank tables.
- Cargo = corrected displacement − deductibles − lightship − constant; at a light-ship (initial) survey with no cargo the same output gives the vessel constant. Heel, hog/sag beyond the quarter mean, and draft-mark reading error (±1 cm ≈ ±TPC tonnes each) are not corrected.
- The result is an estimate for commercial draft surveys with a typical accuracy of ±0.5 % of cargo under good conditions; it is not a substitute for the surveyor's judgement of sea state, list and reading conditions.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Design decision: sign conventions follow surveying practice — trim positive by the stern, LCF from midships positive forward, mark distances positive inboard of the perpendiculars; the first trim correction is coded as −trim × LCF × TPC / LBP so that LCF aft with stern trim gives a positive correction, as the UN ECE code requires.
- Verification 2026-10-30: mark corrections, quarter mean, both trim corrections and the density correction were checked by hand on a 180 m example (FTC +91.2 t, STC +6.2 t, 47 329 → 47 099 t at 1.020).
- Design decision: no hydrostatic tables are embedded; the user enters the ship's values at the quarter-mean draft, which keeps the calculator ship-independent and avoids a false sense of precision.
- Design decision: the same output serves both surveys — with constant = 0 and no cargo it returns the constant; with the constant entered it returns the cargo.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Port/starboard draft difference up to … cm: the ship is listing; the midship mean only approximates the displacement and the survey accuracy degrades.
- Trim exceeds 1 % of LBP: the trim corrections are large and the tables\' LCF/MCTC should be read at the actual trimmed waterline where available.
- Hog/sag of … cm: the quarter-mean draft only approximates the deflected hull; large deflection adds uncertainty.
- Negative cargo: check the constant, lightship and deductibles — at an initial survey enter constant = 0 to obtain the constant itself.
- MCTC at the deeper draft is lower than at the shallower draft, which is unusual — check the two MCTC values.
- A 1 cm error in the quarter-mean draft moves the result by about … t; read both sides at the same moment and average several wave cycles.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Length between marks must be positive — check the mark distances against LBP

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Even keel, no mark offsets, dock water 1.025: no corrections; cargo = 47 232 − 1 000 − 10 000 − 300 = 35 932 t
  - Source: UN ECE Code (1992) survey sequence: displacement − deductibles − lightship − constant = cargo
- Mark corrections: F 9.50 / A 10.50 at marks 3 m aft of FP and 6 m fwd of AP (LBM 171 m): FP 9.4825, AP 10.5351, true trim 1.0526 m
  - Source: UN ECE Code (1992) §: draft correction = distance to perpendicular × apparent trim / LBM; Isbester, Bulk Carrier Practice, "Draught surveys"
- Midship marks 2 m aft of midships with 1 m apparent trim over 171 m move the midship draft by −1.17 cm
  - Source: Same proportional correction applied to the midship marks (Dibble & Mitchell, Draught Surveys, 2009)
- First trim correction: 100 cm by the stern with LCF 3 m aft of midships and TPC 50 on 180 m = +83.3 t; LCF 3 m forward gives −83.3 t
  - Source: UN ECE Code (1992): FTC = trim × LCF × TPC / LBP, positive when LCF is on the side of the deeper draft
- Second trim correction (Nemoto): 1.0 m trim, MCTC 460/440 on 180 m = 50 × 1² × 20 / 180 = 5.56 t, always positive; 0.5 m trim gives a quarter of it
  - Source: UN ECE Code (1992) second trim correction 50 × trim² × (MCTC₊ − MCTC₋) / LBP
- Density correction: 47 232 t from tables in 1.025 floating in 1.010 → 46 540.8 t
  - Source: UN ECE Code (1992): displacement × ρ_dock / ρ_table
- Hog/sag: F 9.90, A 10.10, M 10.05 → sag +5 cm; quarter mean 10.0375 m (M weighted 6/8)
  - Source: Mean-of-means (quarter mean) definition (F + A + 6M)/8, UN ECE Code (1992)
- Default survey (trim 1.05 m by stern, LCF 3 m aft, dock 1.020): FTC +91.2 t, STC +6.2 t, displacement 47 329.4 × 1.020/1.025 = 47 098.5 t, cargo 33 288.5 t
  - Source: Hand calculation with the formulas above
- Warnings: 15 cm list, negative cargo and inverted MCTC values are flagged
  - Source: Survey good-practice notes (Dibble & Mitchell 2009)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: marks outside the hull (LBM ≤ 0), negative draft, zero TPC
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.00 m, 9.482 m, 10.535 m, 1.053 m, 2.1 cm, 10.025 m, 91.2 t, 6.2 t to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- UN ECE, Code of Uniform Standards and Procedures for the Performance of Draught Surveys of Coal Cargoes (ECE/ENERGY/19, 1992)
- J. Isbester, Bulk Carrier Practice (Nautical Institute, 2nd ed. 2010), ch. "Draught surveys"
- W.J. Dibble & P. Mitchell, Draught Surveys — A Guide to Good Practice (North of England P&I Club, 2009)
- Barrass & Derrett, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed. (2012), trim and TPC chapters

## Drag and lift force calculator

<a id="drag-lift"></a>

Folder `drag-lift/` · Automotive · Aerodynamic drag or lift force from ½ρv²CA, the power to overcome drag, and air density from altitude and temperature, with typical Cd values.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The force is F = ½ ρ v² C A with the coefficient referred to the area given: the frontal area for drag coefficients of cars, cyclists and bluff bodies, the wing planform area for lift coefficients.
- The coefficient is taken as constant; real coefficients change with Reynolds number (a sphere drops from 0.47 to about 0.2 when its boundary layer turns turbulent), yaw angle and, near Mach 0.3 and above, compressibility.
- The speed is the air speed relative to the body: for a car or cyclist in still air it is the road speed; add a head wind, subtract a tail wind.
- Air density comes from the standard-atmosphere pressure at the altitude and the actual temperature for dry air, or can be entered directly; humidity lowers it slightly (saturated air at 30 °C is 1.6 % lighter than dry air).
- The power is the drag force times the speed; the engine or rider must also supply rolling resistance and drivetrain losses, which are not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: Cd 0.30, 24 ft² frontal area, 70 mph at sea level and 59 °F: ρ 1.225 kg/m³, q 12.53 psf, drag 90.2 lbf, 16.84 hp to overcome it. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above about Mach 0.3 (230 mph) compressibility changes the coefficients; use data measured at that speed.
- A lift coefficient above 2.5 is beyond most wings even with full flaps; check the value.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Car, Cd 0.30 on 24 ft², 70 mph at sea level and 15 °C: q 599.8 Pa, drag 401.2 N (90.2 lbf), 16.84 hp
  - Source: Hand calculation, F = ½ ρ v² Cd A with ρ = 1.2250 kg/m³ (ISA sea level)
- Drag power grows with the cube of speed: twice the speed needs eight times the power
  - Source: P = ½ ρ v³ Cd A
- Racing cyclist, Cd 0.88 on 0.36 m², at 10 m/s in 1.225 kg/m³ air: 19.40 N and 194 W
  - Source: Munson, Young and Okiishi, typical drag coefficients (racing bicycle 0.88 on 0.36 m²); hand calculation
- Lift: CL 0.3 on a 16.2 m² wing at 60 m/s in 1.225 kg/m³ air is 10 716 N; no drag power for lift
  - Source: L = ½ ρ v² CL S
- At 5 280 ft and 30 °C the density is 0.9588 kg/m³ and the drag 21.7 % lower than the sea-level standard
  - Source: ASHRAE standard pressure p = 101 325 (1 − 2.25577e−5 Z)^5.2559 and ρ = p / (287.042 T)
- A zero area, a negative coefficient and an unknown body are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.225 kg/m³, 12.53 psf, 90.2 lbf, 16.84 hp to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- S.F. Hoerner, Fluid-Dynamic Drag, published by the author, 1965, Chapter 3 (flat plates and discs normal to the flow, C_D ≈ 1.17; sphere 0.47 subcritical)
- Y.A. Çengel and J.M. Cimbala, Fluid Mechanics: Fundamentals and Applications, 4th ed., McGraw-Hill 2018, Table 11-2 (passenger car C_D ≈ 0.3)
- B.R. Munson, D.F. Young and T.H. Okiishi, Fundamentals of Fluid Mechanics, Wiley, figure of typical drag coefficients (bicycle upright 1.1 on 0.5 m², racing 0.88 on 0.36 m²)
- ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals, Chapter 1, eq. (3) standard atmospheric pressure, via the shared psychrometric module

## Drain pipe size calculator (Manning)

<a id="drain-pipe-size"></a>

Folder `drain-pipe-size/` · Civil · Gravity drain and sewer pipe sizing by Manning: full-flow capacity and velocity, smallest standard diameter for a flow, flow depth and self-cleansing check.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Steady, uniform gravity flow in a straight circular pipe of constant slope; the hydraulic gradient equals the pipe slope. Surcharged pipes, backwater from a downstream pipe and losses at manholes and bends are not included.
- Manning's n is a property of the pipe surface in service: smooth PVC tests near 0.009, but many agencies require 0.013 for every material to allow for joints, slime and deposits.
- The nominal size is taken as the inside diameter. PVC sewer pipe and some plastic pipes have a slightly smaller bore, so enter the actual inside diameter for a close check.
- The self-cleansing check uses the Ten States Standards rule of at least 2.0 ft/s (0.61 m/s) with the pipe flowing full; at low flows the actual velocity is lower, so check the partial-flow velocity too.
- This page sizes the pipe hydraulically. Building drains are sized by plumbing-code drainage fixture unit tables, which are not reproduced here.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: an 8 in pipe at 0.40 % with n = 0.013 carries 0.764 ft³/s (343 US gpm) at 2.19 ft/s flowing full, meeting the Ten States 2 ft/s rule that sets 0.40 % as the minimum slope for 8 in. A design flow of 150 gpm runs 0.46 of the diameter deep at 2.12 ft/s; 6 in is the smallest US size that carries it full. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The design flow exceeds the free-surface capacity of this pipe: it would run surcharged under pressure; choose a larger pipe or a steeper slope.
- Design flow deeper than 75 % of the diameter: many sewer standards limit the depth to 50 to 75 % to leave room for ventilation and peaks.
- Velocity flowing full above 10 ft/s (3 m/s): check the pipe for abrasion and anchor it on steep slopes.
- Public gravity sewers are usually at least 8 in (200 mm); smaller sizes are building drains and laterals sized by the plumbing code.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 8 in at 0.40 %, n 0.013: 0.764 ft³/s (343 US gpm) at 2.19 ft/s flowing full
  - Source: Hand calculation, US Manning: Q = 1.486/0.013 × 0.3491 ft² × (0.1667)^(2/3) × 0.004^0.5 = 0.764 ft³/s
- Ten States §33.41 minimum slopes give at least 2.0 ft/s flowing full with n 0.013: 8 in 0.40 %, 10 in 0.28 %, 12 in 0.22 %, 15 in 0.15 %
  - Source: Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (2014), §33.41 table of minimum slopes
- Partial flow: half the full flow runs at y/D = 0.500 with the full-pipe velocity; 150 gpm in 8 in at 0.40 % is 0.46 deep at 2.12 ft/s
  - Source: Circular section geometry: at half depth R = D/4, so V equals the full-pipe value and Q is half (Chow, partially full circular sections)
- Smallest standard size: 150 gpm at 0.40 % needs 6 in (n 0.013); 2 ft³/s needs 12 in; DN series gives 150 mm for 150 gpm
  - Source: Full-flow Manning capacities: 6 in 159 gpm, 10 in 1.39 ft³/s, 12 in 2.26 ft³/s at 0.40 %
- PVC n 0.009 carries 13/9 of the concrete flow; a flow beyond the free-surface capacity gives no depth; bad inputs are rejected
  - Source: Manning: Q ∝ 1/n; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 343 US gpm, 2.19 ft/s, 0.46, 2.12 ft/s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Great Lakes–Upper Mississippi River Board (Ten States Standards), Recommended Standards for Wastewater Facilities (2014), §33.41 minimum slopes for 2.0 ft/s flowing full with n = 0.013
- Uni-Bell PVC Pipe Association, Manning's n for PVC gravity sewer pipe (n = 0.009 for design), and Handbook of PVC Pipe Design and Construction, 5th ed.
- V. T. Chow, Open-Channel Hydraulics (McGraw-Hill, 1959), ch. 5 and 6: Manning formula, Table 5-6 roughness, partially full circular sections

## Drill point length calculator

<a id="drill-point-length"></a>

Folder `drill-point-length/` · Manufacturing · Length of a drill point from diameter and point angle (118°, 135°, 140°), and the depth to drill for a full-diameter blind hole or a through hole.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The point is a sharp cone with the included point angle of the drill; the chisel edge, thinning and corner chamfers change its length by a small amount.
- For a blind hole the full-diameter depth is the depth on the drawing; the drill tip goes one point length deeper, and the cone at the bottom stays in the part.
- For a through hole the whole point must leave the part, plus a breakthrough allowance so that the corners clear the exit edge.
- Flat-bottom (180°) drills have no point; point angles of 60° to 180° are accepted.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 1/2 in drill with a 118° point has a point length of 0.25 / tan 59° = 0.1502 in (0.3004 D); to drill 1 in at full diameter the tip goes to 1.1502 in. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The hole is deeper than 10 diameters: check chip evacuation; peck drilling or a deep-hole drill may be needed.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Material thickness: enter the thickness of the part for a through hole.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Haas: point length 0.30043 D at 118° and 0.207 D at 135°; 140° gives 0.1820 D
  - Source: Haas Automation, Working out drill depth; L = (D/2) / tan(θ/2)
- Blind hole: 1/2 in drill at 118°, 1 in full depth: point 0.1502 in, drill to 1.1502 in
  - Source: Tip depth = depth + point length (hand calculation)
- Metric Haas example basis: a 12 mm drill at 135° adds 0.207 × 12 = 2.485 mm; through 10 mm plate with 1 mm breakthrough travels 13.485 mm
  - Source: Haas Automation 135° multiplier (hand calculation)
- Limiting cases: a 180° (flat) drill has no point; a 90° point is half the diameter; the table lists six angles
  - Source: Cone geometry
- A point angle below 60°, zero thickness for a through hole and zero diameter are rejected; a hole over 10 D warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.1502 in, 0.3004, 1.1502 in to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Haas Automation (UK), Working out drill depth: tip length 0.3 × D for a 118° point and 0.207 × D for 135°, added to the full-diameter depth
- Machinery's Handbook Pocket Companion (Industrial Press), Drilling and reaming: typical point angles, 118° for general work

## Dry-docking critical instant

<a id="drydock-critical-instant"></a>

Folder `drydock-critical-instant/` · Maritime · Upthrust on the keel blocks and the virtual loss of GM at the critical instant of dry-docking, the draft then, and the largest safe trim.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The ship enters the dock trimmed by the stern; as the water falls the after end of the keel lands on the blocks first and the upthrust P there grows until the keel touches along its whole length (the critical instant). Up to that moment the ship trims about its LCF and the trim removed equals P·l/MCTC, so P = MCTC × trim (cm) / l with l the distance from the point of contact to the LCF.
- The upthrust acts at the keel and reduces stability exactly like a weight removed from the keel: method 1 treats it as lost buoyancy at the keel with W unchanged (loss = P·KM/W), method 2 as a weight removed at the keel with KM taken at the reduced displacement (loss = P·KG/(W − P), the KM at the critical-instant draft can be entered); both are standard and differ slightly — the smaller GM governs.
- The free-surface correction of slack tanks is included in the initial GM (FSM/W in method 1, FSM/(W − P) in method 2); hydrostatic values (MCTC, TPC, LCF, KM) are those at the draft before docking and are taken as constant during the small change of draft.
- Side blocks and shores take load only after the critical instant; until then the ship must have positive GM on its own. The required GM at the critical instant is set by the dock master and the docking plan.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: W = 6000 t trimmed 30 cm by the stern with MCTC 90 t·m/cm and the LCF 45 m from the point of contact gives P = 90 × 30 / 45 = 60 t; with KM 7.5 m and KG 6.0 m the loss of GM is 60 × 7.5 / 6000 = 0.075 m by method 1 and 60 × 6.0 / 5940 = 0.0606 m by method 2.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Slack tanks reduce GM throughout docking: press up or empty tanks where possible.
- Trim over 1.5 m: large upthrust on the after blocks; check the block loading with the dock master.
- Hydrostatics at the pre-docking draft are taken as constant; the docking plan and the dock master\'s requirements govern.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The ship is trimmed by the head: it would land forward first; this calculator is for docking trimmed by the stern
- The point of contact must be aft of the LCF
- The upthrust would exceed the displacement: check the trim, MCTC and lever

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Upthrust: 6000 t trimmed 30 cm by the stern, MCTC 90 t·m/cm, contact 45 m aft of the LCF → P = 90 × 30 / 45 = 60 t
  - Source: Barrass & Derrett, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, "Drydocking and grounding": P = MCTC × t / l
- Loss of GM: method 1 P·KM/W = 60 × 7.5/6000 = 0.075 m (GM 1.425 m); method 2 P·KG/(W − P) = 60 × 6.0/5940 = 0.0606 m (GM 1.4394 m)
  - Source: Barrass & Derrett: the two methods for the virtual loss of GM at the critical instant
- Draft at the critical instant: draft at the LCF 4.45 − 0.30 × 45/120 = 4.3375 m, less the bodily rise 60 t / 15 t/cm = 4 cm → 4.2975 m even keel
  - Source: Trim about the LCF and parallel rise P/TPC
- Trim limit and free surface: the largest trim for GM 0.15 m is P_max·l/MCTC with P_max = W(GM − 0.15)/KM = 1080 t → 540 cm; 300 t·m of free surface lowers both GMs and the limit
  - Source: Method 1 solved for the trim; free-surface correction FSM/W
- Unsafe case: a tender ship (KG 7.4 m, GM 0.10 m) trimmed 1.5 m by the stern loses its GM before the critical instant and is reported unsafe
  - Source: Critical-instant stability requirement (positive GM until the keel lands)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: trimmed by the head, contact point forward of the LCF, zero MCTC
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 30 cm, 60 t, 1.50 m, 0.075 m, 1.425 m, 0.061 m, 1.439 m, 4.30 m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- C. B. Barrass, D. R. Derrett, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed., Butterworth-Heinemann 2012 — chapter "Drydocking and grounding" (upthrust, critical instant, both methods)
- Rawson & Tupper, Basic Ship Theory, 5th ed., ch. 4 (stability during docking)
- US Navy Naval Ships' Technical Manual (NSTM) chapter 997 Docking instructions — docking stability

## Duct size calculator

<a id="duct-size"></a>

Folder `duct-size/` · HVAC · Round and rectangular duct size for an airflow by friction rate or velocity, with the velocity, pressure loss per 100 ft or per metre, and standard sizes.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Friction follows Darcy–Weisbach with the Colebrook friction factor, the method of ASHRAE Fundamentals Chapter 21, for standard air at 20 °C (1.204 kg/m³); a duct friction chart (ductulator) gives the same results within its reading accuracy.
- The default roughness 0.09 mm is galvanized steel with joints every 1.2 m (ASHRAE "medium smooth"); flexible duct is much rougher and needs a larger size, especially when not fully stretched.
- The rectangular duct has the same friction loss as the round size at the same airflow (Huebscher equivalent diameter); keep the aspect ratio below about 4 : 1.
- Only straight-duct friction is sized here; fittings add losses that the system design must include. The equal-friction rate 0.08 to 0.1 in. w.c. per 100 ft (0.65 to 0.8 Pa/m) is common for residential and low-pressure supply ducts.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: at 0.10 in. w.c. per 100 ft the calculator gives 5.8 in for 100 cfm, 9.7 in for 400 cfm, 13.65 in for 1 000 cfm and 17.7 in for 2 000 cfm, matching readings of the ASHRAE friction chart for galvanized duct (6, 10, 14 and 18 in standard sizes).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The fixed side is too small to reach this size at any reasonable width; enter a larger fixed side.
- Aspect ratio above 4 : 1: friction, noise and material rise; choose a squarer duct.
- Velocity above 1 000 ft/min (5 m/s): fine for mains, but branches and runouts in homes are usually kept below 600–900 ft/min to limit noise.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 1 000 cfm at 0.10 in. w.c./100 ft: 13.65 in round at 983 ft/min, next standard 14 in (400 mm); the friction at that size is the target
  - Source: ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 21, Darcy–Weisbach and Colebrook, galvanized ε = 0.09 mm, standard air
- Friction chart readings at 0.1 in./100 ft: 100 cfm → 6 in, 400 cfm → 10 in, 2 000 cfm → 18 in standard round
  - Source: ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 21 Fig. 10 (friction chart, galvanized round duct), read to the next standard size
- Colebrook agrees with the explicit Haaland formula within 1.5 % at Re 1e5 and ε/D 1e-4; laminar flow gives 64/Re
  - Source: Haaland (1983), J. Fluids Eng. 105(1): 1/√f = −1.8 log[(ε/D/3.7)^1.11 + 6.9/Re]
- Velocity method: 1 000 cfm at 900 ft/min needs 14.27 in; Huebscher 12 × 12 in = 13.1 in round and the inverse returns 12 in
  - Source: A = Q / V; ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 21 eq. (25) and Table 2 (12 × 12 in → 13.1 in)
- A fixed side too small warns; an extreme aspect ratio warns; zero airflow and unknown methods are rejected
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 13.65 in, 983 ft/min to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals (SI), Chapter 21 Duct Design: eqs. (18) Darcy–Weisbach, (19) Colebrook, (25) Huebscher equivalent diameter; Table 1 duct roughness
- EN 1506:2007 Ventilation for buildings — Sheet metal air ducts with circular cross-section (nominal diameters)

## Earthwork cut and fill volumes

<a id="earthwork-volume"></a>

Folder `earthwork-volume/` · Civil · Volumes by the average end area and prismoidal methods from cross-sections, with swell, shrinkage and haul mass.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Volume between two parallel cross-sections of areas A₁ and A₂ a distance L apart: average end area V = L (A₁ + A₂)/2, exact for prismoids with linearly varying area and over-estimating when the sections differ greatly (up to 25 % for a pyramid); prismoidal formula V = L (A₁ + 4 A_m + A₂)/6 with the true mid-section area A_m, exact for any prismoid — when A_m is not measured it is estimated from the mean of the linear dimensions, A_m ≈ ((√A₁ + √A₂)/2)², which is exact for similar sections.
- The section areas are net cut or fill areas from the cross-sections (ground minus design); cut and fill between the same stations are handled as two separate calculations; curved alignments need the curvature correction (Pappus) which is not applied.
- Earth states: bank (in place) volume is what the cross-sections give; excavated material swells to the loose volume hauled in trucks, V_loose = V_bank (1 + swell); placed and compacted fill occupies V_compacted = V_bank (1 − shrinkage) — blasted rock bulks instead of shrinking (negative shrinkage); typical factors (sand 12 %, loam 25 %/10 %, clay 33 %/10 %, topsoil 25 %/15 %, rock 50 %/−30 %) vary by ±30 % and should be replaced by project test data.
- Fill required: the compacted fill volume needed divided by (1 − shrinkage) gives the bank volume to excavate, and ×(1 + swell) the loose volume to haul; truck loads = loose volume / truck capacity (struck or heaped as entered); mass from the bank density (loose density = bank density/(1 + swell)).
- No allowance for topsoil stripping, over-excavation, unsuitable material, settlement of the foundation or compaction testing; quantities are for estimating and mass-haul planning, not for payment unless the contract uses these methods.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: the published example A₁ 150.25 m², A_m 201.375 m², A₂ 259.375 m², L 20 m gives 4 050.42 m³ by the prismoidal formula and 4 096.25 m³ by the average end area, as tabulated in the earthworks lecture notes; the clay factors (swell 33 %, shrink to 90 %) match the quoted reference values.
- Design decision: the mid-section area may be entered or estimated; the estimate is flagged in the output so a surveyed A_m is preferred for payment quantities.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Mid-section area estimated from A₁ and A₂ assuming similar sections; survey the mid-section for payment quantities.
- End areas differ by a factor …: the average end area over-estimates (correction … %); use the prismoidal volume or shorter intervals.
- Typical factors for … (swell … %, shrinkage … %): project test data vary by ±30 %.
- Negative shrinkage: blasted rock bulks when placed and never returns to bank volume.
- Cut and fill between the same stations are separate calculations; curved alignments need the curvature (Pappus) correction; topsoil strip, over-break and unsuitable material are extra.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Both cross-section areas are zero

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Published example: A₁ 150.25, A_m 201.375, A₂ 259.375 m², L 20 m → prismoidal 4 050.42 m³, average end area 4 096.25 m³, correction 45.8 m³ (1.1 %)
  - Source: Earthworks lecture notes (Scribd "Earthworks" ch. 5) worked example: V_p = 4 050.42 m³, V_AEA = 4 096.25 m³
- Mid-area estimate for similar sections ((√A₁ + √A₂)/2)² = 201.11 m² (measured 201.375) → 4 046.9 m³, within 0.1 % of the measured-mid result; exact for a pyramid: A₁ 100, A₂ 0 → estimate 25, prismoidal 333.3 vs AEA 500 (the classic 50 % over-estimate)
  - Source: Prismoidal formula exactness for prismoids; pyramid volume L A/3
- Cut in clay (swell 33 %, shrinkage 10 %): 4 050 m³ bank → 5 387 m³ loose, 3 645 m³ compacted, 7 291 t at 1 800 kg/m³, loose density 1 353 kg/m³, 449 truck loads of 12 m³
  - Source: Bank/loose/compacted relations (Peurifoy & Schexnayder); clay 33 % swell and 90 % compacted (reference values)
- Fill mode: 4 050 m³ of compacted clay fill needs 4 500 m³ of bank excavation and 5 986 m³ of loose haul; rock bulks (shrinkage −30 %): 1 000 m³ bank → 1 300 m³ placed
  - Source: V_bank = V_compacted/(1 − shrinkage); blasted rock bulking
- Intervals and custom factors: 10 identical intervals multiply all volumes by 10; custom swell 20 % / shrinkage 5 % / density 1 600 are honoured
  - Source: Arithmetic; custom-material path
- Warnings and validation: end areas differing by more than 2× trigger the over-estimate warning; both areas zero, zero length and unknown material are rejected
  - Source: Average end area error for dissimilar sections (FHWA ch. 9); validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 4 096.25 m³, 4 050.42 m³, 45.8 m³, 1.1 %, 4 050.42 m³, 5 387 m³, 3 645 m³, 7 290 t to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- FHWA Federal Lands Highway Project Development and Design Manual, ch. 9 Earthwork design (average end area, prismoidal, mass haul)
- Caterpillar Performance Handbook (material swell and load factors); Peurifoy & Schexnayder, Construction Planning, Equipment and Methods (swell, shrinkage, bank/loose/compacted)
- Earthworks and mass diagram lecture notes (Scribd, "Earthworks" ch. 5) — worked example 4 050.42 / 4 096.25 m³
- BS 6031:2009 Code of practice for earthworks; Specification for Highway Works Series 600 (bulking and compaction)

## Elastic constants calculator (E, G, K, Poisson's ratio)

<a id="elastic-constants"></a>

Folder `elastic-constants/` · Mechanical · Young's modulus, shear modulus, bulk modulus and Poisson's ratio of an isotropic material from any two of them, with Lamé's constant.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The material is isotropic and linear elastic, so two constants define all the others. Wood, fibre composites, rolled single crystals and many plastics are anisotropic, and these relations do not hold for them.
- Poisson's ratio must lie between −1 and 0.5 for a stable isotropic solid; at 0.5 the material is incompressible and the bulk modulus is infinite, so the calculator refuses ν ≥ 0.5.
- Measured E, G and ν of real alloys are often not exactly consistent with G = E/(2(1 + ν)), because they come from different tests and textured products; differences of a few per cent are normal.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: steel with E = 210 GPa and ν = 0.3 gives G = 80.77 GPa (EN 1993-1-1 rounds to 81 GPa), K = 175.0 GPa, λ = 121.2 GPa and M = 282.7 GPa. Checked by hand.
- Data check: EN 1999-1-1 gives aluminium E = 70 000 MPa, G = 27 000 MPa and ν = 0.3; the relation gives G = 26 923 MPa, so the code value is rounded. Copper C11000 (National Bronze data sheet, E 17 000 ksi, G 6 400 ksi) implies ν = 0.328.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Negative Poisson\'s ratio (auxetic): possible for foams and lattices, but no common engineering metal or plastic behaves this way; check the inputs.
- ν above 0.45: nearly incompressible (rubber-like); the bulk modulus is very sensitive to small changes in ν.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Known constants: unknown pair …
- …: the values give ν = …, outside −1 < ν < 0.5 for a stable isotropic solid….

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Steel E 210 GPa, ν 0.3: G = 210/2.6 = 80.77 GPa, K = 210/1.2 = 175 GPa, λ = 121.15 GPa, M = 282.69 GPa
  - Source: G = E/(2(1 + ν)), K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)), λ = Eν/((1 + ν)(1 − 2ν)) (Timoshenko and Goodier); EN 1993-1-1 §3.2.6 rounds G to 81 GPa
- Every pair returns the same set: from (E, G), (E, K), (G, ν), (G, K) and (K, ν) of steel back to E 210 GPa and ν 0.3
  - Source: Consistency of the isotropic relations (round trip)
- EN 1999-1-1 aluminium E 70 GPa, G 27 GPa gives ν = 0.2963 (the code rounds ν to 0.3)
  - Source: EN 1999-1-1:2007 §3.2.5; ν = E/(2G) − 1
- Copper C11000 data sheet: E 17 000 ksi, G 6 400 ksi gives ν = 0.328
  - Source: National Bronze & Metals C11000 data sheet (modulus of elasticity in tension and modulus of rigidity)
- Limiting cases: ν = 0 gives G = E/2 and K = E/3; ν → 0.5 makes K grow without bound and G → E/3
  - Source: Limits of G = E/(2(1 + ν)) and K = E/(3(1 − 2ν))
- Impossible pairs are refused: G below E/3, E above 9K, ν of 0.5 or more; zero E is rejected
  - Source: Validation contract (−1 < ν < 0.5)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 80.77 GPa, 175.0 GPa, 121.2 GPa to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Timoshenko and Goodier, Theory of Elasticity, 3rd ed., §3–§7 (relations between the elastic constants of an isotropic body)
- Gere and Goodno, Mechanics of Materials, 9th ed., §3.6 (G = E/(2(1 + ν))) and §7.5 (bulk modulus K = E/(3(1 − 2ν)))
- EN 1993-1-1:2005 §3.2.6 (steel E 210 GPa, G 81 GPa, ν 0.3); EN 1999-1-1:2007 §3.2.5 (aluminium E 70 GPa, G 27 GPa, ν 0.3)

## Electricity cost and energy use

<a id="electricity-cost"></a>

Folder `electricity-cost/` · Electrical · Energy use and running cost of any appliance or load per hour, day, month and year, from its power, hours of use and the price per kWh.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The power is the real power the load draws while it runs (the watts on the rating plate or measured with a plug-in meter); for motors and heaters on a thermostat, the duty cycle sets the share of time it actually draws that power.
- The price is a flat price per kWh; time-of-use tariffs, standing charges, demand charges and taxes are not included.
- A month is the average 30.44 days and a year 365.25 days; days per week below 7 scale both.
- Standby power can be added as a second load, entered with 24 hours a day.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 2 kW heater 4 h a day at 0.25 per kWh uses 8 kWh and costs 2.00 a day, 730.50 a year (2 922 kWh). Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A large load running many hours: industrial tariffs usually add a demand charge on the peak kW, which this flat-rate estimate leaves out.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- A 2 kW heater 4 h a day at 0.25 per kWh: 8 kWh and 2.00 a day, 243.5 kWh and 60.88 a month, 2 922 kWh and 730.50 a year
  - Source: Energy W = P t (ISO 80000-6, 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ); average month 365.25 / 12 days
- A 150 W fridge compressor running 40 % of the time, 24 h a day: 1.44 kWh a day, 526 kWh a year
  - Source: E = P × duty × t; typical refrigerator duty cycle 30–50 %
- Five working days a week cut the monthly and yearly figures to 5/7 but leave the cost per day of use unchanged
  - Source: Scaling by days of use per week
- A 5 W standby load all year costs 43.83 kWh, 13.15 at 0.30 per kWh
  - Source: IEC 62301 standby power; E = 5 W × 8766 h
- Zero hours or zero price give zero cost; more than 24 hours a day is rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 8 kWh, 2 922 kWh, 2.00, 730.50 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)
