## Enclosed space purge time

<a id="enclosed-space-purge"></a>

Folder `enclosed-space-purge/` · Maritime · Ventilation time for a tank or enclosed space to reach the entry criteria for oxygen, flammable and toxic gas, by dilution with a mixing factor.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Dilution ventilation of a stirred volume: fresh air at Q replaces the atmosphere, and each concentration moves exponentially from its initial value towards that of the supply air, C(t) = C_fresh + (C_0 − C_fresh) e^(−Q t/(K V)); oxygen rises towards 20.9 %, flammable and toxic gases fall towards zero (purge equation of the ACGIH Industrial Ventilation manual).
- Mixing factor K = 1 for perfect mixing; real spaces with structure, a single fan duct or short-circuiting flow need more air, and K of 3 to 10 is a matter of judgement. The ideal time with K = 1 is shown for comparison.
- No new gas is generated during ventilation (no cargo off-gassing, rusting or residues), and the fresh air contains no contaminant unless one is entered; displacement purging of stratified gas can be faster than dilution and is not modelled.
- Entry criteria of MSC.581(110) (2025), 7.4: steady readings of 20.9 % oxygen by volume, less than 0.5 % carbon dioxide, less than 1 % of the lower flammable limit, and less than 50 % of the occupational exposure limit of any toxic gas; the readings are taken with the ventilation stopped and after conditions have stabilised (7.6), at several levels.
- An oxygen meter cannot show 20.9 % before the atmosphere is practically all fresh air, which dilution only approaches; the oxygen target is therefore entered just below 20.9 %, and entry still requires the steady reading.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: a 1200 m³ tank with 5000 m³/h of fresh air (V/Q = 14.4 min) and K = 3 needs 43.2 min × ln 29 = 145.5 min for oxygen from 18 % to 20.8 %, 43.2 × ln 10 = 99.5 min for 10 % LFL to 1 % and 43.2 × ln 4 = 59.9 min for 50 to 12.5 ppm; oxygen governs at 10.1 air changes.
- Design decision: the default toxic example is 50 % of a 25 ppm exposure limit; enter the limit of the gas actually expected.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- All entered values already meet their targets; test the atmosphere before entry.
- A mixing factor below 2 assumes nearly perfect mixing, rarely achieved in tanks with internal structure.
- An oxygen target this close to 20.9 % takes many air changes; the steady 20.9 % reading on the meter is the criterion.
- The time is an estimate: test at several levels with the ventilation stopped after conditions have stabilised, and keep ventilating while the space is occupied (MSC.581(110)).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- the supply air (…) does not get past the target …, so dilution cannot reach it
- ……: …

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Washout: a contaminant falls to 1/e of its value in one time constant, and a tenfold reduction takes ln 10 = 2.30 air changes with perfect mixing
  - Source: ACGIH Industrial Ventilation manual, purge equation t = (K V/Q) ln(C0/C)
- Default tank: 1200 m³, 5000 m³/h, K = 3: oxygen 18 → 20.8 % takes 43.2 ln 29 = 145.5 min and governs; 10 → 1 % LFL 99.5 min; 50 → 12.5 ppm 59.9 min
  - Source: Dilution towards 20.9 % oxygen and zero contaminant; MSC.581(110) 7.4 entry criteria
- The mixing factor scales the time: K = 3 needs three times the ideal time of perfect mixing
  - Source: Effective dilution flow Q/K
- Values already meeting their criteria need no ventilation time, and the table shows the atmosphere at the end of the purge
  - Source: Criteria met at the start
- Unreachable targets are rejected: supply air above the toxic target, an oxygen target of 21 %
  - Source: Dilution only approaches the supply air composition
- Invalid inputs are rejected: zero fan flow, a mixing factor below 1
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 145.5 min, 99.5 min, 59.9 min, 145.5 min, 10.1 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IMO, Resolution MSC.581(110) (2025), Revised recommendations for entering enclosed spaces aboard ships — 7.4 to 7.6
- ACGIH, Industrial Ventilation: A Manual of Recommended Practice for Design — dilution ventilation and the purge equation with mixing factor K
- O. Levenspiel, Chemical Reaction Engineering, 3rd ed., Wiley 1999, chapter 11 — washout of a stirred volume

## Engine BMEP, torque and power

<a id="engine-bmep"></a>

Folder `engine-bmep/` · Mechanical · Swept volume, brake mean effective pressure, torque, mean piston speed and specific power of a reciprocating engine from bore, stroke, cylinders and rpm.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Brake mean effective pressure is the work per cycle per unit swept volume: P = p_me V_d N/(60 n_R), with n_R = 2 revolutions per power stroke for a four-stroke engine and 1 for a two-stroke (Heywood eq. 2.5); it is a measure of how hard the engine is loaded independent of its size, not a pressure that exists in the cylinder.
- Swept volume per cylinder V_d = (π/4) D² S from bore and stroke; the compression volume and any valve or port timing effects are irrelevant to the mean-effective-pressure definition.
- Indicated mean effective pressure IMEP = BMEP/η_m and friction mean effective pressure FMEP = IMEP − BMEP follow from the mechanical efficiency entered (0.85–0.92 at rated load for marine diesels, falling at part load); auxiliary drives are counted as friction.
- Torque T = 60 P/(2π N) is the mean brake torque at the crankshaft; the propeller-law relation (P ∝ N³, so T ∝ N²) is used only for the optional part-load note and is not a property of the engine.
- Mean piston speed c_m = 2 S N/60 and typical ranges (low-speed two-stroke 8–9 m/s, medium-speed 9–11 m/s, high-speed up to 14 m/s; BMEP 18–21 bar for large two-strokes, 22–28 bar for medium-speed four-strokes) are indicative design limits, not regulations.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: a 6-cylinder 320 × 400 mm four-stroke at 750 rpm delivering 3 000 kW → V_d 32.17 L per cylinder, 193.0 L total, BMEP 24.87 bar, torque 38.2 kN·m, c_m 10.0 m/s, 15.5 kW/L — typical of a modern medium-speed marine diesel; a two-stroke 500 × 2 214 mm cylinder at 127 rpm with 1 780 kW gives 19.3 bar, the catalogue order of magnitude (about 20 bar) for that engine class.
- Design decision: both directions (power → BMEP and BMEP → power) are offered because catalogue work goes one way and performance analysis the other; the mechanical-efficiency split is kept simple (no friction model).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Mean piston speed … m/s is high: above the usual 9–11 m/s of medium-speed and 8–9 m/s of low-speed marine engines (high-speed engines reach 12–14 m/s).
- A two-stroke above 300 rpm is unusual for marine propulsion (large two-strokes run 60–250 rpm).
- Stroke/bore above 1.6 on a four-stroke is unusual; check bore and stroke are not swapped.
- Mechanical efficiency below 0.75: part load or heavy auxiliary drives; the IMEP/FMEP split is only as good as this input.
- Mean effective pressures are load measures, not cylinder pressures; peak firing pressure is 5–8 × BMEP and comes from the indicator diagram.
- Torque and power are mean brake values at the crankshaft; shaft losses to the propeller (gearbox, bearings) are separate.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Medium-speed four-stroke 6 × 320 × 400 mm at 750 rpm, 3 000 kW: V_d = π/4 × 0.32² × 0.4 = 32.17 L per cylinder (193.0 L total), BMEP = P × 60 × 2/(V_d,tot N) = 24.87 bar
  - Source: Heywood, Internal Combustion Engine Fundamentals, eq. 2.5 (P = p_me V_d N/(60 n_R), n_R = 2)
- Torque, piston speed and specific power: T = 60 × 3e6/(2π × 750) = 38.20 kN·m, c_m = 2 × 0.4 × 750/60 = 10.0 m/s, 15.5 kW/L, stroke/bore 1.25, work per cycle 80 kJ
  - Source: Heywood eqs. 2.2 (torque) and 2.9 (mean piston speed)
- Two-stroke cylinder 500 × 2 214 mm at 127 rpm with 1 780 kW: n_R = 1 → BMEP 19.3 bar (catalogue order 20 bar), c_m = 9.37 m/s
  - Source: MAN B&W S50ME-C class data (L1 point ≈ 1 780 kW/cyl at 127 rpm, MEP ≈ 20 bar); Heywood eq. 2.5 with n_R = 1
- Inverse mode: BMEP 24.87 bar on the same engine returns 3 000 kW; IMEP = BMEP/0.9 = 27.63 bar, FMEP 2.76 bar; halving the speed at constant BMEP halves the power and leaves the torque unchanged
  - Source: Definitions of IMEP, FMEP and mechanical efficiency (Heywood §2.4); P ∝ N at constant p_me
- Warnings and validation: a high-speed engine at 14 m/s piston speed is flagged; a two-stroke at 1 000 rpm is flagged; fractional cylinders, zero bore and an unknown cycle are rejected
  - Source: Typical piston-speed ranges (Pounder's); validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 32.2 L, 0.193 m³, 24.9 bar, 3 000 kW, 38.2 kN·m, 10.0 m/s, 15.5, 27.6 bar to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- J. B. Heywood, Internal Combustion Engine Fundamentals, 2nd ed., McGraw-Hill 2018, ch. 2 (eqs. 2.5–2.12: power, torque, mean effective pressure, mean piston speed)
- D. Woodyard (ed.), Pounder's Marine Diesel Engines and Gas Turbines, 9th ed., Butterworth-Heinemann 2009 — typical BMEP and piston speed ranges
- MAN Energy Solutions, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion (2018) — engine layout diagram, propeller law
- ISO 3046-1:2002 — declared power definitions

## Engine displacement calculator

<a id="engine-displacement"></a>

Folder `engine-displacement/` · Automotive · Engine displacement in cc, litres and cubic inches from bore, stroke and cylinders, or the bore or stroke for a target size, with mean piston speed.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Displacement is the swept volume of all cylinders, π/4 × bore² × stroke × cylinders, for a four-stroke or a two-stroke piston engine alike; it does not apply to rotary (Wankel) engines.
- Bore and stroke are the finished dimensions; an overbore of 0.030 in or 0.5 mm is added to the bore before calculating.
- Manufacturers round displacement to the nearest 0.1 L for the badge (5 733 cc is sold as a 5.7) and sometimes to whole cubic inches.
- The mean piston speed is 2 × stroke × rpm; it is the average over a revolution, and the peak speed near mid-stroke is about 1.6 times higher for usual connecting-rod lengths.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: GM LS3, bore 4.065 in, stroke 3.622 in, 8 cylinders: 376.1 in³, 6.16 L (GM rates it 6.2 L, 376 cu in); mean piston speed at 6 600 rpm 3 984 ft/min. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The bore/stroke ratio is far outside the 0.6 to 1.6 of car and motorcycle engines; check the bore and stroke.
- Mean piston speed above 25 m/s (4 900 ft/min) is in the range of top racing engines; check the stroke and the rpm.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Honda K20: 86 × 86 mm, 4 cylinders is 1 998 cc; Toyota 2JZ: 86 × 86 mm, 6 cylinders is 2 997 cc
  - Source: Honda and Toyota published specifications (1 998 cc and 2 997 cc)
- GM LS3: 4.065 × 3.622 in × 8 is 376 cu in (6.2 L); small-block 350: 4.00 × 3.48 in is 349.9 cu in
  - Source: GM published specifications (LS3 6.2 L / 376 cu in; 350 cu in, 5.7 L)
- Inverse: 350 cu in with a 3.48 in stroke needs a 4.001 in bore; 2.0 L from an 86 mm bore and 4 cylinders needs an 86.08 mm stroke
  - Source: Rearranged V = π/4 b² s n; consistency with the forward calculation
- Mean piston speed: 3.622 in stroke at 6 600 rpm is 2 × 3.622/12 × 6 600 = 3 984 ft/min (20.24 m/s)
  - Source: Heywood Section 2.2, S_p = 2 L N
- Fractional cylinders, zero bore and an unknown mode are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 376.1 in³, 6.16 L, 770.3 mL, 1.122, 3 984 ft/min to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- J.B. Heywood, Internal Combustion Engine Fundamentals, McGraw-Hill 1988, Section 2.2 (displaced volume V_d = π B² L / 4 and mean piston speed 2 L N)
- Manufacturer data for the test engines: GM small-block 350 (4.00 × 3.48 in), GM LS3 (4.065 × 3.622 in, 6.2 L), Honda K20 (86 × 86 mm, 1 998 cc), Toyota 2JZ-GTE (86 × 86 mm, 2 997 cc)

## Engine-room ventilation (ISO 8861)

<a id="engine-room-ventilation"></a>

Folder `engine-room-ventilation/` · Maritime · Combustion air and heat-removal airflow for an engine room from installed power and heat emissions, fan capacity and air changes.

### Assumptions and caveats

- ISO 8861:1998 method: airflow for combustion q_c = q_dp + q_dg + q_b with m_ad = 0.0023 kg/(kW·s) for 2-stroke and 0.0020 for 4-stroke diesel engines (manufacturer data preferred), air density 1.13 kg/m³ (35 °C, 70 % RH, 101.3 kPa); boiler air from the fuel consumption (0.11 kg fuel per kWh of thermal capacity, 0.077 kg fuel per kg steam) and 15.7 kg air per kg fuel.
- Airflow for heat evacuation q_h = Σφ/(ρ c ΔT) − 0.4 (q_dp + q_dg) − q_b with c = 1.01 kJ/(kg·K) and ΔT = 12.5 K between the air inlet and the casing entrance; the 0.4 factor credits the heat carried away by the engines' own combustion air with the usual duct arrangement — "in case of special arrangements the value of the factor should be considered".
- Heat emission of diesel engines φ = P × h_d/100 with h_d the maker's radiation/convection heat loss in % of MCR (large two-strokes about 1–1.5 %, medium-speed four-strokes 2–4 %; ISO 8861 clause 7.1 gives guidance curves when data are missing) — here an input; boiler heat emission as a percentage of capacity; electrical generator losses as P_el (1/η − 1); exhaust pipes, hot tanks, electrical installations and other components as entered kilowatts.
- Total airflow Q is the larger of q_c + q_h and 1.5 q_c (combustion air plus 50 %); calculations are for simultaneous maximum rating of all machinery at sea; stand-by generators are excluded; equipment inside the casing/funnel is excluded; separate spaces (purifier rooms, auxiliary engine rooms) are calculated separately.
- Air changes per hour and fan duties are derived quantities (room volume and number of supply fans entered); ISO 8861 does not set an air-change requirement, and the exhaust (natural through the casing or mechanical) is not sized here.
- No allowance for tropical over-temperature beyond 35 °C ambient, for inert-gas or cargo-area requirements, or for the SOLAS/class requirement that ventilation is independent of other spaces.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: constants transcribed from the ISO 8861:1998 text (clauses 5.1–6.3): m_ad 0.0023/0.0020, ρ 1.13, c 1.01, ΔT 12.5, factor 0.4, m_fs 0.077 kg/kg steam, m_af 15.7; the boiler thermal-capacity fuel rate printed as "0,11 kg s⁻¹ kW⁻¹" in the sample is interpreted as 0.11 kg per kWh (the only physically consistent reading, ≈ 30 % boiler efficiency margin over 42.7 MJ/kg fuel).
- Design decision: heat-loss percentages are inputs with typical ranges rather than the clause 7.1 guidance curve, which is not reproducible from the standard's preview.
- Verification: 10 MW two-stroke + 3 MW generators + 2 MW boiler default gives q_c 26.5 m³/s and Q 61.7 m³/s (222 000 m³/h), 14.8 air changes per hour in 15 000 m³ — in the usual 15–30 range for merchant-ship engine rooms.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Heat-evacuation airflow is negative: the combustion air alone carries away the heat; the 1.5 × q_c minimum governs.
- Heat-loss percentages left at typical values: ISO 8861 requires the manufacturers\' data where available.
- Fewer than 10 air changes per hour: check the heat emissions entered — engine rooms usually see 15–30.
- No generator engines: ISO 8861 counts all generators running at sea (not stand-by) — confirm the sea-going plant configuration.
- Calculation at simultaneous MCR of all machinery, 35 °C ambient and 12.5 K rise (ISO 8861); separate spaces such as purifier rooms are calculated separately.
- Fan duty is the supply side only; the exhaust via casing or extraction fans must pass Q − q_c and the space is to be kept at slight over-pressure.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- No machinery entered: give at least one engine or boiler power

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- ISO 8861 constants: m_ad 0.0023 (2-stroke) and 0.0020 kg/(kW·s) (4-stroke), ρ 1.13 kg/m³, c 1.01 kJ/(kg·K), ΔT 12.5 K, boiler 15.7 kg air/kg fuel, heat recovery factor 0.4
  - Source: ISO 8861:1998 clauses 5.2.2–5.3 (standard text, iTeh preview)
- Combustion air: 10 000 kW 2-stroke → 10 000 × 0.0023/1.13 = 20.35 m³/s; 3 000 kW 4-stroke → 5.31 m³/s; 2 000 kW boiler → 2 000 × 0.11/3600 × 15.7/1.13 = 0.849 m³/s; q_c = 26.51 m³/s
  - Source: ISO 8861 §5.2.2–5.2.4
- Heat emission: main 150 kW (1.5 %), generators 90 kW + alternator losses 2 850 × (1/0.95 − 1) = 150 kW, boiler 20 kW, others 230 kW → Σφ = 640 kW; gross airflow 640/(1.13 × 1.01 × 12.5) = 44.86 m³/s
  - Source: ISO 8861 §6.1–6.2 (φ = P h_d/100), §6.5 (electrical generator losses), §5.3 denominator ρ c ΔT
- Heat-evacuation airflow with credits: q_h = 44.86 − 0.4 × (20.35 + 5.31) − 0.85 = 33.74 m³/s; total Q = q_c + q_h = 60.25 m³/s (216 900 m³/h) > 1.5 q_c = 39.8 → combustion + heat governs; 14.5 air changes/h; 15.06 m³/s per fan; exhaust Q − q_c = 33.7
  - Source: ISO 8861 §5.1 (larger of q_c + q_h and 1.5 q_c) and §5.3
- Minimum rule governs for a cool plant: heat losses set to zero → q_h negative, Q = 1.5 q_c = 39.77 m³/s, warning issued, and the resulting temperature rise is below 12.5 K
  - Source: ISO 8861 §5.1 b (airflow for combustion + 50 %)
- Engine type and boiler: switching the main engine to 4-stroke lowers q_dp by 0.0020/0.0023; removing the boiler removes q_b and its heat; stand-by generators excluded by entering only running sets
  - Source: ISO 8861 §5.2.2 (m_ad by engine type), §5.2.4
- Invalid inputs fail fast: no machinery at all, fractional fan count, heat loss above 30 %
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 20.35 m³/s, 26.5 m³/s, 640 kW, 150 kW, 44.9 m³/s, 33.7 m³/s, 60.3 m³/s, 14.5 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 8861:1998, Shipbuilding — Engine-room ventilation in diesel-engined ships — Design requirements and basis of calculations, clauses 4–6
- MAN Energy Solutions and Wärtsilä project guides — engine radiation heat and combustion air data (percentage heat loss, specific air consumption)
- Heinen & Hopman, "Engine room ventilation explained" (2022) — application notes on ISO 8861 constants
- SOLAS Ch. II-1 Reg. 35 and class rules — ventilation of machinery spaces (requirements, not calculation)

## Energy-saving device payback

<a id="esd-payback"></a>

Folder `esd-payback/` · Maritime · Payback, NPV, IRR and levelized cost of a fuel-saving retrofit from the saving, fuel and ETS prices, life and discount rate.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The device saves a fixed percentage of the fuel consumption entered (main engine at sea, or total, as the user decides) for the sea days per year entered; the percentage may decline each year by the degradation entered (coating wear, fouling of the device); savings from an ESD measured in trials or by ISO 19030-type monitoring carry ±1–3 % absolute uncertainty, which usually dominates the result.
- Benefits are the fuel saved × fuel price (escalating at the rate entered) plus the CO₂ saved × allowance price × the share of emissions under the EU ETS (100 % for intra-EU voyages, 50 % for voyages to/from the EU, 0 outside), less the annual maintenance of the device; FuelEU penalties, CII rating value, charter-party premiums and residual value are not priced.
- The investment is the capex plus the off-hire days for installation × daily hire (opportunity cost), all at year 0; cash flows are annual at year end, discounted at the nominal rate entered with prices also nominal (use a real rate with zero escalation for a real analysis).
- Simple payback = investment / first-year net benefit; discounted payback interpolates the year in which the cumulative discounted benefit reaches the investment; IRR is the rate that zeroes the NPV (bisection between −90 % and 1 000 %, undefined if the cash flows never pay back); the levelized cost of saved fuel = (capital recovery factor × investment + maintenance) / fuel saved per year, to compare directly with the fuel price.
- One currency throughout; the allowance price must be entered in that currency.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: the textbook annuity (300 000 invested, 100 000 net per year for 5 years at 10 %) gives NPV 79 079, IRR 19.86 %, payback 3.0 years and discounted payback 3.75 years, matching the standard tables; the capital recovery factor 0.26380 at 10 %/5 years matches the engineering-economics tables.
- Design decision: ETS savings are kept at a constant allowance price (no escalation input for EUAs) because the user can fold an expected price path into the price entered; fuel price escalation is separate because bunker prices and allowance prices move independently.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The first-year net benefit is not positive: the saving does not cover the maintenance — no payback.
- Simple payback exceeds the project life: the investment is not recovered.
- Negative NPV at the discount rate entered: the retrofit destroys value unless unpriced benefits (CII, charter premium) justify it.
- Savings above 15 % are rarely verified for a single device: check the claim against independent trials or monitoring.
- The measured saving of an ESD carries ±1–3 % absolute uncertainty (ISO 19030): run the page at the low end of the claimed range too.
- Not priced: FuelEU Maritime penalties or pooling value, CII rating consequences, residual value, financing costs and taxes.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The investment is zero: enter a capex or installation off-hire

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Textbook annuity: 300 000 invested, 100 000 per year for 5 years at 10 % → PV of benefits 379 078.68, NPV 79 078.68, BCR 1.2636, simple payback 3.0 years
  - Source: Newnan et al., Engineering Economic Analysis — (P/A, 10 %, 5) = 3.7908
- IRR 19.86 % and discounted payback 3.751 years (cumulative PV 248 685 after year 3, 316 987 after year 4) for the same annuity; CRF(10 %, 5) = 0.26380 → levelized cost 395.7 per t against 500
  - Source: IRR tables; discounted payback by interpolation; CRF = i(1+i)ⁿ/((1+i)ⁿ−1)
- ETS and CO₂: default case saves 375 t fuel and 1 167.75 t CO₂ (HFO 3.114) per year; allowances 70 at 50 % share → 40 871; fuel 206 250; net 242 121 after 5 000 maintenance; investment 460 000 (incl. 3 × 20 000 off-hire)
  - Source: MEPC.364(79) carbon factors; EU ETS 50 % share for extra-EU voyages
- Escalation and degradation: 2 % fuel escalation makes year-3 fuel savings 1.0404 × year 1 and raises the NPV; 10 % degradation lowers it; zero discount rate gives NPV = Σ benefits − investment and CRF = 1/n
  - Source: Cash-flow definitions; CRF limit at i → 0
- No-payback case: zero saving leaves only maintenance → net benefit negative, payback and IRR null, NPV negative, warnings; a saving above 15 % is flagged
  - Source: Behaviour specification
- Validation: zero investment, fractional project life and unknown fuel are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 460 000, 375, 1 168, 206 250, 40 871, 242 121, 1.9, about 2.1, 3.8, 0.149, 196 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- D. G. Newnan, T. G. Eschenbach, J. P. Lavelle, Engineering Economic Analysis, 13th ed., Oxford University Press 2017 — NPV, IRR, payback, capital recovery factor
- IMO Resolution MEPC.364(79) — carbon factors C_F per fuel (shared/fuels.js); IMO MEPC.1/Circ.896 Guidance on treatment of innovative energy efficiency technologies
- Directive (EU) 2023/959 and Regulation (EU) 2023/957 — extension of the EU ETS to maritime transport (50 % of emissions on voyages to/from the EU, 100 % intra-EU; 40/70/100 % phase-in 2024–2026)
- ISO 19030-1:2016 — measurement of changes in hull and propeller performance (uncertainty of measured savings)

## ETA calculator with time zones

<a id="eta-time-zones"></a>

Folder `eta-time-zones/` · Maritime · Passage ETA in local time at the destination from departure time and UTC offset, distance and speed, with clock changes and the date line.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Offsets are hours from UTC as the clocks show them, east positive: UTC+9 is 9, UTC−5 is −5, India 5.5. A ship's zone description has the opposite sign (ZD −9 for UTC+9).
- The passage time is distance ÷ speed for each leg plus the stops entered. Speed is the planned speed over the ground: allow for current, weather and slow steaming separately.
- The arrival time in UTC and in the destination's local time does not depend on where the clocks are changed on the way; only the description of the clock changes uses the route direction.
- With direction "automatic" the route is taken as the shorter way round: a net clock change of more than 12 hours means the ship crosses the International Date Line. Eastbound the date is repeated, westbound a day is skipped.
- Daylight saving time is not applied automatically: enter the offset in force at departure and at arrival (for example UTC+1 in winter and UTC+2 in summer for Central Europe).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: Yokohama (UTC+9) 2026-11-08 14:00 for 3 400 nmi at 15 kn is 226 h 40 min (9 d 10 h 40 min): UTC 05:00 + 226 h 40 min = 2026-11-17 15:40 UTC, which is 2026-11-17 05:40 at UTC−10. The net clock change is −19 h: eastbound, clocks advanced 5 h and the date repeated once. Checked by hand.
- Design decision: dates are computed with the days-from-civil algorithm rather than the JavaScript Date object, which calc.js files may not use; leap years and the Gregorian century rule are tested.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The offsets and the chosen direction do not fit a normal route: check both offsets and the direction.
- An offset is not a whole number of quarter hours: real time zones are whole, half or three-quarter hours.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- …: write the date and time as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM, for example 2026-11-08 14:30.
- …: the year must be between 1900 and 2200.
- …: the month must be 1 to 12.
- …: …-… has … days.
- …: the time must be between 00:00 and 23:59.
- Legs, line …: write "distance in nmi; speed in knots", for example 240; 12.5
- Legs, line …: the distance "…" must be a number above zero.
- Legs, line …: the speed "…" must be a number above zero and at most 100 kn.
- Legs: enter at least one line "distance; speed".
- Passage time: more than a year. Check the distance and speed.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Yokohama (UTC+9) 2026-11-08 14:00, 3 400 nmi at 15 kn: 9 d 10 h 40 min, ETA 2026-11-17 15:40 UTC = 05:40 local at UTC−10
  - Source: Bowditch ch. 18 (zone time); hand calculation
- Westbound over the date line, Honolulu (UTC−10) to Yokohama (UTC+9): clocks retarded 5 h and a day is skipped; 10 calendar days
  - Source: Bowditch ch. 18 (date line: westbound, advance the date one day); hand calculation
- Year and leap-day rollover: 2026-12-31 23:00 + 2 h is 2027-01-01 01:00; 2028-02-28 22:00 + 3 h is 2028-02-29 01:00
  - Source: Gregorian calendar (2028 is a leap year); days-from-civil algorithm
- Weekdays: 1970-01-01 was a Thursday and 2000-03-01 a Wednesday
  - Source: Calendar facts
- Legs and stops: 120 nmi at 10 kn, 3 000 at 15 and 280 at 12 plus 6 h of stops is 241 h 20 min; India UTC+5.5 is handled
  - Source: Hand calculation (12 + 200 + 23.333 + 6 h)
- Bad dates and legs are rejected: 2027-02-29, 24:10, a missing time and a leg without speed
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 226.7 h to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

## EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime

<a id="eu-ets-fueleu"></a>

Folder `eu-ets-fueleu/` · Maritime · EU ETS allowances and cost with phase-in and voyage scope; FuelEU Maritime GHG intensity against the yearly limit, compliance balance and penalty.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Scope follows both regulations: 100 % of the energy and emissions of voyages between EEA ports and at berth in EEA ports, 50 % of voyages between an EEA port and a third-country port, 0 % elsewhere; the user enters the share of each fuel burned in the first two categories and the remainder is out of scope. Ships ≥ 5 000 GT; exemptions (transhipment ports, islands, PSO routes, ice class) are not modelled.
- FuelEU GHG intensity is the well-to-wake energy-weighted average over ALL fuel in scope: GHGIE = f_wind Σ E_i (WtT_i + TtW_i)/Σ E_i, TtW_i = [(1 − C_slip)(Cf_CO2 + Cf_CH4·GWP_CH4 + Cf_N2O·GWP_N2O) + C_slip·GWP_CH4]/LCV with the RED II GWPs 25 and 298 (Annex I); the limit is 91.16 gCO₂e/MJ reduced by 2 % (2025), 6 % (2030), 14.5 % (2035), 31 % (2040), 62 % (2045) and 80 % (2050).
- Annex II default factors for fossil fuels (table reproduced in the EC guidance of 2025-10-08): the regulation marks CH₄ and N₂O for LPG and methanol as "to be measured" — they are taken as zero here, which slightly understates those fuels. Biofuels, RFNBOs (reward factor 2 until 2033), onshore power supply and the 2 % RFNBO sub-target from 2034 are not modelled; only fossil fuels are offered.
- Compliance balance CB = (GHGIE_target − GHGIE_actual) × E_scope in gCO₂e; penalty = |CB|/(GHGIE_actual × 41 000 MJ/t) × 2 400 EUR per tonne of VLSFO-equivalent energy, multiplied by 1 + (N − 1)/10 for N consecutive deficit years (Annex IV). A surplus can be banked or pooled; borrowing (up to 2 % of the limit × energy, at a 10 % premium) is not computed.
- EU ETS covers CO₂ for 2024–2025 reporting years and adds CH₄ and N₂O as CO₂-equivalent (GWP 28 and 265, Regulation (EU) 2020/1044) from the 2026 reporting year; allowances to surrender are 40 % of 2024, 70 % of 2025 and 100 % of 2026+ verified emissions (surrendered by 30 September of the following year). The emission factors used are the same Annex II/MRV values, with slip treated as unburnt methane. The penalty for non-surrender (100 EUR/t plus the allowances) is not included.
- The EUA price is an input; the cost shown is allowances × price with no hedging, no free allocation (none for shipping) and no administrative costs.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: MGO well-to-wake intensity 90.77 gCO₂e/MJ (EC guidance Table 4.3), LNG Diesel slow-speed 76.08 (Table 4.4), HFO 91.744 (Bettersea worked example); limits 89.34/85.69/77.94/62.90/34.64/18.23 (KR guideline table); wind reward 0.99 × 90.77 = 89.86 (EC guidance Table 4.13).
- Verification 2026-10-30: ETS phase-in 40/70/100 % and the 50 % extra-EEA rule confirmed on the EMSA ETS page; CH₄ and N₂O from 1 January 2026.
- Design decision: three fuel slots with per-fuel scope shares cover dual-fuel ships and pilot fuel; a "none" option disables a slot.
- Design decision: FuelEU and ETS are computed from the same fuel entries so the two costs can be compared per tonne of fuel; the ETS CH₄ factor for LNG uses the slip percentage of the engine class, as the MRV delegated regulation does.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- LPG and fossil methanol: Annex II gives no default CH₄ and N₂O factors yet ("to be measured") — taken as zero, which slightly understates their intensity.
- LNG: the methane slip of the engine class dominates the result (3.1 % Otto medium speed down to 0.2 % Diesel slow speed) and is counted at GWP 25 (FuelEU) or 28 (ETS); certified actual slip may be used instead of the default.
- Compliant with fossil fuel after 2030 is unusual: check the fuel mix — the limit falls to 85.69 in 2030 and 77.94 in 2035.
- Before 2026 the ETS covers CO₂ only; from the 2026 reporting year CH₄ and N₂O are added (GWP 28 and 265).
- Wind reward factor … applied to the attained intensity (Annex I); P_wind must be verified.
- Fossil fuels only: biofuels, RFNBO (reward factor 2 until 2033), OPS electricity, banking/borrowing arithmetic and the 2034 RFNBO sub-target are outside this calculator.
- Exemptions (transhipment ports, outermost regions, islands under 200 000 inhabitants, PSO routes, ice-class adjustments) are not applied.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The intra-EEA and extra-EEA shares add up to more than 100 %
- No fuel in scope: enter a fuel mass and a non-zero EEA share

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- FuelEU limits: 91.16 reference → 89.34 (2025–2029), 85.69 (2030), 77.94 (2035), 62.90 (2040), 34.64 (2045), 18.23 (2050) gCO₂e/MJ
  - Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 Article 4(2); KR FuelEU Guidelines Rev. 2 limits table
- Well-to-wake intensities from Annex II: MGO 90.77 (EC guidance Table 4.3), LNG Diesel slow speed 76.08 (Table 4.4), HFO 91.744, LFO 90.4; LNG Otto medium speed ≈ 89.2 with 3.1 % slip
  - Source: EC Guidance on the FuelEU Maritime Regulation (2025-10-08) Tables 4.2–4.4; Bettersea HFO example 91.744
- HFO-only ship, 5 000 t, 2025, 100 % intra-EEA: energy 202.5 TJ, intensity 91.744 vs limit 89.337 → deficit 487.5 t CO₂e, penalty |CB|/(91.744 × 41 000) × 2 400 = 311 048 EUR
  - Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 Annex IV penalty formula; KR Guidelines §C
- Consecutive deficits: third year in a row multiplies the penalty by 1.2; a compliant ship (LNG Diesel slow speed in 2025) has zero penalty and a banked surplus
  - Source: Annex IV: penalty × (1 + (N − 1)/10); Article 20 banking
- Wind reward factor 0.99 applied to an MGO ship gives 0.99 × 90.77 = 89.86 gCO₂e/MJ (EC guidance Table 4.13)
  - Source: EC Guidance Table 4.12–4.13 (f_wind 0.99 / 0.97 / 0.95)
- Scope: 30 % intra + 50 % extra gives a 55 % factor on energy, emissions and fuel; shares above 100 % are rejected; mixed fuels are energy-weighted
  - Source: Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 Article 2 and Directive 2003/87/EC Article 3ga (100 % intra-EEA and at berth, 50 % extra-EEA)
- EU ETS: 5 000 t HFO, 2025, 40 % intra + 60 % extra → scope 70 %, CO₂ 15 570 t total, 10 899 t in scope, 70 % phase-in → 7 629 EUA, 534 051 EUR at 70 EUR; 2026 → 100 % and CH₄/N₂O added
  - Source: Directive (EU) 2023/959 Article 3gb phase-in (40/70/100 %); MRV CO₂ factor HFO 3.114 (Regulation (EU) 2015/757 Annex I)
- LNG Otto medium speed under the ETS in 2026: CO₂e per gram = 0.969 × (2.75 + 0.00011 × 265) + 0.031 × 28 = 3.561 (slip at GWP 28); before 2026 only 0.969 × 2.75 = 2.665
  - Source: Regulation (EU) 2020/1044 GWPs (28, 265); MRV treatment of methane slip by engine class
- Totals and per-tonne cost: penalty + ETS cost, divided by the in-scope fuel tonnes; invalid inputs fail fast (no fuel in scope, fractional year count, unknown fuel)
  - Source: Arithmetic and validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 91.3 gCO₂e/MJ, −245 t, 157 100, 9 371 t, 70 %, 459 200, 616 300, 208 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (FuelEU Maritime), Articles 2, 4, 20–23, Annex I (GHG intensity formula, GWPs, f_wind), Annex II (default emission factors), Annex IV (penalty)
- European Commission DG MOVE, "Guidance on the FuelEU Maritime Regulation for shipping companies", 2025-10-08 edition, Tables 4.2–4.4 and 4.12–4.13
- Directive (EU) 2023/959 amending Directive 2003/87/EC (EU ETS extension to maritime); Regulation (EU) 2023/957 (MRV amendments); EMSA "ETS extension to maritime" page (phase-in and scope)

## EV charging time and cost calculator

<a id="ev-charging"></a>

Folder `ev-charging/` · Electrical · Electric car charging time and cost from battery size, state of charge, charger power and the car's limit, with charging losses and the range added per hour.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Charging runs at a constant power, the lower of the charger rating and the vehicle limit (the onboard charger for AC, the maximum DC power for fast charging). DC fast charging slows down above about 80 % state of charge, so times to a higher end point are underestimated.
- The efficiency covers the losses from the meter to the battery: onboard charger, cables, battery and cooling. Idaho National Laboratory measured 88.8 % on Level 1 and 90.8 % on Level 2 for the onboard charger of one vehicle; 85 to 90 % from wall to battery is a typical planning range, and cold weather lowers it.
- The capacity is the usable battery energy; the state of charge is the share of that usable energy shown by the car.
- The consumption is the energy taken from the battery per distance, as shown by the trip computer. EPA label figures in kWh/100 mi are measured at the wall (SAE J1634) and include charging losses; with them, set the efficiency to 100 % for the range.
- The price is per kWh drawn from the grid or billed by the station; standing charges, session fees and time-of-use rates are not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 75 kWh battery from 20 to 80 % takes 45.0 kWh; at 90 % efficiency 50.0 kWh from a 7.2 kW Level 2 charger, 6.94 h (6 h 57 min), 7.50 at 0.15 per kWh; at 3.4 mi/kWh the range added is 153 mi, 22.0 mi per hour of charging. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- DC fast charging tapers above about 80 % state of charge: the last part takes much longer than this constant-power estimate.
- AC Level 2 under SAE J1772 goes up to 80 A at 240 V, 19.2 kW; check the charger power.
- DC chargers usually deliver 20 kW or more; check the charger type.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- State of charge at the end: it must be above the state of charge at the start.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 75 kWh from 20 to 80 % on a 7.2 kW Level 2 charger at 90 %: 45 kWh in, 50 kWh drawn, 6.94 h, 7.50 at 0.15, 153 mi at 3.4 mi/kWh
  - Source: Hand calculation: E = C ΔSoC, E_grid = E / η, t = E_grid / P
- Level 1 at 1.92 kW (120 V, 16 A) adds about 5 miles per hour of charging at 3 mi/kWh and 90 %
  - Source: U.S. DOE Alternative Fuels Data Center: Level 1 about 5 miles of range per hour; SAE J1772 Level 1 16 A
- The lower of charger and car sets the power: 11 kW wallbox with a 7.4 kW onboard charger runs at 7.4 kW; a 350 kW DC charger with a 150 kW car at 150 kW
  - Source: Definition of the vehicle limit
- 3.4 mi/kWh = 29.41 kWh/100 mi = 294.1 Wh/mi = 18.28 kWh/100 km = 5.472 km/kWh give the same range
  - Source: Unit definitions (1 mi = 1.609344 km)
- At 100 % efficiency grid energy equals battery energy; the cost per mile is price / (mi/kWh × η)
  - Source: Limiting case; definition of cost per distance
- An end state of charge at or below the start, a consumption out of range and a negative price are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 45.0 kWh, 50.0 kWh, 6.94 h, 7.50, 153 mi, 22.0 mph to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- SAE J1772, SAE Electric Vehicle and Plug-in Hybrid Electric Vehicle Conductive Charge Coupler (AC Level 1 at 120 V up to 16 A; AC Level 2 at 208–240 V up to 80 A)
- U.S. Department of Energy, Alternative Fuels Data Center, Electric Vehicle Charging Stations (Level 1 about 1.9 kW and 5 miles of range per hour; Level 2 up to 19.2 kW, about 25 miles per hour at 7.2 kW)
- Idaho National Laboratory, Advanced Vehicle Testing Activity, Benchmark Testing of the Chevrolet Volt Onboard Charger (2012): AC-to-DC charging efficiency 88.8 % Level 1, 90.8 % Level 2
- SAE J1634, Battery Electric Vehicle Energy Consumption and Range Test Procedure (recharge energy measured at the AC supply)

## Fatigue safety factor calculator (Goodman, Gerber, Soderberg)

<a id="fatigue-goodman"></a>

Folder `fatigue-goodman/` · Mechanical · Endurance limit of a steel part with the Marin factors and the fatigue safety factor by modified Goodman, Gerber, Soderberg and ASME-elliptic criteria.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The method is Shigley's stress-life approach for steel: S_e' = 0.5 S_ut up to 1 400 MPa (700 MPa above), corrected by the Marin factors for surface, size, load, temperature and reliability (Shigley 10th ed. §6-7 to §6-9). It aims at infinite life (10⁶ cycles and beyond).
- The size factor applies to round sections in rotating bending or torsion from 2.79 to 254 mm; a non-rotating round section uses the effective diameter 0.370 d (eq. 6-23). Axial loading has k_b = 1. Other shapes need their own effective diameter.
- The fatigue stress-concentration factor K_f multiplies both the alternating and the mean nominal stress, as for a ductile material that does not yield locally (Shigley Example 6-10). Enter K_f = 1 if the stresses already include it.
- For torsion the load factor is 0.59, and the ultimate and yield strengths are replaced by S_su = 0.67 S_ut (eq. 6-54) and S_sy = 0.577 S_y; enter shear stresses. Combined loading should be reduced to von Mises alternating and mean stresses first and entered as bending.
- A compressive mean stress is treated conservatively: the fatigue factor is S_e/σ_a for every criterion and the yield factor uses |σ_m|. The temperature factor is valid up to 538 °C (1 000 °F).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: Shigley Example 6-10 (1.5 in AISI 1050 CD bar, axial 0 to 16 kip, K_f 1.85, S_ut 100 kpsi, S_y 84 kpsi): k_a = 0.798 (SI constants; 0.797 with kpsi constants), k_c = 0.85, S_e = 33.9 kpsi, σ_a = σ_m = 8.38 kpsi; Gerber n_f = 3.66 (3.67 without rounding the intermediate values), ASME-elliptic 3.75, Langer n_y = 5.01, as printed in the example; Goodman 3.02 and Soderberg 2.88 by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- S_ut above 1 400 MPa: S_e\' is capped at 700 MPa (Shigley eq. 6-8).
- Below 0 °C steels can become brittle; the Marin temperature factor does not cover low-temperature toughness. Check impact properties.
- Compressive mean stress: the fatigue factors are S_e/σ_a, a conservative treatment.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Yield strength: it cannot exceed the ultimate tensile strength.
- Diameter: the size factor of Shigley eq. 6-20 covers effective diameters of 2.79 to 254 mm (got … mm).

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Shigley Example 6-10: S_e = 33.9 kpsi, σa = σm = 8.38 kpsi, Gerber n_f = 3.66, ASME-elliptic 3.75, Langer n_y = 5.01
  - Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., Example 6-10 (1.5 in AISI 1050 CD bar, 0 to 16 kip, K_f 1.85)
- Marin factors: Example 6-3 k_a = 4.51 × 520^−0.265 = 0.860; Example 6-4 k_b = (32/7.62)^−0.107 = 0.858; k_b at 100 mm = 1.51 × 100^−0.157 = 0.733
  - Source: Shigley 10th ed., Examples 6-3 and 6-4, Table 6-2, eq. 6-20
- Temperature factor eq. 6-27 against Table 6-4: 1.000 at 20 °C, 0.975 at 300 °C, 0.768 at 500 °C (within 0.005)
  - Source: Shigley 10th ed., Table 6-4 and eq. 6-27
- Criteria by hand: Goodman 1/(0.2470 + 0.0838) = 3.02, Soderberg 2.88; Gerber ≥ ASME-elliptic ≥ Goodman ≥ Soderberg ordering for this case
  - Source: Shigley 10th ed., Tables 6-6 to 6-8 (hand calculation)
- Limits: zero mean stress gives n = S_e/σ_a for every criterion; S_e' = 0.5 S_ut, capped at 700 MPa above 1 400 MPa; reliability 99 % gives k_e = 0.814
  - Source: Shigley 10th ed., eq. 6-8 and Table 6-5
- Rotating bending of a 32 mm machined shaft uses k_c = 1 and k_b = 0.858; Sy above Sut, a 300 mm shaft and 600 °C are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract; Shigley eq. 6-20 validity range
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.798, 33.9 ksi, 8.375 ksi, 3.02, 3.67, 2.88, 3.75, 5.01 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §6-7 to §6-9: eq. 6-8 (S_e'), eq. 6-18 (Marin equation), Table 6-2 (k_a), eqs. 6-20 and 6-23 (k_b), eq. 6-26 (k_c), eq. 6-27 (k_d), Table 6-5 (k_e)
- Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §6-12 and Tables 6-6 to 6-8 (modified Goodman, Gerber, Soderberg, ASME-elliptic and Langer criteria), eq. 6-54 (torsion), Example 6-10

## Fillet weld strength

<a id="fillet-weld"></a>

Folder `fillet-weld/` · Structural · Throat area and design resistance of fillet welds under shear, tension and bending (Eurocode 3 directional and simplified methods).

### Assumptions and caveats

- EN 1993-1-8 §4.5 fillet welds with equal legs: the throat a is the height of the inscribed triangle (a = z/√2 for leg z), a ≥ 3 mm, and the effective length excludes the end craters (L_eff ≥ 30 mm and ≥ 6a); welds longer than 150 a in lap joints need the β_Lw reduction (not applied — the page warns).
- Simplified method (§4.5.3.3): the resultant of all forces per unit length F_w,Ed ≤ F_w,Rd = f_vw,d a with f_vw,d = f_u/(√3 β_w γ_M2), independent of the load direction — always safe-sided. Directional method (§4.5.3.2): the stresses on the throat plane must satisfy √(σ⊥² + 3(τ⊥² + τ∥²)) ≤ f_u/(β_w γ_M2) and σ⊥ ≤ 0.9 f_u/γ_M2; for a weld loaded transversely σ⊥ = τ⊥ = F/(√2 a L), which gives 22 % more resistance than the simplified method.
- Weld group: n parallel welds of length L; the transverse force and the longitudinal shear are shared equally; an in-plane moment about the weld group is resisted by a force couple M/h between two parallel welds at spacing h (exact for two equal welds, conservative otherwise). Eccentricity, torsion of the group and stress concentrations at the weld ends are not modelled.
- f_u is the nominal ultimate strength of the weaker part joined (EN 1993-1-1 Table 3.1 for t ≤ 40 mm: S235 360, S275 430, S355 490, S420 520, S460 540 MPa), β_w from EN 1993-1-8 Table 4.1 (0.80/0.85/0.90/1.00/1.00) and γ_M2 = 1.25 (recommended; National Annexes may differ); the weld metal must match or over-match the parent metal.
- Static design at ultimate limit state; fatigue (EN 1993-1-9), residual stresses, distortion and inspection levels are outside the calculation.
- The throat limit a ≤ 0.7 t_min of the thinner plate is the usual practical maximum to avoid burn-through; the minimum 3 mm is from EN 1993-1-8 §4.5.2.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: f_vw,d = 360/(√3 × 0.8 × 1.25) = 207.8 MPa for S235 and 251.5 MPa for S355; the UTM worked example with f_u 340 MPa (older S235 grade) gives 196.3 MPa; the directional/simplified ratio for a transverse weld is √3/√2 = 1.225, the classic Eurocode result.
- Design decision: both methods are reported side by side with their utilisations, because designers use the simplified method for quick checks and the directional method to justify slender welds.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Moment resisted by a force couple between two welds at spacing h: conservative for groups of more than two welds (the others are ignored for the moment).
- Long weld: EN 1993-1-8 §4.11 reduces the resistance of lap-joint welds longer than 150 a by β_Lw = 1.2 − 0.2 L/(150 a); not applied here.
- γ_M2 differs from the recommended 1.25: ensure it matches the National Annex.
- Plate thicker than 40 mm: EN 10025 f_u is lower (e.g. S355 470 MPa for 40–80 mm) — use the custom grade.
- Static ULS design to EN 1993-1-8; fatigue (EN 1993-1-9), eccentricity of the weld group and end-crater effects are not covered.
- Weld metal assumed to match or over-match the parent metal; the simplified method is always the conservative check.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Enter at least one force or moment
- An in-plane moment needs at least two parallel welds (force couple)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Design shear strength f_vw,d = f_u/(√3 β_w γ_M2): S235 207.8 MPa, S275 233.6, S355 251.5, S460 249.4; the UTM example with f_u 340 MPa and β_w 0.8 gives 196.3 MPa
  - Source: EN 1993-1-8 §4.5.3.3 eq. 4.4 and Table 4.1; UTM OCW connections lecture worked example (196.3 N/mm²)
- Two S355 welds a 5 mm × 200 mm carrying 300 kN transverse + 100 kN longitudinal: per weld 150 kN and 50 kN → 750 and 250 kN/m, resultant 790.6 kN/m vs F_w,Rd = 251.5 × 5 = 1 257 kN/m → 63 % (simplified)
  - Source: EN 1993-1-8 §4.5.3.3 simplified method F_w,Ed ≤ F_w,Rd = f_vw,d a
- Directional method on the same joint: σ⊥ = τ⊥ = 750/(√2 × 5) = 106.1 MPa, τ∥ = 250/5 = 50 MPa, comparison stress √(σ⊥² + 3(τ⊥² + τ∥²)) = √52 500 = 229.1 MPa vs f_u/(β_w γ_M2) = 435.6 MPa → 52.6 %; σ⊥ ≤ 0.9 f_u/γ_M2 = 352.8 MPa
  - Source: EN 1993-1-8 §4.5.3.2 eqs. 4.1 (directional method) with σ⊥ = τ⊥ for a transverse fillet
- Transverse-only load: directional resistance is √3/√2 = 1.225 × the simplified resistance (classic Eurocode result); longitudinal-only load: both methods coincide
  - Source: EN 1993-1-8 §4.5.3.2 vs §4.5.3.3 for pure transverse and pure longitudinal shear
- Moment couple: 20 kN·m on two welds 200 mm apart adds 100 kN transverse per weld; required throats scale with utilisation (simplified: resultant/f_vw,d); leg input z = 7.07 mm equals a = 5 mm
  - Source: Force couple M/h; a = z/√2
- Geometric limits: a 2.5 mm flagged (< 3 mm); a 8 mm on 10 mm plate flagged (> 0.7 t); 20 mm weld flagged (< 30 mm and 6a); 1.2 m weld on a 5 mm throat flagged (> 150 a) with the β_Lw warning
  - Source: EN 1993-1-8 §4.5.1–4.5.2 and §4.11
- Overload: 900 kN transverse on the same welds → FAIL with the required throat quoted; invalid inputs fail fast (no load, moment with one weld, unknown grade)
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 251.5 MPa, 63 %, 106 MPa, 106 MPa, 50 MPa, 436 MPa, 53 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- EN 1993-1-8:2005 Eurocode 3 — Design of steel structures — Part 1-8: Design of joints, §4.5 (fillet welds), Table 4.1 (β_w), §4.5.3.2 directional method, §4.5.3.3 simplified method
