## Filter cutoff frequency calculator (RC, RL, LC)

<a id="filter-cutoff"></a>

Folder `filter-cutoff/` · Electrical · Cutoff frequency of RC, RL, LC and RLC low-pass and high-pass filters, with Q, attenuation in dB and phase at a frequency, or the component for a target cutoff.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Components are ideal: the inductor has no resistance and the capacitor no leakage or ESR, apart from the resistor R of the circuit; a coil's own resistance can be added to R in the series RLC circuit.
- The source has zero impedance and, for the RC, RL and series RLC circuits, the output drives an open circuit; a load in parallel with the output changes the cutoff and, for second-order filters, the Q.
- In the LC circuit with a load resistor, the inductor (low-pass) or capacitor (high-pass) is in series and the load R sits across the other component, which is the output.
- For second-order filters the −3 dB frequency equals the natural frequency f0 only at Q = 0.707 (Butterworth); the component for a target is chosen so that f0 equals the target, and the resulting −3 dB frequency is shown.
- The cutoff is the −3 dB (half-power) point, where the output voltage is 0.707 of the input and the phase shift is 45° for a first-order filter.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: an RC low-pass of 1 kΩ and 100 nF has f_c = 1.59 kHz and τ = 0.1 ms; at 10 kHz it passes 0.157 of the input (−16.1 dB) with a phase of −81.0°. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Q above 10: the filter rings and has a sharp peak at f0; component tolerances shift the peak noticeably.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Find: an RC filter has no inductor; choose the capacitor or the cutoff frequency.
- Find: an RL filter has no capacitor; choose the inductor or the cutoff frequency.
- Components: the values are so extreme that the response cannot be computed; check the units of R, L and C.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- RC low-pass 1 kΩ, 100 nF: f_c = 1.592 kHz; at 10 kHz |H| = 0.1572 (−16.07 dB), phase −80.96°
  - Source: Horowitz and Hill §1.7, f_3dB = 1/(2πRC) and |H| = 1/√(1 + (f/f_c)²); hand calculation
- At the cutoff a first-order filter is −3.01 dB with ±45° of phase; RL high-pass f_c = R/(2πL) and the L for 1 kHz with 100 Ω is 15.92 mH
  - Source: Definition of the half-power point; Boylestad ch. 21, R-L filters
- Second order: Q = 0.707 puts the −3 dB point at f0 (Butterworth); Q = 0.5 (critical damping) at 0.6436 f0 low-pass and 1.554 f0 high-pass
  - Source: Standard second-order results: √(√2 − 1) = 0.6436 for two equal real poles
- Series RLC with Q = 1: resonant peak 1.25 dB; at f0 the low-pass gain is Q (0 dB) with −90° phase
  - Source: Second-order peaking Q/√(1 − 1/(4Q²)); |H(f0)| = Q
- Component for a target: RC with 10 kΩ for 1 kHz needs 15.92 nF; LC with 10 mH for f0 = 1 kHz needs 2.533 µF
  - Source: C = 1/(2π f R); C = 1/((2π f)² L)
- Invalid entries are rejected: an inductor for an RC filter, zero resistance, zero frequency
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.59 kHz, −16.1, 0.157 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., §1.7 (RC filters, f_3dB = 1/(2πRC)) and §6.2 (LC filters and Q)
- Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, 13th ed., ch. 21 (decibels, filters and Bode plots: R-C and R-L low-pass and high-pass filters)
- Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, 12th ed., the chapters on frequency response and resonance (second-order response, Q and damping)

## Flow rate and pipe velocity

<a id="flow-rate-velocity"></a>

Folder `flow-rate-velocity/` · Thermal and fluids · Velocity from flow rate and pipe bore, flow from velocity, or the bore needed for a flow at a target velocity, checked against usual design velocities.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The pipe runs full with an incompressible fluid, so the mean velocity is the flow divided by the bore area (continuity); gases at high pressure drop need the local density.
- The velocity is the mean over the cross-section; the centre-line velocity is higher (about 1.2 times in turbulent flow, twice in laminar flow).
- The design-velocity ranges are common practice, not a code requirement; noise, erosion, water hammer and the allowable pressure drop decide the final size.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 50 m³/h in a 100 mm bore is 1.77 m/s; for 2 m/s the bore would be 94.0 mm. Checked by hand.
- Design decision: the bore mode returns the exact diameter; choosing the next standard pipe size above it is left to the user, because bores depend on the pipe standard and wall thickness.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The velocity is above the usual range for this service; check the pressure drop and consider a larger pipe.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 50 m³/h in a 100 mm bore: A = 78.54 cm², V = 1.768 m/s, within the 1–3 m/s water range
  - Source: White, Fluid Mechanics, ch. 3: Q = V A; Crane TP-410 reasonable velocities
- Bore for 50 m³/h at 2 m/s: D = √(4Q/πV) = 94.03 mm; 2 m/s in that bore gives back 50 m³/h
  - Source: Continuity solved for D
- 1 m/s in a 50 mm bore carries 1.963 L/s (7.07 m³/h); halving the bore at the same flow quadruples the velocity
  - Source: A = π D² / 4; V ∝ 1/D² at constant Q
- Pump suction at 2 m/s is flagged above 0.6–1.5 m/s with a warning; oil at 0.3 m/s is flagged below its range
  - Source: Crane TP-410 and common practice for suction and oil lines
- Zero flow, zero bore and an unknown mode are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.77 m/s, 78.5 cm² to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- White, F. M., Fluid Mechanics, 7th ed., ch. 3 (continuity: Q = V A)
- Crane Co., Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings and Pipe, Technical Paper 410 (reasonable velocities for liquid lines)

## Flywheel energy calculator (inertia and speed fluctuation)

<a id="flywheel-energy"></a>

Folder `flywheel-energy/` · Mechanical · Flywheel kinetic energy, energy released between two speeds, coefficient of speed fluctuation, and the inertia, disc or rim mass for an energy swing.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The flywheel is a rigid body on a fixed axis: E = ½ I ω². The energy it gives up or absorbs between two speeds is the difference of the kinetic energies (Shigley §16-12).
- The coefficient of speed fluctuation is C_s = (ω₂ − ω₁)/ω with the mean speed ω = (ω₁ + ω₂)/2, so ΔE = C_s I ω² exactly. Typical design values are given by the machine type; the user chooses C_s.
- The energy swing ΔE is the largest difference in the integrated torque–angle diagram over a cycle; this calculator takes it as an input.
- Mass from inertia uses a uniform solid disc (I = ½ m r²) or a thin rim with all the mass at radius r (I = m r²); the inertia of the hub, arms and shaft is neglected, which errs on the safe side for a rim.
- Stresses are elastic centrifugal stresses at the mean speed: ρ v² for a thin rim and (3 + ν)/8 ρ v² at the centre of a solid disc with ν = 0.3; they ignore keyways, bolt holes and overspeed, which the design must add.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: an energy swing of 2 500 J at a mean 300 rpm with C_s = 0.05 needs I = 2 500 / (0.05 × 31.416²) = 50.66 kg·m²; as a solid steel disc of 0.4 m radius that is 633 kg, 160.5 mm thick, with a rim speed of 12.57 m/s and a centre stress of 0.51 MPa; the speed swings between 292.5 and 307.5 rpm. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- C_s above 0.2: a very large speed swing for a flywheel drive; check that the driver and the driven machine tolerate it.
- Rim speed above 50 m/s: check the material, the bursting speed and the overspeed case carefully.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Upper speed: it must be higher than the lower speed.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Energy swing 2 500 J at 300 rpm, C_s 0.05: I = 2 500 / (0.05 × 31.416²) = 50.66 kg·m²; speeds 292.5 and 307.5 rpm
  - Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., eq. 16-62 (hand calculation)
- 50 kg·m² between 285 and 315 rpm: ΔE = ½ × 50 × (32.987² − 29.845²) = 4 934.8 J, C_s = 0.1
  - Source: Shigley eqs. 16-60 and 16-61 (hand calculation)
- Mass and thickness: I 50.66 kg·m² as a 0.4 m solid steel disc is 633.3 kg and 160.5 mm thick; as a thin rim 316.6 kg
  - Source: Solid disc I = ½ m r², thin ring I = m r² (Meriam and Kraige, Dynamics; hand calculation)
- Centrifugal stress at 12.566 m/s in steel: thin rim ρ v² = 1.2396 MPa; solid disc centre (3.3/8) ρ v² = 0.5113 MPa
  - Source: Shigley 10th ed., §3-15 Stresses in rotating rings (ν = 0.3)
- Energy scales with speed squared: doubling the speed band quadruples the energy at each speed
  - Source: E = ½ I ω²
- Upper speed not above the lower, zero energy swing and C_s above 1.5 are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 50.66 kg·m², 633 kg, 160.5 mm, 292.5 rpm, 307.5 rpm to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §16-12 Flywheels, eqs. 16-59 to 16-62 (energy, coefficient of speed fluctuation)
- Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §3-15 Stresses in rotating rings (solid disc and thin rim)
- Meriam and Kraige, Engineering Mechanics: Dynamics, 8th ed., ch. 6 (kinetic energy of rotation, moments of inertia of a disc and a ring)

## Footing size calculator

<a id="footing-size"></a>

Folder `footing-size/` · Civil · Plan size of a square, rectangular, round or strip footing from the column or wall load and the allowable soil bearing pressure, with the actual pressure.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The footing area comes from unfactored (service) loads and the allowable bearing pressure, as ACI 318-19 §13.3.1.1 requires; factored loads are used later for the footing's thickness and reinforcement.
- The load acts at the centre of the footing; moments or eccentricity raise the pressure at one edge and need the full pressure distribution.
- The footing's own weight and the soil above it are subtracted from the allowable pressure (net allowable). Concrete 24 kN/m³ (150 pcf) and soil 18 kN/m³ (115 pcf) by default.
- The allowable bearing pressure comes from the geotechnical report or the building code's presumptive values (for example IBC Table 1806.2); the soil bearing capacity calculator estimates it from soil strength.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 800 kN on soil allowing 200 kPa, with a 0.5 m footing under 0.5 m of soil: net 179 kPa, 4.47 m², 2.114 m square, rounded to 2.15 m, actual 194.1 kPa. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Footings thinner than about 150 mm (6 in) are below common code minimums (ACI 318 §13.3.1.2).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Allowable bearing pressure: the footing and soil above it already use all of it; reduce the depth or check the value.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 800 kN, 200 kPa allowable, 0.5 m footing under 0.5 m soil: net 179 kPa, 4.469 m², 2.114 m → 2.15 m square, 194.1 kPa
  - Source: ACI 318-19 §13.3.1.1: A = P / (q_all − γ_c t − γ_s h_s)
- US: 100 kip on 3 000 psf, 2 ft footing under 2 ft of soil (150 and 115 pcf): net 2 470 psf, 40.49 ft², 6.36 ft square
  - Source: Same relation in US units: 3 000 − 150 × 2 − 115 × 2 = 2 470 psf
- Strip: 150 kN/m needs 0.838 m, rounded to 0.85 m; rectangle 1.5 : 1 gives 1.75 × 2.60 m
  - Source: B = w / q_net; B = √(A/r), L = r B
- Round footing: D = √(4A/π) = 2.385 m for 4.469 m²; actual pressure never exceeds the allowable after rounding up
  - Source: Circle area
- A footing so deep that its weight uses all the allowable pressure is rejected; a thin footing warns
  - Source: Validation contract; ACI 318 §13.3.1.2 minimum depth
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 179 kPa, 4.469 m², 2.114 m, 2.15 m, 194.1 kPa to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ACI 318-19, Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete, §13.3.1.1 (base area from unfactored loads and permissible soil pressure)
- International Building Code 2021, Table 1806.2 (presumptive load-bearing values)
- EN 1997-1:2004 §6 (spread foundations)

## Froude number calculator for ships and boats

<a id="froude-number"></a>

Folder `froude-number/` · Maritime · Length and depth Froude numbers of a ship or boat, the critical speed in shallow water, the hull-speed and hump speeds, and the wave-making regime.

### Assumptions and caveats

- L is the waterline length (or the length between perpendiculars for a ship) and V the speed through the water; the length Froude number compares the speed with the speed of a water wave as long as the hull.
- The depth Froude number uses the undisturbed water depth h. At Fn_h = 1 the ship moves at the speed of the longest shallow-water wave, √(g h): resistance, wash and squat peak just below it.
- Depth regimes follow the Schiffbau-Versuchsanstalt Potsdam: subcritical below 0.9, critical 0.9 to 1.1, supercritical above 1.1. Most empirical squat formulas are fitted only up to about Fn_h 0.7.
- Length regimes are indicative: hull speed at Fn 0.40, the main resistance hump near Fn 0.5. For fast craft the volumetric Froude number Fn_∇ separates displacement (below 1), semi-planing (1 to 3) and planing (above 3) after Savitsky.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a ship 180 m long at 14 kn has Fn = 7.202 / √(9.80665 × 180) = 0.171; in 20 m of water Fn_h = 0.514 and the critical speed √(9.80665 × 20) = 14.00 m/s = 27.2 kn. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Near the critical speed √(g h): resistance, wash and squat peak. Displacement ships should slow down well before this.
- Depth Froude number above 0.7: squat rises steeply and most squat formulas are outside their range.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 180 m ship at 14 kn: Fn = 0.171; in 20 m of water Fn_h = 0.514 and the critical speed is 27.2 kn
  - Source: Lewis, PNA Vol. II ch. 5 (Fn = V/√(gL), critical speed √(gh)); hand calculation
- At hull speed (Fn = 1/√(2π) = 0.399) the transverse wave is exactly as long as the hull
  - Source: Deep-water wave length λ = 2π V²/g (Lewis, PNA Vol. II ch. 5)
- Depth regimes: Fn_h 0.95 is critical and warns, 1.2 is supercritical; no depth means deep water
  - Source: SVA Potsdam: subcritical < 0.9, critical 0.9–1.1, supercritical > 1.1
- Fast craft: 30 kn with ∇ = 3 m³ gives Fn_∇ = 15.433 / √(9.80665 × 1.4422) = 4.10, planing
  - Source: Savitsky (2003): planing above Fn_∇ = 3; hand calculation
- Zero length and a negative depth are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.171, 0.514, 27.2 kn, 19.1 kn, 32.6 kn to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- E.V. Lewis (ed.), Principles of Naval Architecture, 2nd rev. (SNAME, 1988), Vol. II ch. 5: Froude number, wave-making resistance, humps and hollows, and shallow-water effects
- L. Larsson and H.C. Raven, Ship Resistance and Flow (SNAME PNA series, 2010): wave resistance and shallow-water effects
- Schiffbau-Versuchsanstalt Potsdam (SVA), Shallow water: subcritical (Fn_h < 0.9), critical (0.9–1.1) and supercritical (> 1.1) ranges
- D. Savitsky, On the subject of high-speed monohulls, SNAME Greek Section (2003): displacement, semi-planing and planing ranges of the volumetric Froude number

## Fuel blending and heating viscosity

<a id="fuel-blend-heating"></a>

Folder `fuel-blend-heating/` · Maritime · Blend viscosity (Refutas), density and sulphur of two fuels, and the injection or preheating temperature from ASTM D341.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Refutas blending-index method (ASTM D7152 Wright/Refutas family): the viscosity blending index VBI = 14.534 ln(ln(ν + 0.8)) + 10.975 blends linearly by MASS fraction and the result is inverted to the blend viscosity, all at one temperature; it is accurate to a few per cent for miscible petroleum fuels and does not account for the non-ideal behaviour of some residual/distillate pairs.
- Blend density by mass-weighted volumes (1/ρ = Σ w_i/ρ_i) and sulphur by mass fraction; both are ideal mixing and ignore small volume changes on blending.
- The viscosity–temperature relation is ASTM D341 (Walther): log10 log10(ν + 0.7) = A − B log10 T with T in kelvin, fitted through two known points of the fuel (e.g. the ISO 8217 viscosity at 50 °C and the value at 100 °C or another temperature); with only one point the default second point assumes a typical residual-fuel slope and the temperature result is approximate (±5 °C).
- Target viscosities: injection 10–15 cSt for most medium- and slow-speed engines (makers quote 12–14), transfer pumping below about 1 000 cSt, separator inlet about 98 °C for HFO; the minimum distillate viscosity at the injection pump (≈ 2 cSt) limits how hot MGO may be run — the page flags it.
- Compatibility and stability (asphaltene precipitation when a paraffinic distillate cuts an aromatic residual fuel) are NOT predicted: the Refutas method says nothing about them; check spot tests (ASTM D4740) or TSP before blending on board, and never blend across ISO 8217 categories without a compatibility test.
- Lower calorific value and other ISO 8217 parameters (water, ash, CCAI, pour point) are not blended here.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: Refutas indices VBI(10 cSt) = 23.58 and VBI(100 cSt) = 33.20 give a 50/50 mass blend of 26.7 cSt (not the 55 cSt arithmetic mean); a 380 cSt @ 50 °C / 35 cSt @ 100 °C residual fuel needs 128 °C for 15 cSt and 138 °C for 12 cSt by Walther, matching the usual 125–140 °C HFO injection temperatures.
- Design decision: the blend is specified by the mass fraction of fuel A, with modes that solve for the fraction giving a target viscosity or sulphur, because that is how a cutter stock is actually dosed.
- Design decision: the Walther second reference point defaults to a typical residual slope (ν at 100 °C ≈ 35 cSt for a 380 cSt fuel) with a warning; users should enter the certificate value.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The viscosity–temperature line through the two points is too steep to extrapolate to 40, 50 or 100 °C: check the second viscosity point.
- Second viscosity point left at the default (35 cSt at 100 °C, typical of a 380 cSt fuel): enter the certificate value for your fuel or the heating temperature is approximate (±5 °C).
- Required fraction below 5 % or above 95 %: dosing accuracy on board is unlikely to achieve the target reliably.
- Residual fuel cut with a distillate: check compatibility (ASTM D4740 spot test or TSP) — paraffinic distillates can precipitate asphaltenes and sludge the separators.
- Blend heating uses the Walther slope of fuel A through the blend viscosity: an approximation, since the blend\'s slope lies between the two components.
- Blend sulphur … % exceeds the 0.50 % global cap (MARPOL Annex VI) — compliant only with a scrubber; 0.10 % applies in ECAs.
- Blend sulphur above 0.10 %: not compliant inside Emission Control Areas.
- Refutas blending is accurate to a few per cent for miscible fuels; viscosity, density and sulphur blend ideally here — stability, water, ash and CCAI are not predicted.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The two viscosity reference temperatures must differ by at least 5 °C
- Fuels A and B have the same viscosity: no blend fraction changes it
- Target viscosity … cSt is outside the range of the two fuels (…–… cSt)
- Fuels A and B have the same sulphur content: no blend fraction changes it
- Target sulphur … % is outside the range of the two fuels (…–… %)
- Viscosity must decrease with temperature: check the two reference points

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Refutas indices: VBI(10 cSt) = 23.58, VBI(100 cSt) = 33.20; a 50/50 mass blend gives 26.7 cSt, far below the 55 cSt arithmetic mean; the index inverts exactly
  - Source: Refutas blending index VBI = 14.534 ln(ln(ν + 0.8)) + 10.975 (ASTM D7152 family; Maples 2000)
- 80/20 blend of 380 cSt VLSFO (991 kg/m³, 0.50 % S) with 2.5 cSt MGO (860, 0.10 %): 73.7 cSt, 961.8 kg/m³, 0.42 % S, volume fraction of A 77.6 %
  - Source: Refutas (viscosity), ideal mixing by mass (sulphur) and volume (density)
- Target viscosity 180 cSt needs 91.7 % of fuel A (8.3 % MGO); feeding that fraction back gives 180 cSt; target outside the two fuels is rejected
  - Source: Linear blending of the Refutas index: w_A = (VBI_target − VBI_B)/(VBI_A − VBI_B)
- Target sulphur 0.40 % from 0.50 % and 0.10 % fuels needs 75 % of fuel A; same-sulphur fuels are rejected
  - Source: Mass-fraction sulphur blending
- Walther (ASTM D341) through 380 cSt @ 50 °C and 35 cSt @ 100 °C: B = 3.53, A = 9.27; 15 cSt at 128 °C, 12 cSt at 138 °C, 13 cSt at 134 °C; the fit returns both reference points; 1 000 cSt at 36–38 °C
  - Source: ASTM D341 Walther equation log log(ν + 0.7) = A − B log T; typical HFO injection temperatures 125–140 °C (CIMAC)
- Heating the blend (73.7 cSt at 50 °C with the slope of fuel A) needs a lower temperature than fuel A for the same 13 cSt; an MGO (3 cSt at 40 °C) reaching 3.5 cSt below 40 °C gets the distillate remark
  - Source: Walther slope assumption documented in the register
- Warnings: residual cut with distillate → compatibility warning; blend above 0.50 % S → MARPOL warning; above 0.10 % → ECA warning only
  - Source: ASTM D4740 compatibility practice; MARPOL Annex VI Reg. 14 sulphur limits (0.50 % global, 0.10 % ECA)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: reference temperatures too close, viscosity increasing with temperature, unknown mode
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- A viscosity line too steep to extrapolate gives no 40 and 50 °C values and a warning instead of infinite viscosities
  - Source: Range fuzzing (fuzz.js): 10^(10^y) overflows for extreme Walther slopes
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 36.88, 13.55, 73.7 cSt, 962 kg/m³, 0.42 %, 9.27, 3.53, 134 °C to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASTM D7152, Standard Practice for Calculating Viscosity of a Blend of Petroleum Products (Refutas / Wright methods); Refutas, Shell Oil Co. viscosity blending index (as reproduced in Maples, Petroleum Refinery Process Economics, 2000)
- ASTM D341, Standard Practice for Viscosity-Temperature Equations and Charts for Liquid Petroleum or Hydrocarbon Products (Walther equation, MacCoull chart)
- ISO 8217:2017 Petroleum products — Fuels (class F) — Specifications of marine fuels (viscosity at 50 °C for residual grades, at 40 °C for distillates; Annex on viscosity–temperature)
- CIMAC Guideline "Fuel quality guide — ISO 8217:2017" and engine makers' fuel-oil heating recommendations (injection 10–15 cSt)

## Fuel changeover before an ECA

<a id="fuel-changeover"></a>

Folder `fuel-changeover/` · Maritime · Time and distance before an emission control area to start the changeover so that the fuel at the engines meets the sulphur limit, within the temperature rate.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The changeover is a dilution of the fuel already in the booster circuit (MAN Diesel & Turbo 5212208-3): the new fuel first fills the line to the mixing point (plug flow, delay V_line/Q), then mixes with the circuit volume, which is treated as one well-stirred volume with residence time τ = V/Q, Q being the fuel consumed from the circuit.
- The engines keep burning at the entered rate during the changeover, and the circuit volume is constant; sulphur and temperature of the mixture follow the new-fuel fraction linearly (equal specific heats, no heater or cooler action, no heat loss).
- The temperature at the fuel pump inlet should change by no more than 2 °C/min to avoid thermal shock and sticking of the fuel pumps (MAN 5212208-3), and the viscosity should stay between 2 and 20 cSt. When an instant switch would exceed the limit, the feed is blended linearly over the shortest time that keeps the rate within it.
- MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14.6: a written changeover procedure must allow enough time for the fuel oil service system to be fully flushed of non-compliant fuel before entering the ECA, and the tank volumes, date, time and position at completion are logged.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 2 t/h of fuel at 900 kg/m³ through a 3 m³ circuit gives τ = 1.35 h; from 0.50 % to a 0.05 % fuel the 0.10 % limit is reached after the 0.09 h line delay plus τ ln(9) ≈ 2.97 h; an instant switch would cool the fuel by 70 °C at 0.86 °C/min, within the 2 °C/min limit, so no blending is needed.
- Design decision: the circuit is modelled as one mixed volume because the circulating booster pumps return several times the consumption to the mixing tank; a long, unmixed pipe run belongs in the line volume.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Switching at once would change the fuel temperature by … °C/min; blend the new fuel in over … min, or use the heater to control the rate.
- Check that the viscosity at the engine inlet stays above 2 cSt as the fuel cools; a cooler may be needed for the compliant fuel (MAN 5212208-3).
- No safety margin: the fuel reaches the limit exactly at the boundary.
- Check the compatibility of the two fuels before mixing them in the circuit, and watch the filters during the changeover.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The new fuel must have less sulphur than the limit, or the limit is never reached
- The fuel in use already meets the limit: no changeover is needed

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Washout of a stirred volume: one residence time after an instant switch the engines burn 1 − 1/e = 63.2 % new fuel
  - Source: Levenspiel (1999) ch. 11, response of a stirred volume to a step input
- Default: 2 t/h at 900 kg/m³ through 3 m³ gives τ = 1.35 h; 0.50 % to 0.10 % with 0.05 % fuel takes 0.09 h + τ ln 9 = 3.056 h; start 3.306 h, 46.29 nmi before the boundary at 14 kn
  - Source: MAN 5212208-3: changeover by dilution in the booster circuit; MARPOL Annex VI reg. 14.6
- Sulphur and temperature follow the same new-fuel fraction: at the limit the fuel has cooled to 110 − 70 × 8/9 = 47.78 °C
  - Source: Linear mixing of sulphur content and temperature (equal specific heats)
- A 1 m³ circuit and 140 °C fuel would cool at 3.7 °C/min if switched at once; blending over 37.6 min holds the largest rate at exactly 2 °C/min
  - Source: MAN 5212208-3: at most 2 °C/min at the fuel pump inlet; ramp response of a stirred volume
- The blended response is continuous at the end of the blend and approaches the instant switch as the blend shortens
  - Source: Ramp minus delayed ramp through a first-order lag
- Invalid inputs are rejected: a new fuel above the limit, a fuel in use already compliant, zero consumption
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.35 h, 0.86 °C/min, 3.06 h, 3.31 h, 46.3 nmi to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- MAN Diesel & Turbo, Fuel oil change-over procedure, item 5212208-3 (2010) — dilution in the booster circuit, 2 °C/min, 2–20 cSt
- MARPOL Annex VI, regulation 14.6 — written changeover procedure, flushing before entry, log-book entries
- O. Levenspiel, Chemical Reaction Engineering, 3rd ed., Wiley 1999, chapter 11 — residence time distribution and response of a stirred volume

## Fuel injector size calculator

<a id="fuel-injector-size"></a>

Folder `fuel-injector-size/` · Automotive · Fuel injector size in lb/hr and cc/min from horsepower, BSFC, injector count and duty cycle, or the horsepower injectors support, with fuel pressure.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Fuel flow is the flywheel horsepower times the brake specific fuel consumption (BSFC); each injector delivers its share at no more than the maximum duty cycle, the fraction of each engine cycle it is open.
- Typical gasoline BSFC: 0.45 to 0.50 lb/(hp·h) naturally aspirated and 0.55 to 0.75 with a supercharger or turbo, which run richer to control knock (EngineLabs); the presets use 0.50, 0.60 and 0.65.
- E85 needs about 1.5 times the fuel mass of gasoline for the same air (stoichiometric air-fuel ratio 9.8 against 14.7), so its presets are the gasoline values × 1.5; methanol, diesel or other fuels need a BSFC from the engine builder.
- Injector flow rises with the square root of the pressure across the injector (fuel pressure minus manifold pressure), as for any orifice; on a boosted engine with a 1:1 regulator the difference stays at the base pressure.
- lb/hr converts to cc/min with the fuel density: 720 kg/m³ for gasoline, which gives the usual 10.5 cc/min per lb/hr (EN 228 allows 720 to 775 kg/m³), and 780 kg/m³ for E85.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 450 hp naturally aspirated on gasoline (BSFC 0.50), 8 injectors at 80 % duty: total 225 lb/hr, 35.2 lb/hr per injector, 369.1 cc/min at 720 kg/m³; 42 lb/hr injectors support 537.6 hp, or 620.8 hp at 58 psi instead of 43.5 psi. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A duty cycle above 85 % leaves the injector little time to close and open; injector makers generally suggest 85 % at most (EngineLabs).
- A BSFC below 0.35 lb/(hp·h) is better than spark-ignition engines achieve on gasoline; check the value.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 450 hp NA gasoline (BSFC 0.50), 8 injectors at 80 %: 225 lb/hr in total, 35.2 lb/hr each, 369.1 cc/min
  - Source: EngineLabs (Acosta 2024): lb/hr = hp × BSFC / (injectors × duty cycle); hand calculation
- 650 hp at BSFC 0.50 on 8 injectors at 85 % needs 650 × 0.5 / 6.8 = 47.8 lb/hr
  - Source: Same formula; hand calculation
- Gasoline at 720 kg/m³: 1 lb/hr = 453.592 / 60 / 0.72 = 10.50 cc/min, the usual conversion
  - Source: Unit conversion; EN 228 density range 720 to 775 kg/m³
- Reverse: eight 42 lb/hr injectors at 80 % support 42 × 8 × 0.8 / 0.5 = 537.6 hp; at 58 psi instead of 43.5 psi, 620.8 hp
  - Source: hp = flow × n × DC / BSFC; orifice flow ∝ √Δp
- E85 needs 14.7 / 9.8 = 1.5 times the gasoline flow: a turbo E85 engine uses BSFC 0.975
  - Source: Stoichiometric air-fuel ratios 14.7 (gasoline) and 9.8 (E85); Heywood Appendix D
- Fractional injectors, a 5 % duty cycle and an unknown fuel are rejected; 95 % duty warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 225.0 lb/h, 35.2 lb/h, 369.1 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- G. Acosta, How To Calculate What Size Fuel Injectors Your Engine Needs, EngineLabs, 21 June 2024 (lb/hr = hp × BSFC / (injectors × duty cycle); BSFC 0.45–0.50 NA, 0.55–0.75 forced induction; maximum duty cycle about 85 %)
- J.B. Heywood, Internal Combustion Engine Fundamentals, McGraw-Hill 1988, Section 2.9 (brake specific fuel consumption) and Appendix D (stoichiometric air-fuel ratios)
- EN 228 Automotive fuels — Unleaded petrol — Requirements and test methods (density at 15 °C 720.0 to 775.0 kg/m³)

## Fuel net specific energy and CO₂ factor

<a id="fuel-lcv-co2"></a>

Folder `fuel-lcv-co2/` · Maritime · ISO 8217 net and gross specific energy from density, water, ash and sulphur; CO₂ factor by IMO grade or carbon content; g CO₂/MJ.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Net (lower) and gross (higher) specific energy from the ISO 8217:2017 Annex H correlations in density at 15 °C and the water, ash and sulphur mass fractions — H.1/H.2 for residual fuels and H.3/H.4 for distillates — "with a degree of accuracy acceptable for normal purposes" (about ±0.2 MJ/kg); a bomb-calorimeter value (ISO 1928 / ASTM D240) supersedes the estimate, and the correlations do not apply to biofuels, methanol, LNG or other non-petroleum fuels.
- Energy per tonne is Q_net × 1 000 (GJ/t) and energy per litre Q_net × ρ15/1 000 (MJ/L) at 15 °C; the volume-based figure changes with temperature through the VCF (bunker-quantity calculator).
- The CO₂ factor is either the IMO conversion factor for the fuel grade (MEPC.364(79)/CII guidelines: HFO 3.114, LFO 3.151, MGO 3.206 t CO₂/t fuel, derived from typical carbon contents of 84.9/85.9/87.5 %) or computed from a measured carbon content as C_F = w_C × 44.0095/12.011 assuming complete combustion; the fuel-specific value is what the EU MRV/ETS regulation accepts with a laboratory analysis.
- Emission intensity per unit energy g CO₂/MJ = C_F × 1 000/Q_net(MJ/kg) is the tank-to-wake basis FuelEU Maritime uses (HFO 76.9, MGO 75.1 g CO₂/MJ with the default values); well-to-wake and methane/N₂O terms are in the EU ETS and FuelEU calculator.
- The 42 700 kJ/kg reference is the ISO 3046 / ISO 19030 "normal fuel" to which shop-test SFOC and performance baselines refer; mass consumption of the actual fuel = reference-fuel mass × 42 700/Q_net.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: a typical HFO (991 kg/m³, 0.2 % water, 0.05 % ash, 0.5 % sulphur) gives Q_net 40.93 MJ/kg and Q_gross 43.27 MJ/kg; a typical MGO (850 kg/m³, 0.05 % water, 0.01 % ash, 0.1 % sulphur) gives 42.71 MJ/kg — the 40.5–41 and 42.7 MJ/kg values quoted for these grades; HFO 3.114 t/t ÷ 40.5 MJ/kg = 76.9 g CO₂/MJ matches the FuelEU default.
- Transcription from the ISO 8217:2017 PDF (Annex H, formulae H.1–H.4): the sulphur and water terms print as "0,094 2 w_s" and "0,024 49 w_w", i.e. 0.0942 w_s and 0.02449 w_w; the gross formulas have no water term.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Density below 900 kg/m³ with the residual formula: a distillate or light blend — check the fuel class.
- Density above 900 kg/m³ with the distillate formula: likely a residual grade — check the fuel class.
- The ISO 8217 energy correlations are for petroleum fuels: the specific energy shown does not apply to LNG, LPG or alcohols — use the FuelEU default LCV for those.
- Water above 0.5 %: beyond the ISO 8217 limit for most grades; the energy is reduced both by dilution and by evaporation of the water.
- Correlation accuracy about ±0.2 MJ/kg: a bomb-calorimeter test (ISO 1928) supersedes it for custody or ETS purposes.
- CO₂ factor assumes complete combustion of the carbon; CH₄, N₂O and the well-to-wake chain are in the EU ETS / FuelEU calculator.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Residual fuel H.1: ρ 991, 0.2 % water, 0.05 % ash, 0.5 % sulphur → (46.704 − 8.6443 + 3.1385) × 0.9925 + 0.0471 − 0.0049 = 40.93 MJ/kg; gross H.2 = 43.27 MJ/kg
  - Source: ISO 8217:2017 Annex H formulae (H.1), (H.2)
- Distillate H.3: ρ 850, 0.05 % water, 0.01 % ash, 0.1 % sulphur → 42.71 MJ/kg (the usual MGO value); gross 45.50 MJ/kg
  - Source: ISO 8217:2017 Annex H formulae (H.3), (H.4); FuelEU default MGO LCV 42.7 MJ/kg
- Energy per tonne and litre: HFO 40.93 GJ/t and 40.56 MJ/L at 991 kg/m³; MGO 36.30 MJ/L — the distillate has more energy per kg but less per litre
  - Source: Unit conversions at 15 °C
- CO₂ factor: VLSFO grade 3.151 t/t implies 86.0 % carbon; HFO 3.114/40.5 MJ/kg = 76.9 g CO₂/MJ (FuelEU default); measured 86.5 % carbon → C_F = 0.865 × 44.0095/12.011 = 3.169
  - Source: MEPC.364(79) Table 1; FuelEU Annex II defaults; stoichiometry C + O₂ → CO₂
- Reference-fuel scaling: 42 700/40 930 = 1.0432 t of this HFO per tonne of reference fuel; MGO at 42.71 MJ/kg scales by 0.9998; warnings for a mis-classed fuel and for LNG with the petroleum formula
  - Source: ISO 3046 / ISO 19030 42 700 kJ/kg reference; behaviour specification
- Validation: density outside 600–1 200, unknown grade and carbon content above 100 % are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 40.93 MJ/kg, 43.27 MJ/kg, 40.93, 40.6, 3.151, 86.0 %, 77.0, 77.0 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 8217:2017 Petroleum products — Fuels (class F) — Specifications of marine fuels, Annex H (informative) Calculation of specific energy, formulae H.1–H.4
- IMO Resolution MEPC.364(79) 2022 Guidelines on the method of calculation of the attained EEDI, Table 1 (C_F per fuel and carbon content)
- Regulation (EU) 2023/1805 (FuelEU Maritime) Annex II — default emission factors (HFO LCV 0.0405 MJ/g, C_F 3.114; MGO 0.0427, 3.206)
- ISO 3046-1:2002 clause 13 / ISO 19030-3:2016 — 42 700 kJ/kg reference fuel

## Fuel consumption and voyage cost

<a id="fuel-voyage-cost"></a>

Folder `fuel-voyage-cost/` · Maritime · Fuel burned, time at sea, bunker cost and CO₂ for a passage from distance, speed and engine power or daily consumption.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Speed and power are constant over the passage; split the voyage into legs when they are not.
- SFOC must correspond to the power entered and to the fuel in use: shop-test SFOC is on 42 700 kJ/kg reference fuel (scale by 42 700 / LCV), and service SFOC is typically 3–6 % above shop test.
- The margin applies to main-engine fuel only and stands in for weather, fouling and manoeuvring: 10–15 % at the design stage, 0 when the daily figure already comes from recent noon reports.
- Auxiliary and port consumption are flat daily rates; reefers, cargo pumps, tank heating and inert gas generation can raise them substantially.
- CO₂ is tank-to-wake (combustion only) with the IMO MEPC.364(79) carbon factors; well-to-wake factors are larger.
- Cost covers bunkers only — no port dues, canal fees, lubricants or hire; a single currency with no exchange-rate conversion.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the default passage was checked by hand (8 000 kW × 175 g/kWh = 33.6 t/day; × 8.9286 days = 300.0 t; cost 177 277 $) and the CO₂ factors against MEPC.364(79) Table 1.
- Design decision: the CO₂ factors live in shared/fuels.js so the fuel and CII calculators can never disagree.
- Design decision: the margin multiplies main-engine fuel only; auxiliary and port figures are taken as entered because they are usually measured, not modelled.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Speed above 25 kn is unusual for a merchant ship — check the value.
- SFOC below 155 g/kWh is better than the best large two-stroke engines — check the value.
- No margin applied: a shop-test SFOC and calm-water power understate real consumption by typically 10–15 %.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 3 000 nmi at 14 kn takes 214.29 h = 8.9286 days
  - Source: Time = distance / speed; 1 knot = 1 nmi/h by definition (BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed., Table 8)
- 8 000 kW at 175 g/kWh burns 33.6 t/day
  - Source: SFOC definition, ISO 3046-1:2002 §3 and MAN Energy Solutions, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion (2018): fuel = P × SFOC × t
- Default passage: 300.0 t main engine, 22.32 t auxiliaries, cost 177 277 $ at 550 $/t
  - Source: Hand calculation: 33.6 t/day × 8.9286 d = 300.0 t; 2.5 × 8.9286 = 22.321 t; 322.321 t × 550 $/t
- Daily-consumption basis: 30 t/day for a 10-day passage = 300 t, 165 000 $
  - Source: Hand calculation: 3 360 nmi / 14 kn = 240 h = 10 days
- CO₂ factors: 100 t HFO → 311.4 t, MGO → 320.6 t, LNG → 275.0 t
  - Source: IMO Resolution MEPC.364(79), 2022 EEDI calculation guidelines, Table 1 (CF values)
- A 10 % margin raises main-engine fuel from 300 t to 330 t; port fuel 2 days × 3 t/day = 6 t
  - Source: Hand calculation; sea margin practice per MAN Energy Solutions, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion (2018), "Sea margin"
- Unit layer: 3 000 nmi = 5 556 km, 14 kn = 7.2022 m/s, 1 long ton = 1.01605 t
  - Source: 1 nmi = 1852 m (International Hydrographic Conference 1929); 1 long ton = 2240 lb × 0.45359237 kg
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero speed, negative distance, unknown fuel
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 214.3 h, 33.6 t/day, 300.0 t, 22.3 t, 322.3 t, 107.4 kg/nmi, 177 277 $, 59.1 $/nmi to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 3046-1:2002 — reciprocating internal combustion engines, performance (SFOC definition)
- MAN Energy Solutions, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion (2018)
- IMO Resolution MEPC.364(79), 2022 EEDI calculation guidelines, Table 1 (CF factors)
- BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed. (knot and nautical mile definitions)

## Gas compressibility factor Z calculator (natural gas and pure gases)

<a id="gas-compressibility"></a>

Folder `gas-compressibility/` · Process · Real-gas Z factor and density of natural gas by Sutton and Dranchuk–Abou-Kassem (Standing–Katz), with Wichert–Aziz, or of a pure gas from Tc, Pc and ω.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Natural gas: pseudo-critical properties follow Sutton (1985) from the gas specific gravity (fitted for 0.57 to 1.68), and Z follows the Dranchuk–Abou-Kassem (1975) fit of the Standing–Katz chart, used here for reduced temperatures 1.05 (the lowest chart isotherm) to 3.0 and reduced pressures up to 30, with an average error of about 0.5 % against the chart.
- The Wichert–Aziz correction for H₂S and CO₂ applies to sour gases with up to about 50 % acid gas; nitrogen and water vapour are not corrected and should be small.
- Pure gas: the Pitzer second-virial correlation with the Abbott coefficients is valid only at low density; the calculator refuses states where the molar volume falls below twice the critical volume, estimated with Z_c = 0.291 − 0.080 ω.
- Pressures and temperatures are absolute; the gas is a single vapour phase above its dew point.
- Density is P M / (Z R T) with M = 28.964 γ for natural gas; Bg is the reservoir volume per standard volume at 60 °F and 14.696 psia.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a gas of specific gravity 0.65 at 2 000 psia and 200 °F has Tpc = 365.1 °R and ppc = 670.1 psia (Sutton), Tpr = 1.807, ppr = 2.98, and Z = 0.897 by DAK; density 94.95 kg/m³ (5.93 lb/ft³) against 85.20 kg/m³ for an ideal gas. Checked by hand.
- DAK reproduces the Standing–Katz chart readings digitised by Reyes (zFactor package): Tpr 1.3 at ppr 1.5 and 2.5 gives 0.756 and 0.638, Tpr 1.5 0.859 and 0.794, Tpr 2.0 0.956 and 0.941, all within 1 %. Pitzer–Abbott reproduces the n-butane example of Smith, Van Ness and Abbott (510 K, 25 bar: Z = 0.879).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Reduced pressure below 0.2, under the fitted range of the Standing–Katz chart; Z is close to 1 here and the result tends to the ideal gas.
- Reduced temperature below 1.2 near the pseudo-critical pressure: the Standing–Katz chart is steep here and Z is least accurate (a few per cent).
- Below the critical temperature the gas condenses at its vapour pressure: check that the pressure is below the saturation pressure at this temperature.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Temperature: the reduced temperature T/Tpc is …; the Standing–Katz chart and its Dranchuk–Abou-Kassem fit cover 1.05 to 3.0.
- Pressure: the reduced pressure p/ppc is …; the Dranchuk–Abou-Kassem fit is valid up to 30.
- Pressure: no gas-phase Z was found for these reduced conditions; check the pressure and temperature.
- Pressure: the gas is too dense for the second-virial correlation (molar volume below twice the critical volume); use a lower pressure, or the Lee–Kesler tables or a cubic equation of state.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- DAK matches Standing–Katz chart readings within 1 %: Tpr 1.3 → 0.835, 0.756, 0.638; 1.5 → 0.900, 0.859, 0.794; 2.0 → 0.956, 0.941
  - Source: Standing–Katz chart values digitised by Reyes, zFactor R package ("StandingKatz chart" article), Tpr 1.3, 1.5, 2.0 at ppr 1.0, 1.5, 2.5
- n-butane at 510 K and 25 bar (Tc 425.1 K, Pc 37.96 bar, ω 0.200): Tr 1.200, Pr 0.659, Z = 0.879
  - Source: Smith, Van Ness and Abbott, Introduction to Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics, 7th ed., §3.6 n-butane example (virial result Z = 0.879, V ≈ 1 491 cm³/mol)
- Sutton at γ = 0.7: Tpc = 377.59 °R, ppc = 663.34 psia; Wichert–Aziz with 10 % H₂S and 5 % CO₂: ε = 20.74 °R, 356.85 °R, 623.83 psia
  - Source: Ahmed, Reservoir Engineering Handbook, ch. 2 (Sutton 1985 and Wichert–Aziz 1972 equations); hand calculation
- Worked example: γ 0.65 at 2 000 psia and 200 °F gives Tpr 1.807, ppr 2.984, Z 0.897 and 94.95 kg/m³
  - Source: Hand calculation with Sutton (1985) and DAK (1975); ρ = p M / (Z R T) with M = 28.964 γ
- Low pressure tends to the ideal gas: at 15 psia Z is above 0.995 for natural gas and for n-butane far above Tc
  - Source: Limiting case: Z → 1 as P → 0
- Outside the validity ranges the calculator refuses: Tpr below 1.05, ppr above 30, a dense state for the virial method
  - Source: Validation contract (DAK / Standing–Katz range; Poling et al.: second-virial truncation only to half the critical density)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 365.1, 670.1 psi, 1.807, 2.98, 0.897, 94.95 kg/m³ to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Ahmed, T., Reservoir Engineering Handbook, 4th ed., Gulf Professional Publishing, ch. 2: Sutton (1985) pseudo-critical correlations, Wichert–Aziz (1972) correction and the Dranchuk–Abou-Kassem (1975) equation
- Dranchuk, P.M. and Abou-Kassem, J.H. (1975), Calculation of Z factors for natural gases using equations of state, J. Canadian Petroleum Technology 14(3), 34–36; Standing, M.B. and Katz, D.L. (1942), Trans. AIME 146, 140–149
- Smith, J.M., Van Ness, H.C. and Abbott, M.M., Introduction to Chemical Engineering Thermodynamics, 7th ed., §3.6, eqs. 3.61–3.66 (Pitzer correlation, Abbott B⁰ and B¹) and the n-butane worked example
- Poling, B.E., Prausnitz, J.M. and O'Connell, J.P., The Properties of Gases and Liquids, 5th ed., ch. 4 (second-virial truncation adequate up to about half the critical density)

## Gear ratio, rpm and torque

<a id="gear-ratio"></a>

Folder `gear-ratio/` · Mechanical · Gear ratio from tooth counts for one or two stages, with output speed, torque and power after the losses of each stage.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Gears mesh without slip, so the speed ratio is exactly the tooth ratio; belts slip by 1 to 2 %, which this does not include.
- Each stage loses the same fraction of the power it transmits; a spur or helical stage is typically 97 to 99 % efficient, a worm stage much less (50 to 90 %).
- Idler gears change the direction of rotation but not the ratio, so they are left out of the tooth counts.
- The output torque is the steady value; starting, shock and inertia loads are covered by the service factor used when choosing the gearbox.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 12-tooth pinion driving 48 teeth at 1450 rpm and 20 N·m gives a ratio of 4.00, 362.5 rpm and 78.4 N·m at 98 %. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A pinion with fewer than 17 teeth (20° pressure angle) undercuts unless its profile is shifted; check the gear design.
- More than about 8:1 in one spur or helical stage makes a large, heavy wheel; two stages are usual.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 12 teeth driving 48 at 1450 rpm and 20 N·m, 98 %: ratio 4, 362.5 rpm, 78.4 N·m, 3.04 kW in and 60.7 W lost
  - Source: Shigley, Mechanical Engineering Design, ch. 13: n_out = n_in z₁/z₂; T_out = T_in (z₂/z₁) η
- Two stages 12:48 and 15:45 multiply to 12:1; two 98 % stages pass 96.04 % of the power
  - Source: Shigley, ch. 13: train value of a compound train = product of the stage ratios; ISO 14179-1 per-stage losses
- A step-up of 40 teeth driving 20 doubles the speed and halves the torque, before losses
  - Source: Gear ratio below 1 (overdrive)
- A known ratio of 3.5 gives the same output as matching tooth counts 14:49
  - Source: Ratio mode equals tooth mode
- A 12-tooth pinion warns about undercut; fractional teeth and zero speed are rejected
  - Source: Minimum teeth for a 20° full-depth pinion without undercut is 17 (Shigley, ch. 13); validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 4.00, 362.5 rpm, 78.4 N·m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 11th ed., ch. 13 (gear trains: train value e = product of driving teeth / product of driven teeth)
- ISO 14179-1:2001 Gears — Thermal capacity (typical mesh losses of cylindrical gears, about 1 % per stage)

## Gear ratio and vehicle speed calculator

<a id="gear-speed"></a>

Folder `gear-speed/` · Automotive · Vehicle speed from rpm, gear ratio, final drive and tire diameter, the rpm at a speed, and speedometer error after changing tire size.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Road speed is engine rpm divided by the overall ratio (gear × final drive) times the tire circumference; there is no clutch, torque-converter or tire slip.
- The tire diameter is the unloaded overall diameter; under load the rolling radius is a little smaller, so the true speed is a little lower than the result and tire makers list slightly more revolutions per mile.
- With a locked torque converter or a manual gearbox the engine and wheels are tied together; an unlocked converter slips, so the engine then turns faster than calculated.
- The speedometer is assumed to read correctly with the tire diameter it was calibrated for; it counts wheel or output-shaft revolutions, so it reads high with a smaller tire and low with a larger one.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 3 000 rpm, 1.00 gear, 3.73 final drive, 28 in tire: 67.0 mph (3 000 × 28 / (3.73 × 336.13)); 720.3 tire revolutions per mile; with the speedometer calibrated for a 26 in tire it reads 62.2 mph, −7.1 %. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above 9 000 rpm: beyond the redline of most car engines; check the ratios and the speed.
- The tire diameter differs from the speedometer calibration by more than 3 %; the speedometer and odometer should be recalibrated.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 3 000 rpm, direct 1.00 gear, 3.73 axle, 28 in tire: 3 000 × 28 / (3.73 × 336.13) = 67.0 mph
  - Source: Hand calculation, mph = rpm × D[in] / (i × 336.13), 336.13 = 63 360 / (60 π)
- Overdrive 0.70 with 3.73 and 28 in tires turns 2 194 rpm at 70 mph
  - Source: Inverse of the same relation: rpm = mph × i × 336.13 / D
- A 28 in tire makes 63 360 / (π × 28) = 720.3 revolutions per mile
  - Source: Circumference π D; 1 mile = 63 360 in (NIST)
- Speedometer set for 26 in, tire 28 in: at a true 67.0 mph it reads 62.2 mph, −7.1 %; same tire, no error
  - Source: Reading = true speed × D_cal / D (the speedometer counts revolutions)
- A zero gear ratio, a 0.05 m tire and an unknown mode are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 3.730, 67.0 mph, 720.3, 62.2 mph, −7.1 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- T.D. Gillespie, Fundamentals of Vehicle Dynamics, SAE 1992, Chapter 2 Acceleration performance (road speed from engine speed, overall gear ratio and tire radius)
- NIST Handbook 44 and SP 811: 1 mile = 63 360 in, 1 mph = 0.44704 m/s (exact)

## Generator load sharing with droop

<a id="generator-droop"></a>

Folder `generator-droop/` · Electrical · Active load sharing and bus frequency of paralleled generating sets with speed droop, with an optional isochronous set taking the balance.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Each droop governor follows a straight line from its no-load frequency down by D % of the rated frequency at rated power (Woodward application notes 01302 and 50528: droop = (no-load − full-load speed)/rated speed); on a common bus the frequency is where the summed droop lines meet the load.
- Sets with the same droop and the same no-load setting share load in proportion to their ratings; the operator moves a set's line, and so its load, with the speed setting, which does not change the bus frequency when another source holds it.
- One isochronous set holds its set frequency and takes the balance of the load while it stays between no load and its rating; below, it unloads (and would be motored) and the bus frequency rises; above, it stays at its limit and the bus frequency falls until the droop sets take the rest (Woodward 01302).
- Steady state only: governor dynamics, reactive load sharing (voltage droop), engine power limits other than the rating, and load-dependent start and stop are not modelled.
- The deviation from the proportional share is expressed as a percentage of the largest set's rating; the permitted deviation for ships is set by IEC 60092-301 (6.3.2, load sharing) and the class rules.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: three sets of 1000, 1000 and 800 kW, all 4 % droop from 62.4 Hz on a 60 Hz base, carrying 1800 kW: f = 62.4 − 2.4 × 1800/2800 = 60.857 Hz, each set at 64.3 % of its rating; lowering all speed settings by 0.857 Hz restores 60 Hz.
- Design decision: at most one isochronous set is accepted, because two isochronous sets on one bus need a load-sharing link between their controls.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- … is overloaded at … % of its rating.
- … takes negative power (… kW): it is motored and its reverse-power relay will trip it.
- The load exceeds the total rating of … kW.
- The isochronous set is at …; the bus frequency has moved to … Hz.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- …: expected name; rated kW; droop % or iso; frequency Hz
- …: the rating must be a number greater than zero
- …: the droop must be between 0 and 20 %, or "iso"
- …: the frequency must be a number greater than zero
- Enter at least one generating set
- Only one isochronous set can be modelled; the others must run in droop
- The isochronous set alone cannot carry … kW

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Woodward droop definition: a set from 60 Hz at no load with 10 % droop runs at 54 Hz at full load
  - Source: Woodward Application Note 50528: (no-load − full-load speed)/rated = 6/60 = 10 %
- Equal droop and settings share load in proportion to rating: 1800 kW on 1000 + 1000 + 800 kW sets at 64.3 % each and 62.4 − 2.4 × 1800/2800 = 60.857 Hz
  - Source: Woodward Application Note 01302; straight-line droop characteristics
- Unequal droops: every set lies on its own line at the common frequency and the loads add up to 1800 kW
  - Source: P_i = P_r (f_nl − f)/(D f_r), Σ P_i = load
- Isochronous set with a droop set: at 60 Hz the droop set carries 1000 kW and the isochronous set the balance of 800 kW
  - Source: Woodward Application Note 01302, isochronous and droop units on an isolated system
- Beyond the isochronous set's rating the bus slows to 59.76 Hz at 2100 kW; below the droop setting it unloads and the bus rises to 61.68 Hz at 300 kW
  - Source: Woodward Application Note 01302
- Invalid inputs are rejected: two isochronous sets, a droop of 30 %, a line with three fields
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 60.857 Hz to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Woodward, Application Note 01302 Speed droop and power generation (1991)
- Woodward, Application Note 50528 (2003) — measuring droop as (no-load − full-load speed)/rated speed
- IEC 60092-301:2025, Electrical installations in ships — Equipment — Generators and motors, 6.3 parallel operation (load sharing)

## Generator load, kVA and fuel

<a id="generator-load"></a>

Folder `generator-load/` · Electrical · Load factor, kVA, current and N−1 redundancy of parallel diesel generators, the recommended number of sets for a load band, and fuel, cost and CO₂ from SFOC.

### Assumptions and caveats

- All running sets are identical and share the active load equally (isochronous or matched droop); reactive load sharing and unequal set sizes are not modelled.
- Rated kW = rated kVA × rated power factor (0.8 for most marine alternators); the load is limited by the engine kW and by the alternator kVA, whichever is reached first, and both percentages are reported.
- Load percentage limits are planning policy, not physics: the default band is 30–85 % (below ≈ 30 % medium-speed diesels suffer fouling and wet stacking; above ≈ 85–90 % no margin remains for transients), and ISO 8528-1 prime rating allows 10 % overload for one hour in twelve.
- N−1: the load that remains if one set trips is divided among the others; SOLAS II-1 Reg. 41 and class rules require essential services to be supplied with any one generator out of service — the check here is a simple kW comparison without transient analysis or preferential tripping.
- Specific fuel consumption: the entered value is at 100 % load and is scaled with a typical medium-speed part-load curve (×1.02 at 75 %, ×1.10 at 50 %, ×1.27 at 25 %, linear between); engine shop-test curves should replace it for a real plant, and the value refers to the reference fuel (42 700 kJ/kg) unless corrected.
- Fuel per day = electrical load × SFOC × hours; alternator efficiency (≈ 95–97 %) is included only if the SFOC is given per electrical kWh — engine project guides quote per brake kWh, so divide by the alternator efficiency when using them.
- CO₂ uses the IMO MEPC.364(79) carbon factor of the selected fuel (shared/fuels.js).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: 2 × 1 000 kVA at 0.8 with 1 200 kW at 0.85 gives 75 % load, 1 412 kVA, 1 852 A at 440 V, an N−1 load of 150 % (overload) and 6.2 t/day at 214 g/kWh (SFOC 210 × 1.02 at 75 %); the recommended count for 1 200 kW in a 30–85 % band is two sets.
- Design decision: the SFOC part-load curve is a typical multiplier table rather than a fit, to keep the behaviour transparent; users with shop-test data override it by entering the SFOC at the actual load with the curve switched off (set the 100 % value to the known value and read the warning).
- Design decision: both the kW-based (engine) and kVA-based (alternator) load percentages are shown because low power factor loads reach the alternator limit first.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Engine overloaded: the active load exceeds the kW rating of the running sets.
- Alternator overloaded on kVA while the engine is within kW: the load power factor is below the alternator rating — improve the power factor or start another set.
- Low-load operation below the band minimum: medium-speed diesels foul and wet-stack below about 30 %; stop a set if redundancy allows.
- N−1 check fails: with one set tripped the others would be overloaded beyond the 10 % short-time allowance.
- SFOC scaled from the 100 % value with a typical part-load curve (× …); use the shop-test curve for a real plant.
- SFOC per electrical kWh assumed; project-guide values are per brake kWh and must be divided by the alternator efficiency (≈ 0.96).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The maximum of the load band must exceed the minimum

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Two 1 000 kVA sets at 0.8 pf: 1 600 kW installed; 1 200 kW at 0.85 → 75 % on kW, 1 412 kVA = 70.6 % on kVA, 600 kW per set, 1 852 A at 440 V
  - Source: Rated kW = kVA × pf (ISO 8528-1); S = P / pf; I = S / (√3 V)
- N−1: 1 200 kW on one remaining 800 kW set is 150 % → redundancy FAIL and a load-shedding warning; 600 kW load gives 75 % → OK
  - Source: SOLAS II-1 Reg. 41 / IEC 60092-301 (supply with one generator out of service); ISO 8528-1 10 % overload allowance
- Recommended sets for a 30–85 % band: 1 200 kW → 2 sets (75 %); 500 kW → 1 set (62.5 %); 2 000 kW → 3 sets (83 %); 200 kW → 1 set at 25 % with a low-load warning
  - Source: Planning band 30–85 % (common practice; low-load fouling below ≈ 30 %, transient margin above ≈ 85 %)
- Alternator kVA limit: 1 400 kW at pf 0.6 on two 1 000 kVA sets is 87.5 % on kW but 117 % on kVA → overload on the alternator
  - Source: Alternator rated in kVA; low power factor loads reach the kVA limit before the engine kW limit (ISO 8528-3)
- SFOC part-load curve: ×1.0 at 100 %, ×1.02 at 75 %, ×1.10 at 50 %, ×1.27 at 25 %, linear between (×1.06 at 62.5 %); switched off it stays at the entered value
  - Source: Typical medium-speed genset SFOC curves (MAN and Wärtsilä project guides: +2 % at 75 %, +10 % at 50 %, +25–30 % at 25 % load)
- Fuel, cost and CO₂: 1 200 kW × 214.2 g/kWh = 257.0 kg/h, 6.17 t/day, 4 318 $ at 700 $/t, 19.8 t CO₂ (MGO 3.206), 28.8 MWh
  - Source: Fuel = P × SFOC × t; IMO MEPC.364(79) CF for MGO 3.206 t CO₂/t fuel
- Invalid inputs fail fast: fractional set count, band maximum below minimum, unknown fuel
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1 600 kW, 1 412 kVA, 600 kW, 75 %, 70.6 %, 1 852 A, 150 %, 75 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 8528-1:2018, Reciprocating internal combustion engine driven alternating current generating sets — Part 1: Application, ratings and performance (prime, continuous and standby ratings, 10 % overload)
- SOLAS Chapter II-1 Regulation 40–41 and IEC 60092-301 (main source of electrical power: supply with one generator out of service)
- MAN Energy Solutions and Wärtsilä genset project guides (typical SFOC versus load for medium-speed engines)
- IMO Resolution MEPC.364(79) Table 1 (CO₂ carbon factors)

## Generator size calculator

<a id="generator-size"></a>

Folder `generator-size/` · Electrical · What size generator you need: running watts of your loads, the surge of the largest motor starting, and the minimum running, starting and kVA ratings.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Running watts are what each load draws once running; starting (surge) watts are what a motor load draws for a few seconds while it starts. Take both from the nameplate or the manual; the default list is an illustrative example only.
- By default the motors start one at a time, so only the largest surge adds to the running total; choose "all together" if several motors can start at the same moment, for example after a power cut.
- The running rating keeps the load at or below the chosen maximum loading of the generator (80 % by default), which leaves margin for loads switching on and avoids running flat out for hours.
- Portable and inverter generators are rated in watts at unity power factor; standby sets are rated in kVA at a power factor of 0.8 (ISO 8528-1), so their kVA is the kW divided by 0.8.
- Altitude and high ambient temperature reduce the output of an engine-driven generator; apply the derating in the manufacturer's data.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: the default list runs 4 450 W; the furnace fan has the largest surge, 1 550 W, so the peak is 6 000 W and the running rating at 80 % loading is 5 563 W. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- No starting watts entered: motors such as fridges, pumps and air conditioners draw two to three times their running watts for a few seconds when they start.
- Above about 25 kW, a permanently installed standby set with a transfer switch sized by an electrician is the usual choice.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Loads, line …: write "name; running watts; starting watts" (starting watts optional).
- Loads, line …: the running watts "…" is not a number of 0 or more.
- Loads, line …: the starting watts must be a number at least equal to the running watts.
- Loads: enter at least one load.
- Loads: the running watts add up to zero.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Default house list: 4 450 W running, largest surge 1 550 W (furnace fan), peak 6 000 W, 5 563 W running rating at 80 %, 6.95 kVA standby
  - Source: 700 + 1 050 + 800 + 600 + 1 000 + 300 = 4 450 W; max(1 500, 1 100, 1 550) = 1 550 W; 4 450 / 0.8 = 5 562.5 W; ISO 8528-1 kVA at pf 0.8
- All motors starting together add every surge: 4 450 + 1 500 + 1 100 + 1 550 = 8 600 W
  - Source: Simultaneous starting after a power cut
- RV air conditioner 1 800 W running and 3 000 W starting with 400 W of other loads at 100 % loading: 2 200 W running, 3 400 W starting
  - Source: W_peak = W_run + (W_start − W_run) of the air conditioner
- Parser: comments, blank lines, tabs and thousands with spaces are read; starting watts default to running; the running rating is never below the peak in the starting rating
  - Source: Input format of the page
- Bad lines are rejected with their line number: text for watts, starting below running, too many fields, an empty list
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 4 450 W, 1 550 W, 6 000 W, 5 563 W to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 8528-1:2018 Reciprocating internal combustion engine driven alternating current generating sets (ratings, power factor 0.8)
- NFPA 70, National Electrical Code (2023), Article 702 (optional standby systems: the system must carry the load it is connected to)
- NEMA MG 1-2021, Motors and Generators, Part 10 (locked-rotor kVA code letters behind the surge of motor loads)

## Gravel calculator: cubic yards and tons

<a id="gravel"></a>

Folder `gravel/` · Civil · Cubic yards, m³ and tons of gravel, crushed stone, sand or topsoil for an area and depth, with compaction allowance, truck loads and cost.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The area is a rectangle, or an area you enter, covered to a uniform depth; split irregular areas into rectangles and add them.
- Tonnage uses the loose bulk density of the delivered material from the Caterpillar Performance Handbook; the real figure varies with moisture, grading and rock type, so use the supplier's weight per yard when you have it.
- The compaction allowance covers the volume lost when loose material is spread and compacted; 10 to 15 % is usual for base courses and less for loose decorative stone.
- Truck loads are the larger of the volume and weight limits you enter; legal payloads vary by truck and by state.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 20 × 10 ft area 4 in deep is 66.7 ft³ = 2.47 yd³; with 10 % compaction 2.72 yd³; crushed stone at 1 600 kg/m³ (2 697 lb/yd³) gives 7 325 lb = 3.66 short ton, $146.50 at $40 per ton. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Depth under 2 in (50 mm): thin for a path or driveway base, which is usually several inches thick and compacted in layers.
- Topsoil settles a lot after placing; an allowance of 15 to 25 % is common.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 20 × 10 ft, 4 in of crushed stone: 2.47 yd³, 2.72 yd³ with 10 % compaction, 3.66 short ton, $146.50 at $40 per ton
  - Source: Hand calculation: 20 × 10 × 4/12 = 66.67 ft³ / 27 = 2.469 yd³; × 1.1 = 2.716 yd³ × 1 600 kg/m³ = 3 322.5 kg = 3.662 short ton
- Caterpillar loose weights per cubic yard: crushed stone 2 700 lb, gravel 2 850, sand 2 400, sand and gravel 2 900, topsoil 1 600
  - Source: Caterpillar Performance Handbook, weights of materials (loose kg/m³ and lb/yd³ columns, rounded)
- Metric: 5 × 4 m of dry sand 100 mm deep, no allowance: 2.0 m³, 2 840 kg, 85.20 at 30 per tonne
  - Source: Hand calculation: 5 × 4 × 0.1 = 2 m³ × 1 420 kg/m³ = 2 840 kg
- Truck loads take the tighter limit: 30 yd³ of crushed stone (40.5 short ton) is 2 loads of 20 yd³ by volume but 3 loads of 15 ton by weight
  - Source: Hand calculation: 30 × 2 697 lb = 80 910 lb = 40.5 short ton; 40.5 / 15 = 2.7, rounded up to 3
- Custom density is used; a 1 in layer warns; zero depth, an unknown material and a density of 5 000 kg/m³ are rejected
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
