## Great-circle and rhumb-line distance

<a id="great-circle-distance"></a>

Folder `great-circle-distance/` · Maritime · Great-circle distance, initial and final courses, vertex and midpoint, rhumb-line distance and course, WGS-84 geodesic and passage time.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Positions are geographic latitude and longitude in decimal degrees, north and east positive; longitude differences are normalised to ±180°, so tracks crossing the antimeridian are handled.
- Great-circle and rhumb-line results use a spherical Earth: the "nautical" sphere where one minute of arc equals one nautical mile (the convention of Bowditch and the sailings tables), or the IUGG mean radius; the two differ by about 0.07 %.
- The WGS-84 geodesic (Vincenty inverse) is the true shortest distance on the ellipsoid and differs from the spherical great circle by up to about 0.5 %; it is the figure to compare with GPS or ECDIS. Nearly antipodal points may not converge and fall back to the sphere with a warning.
- Courses are true courses measured clockwise from true north; no magnetic variation, deviation, set or drift is applied.
- The rhumb line is a loxodrome of constant true course; its distance is undefined at the poles and the Mercator formula is used only for latitudes within ±89.9°.
- Passage time is distance divided by the entered speed with no allowance for weather, currents, waypoints along the great circle or land in the way; a great-circle track is a sequence of rhumb-line legs in practice.
- The vertex reported is the point of highest latitude on the full great circle; whether the passage actually reaches it is stated separately.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: Vincenty reproduces the Geoscience Australia reference line (Flinders Peak – Buninyong) to 1 mm and both azimuths to 10⁻⁵ °. Note that Vincenty's α₂ is the arrival heading; the published "reverse azimuth" 127°10′25″ is α₂ − 180°, which first tripped the test, not the code.
- Verification: the 60°N parallel-sailing case reproduces Bowditch (2 700 nmi rhumb line, 2 484.6 nmi great circle, vertex 67.8°N) and the New York–London default was checked against the classical vertex formula cos φ_v = cos φ₁ |sin C₁|.
- Design decision: vertex and midpoint are computed with unit vectors (projection of the pole onto the great-circle plane) so that antipodal and equatorial cases are detected explicitly; the classical formula is kept as the test cross-check.
- Design decision: distances are reported in nautical miles with both spherical models selectable and the WGS-84 geodesic always shown alongside.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Rhumb-line sailing is not defined within 0.1° of the poles; rhumb-line outputs are omitted.
- Departure and destination are coincident or antipodal: the great circle is not unique, so vertex and midpoint are omitted.
- Vincenty did not converge (nearly antipodal points); the WGS-84 geodesic shown is the spherical great-circle distance.
- Angular distance above 150°: the great circle passes near the antipode and small position changes swing the route far.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Along the equator from 0°E to 90°E: 90° of arc = 5 400 nmi on the nautical sphere, course 090° both ways of sailing; 5 403.6 nmi with the IUGG radius
  - Source: Definition of the nautical sphere (1′ = 1 nmi, Bowditch ch. 24); IUGG mean radius 6 371.0088 km × π/2 = 10 007.5 km
- Parallel sailing at 60°N over 90° of longitude: rhumb line 2 700 nmi at 090°; great circle 2 484.6 nmi, initial course 049.1°, final 130.9°, vertex 67.79°N at mid-longitude
  - Source: Bowditch ch. 24: parallel sailing p = DLo × cos L; great-circle cos D = sin L1 sin L2 + cos L1 cos L2 cos DLo = 0.75 → D = 41.41° = 2 484.6 nmi; vertex cos Lv = cos L1 sin C
- Meridian sailing 10°N → 50°N on 20°E: 2 400 nmi for both sailings, course 000°; reversed track gives 180° and the same distance
  - Source: Bowditch ch. 24: along a meridian D = Dlat in minutes
- Vincenty inverse on WGS-84, Flinders Peak → Buninyong: 54 972.271 m, forward azimuth 306°52′05.37″, reverse azimuth 127°10′25.07″ (final heading 307°10′25.07″)
  - Source: Vincenty (1975) test line as published by Geoscience Australia (Flinders Peak −37°57′03.72030″ 144°25′29.52440″; Buninyong −37°39′10.15610″ 143°55′35.38390″); the published reverse azimuth is the direction back to the start, i.e. the arrival heading minus 180°
- Crossing the antimeridian: 170°E → 170°W on the equator is 20° = 1 200 nmi eastward, not 340° westward
  - Source: Longitude difference normalised to ±180° (Bowditch: DLo is the smaller arc)
- New York (40.7°N 74.0°W) → London (51.5°N 0.1°W): great circle 3 007 nmi, initial course 051.2°, final 108.3°, vertex 53.8°N 23.1°W; rhumb line 3 128 nmi at 078° (3.9 % longer); WGS-84 geodesic 5 588 km
  - Source: Haversine and Mercator formulas (Bowditch ch. 24); vertex cross-checked with cos φ_v = cos φ₁ |sin C₁| = cos 40.7° × sin 51.2° → 53.8°; JFK–LHR airline great circle 5 555 km for comparison
- Rhumb-line helper: 45°N 0° → 45°N 10°E gives course 090° and distance 600 × cos 45° = 424.3 nmi; vertex helper returns null for antipodes
  - Source: Parallel sailing (Bowditch); antipodal points have no unique great circle
- Invalid inputs fail fast: latitude 95°, longitude 200°, zero speed
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 3 007 nmi, 3 128 nmi, 3.9 %, 5 588 km to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Bowditch, The American Practical Navigator (NGA Pub. 9, 2019), ch. 24 "The Sailings": great-circle, Mercator and parallel sailing formulas
- Vincenty, T., "Direct and inverse solutions of geodesics on the ellipsoid with application of nested equations", Survey Review 23(176), 1975
- Geoscience Australia, Vincenty inverse worked example (Flinders Peak to Buninyong: 54 972.271 m)
- NIMA TR8350.2, Department of Defense World Geodetic System 1984 (ellipsoid parameters); IUGG mean Earth radius 6 371.0088 km
- International Hydrographic Conference 1929 (nautical mile = 1852 m)

## Measurement uncertainty (GUM)

<a id="gum-uncertainty"></a>

Folder `gum-uncertainty/` · General · GUM uncertainty budget: Type A/B components, sensitivity coefficients, combined and expanded uncertainty with Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

### Assumptions and caveats

- GUM law of propagation of uncertainty for uncorrelated input quantities: u_c(y) = √Σ (cᵢ u(xᵢ))², a first-order Taylor expansion of the measurement model; strongly non-linear models, or a dominant non-normal input, need the Monte Carlo method of GUM Supplement 1 (JCGM 101); correlated inputs need the covariance terms of GUM 5.2, which this page does not include.
- Standard uncertainties from the entered value and distribution: normal (the value is u), expanded at k = 2 (u = U/2, as on calibration certificates), rectangular (u = a/√3), triangular (u = a/√6), U-shaped (u = a/√2), and Type A as the experimental standard deviation of the mean s/√n of n readings averaged (with ν = n − 1 unless a pooled value with more degrees of freedom is entered); Type B components have infinite degrees of freedom unless a finite ν is entered (GUM G.4.2).
- Effective degrees of freedom by the Welch–Satterthwaite formula (GUM G.4.1); a non-integer ν_eff is truncated to the next lower integer by default (GUM G.4.1 and EA-4/02 practice, conservative) or used as it is (equivalent to interpolating Table G.2, also allowed by G.4.1), and the coverage factor k = t_p(ν_eff) of the Student distribution for the chosen coverage probability (95.45 % gives k = 2 for large ν, GUM Table G.2); the result assumes the output quantity is approximately normal (central limit theorem).
- The reported result rounds the expanded uncertainty to two significant digits and the measured value to the same decimal place (GUM 7.2.6); all values must be in the same unit as the result (or relative values throughout).
- Component lines: name; type; value; sensitivity coefficient cᵢ (default 1); degrees of freedom νᵢ (number or inf, default ∞, Type A default n − 1); n (Type A only); separated by semicolons or tabs, lines starting with # ignored.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31 (degrees of freedom): the GUM G.4.1 example has ν_eff = 18.9988, printed as 19.0 and read as t₉₅(19) = 2.09; truncation gives ν 18 and k 2.10 — both lead to U₉₅ = 2.2 %, so the option changes the third digit of k only.
- Verification 2026-10-31: EA-4/02 example S2 (calibration of a 10 kg weight: reference U 45 mg at k = 2, drift ±15 mg, s_p 25 mg over 3 readings, comparator ±10 mg, buoyancy ±10 mg) gives u_c = 29.3 mg and U = 59 mg (k = 2), as published; note that EA-4/02 rev00 prints 8.95 mg for the drift row although ±15 mg rectangular is 8.66 mg — the combined value rounds to 29.3 mg either way. GUM G.4.1 example (relative 0.25 %, 0.57 %, 0.82 % with 9, 4, 14 degrees of freedom) gives u_c 1.03 %, ν_eff 19.0, t₉₅(19) 2.09, U₉₅ 2.2 %.
- Design decision: a text table of components rather than fixed input rows, so a budget of any length can be pasted from a spreadsheet; the budget table output shows each contribution and its share of the variance.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- "…" contributes … % of the variance: the combined distribution follows its shape — if it is rectangular, the coverage factor 2 overstates the interval (GUM G.6.5) and a Monte Carlo evaluation (JCGM 101) is advisable.
- Only … effective degrees of freedom: the coverage factor rises to …; more readings or a pooled standard deviation would reduce it.
- All components are zero: check the values.
- Uncorrelated inputs and a linear (first-order) model are assumed; correlated inputs need covariance terms (GUM 5.2).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- …: expected at least name; type; value
- …: unknown type "…" (use normal, k2, rect, tri, arcsine or typeA)
- …: value "…" must be a number ≥ 0
- …: sensitivity coefficient "…" is not a number
- …: Type A needs the number of readings averaged n ≥ 2 in the sixth field
- …: degrees of freedom "…" must be a positive number or inf
- Enter at least one uncertainty component

## GZ curve and intact stability criteria

<a id="gz-criteria"></a>

Folder `gz-criteria/` · Maritime · IS Code 2008 general criteria and the severe wind and rolling (weather) criterion from a pasted GZ curve, with the grain heeling check.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The GZ curve is the righting lever of the loading condition with the free-surface correction already applied, at the trim the ship takes when heeled; it is interpolated with a monotone cubic (PCHIP) through the pasted points and is odd-symmetric (GZ(−θ) = −GZ(θ)) for the roll to windward; areas are in metre-radians.
- General criteria (IS Code 2.2): area 0–30° ≥ 0.055 m·rad, area 0–40° (or 0–θf) ≥ 0.090 m·rad, area 30–40° (or 30–θf) ≥ 0.030 m·rad, GZ ≥ 0.20 m at an angle of 30° or more, maximum GZ at 25° or more, GM0 ≥ 0.15 m.
- Weather criterion (IS Code 2.3): steady wind lever lw1 = P A Z/(1000 g Δ) with P = 504 Pa and g = 9.81 m/s², gust lever lw2 = 1.5 lw1, constant with heel; θ0 at lw1 must not exceed 16° or 80 % of the deck-edge immersion angle; the roll to windward θ1 = 109 k X1 X2 √(r s) uses Tables 2.3.4-1 to -4 (linear interpolation) and, unless a roll period is entered, T = 2 C B/√GM; area b from the first lw2 intercept to θ2 = min(θf, 50°, second intercept) must be at least area a from θ0 − θ1 to the first intercept.
- Grain (International Grain Code A 7): heeling arm λ0 = assumed volumetric heeling moment / (stowage factor × Δ) at 0°, 0.8 λ0 at 40°, linear; heel due to the grain shift ≤ 12° (or the deck-edge immersion angle if less, ships built from 1994); residual area between the GZ and heeling arm curves up to the least of 40°, θf and the angle of maximum difference ≥ 0.075 m·rad; GM0 ≥ 0.30 m.
- Special ship types (passenger ships, timber deck cargo, containerships over 100 m, fishing vessels, offshore vessels) have additional or alternative criteria in Part A chapter 3 and Part B that are not checked here; the calculator does not replace the approved stability booklet or loading computer.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: all four weather tables and the general criteria were transcribed from the MSC.267(85) text; for a wall-sided curve GZ = sin θ (GM + ½BM tan²θ) the areas agree with the closed form GM(1 − cos θ) + ½BM(sec θ + cos θ − 2) to 0.1 %; areas a and b and the grain residual area of a linear test curve agree with their closed forms.
- Design decision: PCHIP interpolation never overshoots between the pasted points, so a coarse curve is not given lever it does not have; the curve must reach every angle a criterion uses, otherwise the page says which angle is missing.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Down-flooding angle at or below 30°: the 30–θf area cannot be met.
- The first segment of the curve has a slope of … m/rad, far from GM0 = … m: check GM0 or add points at small angles.
- The curve ends at …° before θf and 50°: area b is counted only up to …°.
- Roll period above 20 s: the s table is held at its last value (0.035).
- Check against the approved stability booklet: special ship types have additional criteria, and the curve must already include free-surface effects.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- GZ curve line …: expected "heel; GZ" as two numbers
- The GZ curve needs at least 4 points
- GZ curve: heel angles must increase (line with …°)
- GZ curve: the first point must be at 0°
- GZ curve: GZ must be 0 at 0° heel (correct an initial list first)
- The GZ curve ends at …°; a criterion needs …°
- The GZ curve must reach …° (40° or θf); it ends at …°
- The GZ curve never reaches the steady wind lever lw1 = … m: the ship would capsize under the steady wind
- A positive GM0 is needed for the roll period formula (or enter the roll period)
- r × s is negative (G far below the waterline): the roll-back formula does not apply
- The GZ curve never reaches the gust lever lw2 = … m: the weather criterion fails
- The roll to windward reaches …°, beyond the end of the GZ curve
- The GZ curve never exceeds the grain heeling arm: the grain criteria fail

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Wall-sided curve GZ = sin θ (GM + ½BM tan²θ) with GM 0.6 m, BM 3 m given every 5°: areas 0–30° = 0.1115 and 0–40° = 0.2475 m·rad from the closed form GM(1 − cos θ) + ½BM(sec θ + cos θ − 2), within 0.3 %
  - Source: Wall-sided formula (Rawson & Tupper, Basic Ship Theory, ch. 4) integrated analytically
- IS Code tables with linear interpolation: X1(B/d 2.45) = 0.99, X2(CB 0.475) = 0.785, k(1.25) = 0.965, s(T 10 s) = 0.079; values beyond the tables are held (X1 at B/d 2.0 = 1.0, s at 25 s = 0.035)
  - Source: 2008 IS Code (MSC.267(85)) Tables 2.3.4-1 to 2.3.4-4
- Weather criterion on a linear curve GZ = 1.0·θ: lw1 = 504 × 1800 × 14/(1000 × 9.81 × 20 000) = 0.0647 m, θ0 = 3.71°, and areas a and b equal their closed forms with θ2 = 50°
  - Source: 2008 IS Code 2.3.2–2.3.4 with ∫(lw2 − cθ)dθ and ∫(cθ − lw2)dθ evaluated exactly
- Grain on the same linear curve: λ0 = 5000/(1.25 × 20 000) = 0.20 m, heel 10.84° and residual area to 40° = 0.137 m·rad from the closed form
  - Source: International Grain Code A 7 (λ40 = 0.8 λ0, linear heeling arm) solved exactly for GZ = θ
- A poor curve fails: maximum GZ at 20°, 0.18 m at 30° and a small 30–40° area are each reported as FAIL
  - Source: 2008 IS Code 2.2.1–2.2.3
- Invalid inputs fail fast: a curve not starting at 0°, decreasing angles, too few points, a curve that never reaches the wind lever, a curve that ends before 40°
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.152, 0.268, 0.116, 0.69 m, 0.065 m, 19.3 s, 0.301 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IMO Resolution MSC.267(85) International Code on Intact Stability, 2008 (2008 IS Code), Part A 2.2 and 2.3, Tables 2.3.4-1 to 2.3.4-4
- IMO Resolution MSC.23(59) International Code for the Safe Carriage of Grain in Bulk (International Grain Code), A 7 Stability requirements
- MSC.1/Circ.1281 Explanatory notes to the 2008 IS Code; MSC.1/Circ.1537 Unified interpretations of the 2008 IS Code
- F. N. Fritsch, R. E. Carlson, "Monotone piecewise cubic interpolation", SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 17 (1980) 238–246

## Hardness conversion calculator (HRC, HRB, HV, HB)

<a id="hardness-conversion"></a>

Folder `hardness-conversion/` · Mechanical · Approximate conversion of steel hardness between Rockwell C, Rockwell B, Vickers and Brinell, with tensile strength, from ASTM E140 and ISO 18265.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The conversions apply only to non-austenitic carbon and low-alloy steels, in the heat-treated, hot-rolled or annealed condition the tables were built from. Austenitic stainless steel, cold-worked steel, cast iron and non-ferrous metals need their own tables.
- Hardness numbers are converted with ASTM E140 Table 1 (Rockwell C range, HRC 20 to 68) and Table 2 (Rockwell B range, HRB 55 to 100), interpolating linearly between rows. Brinell is the 10 mm tungsten carbide ball at 3 000 kgf (HBW).
- Tensile strength is estimated from the Vickers number with ISO 18265 Table A.1 (HV 80 to 650, Rm 255 to 2 180 MPa). ISO 18265 warns that tensile estimates are the least reliable converted values.
- E140 Tables 1 and 2 meet at about HRB 97 to 100 and HRC 20 to 23 and disagree there by up to about 10 HV; conversions in that band are less certain.
- Values outside a table are refused or shown as "—", never extrapolated. A converted hardness never replaces a test in the scale a specification requires.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 45 HRC converts to 446 HV and 421 HBW (E140 Table 1 row) and to 1 441 MPa tensile strength (ISO 18265: 1 420 + 0.6 × 35); 85 HRB converts to 165 HV and 165 HB and 530 MPa. Checked by hand.
- Table provenance: the E140 HRC, HV and HBW columns were taken from two independent reproductions of E140 (Miki Pulley technical data, Rockwell C hardness conversion; Thread Check Inc., ASTM hardness conversion chart), which agree row by row except HRC 62 (746 against 745 HV; 746 kept). The HRB column comes from the LabTesting.com Rockwell B chart and Thread Check, which agree except HRB 90 (185 against 186 HV; 185 kept, as in a third table by Kemet). The ISO 18265 Rm–HV pairs come from the ws-stahl and Studer-Biennaform reproductions of Table A.1, which agree.
- Spot-check of the tensile estimate against the approximate tensile column of the SAE/ASTM-based table published by Miki Pulley: 1 480 MPa at 45 HRC (ISO 18265 gives 1 441 MPa), 950 MPa at 30 HRC (971 MPa), 760 MPa at 20 HRC (764 MPa); the two methods differ by less than 3 %.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Near the junction of E140 Tables 1 and 2 (about HRB 98 to 100, HRC 20 to 24) the two tables differ by up to 10 HV: the conversion is less certain here.
- Brinell numbers above 650 HBW are outside the range of ISO 6506 and ASTM E10; the value is for comparison only.
- Above 650 HV, ISO 18265 Table A.1 gives no tensile strength: such hard steels are brittle and their tensile strength is not well defined by hardness.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Tensile strength: … MPa is outside ISO 18265 Table A.1 as used here (320 to 2 180 MPa, HV 100 to 650).
- Hardness number: … is outside the conversion table for …, ….

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- E140 Table 1 rows: 60 HRC = 697 HV, 654 HBW; 50 HRC = 513 HV, 481 HBW; 40 HRC = 392 HV, 371 HBW; 30 HRC = 302 HV, 286 HBW
  - Source: ASTM E140 Table 1 (non-austenitic steels, Rockwell C range)
- E140 Table 2 rows: 100 HRB = 240 HV, 90 HRB = 185 HV, 80 HRB = 150 HV, 60 HRB = 107 HV (HB = HV in this range)
  - Source: ASTM E140 Table 2 (non-austenitic steels, Rockwell B range)
- Inverse and interpolation: 446 HV gives 45.0 HRC; 400 HBW gives 43.0 HRC; 45.5 HRC lies half-way between 446 and 458 HV
  - Source: ASTM E140 Table 1, linear interpolation between rows (by hand)
- ISO 18265 tensile strength: 446 HV (45 HRC) ≈ 1 441 MPa; 165 HV (85 HRB) = 530 MPa; 800 MPa ↔ 250 HV
  - Source: ISO 18265 Table A.1 rows (440 HV 1 420 MPa, 450 HV 1 455 MPa, 165 HV 530 MPa, 250 HV 800 MPa)
- Spot-check against a second table: ISO 18265 tensile within 3 % of the SAE/ASTM tensile column (1 480 MPa at 45 HRC, 950 MPa at 30 HRC)
  - Source: Miki Pulley technical data, Rockwell C hardness conversion table (approximate tensile strength column)
- Out of the tables: HRC 18, HRB 105, HV 950 and 3 000 MPa are refused; 68 HRC has no Brinell or tensile value
  - Source: Validation contract (no extrapolation beyond ASTM E140 and ISO 18265)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 446, 421, 1 441 MPa to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASTM E140-12b(2019)e1, Standard Hardness Conversion Tables for Metals, Table 1 (non-austenitic steels, Rockwell C range) and Table 2 (Rockwell B range)
- ISO 18265:2013, Metallic materials — Conversion of hardness values, Annex A, Table A.1 (unalloyed and low-alloy steels and cast steel)
- ASTM A370-24, Standard Test Methods and Definitions for Mechanical Testing of Steel Products, §17 and Tables 3–4 (use of hardness conversions)

## Hazen–Williams head loss calculator

<a id="hazen-williams"></a>

Folder `hazen-williams/` · Mechanical · Hazen–Williams friction loss of water in a pressure pipe, or the flow or pipe diameter for an allowed loss, with velocity, pressure drop and C-factors.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Hazen–Williams is an empirical formula for water at ordinary temperatures, about 15 °C (60 °F), in full pipes in turbulent flow; it ignores viscosity, so it does not apply to oils, hot water or other liquids, where Darcy–Weisbach must be used.
- It is normally used for pipes of about 50 mm (2 in) bore and larger at velocities of about 0.3 to 3 m/s (1 to 10 ft/s); outside that range it can differ widely from Darcy–Weisbach, and the page warns.
- C values are the design values of NFPA 13 Table 28.3.4.8.1, the same for every pipe size; old, corroded or tuberculated pipe can fall well below them, and the authority having jurisdiction may require other values.
- Only straight-pipe friction is calculated: add fittings and valves as equivalent length or with the minor losses calculator, and elevation separately. The pressure drop uses water at 15 °C (999.1 kg/m³).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 500 US gpm of water through 1 000 ft of 6 in bore pipe with C = 150 loses 15.7 ft (6.82 psi) at 5.67 ft/s; the NFPA 13 form 4.52 Q^1.85/(C^1.85 d^4.87) gives 6.81 psi for the same pipe. Checked by hand.
- Verification: 20 L/s through 1 000 m of 150 mm PVC (C = 150) gives 7.32 m by Hazen–Williams and 7.25 m by Darcy–Weisbach with Colebrook (ε = 0.0015 mm, ν = 1.139 mm²/s at 15 °C, shared/pipes.js), 1 % apart.
- Constants: 10.67 and the exponents 1.852 and 4.8704 follow from the velocity form V = 0.849 C R^0.63 S^0.54; converted to psi per foot with Q in gpm and d in inches they give 4.523, the NFPA 13 constant 4.52 to 0.1 %.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Velocity below about 0.3 m/s (1 ft/s): Hazen–Williams is outside its usual range here; check with Darcy–Weisbach.
- Velocity above about 3 m/s (10 ft/s): Hazen–Williams is outside its usual range, and water hammer and erosion become concerns; check with Darcy–Weisbach.
- Bore below 50 mm (2 in): Hazen–Williams was fitted to larger pipes; Darcy–Weisbach is more reliable for small tubes.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 500 US gpm through 1 000 ft of 6 in bore pipe, C = 150: 15.7 ft of head, 6.82 psi, within 0.3 % of the NFPA 13 form 4.52 Q^1.85/(C^1.85 d^4.87) = 6.81 psi
  - Source: NFPA 13, hydraulic calculation procedures (Hazen–Williams in psi per foot, Q in gpm, d in inches)
- The SI constant follows from V = 0.849 C R^0.63 S^0.54: (0.849 × π/4 × 4^−0.63)^−1.852 = 10.67, and the US conversion gives 4.52 psi per foot
  - Source: Williams & Hazen, Hydraulic Tables, 3rd ed. (1920); unit conversion of the head-loss form
- Cross-check with Darcy–Weisbach: 20 L/s in 1 000 m of 150 mm PVC (C = 150) loses 7.32 m; Colebrook with ε = 0.0015 mm at 15 °C gives 7.25 m, 1 % less
  - Source: Darcy–Weisbach with the Colebrook friction factor of shared/pipes.js; ν = 1.139 mm²/s for water at 15 °C
- Solving for flow or diameter inverts the head-loss form exactly; doubling the flow multiplies the loss by 2^1.852 = 3.61
  - Source: Algebra of h_f = 10.67 L Q^1.852 / (C^1.852 d^4.8704)
- Warnings outside the usual range: 1.9 in bore at 50 gpm (velocity 1.72 m/s) warns only for the bore; 1 000 gpm in 6 in (3.46 m/s) and 20 gpm in 6 in (0.07 m/s) warn for velocity
  - Source: Validity range of Hazen–Williams for water distribution practice (d ≥ 50 mm, 0.3–3 m/s)
- Invalid inputs: zero flow, zero length, a custom C above 160 and an unknown material are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 15.7 ft, 6.82 psi, 1.57, 5.67 ft/s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Williams, G.S. & Hazen, A., Hydraulic Tables, 3rd ed., Wiley, 1920 (V = 1.318 C R^0.63 S^0.54 in US units, 0.849 in SI)
- NFPA 13, Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems, 2025 ed., hydraulic calculation formula p = 4.52 Q^1.85/(C^1.85 d^4.87) and Table 28.3.4.8.1 Hazen–Williams C values
- AWWA Manual M23, PVC Pipe — Design and Installation (C = 150 for PVC)

## Heat exchanger LMTD

<a id="heat-exchanger-lmtd"></a>

Folder `heat-exchanger-lmtd/` · Thermal and fluids · LMTD for counter, parallel and 1-2 shell-and-tube flow, duty from either stream, F correction, fouling and required area from U.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Steady state, no heat loss to the surroundings, constant specific heats and constant U along the exchanger; split the exchanger into zones for phase change or large property changes.
- The LMTD method needs all four terminal temperatures (sizing problem); effectiveness, NTU and capacity ratio are reported as the bridge to the ε-NTU rating method.
- F is the Bowman analytical correction for one shell pass with any even number of tube passes, applied to the counterflow LMTD; multi-shell, cross-flow and plate arrangements have different F curves. F below 0.75 is flagged.
- Parallel flow cannot deliver a temperature cross and one shell pass cannot achieve crosses beyond the Bowman limit; both raise an error instead of a number.
- Fouling is a total resistance in series with 1/U (TEMA design values); actual fouling depends on velocity, temperature and cleaning interval, and both sides should be referred to the same area basis as U.
- The U ranges in the help text are pre-sizing orders of magnitude; a real design computes U from film coefficients, wall resistance and fin efficiency.
- Duty from the cold or hot stream uses the entered mass flow and c_p; the other stream is not checked for energy balance.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: Incropera Example 11.1 is reproduced to the published tube length (65.9 m); the Bowman factor F(R = 1, P = 0.5) = 0.802 matches the chart; the ε-NTU counterflow relation closes on the LMTD result to 10⁻⁶.
- Design decision: the one-shell-pass F factor is computed analytically (Bowman 1940) instead of read from charts, with a hard error when the temperature cross is not achievable.
- Design decision: effectiveness, NTU and capacity ratio are derived from the four temperatures alone, which is possible because the stream with the larger temperature change is C_min.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- F below 0.75: the exchanger would operate near the steep part of the F curve. Add shell passes or go to counterflow.
- Temperature cross (cold outlet above hot outlet): only counterflow or multi-shell arrangements can achieve this.
- No fouling allowance: design practice adds TEMA fouling resistances, which typically increase the area by 10–40 %.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Terminal temperature differences must be positive (got … and …)
- Hot fluid must cool down: T_h,in must exceed T_h,out
- Cold fluid must warm up: T_c,out must exceed T_c,in
- Hot inlet must be warmer than cold inlet
- Parallel flow cannot deliver a cold outlet at or above the hot outlet — use counterflow
- Cold outlet must stay below the hot inlet
- Hot outlet must stay above the cold inlet
- This temperature cross is not achievable with one shell pass — use counterflow or more shell passes in series

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Incropera Example 11.1: q = 8 524 W, ΔT_lm = 43.2 °C, area 5.18 m² (tube length 65.9 m on Ø25 mm)
  - Source: Incropera, DeWitt, Bergman & Lavine, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, 6th ed., Example 11.1 (counterflow oil cooler)
- Same temperatures in parallel flow: ΔT₁ = 70, ΔT₂ = 19.8, LMTD = 39.75 K (lower than counterflow)
  - Source: Parallel-flow LMTD definition, Incropera §11.3; value computed by hand: (70 − 19.8)/ln(70/19.8)
- Equal terminal differences: 100→60 against 20→60 counterflow gives LMTD = 40 K (limit of the log mean)
  - Source: Limit of (ΔT₁ − ΔT₂)/ln(ΔT₁/ΔT₂) as ΔT₁ → ΔT₂ (Incropera §11.3)
- Bowman F for 1 shell pass: R = 1, P = 0.5 → F = 0.802; R = 2, P = 0.1 → F = 0.995; P → 0 gives F → 1
  - Source: Bowman, Mueller & Nagle, Trans. ASME 62 (1940); chart reproduced as Incropera Fig. 11.10 (R = 1, P = 0.5 reads ≈ 0.80)
- Effectiveness and NTU from temperatures: ε = 40/70 = 0.5714, NTU = 0.926, C_r = 0.255 — consistent with the counterflow ε-NTU relation
  - Source: ε-NTU method, Incropera §11.4, Table 11.3 counterflow: ε = [1 − exp(−NTU(1 − C_r))] / [1 − C_r exp(−NTU(1 − C_r))]
- Fouling: U = 1 000 with R_f = 0.0005 m²·K/W gives U_service = 666.7 and 1.5 × the clean area
  - Source: 1/U_service = 1/U_clean + R_f — TEMA Standards, 10th ed., §RGP-T-2.4 (fouling resistances)
- Duty from the cold stream or given directly reproduces the hot-stream duty (energy balance)
  - Source: Energy balance q = ṁ_h c_p,h ΔT_h = ṁ_c c_p,c ΔT_c, Incropera eq. 11.6–11.7 (water outlet 40.2 °C from Example 11.1)
- Unit layer: 100 °C = 212 °F, 20 °C = 293.15 K, a 10 K difference = 18 °F
  - Source: Temperature scale definitions (BIPM SI Brochure, 9th ed.)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: parallel flow with a temperature cross, hot fluid warming up, one-shell cross too deep
  - Source: Second law: parallel flow cannot cross; Bowman F undefined beyond the achievable P for given R
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 59.8 K, 30 K, 43.2 K, 43.2 K, 5.18 m², 5.18 m², 0.255 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Incropera, DeWitt, Bergman & Lavine, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, 6th ed., ch. 11 (Example 11.1, Fig. 11.10, Table 11.3)
- R.A. Bowman, A.C. Mueller & W.M. Nagle, "Mean temperature difference in design", Trans. ASME 62 (1940)
- TEMA Standards of the Tubular Exchanger Manufacturers Association, 10th ed., §RGP-T-2.4 (fouling resistances)

## Heat exchanger effectiveness–NTU calculator

<a id="heat-exchanger-ntu"></a>

Folder `heat-exchanger-ntu/` · Thermal and fluids · Effectiveness, NTU, duty and both outlet temperatures of a heat exchanger from UA and the inlet conditions: counter, parallel, shell-and-tube, cross-flow.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Steady state, no heat loss to the surroundings, constant specific heats and a uniform overall coefficient U over the whole area, as in the ε-NTU relations of Incropera Table 11.3.
- The shell-and-tube relation is for n identical shells in series, each with one shell pass and an even number of tube passes; the cross-flow relation for both fluids unmixed is the usual approximation (eq. 11.32): it is exact as C_r tends to 0 and stays within 4 % of the exact series for C_r up to 1 and NTU from 0.25 to 5 (1.6 % low at C_r = 1, NTU = 1).
- A condensing or boiling stream is treated as having an infinite heat capacity rate (C_r = 0) at its inlet temperature; subcooling or superheat sections need a separate zone.
- UA is the clean or service value the user enters; fouling, fin efficiency and wall resistance must already be in it.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: Incropera Example 11.1 rated with ε-NTU (oil 0.1 kg/s, 2 131 J/(kg·K), 100 °C in; water 0.2 kg/s, 4 178 J/(kg·K), 30 °C in; U = 38.1 W/(m²·K), A = 5.176 m², counterflow) gives NTU 0.925, C_r 0.255, ε 0.571, q = 8 521 W, oil out 60.0 °C and water out 40.2 °C, matching the LMTD solution of the example and the heat-exchanger-lmtd calculator. Checked by hand.
- Verification: for one shell pass the duty equals U A F LMTD with the Bowman F factor of the LMTD calculator to 10⁻⁹, and the cross-flow approximation stays within 4 % of the exact series (Kays and London: ε = 0.476 at C_r = 1, NTU = 1) for C_r 0.25 to 1 and NTU 0.25 to 5.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- NTU above 5: the effectiveness is close to its limit, so extra area adds little duty.
- Parallel flow can never exceed ε = 1/(1 + C_r); counterflow gives more duty from the same area.
- Temperature cross in a single shell: the LMTD correction factor is low here; consider more shells in series or counterflow.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Flow arrangement: unknown arrangement …
- Hot fluid inlet: it must be warmer than the cold fluid inlet.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Incropera Example 11.1 rated by ε-NTU: counterflow oil cooler with U 38.1 W/(m²·K) on a 25 mm tube 65.9 m long returns oil at 60.0 °C, water at 40.2 °C and q ≈ 8 524 W
  - Source: Incropera et al., Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, 7th ed., Example 11.1 (q = 8 524 W, L = 65.9 m)
- Same duty as the LMTD method: counterflow q = UA × LMTD and one shell pass q = UA × F × LMTD with the Bowman F, from the outlet temperatures found here
  - Source: Incropera 7th ed., §11.3 (q = UA ΔT_lm and the F factor); Bowman, Mueller & Nagle, Trans. ASME 62 (1940)
- Table 11.3 limits: counterflow C_r = 1, NTU 1 gives ε = 0.5; C_r → 0 gives 1 − e^−NTU for every arrangement; parallel flow tends to 1/(1 + C_r); many shells tend to counterflow
  - Source: Incropera 7th ed., Table 11.3, eqs. 11.28a, 11.29a, 11.31a, 11.35a
- Cross-flow, both unmixed: the exact series gives ε = 0.476 at C_r = 1, NTU = 1 (Kays and London); the eq. 11.32 approximation is within 4 % from NTU 0.25 to 5
  - Source: Kays & London, Compact Heat Exchangers, 3rd ed., cross-flow both fluids unmixed table; Incropera 7th ed., eq. 11.32
- Condensing steam at 100 °C heating 0.2 kg/s of water from 30 °C with UA 1 000 W/K: ε = 1 − e^−1.197 = 0.698, water out 78.8 °C, 40.8 kW, 65.1 kg/h of condensate at 2 257 kJ/kg
  - Source: Incropera 7th ed., eq. 11.35a (C_r = 0); hand calculation
- Invalid inputs: hot inlet not above cold inlet, zero flow, a fractional number of shells and an unknown arrangement are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 213.1, 835.6, 0.255, 197.2, 0.925, 8.52 kW, 60.0 °C, 40.2 °C to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

## Building heat loss calculator (U-values)

<a id="heat-loss"></a>

Folder `heat-loss/` · HVAC · Heat loss of a room or house through walls, windows, roof and floor from U- or R-values, plus ventilation, in W, kW and Btu/h, with yearly heating energy.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Fabric loss is U × A × ΔT for each element at the design indoor and outdoor temperatures (EN 12831-1, ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 18); thermal bridges can add 10 to 20 % to older buildings and are not included unless entered as an element.
- Floors on the ground and walls to unheated spaces lose heat to a temperature above the outdoor one; using the outdoor temperature for them errs on the safe side. Enter a reduced U-value or area to account for this.
- Ventilation and infiltration loss uses standard air (1.204 kg/m³, 1 006 J/(kg·K)), i.e. 0.336 W per m³/h per K or 1.08 Btu/h per cfm per °F. Heat recovery reduces it by its efficiency.
- R-values are entered with an R prefix (R13, R-4.5) in the same unit system as the areas; U = 1/R. Imperial U-values are Btu/(h·ft²·°F).
- The yearly energy from heating degree-days assumes the same heat loss coefficient all season and ignores solar and internal gains, so it overestimates the bill for well-glazed or busy buildings.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: the default house (walls 100 m² at 0.30, windows 20 m² at 1.4, roof 60 m² at 0.18, floor 60 m² at 0.25, door 2 m² at 1.8, 150 m³ at 0.5 ACH, 21 °C inside and −3 °C outside) loses 2 098 W through the fabric and 606 W by ventilation, 2 703 W in total. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- U-values above 3 W/(m²·K) on …: that is uninsulated single-skin construction; check the value and its units.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Building elements, line …: write "name; area; U-value" or "name; area; R-value" such as R13.
- Building elements, line …: the area "…" must be a number above zero.
- Building elements, line …: the …-value "…" must be a number above zero.
- Building elements: enter at least one wall, window, roof or floor.
- Outdoor design temperature: it must be below the indoor temperature for a heat loss.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Default house, ΔT 24 K: fabric 87.4 W/K = 2 098 W, ventilation 0.336 × 0.5 × 150 × 24 = 606 W, total 2 703 W; walls are the largest loss
  - Source: EN 12831-1: Φ = Σ U A ΔT + ρ c_p n V ΔT / 3600
- US units: 1 000 ft² of R13 wall and 150 ft² of U-0.30 windows at 70 °F inside and 20 °F outside lose 6 096 Btu/h
  - Source: ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 18: q = U A ΔT with U = 1/R; (1 000/13 + 150 × 0.30) × 50 = 6 096 Btu/h
- Ventilation constant: 100 cfm at 50 °F difference is 1.08 × 100 × 50 = 5 400 Btu/h within 0.5 %; heat recovery of 80 % removes 80 % of it
  - Source: ASHRAE sensible heat formula q = 1.08 × cfm × ΔT (standard air)
- Degree-days: H 112.63 W/K × 2 500 K·day × 24 h = 6 758 kWh a year; the parser reads R-values and tabs
  - Source: CIBSE Guide A degree-day method: E = H × HDD × 24
- Outdoor not below indoor, bad lines and an implausible wall U-value are caught
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2 098 W, 606 W, 2 703 W to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- EN 12831-1:2017 Energy performance of buildings — Method for calculation of the design heat load (transmission and ventilation heat loss)
- ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals, Chapter 18 Nonresidential Cooling and Heating Load Calculations, and Chapter 26 (U-factor = 1/ΣR)
- CIBSE Guide A: Environmental design (degree-day method for yearly heating energy)

## Heat pump vs gas boiler running cost calculator

<a id="heat-pump-cost"></a>

Folder `heat-pump-cost/` · Electrical · Heat pump running cost and CO₂ against a gas or oil boiler from the yearly heat demand, SCOP, boiler efficiency and prices, with the saving and break-even COP.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Both systems deliver the same yearly heat to the home. The heat pump uses heat / SCOP of electricity, where the SCOP is the seasonal coefficient of performance for the climate and flow temperature (EN 14825); the boiler uses heat / efficiency of fuel.
- Fuel energy and boiler efficiency are both on the gross (higher heating value) basis, as US AFUE ratings and UK SEDBUK figures are. Gas and oil price units convert with the EPA heat contents: 1 026 Btu per cubic foot of natural gas and 138 000 Btu per US gallon of No. 2 heating oil; a therm is 100 000 Btu.
- Default CO₂ factors are examples: natural gas 0.181 and heating oil 0.252 kg CO₂ per kWh of fuel from the EPA factors (53.06 and 73.96 kg per MMBtu); the electricity factor depends on the grid and the year, so enter your supplier's or country's figure.
- Standing charges, maintenance, boiler servicing, time-of-use tariffs and the electricity a boiler's pump and fan use are not included; a gas standing charge you no longer pay after removing the boiler adds to the heat pump's saving.
- The break-even COP is the seasonal COP at which the two running costs are equal; a heat pump with a higher SCOP is cheaper to run.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 12 000 kWh of heat at SCOP 3.2 takes 3 750 kWh of electricity, 750.00 at 0.20; a 90 % gas boiler burns 13 333 kWh, 933.33 at 0.07, so the heat pump saves 183.33 a year; break-even COP 2.57. CO₂: 938 kg at 0.25 kg/kWh against 2 413 kg at 0.181 kg/kWh. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- An SCOP below 2.5 is low for a modern heat pump; a lower flow temperature, with larger radiators or underfloor heating, usually raises it.
- An SCOP above 5 is unusually high; check that it is a seasonal figure for your climate and flow temperature.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 12 000 kWh at SCOP 3.2 and 0.20/kWh: 3 750 kWh, 750.00; 90 % gas boiler at 0.07/kWh: 13 333 kWh, 933.33; saving 183.33; break-even COP 2.571
  - Source: Hand calculation: E = Q / SCOP, E = Q / η, COP_be = p_e η / p_f
- EPA heat contents: a therm is 29.307 kWh, a ccf of gas 30.07 kWh, a US gallon of No. 2 oil 40.44 kWh, a litre 10.68 kWh
  - Source: EPA GHG Emission Factors Hub Table 1 (1 026 Btu/scf, 0.138 MMBtu/gal); 1 therm = 100 000 Btu; 1 Btu = 1 055.05585262 J
- EPA CO₂ factors: natural gas 53.06 kg/MMBtu = 0.1810 kg/kWh, No. 2 oil 73.96 kg/MMBtu = 0.2524 kg/kWh
  - Source: EPA GHG Emission Factors Hub Table 1; 1 MMBtu = 293.071 kWh
- At the break-even COP the heat pump and the boiler cost the same; above it the heat pump is cheaper
  - Source: Definition of the break-even COP
- Oil at 3.50 per US gallon in an 85 % boiler: 14 118 kWh, 349.1 gal, 1 221.74 a year
  - Source: Hand calculation with 40.444 kWh per gallon (EPA)
- A zero electricity price, an SCOP below 1 and an unknown fuel are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 3 750 kWh, 750.00, 13 333 kWh, 933.33, 183.33, 2.57, 2 413 kg to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- U.S. EPA, Emission Factors for Greenhouse Gas Inventories (GHG Emission Factors Hub), Table 1: natural gas 1 026 Btu/scf and 53.06 kg CO₂/MMBtu; distillate fuel oil No. 2 0.138 MMBtu/gal and 73.96 kg CO₂/MMBtu
- EN 14825:2022 Air conditioners, liquid chilling packages and heat pumps — Testing and rating at part load conditions and calculation of seasonal performance (SCOP)

## Heat transfer calculator: conduction, convection, radiation

<a id="heat-transfer"></a>

Folder `heat-transfer/` · Thermal and fluids · Heat flow by conduction through a wall (Fourier), convection from a surface (Newton) and radiation (Stefan–Boltzmann), with heat flux and thermal resistance.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Steady state, one-dimensional heat flow; properties constant. Conduction is through a flat wall of uniform thickness; for pipes and cylinders use the pipe insulation calculator.
- The convection coefficient h depends on the flow: about 2–25 W/(m²·K) for free convection in gases, 25–250 for forced convection in gases, 50–1 000 for free and 100–20 000 for forced convection in liquids (Incropera Table 1.1).
- Radiation is between a small grey surface and large surroundings at T_sur (view factor 1); the emissivity ε is 0.9–0.95 for paint, brick and most non-metals, 0.05–0.1 for polished metal.
- Conductivities are typical values near room temperature; insulation values depend on density and moisture.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 200 mm brick wall of 10 m² with 20 K across it conducts 0.72 × 10 × 20 / 0.2 = 720 W; a black (ε = 1) surface at 100 °C radiates 680.6 W/m² net to 20 °C surroundings (1 099 W/m² gross). Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- h above 250 W/(m²·K) implies a liquid or a fast gas flow; check the value for gases.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Temperatures: they must differ for heat to flow.
- Temperatures: they must be above absolute zero.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Conduction: 200 mm brick (0.72 W/m·K), 10 m², 20 K: Q = 0.72 × 10 × 20 / 0.2 = 720 W, 72 W/m², R = 0.0278 K/W
  - Source: Fourier's law, Incropera eq. 1.2; k_brick = 0.72 W/(m·K) (Table A.3)
- Convection: h = 25 W/(m²·K), 2 m², surface 80 °C in 20 °C air: 3 000 W
  - Source: Newton's law of cooling, Incropera eq. 1.3a
- Radiation: a black surface at 100 °C to 20 °C surroundings emits σ (373.15⁴ − 293.15⁴) = 680.6 W/m² net; ε = 0.9 gives 612.5 W/m²
  - Source: Stefan–Boltzmann, Incropera eq. 1.7; σ = 5.670374419e−8 (CODATA 2018)
- Insulation: 100 mm extruded polystyrene (0.027) lets through 1/26.7 of what 200 mm brick does for the same ΔT and area
  - Source: Q ∝ k / L
- Equal temperatures and zero thickness are rejected; heat flows backwards with a negative sign when the cold side is warmer
  - Source: Validation contract; sign convention
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 720 W, 72.00 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Incropera, F.P., DeWitt, D.P., Bergman, T.L. and Lavine, A.S., Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, 7th ed., eqs. 1.2, 1.3a, 1.7; Table 1.1; Appendix A (Tables A.1, A.3, A.6)
- CODATA 2018 value of the Stefan–Boltzmann constant, 5.670374419 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴

## Spring rate calculator (helical compression spring)

<a id="helical-spring"></a>

Folder `helical-spring/` · Mechanical · Spring rate, deflection, shear stress with the Wahl factor, solid height and buckling check for round-wire compression springs.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Round-wire helical compression spring under axial static load, analysed per Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design ch. 10: rate k = d⁴G/(8 D³ N_a), torsional stress τ = K 8FD/(π d³) with the curvature correction K — Wahl K_W = (4C − 1)/(4C − 4) + 0.615/C or Bergsträsser K_B = (4C + 2)/(4C − 3) (within 1 % of each other); Shigley uses K_B for both static and fatigue.
- Wire tensile strength from S_ut = A/d^m with the Shigley Table 10-4 constants (music wire A 2211 MPa·mm^m, m 0.145; hard-drawn 1783/0.190; oil-tempered 1855/0.187; chrome-vanadium 2005/0.168; chrome-silicon 1974/0.108; stainless 302 1867/0.146), valid only inside each wire's diameter range; the torsional yield strength for static service is a fraction of S_ut (Table 10-6: 45 % music wire and hard-drawn, 50 % hardened and tempered alloy wires, 35 % austenitic stainless) — set-removed springs may be allowed more.
- Shear modulus per material (Table 10-5: music wire 81.0 GPa, hard-drawn 79.3, oil-tempered/Cr-V/Cr-Si 77.2, stainless 69.0); the small variation of G with wire diameter is ignored.
- End geometry per Shigley Table 10-1: total coils N_t = N_a + 0/1/2/2 and solid height L_s = d(N_t + 1), d N_t, d(N_t + 1), d N_t for plain, plain-ground, squared and squared-ground ends; the spring index C = D/d should be 4–12 (below 4 hard to form, above 12 tangles).
- Static design only: no fatigue (Goodman/Gerber with Zimmerli data), no shot-peening or presetting credit, no temperature or corrosion effects; a safety factor against the solid-height stress of about 1.2 is the usual minimum (Shigley's design recommendation).
- Buckling criterion L₀ < 2.63 D/α (Shigley eq. 10-13 with the end-condition constants α); surge (natural) frequency f = ½ √(k/m) for a spring between flat plates with m the active-coil mass (ρ 7 850 kg/m³); keep operating frequencies below f/15–f/20.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: Shigley Example 10-1 (music wire d 0.037 in, OD 0.4375 in, 12.5 total coils squared and ground, L₀ 1.25 in, G 11.75 Mpsi) reproduced in SI: C 10.8, K_B 1.124, k 4.08 lbf/in (714 N/m), L_s 0.4625 in, F_s 3.21 lbf, S_ut 324 kpsi, τ_s 72.6 kpsi, n_s 2.0, 2.63 D/α 2.11 in > L₀ (stable).
- Design decision: both Wahl and Bergsträsser factors are offered; the strength fractions of Table 10-6 are applied automatically by material class with a custom override.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Wire diameter … mm is outside the …–… mm range of the S_ut = A/d^m fit for this material.
- Spring index below 4: difficult to coil and high curvature stress.
- Spring index above 12: springs tangle and buckle easily; tolerances widen.
- The working deflection closes the spring solid — the force output is the solid-height force.
- Shigley recommends a safety factor of at least 1.2 at the solid height so that accidental closing does not set the spring.
- Static analysis: cyclic loading needs a fatigue check (Zimmerli endurance data with Goodman or Gerber) and ratio-dependent allowable stresses.
- Curvature factor applied to the static stress as Shigley does; some design codes (EN 13906) omit it for static set-removed springs.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Mean coil diameter must exceed the wire diameter (check OD versus d)
- Fewer than one active coil: increase the total coils for this end type
- Free length … mm is not greater than the solid height … mm

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Shigley Example 10-1 geometry: D = 0.4375 − 0.037 = 0.4005 in, C = 10.8, K_B = (4C + 2)/(4C − 3) = 1.124, N_a = 10.5, L_s = d N_t = 0.4625 in
  - Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, Example 10-1, Tables 10-1 and eq. 10-6
- Shigley Example 10-1 rate and solid force: k = d⁴G/(8D³N_a) = 4.08 lbf/in (714 N/m); deflection to solid 0.7875 in; F_s = 3.21 lbf
  - Source: Shigley Example 10-1 (a)–(c): k 4.08 lbf/in, y_s 0.7875 in, F_s 3.21 lbf
- Shigley Example 10-1 stress: S_ut = A/d^m = 201/0.037^0.145 = 324 kpsi (SI constants give 2 231 MPa for 0.94 mm), S_sy = 0.45 S_ut = 146 kpsi, τ_s = K_B 8 F_s D/(π d³) = 72.6 kpsi, n_s = 2.0; buckling 2.63 D/α = 2.11 in > L₀ → stable
  - Source: Shigley Example 10-1 (d)–(f): S_ut 324 kpsi, τ_s 72.6 kpsi, n_s 2.01, stable
- Material table (Shigley 10-4/10-5/10-6): music wire 2211/0.145/45 %/81 GPa, hard-drawn 1783/0.190, oil-tempered 1855/0.187/50 %, Cr-V 2005/0.168, Cr-Si 1974/0.108, stainless 302 1867/0.146/35 %; S_ut of 2 mm hard-drawn wire = 1783/2^0.19 = 1563 MPa
  - Source: Shigley Tables 10-4 (A, m), 10-5 (G) and 10-6 (static torsional yield fraction)
- Wahl versus Bergsträsser: at C = 6 K_W = 23/20 + 0.1025 = 1.2525 and K_B = 26/21 = 1.2381 (1.2 % apart); end types: plain N_t = N_a, plain-ground +1, squared +2, squared-ground +2 with the Table 10-1 solid heights
  - Source: Shigley eqs. 10-5/10-6 and Table 10-1
- Working point: 2 lbf on the Example 10-1 spring deflects 0.49 in (F/k), stress 45.2 kpsi, safety 3.2; deflection mode returns the same force; a 5 lbf request closes the spring solid and is capped at F_s with a warning
  - Source: Linear spring F = k y; solid-height cap
- Surge frequency: music-wire spring of Example 10-1 has active mass 7850 × (π d²/4) × π D N_a = 2.6 g and f = ½ √(k/m) ≈ 260 Hz; a long slender spring (L₀ 60 mm, D 10 mm, fixed–free) is flagged for buckling
  - Source: Shigley eq. 10-25 (f = ½ √(k g/W) for fixed ends) and eq. 10-13 (buckling)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: outside diameter not larger than the wire, free length below the solid height, unknown material
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 10.17 mm, 10.8, 1.124, 10.5, 4.08 lbf/in, 2 231 MPa, 11.75 mm, 0.7875 in to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- R. G. Budynas & J. K. Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 9th–10th ed. (McGraw-Hill), ch. 10 Mechanical Springs: Tables 10-1 to 10-6, eqs. 10-3 to 10-13, Example 10-1
- Associated Spring (Barnes Group), Design Handbook — Engineering Guide to Spring Design (end types, buckling, allowable stresses)
- ASTM A228 / A227 / A229 / A232 / A401 / A313 wire specifications (tensile strength versus diameter)

## Holtrop–Mennen resistance and power

<a id="holtrop-mennen"></a>

Folder `holtrop-mennen/` · Maritime · Holtrop–Mennen (1982/1984) resistance components, effective and brake power, wake fraction and thrust deduction from main particulars.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Statistical regression method (334 models and 168 full-scale trials in the 1984 sample): valid for hull forms resembling the sample — roughly Cp 0.55–0.85, L/B 3.9–15, B/T 2.1–4.0, Fn below about 0.45 for the 1982 formulae and up to 0.8 for the 1984 high-speed formula — and uncertain to ±5–10 % even inside the range; outside it the formulas extrapolate and the page warns.
- ITTC-1957 friction line C_F = 0.075/(log10 Rn − 2)² with the viscosity and density entered (defaults: sea water 15 °C, ν = 1.18831·10⁻⁶ m²/s, ρ = 1025 kg/m³); the form factor 1+k1 multiplies R_F only, and the appendage resistance uses the same C_F with an equivalent 1+k2 from the paper's table (rudder behind stern 1.3–1.5, bilge keels 1.4, shaft brackets 3.0).
- Wave resistance: the 1982 formula uses m2 = c15 Cp² exp(−0.1 Fn⁻²); the 1984 re-analysis replaces it with m4 = 0.4 c15 exp(−0.034 Fn^−3.29) for Fn ≤ 0.40, uses the Series-64 based R_W-B (c17, m3) for Fn ≥ 0.55 and interpolates linearly between — the interpolation is described in the paper as "more or less arbitrary".
- Bulb and transom terms follow the 1982 paper unchanged (the 1984 paper made no new analysis); the 1984 variant caps the bulb centre height h_B at 0.6 T_F as the paper recommends. With A_BT = 0 or A_T = 0 the terms vanish.
- Correlation allowance C_A (1982 trial-based formula, 150 µm hull roughness) with the roughness increase (0.105 k_s^(1/3) − 0.005579)/L^(1/3) for rougher hulls; the 1984 paper notes new ships average 91 % of this C_A but recommends keeping the formula. Still-air resistance is inside C_A; wind, waves, shallow water and fouling are not included.
- Propulsion factors: single-screw conventional-stern wake and thrust deduction from the chosen variant (1982: c8–c11 formula; 1984: c19/c20 formula), relative-rotative efficiency 0.9922 − 0.05908 A_E/A_0 + 0.07424 (Cp − 0.0225 lcb); twin-screw formulas from 1982. The open-water efficiency η_O is an input (use the B-series calculator), shaft efficiency 0.99 by default; P_S is the shaft power at ideal trial conditions.
- lcb is the longitudinal centre of buoyancy forward of ½L_WL in % of L_WL (negative aft). The paper's example prints −2.02 % relative to ½L_PP; in the formulas it enters as −0.75 % of L_WL, which is the value that reproduces every printed intermediate (L_R 81.385 m, C_P1 0.5477).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30, corrected 2026-10-31: the 1982 variant reproduces the numerical example of the paper (L 205 m, 25 kn) within rounding on 1+k1 1.156, S 7381.45 m², C_F 0.001390, R_F 869.63 kN, R_APP 8.83 kN, i_E 12.08°, c1 1.398, c2 0.7595, c5 0.9592, λ 0.6513, m1 −2.1274, m2 −0.17087, P_B 0.6261, R_B 0.049 kN, Fn_T 5.433, C_A 0.000352, w 0.2584, t 0.1747 and η_R 0.9931. It does not reproduce the printed R_A: 220.57 kN against 221.98 kN (−0.6 %). The printed figure equals ½ρV² C_A over S + S_APP (222.07 kN), so the paper appears to apply C_A to the appendage area as well, while this calculator follows the formula R_A = ½ρV² S C_A. With R_W 556.95 kN (printed 557.11) the totals are R_T 1792.10 kN (1793.26), P_E 23 048 kW (23 063), thrust 2171.3 kN (2172.75) and P_S 32 619 kW (32 621) with η_O 0.6461, all within 0.07 %.
- Article check 2026-10-31 (schema.example): the worked example of content.md had printed the figures of the paper instead of the results of this calculator, and R_F(1+k1) 1 005 instead of 1 006 kN, η_H 1.113 instead of 1.112, and a rise of about 3 % instead of 1.2 % in total resistance for the 1984 variant; corrected, with the difference to the paper explained there.
- Formulas transcribed from the OCR text of both papers (ISP 29 pp. 166–170 and ISP 31 pp. 272–276, fetched 2026-10-30); every coefficient was cross-checked against the reproduced example or against standard reproductions (Birk 2019 ch. 50, Molland et al. 2017).
- Design decision: both variants are offered because most textbooks and codes use the 1982 form factor with the 1984 wave resistance; here each variant is internally consistent with its paper. For the example ship the 1984 form factor is 2.5 % higher (1.185 vs 1.156).
- Design decision: wake, thrust deduction and η_R are reported as information and used for P_D; η_O must be supplied (default 0.62) because the propeller is not designed here — the B-series calculator does that.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Froude number … is above the range of the … formulas (≈ …): extrapolation.
- 0.40 < Fn < 0.55: the wave resistance is the paper\'s linear interpolation between the low- and high-speed formulas ("more or less arbitrary").
- Prismatic coefficient … is outside the 0.55–0.85 core of the regression sample.
- L/B = … is outside the 3.9–15 range of the sample.
- B/T = … is outside the 2.1–4.0 range of the sample.
- Bulb centre height h_B capped at 0.6 T_F = … m as recommended in the 1984 paper.
- Half angle of entrance estimated at …° from the hull coefficients; enter the actual value from the lines plan if known.
- L³/∇ > 1727 (very slender hull): the hump coefficient c15 is zero.
- Ideal trial conditions: calm water, deep water, clean hull (150 µm) — add service margins for wind, waves and fouling.
- Open-water efficiency η_O = … is an input; design the propeller with the B-series calculator for a consistent value.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Prismatic coefficient … is outside the method (0.30 ≤ C_P < 0.95): check ∇, L, B, T and C_M
- Length of run is not positive: check lcb and C_P
- L/B = … is outside the Holtrop–Mennen method: the wave resistance terms need L/B greater than 2
- Bulb centre too high: T_F − 1.5 h_B must be positive (T_F … m, h_B … m)
- Bulb immersion T_F − h_B − 0.25 √A_BT must be positive
- C_P1 = 1.45 C_P − 0.315 − 0.0225 lcb = … is 1 or more: the single-screw wake formula does not apply to so full an afterbody
- The pram-with-gondola stern coefficient (−25) exists only in the 1984 re-analysis

  - Source: Holtrop & Mennen (1982) example

## Horsepower calculator

<a id="horsepower"></a>

Folder `horsepower/` · Automotive · Horsepower from torque and rpm, or estimated from quarter-mile time or trap speed and weight, in hp, kW and PS, at the crank and the wheels.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Power from torque is exact: P = T × 2π × rpm / 60, which is hp = lbf·ft × rpm / 5 252 with 1 hp = 550 ft·lbf/s; torque and horsepower curves therefore cross at 5 252 rpm.
- The elapsed-time and trap-speed formulas are empirical estimates from drag-strip data: hp = W (K_t / ET)³ and hp = W (mph / K_v)³ with the race weight W in lb (car, driver and fuel). They give engine (flywheel) horsepower, as the Wallace Racing calculator that uses the same form states.
- Trap speed estimates power better than elapsed time, because the launch, traction and shifting affect the ET far more than the speed at the end of the run.
- Wheel horsepower is crank horsepower times (1 − drivetrain loss); the loss is an assumption, often taken as 15 % for a manual rear-drive car and higher for automatics and all-wheel drive.
- kW and PS (metric horsepower, 75 kgf·m/s = 735.5 W) are the same power in other units; 1 hp (mechanical) = 745.7 W.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 400 lbf·ft at 5 000 rpm is 380.8 hp, 284.0 kW, 386.1 PS at the crank and 323.7 hp at the wheels with a 15 % loss. A 3 500 lb car trapping 113.6 mph gives 400.5 hp by the Hale constants (3 500 × (113.6 / 234)³). Checked by hand.
- The constants are those tabulated by McCaul (2014, Table 2) for Patrick Hale (Quarter Jr.), Geoffrey Fox and Roger Huntington; ET × mph is the same constant for every car with one set of constants (5.825 × 234 = 1 363).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Elapsed time depends heavily on launch, traction and shifting; the trap-speed estimate is usually closer to the real power.
- Below 1.5 lb per hp the car is in pro drag-racing territory, where the empirical formulas were not fitted; treat the estimate as rough.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 400 lbf·ft at 5 000 rpm is 400 × 5 000 / 5 252.1 = 380.8 hp, 284.0 kW, 386.1 PS; 323.7 hp at the wheels with 15 % loss
  - Source: P = T ω with 1 hp = 550 ft·lbf/s (33 000 / 2π = 5 252.11); 1 PS = 735.49875 W
- Torque and horsepower cross at 5 252 rpm: 300 lbf·ft there is 300 hp
  - Source: hp = lbf·ft × rpm / 5 252 (definition of the mechanical horsepower)
- Chassis dyno: 300 hp at the wheels with a 15 % loss is 352.9 hp at the crank
  - Source: Wheel = crank × (1 − loss)
- Hale constants: 3 500 lb trapping 113.6 mph is 400.5 hp; the same car at 12.00 s is 400.3 hp
  - Source: McCaul 2014, Table 2: Patrick Hale / Quarter Jr. K_t = 5.825, K_v = 234.0; hp = W (mph/K_v)³ = W (K_t/ET)³
- 1970 AAR ’Cuda (3 585 lb, 14.30 s, rated 290 hp): Huntington’s ET formula gives 305.1 hp, within 6 % of the rating
  - Source: McCaul 2014, test data of the AAR ’Cuda and Huntington constants K_t = 6.29, K_v = 224

  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 380.8 hp, 284.0 kW, 386.1 PS, 323.7 hp to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)
