## Optimal hull cleaning interval

<a id="hull-cleaning-interval"></a>

Folder `hull-cleaning-interval/` · Maritime · Cleaning interval that minimises fuel penalty plus cleaning cost, from the fouling growth rate, fuel and ETS prices and the cost per cleaning.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The fouling fuel penalty grows linearly with time since cleaning, p(t) = p₀ + r t in per cent of the clean-hull consumption at sea, with a residual p₀ right after cleaning (0 for a full clean, 1–3 % when cleaning does not restore the coating) and a rate r in % per month; real growth is seasonal and stepwise (slime in weeks, calcareous fouling after idle periods), so r is the average over the cycle and the result is a planning interval, not a forecast.
- Each percentage point of penalty costs c₁ = F × d × (p + s C_F e)/100 per month, where F is the clean consumption at sea (t/day), d the sea days per month, p the fuel price, e the CO₂ allowance price, C_F the carbon factor and s the share of emissions under the ETS; the CII and FuelEU consequences are not priced.
- A cleaning costs C = diver/ROV cost + off-hire days × daily hire (or opportunity cost); the cleaning is assumed to take the hull back to the residual p₀ instantly and to be feasible anywhere (port-state and coating-manufacturer restrictions, capture requirements and the IMO 2023 Biofouling Guidelines are outside the model).
- Minimising the average monthly cost A(T) = C/T + c₁ p₀ + c₁ r T/2 gives the age-replacement optimum T* = √(2C/(c₁ r)) (Jardine & Tsang); A(T*) = c₁ p₀ + √(2 C c₁ r). The interval cannot exceed the docking interval entered, where a full recoating resets the cycle anyway.
- Cost to the owner/operator only, in one currency; discounting is ignored over the cycle (months), and the fuel penalty is charged whether the ship is on time charter or spot (whoever pays the fuel bears it).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: default case (30 t/day, 22 sea days/month, 550 per t fuel, 70 per t CO₂ at 50 % ETS, 1 %/month, cleaning 60 000 + 1 day off-hire at 20 000) gives c₁ 4 349 per % per month, T* 6.07 months and 26 380 per month; a 12-month interval costs 32 763 per month, so cleaning twice as often saves about 76 600 per year — the same order as the Schultz et al. (2011) frigate study (slime-level fouling dominating the cost).
- Design decision: a single linear growth rate because the published data do not support a more detailed universal curve; the chosen-interval outputs let the user compare any policy against the optimum.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Zero penalty growth: there is no optimum — clean only at docking (interval set to the docking interval).
- Zero cleaning cost: the optimum is to clean continuously; the docking interval is shown instead.
- The economic optimum … months exceeds the docking interval: clean only at docking (penalty too slow or cleaning too expensive to pay off).
- Optimum below two months: the linear-growth model and the instant-cleaning assumption are stretched; check the growth rate and consider a better coating.
- Residual penalty … % after cleaning adds a fixed … per year that no interval removes — only recoating does.
- Average linear fouling growth over the cycle: idle periods in warm water accelerate calcareous fouling far beyond the average rate.
- Cleaning feasibility (port rules, capture systems, coating damage from aggressive brushes) and the CII/FuelEU value of the saved fuel are outside the model.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The fuel penalty has no cost: enter sea days and a fuel or allowance price

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Cost per point and per cleaning: c₁ = 30 × 22 × (550 + 0.5 × 3.114 × 70)/100 = 4 349.3 per % per month; C = 60 000 + 1 × 20 000 = 80 000
  - Source: Model definition (fuel + ETS cost of one percentage point; cleaning plus off-hire)
- Optimum: T* = √(2 × 80 000/(4 349.3 × 1)) = 6.065 months, A(T*) = √(2 C c₁ r) = 26 380 per month = 316 557 per year; 1.98 cleanings per year; penalty 6.07 % just before cleaning
  - Source: Jardine & Tsang age-replacement optimum with linearly increasing cost
- The optimum is a minimum: A(T*) ≤ A(T) for T = 3, 4.5, 9, 12, 24 months; the compared 12-month policy costs 32 763 per month, so the saving is 12 × (32 763 − 26 380) = 76 595 per year
  - Source: Convexity of C/T + a T/2; arithmetic
- Fuel wasted at 12 months: 30 × 22 × 12 × (0 + 12/2)/100 = 475.2 t/yr and 1 479.8 t CO₂; at the optimum 240.2 t/yr
  - Source: Average penalty over a cycle = p₀ + r T/2
- Residual penalty shifts the cost but not the interval: p₀ 2 % leaves T* at 6.065 months and adds 2 × 4 349.3 × 12 = 104 383 per year, with a warning
  - Source: A(T) = C/T + c₁ p₀ + c₁ r T/2 — the p₀ term is constant in T
- Edge cases: zero growth → no optimum, docking interval used and warned; slow growth 0.05 %/month → T* 27.1 months capped at a 24-month docking interval; zero fuel cost rejected
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 6.1 %, 475 t, 1 480 t to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- M. P. Schultz, J. A. Bendick, E. R. Holm, W. M. Hertel, "Economic impact of biofouling on a naval surface ship", Biofouling 27(1), 2011, 87–98
- M. P. Schultz, "Effects of coating roughness and biofouling on ship resistance and powering", Biofouling 23(5), 2007 (penalty magnitudes per condition)
- A. K. S. Jardine, A. H. C. Tsang, Maintenance, Replacement, and Reliability: Theory and Applications, 2nd ed., CRC Press 2013 — replacement interval with linearly increasing operating cost, T* = √(2C/a)
- IMO Resolution MEPC.378(80), 2023 Guidelines for the control and management of ships' biofouling (inspection and cleaning practice)

## Hull roughness and fouling penalty

<a id="hull-roughness-penalty"></a>

Folder `hull-roughness-penalty/` · Maritime · Added resistance, power, fuel and speed loss from hull roughness or fouling via the ITTC-57 line and the ISO 15016 roughness allowance.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Roughness acts only on the frictional part of the resistance through the roughness allowance ΔC_F; the viscous resistance of the clean hull is (1 + k) C_F ½ρSV² with the ITTC-1957 line and a form factor (1 + k), and ΔC_F is added without the form factor, as in the 1978 ITTC performance prediction method and ISO 15016:2025 (G.5).
- The roughness allowance follows ISO 15016:2025 E.7/G.8 (Townsin form, ΔC_F = 0.044[(k_s/L)^(1/3) − 10 Re^(−1/3)] + 0.000125, minimum 0) or the 1978 ITTC form [105 (k_s/L)^(1/3) − 0.64]·10⁻³; both treat k_s as a single equivalent sand roughness, which for coatings is close to the 50 mm cut-off hull roughness Rt50 and for fouling is the Schultz (2007) equivalent value — fouling is not sand roughness, so the equivalence is approximate (±30 %).
- The fouled condition is compared with the clean, newly coated hull (default 150 µm, the ISO default when no roughness survey exists): ΔR = ½ρSV² [ΔC_F(k_s,fouled) − ΔC_F(k_s,clean)].
- Power increase at constant speed ΔP/P = ΔR/R_T assumes the propulsive efficiency does not change with the added resistance (in reality the heavier propeller loading lowers it slightly, making the real penalty 5–10 % larger than computed); the total resistance comes either from the delivered power and η_D entered or from the clean viscous resistance divided by an assumed viscous share of the total.
- Speed loss at constant power uses the cubic law P ∝ V³: ΔV/V = 1 − (1 + ΔP/P)^(−1/3); fuel from the added power × SFOC × 24 h; CO₂ with the carbon factor entered (HFO 3.114 by default).
- Sea water density and viscosity from the ITTC 7.5-02-01-03 table at the temperature and salinity entered (shared/seawater.js).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: for L 180 m at 6.5 m/s in 15 °C sea water (Re 9.846e8) the allowances reproduce the atlas_physics production pins (150 µm 9.677e-5, 300 µm 2.044e-4, 1 000 µm 4.620e-4, 10 000 µm 1.362e-3); heavy slime on a 5 500 m² hull with 3 200 kW delivered adds 29.0 kN, 8.66 % power, 1.16 t/day — inside the 10–20 % band Schultz (2007) predicts for heavy slime on a frigate.
- Design decision: the clean reference roughness is an input (not fixed at 150 µm) so a measured as-docked Rt50 can be used; the Schultz conditions are offered as presets with the custom value for survey data.
- Article check 2026-10-31 (schema.example): the worked example had been worked by hand with the speed rounded to 6.5 m/s (12.6 kn is 6.482 m/s), so its ½ρSV² (119.2 MN), ΔR (29.0 kN), ΔP/P (8.66 %), fuel (1.16 t/day, 291 t/year) and CO₂ (906 t) were 0.6–0.8 % high; restated in content.md with the results of this calculator.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Water temperature outside the 0–35 °C ITTC table: properties held at the table end.
- Present roughness is smoother than the clean reference: the penalty is negative (a credit), check the two roughness values.
- Reynolds number below 1e7 (model scale or very low speed): the roughness allowance was derived for full-scale ships.
- Total resistance estimated from a … % viscous share: use the delivered power at this speed when known.
- Power increase above 50 %: the constant-efficiency and cubic-law assumptions no longer hold; the propeller may not absorb the power.
- Fouling is not sand-grain roughness: the Schultz equivalent k_s values carry about ±30 % uncertainty, and the propulsive efficiency drop with heavier propeller loading (5–10 % of the penalty) is not included.
- Hull only: propeller roughness and fouling (typically a further 2–6 % of power) are a separate penalty.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The roughness credit exceeds the total resistance implied by the power or viscous share entered: check the power, speed, wetted surface and the two roughness values

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Friction and allowance pins: L 180 m at 6.5 m/s in 15 °C sea water → Re 9.846e8, C_F 1.5336e-3, ΔC_F 9.677e-5 (150 µm), 3.400e-4 (600 µm), 1.3616e-3 (10 000 µm)
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 E.5–E.7 as implemented in atlas_physics (pins 2026-10-31); ITTC 7.5-02-01-03 water properties
- Heavy slime penalty: ½ρSV² = 119.20 MN, ΔC_F increase 2.432e-4 → ΔR 28.99 kN; clean viscous resistance 219.4 kN; R_T from 3 200 kW and η_D 0.68 = 334.8 kN → ΔP/P 8.66 %, 277 kW, 1.164 t/day, 291 t/yr, 160 k/yr, 906 t CO₂/yr
  - Source: ITTC-78 resistance decomposition; Schultz (2007) heavy slime 10–20 % band; arithmetic
- Speed loss at constant power: ΔV/V = 1 − (1.0866)^(−1/3) = 2.73 %; the cubic law gives ΔP/P ≈ 3 ΔV/V for small penalties
  - Source: Cubic speed-power law (ISO 19030-2 speed-loss indicator logic)
- Viscous-share mode: R_T = (219.4 + 11.5 kN)/0.8 = 288.6 kN, delivered power 2 759 kW, ΔP/P 10.0 % — flagged as an estimate
  - Source: Resistance decomposition with an assumed viscous share
- ITTC-78 allowance and the condition table: 150 µm → 3.481e-4, 600 µm → 9.285e-4 with the 1978 formula; custom 600 µm equals the heavy-slime preset; Schultz table 150/300/600/1 000/3 000/10 000 µm
  - Source: ITTC 7.5-02-03-01.4 (1978) ΔC_F = [105 (k_s/L)^(1/3) − 0.64]·10⁻³; Schultz 2007 Table 1
- Credit and validation: a 100 µm hull against a 150 µm reference gives a negative penalty with a warning; zero wetted surface, unknown condition and η_D above 1 are rejected
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
- A roughness credit larger than the whole resistance (smoother "fouled" hull and a tiny power) is rejected instead of a NaN speed loss
  - Source: Range fuzzing (fuzz.js): (1 + ΔP/P)^(−1/3) needs ΔP/P > −1
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 218 kN, 336 kN, 28.8 kN, 8.59 %, 275 kW, 2.7 %, 1.15, 289, about 159 000, 899 t to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ITTC Recommended Procedure 7.5-02-03-01.4, 1978 ITTC Performance Prediction Method (roughness allowance, form factor, ITTC-57 line)
- ISO 15016:2025, Annex E (E.5–E.7) and Annex G (G.5–G.8) — friction coefficient and roughness allowance with k_s default 150 µm
- M. P. Schultz, "Effects of coating roughness and biofouling on ship resistance and powering", Biofouling 23(5), 2007, 331–341 — Table 1 hull conditions (150, 300, 600, 1 000, 3 000, 10 000 µm)
- R. L. Townsin, "The ITTC line — its genesis and correlation allowance", The Naval Architect, 1985; ITTC 7.5-02-01-03 water properties

## Hull speed calculator

<a id="hull-speed"></a>

Folder `hull-speed/` · Maritime · Displacement hull speed from waterline length (1.34 √LWL), speed–length ratio, Froude number, speed regime and Gerr's top speed for light hulls.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Hull speed is the speed at which the bow wave is as long as the waterline: S/L = 1.34, Froude number 0.40. It is a practical limit for heavy displacement hulls, not a physical barrier.
- LWL is the waterline length in the loaded condition; overhangs that immerse as the boat heels or squats lengthen the effective waterline a little.
- Speed regimes follow Gerr: displacement up to S/L 1.34, semi-displacement from about 1.45 to 3.0 with enough power and a light hull, planing above S/L 3.0.
- Gerr's formula S/L = 8.26 / (D/L)^0.311 estimates the top speed a hull of that displacement–length ratio can reach without planing; it is an empirical fit, not a resistance calculation.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: LWL 30 ft gives 1.34 × √30 = 7.34 kn (2.43 × √9.144 m gives the same); at 6 kn S/L = 1.10 and Fn = 0.326; 10 000 lb gives D/L = 165 and Gerr S/L 1.69, 9.24 kn. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Gerr\'s formula gives less than S/L 1.34 for this heavy hull: in practice it is limited to about hull speed.
- Gerr\'s formula gives more than S/L 3.0: a hull this light can plane, so use the planing speed calculator instead.
- The displacement–length ratio is outside the usual range for boats (about 50 to 500): check the displacement and its unit.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- LWL 30 ft: hull speed 1.34 × √30 = 7.34 kn; the metric form 2.43 × √9.144 m agrees within 0.2 %
  - Source: Gerr, The Propeller Handbook, ch. 2 (V = 1.34 √LWL); hand calculation
- At hull speed the Froude number is 0.40 and the bow wave is as long as the waterline
  - Source: Lewis, PNA Vol. II ch. 5: λ = 2π V²/g, so λ = L at Fn = 1/√(2π) = 0.399
- Gerr: 10 000 lb on 30 ft LWL is D/L 165, maximum S/L 1.69 and about 9.24 kn
  - Source: Gerr, The Propeller Handbook, ch. 2 (D/L = long tons / (0.01 LWL)³, S/L = 8.26 / (D/L)^0.311); hand calculation
- Regimes: S/L 1.0 is displacement, 2.0 semi-displacement, 3.5 planing; planing starts at 3.0 √LWL
  - Source: Gerr (displacement ≤ 1.34, semi-displacement 1.45–3.0, planing above 3.0)
- A displacement of 0 skips Gerr; zero length is rejected; a very heavy hull warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 7.34 kn, 1.10, 0.326, 165, 1.69, 9.24 kn to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- D. Gerr, The Propeller Handbook (International Marine, 1989), ch. 2: speed–length ratio, displacement–length ratio and the maximum S/L of semi-displacement hulls
- E.V. Lewis (ed.), Principles of Naval Architecture, 2nd rev. (SNAME, 1988), Vol. II ch. 5: Froude number and ship-generated waves (λ = 2π V²/g)
- L. Larsson and H.C. Raven, Ship Resistance and Flow (SNAME PNA series, 2010): wave resistance

## Hydraulic cylinder force and speed

<a id="hydraulic-cylinder"></a>

Folder `hydraulic-cylinder/` · Mechanical · Push and pull force, extend and retract speed, regenerative mode, hydraulic power, oil volumes and rod buckling margin from bore, rod, pressure and flow.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Force = pressure × effective piston area × mechanical efficiency; the pressure is the differential across the piston (supply minus the back-pressure on the other side), which the user enters as one effective value. Seal friction and breakaway are lumped into the efficiency (0.85–0.95 typical).
- Speed = flow ÷ area with the full pump flow available to the cylinder; valve pressure drops, pump slip and compensator behaviour are not modelled, and the extend and retract times exclude acceleration and cushioning.
- Regenerative (differential) extension connects the annulus to the cap side: speed Q / A_rod and force p A_rod, valid only while the load is below that force.
- Hydraulic power p Q is the power delivered to the cylinder; the pump input power is higher by the pump and drive efficiencies.
- Rod buckling uses the Euler formula on the rod alone with the full extended length and the mounting K factor, which is the conservative catalogue approach; manufacturers' buckling charts also credit the cylinder tube stiffness and apply a safety factor of 3.5 (Parker) or 2.5–4 depending on the standard.
- The pressure vessel aspects (tube wall thickness, end caps, tie rods) are not checked — see the pressure-vessel calculator with the cylinder bore as inside diameter.
- Oil compressibility and hose expansion are ignored; they matter for positioning accuracy and natural frequency, not for the static figures here.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the 100/56 mm cylinder at 200 bar with 40 L/min gives 157.1 kN push, 107.8 kN pull, 0.0849 m/s extend (5.09 m/min) and 13.3 kW hydraulic power, all checked by hand against the standard catalogue formulas; the rod Euler load of 4.0 MN at 0.5 m confirms the familiar result that short strokes never buckle and a 3 m stroke of the same rod would.
- Design decision: ISO 3320 preferred bores and rods are not enforced — any dimensions are accepted — but the 100/56 default is a standard pairing (area ratio 1.46).
- Design decision: the rod section comes from shared/sections.js so the buckling check is consistent with the column calculator.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Rod buckling factor … is below the required …: shorten the stroke, use a larger rod or add a stop tube / better guiding.
- Pressure above 350 bar exceeds the usual industrial cylinder rating; check the cylinder series.
- Extend speed above 0.5 m/s: cushioning and seal speed limits need checking (standard seals are rated to about 0.5–1 m/s).
- Efficiency 1.0 ignores seal friction; catalogue practice uses 0.85–0.95.
- Static figures with the full pump flow and the entered differential pressure; valve losses, back-pressure and acceleration are not included.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Rod diameter must be smaller than the bore

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Areas of a 100/56 cylinder: cap 78.54 cm², annulus 53.91 cm², ratio φ = 1.457 (ISO 3320 standard pairing)
  - Source: A = π D²/4; ISO 3320 bore/rod series (100 mm bore with 56 mm rod, ratio ≈ 1.46)
- Forces at 200 bar: push 157.1 kN, pull 107.8 kN; with η = 0.9 both drop by 10 %
  - Source: Parker HY08-1114 / Bosch Rexroth: F = p × A (× efficiency)
- Speeds at 40 L/min: extend 0.0849 m/s (5.09 m/min) in 5.89 s, retract 0.1237 m/s in 4.04 s; return flow while extending 27.5 L/min
  - Source: v = Q / A; t = s / v; return flow Q × A_ann / A_cap (Rexroth Hydraulic Trainer Vol. 1)
- Regenerative extension: speed Q / A_rod = 0.271 m/s (3.2 × normal) at a force of p A_rod = 49.3 kN
  - Source: Differential circuit: both sides at pressure, net area = rod area (Rexroth Hydraulic Trainer Vol. 1, regenerative circuits)
- Hydraulic power p Q = 200 bar × 40 L/min = 13.33 kW; oil volumes 3.93 L to extend and 2.70 L to retract
  - Source: P = p Q (1 bar × 1 L/min = 1.667 W); V = A × stroke
- Rod buckling: 56 mm rod, I = π d⁴/64 = 48.3 cm⁴, Euler load at 0.5 m pinned = 4.0 MN (factor 25); at 3 m stroke 111 kN, below the push force → warning; K = 2 quarters the load
  - Source: Euler P_cr = π² E I / (K L)² (Shigley §4-12); Parker column-load practice with safety factor 3.5
- Maximum stroke for the safety factor: with FS 3.5 the 56 mm rod at 157 kN may extend to √(π² E I / (3.5 F)) = 1.35 m pinned; the Euler load at that stroke is exactly 3.5 × the push force
  - Source: Inversion of the Euler formula for the length
- Unit layer: 200 bar = 2 900 psi, 40 L/min = 10.57 US gpm, 157 kN = 35 310 lbf
  - Source: NIST SP 811 conversion factors
- Invalid inputs fail fast: rod not smaller than the bore, zero stroke, unknown mounting
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 78.5 cm², 53.9 cm², 1.46, 141 kN, 97 kN, 0.085 m/s, 0.124 m/s, 5.9 s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

- Bosch Rexroth, Hydraulic Formulae and Hydraulic Trainer Vol. 1 (F = p A, v = Q / A, P = p Q)

## Hydrostatic pressure at depth

<a id="hydrostatic-pressure"></a>

Folder `hydrostatic-pressure/` · Thermal and fluids · Gauge and absolute pressure at a depth in water, sea water, fuel or any liquid, its head in metres of water, and the force on a flat surface.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The liquid is at rest and of uniform density; a column with temperature or salinity layers needs an average density.
- Gravity is the standard 9.806 65 m/s²; local gravity varies by up to 0.3 % with latitude and height.
- The surface pressure is the standard atmosphere (101.325 kPa) unless another is entered, for example a pressurised tank or a different altitude.
- The force is on a horizontal surface at the given depth, where the pressure is uniform; a vertical or sloping wall needs the pressure at its centroid.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: sea water at 30 m gives 301.8 kPa gauge and 403.1 kPa absolute; fresh water at 10 m gives 97.9 kPa, the familiar "one atmosphere per ten metres". Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Below about 1000 m water compresses noticeably (about 0.5 % per 1000 m); the constant-density result slightly understates the pressure.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Sea water (1025.87 kg/m³) at 30 m: 301.81 kPa gauge, 403.14 kPa absolute, 3.018 bar
  - Source: White, Fluid Mechanics, ch. 2.3: p = p₀ + ρ g h; ITTC 7.5-02-01-03 sea water at 15 °C; ISO 2533 atmosphere
- Fresh water at 10 m: 97.9 kPa, close to one atmosphere, and a head of 9.98 m of 1000 kg/m³ water
  - Source: ρ water 20 °C = 998.2 kg/m³; conventional metre of water column at 1000 kg/m³ (ISO 80000-4)
- A 1.5 m² hatch 4 m below a fuel oil surface (830 kg/m³) carries 48.8 kN
  - Source: Force on a horizontal plane F = p A (White, ch. 2.5)
- A 760 mm mercury column (13 595.1 kg/m³ at 0 °C) equals one standard atmosphere
  - Source: Definition of 760 mmHg = 101 325 Pa with mercury at 0 °C and standard gravity
- At the surface the gauge pressure is zero and the absolute pressure is the surface pressure; very deep water warns
  - Source: p = p₀ at h = 0; water compressibility about 0.5 % per 1000 m
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 301.8 kPa, 403.1 kPa, 3.02 bar to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- White, F. M., Fluid Mechanics, 7th ed., ch. 2.3 (hydrostatic pressure distribution p = p₀ + ρ g h) and ch. 2.5 (forces on plane surfaces)
- ISO 2533:1975 Standard Atmosphere (101 325 Pa at sea level); ISO 80000-3 standard gravity 9.806 65 m/s²

## Hydrostatics basics

<a id="hydrostatics"></a>

Folder `hydrostatics/` · Maritime · Displacement from draft and block coefficient, TPC, fresh and dock water allowance, trim and end drafts from LCG, LCB and MCTC.

### Assumptions and caveats

- C_B and C_W are the coefficients at the draft entered, not design values; both fall as the draft decreases, so summer-load values at ballast draft overstate displacement.
- Longitudinal positions are measured from the aft perpendicular, positive forward; trim is positive by the stern, negative by the head.
- The fresh water allowance assumes sea water of 1.025 t/m³ and a constant TPC over the small draft change (Load Line convention), with DWA scaled linearly to the dock density.
- Trim is treated as small: TPC, MCTC and LCF are constant and the draft at the LCF is unchanged by the trim; above about 1 % of the length use the hydrostatic tables iteratively.
- Barrass's MCTC ≈ 7.31 × TPC² / B is an order-of-magnitude estimate (±15 % or worse) for merchant forms in salt water and must not be used for a real loading condition.
- All drafts are moulded; add keel thickness for extreme drafts and apply hog/sag corrections separately.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the FWA formula Δ/(4 TPC) was cross-checked independently against the volume change from 1.025 to 1.000 t/m³ on a box barge (125 mm both ways).
- Design decision: longitudinal positions are from the aft perpendicular, positive forward, and trim is positive by the stern, to match the way hydrostatic tables are printed; the draft-survey calculator uses LCF from midships instead because surveys do.
- Provenance: Barrass's MCTC ≈ 7.31 TPC²/B is quoted from Ship Design and Performance for Masters and Mates (2004) and kept only as a labelled estimate.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Block coefficient outside 0.45–0.90 is unusual for a displacement ship — check the value.
- Waterplane coefficient is below the block coefficient, which no normal hull form has — check both values.
- MCTC is Barrass\'s rough estimate (±15 % or worse). Use the hydrostatic tables for any real trim calculation.
- Trim exceeds 1 % of the ship length; the linear trim formulas lose accuracy and LCF moves — recheck LCG and MCTC.
- An end draft is negative: the combination of draft and trim is not physical.
- C_W is well below the usual (1 + 2 C_B) / 3 relation for merchant hulls — TPC may be underestimated.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Box barge 100 × 10 × 5 m in salt water: ∇ 5 000 m³, Δ 5 125 t, A_W 1 000 m², TPC 10.25 t/cm
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed. (2012), ch. 2 "Form coefficients" and ch. 9 "TPC"; TPC = A_W × ρ / 100
- FWA = Δ / (4 TPC) = 125 mm, verified against the volume change from 1.025 to 1.000 t/m³
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass (2012), ch. 10 "Fresh water allowance": FWA (mm) = W / (4 × TPC); independent check 5 125 t × (1/1.000 − 1/1.025) ÷ 1 000 m² = 0.125 m
- Dock water allowance at 1.010 t/m³ is 75 mm (FWA × (1025 − 1010) / 25)
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass (2012), ch. 10: DWA = FWA × (1025 − ρ_DW) / 25
- Δ 8 000 t with LCG 1 m aft of LCB and MCTC 100 t·m/cm trims 80 cm by the stern; drafts 5.40 / 4.60 m
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass (2012), ch. 15 "Trim": trim = Δ × (LCB − LCG) / MCTC; change aft = trim × LCF/L, forward = trim × (L − LCF)/L
- LCF 40 m from AP splits the same 80 cm trim unequally: aft +32 cm, forward −48 cm
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass (2012), ch. 15: draft changes are proportional to the distance of each perpendicular from the LCF
- LCG forward of LCB trims by the head (negative trim, text "by the head"); even keel when LCG = LCB
  - Source: Sign convention of this calculator (README) and Derrett & Barrass (2012), ch. 15
- Barrass MCTC estimate: 7.31 × 10.25² / 10 = 76.80 t·m/cm, flagged as an estimate
  - Source: C.B. Barrass, Ship Design and Performance for Masters and Mates (2004): MCTC ≈ 7.31 × TPC² / B
- Default ship 180 × 32 × 10 m, C_B 0.80, C_W 0.88: Δ 47 232 t, TPC 51.96 t/cm, FWA 227 mm
  - Source: Hand calculation with the Derrett & Barrass formulas above
- Unit layer: TPC 10.25 t/cm = 25.62 long tons per inch; MCTC 100 t·m/cm = 820.2 long ton·ft/in
  - Source: 1 long ton = 1.0160469 t, 1 in = 2.54 cm, 1 ft = 0.3048 m (exact definitions)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: LCG beyond the ship length, zero draft, block coefficient above 1
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 8 000 m³, 8 000 t, 1 600 m², 16.0 t/cm, 8 000 t·m, 80 cm, 5.40 m, 4.60 m to the digits printed

## Ideal gas law (PV = nRT)

<a id="ideal-gas-law"></a>

Folder `ideal-gas-law/` · Thermal and fluids · Pressure, volume, temperature or amount of a gas from PV = nRT, with its mass, density and specific gas constant for air, N₂, CO₂, H₂ and more.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The gas is ideal: its molecules have no volume and no attraction. Real gases follow PV = nRT closely at low pressure and well above their boiling point; at high pressure the compressibility factor Z multiplies the right-hand side.
- Pressure is absolute. A gauge reading must have the atmospheric pressure (about 1.013 bar at sea level) added before it is entered.
- Temperature is absolute (kelvin); the calculator converts °C and °F, but the law itself only holds on an absolute scale.
- Molar masses are for the pure gas (dry air for air); humid air is slightly lighter, and natural gas varies with its composition.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: dry air at 101.325 kPa and 20 °C gives 1.204 kg/m³, the standard value; 1 mol at 0 °C and 101.325 kPa occupies 22.414 L (the textbook molar volume).
- Design decision: one page solves for any of the four variables, because searches for the ideal gas law come from every direction (pressure in a tank, volume of a gas, temperature after heating).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above about 10 bar real gases depart from PV = nRT; at 200 bar nitrogen holds a few per cent less gas than the ideal value. Multiply by the compressibility factor Z for high-pressure work.
- Below its critical temperature this gas can condense under pressure; the ideal gas law does not apply to the liquid or near saturation.
- Below about 150 K most gases are near condensation, where the ideal gas law is unreliable.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Unknown variable "…"

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- One mole at 0 °C and 101.325 kPa occupies 22.414 L, the standard molar volume
  - Source: CODATA 2018: R = 8.314 462 618 J/(mol·K); molar volume of an ideal gas at 273.15 K and 101.325 kPa = 22.413 969 54 L/mol
- Dry air at the ISO standard atmosphere (101.325 kPa, 15 °C) has a density of 1.225 kg/m³
  - Source: ISO 2533:1975 Standard Atmosphere: ρ₀ = 1.2250 kg/m³ at sea level, 288.15 K
- Specific gas constants: air 287.05, nitrogen 296.80, CO₂ 188.92, hydrogen 4124.5 J/(kg·K)
  - Source: Çengel and Boles, Thermodynamics, Table A-1 (R = R_u / M)
- A 50 L nitrogen cylinder at 200 bar absolute and 15 °C holds 417.4 mol, 11.69 kg as an ideal gas, with a high-pressure warning
  - Source: PV = nRT (Çengel and Boles, ch. 3); M(N₂) = 28.0134 g/mol (IUPAC 2021)
- Round trip: solving for each variable in turn returns the other three unchanged
  - Source: Consistency of PV = nRT
- Heating a closed vessel: 1 bar at 20 °C rises to 1.341 bar at 120 °C (Gay-Lussac, P/T constant)
  - Source: Çengel and Boles, ch. 3: P₁/T₁ = P₂/T₂ at constant V and n
- Custom gas with M = 44.0095 g/mol matches the built-in CO₂; CO₂ below 31 °C warns about condensation
  - Source: IUPAC 2021 molar mass of CO₂; critical temperature of CO₂ 304.13 K (NIST Chemistry WebBook)
- Zero absolute temperature, zero volume and an unknown gas are rejected
  - Source: Input validation contract (shared/validate.js)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2 079, 60.2 kg, 1.204 kg/m³, 287.1 J/(kg·K) to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- CODATA 2018 recommended values: molar gas constant R = 8.314 462 618 J/(mol·K), exact
- Çengel and Boles, Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, 9th ed., ch. 3 (ideal-gas equation of state, compressibility factor)
- IUPAC Commission on Isotopic Abundances and Atomic Weights, standard atomic weights 2021 (molar masses)
- ISO 2533:1975 Standard Atmosphere (dry air molar mass 28.9644 g/mol, 1.225 kg/m³ at 15 °C)

## Inclining experiment

<a id="inclining-experiment"></a>

Folder `inclining-experiment/` · Maritime · GM and lightship KG from an inclining test: weight-movement moments against pendulum tangents by least squares, free surface and the lightweight survey.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Small-angle stability: within the 1°–4° of an inclining test the heeling moment and the tangent of the heel are proportional, tan θ = W·x/(Δ·GM); the moments of the weight movements are plotted against the tangents and fitted by a least-squares straight line, which (as the IS Code guidance stresses) need not pass through the origin, so a constant zero error of the pendulums does not affect GM.
- The tangent of each reading is the mean over the pendulums used of the deflection divided by that pendulum's length; the displacement and KM are those of the test condition from the draft readings, water density and hydrostatics at the actual trim, which this calculator takes as inputs.
- The measured metacentric height includes the free-surface effect of slack tanks at the time of the test; the free-surface moment entered is removed to obtain the solid KG.
- Lightweight survey: every item on board that is not part of the lightship (the inclining weights themselves, people, tools, liquids) is removed and every missing item added, each with its own vertical centre of gravity; their sum gives the lightship displacement and KG. Longitudinal centre and the hydrostatic corrections for trim and hog/sag are outside this calculator.
- IS Code limits checked as warnings: heel between 1° and 4° each side, a pendulum deflection of at least 15 cm, pendulums of at least 3 m, at least two pendulums, the zero point plus at least six movements, and a straight-line fit: R² below 0.99, or a reading whose externally studentized residual exceeds 3 and whose deviation exceeds about 1 mm on a 6 m pendulum, points to wind, mooring lines, liquids or people moving.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: readings generated for Δ = 9000 t and GM = 1.20 m (6.0 m and 5.5 m pendulums, rounded to whole millimetres) give GM = 1.20 m; adding a 3 mm zero error to every reading leaves GM unchanged; with KM 9.50 m and a free-surface moment of 150 t·m the solid KG is 8.283 m, and the lightweight survey of the default items gives 8948.5 t at a KG of 8.269 m.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- R² = …: the points do not lie on a straight line — look for wind, mooring lines, free liquids or people moving during the test, and repeat the bad movements.
- Reading on line … is off the line (studentized residual …): check it or repeat that movement.
- Largest heel …°: the IS Code asks for 1° to 4° each side.
- Largest deflection … mm: at least 150 mm each side is recommended (longer pendulums or heavier weights).
- A pendulum shorter than 3 m: 4–6 m is recommended.
- Only one pendulum: at least two are required and three recommended, to identify bad readings.
- Fewer than seven readings: the standard test is the zero point and eight weight movements (at least six with a straight-line plot).
- Very small GM: the ship is tender — the test may not be valid and the condition may be unsafe.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Readings line …: expected a moment and at least one deflection, all numbers
- Readings line …: … pendulums are in use but only … deflection(s) are given
- Survey line …: expected item; weight; VCG
- Survey line …: weight and VCG must be numbers
- Give the length of at least one pendulum
- Number the pendulums in use from 1 without gaps (pendulum 2 is used only together with pendulum 1)
- At least three readings are needed for the fit
- The heeling moments are all equal: move the weights
- The tangents do not increase with the heeling moment: check the signs (+ to starboard) of moments and deflections
- The survey removes more than the test displacement

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Exact readings for Δ = 9000 t and GM = 1.20 m (tan θ = W·x/(Δ·GM)) give GM = 1.200 m with R² = 1; the rounded default readings give 1.20 m within 1 cm
  - Source: IS Code 2008 Annex 1 §4.3: heeling moment against tangent, GM = W·x/(Δ tan θ)
- A constant 3 mm zero error on every pendulum reading shifts the fitted line but leaves GM unchanged, as the guidance says the line need not pass through the origin
  - Source: IS Code 2008 Annex 1 §4.3.2 (regression line not forced through the origin)
- KG and free surface: KM 9.50 m − GM 1.20 m = 8.30 m including free surface; FSM 150 t·m / 9000 t = 0.0167 m, so the solid KG is 8.2833 m
  - Source: KG = KM − GM; free-surface correction FSM/Δ (IS Code 2008 Part B 3.1)
- Lightweight survey of the default items: 9000 − 40 − 1.5 + 2 − 12 = 8948.5 t, KG = (74 550 − 500 − 22.5 + 36 − 72)/8948.5 = 8.2686 m
  - Source: Moments about the keel (IS Code 2008 Part B 8.1 lightweight survey)
- A bad reading is flagged: 20 mm added to one deflection lowers R² below 0.99 and the line is named in a warning
  - Source: IS Code 2008 Annex 1 §4.3.2 (deviations from a straight line indicate other moments)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: two readings only, pendulum 2 without pendulum 1, a missing deflection, inverted signs
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.201 m, 0.99999, 8.299 m, 0.017 m, 8.282 m, 8948.5 t, 8.27 m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IMO Resolution MSC.267(85) 2008 IS Code, Part B chapter 8 (determination of lightship parameters) and Annex 1 (detailed guidance for the conduct of an inclining test)
- ASTM F1321 Standard Guide for Conducting a Stability Test (Lightweight Survey and Inclining Experiment) to Determine the Light Ship Displacement and Centers of Gravity of a Vessel
- Rawson & Tupper, Basic Ship Theory, 5th ed., ch. 4 (the inclining experiment)

## Initial stability GM and list

<a id="initial-stability"></a>

Folder `initial-stability/` · Maritime · GM from KM and KG with free-surface correction, list from a weight shift, loading or discharge, rolling period and the IMO minimum-GM check.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Initial (small-angle) stability only: GM describes the righting lever for heel angles up to about 10°; list angles above that are reported with a warning and the full GZ curve (cross curves / KN) is needed instead.
- KM is taken from the hydrostatic tables at the present draft and is held constant through a loading or discharge operation; for large weights re-enter KM at the new displacement.
- Free surface is a virtual rise of G: FSC = Σ(l b³/12 × ρ_liquid) / Δ for rectangular tank surfaces, divided by n² for n equal longitudinal subdivisions; irregular tank shapes need the free-surface moments from the tank tables, and the moment is independent of how full the tank is (as long as it is slack).
- List assumes the heeling moment acts statically and the ship floats at the same KM; wind heeling, cargo shifting and grain heeling moments are not covered.
- Transverse distances are positive to starboard: a positive list is to starboard.
- The rolling period uses the IMO 2008 IS Code weather-criterion formula T = 2 C B / √GM with C = 0.373 + 0.023 B/d − 0.043 L_wl/100; it is an estimate for conventional hull forms and actual periods vary with loading and radius of gyration.
- The IMO check is the 0.15 m minimum corrected GM only; the area-under-GZ and weather criteria of the IS Code are not evaluated.
- The "stiff / tender" classification by rolling period is a rule of thumb for crew comfort and cargo securing, not a regulatory criterion.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Design decision: KM is held constant for load/discharge operations (stated in the assumptions) so the calculator stays table-independent; the warning asks for re-entry when the weight exceeds 2 % of displacement.
- Verification 2026-10-30: free-surface moments (20 × 10 m tank, 1 666.7 t·m; two compartments 416.7 t·m), list for a 200 t shift (1.65°) and the loading case (KG 11.042 m) checked by hand against the Derrett formulas; rolling period C = 0.369 for B/d = 3.2, L = 180 m.
- Design decision: a negative fluid GM raises an error rather than a list, because the ship would then take an angle of loll, which is not a list calculation.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- List exceeds 10°: the initial-stability (GM) formula is no longer accurate; use the GZ curve for the actual angle.
- Fluid GM is below the IMO 2008 IS Code minimum of 0.15 m.
- The weight exceeds 2 % of displacement: KM changes with draft — re-enter KM from the tables at the new displacement.
- No free surface moment entered: any slack tank reduces GM; the fluid GM equals the solid GM here.
- The operation removes more than half of the initial GM.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Discharged weight must be less than the displacement
- Fluid GM after the operation is … m (zero or negative): the ship would loll, not list — reduce KG or free surface

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- GM = KM − KG = 1.500 m; FSC = 1 500 / 47 232 = 0.0318 m; fluid GM 1.468 m
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed., ch. 5 and ch. 21 (free surface correction = FSM / Δ)
- Free surface moment of a 20 × 10 m fresh-water tank = l b³/12 × ρ = 1 666.7 t·m; two equal compartments reduce it to a quarter (416.7 t·m)
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass ch. 21: i = l b³/12, FSM = i × ρ, subdivision into n equal parts divides the moment by n²
- List from shifting 200 t by 10 m to starboard: tan θ = 2 000 / (47 232 × 1.468) → 1.65° to starboard
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass ch. 17 "List": tan θ = w d / (W × GM)
- Loading 500 t at Kg 15 m, 8 m to starboard: Δ 47 732 t, KG 11.042 m, fluid GM 1.427 m, list 3.36°; discharging the same weight lists to port
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass ch. 7 (final KG by moments about the keel) and ch. 17
- Vertical shift of 200 t by 5 m upwards raises KG by w d / Δ = 0.0212 m
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass ch. 7: GG₁ = w × d / W
- Rolling period: C = 0.373 + 0.023 × 3.2 − 0.043 × 1.8 = 0.369; T = 2 × 0.369 × 32 / √1.468 = 19.5 s
  - Source: IMO 2008 IS Code (MSC.267(85)) Part A 2.3.4: T = 2 C B / √GM, C = 0.373 + 0.023 (B/d) − 0.043 (L_wl/100)
- IMO check: fluid GM 0.12 m fails the 0.15 m minimum and raises a warning; 1.47 m passes
  - Source: IMO 2008 IS Code Part A 2.2.4
- Large list (> 10°) and negative GM are handled: 2 000 t shifted 10 m gives 15.3° with a warning; KG above KM throws
  - Source: Small-angle validity of the GM method (Derrett ch. 17); angle of loll when GM < 0 (ch. 6)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero displacement, discharging more than the displacement, fractional subdivisions
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.50 m, 0.032 m, 1.468 m, 1.468 m, 2 000 t·m, 19.5 s, 0.369 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Derrett & Barrass, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed. (2012): ch. 5 "Transverse statical stability", ch. 17 "List", ch. 21 "Free surface effect"
- IMO Resolution MSC.267(85), International Code on Intact Stability, 2008 (2008 IS Code), Part A 2.2.4 (GM ≥ 0.15 m) and 2.3 (weather criterion, rolling period formula)
- Rawson & Tupper, Basic Ship Theory, 5th ed., ch. 4 (stability) and ch. 11 (rolling)

## Injection molding clamp tonnage calculator

<a id="injection-clamp-tonnage"></a>

Folder `injection-clamp-tonnage/` · Manufacturing · Clamp force for an injection mould from projected area, cavities, cold runner and clamp factor or cavity pressure, with the machine size for a margin.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Clamp force is the projected area of everything under melt pressure at the parting line (all cavities and a cold runner) times the clamp factor, which is the mean cavity pressure over that area; 1 US ton/in² equals 2 000 psi or 13.8 MPa.
- Clamp factors depend on the resin, wall thickness and flow length: RJG gives 2 to 10 tons/in² with 3 as a starting point; the SABIC Lexan guide gives 3 to 5 tons/in² for polycarbonate and about 1 ton/in² more for glass-reinforced grades; resin datasheets give the value for a grade.
- Projected area is the area seen along the direction of mould opening, with through-holes and cored-out areas taken away; side cores and hot runners are not included.
- The machine should run below its rating: Autodesk Moldflow advises keeping the peak clamp force under about 80 % of the machine limit.
- Too much clamp force can damage the mould: RJG reports a cavity block that failed when clamped at four times the required tonnage, so size to the need.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: RJG example, a 4.6 × 4.6 in part (21.16 in²) in 8 cavities at 3 tons/in² needs 169.28 × 3 = 507.84 US tons; at an 80 % limit the machine should be rated at least 634.8 tons. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The clamp factor is outside the 2 to 10 tons/in² range RJG quotes for most moulding: check the units of the pressure.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- RJG: 21.16 in² × 8 cavities = 169.28 in² × 3 tons/in² = 507.84 tons; the 2–3 tons/in² range gives 339 to 508 tons
  - Source: RJG Inc., Clamp Tonnage: More is Better, Right? (worked example)
- Units: 3 US tons/in² = 6 000 psi = 41.37 MPa = 4.14 kN/cm²; Makrolon 3.0–5.0 tons/in² is 4.1–6.9 kN/cm²
  - Source: 1 US ton = 2 000 lbf; Covestro Makrolon 2558 datasheet (clamp tonnage 3.0–5.0 tons/in², 4.1–6.9 kN/cm²)
- Machine size: 507.84 tons at an 80 % limit needs 634.8 tons; polycarbonate at 4 tons/in² needs 677.1 tons of clamp
  - Source: Autodesk Moldflow (80 % of machine limit); SABIC Lexan guide 3–5 tons/in² (middle value 4)
- A cold runner adds its own area: 8 × 21.16 + 20 in² = 189.28 in²; one cavity of 10 in² at 3 tons/in² needs 30 tons
  - Source: RJG method: add the projected area of a cold runner (hand calculation)
- A factor outside 2–10 tons/in² warns; zero area, fractional cavities and a utilisation of 20 % are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 169.28 in², 507.8, 634.8, 4 518 kN to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- RJG Inc., Clamp Tonnage: More is Better, Right? (2017): projected area × cavities + cold runner × tonnage factor; 2–10 tons/in², 3 as a start; example 507.84 tons
- SABIC (GE Plastics) LEXAN resin processing guide: 3 to 5 tons of clamp force per in² of projected area, about 1 ton/in² more for glass-reinforced grades; Covestro Makrolon 2558 datasheet 3.0–5.0 tons/in² (4.1–6.9 kN/cm²)
- Autodesk Moldflow Insight help, Clamp force result: keep the maximum clamp force below approximately 80 % of the machine limit

## Interference fit

<a id="interference-fit"></a>

Folder `interference-fit/` · Mechanical · Contact pressure, torque and axial force capacity, bore stresses and shrink-fit temperature of a hub on a solid or hollow shaft.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Thick-walled cylinders in plane stress (Lamé): a hub of outer diameter D_o on a shaft of bore d_i with the diametral interference δ at the nominal fit diameter d; the contact pressure is uniform over the fit length and the parts stay elastic (Shigley, press and shrink fits).
- Torque and axial force are carried by friction, T = μ p π d² L/2 and F = μ p π d L; combined torque and axial load share the same friction, and the friction coefficient for a shrink fit differs from that for pressing in or out.
- The interference is the effective one: surface smoothing on assembly reduces the measured interference, and DIN 7190-1 gives the allowance; centrifugal expansion and differences in operating temperature are not included.
- Stresses at the bore: hoop stress σ_t = p (D_o² + d²)/(D_o² − d²) and radial stress −p in the hub; the von Mises stress from them is compared with the hub yield strength. Stress concentrations at the hub ends are not included.
- Shrink assembly: the hub is heated by ΔT = (δ + clearance)/(α d) above the shaft temperature so that it slides on with the chosen clearance.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: equal steel hub and solid shaft (E = 210 GPa), d = 100 mm, D_o = 200 mm, δ = 0.08 mm give p = E δ (D_o² − d²)/(2 d D_o²) = 63.0 MPa, the same-material closed form; with μ = 0.14 and L = 120 mm the fit carries 16.6 kN·m.
- Design decision: the assembly clearance and the ambient temperature are inputs; the heating temperature is the ambient plus ΔT and should stay below the temperature that would change the heat treatment of the hub.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The hub yields at the bore: von Mises … MPa against … MPa; the elastic solution no longer holds.
- Heating the hub to … °C may affect its heat treatment; consider cooling the shaft or a hydraulic fit.
- A fit longer than twice its diameter has pressure peaks at the hub ends that the uniform-pressure solution does not show.
- No interference: the fit carries no torque by friction.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The hub outer diameter must be larger than the fit diameter
- The shaft bore must be smaller than the fit diameter

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Equal steel parts, solid shaft: p = E δ (D² − d²)/(2 d D²) = 210 000 × 0.08 × 30 000/(2 × 100 × 40 000) = 63.0 MPa
  - Source: Shigley (10th ed.) 3-16, contact pressure for equal materials
- Equal steel parts, shaft bored to 50 mm: p = E δ (D² − d²)(d² − d_i²)/(2 d³ (D² − d_i²)) = 50.4 MPa
  - Source: Shigley (10th ed.) 3-16, equal materials with a hollow shaft
- A rigid hub on a solid shaft gives p = δ E/(d (1 − ν)) = 240 MPa
  - Source: Limit of the general two-material formula as E_hub → ∞
- Friction capacity: T = μ p π d² L/2 = 16.63 kN·m and F = μ p π d L = 2T/d = 332.5 kN
  - Source: Torque and axial force carried by friction over the fit
- Bore stresses: hub hoop p (D² + d²)/(D² − d²) = 5/3 × 63 = 105 MPa, von Mises √(105² + 105 × 63 + 63²) = 147 MPa, solid shaft hoop −p
  - Source: Lamé thick-cylinder stresses (Shigley 3-14 and 3-16)
- Shrink assembly: (0.08 + 0.05) mm/(12 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 mm) = 108.3 °C of heating, the hub at 128.3 °C
  - Source: Free thermal expansion of the hub bore
- Invalid inputs are rejected: a hub no larger than the fit, a shaft bore as large as the fit
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 63.0 MPa, 16.6 kN·m, 333 kN, 105 MPa, 147 MPa, 108 °C, 128 °C to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- R. G. Budynas, J. K. Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., McGraw-Hill 2015, 3-16 Press and shrink fits — contact pressure for different materials and for equal materials
- DIN 7190-1:2017, Interference fits — calculation and design rules (smoothing of the interference, friction coefficients)

## Inverter size calculator

<a id="inverter-size"></a>

Folder `inverter-size/` · Electrical · What size power inverter you need: running watts and VA of your loads, motor starting surge, design margin, the next common size and the DC battery current.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Running watts are what each load draws once running and starting watts what a motor draws for a few seconds while it starts; take both from the nameplate or manual. The default list is an illustrative example only.
- Apparent power is the sum of each load's watts divided by its power factor; adding the VA arithmetically ignores the different phase angles and errs on the safe side. Loads without a power factor are taken as resistive (1).
- By default the motors start one at a time, so only the largest surge adds to the running total; choose "all together" if several can start at once. The inverter's surge rating is its continuous rating times the surge multiple from its data sheet, held for a few seconds.
- The recommended size is the next common catalogue rating above both requirements; inverter ratings are not a standard series, so check the sizes the maker offers.
- Battery current is the AC output power divided by the battery voltage and the inverter efficiency; it is highest at the low-voltage cutoff, which sets the cable and fuse sizes.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: the default list runs 2 360 W and 2 664 VA; the pump's 1 600 W surge gives a 3 960 W peak; with 25 % margin 3 330 VA continuous, surge needs 1 980 W at 2×, so 3 500 W; at 24 V and 90 % the battery current is 109 A running and 209 A at the peak with the 21 V cutoff. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- No starting watts entered: motors such as fridges, pumps and compressors draw several times their running watts for a few seconds when they start.
- Above about 2 kW a 12 V battery has to supply very high currents; a 24 V or 48 V system needs thinner cables and smaller fuses.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Loads, line …: write "name; running watts; starting watts; power factor" (the last two are optional).
- Loads, line …: the running watts "…" is not a number of 0 or more.
- Loads, line …: the starting watts must be a number at least equal to the running watts.
- Loads, line …: the power factor must be between 0.1 and 1.
- Loads: enter at least one load.
- Loads: the running watts add up to zero.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Default list: 2 360 W, 2 664 VA, pump surge 1 600 W, peak 3 960 W, 3 330 VA with 25 % margin, 3 500 W inverter, 109.3 A at 24 V and 90 %
  - Source: Hand calculation: Σ W, Σ W/PF, largest (start − run), I = P / (V η)
- A 1 000 W pump starting at 3 000 W alone with a 2× surge inverter needs 1 500 W, set by the surge, not the 1 250 VA running load
  - Source: Hand calculation: peak / surge multiple = 3 000 / 2
- All motors starting together add every surge: 600 + 1 600 = 2 200 W on the default list
  - Source: Definition of simultaneous starting
- 1 000 W from a 12 V battery through a 90 % inverter draws 92.6 A, and 105.8 A at the 10.5 V cutoff
  - Source: I = P / (V η)
- A load above the largest common size gives no size and says so; the parser fills in starting watts and power factor
  - Source: Design decision; parser contract
- A power factor above 1, starting watts below running watts, an empty list and zero watts are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2 360 W, 2 664 VA, 3 960 W, 3 330 VA, 3 500 W, 109 A, 209.5 A to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Sandia National Laboratories, Stand-Alone Photovoltaic Systems: A Handbook of Recommended Design Practices, SAND87-7023 (inverter sizing for continuous and surge loads)
- IEEE Std 1562-2007, Guide for Array and Battery Sizing in Stand-Alone Photovoltaic Systems (load determination)
- NEMA MG 1-2021, Motors and Generators, Part 10 (locked-rotor kVA code letters behind the starting surge of motor loads)

## Joist span calculator (bending and deflection)

<a id="joist-span"></a>

Folder `joist-span/` · Structural · Maximum span of a wood floor joist or rafter from its size, spacing, grade and loads, by bending and deflection mechanics with NDS adjustment factors.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Spans are computed from mechanics for a simply supported member under uniform load: M = wL²/8 and Δ = 5wL⁴/(384EI). They are not copied from code span tables, which may include other checks and rounding.
- Allowable bending stress F'b = Fb × C_D × C_F × C_r by the NDS: dry service, normal temperature, the compression edge held by sheathing (C_L = 1) and C_r = 1.15 for joists at 24 in or less with at least three members sharing the load.
- The dead load is also checked alone with C_D = 0.9. Shear, bearing at the supports, vibration and notches are not checked; shear rarely governs uniformly loaded joists of usual spans.
- Loads are area loads on plan for floors; for a sloping rafter enter the horizontal projection of the span and loads per horizontal area. Self-weight belongs in the dead load.
- The preset grades use NDS Supplement Table 4A reference values for 2 in thick dimension lumber, with C_F from the depth; other species, grades or sizes take Fb, E and C_F as entered.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a Douglas Fir-Larch No. 2 2×10 at 16 in with 10 psf dead and 40 psf live: F'b = 900 × 1.0 × 1.1 × 1.15 = 1 138.5 psi, S = 21.39 in³, I = 98.93 in⁴; bending allows 187.3 in (15.6 ft), live deflection L/360 allows 16.4 ft and total L/240 17.4 ft, so bending governs at 15.6 ft. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- C_r = 1.15 applies only to members at 24 in (610 mm) or less; it is not used at this spacing.
- The span is more than 30 times the depth: check floor vibration, which deflection limits alone do not control.
- The span is less than 10 times the depth: check shear and bearing, which this page does not.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Actual depth d: the joist must be deeper than it is wide; enter the larger dimension as the depth.
- Actual width b: the preset grades use the size factors for 2 in and 3 in thick lumber (up to 2.5 in actual); choose "Other" for thicker members.
- Live or snow load: enter a dead or a live load.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- DF-L No. 2 2×10 at 16 in, 10 + 40 psf: F'b = 900 × 1.1 × 1.15 = 1 138.5 psi; bending span √(8 × 1 138.5 × 21.39 / 5.556) = 187.3 in = 15.61 ft governs
  - Source: Hand calculation in inch-pound units: S = 1.5 × 9.25²/6, w = 50 psf × 16/12 ft = 66.67 lb/ft; NDS 2018 C_F = 1.1 and C_r = 1.15
- Deflection spans of the same joist: L/360 under 40 psf gives (384 × 1.6e6 × 98.93 / (5 × 4.444 × 360))^⅓ = 196.6 in; L/240 under 50 psf gives 208.9 in
  - Source: Δ = 5 w L⁴ / (384 E I) solved for L; I = 1.5 × 9.25³/12 = 98.93 in⁴
- NDS size factors for 2 in lumber: 2×4 1.5, 2×6 1.3, 2×8 1.2, 2×10 1.1, 2×12 1.0, 2×14 0.9; C_r drops to 1.0 beyond 24 in spacing
  - Source: AWC NDS Supplement 2018, Table 4A size factors (2" and 3" thick); NDS 4.3.9 repetitive member factor
- Heavy dead load: with 60 psf dead and 5 psf live, dead alone at C_D 0.9 governs bending (60/65 > 0.9/1.0)
  - Source: NDS 2018 2.3.2: each load combination is checked with the C_D of its shortest-duration load
- Span check at 15 ft: stress ratio (15/15.606)² = 92.4 %; live deflection 0.384 in (L/469); a flat member, thick preset lumber and no load are refused
  - Source: Hand calculation; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1 139 psi, 15.61 ft, 16.38 ft, 17.41 ft, 15.61 ft to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- AWC National Design Specification (NDS) for Wood Construction, 2018 ed., 4.3 adjustment factors (C_D Table 2.3.2, C_F, C_r 4.3.9) and 3.3 bending members
- AWC NDS Supplement, Design Values for Wood Construction, 2018 ed., Table 1B (section properties of standard dressed lumber) and Table 4A (reference values and size factors)
- Gere, J.M. and Goodno, B.J., Mechanics of Materials, Cengage (simply supported beam under uniform load: M = wL²/8, Δ = 5wL⁴/384EI)

## kVA to amps

<a id="kva-to-amps"></a>

Folder `kva-to-amps/` · Electrical · Line current from kVA and voltage for single-phase and three-phase supplies, kVA from amps, and the kW at a given power factor.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The supply is balanced and sinusoidal; for three-phase the voltage is the line-to-line voltage and the current the line current, whatever the connection (star or delta).
- Apparent power (kVA) sets the current; the power factor only converts it to active power (kW), so a generator or transformer rated in kVA carries its rated current at any power factor.
- For a transformer, the current is the rated current of the winding at the voltage entered; enter the secondary voltage for the secondary current.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 1000 kVA at 400 V three-phase gives 1 443 A; at 0.8 power factor that is 800 kW. 10 kVA at 230 V single-phase is 43.5 A. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above about 4000 A a low-voltage busbar or several parallel cables are needed; check the switchgear rating.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 1000 kVA at 400 V three-phase: I = 10⁶ / (√3 × 400) = 1443.4 A; 800 kW and 600 kvar at 0.8 power factor
  - Source: Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, ch. "Three-phase systems": S = √3 V_L I_L, P = S cos φ
- 10 kVA single-phase at 230 V is 43.48 A
  - Source: S = V I for single-phase
- A 630 kVA transformer secondary at 400 V carries 909.3 A; at 11 kV its primary carries 33.07 A
  - Source: IEC 60076-1 clause 3.4: rated current from rated power and rated voltage
- Amps to kVA: 100 A at 400 V three-phase is 69.28 kVA; converting back returns 100 A
  - Source: S = √3 V I
- Zero voltage and an unknown supply are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1 443 A, 800 kW to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, 12th ed., ch. "Three-phase systems" (S = √3 V_L I_L)
- IEC 60076-1:2011 Power transformers, clause 3.4 (rated power and rated current)

## kVA to kW

<a id="kva-to-kw"></a>

Folder `kva-to-kw/` · Electrical · Real power in kW from a kVA rating at the power factor, with the kvar and the rated line current of a generator, transformer or UPS.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The kVA is the rated or measured apparent power; the kW available depends on the power factor of the load connected, not on the equipment.
- For generators the engine also limits the kW: a set rated 500 kVA at 0.8 delivers at most 400 kW even to a unity power factor load (ISO 8528-1).
- Harmonics from non-linear loads add current without kW, reducing the kW a kVA rating can carry.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 500 kVA at 0.8 gives 400 kW and 300 kvar; at 400 V three-phase its rated current is 722 A. Checked by hand.

- (none — all conditions are hard errors or silent)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

- A 10 kVA single-phase UPS at power factor 0.9 supplies 9 kW at 43.5 A on 230 V
  - Source: P = S cos φ; I = S / V
- Inverse of kW to kVA: P → S → P returns the same value
  - Source: S = P / cos φ and P = S cos φ
- A 1600 kVA transformer at 11 kV draws 83.98 A on the primary
  - Source: IEC 60076-1 rated current I = S / (√3 U)
- Zero kVA and a power factor of zero are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 400 kW, 300 kvar, 722 A to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

## kW to amps

<a id="kw-to-amps"></a>

Folder `kw-to-amps/` · Electrical · Current from kW for single-phase, three-phase and DC loads, including motors from their shaft kW and efficiency, with the power factor.

### Assumptions and caveats

- An electrical load's kW is the power it draws; a motor's nameplate kW is its shaft output, so the electrical input is the output divided by the efficiency.
- The power factor is the running value at that load; motors at part load have a lower power factor, so their current falls less than their kW.
- For three-phase the load is balanced and the voltage is line-to-line.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 22 kW electrical load at 400 V three-phase and 0.85 draws 37.4 A; a 22 kW motor at 93 % efficiency draws 40.2 A. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- This is the full-load running current; direct-on-line starting draws 6 to 8 times as much for a few seconds.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

  - Source: Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, ch. "Three-phase systems": I = P / (√3 V_L cos φ)
- A 22 kW motor at 93 % efficiency draws 23.66 kW and 40.17 A, with a starting-current note
  - Source: IEC 60034-1: rated output is the shaft power; input = output / η
- Agrees with the three-phase power calculator's motor mode for 30 kW, η 0.92, cos φ 0.85 at 400 V (55.37 A)
  - Source: Cross-check against three-phase-power (catalogue band 55–57 A)
- Single-phase 3 kW at 230 V and 0.95 is 13.73 A; DC 2 kW at 48 V is 41.67 A
  - Source: I = P / (V cos φ); I = P / V
- At 480 V the same 22 kW load draws 400/480 of the 400 V current
  - Source: I ∝ 1/V at constant P
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 37.4 A, 25.9 kVA to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)
