## kW to kVA

<a id="kw-to-kva"></a>

Folder `kw-to-kva/` · Electrical · Apparent power in kVA for a load in kW at its power factor, with kvar and the line current, to size a generator, transformer or UPS.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The power factor is the overall power factor of the load; for a mix of loads use the combined value (total kW over total kVA), not an average of power factors.
- Generators are rated in kVA at 0.8 power factor by convention (ISO 8528-1); the engine limits the kW and the alternator the kVA.
- The result is the running load; motor starting, inrush and future growth need margin on top when sizing equipment.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 400 kW at 0.8 power factor needs 500 kVA and 300 kvar, 722 A at 400 V three-phase. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A power factor below 0.7 makes the kVA much larger than the kW; power-factor correction would cut the generator or transformer size.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 400 kW at 0.8: 500 kVA, 300 kvar, 721.7 A at 400 V three-phase
  - Source: Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, ch. "Three-phase systems": S = P / cos φ, Q = S sin φ, I = S / (√3 V)
- At unity power factor kVA equals kW and kvar is zero
  - Source: cos φ = 1
- A generator rated 1000 kVA at 0.8 delivers 800 kW: 800 kW at 0.8 is exactly 1000 kVA
  - Source: ISO 8528-1: rated power stated at power factor 0.8
- Single-phase 5 kW at 0.9 and 230 V: 5.556 kVA, 24.15 A; a power factor of 0.6 warns
  - Source: S = P / cos φ; I = S / V
- Zero power and an unknown supply are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 500 kVA, 300 kvar, 722 A to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, 12th ed., ch. "Three-phase systems" (power triangle S = P / cos φ)
- ISO 8528-1:2018 Reciprocating internal combustion engine driven alternating current generating sets (rated power at power factor 0.8)

## Latent and sensible heat calculator (air and water)

<a id="latent-sensible-heat"></a>

Folder `latent-sensible-heat/` · HVAC · Sensible, latent and total heat of an airstream by psychrometrics and the 1.08 and 4840 rules, SHR and coil load; and the heat to melt or boil water.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The airflow is the volume at the entering condition; it is converted to dry air mass with the moist-air specific volume (ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 1) at the standard pressure of the altitude entered.
- The exact split takes the latent heat as the enthalpy change of removing the moisture at the entering temperature, (W1 − W2)(2 501 + 1.86 t1), and the sensible heat as the cooling of the drier air; the two add up to the total enthalpy change.
- The rules use standard air (0.075 lb/ft³): 1.08 Btu/h per cfm per °F with c_p = 0.24, or 1.10 with the moist-air c_p of ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 18, 4 840 per cfm per lb/lb of humidity ratio and 4.5 per cfm per Btu/lb of enthalpy; SI equivalents 1.21 or 1.23 W per L/s per K, 3 010 and 1.20.
- Positive heat is removed from the air (cooling); a negative value means heat or moisture is added. The coil load subtracts the enthalpy of the condensate leaving at the air outlet temperature.
- Water phase changes are at atmospheric pressure: melting at 0 °C and boiling at 100 °C, with constant specific heats; the latent heats default to 334 kJ/kg for fusion and 2 257 kJ/kg for vaporisation and can be changed.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 1 000 cfm cooled from 80 °F db / 67 °F wb to 55 °F db / 54 °F wb at sea level: sensible 26 440 Btu/h, latent 12 040 Btu/h, total 38 480 Btu/h, SHR 0.69, coil load 3.19 tons, condensate 11.0 lb/h; the 1.08 rule gives 27 000 Btu/h sensible (standard air is denser than air at 80 °F). Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The leaving air is cooler but more humid than the entering air: this is evaporative cooling or humidification, not a cooling coil; check the states.
- The sensible and latent heats have opposite signs, so the sensible heat ratio is outside 0 to 1.
- Above about 2 000 ft (600 m) the rule constants overstate the heat: they assume sea-level air density. Use the exact values.
- The final state has less latent heat but the total is positive: check the states and temperatures.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- … relative humidity: the vapour pressure reaches the total pressure.
- … wet bulb: it cannot be above the dry bulb temperature.
- … wet bulb: too low for this dry bulb; the air would have negative moisture.
- …: ice must be at or below 0 °C at atmospheric pressure.
- …: liquid water must be between 0 and 100 °C at atmospheric pressure.
- …: steam must be at or above 100 °C at atmospheric pressure.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Rules for 1 000 cfm cooled 25 °F: 1.08 × 1 000 × 25 = 27 000 Btu/h, 1.10 gives 27 500; latent 4 840 cfm ΔW; total 4.5 cfm Δh
  - Source: ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals Ch. 18 (q_s = 1.10 Q Δt, q_l = 4 840 Q ΔW, q_t = 4.5 Q Δh); classic 1.08 = 0.075 × 60 × 0.24
- Exact split for 80/67 °F to 55/54 °F at 1 000 cfm: sensible 26 440, latent 12 040, total 38 480 Btu/h; sensible + latent = total
  - Source: ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 1 eq. 30, h = 1.006 t + W (2 501 + 1.86 t); hand calculation (ṁ = 0.546 kg/s, Δh = 20.66 kJ/kg)
- Dry air at 70 °F (0.0749 lb/ft³, close to standard 0.075) cooled by 10 °F: the exact sensible heat equals the 1.08 rule within 0.1 %
  - Source: Standard air 0.075 lb/ft³ and c_p 0.24 Btu/(lb·°F) behind the 1.08 constant; ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 1
- Serway heating curve: 1 g of ice at −30 °C to steam at 120 °C needs 62.7 + 333 + 419 + 2 260 + 40.2 J = 3.11 kJ
  - Source: Serway & Jewett, Physics for Scientists and Engineers, 9th ed., Ch. 20 (c_ice 2 090, c_w 4 186, c_steam 2 010 J/(kg·K); L_f 3.33e5, L_v 2.26e6 J/kg)
- Latent heats: melting 1 kg of ice at 0 °C takes 334 kJ, boiling 1 kg at 100 °C 2 257 kJ; condensing gives them back; 1 kW boils it in 37.6 min
  - Source: Latent heats of water 334 and 2 257 kJ/kg (IAPWS-IF97: 2 256.5 kJ/kg at 1 atm)
- Invalid input: ice above 0 °C, steam below 100 °C, a wet bulb above the dry bulb and zero airflow are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 26 440 Btu/h, 12 040 Btu/h, 38 480 Btu/h, 0.69, 3.19 TR, 27 000 Btu/h to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals (2017), Ch. 1 Psychrometrics (enthalpy eq. 30, wet bulb eqs. 33/35, moist-air cooling and dehumidification) and Ch. 18 (q_s = 1.10 Q Δt, q_l = 4 840 Q ΔW, q_t = 4.5 Q Δh; SI 1.23, 3 010, 1.20)
- R. A. Serway & J. W. Jewett, Physics for Scientists and Engineers, 9th ed., Ch. 20 (specific and latent heats of water; heating 1 g of ice at −30 °C to steam at 120 °C needs 3.11 kJ)
- IAPWS-IF97: enthalpy of vaporisation of water at 1 atm, 2 256.5 kJ/kg (the 2 257 kJ/kg default)

## Latitude/longitude to UTM converter (WGS84)

<a id="latlon-utm"></a>

Folder `latlon-utm/` · Civil · Convert WGS84 latitude and longitude to UTM zone, easting and northing and back, to well under a millimetre, with grid convergence and scale factor.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Coordinates are on the WGS84 ellipsoid (a = 6 378 137 m, f = 1/298.257223563). Positions on another datum such as NAD27 or ED50 must be transformed first; the datum shift can be over 100 m.
- The projection uses the Krüger series to sixth order (Karney 2011), which is accurate to a few nanometres within the zone and to far better than a millimetre up to 9° from the central meridian.
- The zone follows the standard 6° grid with the Norway (32V) and Svalbard (31X to 37X) exceptions. A zone can be forced to work in a neighbouring zone, up to 9° from its central meridian.
- UTM covers 80° S to 84° N. The polar regions use the Universal Polar Stereographic grid, which this page does not compute.
- Northings in the southern hemisphere carry the 10 000 000 m false northing; eastings carry the 500 000 m false easting.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 48.8582° N, 2.2945° E (Eiffel Tower) gives zone 31U, E 448 251.795 m, N 5 411 932.678 m, as in the Veness geodesy library example; 38N 444 500 3 688 500 gives 33.33424° N, 44.40363° E as in the GeoConvert manual. Fourteen points agree with the exact transverse Mercator (pygeodesy 26.10, elliptic-function method) within 0.01 mm. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The point lies in zone …; the coordinates are given in the forced zone ….
- The point is more than 3.5° from the central meridian: the scale error exceeds 1 part in 1 000 near the equator.
- The point is outside its 6° zone (more than 3.5° from the central meridian); check the zone number.
- A southern northing below 1 000 000 m is near the South Pole limit; check the hemisphere.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Force a zone: the point is …° from the central meridian of zone …; use a zone within 9°.
- Easting: a UTM easting lies between about 100 000 and 900 000 m (500 000 m on the central meridian).
- Northing: the point is outside the UTM latitude range of 80° S to 84° N.
- Easting: the point is more than 9° from the central meridian.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Eiffel Tower 48.8582° N, 2.2945° E: zone 31U, E 448 251.795 m, N 5 411 932.678 m; back to 48°51′29.52″ N, 2°17′40.20″ E
  - Source: C. Veness, Geodesy functions library (utm.js) documented example: 31 N 448251.795 5411932.678 ↔ 48°51′29.52″N, 002°17′40.20″E
- GeoConvert manual: 38n 444500 3688500 is 33.33424° N, 44.40363° E (33°20′03.25″ N, 44°24′13.06″ E)
  - Source: GeographicLib GeoConvert(1) manual page, EXAMPLES (echo 38SMB4488 | GeoConvert, -: -p 1 and -u)
- Eight points in both hemispheres, in Svalbard, near 80° S and 84° N and 8.9° off the central meridian agree with the exact transverse Mercator within 0.05 mm, 1e-8° and 1e-9
  - Source: Karney (2011), J. Geodesy 85: exact TM by elliptic functions (pygeodesy ExactTransverseMercator), WGS84, k0 = 0.9996
- Round trip forward then inverse returns the position within 1e-9° (0.1 mm); scale on the central meridian at the equator is exactly k0 = 0.9996
  - Source: Consistency of the α and β Krüger series (Karney 2011); UTM definition k0 = 0.9996
- Zones: London 30U, New York 18T, Bergen at 5° E is 32V (Norway), Longyearbyen at 15.6° E is 33X (Svalbard); 180° E is zone 60
  - Source: NGA.SIG.0012 UTM zone and band definitions with the 32V and 31X–37X exceptions
- Outside UTM (above 84° N), a forced zone more than 9° away and an easting outside 100–900 km are refused; a forced neighbouring zone warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 448 251.795 m, 5 411 932.678 m, 0.9996329 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Karney, C.F.F. (2011), "Transverse Mercator with an accuracy of a few nanometers", Journal of Geodesy 85(8), 475–485 (sixth-order Krüger series, conformal latitude, convergence and scale)
- NGA.SIG.0012_2.0.0_UTMUPS (2014), The Universal Grids and the Transverse Mercator and Polar Stereographic Map Projections, National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency
- NIMA TR8350.2 (2000), Department of Defense World Geodetic System 1984 (ellipsoid parameters)
- GeographicLib GeoConvert manual, Examples (38SMB4488 = 38n 444500 3688500 = 33.33424 44.40363)

## LC resonant frequency calculator

<a id="lc-resonance"></a>

Folder `lc-resonance/` · Electrical · Resonant frequency of an LC circuit, or the L or C for a target frequency, with characteristic impedance, Q and bandwidth from the series resistance.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The inductor and capacitor are ideal apart from one resistance R in series with them, which stands for the coil's winding and skin-effect resistance and any capacitor ESR at the resonant frequency.
- Q, bandwidth and the −3 dB frequencies are those of the series RLC circuit; for high Q they also describe a parallel tank whose coil has the series resistance R.
- A parallel tank with a lossy coil resonates, in the sense of a purely resistive impedance, at f0 √(1 − 1/Q²); the difference from f0 is 0.5 % at Q = 10 and smaller above.
- Stray capacitance of the coil and the wiring adds to C and lowers the frequency; at high frequencies it can be several picofarads.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 10 µH and 100 pF resonate at 5.03 MHz with Z0 = 316 Ω; with 5 Ω series resistance Q = 63.2, the bandwidth is 79.6 kHz and the parallel dynamic resistance 20 kΩ. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Q is below 0.5: the circuit is overdamped and has no sharp resonance; the bandwidth figures describe a broad response.
- With zero resistance Q and the dynamic resistance are unlimited; enter the coil\'s resistance at the frequency for real values.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 10 µH and 100 pF: f0 = 5.033 MHz, Z0 = 316.2 Ω; with 5 Ω, Q = 63.25, BW = 79.58 kHz, R_D = 20 kΩ
  - Source: Hand calculation from f0 = 1/(2π√(LC)), Q = √(L/C)/R, BW = R/(2πL), R_D = L/(CR)
- Medium-wave tuning: 1 MHz with 100 pF needs 253.3 µH, and 253.3 µH needs 100 pF back
  - Source: L = 1/((2πf)² C), C = 1/((2πf)² L); the textbook 1 MHz / 100 pF / 253 µH broadcast-band case
- The −3 dB frequencies are geometric about f0 (f1 f2 = f0²) and differ by exactly the bandwidth
  - Source: Series RLC half-power frequencies f1,2 = f0(√(1 + 1/(4Q²)) ∓ 1/(2Q))
- Limiting case: zero resistance gives no Q, bandwidth or dynamic resistance, and a warning
  - Source: Q = Z0/R → ∞ as R → 0
- Invalid entries are rejected: zero inductance, zero capacitance, negative resistance
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 5.03 MHz, 316 Ω, 63.2, 79.6 kHz, 20 kΩ to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, 12th ed., the chapters on series and parallel resonance (Q factor, bandwidth f0 / Q)
- Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, 13th ed., ch. 20 (resonance: f_s = 1/(2π√(LC)), Q_s = X_L/R, BW = f_s/Q_s, half-power frequencies)
- ARRL Handbook for Radio Communications, Electrical Fundamentals chapter (resonant circuits, Q, dynamic resistance of a parallel tank R_D = Q² R)

## LED series resistor

<a id="led-resistor"></a>

Folder `led-resistor/` · Electrical · Series resistor for an LED or a string of LEDs: exact value, next standard value, actual current, resistor power and the rating to buy.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The LED forward voltage is taken as constant at the design current; the built-in values are typical at about 20 mA, and the data sheet value of the actual part is better.
- The supply is a steady DC voltage; with a battery, design for its highest voltage so the current never exceeds the LED rating when the battery is fresh.
- The standard resistor is the next E-series value above the exact value, so the actual current is at or below the target.
- The resistor rating is chosen with a factor of two on its dissipation, so it runs well below its maximum temperature.
- All LEDs in a string carry the same current; parallel strings each need their own resistor.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 5 V and one white LED at 20 mA need 90 Ω exactly; the E24 value 91 Ω gives 19.8 mA and 36 mW, so a 1/8 W resistor is enough. Checked by hand.
- Design decision: the next value above, not the nearest, is chosen, because rounding down would push the LED above its rated current.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Less than 1 V is left across the resistor, so small changes in supply or forward voltage swing the current a lot; use fewer LEDs in series or a higher supply.
- More than 30 mA is above the rating of most indicator LEDs; check the data sheet, and consider a constant-current driver for power LEDs.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The supply must exceed the LEDs' total forward voltage (… × … V = … V is not below … V)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- One white LED (3.2 V) on 5 V at 20 mA: R = 90 Ω, next E24 value 91 Ω gives 19.8 mA and 36 mW, a 1/8 W part
  - Source: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §2.1.1: R = (V_s − V_f) / I; IEC 60063 E24
- Three red LEDs (3 × 2.0 V) on 12 V at 20 mA: R = 300 Ω exactly (an E24 value), 120 mW, a 1/4 W part; LEDs take half the supply power
  - Source: R = (V_s − n V_f) / I; P = I² R; P_LED / P_supply = n V_f / V_s
- E12 rounds 90 Ω up to 100 Ω, so the current falls to 18 mA; the chosen value is never below the exact one
  - Source: IEC 60063 E12; next value above keeps I ≤ I_target
- Ratings: 36 mW needs 1/8 W, 120 mW needs 1/4 W, 0.3 W needs 1 W; above 5 W a driver is advised
  - Source: Common resistor ratings with a factor of two on dissipation (design practice)
- Little headroom warns; a supply below the total forward voltage and a fractional LED count are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract; current sensitivity grows as V_s − n V_f shrinks
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 90 Ω, 91 Ω, 19.8 mA, 0.036 W to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., §2.1.1 and §12.4 (LEDs and current limiting)
- Kingbright and Vishay indicator LED data sheets (typical forward voltage at 20 mA by colour)
- IEC 60063:2015 Preferred number series for resistors and capacitors (E12, E24)

## Lifting sling and wire rope load

<a id="lifting-sling"></a>

Folder `lifting-sling/` · Mechanical · Sling leg tension from load, legs and angle or geometry with dynamic and hitch factors; chain, wire-rope or rated WLL; utilisation and maximum load.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The load is shared equally by the effective legs and each leg makes the same angle β with the vertical; by EN 13414-1 and ASME B30.9 practice a 3- or 4-leg sling is rated on three legs unless the lift points and leg lengths guarantee equal sharing (the calculator defaults to 3 effective legs for 4-leg slings and lets you override).
- β is the angle from the vertical (0° = legs hanging straight). The common field rule "60° included angle" corresponds to β = 30°; EN 13414-1 limits β to 60° (tension = full load per leg) and recommends 45° or less.
- The dynamic amplification factor multiplies the static weight to cover acceleration, swing and snatch: 1.1–1.25 for slow crane lifts in a workshop, 1.3 or more for offshore lifts (DNV-ST-N001) — the calculator does not derive it.
- Sling working load limits: Grade 8 chain WLL ≈ 0.0314 d² t (EN 818-4, factor 4 on breaking load); wire rope 6×36 IWRC 1770 MPa MBL = 0.356 d² × 1770/1000 kN with ferrule-secured eyes (termination efficiency 0.9) and safety factor 5 (EN 13414-1). Other constructions, grades and terminations differ; the tag WLL always governs.
- Hitch factors: choke 0.8 and basket 2.0 (legs vertical) per EN 13414-1 / ASME B30.9; a basket hitch with inclined legs needs the angle reduction as well, and bending over small diameters (D/d < 20 for wire rope) reduces the capacity further.
- The centre of gravity is assumed under the hook; an off-centre CoG loads the near legs more than this calculation shows and needs a moment balance.
- Shackles, hooks, master links, lifting lugs and the hook block are not checked; each must have at least the leg tension (or the total load) as WLL, with the correct angle factors for shackles loaded in-line.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: 10 t on two legs at β = 30° gives 5.77 t per leg and at 60° the full 10 t per leg, the standard sling-angle demonstration; chain WLL 13 mm → 5.3 t matches the EN 818-4 table; the geometry mode reproduces β = 30° for a 4 m spread with 4 m legs.
- Design decision: 4-leg slings default to 3 effective legs (EN 13414-1 / ASME B30.9 practice) with an override, because equal sharing on four legs requires adjustable legs or a very rigid load.
- Design decision: the WLL output always states the basis (formula or tag) so the register and the user can see what the utilisation is measured against.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Leg angle above 60° to the vertical: not permitted by EN 13414-1 / ASME B30.9 — use longer slings or a spreader beam.
- Leg angle between 45° and 60°: allowed but the tension exceeds 1.41 × the share of the load; 45° or less is recommended.
- All legs assumed to share the load: valid only with adjustable legs or a rigid load and exact lift-point geometry; standards rate 3- and 4-leg slings on three legs.
- Leg tension exceeds the sling capacity in this hitch — the lift is not permitted with this sling.
- No dynamic factor: even a slow crane lift sees 10–25 % overload from acceleration and swing.
- Basket hitch with inclined legs: the ×2 factor applies only to vertical legs; the angle factor has been applied on top, but check the standard\'s combined table.
- Centre of gravity assumed under the hook; off-centre loads overload the near legs. Shackles, hooks, lugs and the hook block need their own WLL checks.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Effective legs (…) cannot exceed the number of legs (…)
- Half the spread must be less than the leg length — the legs cannot reach

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Sling angle: 10 t on two legs at β = 30° gives 5.77 t per leg (factor 1.155); at 45° 7.07 t; at 60° each leg carries the full 10 t
  - Source: ASME B30.9 / EN 13414-1 sling-angle relation T = W / (n cos β); the 60°-to-vertical limit where T = W
- Geometry: 4 m spread with 4 m legs gives β = asin(2/4) = 30°, the same tension as the angle input; included angle 60°
  - Source: Right-triangle geometry sin β = (spread/2) / leg length (LEEA guidance)
- Dynamic factor and effective legs: DAF 1.25 raises the hook load to 122.6 kN; a 4-leg sling is rated on 3 legs by default (3.92 t per leg at 30°) and on 4 only when overridden
  - Source: DNV-ST-N001 dynamic amplification; EN 13414-1 / ASME B30.9 three-leg assumption for four-leg slings
- Grade 8 chain WLL ≈ 0.0314 d²: 8 mm 2.0 t, 10 mm 3.14 t (table 3.15), 13 mm 5.3 t, 16 mm 8.0 t, 20 mm 12.6 t (table 12.5)
  - Source: EN 818-4 Table (Grade 8 single-leg chain sling WLL)
- Wire rope sling 20 mm 6×36 IWRC 1770: MBL = 0.356 × 20² × 1770/1000 = 252 kN; WLL = 252 × 0.9 / 5 = 45.4 kN = 4.62 t
  - Source: EN 12385-4 minimum breaking force (K = 0.356 for 6×36 IWRC); EN 13414-1 termination efficiency 0.9 and safety factor 5
- Hitch factors: choke 0.8 halves nothing but reduces capacity to 6.4 t for an 8 t sling; basket with vertical legs doubles to 16 t
  - Source: EN 13414-1 mode factors; ASME B30.9 choker (0.8) and basket (2.0) hitches
- Utilisation and maximum load: 10 t at 30° on two 8 t legs = 72 %; maximum load 13.86 t; 16 t at 30° exceeds the capacity
  - Source: Utilisation = T / (WLL × hitch factor); maximum W = WLL n cos β / DAF
- Angle warnings: 50° is allowed with a recommendation, 65° is not permitted
  - Source: EN 13414-1 (β ≤ 60°, 45° recommended); ASME B30.9
- Invalid inputs fail fast: more effective legs than legs, legs too short for the spread, zero chain diameter
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 107.9 kN, 62.3 kN, 6.35 t, 1.155, 31.1 kN, 8.04 t, 8.04 t, 79 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- EN 13414-1:2003+A2:2008, Steel wire rope slings — Safety — Part 1: Slings for general lifting service (mode factors, angle limits, safety factor 5, termination efficiency)
- EN 818-4:1996+A1:2008, Short link chain for lifting purposes — Chain slings Grade 8 (WLL table)
- EN 12385-4:2002+A1:2008, Steel wire ropes — Stranded ropes for general lifting applications (minimum breaking force K factors)
- ASME B30.9-2021, Slings (sling angle, choker and basket hitch factors, 3-leg assumption for 4-leg slings)
- DNV-ST-N001 Marine operations and marine warranty (dynamic amplification factors); LEEA Code of Practice for the Safe Use of Lifting Equipment

## Light, radar and VHF range

<a id="light-range"></a>

Folder `light-range/` · Maritime · Geographic and luminous range of a light, radar and VHF line-of-sight ranges, and the COLREG minimum intensity of a navigation light.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Geographic range is the sum of the distances to the sea horizon from the light and from the eye. The default horizon model is Bowditch Table 12, d = √(2Rh/β) with R = 3440.1 nmi and the refraction parameter β = 0.8279 (1.17 √h for h in feet, 2.12 √h for h in metres); "2.08 √h" is a common rounded rule and "geometric" leaves refraction out (1.93 √h). Abnormal refraction (super-refraction over cold water, sub-refraction) can change the range considerably.
- Heights are above the actual sea level: charted light elevations refer to a high-water datum (MHWS in British charts), so at lower states of the tide the light stands higher and the geographic range is slightly greater.
- Luminous range by Allard's law for a point source at night, E = I·T^d/(1852 d)², with the IALA threshold illuminance of 2·10⁻⁷ lux and the transmissivity per nautical mile T = 0.05^(1/V) for a meteorological visibility V; the nominal range is the luminous range at V = 10 nmi (T = 0.741). Background lighting (a lit coastline) raises the threshold and shortens the range; daytime ranges are not covered.
- A light is seen at the lesser of its geographic and luminous ranges; the loom of a powerful light can be visible beyond the geographic range.
- Radar and VHF ranges are line-of-sight horizons in the standard atmosphere with an effective earth radius of 4/3 of the true one (radar 2.23 √h); whether a target is actually detected or a call heard also depends on its radar cross-section or the transmitter power, antenna gains and sea clutter, which are not modelled.
- The COLREG Annex I minimum intensity uses the regulation's own formula and K = 0.8 (meteorological visibility of about 13 nmi), which is why it differs from an IALA nominal-range intensity.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: Bowditch Table 12 gives 12.8 nmi for 120 ft; the 2.08 rule gives 11.39 + 3.60 = 15.0 nmi for a 30 m light and a 3 m eye; the COLREG Annex I §8 table (0.9, 4.3, 12, 27, 52, 94 cd for 1–6 nmi) is reproduced; a 10 nmi nominal range needs 2·10⁻⁷ × 1852² × 100 × 20 = 1372 cd.
- Design decision: the Allard equation is solved by bisection on its logarithm, which is monotonic in distance, so every intensity and visibility has exactly one luminous range.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Visibility under 2 nmi: restricted visibility (COLREG Rule 19) — lights are of little help; rely on radar and sound signals.
- A height of zero means that eye or light is at the sea surface: its horizon distance is zero.
- Nominal ranges above about 30 nmi are rare: check the light list entry.
- Abnormal refraction can change geographic and radar ranges a lot; background lights on shore raise the visibility threshold and shorten the luminous range.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Bowditch Table 12: a height of 120 ft gives 12.8 nmi to the horizon, i.e. 1.17 √h with h in feet (2.12 √h in metres)
  - Source: The American Practical Navigator (Bowditch), Table 12 "Distance of the horizon" (R = 3440.1 nmi, β = 0.8279)
- Rounded 2.08 rule: a 30 m light seen from a 3 m height of eye has a geographic range of 11.39 + 3.60 = 15.0 nmi
  - Source: Geographic range = 2.08 (√H + √h) nmi, H and h in metres (the common rounded rule)
- COLREG Annex I §8 table of minimum luminous intensity: 1 nmi 0.9 cd, 2 nmi 4.3, 3 nmi 12, 4 nmi 27, 5 nmi 52, 6 nmi 94
  - Source: COLREG 1972 Annex I section 8(b) table; 33 CFR 84.14
- Allard's law: a 10 nmi nominal range needs 2·10⁻⁷ × 1852² × 100 × 20 = 1372 cd, and that light's luminous range at 10 nmi visibility is exactly 10 nmi; less visibility always means less range
  - Source: IALA Recommendation E-200-2 (Allard's law, T = 0.05^(1/V), threshold 2·10⁻⁷ lx)
- Radar horizon in the 4/3 atmosphere is 2.23 √h nmi (within 1 % of Bowditch's 1.22 √h for h in feet); target range adds the two horizons; the light is seen at the lesser of luminous and geographic range
  - Source: Bowditch (radar horizon 1.22 √h ft); ITU-R effective earth radius factor 4/3
- Invalid inputs fail fast: negative heights, zero visibility, zero intensity and an unknown horizon model
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 8.2 nmi, 13.4 nmi, 21.6 nmi, 110 000, 11.8 nmi, 11.8 nmi to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- The American Practical Navigator (Bowditch), NGA Pub. 9 — Table 12 "Distance of the horizon" (R = 3440.1 nmi, β = 0.8279) and the radar horizon
- IALA Recommendation E-200-2 (2008), now IALA R0202 — Allard's law, threshold illuminance 2·10⁻⁷ lx, luminous and nominal range
- COLREG 1972 Annex I, section 8 (intensity of lights) — I = 3.43·10⁶ × T × D² × K⁻ᴰ with T = 2·10⁻⁷ and K = 0.8; also 33 CFR 84.14
- ITU-R Recommendation P.453 / P.834 — effective earth radius factor 4/3 for radio and radar propagation in the standard atmosphere

## Lighting design (lumen method)

<a id="lighting-lumen"></a>

Folder `lighting-lumen/` · Electrical · Number of luminaires for a target illuminance from room index, utilisation and maintenance factors; power density.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Lumen (zonal cavity) method for a uniform general lighting layout: average maintained illuminance on the horizontal working plane E = N Φ UF MF / A, where Φ is the initial luminous flux of one luminaire (lamp lumens × lamps × luminaire light-output ratio, or the luminaire lumens of an LED fitting), UF the utilisation factor and MF the maintenance factor; it gives the average, not the uniformity, and ignores task lighting, daylight and obstructions.
- Room index K = L W/(h_m (L + W)) with h_m the mounting height above the working plane (0.75–0.85 m above the floor in offices, 0 for floor-level tasks), valid for rooms whose length is less than about four times the width.
- Utilisation factor: the built-in table is a typical direct-distribution luminaire (recessed louvre or diffuser) for three reflectance sets (ceiling/walls/floor 70/50/20, 50/30/20, 30/30/20) interpolated in K; it is indicative within about ±10 %, and the manufacturer's photometric UF table for the actual luminaire and reflectances should be entered when available.
- Maintenance factor MF = LLMF × LSF × LMF × RSMF (lamp lumen maintenance, lamp survival, luminaire maintenance, room surface maintenance): 0.8 is the usual clean-room default, 0.67 for dirty industrial spaces, 0.9 for sealed LED fittings in clean offices — entered by the user as a single factor.
- Layout: the luminaires are arranged in a rectangular grid with rows along the width and columns along the length; the spacing-to-height ratio (SHR = spacing/h_m) should not exceed the luminaire's maximum (1.25–1.5 for most direct fittings) for acceptable uniformity; the page rounds N up to a grid and reports the resulting SHR.
- Target illuminances are EN 12464-1 maintained values (offices 500 lx, drawing 750, corridors 100, workshops 300–500) and the engine-room value of ISO 8995 / class practice (200 lx); glare (UGR), colour rendering and emergency lighting are separate requirements.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 12 × 8 m office, h_m 2.3 m → K 2.09; 500 lx with 4 000 lm luminaires, UF 0.55, MF 0.8 → N = 27.3 → 28 (4 × 7 grid), achieved 513 lx, 10.5 W/m² for 36 W fittings — within the EN 15193 benchmark range for LED offices (8–12 W/m²).
- Design decision: a typical UF table is built in so the page works without photometric data, with a warning that it is indicative; a custom UF overrides it.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Utilisation factor … from the typical direct-luminaire table for … reflectances (±10 %): use the manufacturer's UF table for the actual fitting.
- Room length more than four times the width: the room-index method is unreliable — split the room into zones.
- Spacing-to-height ratio exceeded: the average may be met but the uniformity (E_min/E_avg ≥ 0.6 for task areas) will not.
- Maintenance factor above 0.85 assumes sealed LED luminaires in a clean, regularly cleaned space.
- Average illuminance only: glare (UGR), uniformity, colour rendering, task lighting and emergency lighting are separate requirements (EN 12464-1).
- Daylight, obstructions (machinery, racks) and dark equipment surfaces reduce the real illuminance below the lumen-method average.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Room index: 12 × 8 m at h_m 2.3 m → K = 96/(2.3 × 20) = 2.087; a square 10 × 10 m room at 3 m → 1.67; K is symmetric in L and W
  - Source: CIBSE/SLL Lighting Handbook, room index K = LW/(h_m(L + W))
- Lumen method: 500 lx over 96 m² with 4 000 lm luminaires, UF 0.55, MF 0.8 → N = 48 000/1 760 = 27.3 → 28 in a 4 × 7 grid; achieved 513 lx, initial 642 lx
  - Source: N = E A/(Φ UF MF) (SLL Code for Lighting); E_achieved = N Φ UF MF/A
- Layout and SHR: 4 × 7 grid gives spacings 1.71 m (length) and 2.0 m (width), SHR = 2.0/2.3 = 0.87 ≤ 1.5 OK; a high bay at h_m 8 m with few fittings exceeds SHR and is flagged
  - Source: SLL spacing-to-height ratio criterion for uniformity
- Typical UF table: 70/50/20 at K 2.0 = 0.59, interpolated 0.61 at K 2.25; darker 30/30/20 surfaces give 0.52 at K 2.0; table mode on the office (K 2.09) gives UF ≈ 0.60 and 25.1 luminaires required (still 28 installed on the 4 × 7 grid)
  - Source: Indicative UF values for a recessed direct luminaire (SLL/CIBSE pattern); manufacturer data governs
- Power and energy: 28 × 36 W = 1 008 W, 10.5 W/m², efficacy 111 lm/W, 2 520 kWh/year at 2 500 h; EN 12464-1 presets (office 500, drawing 750, corridor 100, engine room 200)
  - Source: EN 12464-1 maintained illuminance; EN 15193 lighting power density benchmarks (LED offices 8–12 W/m²)
- Long room warning (L > 4W) and invalid inputs: zero height, UF above 1, unknown task
  - Source: Room-index validity (SLL); validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 500, 2.09, 27.3, 28, 2.0 m, 1.71 m, 0.87, 513, 642, 1 008 W, 10.5, 111 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- CIBSE/SLL Lighting Handbook (2018) and SLL Code for Lighting — lumen method, room index, utilisation factor tables, maintenance factor
- EN 12464-1:2021 Light and lighting — Lighting of work places — Part 1: Indoor work places (maintained illuminance, UGR, uniformity)
- ISO 8995-1:2002 / CIE S 008 Lighting of indoor work places; IMO/class lighting practice for machinery spaces (ABS/DNV ergonomics notations)
- CIE 97:2005 Guide on the maintenance of indoor electric lighting systems (maintenance factor components)

## Load combinations calculator (ASCE 7 LRFD/ASD and Eurocode)

<a id="load-combinations"></a>

Folder `load-combinations/` · Structural · Factored load combinations from dead, live, roof, snow, rain, wind and seismic loads by ASCE 7-16 LRFD or ASD, or EN 1990 6.10, with the governing case.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Each load is the effect of one load case on the same quantity (a reaction, a moment, an axial force) in one consistent unit, positive in the direction of gravity.
- Wind and earthquake effects act in either direction, so every combination with W or E is evaluated with both signs; the minimum shows uplift or reversal.
- ASCE 7-16: the load factor on L in combinations 3, 4 and 5 may be 0.5 where the live load is 100 psf or less, except in garages and places of public assembly (2.3.1 Exception 1). E is the combined seismic load effect of 12.4; the special combinations of 2.3.6 with E_v are not split out.
- EN 1990: expressions 6.10 or 6.10a and 6.10b for persistent and transient STR design with the recommended γ_G = 1.35 (1.00 when favourable), γ_Q = 1.5 and ψ factors of Table A1.1; variable actions enter only where unfavourable, and roof imposed loads are not combined with snow or wind (A1.2.1(3)). National annexes can change the values. Rain R has no EN 1990 counterpart and is ignored there.
- The seismic combination of EN 1990 6.12b takes E as the design seismic action A_Ed with ψ2 on the imposed and snow loads.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: D 10, L 8, Lr 2, S 5, W 6: ASCE 7-16 LRFD maximum 1.2 × 10 + 6 + 8 + 0.5 × 5 = 28.5 (combination 4), minimum 0.9 × 10 − 6 = 3.0 (combination 6); ASD maximum 22.45 (6a), minimum 2.4 (7); EN 1990 6.10 maximum 34.8 with snow leading (category A, altitude ≤ 1 000 m). Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- EN 1990 has no separate rain load; R is ignored in the Eurocode combinations.
- The dead load is negative: check the sign convention (gravity positive).
- The minimum is negative: the load effect reverses (uplift or tension); check the connections and anchorage for it.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- ASCE 7-16 LRFD with D 10, L 8, Lr 2, S 5, W 6: 1.4D = 14; 2(S) = 27.3; 3(S, L) = 28; 4(+W, S) = 28.5 governs; 6(−W) = 0.9 × 10 − 6 = 3.0 is the minimum
  - Source: ASCE/SEI 7-16, 2.3.1 combinations 1 to 7; hand calculation
- ASCE 7-16 LRFD exception: with 0.5 on L, combination 4 drops to 24.5; seismic E 7 gives 1.2D + E + L + 0.2S = 28 and 0.9D − E = 2
  - Source: ASCE/SEI 7-16, 2.3.1 Exception 1 and combinations 5 and 7
- ASCE 7-16 ASD: D + L = 18; D + 0.75L + 0.75(0.6W) + 0.75S = 22.45 governs; 0.6D − 0.6W = 2.4 is the minimum; 0.6D + 0.7E with E 10 is 13
  - Source: ASCE/SEI 7-16, 2.4.1 combinations 1 to 8; hand calculation
- EN 1990 6.10, category A, snow below 1 000 m: snow leading 1.35 × 10 + 1.5 × 5 + 1.5 × 0.7 × 8 + 1.5 × 0.6 × 6 = 34.8; roof load leading excludes snow and wind (24.9); uplift 1.0 × 10 − 1.5 × 6 = 1.0
  - Source: EN 1990 6.10 with Table A1.1 ψ0 (A 0.7, snow 0.5, wind 0.6, H 0) and Table A1.2(B) γ factors; A1.2.1(3)
- EN 1990 6.10a/b: 6.10a = 1.35 × 10 + 1.5(0.7 × 8 + 0.5 × 5 + 0.6 × 6) = 31.05; 6.10b snow leading 0.85 × 1.35 × 10 + 7.5 + 8.4 + 5.4 = 32.775 governs; seismic 6.12b G + E + 0.3 L = 22.4 for E 10; rain is ignored and bad input refused
  - Source: EN 1990 expressions 6.10a, 6.10b (ξ = 0.85) and 6.12b with ψ2 = 0.3 for category A
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 28.5, 3.0 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASCE/SEI 7-16 Minimum Design Loads and Associated Criteria for Buildings and Other Structures, 2.3.1 (LRFD basic combinations), 2.3.6 and 2.4.1 (ASD basic combinations)
- EN 1990:2002+A1:2005 Eurocode — Basis of structural design, 6.4.3.2 expressions 6.10, 6.10a, 6.10b; 6.4.3.4 expression 6.12b; Annex A1, Table A1.1 (ψ factors) and Table A1.2(B) (γ factors)
- International Building Code 2021, section 1605 Load Combinations (adopting the ASCE 7 combinations)

## Loading condition from an item list

<a id="loading-condition"></a>

Folder `loading-condition/` · Maritime · Displacement, deadweight, KG with free surface, GM, trim, end drafts and list from a pasted list of weights and centres and a hydrostatic table.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Weights are summed with their vertical, longitudinal and transverse centres; the first line is taken as the lightship for the deadweight. Free-surface moments of slack tanks (FSM = ρ·i, t·m) are summed and divided by the displacement as a virtual rise of G.
- Hydrostatic particulars (mean draft, KM, LCB, LCF, MCTC, TPC) are interpolated linearly by displacement in the pasted table, which is for even keel in water of the table density; for other water the displacement is converted to the table density first, and MCTC and TPC are scaled with the density.
- Trim by the stern = Δ(LCB − LCG)/(100 MCTC) about the LCF, with the table draft taken at the LCF; this is the usual small-trim method of stability booklets and loses accuracy at large trims, where a trimmed-hydrostatics (or direct) calculation is needed.
- List from the transverse centre of gravity by the small-angle formula tan φ = TCG/GM; it is not valid near or beyond the deck-edge immersion or with GM close to zero (angle of loll).
- The calculation does not include longitudinal strength (shear forces and bending moments), grain or dangerous goods requirements; use the approved loading computer for the official condition.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: the default condition sums to 13 690 t (deadweight 9490 t); interpolated in the sample table it floats at 6.79 m with KM 8.43 m, GM 1.30 m after 0.031 m of free surface, and trims 1.00 m by the stern; the sums of moments reproduce KG, LCG and TCG independently computed in the tests, and a weight moved 10 m to starboard lists the ship by atan(w·10/(Δ·GM)).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- GM corrected for free surface is … m: the ship is unstable upright (angle of loll) — do not sail.
- GM … m is below the IS Code minimum of 0.15 m.
- List of …° to …: correct it by transferring ballast or fuel.
- Trim of … m is more than 1.5 % of the length: even-keel hydrostatics lose accuracy; use trimmed hydrostatics.
- Free surface costs … m of GM: press up or empty slack tanks where possible.
- Longitudinal strength, the GZ curve and the stability criteria are not checked here; the approved loading computer governs.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- … line …: expected … numbers…
- Displacement … t (at the table density) is outside the hydrostatic table (…–… t)
- Enter at least the lightship line
- Item "…": weight must be greater than zero
- Item "…": free-surface moment must not be negative
- The hydrostatic table needs at least two drafts
- Hydrostatic table line …: displacements must increase

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Moment sums: 5000 t at 8 m, 6000 t at 6 m and 600 t at 1 m give Δ 11 600 t and KG 6.6034 m; LCG 66.724 m; deadweight 6600 t; FSM 300 t·m adds 0.0259 m
  - Source: Sum of moments about the keel and the aft perpendicular (Barrass & Derrett, loading condition tables)
- Hydrostatics: at exactly 11 600 t the table row is returned (draft 6.0 m, KM 8.55 m); halfway between rows every column is the mean
  - Source: Linear interpolation by displacement in the hydrostatic table
- Trim and drafts: Δ(LCB − LCG)/(100 MCTC) with LCB 71.5 m, MCTC 175 t·m/cm; the drafts differ by the trim and the draft at the LCF is the table draft
  - Source: Trim by the moment to change trim about the LCF (Barrass & Derrett)
- List: moving 100 t of the cargo 10 m to starboard lists the ship by atan(1000/(Δ · GM)); the GM is KM − KG − FSC
  - Source: Small-angle list tan φ = w·d / (Δ·GM)
- Density: in fresh water (1.000 t/m³) the same 11 600 t corresponds to 11 890 t of sea water in the table, so the ship floats deeper; MCTC and TPC scale with the density
  - Source: Displacement = volume × density; table particulars in sea water 1.025 t/m³
- Invalid inputs fail fast: a displacement outside the table, a zero weight, a table with falling displacements, a malformed line
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 13 690 t, 9490 t, 7.102 m, 420 t·m, 0.031 m, 8.43 m, 1.30 m, 69.93 m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- C. B. Barrass, D. R. Derrett, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed. — loading condition tables, trim and drafts by MCTC, free-surface correction
- IMO Resolution MSC.267(85) 2008 IS Code, Part B chapter 3 (calculation of loading conditions, free-surface effects)
- IACS Recommendation No. 48 Requirements for loading conditions, loading manuals and loading instruments

## Speed of sound and Mach number calculator

<a id="mach-number"></a>

Folder `mach-number/` · Automotive · Speed of sound from temperature or altitude, Mach number from a speed, and the speed for a given Mach, in mph, knots, km/h and m/s.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Air is an ideal gas with γ = 1.4 and R = 287.05 J/(kg·K) (ICAO Doc 7488), so the speed of sound depends on temperature only, not on pressure or altitude as such; at very high temperatures γ falls and the formula reads slightly high.
- The altitude option uses the ICAO standard atmosphere temperature: 15 °C at sea level, falling 6.5 °C per km to −56.5 °C at 11 km (36 089 ft), constant to 20 km; altitudes are geopotential, which differ from geometric height by less than 0.3 % below 20 km.
- Humidity raises the speed of sound slightly; the calculator uses dry air.
- Another gas can be entered with its own ratio of specific heats and specific gas constant, such as γ = 1.67 and R = 2 077 J/(kg·K) for helium.
- The regime bands (subsonic below 0.8, transonic 0.8 to 1.2, supersonic to 5, hypersonic beyond) are the usual aerodynamic classification.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: ISA sea level (15 °C) a = 340.29 m/s = 761.2 mph = 661.5 kn; 500 mph at 35 000 ft (ISA −54.3 °C, a = 663.3 mph) is Mach 0.754; total temperature −29.5 °C. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above Mach 5 the air heats so much that γ is no longer 1.4; the total temperature shown is an ideal-gas value and too high.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Sea-level ISA, 15 °C: speed of sound 340.294 m/s, 761.2 mph, 661.48 kn
  - Source: ICAO Doc 7488/3, a0 = 340.294 m/s
- Tropopause and above (−56.5 °C): 295.07 m/s; Mach 2 at 15 km is 590.1 m/s (1 320 mph)
  - Source: ICAO Doc 7488/3 table, a = 295.069 m/s from 11 to 20 km
- 500 mph at 35 000 ft (ISA −54.34 °C): a = 663.3 mph, Mach 0.754, total temperature −29.5 °C
  - Source: Hand calculation, a = √(1.4 × 287.05 × 218.81 K), T_t = T (1 + 0.2 M²)
- Helium at 0 °C (γ = 5/3, R = 2 077 J/(kg·K)): about 972 m/s, nearly three times air
  - Source: a = √(γ R T); handbook speed of sound in helium at 0 °C about 970 m/s
- Regime bands: 0.5 subsonic, 1.0 transonic, 3 supersonic, 7 hypersonic
  - Source: Anderson, Fundamentals of Aerodynamics, Section 1.10
- A temperature below −150 °C, an altitude above 20 km and γ of 2 are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces −54.34 °C, 663.3 mph, 0.754, −29.5 °C to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ICAO Doc 7488/3, Manual of the ICAO Standard Atmosphere, 3rd ed. 1993 (a0 = 340.294 m/s at 288.15 K; γ = 1.4; R = 287.05287 J/(kg·K); temperature profile)
- J.D. Anderson, Fundamentals of Aerodynamics, 6th ed., McGraw-Hill 2017, Section 1.10 (flow regimes by Mach number) and Chapter 8 (speed of sound a = √(γ R T), total temperature)

## Machining time calculator (turning, facing, drilling, milling)

<a id="machining-time"></a>

Folder `machining-time/` · Manufacturing · Cutting time per pass and per part for turning, facing, drilling and milling from length, feed and rpm, and total job time with set-up and handling.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The tool feeds at a constant rate over the whole travel: the length of cut plus the approach and overtravel you enter; rapid moves, tool changes and acceleration are part of the handling time.
- Facing runs at a constant spindle speed from the outside diameter to the centre (or to the bore); a lathe with constant surface speed raises the rpm towards the centre and finishes sooner.
- Drilling travel adds the length of the drill point, D / (2 tan(θ/2)), so that the full diameter reaches the stated depth; add the breakthrough allowance for a through hole.
- In milling the travel is the path length of the cutter centre; for a face mill to clear the part completely the overtravel must include the cutter diameter.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: turning 100 mm plus 3 mm of approach at 0.2 mm/rev and 1 000 rpm takes 0.515 min a pass; two passes are 1.03 min, and 50 parts with 30 min set-up and 0.5 min handling each take 106.5 min. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Facing at a constant rpm: the surface speed falls to zero at the centre; with constant surface speed the face is finished sooner.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Bore diameter d: it must be smaller than the outside diameter.
- Length of cut: the tool travel is zero; enter a length or an approach.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Turning 100 + 3 mm at 0.2 mm/rev and 1 000 rpm: 103 / 200 = 0.515 min a pass; 2 passes 1.03 min; 50 parts + 30 min set-up + 0.5 min each = 106.5 min
  - Source: Groover / Kalpakjian: T_m = L / (f N) (hand calculation)
- Drilling 1 in deep with a 1/2 in 118° drill: point 0.1502 in + 0.1 in approach = 1.2502 in at 0.008 in/rev and 800 rpm takes 0.1954 min
  - Source: Point length D / (2 tan 59°) = 0.3004 D; T = L / (f N) (hand calculation)
- Facing a 2 in bar to the centre with 0.1 in approach at 0.008 in/rev and 800 rpm: 1.1 in at 6.4 in/min = 0.1719 min; a 1 in bore leaves 0.6 in
  - Source: Travel (D − d)/2 + allowance (hand calculation)
- Milling 4 + 0.1 in at 0.003 in/tooth, 4 teeth, 800 rpm: 9.6 in/min, 0.4271 min; three passes take three times as long
  - Source: Groover: f_r = N n_t f, T_m = (L + A) / f_r (hand calculation)
- A bore as large as the outside, zero travel, fractional passes and zero rpm are rejected; facing warns about constant rpm
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.515 min, 1.03 min, 106.5 min to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Groover, M. P., Fundamentals of Modern Manufacturing, Wiley, chapter on machining operations: T_m = L / f_r with f_r = N f (turning, drilling) and T_m = (L + A) / f_r with f_r = N n_t f (milling)
- Kalpakjian, S. and Schmid, S. R., Manufacturing Engineering and Technology, 7th ed., Pearson: cutting time t = l / (f N) for turning and drilling

## mAh to Wh battery capacity

<a id="mah-to-wh"></a>

Folder `mah-to-wh/` · Electrical · Battery capacity in mAh or Ah converted to energy in Wh at the nominal voltage, and back, with the airline carry-on limit it falls under.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Energy is capacity times the nominal voltage, which is the average voltage over a discharge (3.6 or 3.7 V for a lithium-ion cell, 3.2 V for LiFePO4, 2.0 V per lead-acid cell); the voltage falls as the battery empties, so the energy at a high discharge rate is a few per cent lower.
- A pack's capacity in mAh is quoted at its own voltage; a power bank rated in mAh at 3.7 V delivers fewer mAh at its 5 V USB output.
- The airline status follows the IATA limits for lithium-ion batteries carried by passengers; the airline and the country of departure can be stricter, and spare batteries must go in the cabin.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 3000 mAh at 3.7 V is 11.1 Wh; a 20 000 mAh power bank at 3.7 V is 74 Wh, under the 100 Wh limit. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above 60 V DC the battery is no longer extra-low voltage; it needs protection against electric shock.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 3000 mAh at 3.7 V is 11.1 Wh (3 Ah)
  - Source: Linden's Handbook of Batteries, ch. 1: energy = capacity × nominal voltage
- A 100 Ah, 12 V lead-acid battery stores 1.2 kWh; 1.2 kWh at 12 V is back to 100 Ah
  - Source: E = Q V; Q = E / V
- Airline limits: 99.9 Wh free, 100 Wh free, 100.1 Wh needs approval, 160 Wh needs approval, 160.1 Wh not allowed
  - Source: IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations, Table 2.3.A, lithium-ion batteries carried by passengers
- A 20 000 mAh power bank at 3.7 V is 74 Wh, allowed; 27 000 mAh is 99.9 Wh, just under the limit
  - Source: IATA Lithium Battery Guidance Document (power banks)
- A 100 Wh LiFePO4 pack at 12.8 V holds 7812.5 mAh; zero voltage is rejected
  - Source: Q = E / V; LiFePO4 4 cells × 3.2 V; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 11.1 Wh, 3 Ah to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

- IEC 61960-3:2017 Secondary lithium cells and batteries for portable applications (rated capacity, nominal voltage)

## Open-channel flow (Manning)

<a id="manning-channel-flow"></a>

Folder `manning-channel-flow/` · Civil · Manning flow in rectangular, trapezoidal, triangular and circular channels: velocity, discharge or normal depth, Froude number, critical depth, shear stress.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Steady uniform flow: the water surface is parallel to the channel bed, so the bed slope equals the energy slope; backwater, drawdown, bends, hydraulic jumps and unsteady flow need gradually varied or unsteady flow analysis.
- Manning's equation is empirical and dimensional (the 1/n coefficient is in SI with R in metres); it applies to fully rough turbulent flow, which excludes very smooth linings at low velocities and very shallow laminar sheet flow.
- The roughness coefficient n is the dominant uncertainty (±15–25 % between the minimum and maximum of Chow's ranges for one description); presets are Chow's "normal" values for clean, maintained channels and natural channels vary with stage, vegetation and season.
- Prismatic channel with a constant cross-section; the circular section assumes a free surface (the full-pipe case is the limit where the hydraulic radius is D/4, and the maximum discharge of a circular pipe occurs at about 94 % depth).
- Froude number uses the hydraulic depth A/T; the critical depth is found by bisection on Fr = 1 for the same discharge and section, and the specific energy is referred to the channel bottom.
- Boundary shear stress τ₀ = ρ g R S is the mean over the wetted perimeter; local values at the bed centre are higher (about 1.5 × on the bed of a wide channel), which matters for erosion checks.
- Water at 1 000 kg/m³; sediment-laden or saline water changes the density slightly and the roughness considerably.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: a 3 m rectangular concrete channel 1 m deep on 0.1 % gives 1.73 m/s and 5.19 m³/s, with a Froude number of 0.55 and a critical depth of 0.673 m; the half-full and full circular pipe both give R = D/4 and the maximum discharge appears near 94 % depth, as in Chow.
- Design decision: normal depth and critical depth are found by bisection rather than iteration formulas, so every section shape is handled identically.
- Design decision: Manning n presets are the 'normal' column of Chow's Table 5-6; the register notes the range so users know the ±20 % band.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Froude number within ±15 % of unity: standing waves and an unstable surface; change the slope or section.
- Velocity above 3 m/s: erosive for earth and most lined channels; check the lining permissible velocity or shear stress.
- Velocity below 0.6 m/s: sediment deposition likely in channels carrying silt.
- Pipe more than 80 % full: air entrainment and surging; free-surface capacity peaks near 94 % and falls to the full-pipe value at 100 %.
- Manning's n = … is the normal value for this description; Chow's range for the same description spans roughly ±20 %.
- Uniform flow: the bed slope is taken as the energy slope; backwater or a downstream control changes the depth.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Unknown channel section "…"
- Discharge … m³/s exceeds the capacity of the pipe flowing with a free surface (… m³/s at 94 % depth)
- Flow depth … m exceeds the pipe diameter … m

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Rectangular concrete channel 3 m wide, 1 m deep, S = 0.001, n = 0.013: A 3 m², P 5 m, R 0.6 m, V = (1/0.013) × 0.6^(2/3) × 0.001^(1/2) = 1.730 m/s, Q = 5.19 m³/s
  - Source: Manning's equation in SI (Chow 1959, eq. 5-7); n = 0.013 for finished concrete (Chow Table 5-6)
- Trapezoidal earth channel b = 6 m, z = 2, y = 1.5 m, S = 0.0016, n = 0.025: A 13.5 m², P 12.71 m, R 1.062 m, V 1.666 m/s, Q 22.5 m³/s
  - Source: Trapezoidal geometry A = (b + z y) y, P = b + 2 y √(1 + z²) (Chow Table 2-1); Manning with n = 0.025
- Circular pipe: half full and completely full both have R = D/4; the free-surface discharge peaks near 94 % depth at about 1.08 × the full-pipe discharge
  - Source: Chow (1959) §6-4 and French (1985): hydraulic elements of a circular section, maximum discharge at y/D ≈ 0.938
- Normal depth by bisection: 5.191 m³/s in the 3 m channel returns y = 1.000 m; the circular pipe refuses a discharge above its free-surface capacity
  - Source: Inverse of Manning for the depth (Chow §6-4, uniform flow computation)
- Froude number and critical depth: 1.73 m/s at 1 m depth → Fr = 0.553 (subcritical); critical depth (q²/g)^(1/3) = 0.673 m for q = 1.73 m²/s; at y_c the Froude number is 1
  - Source: Henderson (1966) ch. 2: Fr = V/√(g y) for a rectangle, y_c = (q²/g)^(1/3)
- Specific energy E = y + V²/2g = 1.153 m and mean shear stress ρ g R S = 5.88 Pa for the 3 m channel
  - Source: Henderson ch. 2 (specific energy); Chow ch. 7 unit tractive force τ₀ = γ R S
- Triangular ditch z = 2 at 0.5 m: A = 0.5 m², P = 2.236 m, T = 2 m; supercritical on a 5 % slope with a steep-slope regime text
  - Source: Triangular geometry A = z y², P = 2 y √(1 + z²) (Chow Table 2-1)
- Warnings: velocity above 3 m/s (steep channel) and below 0.6 m/s (flat channel) are flagged; at the critical slope (≈ 0.31 %) Fr = 1 and near-critical flow is flagged
  - Source: Permissible velocities (Chow Table 7-3, Fortier and Scobey), deposition limit ≈ 0.6 m/s, critical slope from V_c = √(g y_c) in Manning
- Invalid inputs fail fast: depth above the pipe diameter, zero slope, unknown roughness
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 3.0 m², 5.0 m, 0.60 m, 1.73 m/s, 5.19 m³/s, 0.67 m, 1.15 m, 5.9 Pa to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- V. T. Chow, Open-Channel Hydraulics (McGraw-Hill, 1959), ch. 5 (Manning formula, Table 5-6 roughness coefficients) and ch. 6 (uniform flow computation)
- F. M. Henderson, Open Channel Flow (Macmillan, 1966), ch. 2 (critical flow) and ch. 4 (uniform flow)
- R. H. French, Open-Channel Hydraulics (McGraw-Hill, 1985), circular sections and the maximum-discharge depth
- USGS Water-Supply Paper 2339 (Arcement & Schneider, 1989), roughness coefficients for natural channels

## Mass balance calculator: mixing streams (flow, concentration, temperature)

<a id="mass-balance"></a>

Folder `mass-balance/` · Process · Mix two or three streams to find the combined flow, concentration and temperature, or find the stream 2 flow that reaches a target concentration or temperature.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Steady state with no reaction, accumulation or losses: total mass and the mass of each component are conserved, so the mixed concentration is the flow-weighted mean of the stream concentrations.
- Concentrations are mass fractions of one component (% w/w, ppm by mass) and flows are mass flows; for volume flows and mg/L the same equations hold only when the densities are equal.
- The mixed temperature is the c_p-weighted mean: no heat of mixing or dilution, no phase change and no heat loss; dissolving or diluting acids, caustic soda and some salts releases heat and gives a hotter mix.
- In the required-stream form, stream 2 must be weaker (or colder) than the target when stream 1 is stronger (or hotter), and the target must lie between the two.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 1 000 kg/h of 26 % brine diluted to 10 % needs 1 000 × (26 − 10) / (10 − 0) = 1 600 kg/h of water, giving 2 600 kg/h of product. Checked by hand.
- Felder and Rousseau, mixing unit example: 200 g of 40 wt% methanol and 150 g of 70 wt% methanol give 350 g of 52.9 wt% methanol, reproduced in the tests.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The streams differ by more than 50 K: check for boiling, flashing or a heat of mixing, which this energy balance ignores.
- Stream 2 is more than 100 times stream 1: the target is very close to the concentration or temperature of stream 2.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Stream mass flows: at least one stream must have a flow above zero.
- Stream 1: mass flow must be greater than zero to find the flow of stream 2.
- Target concentration: it equals the concentration of stream 2, which no finite flow can reach.
- Target concentration: it must lie between the concentrations of stream 1 and stream 2.
- Target temperature: it equals the temperature of stream 2, which no finite flow can reach.
- Target temperature: it must lie between the temperatures of stream 1 and stream 2.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 200 g of 40 wt% methanol mixed with 150 g of 70 wt% methanol gives 350 g of 52.9 wt% methanol
  - Source: Felder and Rousseau, Elementary Principles of Chemical Processes, 3rd ed., ch. 4, balances on a mixing unit
- 1 000 kg/h of 26 % brine diluted to 10 % needs 1 600 kg/h of water and gives 2 600 kg/h
  - Source: Component balance by hand: ṁ2 = ṁ1 (x1 − x_t) / (x_t − x2)
- Three streams of 100, 200 and 300 kg/h at 10, 20 and 30 % and 10, 20 and 30 °C mix to 600 kg/h at 23.33 % and 23.33 °C
  - Source: Flow-weighted means by hand (equal c_p)
- Energy balance with different c_p: 1 kg/s of water at 80 °C and 2 kg/s of oil (2.0 kJ/(kg·K)) at 20 °C mix at 50.68 °C
  - Source: Felder and Rousseau ch. 8: adiabatic mixing with constant c_p, by hand
- Required cold stream: 1 kg/s at 60 °C cooled to 40 °C by water at 10 °C needs 0.667 kg/s
  - Source: Energy balance by hand: ṁ2 = ṁ1 c_p1 (T1 − T_t) / (c_p2 (T_t − T2))
- A target outside the two streams, a target equal to stream 2 and no flow at all are rejected; large temperature spreads warn
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1 600 kg/h, 2 600 kg/h, 1.600 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Felder, R.M. and Rousseau, R.W., Elementary Principles of Chemical Processes, 3rd ed., Wiley, ch. 4 (material balances on a mixing unit) and ch. 7–8 (energy balances)
- Himmelblau, D.M. and Riggs, J.B., Basic Principles and Calculations in Chemical Engineering, 8th ed., Part II (material balances)

## Mass flow rate calculator (kg/h, m³/h, velocity, Nm³/h, SCFM)

<a id="mass-flow"></a>

Folder `mass-flow/` · Process · Mass flow, volume flow and pipe velocity from any one of them, with gas density from P, T and Z and conversion between actual and standard flow (Nm³/h, SCFM).

### Assumptions and caveats

- Mass flow equals density × volume flow, and volume flow equals velocity × the inside cross-section of the pipe; the velocity is the average over the section.
- Gas density follows the real-gas law ρ = P M / (Z R T) at the flowing pressure and temperature; enter Z = 1 for an ideal gas, which is within 1 % for air and nitrogen below about 20 bar near room temperature.
- Standard and normal flows are the volume the same mass would occupy at the reference state, taken as an ideal gas there (Z = 1); the references are 0 °C and 101.325 kPa (Nm³), 15 °C and 101.325 kPa (Sm³), 60 °F and 14.696 psia (SCF) and 20 °C and 100 kPa for compressed air.
- Pressure is absolute: add the atmospheric pressure, about 1.013 bar or 14.7 psi, to a gauge reading.
- Water vapour is not separated out: a humid gas gives a wet standard flow; dry-basis flows need the moisture content removed first.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 500 Nm³/h of air (28.964 g/mol) is 646.1 kg/h; at 8 bar absolute and 20 °C its density is 9.507 kg/m³, so it flows at 67.97 m³/h, 40.0 ACFM, and 9.62 m/s in a 50 mm bore. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Gas velocity above 30 m/s (100 ft/s): expect noise and a high pressure drop; a larger pipe is usual.
- Liquid velocity above 3 m/s (10 ft/s): expect a high pressure drop, erosion and water hammer risk; 1 to 3 m/s is the usual design range.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Known flow: standard volume flow applies to gases; choose Gas or give the actual flow of the liquid.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 500 Nm³/h of air: 646.1 kg/h; at 8 bar(a) and 20 °C 9.507 kg/m³, 67.97 m³/h, 40.0 ACFM, 9.62 m/s in 50 mm
  - Source: Hand calculation: ρ = P M / (R T), ṁ = ρ_N Q_N, v = Q / A
- 100 US gpm of water in 2 in Schedule 40 pipe (2.067 in bore) flows at 9.56 ft/s
  - Source: Crane Technical Paper 410, v = 0.4085 Q/d² (gpm, in) and its flow table for 2 in Schedule 40
- Dry air at 60 °F and 14.696 psia is 1.2226 kg/m³ (0.0763 lb/ft³); at 0 °C and 1 atm 1.2922 kg/m³, within 0.1 % of the real 1.2929
  - Source: Ideal gas with M = 28.9644 g/mol (ISO 2533); CRC normal density of air 1.2929 kg/m³
- 100 ACFM of air at 100 psig and 60 °F is 780.5 SCFM; Z = 0.9 at the same conditions gives 867.2 SCFM
  - Source: Q_std = Q (P / P_std)(T_std / T) / Z by hand (14.696 psia atmosphere)
- Velocity input round-trips: 2 m/s in a 100 mm bore is 56.55 m³/h and back
  - Source: Q = v π D² / 4 by hand
- Standard flow of a liquid is refused; a fast liquid warns; zero diameter is rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 646.1 kg/h, 9.507 kg/m³, 67.97 m³/h, 40.0 cfm, 9.62 m/s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 13443:1996 Natural gas — Standard reference conditions (15 °C, 101.325 kPa); DIN 1343:1990 Reference conditions, normal conditions (0 °C, 101.325 kPa)
- ISO 8778:2003 Pneumatic fluid power — Standard reference atmosphere (20 °C, 100 kPa)
- Perry's Chemical Engineers' Handbook, 8th ed., Section 6 (fluid flow: continuity, ṁ = ρ v A) and Section 2 (gas density, compressibility)

## Mass moment of inertia calculator

<a id="mass-moment-of-inertia"></a>

Folder `mass-moment-of-inertia/` · Mechanical · Mass moment of inertia of cylinders, discs, tubes, spheres, rods and blocks, with radius of gyration, parallel-axis shift and flywheel energy.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Bodies are homogeneous: the density is uniform, so the mass centre is at the geometric centre. For a body made of several parts, add the parts' inertias about the same axis.
- The slender rod formulas neglect the rod's thickness; for a thick rod use the cylinder about a transverse axis.
- The thin shell has all its mass on the sphere's surface; the tube formula is exact for any wall thickness.
- The parallel-axis shift I = I_G + m d² applies only from the axis through the centre of mass to a parallel axis.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a steel disc 300 mm across and 50 mm thick weighs 27.74 kg and has I = 0.3121 kg·m²; at 1 500 rpm it stores 3 851 J. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The offset is measured from the axis through the centre of mass, not from the end axis of the rod.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Inside diameter: it must be smaller than the outside diameter.
- Mass from: a thin shell has no volume of its own; enter its mass.
- Mass from: a slender rod is defined by its mass and length; enter its mass.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Steel disc 300 mm × 50 mm: m = 7 850 × π × 0.15² × 0.05 = 27.74 kg, I = m r²/2 = 0.3121 kg·m², k = r/√2 = 106.1 mm, 3 851 J at 1 500 rpm
  - Source: Meriam and Kraige, Dynamics, Appendix D (solid cylinder about its axis); E = ½ I ω²
- Slender rod 3 kg, 1 m: m L²/12 = 0.25 about the centre and m L²/3 = 1.0 about the end; the parallel-axis shift of L/2 links them
  - Source: Beer et al., Dynamics (slender rod); parallel-axis theorem I = I_G + m d²
- Sphere and shell of 5 kg, 200 mm diameter: 2/5 m r² = 0.020 and 2/3 m r² = 0.0333 kg·m²
  - Source: Meriam and Kraige, Dynamics, Appendix D
- Tube 300/200 mm × 50 mm steel: m = 15.41 kg, I = m (r_o² + r_i²)/2 = 0.2505 kg·m²; block 200 × 100 × 50 mm: m (a² + b²)/12
  - Source: Thick-walled cylinder and rectangular prism formulas
- Inside diameter at least the outside, a density for a thin shell or rod, and zero mass are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 27.74 kg, 0.3121 kg·m², 3.851 kJ to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Meriam, J.L. and Kraige, L.G., Engineering Mechanics: Dynamics, Appendix D (properties of homogeneous solids)
- Beer, F.P. et al., Vector Mechanics for Engineers: Dynamics, inside back cover (mass moments of inertia of common shapes)

## Material properties table (steel, aluminium, plastics)

<a id="material-properties"></a>

Folder `material-properties/` · Mechanical · Density, Young's modulus, yield and tensile strength, thermal expansion, conductivity, specific heat and melting range of common materials, with mass.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Each value comes from the standard or data sheet named with the material: code minimums or characteristic values for structural steels, aluminium (EN 1999-1-1), stainless steel (ASTM A240), concrete and timber, and typical data-sheet values for copper, brass, 6061-T6, titanium physical data and plastics. The basis line says which.
- Strengths are room-temperature values for the product form and thickness stated; thicker sections, other tempers, welding and higher temperatures lower them. Use the mill certificate or the design code for a real design.
- Physical properties are at about 20 °C (expansion over the range stated). A dash means no cited value is held for that property rather than a guess.
- Mass is density × volume; specific stiffness E/ρ and specific strength f/ρ use the yield strength, or the tensile or characteristic strength where no yield is defined.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 2 L of 6061-T6 has a mass of 5.40 kg; E/ρ = 68.9 GPa / 2 700 = 25.52 MJ/kg; 276 MPa / 2 700 = 102.2 kJ/kg. S355: E/ρ = 26.75 MJ/kg and 45.2 kJ/kg. Checked by hand.
- Table provenance: EN 1993-1-1 Table 3.1 S355 fu = 490 MPa for t ≤ 40 mm was confirmed against a published implementation of the table (blueprints, EN 1993-1-1:2005 Table 3.1); EN 1999-1-1 Tables 3.2a/b from a reproduction of the standard; stainless physical data read from the Cleveland-Cliffs 304/304L and 316/316L bulletins (2021); copper and brass from the National Bronze data sheets (k 226 and 70 Btu·ft/(h·ft²·°F), α 9.40 and 11.1 µin/(in·°F), c 0.092 and 0.090 Btu/(lb·°F) converted); titanium from the ASM Aerospace Specification Metals data sheets; glass from the AGC Planibel data sheet (2 500 kg/m³, 70 GPa, 9e-6/K, 720 J/(kg·K)).
- Design decision: no melting range, conductivity or expansion is shown for the carbon steels, the EN aluminium alloys, cast iron and timber, because no source read for this page states them for those grades.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Plastics creep under sustained load and lose stiffness as they warm: short-term data-sheet values overstate long-term strength and stiffness.
- Brittle material: there is no yield point, and the tensile strength depends strongly on flaws and section size.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- EN 1993-1-1: S235 fy 235, fu 360; S355 fy 355, fu 490 MPa (t ≤ 40 mm); E 210 GPa, α 12e-6/K, ρ 7 850 kg/m³
  - Source: EN 1993-1-1:2005 Table 3.1 and §3.2.6
- EN 1993-1-2 carbon steel at 20 °C: λ = 54 − 0.0333 × 20 = 53.33 W/(m·K), c = 439.8 J/(kg·K)
  - Source: EN 1993-1-2:2005 §3.4.1.2 (eq. 3.2) and §3.4.1.3 (eq. 3.4)

  - Source: ASTM A36 and A572 minimum properties (1 ksi = 6.894757 MPa)
- Data-sheet values: 304 ρ 8 030, E 193 GPa, k 16.2; copper k 226 Btu·ft/(h·ft²·°F) = 391.1 W/(m·K), α 9.40 µin/(in·°F) = 16.92 µm/(m·K)
  - Source: Cleveland-Cliffs 304/304L bulletin; National Bronze C11000 data sheet
- Derived values: 2 L of 6061-T6 is 5.40 kg; E/ρ 25.52 MJ/kg; 276 MPa / 2 700 = 102.2 kJ/kg; no volume gives no mass
  - Source: m = ρ V, E/ρ, f/ρ (by hand)

## Mechanical advantage calculator (lever, pulley, screw jack)

<a id="mechanical-advantage"></a>

Folder `mechanical-advantage/` · Mechanical · Ideal and actual mechanical advantage and effort for levers, pulley blocks, inclined planes, screw jacks with friction, and wheel and axle.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Loads are static or move slowly at constant speed, so inertia is neglected; the effort is the force that just keeps the load moving (raising for the incline and the screw jack).
- Levers are rigid and turn on a frictionless fulcrum, so their actual and ideal mechanical advantage are equal; arm lengths are measured perpendicular to the forces from the fulcrum.
- A pulley system with n rope parts supporting the moving block has IMA = n; the overall efficiency entered covers sheave friction and rope stiffness and falls as parts are added; take it from the block maker.
- The incline effort acts parallel to the slope with Coulomb friction μ; the screw jack uses the power-screw equations of Shigley §8-2 with thread friction μ, flank half-angle α and a thrust collar of mean diameter d_c and friction μ_c.
- A screw is self-locking when the thread alone needs a positive torque to lower the load (π μ d_m sec α > l); the collar friction adds to the holding torque.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: Shigley Example 8-1 (square thread, d_m 30 mm, double-start 4 mm pitch so l = 8 mm, W = 6.4 kN, μ = μ_c = 0.08, d_c = 40 mm) gives T_R = 15.94 + 10.24 = 26.18 N·m, T_L = −0.466 + 10.24 = 9.77 N·m and efficiency 0.311, reproduced here; with a 300 mm handle the effort is 87.3 N and the AMA 73.3 against an IMA of 235.6.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The screw jack is not self-locking: the load lowers itself unless the screw is held.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Load arm: in a class 2 lever the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort, so the load arm must be shorter than the effort arm.
- Effort arm: in a class 3 lever the effort sits between the fulcrum and the load, so the effort arm must be shorter than the load arm.
- Friction coefficient: with this lead and friction the screw locks solid and no torque can raise the load.
- Lead: a lead larger than the mean circumference is not a practical power screw.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Shigley Example 8-1: square thread d_m 30 mm, l 8 mm, 6.4 kN, μ = μ_c = 0.08, d_c 40 mm: T_R = 15.94 + 10.24 = 26.18 N·m, T_L = −0.466 + 10.24 = 9.77 N·m, e = 0.311
  - Source: Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., Example 8-1
- Acme thread (α 14.5°) needs more torque than a square thread; with no friction the screw efficiency is 100 %
  - Source: Shigley eq. 8-5 (sec α on the friction terms); limiting case μ = μ_c = 0
- Levers: 1.5 m effort arm and 0.3 m load arm give IMA 5 and 1 280 N for 6.4 kN; class 2 and 3 arm order is enforced
  - Source: Moment equilibrium about the fulcrum, F a_e = W a_l (Meriam and Kraige, Statics, ch. 3)
- Pulley block: 4 parts at 85 % lift 6.4 kN with 1 882 N (AMA 3.4); wheel and axle 400/50 mm at 85 % needs 941 N
  - Source: IMA = n and IMA = R/r, AMA = η × IMA (hand calculation)
- Incline 20°, μ 0.08, 6.4 kN: F = W (sin θ + μ cos θ) = 2 670.1 N, IMA 2.924; frictionless F = W sin θ
  - Source: Hibbeler, Statics, §8.2 (block on an incline pushed up the slope; hand calculation)
- A steep, smooth screw is not self-locking and warns; zero load, a fractional rope count and a locked screw are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract; self-locking condition π μ d_m sec α > l (Shigley eq. 8-3)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 26.18 N·m, 9.77 N·m, 87.3 N, 235.6, 73.3, 31.1 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

- Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §8-2 The mechanics of power screws, eqs. 8-1 to 8-6 and Example 8-1
- Meriam and Kraige, Engineering Mechanics: Statics, 8th ed., ch. 6 Friction (wedges, screws, flexible belts) and ch. 4 (levers and pulleys)
