## Mercator (rhumb-line) sailing

<a id="mercator-sailing"></a>

Folder `mercator-sailing/` · Maritime · Rhumb-line course and distance from meridional parts (sphere or WGS84), departure, great-circle comparison and passage time.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Mercator sailing solves the rhumb line (loxodrome, constant true course) between two positions with meridional parts: tan C = DLo/DMP, where DLo is the difference of longitude in minutes (the shorter way round, ≤ 180°) and DMP the difference of meridional parts; MP(φ) = (10800/π)[ln tan(45° + φ/2) − e² sin φ − e⁴ sin³φ/3 − e⁶ sin⁵φ/5] in minutes, with e = 0 on the sphere (7915.7045 log₁₀ tan(45° + φ/2)) and e² = 0.00669438 for WGS84 (the familiar 23.0133633 sin φ correction term).
- Distance by the standard navigational convention that one minute of latitude is one nautical mile: departure = DLo × DLat/DMP (or DLo cos φ on a parallel) and D = √(DLat² + departure²), which equals DLat/cos C away from east–west courses; the true meridian minute on the ellipsoid varies between 1 843 and 1 862 m, so the ellipsoidal course is exact while the distance keeps the 1′ = 1 nmi basis (±0.5 %), as in Bowditch.
- The great-circle comparison uses the haversine formula on the same 1′ = 1 nmi basis (R = 10800/π = 3 437.75 nmi) so that both distances share one convention and the saving is meaningful; the atlas_physics navigation module uses a mean radius of 3 440.065 nmi, 1.000674 × these values.
- The rhumb line cannot pass over a pole; positions within 0.1° of a pole are rejected because the meridional parts diverge; for courses within 0.5° of east–west the parallel-sailing form is used to avoid dividing by a vanishing DMP.
- Positions are geodetic latitude and longitude (east and north positive); no corrections for compass error, current or leeway (see the course-to-steer calculator).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: Piraeus (37.9375 N, 23.6375 E) to Port Said (31.25 N, 32.30 E) gives course 133.19° on the sphere, identical to the production rhumb_course_deg, and 586.2 nmi, which × 1.000674 equals the production 586.62 nmi (different Earth radius convention); a 10° parallel leg (10 N, 10 E → 10 N, 20 E) gives 590.9 nmi = 600′ cos 10°, and a meridian leg of 10° gives exactly 600 nmi; WGS84 changes the Piraeus course by 0.13° (the ellipsoid shrinks the meridional parts by about 0.5 %).
- Design decision: 1′ = 1 nmi is kept for the distance even on the ellipsoid because that is what the Mercator sailing method and sight-reduction tables assume; the note explains the 0.07 % difference to the production spherical radius so the two can be reconciled.
- Article check 2026-10-31 (schema.example): the worked example printed MP₁ 2 453.5′ (a typo for 2 463.5′) and MP₂ 1 963.1′ (the spherical value is 1 975.5′, recomputed independently), hence DMP −490.4′ instead of −488.0′, S 46.7° E instead of S 46.8° E and a great circle of 586.1 instead of 586.0 nmi; the course of 133.2° and the rhumb-line distance were right. Corrected in content.md; the calculator was right.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Latitude above 80°: meridional parts grow fast and the rhumb line becomes a long spiral; use great-circle or composite sailing.
- The great circle is … nmi shorter: consider great-circle or composite sailing for this leg.
- Longitude difference above 90°: a single rhumb line is far from the shortest route; the great-circle comparison matters.
- Distance on the 1′ = 1 nmi convention (±0.5 % against the true ellipsoidal meridian); the course is exact for the figure chosen.
- Geographic positions only: no current, leeway or compass error (course-to-steer calculator).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Departure and arrival positions are identical

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Meridional parts: sphere MP(45°) = 7915.7045 log₁₀ tan 67.5° = 3 029.94′; WGS84 MP(45°) = 3 013.65′ (Bowditch Table 6 form, 23.0134 sin φ leading correction); MP(0) = 0
  - Source: Bowditch ch. 12 and Table 6; WGS84 e² 0.00669438
- Production pins (sphere): Piraeus → Port Said course 133.194° exactly as atlas_physics rhumb_course_deg; distance 586.2 nmi × 1.000674 = 586.62 nmi (production radius 3 440.065); New York → Lizard 78.374°, 2 979.33 nmi
  - Source: atlas_physics.navigation rhumb_distance_nm / rhumb_course_deg (pins computed 2026-10-31); radius ratio 3440.065 / (10800/π)
- Special sailings: a 10° parallel leg at 10° N gives course 090° and 600′ cos 10° = 590.88 nmi (production 591.28 = × 1.000674); a 10° meridian leg gives 000° and exactly 600 nmi; a west-going leg gives a course in the 270° quadrant
  - Source: Parallel and meridian sailing (Bowditch ch. 12)
- WGS84 versus sphere: the Piraeus course changes by 0.13° and the great-circle comparison (haversine) is shorter than the rhumb line; dateline crossing (170° E → −170° E) takes the 20° short way
  - Source: Ellipsoidal meridional parts; haversine great circle; longitude wrap
- Passage time and validation: 586.2 nmi at 12 kn = 48.9 h; identical positions, a latitude of 90° and an unknown figure are rejected
  - Source: Arithmetic; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces −401.25, +519.75, 2 463.5, 1 975.5, −488.0, 133.2°, 427.4 nmi, 586.2 nmi, 586.0 nmi, 48.9 h to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- The American Practical Navigator (Bowditch), NGA Pub. 9, 2019 edition, ch. 12 "The Sailings" — Mercator sailing, meridional parts (Table 6 formula with WGS84 eccentricity)
- Admiralty Manual of Navigation, BR 45, Vol. 1 — Mercator sailing and meridional parts
- NIMA TR8350.2, Department of Defense World Geodetic System 1984 — e² = 0.00669437999014
- atlas_physics.navigation (rhumb_distance_nm, rhumb_course_deg, R = 3440.065 nmi) — cross-check values

## Steel and metal weight calculator

<a id="metal-weight"></a>

Folder `metal-weight/` · Structural · Weight of steel, stainless, aluminium, copper and brass plate, bar, tube, pipe, angle, beam and channel, per metre or foot, per piece and in total.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Weights are theoretical: density × volume with sharp corners. Rolled and formed sections have root fillets or corner radii, and mill tolerances allow ± a few percent, so a weighed piece can differ by up to about 5 %.
- Densities: carbon steel 7 850 kg/m³ (EN 1993-1-1), stainless 304 7 900 and 316 8 000 kg/m³ (EN 10088-1), aluminium 2 700, copper 8 940, brass 8 500, bronze 8 800, grey cast iron 7 200, Ti-6Al-4V 4 430, lead 11 340 kg/m³; alloys vary by a percent or two.
- Pipe and tube use the outside diameter and wall; for standard pipe sizes enter the actual outside diameter (2 in NPS is 60.3 mm), not the nominal size.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 20 mm steel round bar weighs 2.466 kg/m, so 14.80 kg for 6 m; 48.3 × 3.2 mm tube 3.56 kg/m, as in EN 10219 tables (3.56 kg/m). Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- (none — all conditions are hard errors or silent)

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Thickness: the wall must be less than half the outside diameter.
- Thickness: twice the wall must be less than the width and the height.
- Thickness: it must be less than both legs.
- Flange thickness: the flanges and web do not fit inside the overall size.
- Number of pieces: enter 1 or more.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Steel round bar 20 mm × 6 m: 314.2 mm², 2.466 kg/m (1.657 lb/ft), 14.80 kg
  - Source: m = 7 850 × π × 0.02²/4 × 6 (EN 1993-1-1 density)
- Circular hollow section 48.3 × 3.2 mm: 3.56 kg/m, matching EN 10219-2
  - Source: EN 10219-2:2006 Table B.3 (48.3 × 3.2: 3.56 kg/m)
- Steel plate 2 000 × 1 000 × 10 mm weighs 157 kg (78.5 kg/m²); the same in aluminium 54 kg
  - Source: 7 850 × 2 × 1 × 0.01; 2 700 × 0.02
- Angle 50 × 50 × 5: A = t(a + b − t) = 475 mm², 3.73 kg/m (catalogue 3.77 with root fillet); hex 20 mm A/F: (√3/2) s² = 346.4 mm²; 10 pieces sum
  - Source: EN 10056-1 (L 50 × 50 × 5: 3.77 kg/m); hexagon area
- Walls too thick, oversize flanges, zero pieces and an unknown material are rejected; a custom density is used
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 314.2 mm², 2.466 kg/m, 14.80 kg to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- EN 1993-1-1:2005 §3.2.6 (steel density 7 850 kg/m³); EN 10088-1:2014 Annex (densities of stainless steels)

## Micro-hydro power calculator

<a id="micro-hydro"></a>

Folder `micro-hydro/` · Electrical · Hydro power from flow and head: penstock friction by Darcy or Hazen–Williams, net head, electrical power, yearly energy and turbine types for the head.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Power is ρ g Q H_n η, where H_n is the net head: the gross head between intake and turbine minus the friction and fitting losses in the penstock at the design flow (ESHA 2004, eq. 6.1).
- Friction by Darcy–Weisbach uses the Colebrook friction factor with the pipe roughness and the water viscosity (1.307 mm²/s at 10 °C by default); Hazen–Williams is an empirical formula for water at ordinary temperatures in pipes above about 50 mm; the third option takes the loss as a share of the gross head, for a first estimate.
- The efficiency is from water to wire: turbine, drive and generator together. ESHA gives best turbine efficiencies of 0.85 (Turgo) to 0.94 (Francis); the generator, the drive and part-flow running lower the overall figure, so the default is 0.6.
- Yearly energy assumes the design flow for the chosen share of the year; a real stream varies, so the energy should come from the flow duration curve less the residual flow left in the stream.
- Turbine types are suggested from the net head ranges of ESHA Table 6.3 only; flow, speed, cavitation and cost narrow the choice, and manufacturers' selection charts use head and flow together.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 50 L/s through 200 m of 200 mm plastic pipe (0.0015 mm) at 1.59 m/s, Re 243 500, f 0.0151, loses 1.95 m of a 40 m gross head; net head 38.05 m gives 18.66 kW hydraulic and 11.19 kW at 60 % water to wire, 78 400 kWh a year at 80 % running. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The penstock loses more than a third of the gross head: beyond this point more flow gives less power. A larger pipe pays for itself.
- Water velocity above 5 m/s in the penstock: high friction, wear and severe water hammer if a valve closes quickly.
- Laminar or transitional flow in the penstock: check the flow and diameter.
- No turbine type in ESHA Table 6.3 covers this net head (2 to 1 300 m).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Penstock: the losses at this flow use up the whole gross head; choose a larger pipe or a smaller flow.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 1 m³/s over a 10 m net head is 98.07 kW of hydraulic power; at 80 % it delivers 78.45 kW
  - Source: ESHA 2004, eq. 6.1: P = ρ Q g H η with ρ = 1 000 kg/m³, g = 9.80665 m/s²
- 50 L/s, 200 m of 200 mm plastic pipe: v 1.592 m/s, Re 243 500, f 0.0151, loss 1.95 m, net 38.05 m, 11.19 kW at 60 %
  - Source: Hand calculation: Darcy–Weisbach with the Colebrook friction factor (Haaland gives 0.0150, within 1 %)
- Hazen–Williams with C = 150 gives 1.97 m for the same pipe, within 1 % of Darcy–Weisbach; 100 L/s in 300 mm, 1 km, C 130 loses 6.42 m
  - Source: Hazen–Williams SI form h_f = 10.67 L Q^1.852 / (C^1.852 D^4.8704), hand calculation
- ESHA Table 6.3: 3 m Kaplan only; 38 m Kaplan, crossflow, Francis; 100 m crossflow, Francis, Turgo, Pelton; 500 m Pelton only
  - Source: ESHA, Guide on How to Develop a Small Hydropower Plant (2004), Table 6.3 Range of heads
- Fitting losses add K v²/2g: K = 2 at 1.59 m/s adds 0.258 m; a loss above a third of the gross head warns
  - Source: Minor loss definition; maximum of Q (H_g − c Q²) at h_f = H_g/3
- Losses that use up the gross head, a zero flow and an efficiency above 95 % are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.59 m/s, 1.95 m, 38.05 m, 18.66 kW, 11.19 kW, 78 400 kWh to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ESHA (European Small Hydropower Association), Guide on How to Develop a Small Hydropower Plant, 2004: ch. 6, eq. 6.1 (P = ρ Q g H η), Table 6.3 (range of heads) and Table 6.7 (typical turbine efficiencies)
- Colebrook, C. F., Turbulent flow in pipes, with particular reference to the transition region between the smooth and rough pipe laws, J. Inst. Civil Engineers 11 (1939) 133–156
- Williams, G. S. and Hazen, A., Hydraulic Tables, 3rd ed., Wiley 1920 (Hazen–Williams formula; SI form h_f = 10.67 L Q^1.852 / (C^1.852 D^4.87))

## Minor losses calculator (pipe fittings and valves)

<a id="minor-losses"></a>

Folder `minor-losses/` · Mechanical · Head and pressure loss through elbows, tees, valves, entrances and exits by the Crane K method, with total K and the equivalent pipe length.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Resistance coefficients by the Crane TP-410 method: K = f_T × L/D with f_T the fully turbulent friction factor of clean steel pipe of the same bore. The method suits turbulent flow; in laminar flow fitting losses are higher than these K values give.
- Fittings are fully open and separated by at least a few diameters; closely coupled fittings interact and can lose more. Valve K values vary by make; use the manufacturer's K or C_v where available.
- The velocity is the mean velocity in the pipe bore; for a fitting between two sizes, use the K and velocity of the smaller bore.
- The equivalent length is the straight pipe that would lose the same head at the fully turbulent friction factor; at lower Reynolds numbers the real friction factor is higher and the equivalent length shorter.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 10 m³/h of water in a 52.5 mm bore (2 in Sch 40) at 1.28 m/s through 4 standard elbows, a gate valve, a swing check, an entrance and an exit: f_T = 0.0190, ΣK = 5.84, 0.490 m and 4.80 kPa. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- No fittings entered: the minor loss is zero.
- Velocity above 3 m/s (10 ft/s): losses, noise and erosion rise quickly; a larger pipe may pay back.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 2 in Sch 40 (52.5 mm), 10 m³/h: 4 elbows + gate + swing check + entrance + exit: f_T 0.0190, ΣK = 0.0190 × 228 + 1.5 = 5.836, h = 0.490 m, 4.80 kPa
  - Source: Crane TP-410: K = f_T L/D (elbow 30, gate 8, swing check 100), entrance 0.5, exit 1.0; h = K v²/2g
- An exit alone (K = 1) loses exactly one velocity head; a globe valve (340 f_T) loses as much as 17 standard elbows
  - Source: Crane TP-410 Appendix A
- Equivalent length L = ΣK D / f_T: one standard elbow equals 30 diameters of pipe
  - Source: Definition of L/D
- Extra K adds directly; head loss rises with the square of flow; fast flow warns
  - Source: h ∝ v²
- Negative counts, zero diameter and fractional counts are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 5.836, 0.490 m, 4.80 kPa to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Crane Co., Technical Paper No. 410 (2018), eq. 2-11 (h_L = K v²/2g) and Appendix A (representative resistance coefficients K and L/D)

## Mixed air temperature calculator (outdoor and return air)

<a id="mixed-air-temperature"></a>

Folder `mixed-air-temperature/` · HVAC · Mixed air dry bulb, humidity ratio, enthalpy, RH and wet bulb of outdoor and return air streams by psychrometric mass balance, and the outdoor-air fraction.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Mixing is adiabatic and at constant pressure: dry air, water and energy are conserved, and the mixed state lies on the straight line between the two states on a psychrometric chart (ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 1).
- Each airflow is the actual volume at its own temperature and humidity; it is turned into a mass of dry air with the moist-air specific volume. The quick volume-weighted average is shown for comparison and is usually within a few tenths of a degree.
- Moist-air properties follow ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 1 (Hyland–Wexler saturation pressure, ideal-gas mixture); pressure is the standard atmosphere at the altitude entered.
- The outdoor-air fraction from measured temperatures assumes well-mixed air at the sensor and becomes unreliable when the outdoor and return temperatures are close: with 10 °F (5.6 K) between them, a 1 °F sensor error shifts the fraction by 10 points.
- If the mixed state is beyond saturation, the excess moisture appears as fog; the dry bulb is then slightly higher than calculated.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 1 mixing example, 2 m³/s at 4 °C dry bulb and 2 °C wet bulb with 6.25 m³/s at 25 °C and 50 %: mixed 19.6 °C dry bulb (ASHRAE reads 19.5 °C from the chart), 14.6 °C wet bulb as printed, W = 8.25 g/kg, h = 40.7 kJ/kg, 25.8 % outdoor air by mass. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Outdoor and return temperatures differ by less than 10 °F (5.6 K): a small sensor error gives a large error in the fraction.
- The mixture is beyond saturation: the excess moisture forms fog in the mixing box. Preheat the outdoor air or reduce the outdoor-air fraction.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- … relative humidity: the vapour pressure reaches the total pressure.
- … wet bulb: it cannot be above the dry bulb temperature.
- … wet bulb: too low for this dry bulb; the air would have negative moisture.
- Outdoor air dry bulb: it must differ from the return air temperature by at least 0.5 K to find the fraction.
- Measured mixed air dry bulb: it must lie between the outdoor and return temperatures.
- Outdoor airflow: enter at least one airflow above zero.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- ASHRAE example: 2 m³/s at 4 °C db / 2 °C wb mixed with 6.25 m³/s at 25 °C, 50 % gives 19.5 °C db and 14.6 °C wb
  - Source: ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals (2017), Ch. 1, adiabatic mixing example (v1 = 0.789, v2 = 0.858 m³/kg; ṁ1 = 2.535, ṁ2 = 7.284 kg/s)
- Mass and energy balance: W and h of the mix are the dry-air-mass weighted means of the two streams
  - Source: ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 1, eqs. 46–48 (hand calculation from the stream states)
- US case: 2 000 cfm at 95/75 °F with 8 000 cfm at 75 °F, 50 % mixes to 78.9 °F (volume average 79.0 °F), 20 % outdoor air by volume
  - Source: Psychrometric mass balance; volume-weighted check (2 000 × 95 + 8 000 × 75) / 10 000 = 79 °F
- Outdoor-air fraction from temperatures: return 75 °F, outdoor 95 °F, mixed 79 °F gives 20 % and 2 000 of 10 000 cfm
  - Source: Energy balance x = (t_RA − t_MA)/(t_RA − t_OA) (hand calculation)
- Wet bulb and IP enthalpy: W from 25 °C db / 18 °C wb gives back 18 °C wb; 75 °F, 50 % is about 28.1 Btu/lb on the IP chart
  - Source: ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 1 eq. 33 and IP eq. h = 0.240 t + W (1061 + 0.444 t); ASHRAE IP psychrometric chart No. 1
- Cold saturated air mixed with warm humid air fogs (warning); wet bulb above dry bulb and no airflow are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract; ASHRAE Fundamentals Ch. 1 (mixing line crossing the saturation curve)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 19.6 °C, 14.6 °C, 8.25 g/kg, 40.7 kJ/kg, 25.8 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals (2017), Chapter 1 Psychrometrics: eqs. 30, 33, 35 and adiabatic mixing of two moist airstreams (eqs. 46–48) with its worked example
- Y. A. Çengel & M. A. Boles, Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Ch. 14 Gas–vapor mixtures and air-conditioning (adiabatic mixing of airstreams)

## Mohr's circle calculator (principal stress, von Mises)

<a id="mohr-circle"></a>

Folder `mohr-circle/` · Mechanical · Plane-stress Mohr's circle: principal stresses and angle, maximum shear, stresses on a rotated plane, von Mises and Tresca stress and safety factor.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Plane stress: the third principal stress, normal to the plane, is zero. The absolute maximum shear and the Tresca stress include it, so for two principal stresses of the same sign they exceed the in-plane values.
- Sign convention: tension positive; τxy positive when it acts in +y on the face whose normal is +x; angles positive counter-clockwise from the x axis. On the circle drawn with shear positive downward, rotations have the same sense as on the element.
- Yield criteria are those of ductile isotropic metals with equal yield strength in tension and compression: distortion energy (von Mises) and maximum shear stress (Tresca), Shigley §5-4 and §5-5. Brittle materials need Coulomb–Mohr or modified Mohr criteria instead.
- The factors of safety are static: yield strength over equivalent stress. Fluctuating stresses need a fatigue check.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: Shigley Example 3-4 (σx = 80 MPa, σy = 0, τxy = 50 MPa clockwise, i.e. −50 here) gives σ1 = 104.0 MPa, σ2 = −24.0 MPa, τmax = 64.0 MPa and the principal direction 25.7° clockwise from x; with Sy = 250 MPa the von Mises stress is 117.9 MPa and n = 2.12. Shigley Example 5-1 (Sy = 100 kpsi) factors of safety are reproduced in the tests.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The von Mises stress exceeds the yield strength: the material yields at this point.
- Both in-plane principal stresses have the same sign: the absolute maximum shear acts out of the plane and is larger than the circle radius.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Shigley Example 3-4: σx 80, τxy 50 MPa cw: σ1 = 104 MPa, σ2 = −24 MPa, τ1 = 64 MPa, σ1 at 25.7° cw from x
  - Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., Example 3-4
- Shigley Example 5-1 (Sy 100 kpsi): (b) σx 60, σy 40, τ −15: n = 1.47 (MSS), 1.70 (DE); (c) σy 40, τ 45: n = 1.02, 1.14; (d) σx −40, σy −60, τ 15: 1.47, 1.70
  - Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., Example 5-1
- Rotated element: σx −80, σy 50, τxy −25 MPa turned 30° clockwise gives σx' = −25.8, σy' = −4.15, τx'y' = −68.8 MPa
  - Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, §9.2, eqs. 9-1 to 9-3 (hand calculation)
- Invariants: rotating to θp gives σx' = σ1 and τx'y' = 0; σx' + σy' is the same at any angle
  - Source: Properties of the transformation equations (Mohr circle centre and radius)
- Pure shear τ: σ1 = τ, σ2 = −τ, von Mises √3 τ, Tresca 2τ; uniaxial σ: von Mises = Tresca = σ
  - Source: Limiting cases of Shigley eqs. 5-3 and 5-15
- Yield warning when σ' > Sy; no yield strength gives no safety factor; non-numeric stress is rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 104.0 MPa, −24.0 MPa, 64.0 MPa, 117.9 MPa, 128.1 MPa, 2.12, 1.95 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §3-6 and §3-7 (plane stress, Mohr's circle, eqs. 3-8 to 3-13, Example 3-4)
- Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §5-4 and §5-5 (maximum-shear-stress and distortion-energy theories, eqs. 5-3 and 5-15, Example 5-1)
- Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, 10th ed., §9.2 to §9.4 (stress transformation equations, principal stresses, Mohr's circle)

## Molarity calculator (moles, mass, volume, normality)

<a id="molarity"></a>

Folder `molarity/` · Process · Molarity, mass of solute or volume of solution from the other two, with molar masses of common reagents, moles, normality, molality and % w/w.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Molarity is moles of solute per litre of final solution (not per litre of solvent): dissolve the solute and then make up to the volume.
- Molar masses are computed from the IUPAC 2021 abridged standard atomic weights; hydrates include their water, so weigh the form named on the bottle.
- Normality uses the acid–base equivalents per mole in the table (H₂SO₄ 2, H₃PO₄ 3, Na₂CO₃ 2 to carbonic acid); redox and precipitation normalities differ and must be entered for the reaction.
- Molality and % w/w need the density of the solution, which depends on the concentration and temperature; leave it at zero to skip them.
- Purity is taken as 100 %; divide the mass by the assay fraction for a technical-grade reagent.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 250 mL of 0.5 M sodium chloride (58.44 g/mol) needs 0.125 mol, 7.305 g. Checked by hand.
- Harris, Quantitative Chemical Analysis: reagent hydrochloric acid of 37.0 wt% and density 1.18 g/mL is 12.0 M; reproduced in the tests.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above 20 mol/L only a few liquids exist in pure form (water is 55.5 mol/L); check the amounts and units.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Solution density: the solute alone outweighs the solution at this density; check the density and the amounts.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 250 mL of 0.5 M NaCl: 0.125 mol, 7.305 g (29.22 g/L)
  - Source: Hand calculation: m = c V M with M(NaCl) = 58.44 g/mol
- Reagent HCl, 37.0 wt% with density 1.18 g/mL, is 12.0 M (molality 16.1 mol/kg)
  - Source: Harris, Quantitative Chemical Analysis, ch. 1: molarity of 37.0 wt% HCl from its density
- Molar masses agree with published values within 0.01 %: NaCl 58.44, NaOH 40.00, H₂SO₄ 98.08, glucose 180.16, KMnO₄ 158.03, CuSO₄·5H₂O 249.69
  - Source: IUPAC 2021 atomic weights; CRC Handbook formula weights
- Normality: 0.5 M H₂SO₄ is 1.0 N, 0.1 M H₃PO₄ is 0.3 N; a salt has no table normality unless equivalents are entered
  - Source: Acid–base equivalents per mole (Harris ch. 1; IUPAC equivalent entity)
- Round trip: 10 g of glucose in 500 mL is 0.1110 M, and 10 g at that molarity fills 500 mL
  - Source: c = m / (M V) and V = m / (M c) by hand
- A density too low for the solute, zero volume and an unknown reagent are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.125, 7.305 g to the digits printed

## Moment of inertia calculator (section properties)

<a id="moment-of-inertia"></a>

Folder `moment-of-inertia/` · Structural · Area moment of inertia, section modulus, plastic modulus, centroid and radius of gyration of rectangles, tubes, I-beams, T and channel sections.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Sections are made of straight-sided rectangles with sharp corners; rolled steel sections also have root fillets and tapered flanges, so catalogue values of I are typically 2 to 6 % higher than this idealised shape.
- Ix is about the horizontal axis through the centroid, Iy about the vertical one; for the T, channel and triangle the centroid is not at mid-height or mid-width and is reported.
- Elastic section modulus S = I / c uses the extreme fibre farthest from the centroid; the plastic modulus Z uses the axis that splits the area in half.
- The polar moment for round sections is the torsion constant J; for other shapes Ix + Iy is given, which is not the torsion constant of an open section.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 100 × 200 mm rectangle gives A = 20 000 mm², Ix = 6 667 cm⁴, Sx = 667 cm³, Zx = 1 000 cm³ and rx = 57.7 mm (closed forms); the composite routine reproduces the I-beam and tube closed forms.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Very thin walls: local buckling will govern long before the section reaches its plastic moment.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Wall thickness: it must be less than half the outside diameter.
- Wall thickness: twice the wall must be less than the width and the height.
- Web thickness: it must be less than the width.
- Flange thickness: the flanges are thicker than the section is deep.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Rectangle 100 × 200 mm: A 20 000 mm², Ix = bh³/12 = 6 667 cm⁴, Iy 1 667 cm⁴, Sx = bh²/6 = 666.7 cm³, Zx = bh²/4 = 1 000 cm³, rx = h/√12 = 57.7 mm
  - Source: Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain, Table A.1 case 1
- I-beam 200 × 100 × 5.6 × 8.5 mm (IPE 200 without fillets): Ix = [bh³ − (b − tw)(h − 2tf)³]/12 = 1 845.6 cm⁴, about 5 % below the catalogue 1 943 cm⁴ that includes root fillets
  - Source: Closed form for a doubly symmetric I; EN 10365 IPE 200 catalogue Iy = 1 943 cm⁴
- T-section 100 × 100 × 10 × 10 mm: centroid 71.32 mm up, Ix 180.0 cm⁴, plastic axis 90.5 mm up, Zx 45.47 cm³
  - Source: Parallel-axis theorem by hand: (95 × 1 000 + 45 × 900)/1 900; Z = 900 × 45.5 + 50 × 0.25 + 950 × 4.75
- 4 in Schedule 40 pipe (114.3 × 6.02 mm): I = 7.23 in⁴ = 300.9 cm⁴, J = 2I; solid 100 mm bar Z = d³/6 = 166.7 cm³
  - Source: ASME B36.10M pipe dimensions; published Schedule 40 property tables (4 in: I = 7.23 in⁴)
- The rectangle routine agrees with box and triangle closed forms; impossible walls and flanges are rejected
  - Source: Box: (bh³ − b_i h_i³)/12; triangle: bh³/36 with centroid at h/3
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 20 000 mm², 6 667 cm⁴, 666.7 cm³, 1 000 cm³, 57.7 mm to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Young, W.C. and Budynas, R.G., Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain, 8th ed., Table A.1 (properties of sections)
- Gere, J.M. and Goodno, B.J., Mechanics of Materials, Appendix E (moments of inertia of plane areas; parallel-axis theorem)
- EN 1993-1-1:2005 §6.2.5 and AISC 360-22 Chapter F (use of elastic and plastic section moduli)

## Mooring line and winch brake (MEG4)

<a id="mooring-line-meg4"></a>

Folder `mooring-line-meg4/` · Maritime · OCIMF MEG4 values from the ship design MBL: line LDBF range, WLL, tail strength, fitting SWL, brake holding and rendering, and the drum-layer derating.

### Assumptions and caveats

- OCIMF Mooring Equipment Guidelines 4th edition (MEG4, 2018) terminology: the Ship Design Minimum Breaking Load (SDMBL) is the strength the mooring system is designed around (from the environmental criteria, typically 60 kn wind and 3 kn current); mooring lines are specified with a Line Design Break Force (LDBF) of 100–105 % of the SDMBL (synthetic lines tested wet and spliced), with the Working Load Limit (WLL) 50 % of the SDMBL as the maximum load in normal operation; the ranges are MEG4 recommendations, and the ship's Mooring System Management Plan (MSMP) governs.
- Tails: the Tail Design Break Force should be 125–130 % of the SDMBL (the higher figure for tails on steel wire lines) so that the tail, which fatigues fastest, never governs the system; the line-to-tail connection and the replacement criteria are in the Line Management Plan.
- Winch brakes: the brake design holding capacity is 80 % of the SDMBL and the brake is set in service to render (slip) at 60 % of the SDMBL, so that the line slips before it breaks; the rendering load is verified by the annual brake test with a jack on the first layer. Mooring fittings (bollards, fairleads, chocks) are rated by their Safe Working Load not less than 1.25 × the SDMBL (MSC.1/Circ.1175 / IACS UR A2, as referenced by MEG4) and marked accordingly.
- Drum layers: the brake acts on the drum, so the torque at rendering is constant and the line load at rendering falls with the effective radius: load on layer k = set point × r₁/r_k with r_k = D_drum/2 + (k − 0.5) d_rope; with more than one layer under tension the outer layers can also crush the inner ones — MEG4 recommends mooring on the first layer or de-rating the brake setting for the layer in use.
- Loads are compared statically; dynamic loads from passing ships, surge and long-period waves, line elasticity and the sharing between lines are in the mooring analysis (OPTIMOOR or equivalent), not here.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: SDMBL 1 000 kN → LDBF 1 000–1 050 kN, WLL 500 kN, tail ≥ 1 250 kN, brake design 800 kN, rendering 600 kN, fitting SWL ≥ 1 250 kN; a 600 mm drum with 44 mm rope on the third layer renders at 600 × 322/410 = 471 kN (47 % SDMBL), which is why MEG4 asks for first-layer mooring or a layer-adjusted setting.
- Design decision: the percentages are editable constants (MEG4 object) with the MEG4 defaults; the tail factor is a select so the steel-wire case is explicit.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Line break force below the SDMBL: the line is weaker than the system design — it will govern and may part before the brake renders.
- Line break force above 105 % of the SDMBL: a line stronger than the design overloads fittings and winch before it parts — MEG4 limits the LDBF to 105 %.
- Tail weaker than the MEG4 minimum: the tail will fail first; fit tails of 125–130 % of the SDMBL.
- Expected line load exceeds the WLL (50 % SDMBL): add lines, re-arrange the pattern or restrict the operating conditions.
- Mooring on layer …: the brake renders at … kN (… % SDMBL) instead of 60 % — moor on the first layer or adjust the brake setting for the layer in use (MEG4).
- Last brake test … the 60 % set point by … %: … — re-adjust and re-test.
- MEG4 recommendations; the ship\'s Mooring System Management Plan and Line Management Plan govern, and terminal requirements (e.g. OCIMF SIRE questions) may be stricter.
- Static comparison only: dynamic loads, line sharing, elasticity and fatigue are in the mooring analysis.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- MEG4 values for SDMBL 1 000 kN: LDBF 1 000–1 050 kN, WLL 500 kN, tail ≥ 1 250 kN (synthetic) / 1 300 kN (wire), fitting SWL ≥ 1 250 kN, brake design 800 kN, rendering 600 kN
  - Source: OCIMF MEG4 (2018) sections 5 and 6; MSC.1/Circ.1175 (fittings 1.25 × MBL)
- Drum layers: 600 mm drum, 44 mm rope → r₁ 322 mm, r₃ 410 mm, factor 0.785 → rendering 471 kN (47.1 % SDMBL) on the third layer; first layer factor 1
  - Source: Constant brake torque: load ∝ 1/effective radius (MEG4 section 6)
- Line checks: 1 030 kN is within range (103 %); 950 kN too weak; 1 100 kN too strong (overloads fittings); expected load 350 kN = 70 % of WLL; 600 kN exceeds the WLL with a warning
  - Source: MEG4 LDBF 100–105 % and WLL 50 % of SDMBL
- Tail and brake test: a 1 200 kN tail is too weak for a 1 000 kN SDMBL; a brake test at 700 kN (+16.7 %) or 500 kN (−16.7 %) calls for re-adjustment, 630 kN (+5 %) is OK
  - Source: MEG4 tails 125–130 %; brake test tolerance (±10 % practice)
- Scaling and validation: all values scale linearly with the SDMBL (2 000 kN doubles them); zero SDMBL, a fractional layer and an unknown tail type are rejected
  - Source: Linearity of the MEG4 percentages; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1 050 kN, 500 kN, 70 %, 1 250 kN, 1 250 kN, 800 kN, 471 kN, 47 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- OCIMF, Mooring Equipment Guidelines, 4th edition (MEG4), 2018 — sections 4 (mooring system design), 5 (mooring lines: SDMBL, LDBF, WLL, tails) and 6 (winches: brake holding capacity, rendering)
- IMO MSC.1/Circ.1175 Guidance on shipboard towing and mooring equipment; IACS Unified Requirement A2 — fitting SWL ≥ 1.25 × line MBL
- Wärtsilä Encyclopedia of Marine Technology — "Mooring winch brake design capacity / brake holding capacity" (80 % / 60 %)
- Steamship Mutual Risk Alert 50 — mooring winch brake holding capacity and rendering tests

## Motor starting current and voltage dip

<a id="motor-starting"></a>

Folder `motor-starting/` · Electrical · Starting current and kVA by method (DOL, star-delta, autotransformer, soft starter, VFD), voltage dip on a generator or network, torque at reduced voltage.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Rated current I_n = P/(√3 V η cos φ) from the rated shaft power, voltage, efficiency and power factor; the locked-rotor (direct-on-line) starting current is the multiple of I_n from the motor data sheet (5–8 for standard IEC motors, IEC 60034-12 design N), and the starting methods reduce it: star-delta to 1/3, an autotransformer with tap a to a², a soft starter to its current limit, a variable-speed drive to about its overload current (1.0–1.5 I_n).
- Voltage dip by the voltage-divider estimate: the starting motor is a constant impedance equal to the locked-rotor kVA, the source an EMF behind a reactance — for a generator dip = X s/(1 + X s) with s = S_start/S_gen and X its transient reactance X'd (conservative; the subtransient X''d gives the initial dip, the AVR then recovers), for a network dip = S_start/(S_sc + S_start); magnitudes are added, ignoring the locked-rotor power factor (0.2–0.4) and the pre-existing load, which makes the estimate conservative by a few per cent; time-domain AVR and governor response is not modelled.
- Starting torque scales with the square of the motor terminal voltage: T_start/T_n = (locked-rotor torque multiple) × (method torque factor: DOL 1, star-delta 1/3, autotransformer a², soft starter (I_limit/I_LR)²) × (1 − dip)²; for a drive the available starting torque is about its current multiple (field-oriented control). The motor accelerates only if this exceeds the load's breakaway and acceleration torque with margin (here 10 % above the load torque entered: 10–30 % for centrifugal pumps and fans, 100 % or more for loaded compressors and conveyors).
- Dip limits are user inputs; references: ISO 8528-5 maximum transient voltage dip on load increase −25 / −20 / −15 % for performance classes G1 / G2 / G3 (for the standard load steps), and IACS UR E5 for ship a.c. systems: ±20 % transient with recovery within 1.5 s; contactors drop out and electronics trip below about 70–80 % voltage.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 200 kW, 440 V, η 0.94, cos φ 0.85 → I_n 328.5 A; DOL at 7 × I_n = 2 299 A, 1 752 kVA on a 1 500 kVA generator with X'd 0.25 → s 1.168, dip 22.6 % (exceeds 15 %); star-delta 584 kVA → dip 8.9 % with 0.55 × rated torque available, enough for a centrifugal pump (0.3); the divider formula is the one in Cummins' motor starting white paper (dip = S_start/(S_gen/X + S_start)).
- Design decision: the transient reactance X'd is the default because it gives the larger (conservative) dip; the subtransient value can be entered for the initial dip.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Voltage dip … % exceeds the … % limit: use a reduced-voltage start (star-delta, autotransformer, soft starter, drive) or add generating capacity.
- Starting torque … × rated is below the load torque plus 10 % margin (…): the motor may stall or take too long to accelerate.
- Starting kVA exceeds the generator rating: the generator may also be limited by its excitation and the engine by the step load — check with the generator maker\'s motor-starting curve.
- Voltage below 80 % during start: contactors may drop out and other drives trip.
- Star-delta changeover causes a transient current peak; the motor must reach about 80 % speed in star, which needs a light load at start.
- Divider estimate with magnitudes (conservative); AVR and governor response, pre-existing load and the locked-rotor power factor are not modelled — confirm with the generator maker\'s motor-starting data.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Rated current: 200 kW at 440 V, η 0.94, cos φ 0.85 → input 250.3 kVA, I_n = 250 313/(√3 × 440) = 328.4 A; DOL 7 × I_n = 2 299 A, 1 752 kVA
  - Source: I_n = P/(√3 V η cos φ); S = √3 V I
- Generator dip (divider, Cummins form): s = 1 752/1 500 = 1.168, X'd 0.25 → dip = 0.292/1.292 = 22.6 % → EXCEEDED against 15 %; DOL torque 2 × (1 − 0.226)² = 1.20
  - Source: Cummins motor-starting white paper: dip = S_start/(S_gen/X + S_start)
- Star-delta: 1/3 of DOL → 584.1 kVA, dip 8.87 % → OK; torque 2/3 × (1 − 0.0887)² = 0.554 ≥ 0.33 (30 % + 10 %) → OK; DOL dip still reported for comparison (22.6 %)
  - Source: Star-delta current and torque factor 1/3
- Autotransformer 65 % tap: current and torque × 0.4225; soft starter at 3.5 × I_n: torque factor (3.5/7)² = 0.25; drive at 1.2 × I_n gives 1.2 × rated torque and a dip of about 4.7 %
  - Source: Reduced-voltage starting relations (IEC 60034-12 background; manufacturer practice)
- Network supply: S_sc 20 MVA, DOL 1.752 MVA → dip = 1.752/(20 + 1.752) = 8.05 %; a weak 5 MVA supply gives 25.9 % with warnings
  - Source: dip = S_start/(S_sc + S_start)
- Torque shortfall and validation: a loaded conveyor (110 % load torque) cannot start on star-delta → INSUFFICIENT with warning; zero voltage and an unknown method are rejected
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 328 A, 2 299 A, 1 752 kVA, 1.168, 22.6 %, 22.6 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources
