## Newton's law of cooling calculator

<a id="newtons-cooling"></a>

Folder `newtons-cooling/` · Thermal and fluids · Temperature after a time or time to cool or heat by Newton's law of cooling, with the time constant from h, A, m, c (Biot check) or from two readings.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The body has one uniform temperature at any instant (lumped capacitance). This holds when the Biot number h L_c / k, with L_c = V/A, is below 0.1 (Incropera Section 5.2); above that the surface cools faster than the core and the result is only indicative.
- The surrounding temperature T∞, the heat transfer coefficient h and the properties are constant. Radiation can be included in h as a linearised coefficient; for large temperature differences it varies and the curve is no longer a pure exponential.
- The same equation covers heating: a body colder than its surroundings approaches T∞ from below with the same time constant.
- From two readings, the first is taken as the start (t = 0) and the time constant follows from the ratio of the temperature differences; both readings must lie on the same side of T∞.
- A cylinder includes both ends in its surface area; for a long rod or wire whose ends are insulated, use the custom shape.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: Incropera Example 5.1, thermocouple bead D = 0.706 mm, h = 400 W/(m²·K), k = 20 W/(m·K), c = 400 J/(kg·K), ρ = 8 500 kg/m³: τ = 1.00 s, Bi = 2.35 × 10⁻³, 25 → 199 °C in a 200 °C gas stream in 5.2 s. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Biot number 0.1 or more: the temperature inside the body is not uniform, so the lumped result is only an estimate (Incropera Section 5.2).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Initial temperature: it equals the surrounding temperature, so nothing changes.
- Temperature at the second reading: it must lie between the first reading and the surrounding temperature.
- Target temperature: it must lie between the initial and the surrounding temperature; the body only approaches T∞ and never passes it.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Incropera Example 5.1: thermocouple bead 0.706 mm has τ = 1 s, Bi = 2.35 × 10⁻³, and reaches 199 °C from 25 °C in 5.2 s
  - Source: Incropera et al., Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, 7th ed., Example 5.1 (D, τ and t); Bi = h (D/6)/k by hand
- After one time constant 36.8 % of the initial difference remains; the difference halves in τ ln 2
  - Source: Newton's law of cooling T = T∞ + (T0 − T∞) e^(−t/τ) (Incropera eq. 5.6)
- Two readings: coffee 90 °C falls to 70 °C in 10 min in a 20 °C room, so τ = 10 / ln(70/50) = 29.7 min and it is 45.5 °C after 30 min
  - Source: τ = t1 / ln[(T0 − T∞)/(T1 − T∞)] (hand calculation)
- Geometry and Biot: a 100 mm steel ball (k 50) quenched in water at h = 1 000 has Bi = 0.33 and warns; cylinder V and A by hand
  - Source: Bi = h (V/A)/k with V/A = D/6 for a sphere; Incropera Section 5.2 criterion Bi < 0.1
- Heating works the same way: a 4 °C drink in a 24 °C room with τ = 1 h reaches 14 °C in 41.6 min; heat gained is m c ΔT
  - Source: Newton's law of cooling applied to warming (hand calculation)
- Invalid input: a target beyond T∞, a second reading on the wrong side and a zero diameter are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.00 s, 5.2 s, 0.00235 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- F. P. Incropera, D. P. DeWitt, T. L. Bergman & A. S. Lavine, Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, 7th ed., Sections 5.1–5.2 (lumped capacitance, eqs. 5.6 and 5.10, Biot number criterion) and Example 5.1
- Y. A. Çengel & A. J. Ghajar, Heat and Mass Transfer: Fundamentals and Applications, 5th ed., Section 4.1 (lumped system analysis, Bi ≤ 0.1)

## NOx tier limit by engine speed

<a id="nox-tier-limit"></a>

Folder `nox-tier-limit/` · Maritime · MARPOL Annex VI Reg. 13 Tier I/II/III NOx limits from rated speed, the applicable tier, the margin of the certified value and annual NOx mass.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Limits per MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 13 as a function of the rated engine speed n (rpm): Tier I 17.0 g/kWh below 130 rpm, 45 n^−0.2 from 130 to below 2 000 rpm, 9.8 at 2 000 rpm and above; Tier II 14.4 / 44 n^−0.23 / 7.7; Tier III 3.4 / 9 n^−0.2 / 2.0; the value is the weighted average over the NOx Technical Code test cycle (E2/E3/D2/C1), not an instantaneous limit.
- Applicability: Regulation 13 covers marine diesel engines above 130 kW installed on ships; Tier I applies to ships constructed (keel laid) from 1 January 2000, Tier II from 1 January 2011 worldwide, Tier III only when operating inside a NOx Emission Control Area for ships constructed on or after 1 January 2016 (North American and US Caribbean Sea ECAs) or 1 January 2021 (Baltic and North Sea ECAs); outside an ECA a Tier III ship meets Tier II; emines for emergency use, lifeboats and engines solely on ships in national waters with alternative measures are exempt (Reg. 13.1.2).
- Engines of pre-2000 ships (built 1990–1999, over 5 000 kW and over 90 L/cylinder) must meet Tier I where an approved method exists (Reg. 13.7); "major conversions" bring an engine to the tier of the conversion date; a certified value is the parent-engine value on the EIAPP certificate and applies at the test-cycle weighting.
- Annual NOx mass = power × load factor × hours × (g/kWh)/10⁶ in tonnes, a planning figure at the certified (or limit) value; actual emissions vary with load, ambient conditions and fuel, and the EIAPP value is a certification figure, not a measurement of in-service emissions.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 500 rpm → Tier I 12.98, Tier II 10.54, Tier III 2.60 g/kWh; the piecewise curves are continuous within 1 % at both breakpoints (130 rpm: 45 × 130^−0.2 = 17.0; 2 000 rpm: 45 × 2000^−0.2 = 9.84 vs 9.8; 44 × 2000^−0.23 = 7.66 vs 7.7; 9 × 2000^−0.2 = 1.97 vs 2.0), confirming the coefficients.
- Design decision: the applicable tier is derived from the construction date and the ECA switch, with the three limits always shown so a Tier III ship's Tier II value outside the ECA is visible.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Regulation 13 applies to engines above 130 kW: this engine is below the threshold.
- Tier III applies only while operating inside the NECA; outside it the same engine must meet Tier II (both limits are shown). Tier III needs SCR, EGR or LNG/dual-fuel operation.
- Certified value exceeds the applicable limit: the engine cannot be certified for this tier without a NOx-reducing method.
- Within the speed-dependent band: the limit falls with rpm because slow engines have longer residence times and higher NOx formation.
- Limits and certified values are NOx Technical Code test-cycle weighted averages (E2/E3/D2/C1), not instantaneous or in-service values; annual tonnes are a planning estimate.
- Exemptions (emergency engines, lifeboats, national-waters alternatives) and the major-conversion rules are not evaluated here.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Curves at 500 rpm: Tier I 45 × 500^−0.2 = 12.98, Tier II 44 × 500^−0.23 = 10.54, Tier III 9 × 500^−0.2 = 2.60 g/kWh; Tier III is 75.4 % below Tier II
  - Source: MARPOL Annex VI Regulation 13.3, 13.4, 13.5
- Plateaus and continuity: below 130 rpm 17.0/14.4/3.4; at and above 2 000 rpm 9.8/7.7/2.0; the curves meet the plateaus within 1 % at 130 and 2 000 rpm (Tier II: 7.66 vs 7.7)
  - Source: Regulation 13 breakpoints (n < 130, 130 ≤ n < 2000, n ≥ 2000)
- Applicability: built 2018 in the Baltic/North Sea NECA → Tier II (NECA date 2021); built 2022 there → Tier III; built 2018 in the North American NECA → Tier III (2016); built 2005 → Tier I; built 1995 → no tier (Reg. 13.7 note)
  - Source: Regulation 13.5.1 NECA dates (MEPC.286(71)); Reg. 13.3–13.4 construction dates; Reg. 13.7
- Compliance and margin: 2.2 g/kWh against Tier III 2.60 at 500 rpm → complies with 15.3 % margin; 3.0 g/kWh exceeds; annual NOx at 4 000 kW × 0.75 × 6 000 h: 46.7 t at the limit, 39.6 t certified
  - Source: Arithmetic; EIAPP certified value against the limit
- Validation and threshold: an engine of 100 kW is flagged as below the 130 kW threshold; a fractional construction year, zero rpm and an unknown area are rejected
  - Source: Regulation 13.1.1 (engines > 130 kW); validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 12.98, 10.54, 2.60, 10.54, 39.6 t, 75 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IMO MARPOL Annex VI, Regulation 13 — Nitrogen Oxides (NOx), as amended by MEPC.176(58), MEPC.251(66), MEPC.286(71) (Baltic/North Sea NECA)
- IMO NOx Technical Code 2008 (resolution MEPC.177(58) as amended) — test cycles and weighting factors
- IMO, "Nitrogen Oxides (NOx) — Regulation 13" guidance page (tier applicability dates)
- EIAPP certificate / Technical File requirements (NOx Technical Code chapter 2)

## Nozzle flow calculator (orifice, fire nozzle and K-factor)

<a id="nozzle-flow"></a>

Folder `nozzle-flow/` · Mechanical · Water flow, pressure or orifice size of a nozzle, hydrant outlet or sprinkler from Q = Cd A √(2Δp/ρ), 29.84 c d² √p or Q = K√p, with nozzle reaction.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The nozzle discharges a liquid to the atmosphere; the pressure is the gauge pressure at the nozzle inlet (or the pitot pressure in the jet), and the velocity of approach in the hose or pipe is neglected.
- The discharge coefficient Cd takes account of jet contraction and friction: about 0.97 to 1.0 for a smooth-bore fire nozzle, 0.90 for a smooth rounded hydrant outlet, 0.80 for a square sharp one and 0.70 for one projecting into the barrel (NFPA 291), and about 0.6 for a sharp-edged hole.
- A K-factor already contains the orifice area and discharge coefficient; it is converted between US units (gpm/psi^½) and metric units (L/min/bar^½) with the factor 14.42.
- The reaction force is the jet momentum ρ Q v with the ideal jet velocity √(2Δp/ρ); for a smooth bore with Cd = 1 it equals the IFSTA formula 1.57 d² p. The IFSTA fog-nozzle formula 0.0505 Q √p is shown as well and gives about 4 % less.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: NFPA 291 hydrant outlet 2.5 in, c = 0.90, pitot 23 psi: Freeman formula 805 gpm (Temecula fire flow examples print 804 gpm), orifice equation at 999 kg/m³ also 805 gpm, K-factor 167.8 gpm/psi½, ideal jet velocity 58.5 ft/s, reaction 203 lbf. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Pressure below 7 psi (0.5 bar): NFPA 13 requires at least 7 psi at any operating sprinkler.
- Orifice above 200 mm (8 in): check that the velocity of approach in the supply pipe is still small compared with the jet velocity.
- Pressure above 200 bar (2 900 psi): this is a jetting or cleaning nozzle; check the discharge coefficient with the maker.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Hydrant flow test: 2½ in outlet, c = 0.90, pitot 23 psi gives 804–805 gpm by 29.84 c d² √p and by the orifice equation
  - Source: NFPA 291 Q = 29.84 c d² √p; City of Temecula fire flow calculation examples (804 gpm)
- Smooth bore 7/8 in at 50 psi: 161 gpm (29.7 d² √NP) and 60 lb reaction (1.57 d² NP)
  - Source: IFSTA smooth-bore formulas; Fire Apparatus Magazine "Nozzle reaction" (161 gpm, 60 lb)
- Fog nozzle 150 gpm at 50 psi: IFSTA reaction 0.0505 × 150 × √50 = 53.6 lb (about 54 lb); jet momentum 4 % more
  - Source: IFSTA fog-nozzle reaction formula; Fire Apparatus Magazine "Nozzle reaction" (about 54 lb)
- Sprinkler K 5.6 at 7 psi flows 14.8 gpm; 20 gpm needs 12.8 psi; K 5.6 is K80.7 metric; K80 at 0.5 bar flows 56.6 L/min
  - Source: NFPA 13 Q = K √p; 1 gpm/psi½ = 3.785 × √14.504 = 14.42 L/min/bar½
- Round trip: the pressure for the computed flow, and the size for that flow and pressure, return the inputs
  - Source: Q = Cd A √(2Δp/ρ) solved for each unknown
- A sprinkler below 7 psi warns; zero pressure, Cd above 1 and an unknown option are rejected
  - Source: NFPA 13 minimum operating pressure; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 805 US gpm, 805 US gpm, 167.8, 58.5 ft/s, 203 lbf to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- NFPA 291, Recommended Practice for Water Flow Testing and Marking of Hydrants (2022): Q = 29.84 c d² √p and outlet coefficients 0.90 / 0.80 / 0.70
- NFPA 13, Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems (2022), hydraulic calculations: sprinkler discharge Q = K √p, minimum operating pressure 7 psi (0.5 bar)
- IFSTA, Pumping and Aerial Apparatus Driver/Operator Handbook, fire-stream hydraulics: smooth-bore flow 29.7 d² √NP, nozzle reaction 1.57 d² NP and 0.0505 Q √NP
- F. M. White, Fluid Mechanics, 7th ed., Ch. 3 (momentum of a free jet) and Ch. 6 (orifice discharge coefficient)

## OEE and takt time calculator

<a id="oee-takt"></a>

Folder `oee-takt/` · Manufacturing · OEE from availability, performance and quality using shift times and part counts, plus takt time from demand and a cycle-time check against it.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Planned production time is the shift minus planned stops (breaks, meals, planned maintenance); downtime is every unplanned stop and changeover inside it.
- Performance compares the ideal (fastest sustainable) cycle time with the run time; a value above 100 % means the ideal cycle time is set too slow.
- Quality counts only parts good the first time; reworked parts count as rejects.
- Takt time is the planned production time divided by the customer demand for the same period; a line meets demand when its planned time per good part is at or below takt.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: the oee.com example (480 min shift, 60 min of breaks, 47 min downtime, 1.0 s ideal cycle, 19 271 parts, 423 rejects) gives availability 88.81 %, performance 86.11 %, quality 97.80 % and OEE 74.79 %; for a demand of 18 000 parts takt is 1.40 s. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Performance is above 100 %: the ideal cycle time is slower than the machine really ran; use the nameplate or best demonstrated cycle time.
- The ideal cycle time is longer than takt: even at 100 % OEE one machine cannot meet the demand.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Planned stops: they must be shorter than the shift.
- Unplanned downtime: it must be shorter than the planned production time.
- Rejected parts: they cannot exceed the total parts made.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- OEE.com example: availability 0.8881, performance 0.8611, quality 0.9780, OEE 0.7479
  - Source: Vorne Industries, OEE.com, Calculate OEE (published worked example)
- Simple OEE identity: OEE = ideal cycle × good parts / planned time = 1.0 × 18 848 / 25 200 s
  - Source: OEE.com simple calculation (fully productive time ÷ planned production time)
- Takt: 420 min for 18 000 parts is 1.40 s; 1.337 s per good part meets it; at 20 000 parts (1.26 s) it falls short
  - Source: Takt time = available time / demand (hand calculation)
- Limiting cases: no downtime, ideal speed and no rejects give OEE 100 %; a too-slow ideal cycle warns (performance above 100 %)
  - Source: Definitions (limiting cases)
- Breaks longer than the shift, downtime longer than planned time and more rejects than parts are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 88.81 %, 86.11 %, 97.80 %, 74.79 %, 1.40 s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Vorne Industries, OEE.com, Calculate OEE: definitions and worked example (availability 88.81 %, performance 86.11 %, quality 97.80 %, OEE 74.79 %)
- ISO 22400-2:2014 Automation systems and integration — Key performance indicators for manufacturing operations management, Part 2: OEE index = availability × effectiveness × quality ratio
- Nakajima, S., Introduction to TPM: Total Productive Maintenance, Productivity Press, 1988 (the six big losses and OEE)

## Ohm's law and electrical power

<a id="ohms-law"></a>

Folder `ohms-law/` · Electrical · Voltage, current, resistance and power from any two of them, with Ohm's law V = I R and P = V I, for DC and resistive AC circuits.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The circuit element is a linear resistor: its resistance does not change with the voltage or current applied (no diodes, lamps warming up, or semiconductors).
- For AC, the voltage and current are RMS values and the load is purely resistive (power factor 1). Inductive or capacitive loads need the power factor; use the three-phase power calculator for those.
- Resistance is taken at its operating temperature; a conductor heated by the current has a higher resistance than its cold value (copper rises about 0.39 % per kelvin).
- All four quantities refer to the same element: the voltage across it, the current through it, its resistance and the power it dissipates.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: every pair mode reproduces the same four values for the worked example (24 V, 0.5 A, 48 Ω, 12 W), and the 1 kW, 230 V heater and 100 W, 4 Ω loudspeaker cases were checked by hand.
- Design decision: one page for all six pairs, because people search for "Ohm's law calculator" whichever two values they know; the pair selector keeps only the two inputs that matter visible.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- More than 2 kW at extra-low voltage means a very large current: check the conductor size and the protective device.
- Resistance below 0.01 Ω is close to a short circuit; contact and lead resistance will dominate a real measurement.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Unknown pair "…"

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Voltage and current: 12 V across a resistor carrying 2 A gives R = 6 Ω and P = 24 W
  - Source: Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, ch. 2: R = V / I, P = V I
- A 1 kW heater on 230 V: I = 4.348 A and R = 52.9 Ω; from voltage and resistance the power is back to 1000 W
  - Source: Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, ch. 4: P = V² / R, I = P / V
- A 100 W, 4 Ω loudspeaker: I = √(P/R) = 5 A and V = 20 V RMS
  - Source: Hughes, ch. 2: P = I² R; RMS power into a resistive load
- Power and current: 60 W at 5 A means 12 V and 2.4 Ω; current and resistance: 0.5 A through 48 Ω drops 24 V and dissipates 12 W
  - Source: Ohm (1827): V = I R; Joule heating P = I² R (Boylestad ch. 4)
- Every pair gives the same four values for the worked example (24 V, 0.5 A, 48 Ω, 12 W)
  - Source: Consistency of V = I R and P = V I across all six pairs
- Zero or negative values are rejected, and an unknown pair is refused
  - Source: Input validation contract (shared/validate.js)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.5 A, 12 W to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Ohm, G. S., Die galvanische Kette, mathematisch bearbeitet, Berlin, 1827 (V = I R)
- Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, 12th ed., ch. 2 "Simple DC circuits" (Ohm's law, power P = V I = I² R = V² / R)
- Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, 13th ed., ch. 4 "Ohm's law, power and energy"
- IEC 60050-131:2002, International Electrotechnical Vocabulary, circuit theory (resistance, power)

## Optimal speed under charter

<a id="optimal-speed-charter"></a>

Folder `optimal-speed-charter/` · Maritime · Cost-minimising speed on time charter and profit-maximising speed on a voyage charter from the fuel-speed law, prices, hire or freight and port time.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Daily fuel consumption at sea follows a power law of speed, F(v) = F₀ (v/v₀)ⁿ with n ≈ 3 (the cubic law) for displacement ships near their design speed; the exponent drifts above 3 at high speed and below 3 at very low speed (hotel and auxiliary loads make the fuel per mile rise again), so the result is valid within the speed range the law was fitted to, which the speed bounds should reflect.
- Time charter: the charterer pays hire and fuel, so the voyage cost C(v) = H (D/24v + T_p) + p_eff F(v) D/24v is minimised; the closed-form optimum is Ronen's v* = v₀ [H/((n−1) p_eff F₀)]^(1/n), independent of distance and port time.
- Voyage charter: the owner earns a fixed freight R per voyage and pays fuel and daily operating costs, so the profit per day over the whole cycle (sea + port days) is maximised; port time LOWERS the optimal speed in this model — the fixed freight is spread over more days, so each sea day saved is worth less (the opposite holds when more voyages per year bring more freight at a rate per day, which is the time-charter case); the closed form for zero port time and zero operating cost, v* = [24 R v₀ⁿ/(n p_eff F₀ D)]^(1/(n−1)), is reported for reference and the numeric optimum (golden-section search within the bounds) is the answer.
- The effective fuel price p_eff = fuel price + ETS share × C_F × allowance price prices the CO₂ of the fuel; FuelEU intensity penalties, CII rating effects, canal dues, cargo inventory cost, laycan constraints and weather are outside the model (the latter two usually dominate real voyage planning).
- Port fuel (auxiliary engines and boilers) is a constant per port day added to the voyage fuel; it does not affect the optimum.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: time charter 18 000/day, 14 kn with 35 t/day, fuel 550 → v* = 14 × (18 000/(2 × 550 × 35))^(1/3) = 10.87 kn (Ronen formula) and the numeric minimiser agrees to 0.001 kn; a voyage charter of 1.2 million over 5 000 nmi with no port time gives v* = √(8 R v₀³/(p F₀ D)) = 16.5 kn, and adding 4 port days lowers the optimum to 15.1 kn (first-order condition R = 3K/s² + 2K T_p/s³ in sea days s, solved for larger s).
- Design decision: a numeric optimiser is used for the voyage case so that port time and operating cost are included exactly; the closed forms are shown so the user can see the textbook result.
- Article check 2026-10-31 (schema.example): the worked example printed the voyage cost at 14 kn as 632 000 (it is 632 915) and the saving as 5.7 % (5.79 %); corrected to 633 000 and 5.8 % in content.md.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The optimum sits on a speed bound (… kn): the unconstrained optimum is outside the feasible range… kn)` : ''}.
- Optimum far from the reference speed: the power law was fitted near v₀ and the consumption extrapolation is uncertain — re-anchor F₀ at a speed closer to the result.
- Negative profit per day even at the best speed: the freight does not cover fuel and operating costs.
- Port days lower the optimal speed below the zero-port-time closed form: the fixed freight is spread over more days, so a sea day saved is worth less.
- Laycan and ETA constraints, weather, canal dues, cargo inventory cost, FuelEU penalties and CII consequences are outside the model and often dominate the decision.
- The fuel-speed exponent is an average: below about 60 % of design speed the fuel per mile rises again because hotel and auxiliary loads do not slow down.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Minimum speed must be below the maximum speed
- Enter a fuel price or a hire rate

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Time charter (Ronen): v* = 14 × (18 000/(2 × 550 × 35))^(1/3) = 10.866 kn; the numeric minimiser agrees within 0.002 kn; cost per voyage at v* is below the cost at 14 kn
  - Source: Ronen (1982) cost-minimising speed v* = v₀ [H/((n−1) p F₀)]^(1/n)
- Time-charter arithmetic at v*: sea days 5000/(24 × 10.866) = 19.18, fuel 35 × (10.866/14)³ = 16.36 t/day → 313.8 t + 12 t port, hire 18 000 × 23.18 = 417 200; cost per nmi = total/5 000
  - Source: Voyage cost C(v) = H (D/24v + T_p) + p F₀ (v/v₀)ⁿ D/24v
- Voyage charter with zero port time and zero opex: numeric optimum equals the closed form √(8 R v₀³/(p F₀ D)) = 16.54 kn within 0.01 kn
  - Source: Profit-per-day maximisation with T_p = 0 (Ronen 1982; Psaraftis & Kontovas 2013)
- Port time lowers the voyage-charter optimum (4 port days → 15.1 kn against 16.54 kn with none, first-order condition R = 3K/s² + 2K T_p/s³); a higher fuel price lowers it; the ETS adds 0.5 × 3.114 × 70 = 108.99 to the effective price
  - Source: Profit-per-day model derivative; price sensitivity; ETS cost per tonne of fuel
- Bounds: with v_max 16 kn and no port time the voyage-charter optimum (16.5 kn unconstrained) sits on the bound with a warning; the golden-section minimiser finds the minimum of (x − 3)² at 3 and respects the edges
  - Source: Behaviour specification; golden-section search
- Validation: minimum speed at or above the maximum, zero distance and an unknown mode are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 10.87 kn, 19.2, 16.4, 417 000, 179 000, 596 000, 633 000, 5.8 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- D. Ronen, "The effect of oil price on the optimal speed of ships", Journal of the Operational Research Society 33, 1982, 1035–1040
- H. N. Psaraftis, C. A. Kontovas, "Speed models for energy-efficient maritime transportation: A taxonomy and survey", Transportation Research Part C 26, 2013, 331–351
- M. Stopford, Maritime Economics, 3rd ed., Routledge 2009 — speed, fuel consumption and the cubic law (ch. 6)
- IMO MEPC.364(79) carbon factors; Directive (EU) 2023/959 (ETS share of maritime emissions)

## Orifice and venturi flow (ISO 5167)

<a id="orifice-flow"></a>

Folder `orifice-flow/` · Thermal and fluids · Flow from differential pressure for orifice plates and venturis with the Reader-Harris/Gallagher discharge coefficient and expansibility.

### Assumptions and caveats

- ISO 5167 applies to steady, single-phase, subsonic flow in a circular pipe running full, with the straight lengths and plate/tube geometry of the standard; the discharge coefficient is the Reader-Harris/Gallagher (1998) equation of ISO 5167-2:2003 eq. 4 for orifice plates (corner, flange or D and D/2 tappings, with the extra term for D < 71.12 mm) and the constant coefficients of ISO 5167-4 for classical Venturi tubes (0.995 machined, 0.984 as-cast, 0.985 rough-welded).
- The flow depends on the Reynolds number through C and vice versa, so the flow-from-Δp mode iterates until the Reynolds number is consistent (the standard's iterative procedure); the Δp-from-flow mode is direct.
- Expansibility for gases: ε = 1 − (0.351 + 0.256 β⁴ + 0.93 β⁸)[1 − (p₂/p₁)^(1/κ)] for orifice plates (ISO 5167-2 eq. 5, valid for p₂/p₁ ≥ 0.75) and the isentropic Venturi expression of ISO 5167-4 eq. 3; liquids have ε = 1. The density is the upstream density at p₁ and T₁.
- Permanent pressure loss for orifice plates Δϖ = [√(1 − β⁴(1 − C²)) − C β²]/[√(1 − β⁴(1 − C²)) + C β²] Δp (ISO 5167-2 §5.4.1); for classical Venturis the loss is taken as 10 % of Δp (ISO 5167-4 gives 5–20 % depending on the divergent angle).
- Validity limits checked and reported: orifice d ≥ 12.5 mm, 50 ≤ D ≤ 1 000 mm, 0.10 ≤ β ≤ 0.75, Re_D ≥ 5 000 (and ≥ 16 000 β² for β > 0.56 with corner or D–D/2 taps; flange taps also Re_D ≥ 170 β² D/mm); Venturi β, Re_D and D ranges per type; outside them the uncertainty of the standard (0.5–0.75 % on C) no longer applies and the page warns.
- Pipe roughness, plate edge sharpness, bending of the plate and upstream disturbances are assumed within the standard's limits; drain holes, wet gas and pulsating flow are excluded.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the Reader-Harris/Gallagher equation was transcribed term by term against the HydrauCalc reproduction of ISO 5167-2:2003 eq. 4; the flange-tap case D 102.26 mm, d 51.13 mm, water 998.2 kg/m³ / 1.002 mPa·s, Δp 250 mbar converges to Re_D 112 800, C 0.6059, 9.078 kg/s (32.74 m³/h), the published calculator result; the gas expansibility for β 0.5, p₂/p₁ 0.9, κ 1.4 is 0.9731 by hand.
- Design decision: three orifice tapping arrangements and three Venturi types are offered through one device select; the ISA 1932 and long-radius nozzles of ISO 5167-3 are not included.
- Design decision: mode "Δp from flow" is included because transmitter ranging needs it; it accepts mass or volume flow.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Operating point outside the standard\'s validity: the discharge coefficient equation is being extrapolated.
- Classical Venturi: constant discharge coefficient of ISO 5167-4 within its Reynolds range; permanent loss taken as 10 % of Δp (5–20 % depending on the divergent angle).
- Gas: density and volume flow refer to upstream conditions p₁, T₁; the expansibility equation holds for p₂/p₁ ≥ 0.75.
- β above 0.65: the standard\'s uncertainty on C grows (up to 0.75 %) and the permanent pressure loss is small but the plate is sensitive to upstream disturbances.
- Uncertainty of C per ISO 5167: 0.5 % (β ≤ 0.6) to 0.75 % for orifice plates, 1–1.5 % for Venturi tubes; add Δp, density and diameter uncertainties for the flow uncertainty.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Bore … mm must be smaller than the pipe diameter … mm
- Differential pressure exceeds the upstream absolute pressure

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Published case: flange taps, D 102.26 mm, d 51.13 mm (β 0.5), water 998.2 kg/m³ / 1.002 mPa·s, Δp 250 mbar → Re_D 112 800, C 0.6059, q_m 9.078 kg/s, q_v 32.74 m³/h, pipe velocity 1.107 m/s
  - Source: instrumentationblog.in ISO 5167-2 orifice calculator worked example (C 0.6059, 32 680 kg/h, 32.739 m³/h, 1.107 m/s)
- Reader-Harris/Gallagher structure: at very high Re_D the corner-tap coefficient tends to 0.5961 + 0.0261β² − 0.216β⁸ (the L1 bracket 0.043 + 0.080 − 0.123 vanishes for corner taps); flange and D–D/2 taps differ only through L1 and M′2; the small-pipe term adds for D < 71.12 mm
  - Source: ISO 5167-2:2003 eq. 4 (as reproduced by HydrauCalc, March 2019)
- Δp from flow inverts the flow mode: 9.078 kg/s (32.74 m³/h) through the same plate gives 250 mbar; mass and volume bases agree
  - Source: Inverse of q_m = C E ε (π/4) d² √(2 Δp ρ)
- Gas expansibility: β 0.5, p₂/p₁ 0.9, κ 1.4 → ε = 1 − (0.351 + 0.256·0.0625 + 0.93·0.0039)(1 − 0.9^(1/1.4)) = 0.9731; ε → 1 as Δp → 0; the isentropic Venturi ε at the same point is lower (0.9405)
  - Source: ISO 5167-2:2003 eq. 5; ISO 5167-4:2003 eq. 3
- Venturi (machined, C 0.995): same geometry and Δp gives (0.995/0.6059) × the orifice flow; permanent loss 10 % of Δp vs the orifice formula [√(1−β⁴(1−C²)) − Cβ²]/[√(1−β⁴(1−C²)) + Cβ²] = 0.737 at β 0.5
  - Source: ISO 5167-4 discharge coefficients; ISO 5167-2 §5.4.1 pressure loss
- Validity flags: β 0.8 or Re_D below 5 000 is reported as outside ISO 5167-2; a 40 mm pipe is outside the 50–1 000 mm range; Venturi below Re_D 2·10⁵ is flagged
  - Source: ISO 5167-2 §5.3.1 and ISO 5167-4 §5.5 limits of use
- Invalid inputs fail fast: bore not smaller than the pipe, Δp above the upstream gas pressure, unknown device
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.6059, 9.08 kg/s, 32.7 m³/h, 1.11 m/s, 4.43 m/s, 1.033 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 5167-1:2003 General principles and requirements; ISO 5167-2:2003 Orifice plates (eq. 4 discharge coefficient, eq. 5 expansibility, §5.4 pressure loss); ISO 5167-4:2003 Venturi tubes
- M. J. Reader-Harris & J. A. Sattary, "The orifice plate discharge coefficient equation — further work" (NEL, Flow Measurement and Instrumentation 1996/1998)
- HydrauCalc, "Square-edge orifice flowmeter ISO 5167-2:2003" application notes (corner, D–D/2 tappings), March 2019 — reproduction of the equations used for transcription checking
- R. W. Miller, Flow Measurement Engineering Handbook, 3rd ed. (McGraw-Hill 1996) — background and iteration procedure

## Crane outrigger pad bearing pressure

<a id="outrigger-pad-pressure"></a>

Folder `outrigger-pad-pressure/` · Civil · Outrigger load, float and mat bearing pressure, effective mat area by load spread, ground utilisation and required mat size for a mobile crane.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The maximum outrigger load is best taken from the crane manufacturer's outrigger-load calculator for the lift (slew position, radius, counterweight); for planning the page offers the estimate 0.65 × (crane + load + rigging) quoted from the Queensland mobile crane code of practice and the upper bound of the whole crane and load on one outrigger.
- Bearing pressure is uniform under the float and under the mat (rigid-body assumption); with a "rigid" mat the whole mat is effective, which requires a mat stiff and strong enough to spread the load — checked here only by a one-way cantilever bending stress σ = 3 q c²/t² against the mat's allowable bending stress (conservative for two-way action; shear, deflection and the mat maker's rating are separate); with "load spread" the effective dimensions grow from the float by 2 t tan θ through the mat thickness (θ 45° typical — a designer's assumption, not a property of the mat), capped at the mat size.
- Allowable ground bearing pressures are the BS 8004:1986 presumed values (lower bound of each range) for preliminary design: they assume a foundation width of at least 1 m, the water table at least one width below the base, and they guard against shear failure, not settlement; soft clays, loose sands and fills (below 75–100 kPa) must be tested — use the tested or specified value option.
- Mat self-weight is added over the full mat area; dynamic effects (slewing, wind, sudden release) are covered only by the margin the user keeps below 100 % utilisation; voids, buried services, slopes and excavations near the outrigger are site checks outside this page.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 400 kN on a 0.6 × 0.6 m float = 1 111 kPa; a rigid 2 × 2 m mat of 0.5 t gives 101.2 kPa (67 % of stiff clay's 150 kPa) with a bending stress of 6.6 MPa for 150 mm thick timber; the same mat by 45° spread is effective over only 0.9 × 0.9 m (495 kPa) — the reason mat stiffness decides the result; the Brilliant Ideas worked example (490.5 kN at 100 kPa → 4.905 m²) is reproduced.
- Design decision: the 0.65 factor is shown as an estimate with its source, never as the default load; the default is the manufacturer value field.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Ground pressure … kPa exceeds the allowable … kPa: a larger or stiffer mat (≥ … m square if fully effective) or a ground improvement is needed.
- No mat: the float bears directly on the ground — only acceptable on rock, concrete or hardstanding designed for it.
- The mat is overstressed in bending: it will not spread the load over its whole area — the rigid-mat pressure is unconservative.
- Outrigger load …: obtain the manufacturer's outrigger load for the actual lift configuration before relying on the result.
- Allowable bearing below 100 kPa: soft or loose ground — base the design on a site investigation and consider a temporary works design.
- BS 8004 presumed values guard against shear failure, not settlement, and assume no voids, services, slopes or excavations near the outrigger; a temporary works designer should check marginal cases.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The mat is smaller than the float: the float would bear directly on the ground

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Load estimates: 0.65 × (60 + 10 + 0.5) t × g = 449.4 kN; upper bound 70.5 t × g = 691.4 kN; manufacturer value used as entered (400 kN)
  - Source: Queensland Mobile Crane Code of Practice 2006 factor 0.65 (as quoted by Cranes and Lifting); g = 9.80665 m/s²
- Float pressure: 400 kN on 0.6 × 0.6 m = 1 111 kPa; on a 0.6 m diameter circular float (0.2827 m²) = 1 415 kPa
  - Source: q = F/A
- Rigid 2 × 2 m mat (0.5 t): q = (400 + 4.90) kN / 4 m² = 101.2 kPa, 67.5 % of stiff clay (150 kPa) → OK; required area 400/150 = 2.667 m² (1.633 m square)
  - Source: Rigid-mat uniform pressure; BS 8004 Table 1 stiff clay 150–300 kPa (lower bound)
- Published sizing example: 490.5 kN at 100 kPa needs 4.905 m²; BS 8004 presets: dense gravel 600, compact sand 300, stiff clay 150, firm clay 75 kPa
  - Source: Brilliant Ideas Ltd load-spread guide worked example; BS 8004:1986 Table 1
- Load spread at 45° through 0.15 m: effective 0.9 × 0.9 m → 400/0.81 + 4.90/4 = 495.0 kPa → EXCEEDED on stiff clay; a 1.0 m thick mat spreads to the full 2 m
  - Source: Load-spread model L_eff = min(L_mat, L_float + 2 t tan θ)
- Mat bending (rigid): cantilever c = 0.7 m, σ = 3 × 101.2 kPa × 0.7²/0.15² = 6.61 MPa ≤ 10 MPa OK; a 75 mm mat gives 26.5 MPa → OVERSTRESSED with a warning
  - Source: One-way cantilever bending of the mat outside the float, σ = 6M/t² with M = q c²/2
- No mat and validation: without a mat the float pressure is the ground pressure (warning); a mat smaller than the float and an unknown ground type are rejected
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 400 kN, 1 111 kPa, 101 kPa, 150 kPa, 67 %, 2.67 m², 1.63 m, 6.6 MPa to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- BS 8004:1986 Code of practice for foundations, Table 1 presumed allowable bearing values (as reproduced in published tables; superseded by BS EN 1997 for design)
- Construction Plant-hire Association (CPA), Ground Conditions for Construction Plant — Good Practice Guide (2014); BS 7121-3 Code of practice for safe use of cranes — Mobile cranes
- Queensland Mobile Crane Code of Practice 2006 — maximum outrigger force ≈ 0.65 × (crane + load), as quoted by Cranes and Lifting (2020)
- Brilliant Ideas Ltd, "How we size a crane mat: the load spread calculation" (area = force ÷ allowable bearing pressure; worked example 490.5 kN / 100 kPa = 4.905 m²); Temporary Works Forum outrigger mat guidance

## Padeye design check

<a id="padeye"></a>

Folder `padeye/` · Structural · Plate geometry around the hole, bearing, and shear and bending of the shackle pin of a lifting padeye to EN 1993-1-8 pin connections.

### Assumptions and caveats

- EN 1993-1-8:2005 3.13 (with corrigenda): the plate with the hole is checked as a type A pin-ended member of given thickness, a ≥ F γM0/(2 t fy) + 2d0/3 beyond the hole in the direction of the load and c ≥ F γM0/(2 t fy) + d0/3 at the sides (Table 3.9); the proportions of type B (t ≥ 0.7 √(F γM0/fy), d0 ≤ 2.5 t) are shown for information.
- Table 3.10: bearing of plate and pin 1.5 t d fy/γM0 with fy the lower of plate and pin; shear of the pin 0.6 A fup/γM2 per shear plane, the shackle pin being in double shear; bending of the pin 1.5 Wel fyp/γM0 with MEd = F (b + 4c + 2a)/8 for the padeye of thickness b between shackle jaws of thickness a with gaps c (Figure 3.11); and the interaction of bending and shear.
- A replaceable pin (a shackle) must also meet the serviceability checks under the characteristic load: bearing 0.6 t d fy/γM6,ser, bending 0.8 Wel fyp/γM6,ser, and the contact stress σh,Ed = 0.591 √(E Fser (d0 − d)/(d² t)) ≤ 2.5 fy/γM6,ser (3.14–3.16).
- Partial factors: γM0 = 1.00 (EN 1993-1-1 6.1), γM2 = 1.25 and γM6,ser = 1.0 (EN 1993-1-8 Table 2.1) as recommended; the National Annex may set others. E = 210 000 MPa.
- The design force must already include the factors of the lifting standard used (dynamic amplification, skew load, consequence); the load acts in the plane of the padeye along its axis. Out-of-plane loads, the welds of the padeye and cheek plates, and the supporting structure are outside this check.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 250 kN on a 30 mm padeye with a 53 mm hole and a 50 mm pin: a ≥ 11.74 + 35.33 = 47.07 mm, c ≥ 29.40 mm; Fb,Rd = 798.8 kN; Fv,Rd = 754.0 kN per plane; MEd = 3.125 kN·m against MRd = 11.78 kN·m; the replaceable-pin contact stress is 706 MPa against 887.5 MPa.
- Design decision: the thickness t is that of the plate at the hole, including cheek plates when they are welded to share the load; with cheek plates of a smaller radius, check the main plate alone for a and c.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Not adequate: … at a utilisation of ….
- The hole is more than 2.5 times the plate thickness (… t), beyond the type B proportions.
- The plate is thinner than 0.7 √(F γM0/fy) = … mm of the type B proportions; the type A distances govern.
- The serviceability force exceeds the design force: check the load combinations.
- Check the welds of the padeye and any cheek plates, out-of-plane and skew loads, and the structure behind the padeye separately; shackle pins are rated by their maker.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The pin diameter must not exceed the hole diameter
- The pin ultimate strength must not be below its yield strength

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Type A geometry: a ≥ 250 000/(2 × 30 × 355) + 2 × 53/3 = 47.07 mm and c ≥ 11.74 + 17.67 = 29.40 mm
  - Source: EN 1993-1-8:2005 Table 3.9, type A (given thickness)
- Bearing 1.5 t d fy/γM0 with fy the lower of plate and pin: 798.75 kN with a 355 MPa plate, 675 kN when the pin has 300 MPa
  - Source: EN 1993-1-8:2005 Table 3.10, bearing of plate and pin
- Pin shear 0.6 A fup/γM2 = 0.6 × 1963.5 × 800/1.25 = 754.0 kN per plane against F/2 = 125 kN in double shear
  - Source: EN 1993-1-8:2005 Table 3.10, shear of the pin; Table 2.1 γM2 = 1.25
- Pin bending MEd = F (b + 4c + 2a)/8 = 250 × 100/8 = 3125 kN·mm against MRd = 1.5 (π 50³/32) 640 = 11.78 kN·m; interaction 0.098
  - Source: EN 1993-1-8:2005 Figure 3.11 and Table 3.10
- Replaceable pin: σh,Ed = 0.591 √(210 000 × 170 000 × 3/(50² × 30)) = 706.2 MPa against 2.5 × 355 = 887.5 MPa governs at 0.80
  - Source: EN 1993-1-8:2005 eqs (3.14)–(3.16)
- At 900 kN the pin fails in combined bending and shear (1.27) and the failure is flagged
  - Source: EN 1993-1-8:2005 Table 3.10, combined shear and bending
- Invalid inputs are rejected: a pin larger than the hole, an ultimate strength below the yield strength
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 47.1 mm, 29.4 mm, 798.8 kN, 754.0 kN, 3.13 kN·m, 11.78 kN·m, 706 MPa to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

## Paint coverage and quantity

<a id="paint-coverage"></a>

Folder `paint-coverage/` · Maritime · Theoretical and practical spreading rate from volume solids and dry film thickness, litres and cost for an area with loss factors.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Theoretical spreading rate TSR = volume solids (%) × 10 / DFT (µm) in m²/L assumes a perfectly smooth, non-absorbent surface, no overspray and the paint applied at its datasheet volume solids (thinning reduces the solids proportionally); it is the figure printed on datasheets and is never achieved in practice.
- Practical spreading rate = TSR × (1 − loss): the loss factor covers overspray, wind, container and line residues, uneven film (the specification usually asks for 80 % of readings ≥ DFT and none < 80 %, which forces a higher average) and masking; typical airless-spray losses are 20–30 % on flat steel, 30–50 % on complex steelwork or lattice and 40–60 % in wind, brush and roller 5–15 % — the presets are industry rules of thumb, not datasheet values.
- Surface profile dead volume: a blast profile fills with paint before any film builds above the peaks; the allowance (typically one third to one half of the profile height, or the datasheet's "add 25 µm for every 25 µm of profile above 75 µm") is added to the first coat's DFT only.
- Wet film thickness WFT = DFT / volume solids is the wet-comb reading to aim for immediately after application, before solvent loss; it increases with thinning.
- Quantities are per coat with the same DFT and product; multi-product systems (primer + intermediate + topcoat) are computed by running each product separately. Stripe coats, touch-up and spot repair are not included unless added to the area.
- Mass and cost use the entered density and price per litre; pack sizes are rounded up to whole containers.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: 55 % solids at 75 µm → 7.33 m²/L (industry worked example); 4.0 m²/L theoretical with 39 % loss → 2.44 m²/L (coatings coverage brochure); 10 000 m² × 2 coats of 150 µm at 60 % solids with 30 % loss → 7 143 L and WFT 250 µm.
- Design decision: loss presets are offered because specifiers rarely have measured consumption data; the register records them as rules of thumb.
- Design decision: the profile allowance is applied only to the first coat, as the dead volume is filled once.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Thinning … % lowers the volume solids to … % and raises the wet film to … µm for the same DFT.
- Wet film above 600 µm per coat: sagging and solvent entrapment risk on vertical surfaces — check the product\'s maximum WFT.
- Loss factor … % is a rule of thumb for "…"; measured consumption from a previous job is better.
- No surface-profile allowance: on freshly blasted steel the first coat fills the profile (allow 25–40 µm for a 50–75 µm profile).
- The 80/20 acceptance rule (ISO 19840) means the applied average DFT typically exceeds the specification by 10–20 %, part of the loss factor.
- Single product and DFT: run primer, intermediate and topcoat separately for a full system.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Theoretical spreading rate: 55 % solids at 75 µm → 7.33 m²/L; 60 % at 150 µm → 4.0 m²/L; 100 % solids at 100 µm → 10 m²/L
  - Source: TSR = VS × 10 / DFT (International Paint, Jotun, Hempel datasheet convention); worked example 55 × 10 / 75 = 7.33
- Practical rate: 4.0 m²/L with 39 % loss → 2.44 m²/L (coverage brochure efficiency 0.61); 30 % loss → 2.8 m²/L
  - Source: Coatings coverage brochure worked case 4.0 × 0.61 = 2.44 m²/L; loss factor convention (1 − loss)
- Hull job: 10 000 m² × 2 coats of 150 µm at 60 % solids, 30 % loss → theoretical 5 000 L, practical 7 143 L, 358 × 20 L containers, 10 000 kg, 57 143 at 8/L (5.71 per m²), WFT 250 µm, total DFT 300 µm
  - Source: Quantity = area × DFT / (10 × VS × (1 − loss)); WFT = DFT / VS
- Thinning 10 % lowers solids to 54.5 %, raises WFT to 275 µm and the quantity by 10 %; dry film mass = theoretical litres × solids × density
  - Source: Volume solids after thinning = VS/(1 + thinner); mass balance of the dry film
- Surface profile allowance of 30 µm on the first coat adds 30/300 = 10 % to the quantity and makes the first coat 180 µm
  - Source: Dead-volume allowance practice (add paint to fill the blast profile before film builds)
- Imperial reading: 4.0 m²/L = 163 ft²/US gal (unit conversion of the spreading-rate group)
  - Source: 1 ft²/US gal = 0.09290 m² / 3.7854 L = 0.02454 m²/L
- Warnings: thinning, high wet film (> 600 µm), no profile allowance, rule-of-thumb loss; invalid inputs fail fast (fractional coats, solids above 100 %)
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 4.0 m²/L, 2.8 m²/L, 250 µm, 5 000 L, 7 143 L, 358, 10 t, 57 143, 5.7 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- International Paint / AkzoNobel, "Calculating paint consumption" (theoretical spreading rate, wet film thickness); Jotun and Hempel technical datasheets (volume solids, TSR, loss factors)
- Industrial Coatings Ltd, "How to work out paint coverage for protective coatings" — loss allowances by application method (airless 20–30 %, complex 30–50 %)
- ISO 19840:2012, Measurement of, and acceptance criteria for, the thickness of dry films on rough surfaces (80/20 rule); ISO 8503 surface profile grades
- Wattyl Protective & Marine info sheet I-09 "Coating coverage, costs and calculations" (coverage efficiency factors)

## Passage plan from waypoints

<a id="passage-plan"></a>

Folder `passage-plan/` · Maritime · Leg courses, distances, times and ETAs from a pasted waypoint list, by rhumb line or great circle, with the passage totals.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The earth is a sphere on which one minute of great-circle arc is one nautical mile (R = 10 800/π nmi), the usual basis of passage planning; on the WGS-84 ellipsoid rhumb-line distances differ by up to about 0.5 % with latitude (the Mercator sailing calculator gives the ellipsoidal values for a single leg).
- Each leg is sailed either on a rhumb line at constant course or on a great circle starting on the initial course shown; a great-circle leg changes course continuously and is normally steered as a series of rhumb lines.
- Waypoint lines are "name; latitude; longitude; speed" separated by semicolons or tabs; coordinates may be decimal degrees with a sign (south and west negative) or degrees and minutes, with optional seconds, followed or preceded by N, S, E or W; the speed on a line applies to the leg that starts at that waypoint, otherwise the default speed; lines starting with # are comments.
- Times are at the speed over the ground entered for each leg, without allowance for current, weather, traffic or manoeuvring; ETAs count from the departure time on day 1 in a single time zone.
- Legs that cross the 180° meridian are handled by taking the shorter way round in longitude.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: a leg from 0° to 1° N along a meridian is 60 nmi on 000°; one degree of longitude along the equator is 60 nmi on 090°, and at 60° N a parallel leg of one degree is 30 nmi; a great-circle leg from 40.7° N 74.0° W to 51.5° N 0.1° W is shorter than the rhumb line, as it must be.
- Design decision: the coordinate parser accepts the forms in which waypoints are copied from ECDIS route tables and pilot books, and reports the line number of anything it cannot read instead of guessing.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Leg … (… to …) has no length: duplicate waypoint.
- Leg … spans more than 90° of longitude: split it into shorter legs for planning.
- Waypoints above 70° latitude: rhumb lines become long spirals near the poles; plan high-latitude legs as great circles.
- Planning figures: times use the entered speeds over the ground without current, weather or traffic allowances.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- empty …
- "…" has more than one hemisphere letter
- "…" is a longitude, expected a latitude (N or S)
- "…" is a latitude, expected a longitude (E or W)
- cannot read "…"
- "…": degrees must be whole when minutes follow
- "…": minutes and seconds must be below 60
- "…": use either a minus sign or S/W, not both
- "…" is outside ±…°
- …: expected name; latitude; longitude[; speed]
- …: …
- …: speed "…" must be a number greater than zero
- At most … waypoints
- Enter at least two waypoints

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Coordinates: 37 55.5 N = 37.925°, 023°35.0′E = 23.5833°, 37 55 30 N = 37.925°, −12.5 and 12 30.0 S = −12.5°, 74 00.0 W = −74°; a decimal comma is accepted
  - Source: Degrees, decimal minutes and seconds notation (Bowditch); ECDIS route table formats
- Basic legs: 0° to 1° N on a meridian is 60 nmi on 000°; one degree of longitude on the equator is 60 nmi on 090° by both sailings; at 60° N one degree of longitude is 60 cos 60° = 30 nmi by rhumb line
  - Source: One minute of latitude = one nautical mile; departure = d.long × cos lat (parallel sailing)
- Long leg 40.7° N 74.0° W to 51.5° N 0.1° W: the great circle equals the haversine distance on R = 10 800/π nmi and is shorter than the rhumb line, which equals Δφ/cos(course) × R
  - Source: Bowditch: great-circle sailing and Mercator sailing
- Timing: two legs of 60 nmi at 12 and 10 kn take 5 h and 6 h; leaving at 20:00 the arrival is Day 2 07:00 and the average speed 120/11 kn
  - Source: Time = distance / speed; clock arithmetic across midnight
- Default speed and the date line: a leg without a speed uses the default; a leg from 179° E to 179° W is 2° of longitude the short way
  - Source: Waypoint format of this calculator; longitude difference reduced to ±180°
- Invalid inputs fail fast with the line number: a missing longitude, an unreadable latitude, a zero speed, a single waypoint
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 214.8 nmi, 214.8 nmi, 15.7 h, 14 kn to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- The American Practical Navigator (Bowditch), NGA Pub. 9 — Mercator and great-circle sailing
- IMO Resolution A.893(21) Guidelines for voyage planning
- IHO S-421 Route Plan Based on S-100 / IEC 61174 (RTZ) — waypoint and leg conventions of ECDIS routes

## PCB trace width calculator (IPC-2221)

<a id="pcb-trace-width"></a>

Folder `pcb-trace-width/` · Electrical · PCB trace width for a current by IPC-2221 from copper weight and allowed temperature rise, with the trace resistance, voltage drop and power loss.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The width comes from the curve fit to the IPC-2221 current charts, I = k ΔT^0.44 A^0.725, with k = 0.048 for outer layers and 0.024 for inner layers; the inner-layer chart is the outer one at half the current.
- The fit is used only within the charts it was drawn from: currents up to 35 A on outer and 17.5 A on inner layers, widths up to 400 mil (10.2 mm), temperature rises of 10 to 100 °C and copper of 0.5 to 3 oz/ft²; outside that range the calculator refuses rather than extrapolates.
- IPC-2221 is conservative. IPC-2152 (2009) is based on newer measurements and takes the board material, thickness and copper planes into account; it usually allows narrower traces, especially on inner layers.
- Copper thickness is the nominal 1.378 mil (35 µm) per oz/ft²; plating on outer layers adds thickness and etching removes some, so the real cross-section differs.
- Resistance uses annealed copper, 1.7241 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 20 °C with 0.393 % per K, at the ambient temperature plus the temperature rise; electrodeposited PCB copper is a few per cent more resistive.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 2 A on an outer layer of 1 oz copper with a 10 °C rise needs 42.4 mil² and 30.8 mil (0.781 mm); 2 in of it at 35 °C has 33.9 mΩ, drops 67.8 mV and dissipates 0.136 W. 1 A gives 11.8 mil (0.30 mm), the commonly tabulated value. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Under about 4 mil (0.1 mm) the width is below what many board makers etch as standard; check the fabricator\'s minimum.
- On the other layer type the same current needs more than the 400 mil the charts cover.
- The trace runs above 105 °C: check the board material\'s maximum operating temperature (FR-4 glass transition is typically 130 to 180 °C).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Current: the IPC-2221 charts end at … A on … layers (got … A); use IPC-2152, several traces or a copper pour.
- Current: the width comes out at … mil, beyond the 400 mil the IPC-2221 charts cover; use heavier copper, a larger temperature rise, or IPC-2152.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 1 A, 1 oz, 10 °C rise, outer layer: 16.3 mil² and 11.8 mil (0.30 mm), the value printed in IPC-2221 trace-width tables
  - Source: IPC-2221B Figure 6-4 curve fit, I = 0.048 ΔT^0.44 A^0.725; 1 oz = 1.378 mil
- The fitted current from the computed area returns the input current (inverse of I = k ΔT^0.44 A^0.725)
  - Source: IPC-2221B curve fit, hand inversion
- Inner layer at 1 A needs the same copper as an outer layer at 2 A (k = 0.024 is half of 0.048)
  - Source: IPC-2221B: the internal chart is the external chart at half the current
- 2 A worked example: 2 in at 35 °C is 33.9 mΩ (R = ρ L / A with ρ = 1.7241e-8 × (1 + 0.00393 × 15)), 67.8 mV, 0.136 W
  - Source: IEC 60028 copper resistivity and temperature coefficient; hand calculation
- Outside the IPC-2221 charts the calculator refuses: 20 A on an inner layer, a width over 400 mil, a 5 °C rise, 4 oz copper
  - Source: IPC-2221B chart extent (35 A outer, 17.5 A inner, 400 mil, 10–100 °C, 0.5–3 oz)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 42.4, 30.8 mil, 0.781 mm, 33.9 mΩ, 67.8 mV, 0.136 W to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IPC-2221B, Generic Standard on Printed Board Design (2012), §6.2 Conductive material requirements and Figure 6-4, conductor current-carrying capacity charts for internal and external conductors
- IPC-2152, Standard for Determining Current Carrying Capacity in Printed Board Design (2009), named for comparison
- IEC 60028:1925 International standard of resistance for copper (1/58 Ω·mm²/m at 20 °C, 0.00393 per K)

## Pile capacity calculator (driven and bored piles)

<a id="pile-capacity"></a>

Folder `pile-capacity/` · Civil · Axial capacity of a single driven or bored pile in layered clay and sand: shaft friction by the α and β methods plus end bearing, with a factor of safety.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Driven piles follow API RP 2GEO: the α method in clay and the β method with the Table 1 limits in sand and silt, by relative density. API gives no values for loose sand, so a loose layer is refused for driven piles. The pile is assumed plugged, with end bearing on its full area.
- Bored piles (drilled shafts) follow O'Neill and Reese (FHWA, 1999): α = 0.55 in clay with no friction in the top 1.5 m and the bottom one diameter, β = 1.5 − 0.245 √z in sand, and end bearing from N60 in sand.
- Sand and silt layers take an SPT N60 value, from which the relative density follows Terzaghi and Peck; driven piles also accept the words medium dense, dense or very dense. Use effective (submerged) unit weights below the water table.
- The capacity is geotechnical only: the pile weight, negative skin friction, group effects, settlement and the strength of the pile itself are not checked.
- The allowable load is the ultimate capacity divided by one factor of safety, commonly 2 to 3; LRFD design uses resistance factors instead, and load tests can justify lower factors.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a driven 610 mm closed-end pipe pile 20 m long through 6 m of clay (s_u 40 kPa, γ' 8), 8 m of clay (s_u 80 kPa, γ' 9) and into dense sand (N60 35, γ' 10) has shaft friction 100.97 + 332.67 + 414.0 = 847.6 kN per metre of perimeter, Q_s = 1 624 kN, end bearing 40 × 180 = 7 200 kPa, Q_b = 2 104 kN, Q_ult = 3 729 kN and 1 491 kN at FS 2.5 (integrals by hand).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- N60 above 50 at the tip is taken as 50; very dense soil may be treated as an intermediate geomaterial for a higher value.
- The tip is less than three diameters above the next layer; if that layer is weaker, it controls the end bearing.
- Clay at the base has s_u below 96 kPa (2 ksf): O\'Neill and Reese reduce the base resistance there because settlement governs.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Soil layers, line …: write "thickness; clay or sand or silt; s_u or N60; effective unit weight".
- Soil layers, line …: the thickness "…" must be a number above zero.
- Soil layers, line …: the soil "…" must be clay, sand or silt.
- Soil layers, line …: the effective unit weight "…" must be above zero and at most … (use the submerged weight below the water table).
- Soil layers, line …: the undrained shear strength "…" must be a number above zero.
- Soil layers, line …: N60 "…" must be between 0 and 200 blows per 300 mm.
- Soil layers, line …: give N60 as a number or the density as medium dense, dense or very dense.
- Soil layers: enter at least one layer.
- Embedded length L: the soil layers end at … ft` : `… m`}, above the pile tip; describe the soil down to the tip.
- Soil layers, line …: s_u above 2.5 atmospheres (253 kPa) is outside O'Neill and Reese's clay method; treat it as an intermediate geomaterial.
- Soil layers, line …: API RP 2GEO gives no design values for … …; use CPT-based methods or a geotechnical engineer.
- Soil layers, line …: bored piles in sand need the N60 blow count as a number.
- Soil layers, line …: API RP 2GEO gives no design values for loose sand at the tip.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- API α: ψ = 0.25 gives α = 1.0 (cap), ψ = 1 gives 0.5, ψ = 4 gives 0.354; a uniform clay with s_u = σ'v has f = 0.5 s_u
  - Source: API RP 2GEO (2011) 8.1: α = 0.5 ψ^−0.5 for ψ ≤ 1, 0.5 ψ^−0.25 for ψ > 1, α ≤ 1
- API Table 1: dense sand β 0.46, f_lim 96 kPa, N_q 40, q_lim 10 MPa; N60 35 is dense, 20 medium dense, 60 very dense; loose sand is refused for driven piles
  - Source: API RP 2GEO (2011) Table 1; Terzaghi, Peck and Mesri (1996) relative density by SPT N
- Worked example, driven 610 mm pipe pile, 20 m: shaft 100.97 + 332.67 + 414.0 = 847.6 kN/m × π × 0.61 = 1 624 kN; tip 40 × 180 = 7 200 kPa × 0.2922 m² = 2 104 kN
  - Source: Hand integration of the API α and β formulas over each layer (closed-form integrals of z^0.25 and z^0.5 terms)
- Bored pile in clay (s_u 60 kPa, D 1 m, L 15 m): f = 0.55 × 60 = 33 kPa over 1.5–14 m = 1 296 kN; N_c = 9, base 540 kPa × 0.785 = 424 kN
  - Source: O'Neill & Reese (1999) FHWA-IF-99-025: α = 0.55, top 1.5 m and bottom D excluded, N_c = 6 (1 + 0.2 L/D) ≤ 9
- Bored pile in sand (N60 30, γ' 10, D 1 m, L 10 m): β = 1.5 − 0.245 √z ≤ 1.2, f = β σ'v integrated by hand; base 57.5 × 30 = 1 725 kPa; N60 10 scales β by 10/15
  - Source: O'Neill & Reese (1999): β method for cohesionless soil and q_b = 0.6 N60 tsf (57.5 N60 kPa) ≤ 30 tsf
- US units give the same capacity as SI; layers ending above the tip, bad lines, stiff clay for bored piles and a word for N60 in bored sand are refused
  - Source: Unit definitions (ft 0.3048 m, psf 0.04788 kPa, pcf 0.1571 kN/m³); validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1 624 kN, 2 104 kN, 3 729 kN, 1 491 kN to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

## Pipe flow and pressure drop

<a id="pipe-flow"></a>

Folder `pipe-flow/` · Thermal and fluids · Velocity, Reynolds number, Darcy friction factor (Colebrook, Swamee–Jain) and pressure drop for a straight pipe with fittings.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Steady, fully developed, incompressible flow in a circular pipe running full; for gases the result holds while the pressure drop stays below about 10 % of the absolute pressure.
- The friction factor is the Darcy factor (4 × Fanning): laminar f = 64/Re below Re 2 300, Colebrook–White iterated to convergence above; in the transitional band 2 300–4 000 the turbulent value is used and a warning is raised.
- Swamee–Jain is shown for comparison only (within about 1 % of Colebrook for 5 000 ≤ Re ≤ 10⁸ and 10⁻⁶ ≤ ε/D ≤ 10⁻²).
- Minor losses are lumped as ΣK × dynamic pressure; handbook K values vary by ±30 % and depend on Reynolds number and fitting geometry.
- Roughness presets are for new, clean pipe (Moody 1944 / White Table 6.1); aged or scaled pipe can have several times the roughness and a reduced bore, and losses scale with D⁻⁵ at fixed flow.
- Fuel and lubricating-oil presets are typical values at the stated temperature, not standard properties; HFO viscosity roughly halves for a 10 °C rise.
- Non-circular ducts: use the hydraulic diameter 4A/P in place of D; accuracy about ±15 % in turbulent flow and poor in laminar flow.
- Elevation enters as the static term ρ g Δz; the outlet pressure requirement and velocity-head changes between different inlet and outlet diameters are not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the laminar case is checked against Hagen–Poiseuille independently (320 Pa both ways); the smooth-pipe limit against the Prandtl law (0.0180 at Re 10⁵) and the fully rough limit against von Kármán (0.0379 at ε/D 0.01); the Moody chart point Re 10⁵, ε/D 0.001 reads 0.0222 against Colebrook 0.02217.
- Design decision: Colebrook is iterated to 10⁻¹³ from a Swamee–Jain start and both values are shown, so users can see the explicit approximation error (about 0.8 % at the test point).
- Design decision: in the transitional band the turbulent factor is used as the conservative choice and a warning is raised rather than interpolating.
- Article check 2026-10-31 (schema.example): the worked example printed the Colebrook factor as 0.0180 and the Swamee–Jain factor as 0.0181; recomputed independently (Re 2.98·10⁵, ε/D 4.5·10⁻⁴) they are 0.01793 and 0.01805, as this calculator gives, so the friction loss is 115.1 kPa (11.4 m) instead of 115.5 kPa (11.5 m) and the total head 24.6 m instead of 24.7 m. Corrected in content.md.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Transitional regime: the friction factor is uncertain by ±30 %; the turbulent value is shown as the conservative choice.
- Relative roughness above 0.05 is outside the Moody chart; the Colebrook result is an extrapolation.
- Liquid velocity above 3 m/s: expect noise, erosion and water hammer risk; typical design 1–3 m/s.
- Gas pressure drop exceeds about 10 % of absolute pressure: incompressible flow assumptions no longer hold.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Laminar flow Re = 1 000: f = 64/Re = 0.064 and Δp = 320 Pa, equal to Hagen–Poiseuille 32 μ L V / D²
  - Source: Hagen–Poiseuille law; White, Fluid Mechanics, 7th ed., §6.4 (f = 64/Re for laminar pipe flow)
- Smooth pipe, Re = 10⁵: Colebrook gives f = 0.0180 (Prandtl–von Kármán smooth-pipe law, Moody chart)
  - Source: Moody (1944) chart; Prandtl universal law 1/√f = 2 log(Re√f) − 0.8 → 0.0180 at Re = 10⁵ (White, Fluid Mechanics, eq. 6.54)
- Fully rough pipe, ε/D = 0.01 at Re = 10⁹: f = [2 log(3.7 D/ε)]⁻² = 0.0379 (von Kármán rough-pipe law)
  - Source: Nikuradse / von Kármán fully rough law, White, Fluid Mechanics, eq. 6.55; Moody chart ε/D = 0.01 → 0.038
- Moody chart check Re = 10⁵, ε/D = 0.001: Colebrook f ≈ 0.0222; Swamee–Jain within 1 % of Colebrook
  - Source: Moody (1944) chart reading 0.0222 (Çengel & Cimbala, Fluid Mechanics, Fig. A-12); Swamee & Jain (1976) accuracy ±1 %
- Darcy–Weisbach: minor losses ΣK = 5 at 2 m/s → 10 000 Pa (1.02 m); 10 m rise → 98 066.5 Pa static
  - Source: Darcy–Weisbach h = f (L/D) V²/2g and h_minor = K V²/2g — Crane TP-410 (2013), ch. 2; g = 9.80665 m/s²
- Velocity from flow: 100 m³/h in DN100 (0.1 m) = 3.537 m/s; velocity mode returns the same flow
  - Source: Continuity V = Q / (π D²/4)
- Presets: commercial steel ε = 0.045 mm, cast iron 0.26 mm; ITTC sea water 15 °C ρ = 1025.87 kg/m³, ν = 1.18831e-6 m²/s
  - Source: Moody (1944) / White Table 6.1 roughness; ITTC Recommended Procedure 7.5-02-01-03 (2011) fresh and sea water properties
- Unit layer: 1 cSt = 1e-6 m²/s, 100 m³/h = 0.027778 m³/s, 1 bar = 100 kPa
  - Source: SI definitions (BIPM); 1 St = 1 cm²/s
- Zero flow returns zero losses; invalid inputs fail fast: zero diameter, negative length, unknown fluid

- Loss head for a suction line: (Δp_f + Δp_minor)/(ρ g) leaves out the elevation; the density output echoes the fluid

## Pipe and tank insulation heat loss

<a id="pipe-insulation"></a>

Folder `pipe-insulation/` · Thermal and fluids · Heat loss through multi-layer cylindrical or flat insulation, surface temperature and the heating power to hold a fuel tank or line warm.

### Assumptions and caveats

- One-dimensional steady conduction through concentric cylindrical layers (pipe wall, up to two insulation layers) or a flat wall, in series with the inside film coefficient and a combined outside convection-plus-radiation coefficient h_o; axial conduction, supports, flanges, valves and thermal bridges are not included — add 10–20 % for a real line.
- Thermal conductivities are constant at their mean temperature (mineral wool 0.035–0.045 W/(m·K) at 50 °C rising to 0.06–0.08 at 200 °C; the user should enter the value at the mean insulation temperature, iterating once if needed).
- The outside coefficient includes radiation: still air indoors 8–10 W/(m²·K) for cladded insulation at near-ambient surface temperature, 20–30 in wind; the surface temperature result allows the user to check the personnel-protection limit (60 °C for metal cladding per CINI/ASTM C1055).
- Bare-surface comparison uses the same inside film and outside coefficient on the uninsulated pipe wall; in reality the bare hot pipe has a higher h_o (radiation grows with temperature), so the saving is slightly understated.
- The critical radius of insulation r_cr = k/h_o (cylinder) marks where adding insulation stops increasing the loss; it is only relevant for small pipes or cables with poor insulation (a few millimetres for k 0.04 and h 10).
- Heating power equals the steady loss at the design ambient; heat-up from cold, wind chill on exposed decks and tank contents stratification are outside the calculation.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: 4-inch steel pipe (114.3 mm OD, 6 mm wall, k 50) at 150 °C with 50 mm mineral wool (k 0.04) in 25 °C air (h_i 1 000, h_o 10): resistances 0.00311 + 0.00035 + 2.501 + 0.1485 = 2.653 K·m/W → 47.1 W/m, surface 32.0 °C; bare pipe 443 W/m (R 0.282) → 89 % saving; critical radius 4 mm. Flat-wall check: 100 mm of k 0.04 with h_o 10 and h_i 1 000 at ΔT 125 K → 48.0 W/m².
- Design decision: the outside coefficient is a single input rather than computed from wind and emissivity, because the free-convection and radiation correlations would add a dozen inputs for a 10–20 % effect; the register records the typical values.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- No insulation entered: the result is the bare-surface loss.
- Outer radius below the critical radius k/h_o: this insulation INCREASES the heat loss (small pipe, poor insulation).
- Mean insulation temperature is high: mineral-wool conductivity rises with temperature (≈ 0.06–0.08 W/(m·K) at 200 °C) — enter k at the mean layer temperature.
- Outside coefficient for still air; on an open deck or in wind use 20–30 W/(m²·K), which raises the loss slightly and lowers the surface temperature.
- Thermal bridges (supports, flanges, valves, uninsulated fittings) add 10–20 % to a real line; axial conduction and heat-up transients are not included.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Inside and ambient temperatures are equal: no heat flow
- Wall thickness must be less than the pipe radius

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 4-inch pipe, 6 mm wall, 50 mm mineral wool, 150 °C inside, 25 °C ambient, h_i 1000, h_o 10: R = 0.00311 + 0.00035 + 2.501 + 0.1485 = 2.653 K·m/W → 47.1 W/m, 471 W for 10 m
  - Source: Incropera & DeWitt §3.3.1 radial systems: R_cyl = ln(r₂/r₁)/(2πkL), R_film = 1/(h 2πrL)
- Surface and interface temperatures: cladding 25 + 47.1 × 0.1485 = 32.0 °C (OK ≤ 60 °C); steel/insulation interface 150 − 47.1 × 0.00346 = 149.8 °C
  - Source: Temperature drop proportional to resistance in a series network
- Bare pipe with the same coefficients: R = 0.00311 + 0.00035 + 0.2785 = 0.282 K·m/W → 443 W/m; the 50 mm insulation saves 89 %; critical radius k/h_o = 4 mm
  - Source: Incropera Example 3.6 / §3.3.2 critical insulation radius r_cr = k/h
- Two layers: adding 25 mm of k 0.03 outside the mineral wool adds ln(132.15/107.15)/(2π·0.03) = 1.113 K·m/W (the outside film falls to 0.120) and cuts the loss to 33.4 W/m
  - Source: Series resistances of concentric cylinders
- Flat wall (tank side): 6 mm steel + 100 mm of k 0.04 with h_i 1000 and h_o 10 at ΔT 125 K → R = 0.001 + 0.00012 + 2.5 + 0.1 = 2.601 K·m²/W → 48.0 W/m², 4.8 kW for 100 m², 28.8 MWh/year at 6 000 h
  - Source: Çengel ch. 3 plane-wall resistance network R = L/(kA) + 1/(hA)
- Critical radius effect: a 10 mm cable (k_ins 0.15, h_o 10 → r_cr 15 mm) loses MORE heat with 3 mm of insulation than bare, and the page warns
  - Source: Incropera §3.3.2: for r < r_cr adding insulation increases the heat loss
- Cold service: −20 °C brine pipe in 25 °C air gives a negative loss (heat gain) and a cold-surface condensation remark; invalid inputs fail fast (equal temperatures, wall thicker than the radius)
  - Source: Sign convention and validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2.501, 0.1485, 2.653, 471 W, 32 °C, 149.8 °C, 89 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- F. P. Incropera, D. P. DeWitt et al., Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, 7th ed. (Wiley 2011) §3.3 radial systems, critical insulation radius
- Y. A. Çengel & A. J. Ghajar, Heat and Mass Transfer, 5th ed. (McGraw-Hill 2015) ch. 3 steady conduction, thermal resistance networks

## Pipe volume and mass of contents

<a id="pipe-volume"></a>

Folder `pipe-volume/` · Thermal and fluids · Volume and mass of the liquid in a pipe from its bore and length, the litres per metre, and the time to fill or flush it at a given flow.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The pipe is a straight cylinder of uniform inside diameter running completely full; fittings, valves and bends add volume that can be entered as extra length.
- The inside diameter is the bore, not the nominal size: a DN 100 steel pipe has a bore between about 97 and 108 mm depending on its wall thickness.
- The liquid density is the reference value at the stated temperature; it changes with temperature (water 1 % between 4 and 45 °C).
- Fill time assumes a steady flow that fills the whole bore from the start; venting trapped air and filling uphill take longer in practice.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 150 mm bore 120 m long holds 2.121 m³ (17.67 L per metre) and 2 117 kg of water; at 30 m³/h it fills in 4.24 min. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Heavy fuel oil is only pumpable when heated; its density and volume change by about 0.07 % per kelvin.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)
