## Pipe wall thickness (ASME B31.3)

<a id="pipe-wall-thickness"></a>

Folder `pipe-wall-thickness/` · Mechanical · ASME B31.3 pressure design thickness, allowances and mill tolerance, nominal wall required, schedule check and MAWP of the available wall.

### Assumptions and caveats

- ASME B31.3 para. 304.1.2 for straight pipe under internal pressure with t < D/6: pressure design thickness t = P D/(2 (S E W + P Y)) using the outside diameter D, the basic allowable stress S at the design temperature (Table A-1), the longitudinal weld joint quality factor E (Table A-1B), the weld joint strength reduction factor W (1.0 below about 510 °C for most materials) and the coefficient Y from Table 304.1.1 (0.4 for ferritic steel up to 482 °C and austenitic up to 566 °C, rising to 0.5 and 0.7 at higher temperatures, 0.0 for cast iron); for t ≥ D/6 or P/(S E) > 0.385 the code requires special consideration.
- Minimum required thickness t_m = t + c, where c is the sum of the corrosion/erosion allowance and the mechanical allowance for threading or grooving (thread depth per ASME B1.20.1); the nominal (ordered) wall must satisfy t_nom × (1 − mill tolerance) ≥ t_m, with 12.5 % under-tolerance for seamless and most welded pipe to ASTM A106/A53/A312 (ASTM A530), 10 % or an absolute value for some plate-made pipe.
- MAWP of the available wall inverts the formula with the effective thickness t_eff = t_avail (1 − tol) − c: P = 2 S E W t_eff/(D − 2 Y t_eff); hoop stress at design pressure by Barlow σ = P D/(2 t_eff) is shown as a conventional check; longitudinal, bending, external pressure, thermal and occasional loads (para. 302.3.5–6) and flange ratings are separate.
- Allowable stresses in the material table are the Table A-1 values at or below 100–200 °C for quick sizing; at higher temperatures S falls and must be read from the table for the design temperature (custom material option); the stainless values are the lower "conservative" set, B31.3 also lists higher values where slight deformation is acceptable.
- Marine class rules (e.g. DNV, LR, ABS pipe thickness formulas) use the same form with their own allowances and a minimum wall by diameter; this page follows B31.3 and should be compared with the class table where the class governs.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: NPS 8 (219.1 mm) A106 B seamless at 16 bar: t = 1.6 × 219.1/(2 × (137.9 + 0.64)) = 1.265 mm, t_m 2.77 mm with 1.5 mm corrosion, nominal 3.16 mm with 12.5 % tolerance; schedule 40 (8.18 mm) has MAWP 72.7 bar and the design pressure uses 22 % of it — the familiar result that process pipe in the 10–20 bar range is governed by corrosion, handling and minimum wall rather than pressure.
- Design decision: a short material table with Table A-1 values at low temperature and a custom entry, rather than the whole stress table; the Y coefficient is derived from the material class and the design temperature per Table 304.1.1.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Pressure design thickness at or above D/6: thick-wall pipe — B31.3 requires special consideration (para. 304.1.2(b)); the formula is not valid.
- P/(S E) above 0.385: outside the range of the simple formula (para. 304.1.2(b)).
- Design temperature above 200 °C: the allowable stress of the table value falls with temperature — enter S at the design temperature (custom material).
- Below −29 °C carbon steel needs impact testing or a low-temperature grade (A333) per B31.3 para. 323.2.2.
- Available wall … mm is below the required nominal … mm: choose the next schedule.
- The available wall is consumed by tolerance and allowances: no pressure capacity remains.
- Pressure uses less than 30 % of the available wall: the schedule is governed by corrosion, handling or a minimum-wall rule, not by pressure — normal for low-pressure process pipe.
- Internal pressure only: sustained, occasional and thermal stresses (para. 302.3.5–6), external pressure, bending at supports and flange ratings are separate checks.
- Table values of S are the low-temperature basic allowable stresses; class rules (DNV/LR/ABS) have their own formula constants and minimum wall tables for shipboard piping.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

- Eq. 3a: NPS 8 A106 B seamless at 16 bar (1.6 MPa), S 137.9 MPa, E 1, W 1, Y 0.4 → t = 1.6 × 219.1/(2 × (137.9 + 0.64)) = 1.265 mm; t_m = 2.765 mm with 1.5 mm corrosion; nominal 2.765/0.875 = 3.160 mm

  - Source: B31.3 Table A-1B (E), Table 304.1.1 (Y), Table A-1 (S)

## Planing boat speed calculator (Crouch formula)

<a id="planing-speed"></a>

Folder `planing-speed/` · Maritime · Top speed of a planing boat from shaft horsepower and weight by Crouch's formula, with C by hull type, and the power needed for a target speed.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Crouch's formula V = C / √(W / P) is an empirical fit for planing hulls (speed in knots, weight in pounds, shaft horsepower). It does not apply to displacement or most semi-displacement hulls below a speed–length ratio of about 3.
- W is the loaded weight of the boat as it runs: hull, engines, fuel, water, people and gear. A half-loaded boat is noticeably faster than a fully loaded one.
- P is shaft horsepower delivered to the propeller. Gearboxes and stern drives lose a few percent of the engine's rated power, and the rating itself is at the top of the rpm range.
- The constant C depends on the hull and its propeller: Gerr tabulates 150 for average runabouts and cruisers up to 230 for racing catamarans. The best value comes from a sister boat with a known speed and power.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 5 000 lb runabout (C = 150) with 200 shp runs 150 / √(5 000 / 200) = 30.0 kn; for 35 kn it needs 5 000 × (35 / 150)² = 272 shp. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The speed–length ratio is below 3: the boat is not fully planing at this speed, and Crouch\'s formula overestimates the speed (or underestimates the power).
- More than 100 lb per horsepower: a boat this heavy for its power will probably not plane.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 5 000 lb runabout with 200 shp, C = 150: 25 lb/hp and 150 / √25 = 30.0 kn
  - Source: Crouch's formula and constants as given in Gerr, The Propeller Handbook, ch. 2; hand calculation
- Inverse: 35 kn for the same boat needs 5 000 × (35/150)² = 272.2 shp
  - Source: P = W (V/C)²; hand calculation
- Gerr's constants: 190 high-speed runabouts, 210 race boats, 220 hydroplanes, 230 racing catamarans
  - Source: Gerr, The Propeller Handbook, table of Crouch constants
- Speed scales with √(P/W): four times the power doubles the speed
  - Source: Crouch's formula; consistency check
- A 20 ft waterline at 12 kn is S/L 2.68 and warns that the boat is not planing; zero weight is rejected
  - Source: Gerr: planing above S/L 3.0; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 25.0, 30.0 kn to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- D. Gerr, The Propeller Handbook (International Marine, 1989), ch. 2: Crouch's planing speed formula and the table of Crouch constants C
- D. Savitsky, Hydrodynamic design of planing hulls, Marine Technology 1(1), 1964, pp. 71–95 (the physics-based method for planing resistance behind empirical rules such as Crouch's)

## Power factor correction

<a id="power-factor-correction"></a>

Folder `power-factor-correction/` · Electrical · Capacitor kvar and capacitance to raise the power factor, released kVA and current, loss saving, resonance with the supply and detuning.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Balanced three-phase load of constant active power P at the existing displacement power factor cos φ₁ (sinusoidal voltage and current); the capacitor bank supplies Q_c = P (tan φ₁ − tan φ₂) to reach the target cos φ₂, the classic kvar-per-kW table of the Schneider Electric Installation Guide (chapter L) reproduced exactly; harmonic currents (true power factor) are not included.
- Capacitance per phase from the bank rating at the supply voltage and frequency: C = Q_c/(3 ω V²) for a delta connection (each unit at line voltage) and C = Q_c/(ω V²) for star (each unit at phase voltage); manufacturers rate units in kvar at a rated voltage, and capacitor tolerance (−5/+10 % IEC 60831-1) is not included.
- Released capacity S₁ − S₂ = P/cos φ₁ − P/cos φ₂ and line currents I = S/(√3 V); resistive losses in the cables and transformers upstream of the bank scale with I², so they fall by 1 − (cos φ₁/cos φ₂)² — the saving in kW applies the ratio to the existing losses entered (only upstream of the bank).
- Parallel resonance of the bank with the supply inductance at harmonic order h_r ≈ √(S_sc/Q_c), with S_sc the short-circuit power at the bank's busbar (IEEE 1036 / Schneider guide); h_r within ±10 % of a characteristic harmonic (5, 7, 11, 13) of six-pulse converters is a resonance risk and calls for a detuned bank.
- Detuned (series reactor) bank with relative reactance p: series tuning order h_t = 1/√p (7 % → 3.78, 189 Hz at 50 Hz) below the 5th harmonic, and the capacitor voltage rises to V/(1 − p) at the fundamental, so the capacitors must be rated for it and the bank's output is taken from the manufacturer's detuned data — the capacitance output is for an undetuned bank.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 500 kW from cos φ 0.75 to 0.93 → tan φ 0.8819 − 0.3952 = 0.4867 kvar/kW (Schneider table 0.487), Q_c 243.3 kvar, 1 614 µF per phase in delta at 400 V 50 Hz, released 129.0 kVA, current 962 → 776 A, losses −35.0 %; with S_sc 10 MVA the resonance order is 6.41 (321 Hz), within 10 % of the 7th harmonic — flagged.
- Design decision: the loss saving is expressed against existing upstream losses entered by the user rather than a cable model, because the I² ratio is exact while the absolute losses depend on the installation.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Target above 0.98: at light load a fixed bank over-compensates (leading power factor, voltage rise); use an automatic stepped bank.
- Parallel resonance close to the …th harmonic: harmonic currents from drives and rectifiers will be amplified — detune the bank (p 5.67–7 %) or use a filter.
- Bank above 10 % of the short-circuit power: noticeable voltage rise when switched in (ΔV ≈ Q_c/S_sc) — switch in steps.
- With a … % reactor the capacitors see … % of the supply voltage: rate them accordingly and take the bank output from the manufacturer's detuned data.
- Displacement power factor of a sinusoidal load only: harmonic distortion lowers the true power factor and is not corrected by capacitors.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Target power factor must be above the existing power factor

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- kvar/kW factor: cos φ 0.75 → 0.93 gives tan φ 0.8819 − 0.3952 = 0.487 kvar/kW (Schneider table value); 500 kW needs Q_c = 243.3 kvar; 0.80 → 0.95 gives 0.421
  - Source: Schneider Electric Electrical Installation Guide, chapter L, table of kvar per kW (0.75→0.93: 0.487; 0.80→0.95: 0.421)
- Released capacity and currents at 400 V: S 666.7 → 537.6 kVA (129.0 kVA released), I 962.3 → 776.0 A, capacitor current 351.2 A; losses fall by 1 − (0.75/0.93)² = 34.96 %, 2.80 kW of 8 kW, 11 187 kWh/yr
  - Source: S = P/cos φ, I = S/(√3 V), losses ∝ I²
- Capacitance: delta C = Q_c/(3 ω V²) = 243 345/(3 × 314.16 × 400²) = 1 614 µF per phase; star C = Q_c/(ω V²) = 3 × that; at 60 Hz the capacitance falls by 50/60
  - Source: Q = 3 V² ω C (delta), Q = V_LL² ω C (star)
- Resonance: S_sc 10 MVA and Q_c 243 kvar give h_r = √(10 000/243.35) = 6.41 (321 Hz), within 10 % of the 7th → RISK with a warning; S_sc 30 MVA gives h_r 11.1 → near the 11th; S_sc 20 MVA gives h_r 9.07 → no characteristic harmonic within 10 %
  - Source: Schneider guide / IEEE 1036: h_r = √(S_sc/Q_c)
- Detuned bank: p 7 % → tuning order 1/√0.07 = 3.78 (189 Hz at 50 Hz), capacitor voltage factor 1/0.93 = 1.0753, resonance check reports the detuned bank
  - Source: Detuned reactor practice (Schneider guide chapter L; IEC 61642)
- Validation and warnings: target not above existing is rejected; zero voltage rejected; a target of 0.99 warns about over-compensation; a 2 MVar bank on 10 MVA warns about the switching voltage step
  - Source: Behaviour specification
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.882, 0.395, 0.487, 243 kvar, 538 kVA, 129 kVA, 776 A, 351 A to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Schneider Electric, Electrical Installation Guide, chapter L "Power factor correction" — kvar/kW table, resonance f_r = f √(S_sc/Q), detuned reactors
- IEC 60831-1:2014 Shunt power capacitors of the self-healing type for a.c. systems up to 1 000 V — ratings and tolerances
- IEEE Std 1036-2020 Guide for the Application of Shunt Power Capacitors — resonance and harmonic considerations
- IEC 61642:1997 Industrial a.c. networks affected by harmonics — application of filters and shunt capacitors

## PPM concentration converter (mg/L, % w/w, ppmv, mg/m³, mol/L)

<a id="ppm-concentration"></a>

Folder `ppm-concentration/` · Process · Convert ppm and ppb by mass or volume, mg/L, g/L, % w/w, mol/L and mg/m³ for liquids and gases, using the density, molar mass, temperature and pressure.

### Assumptions and caveats

- In a liquid, ppm and ppb are by mass (mg/kg and µg/kg); converting them to mg/L uses the density of the whole solution, so 1 ppm equals 1 mg/L only when the density is 1 000 kg/m³.
- In a gas, ppm and ppb are by volume, which for ideal gases equals the mole fraction; mg/m³ uses the ideal gas molar volume R T / P at the stated temperature and pressure (24.45 L/mol at 25 °C and 1 atm).
- The ppm by mass in a gas is for a binary mixture with dry air (28.964 g/mol); for other carrier gases use the volume fraction and molar masses directly.
- Molarity uses the molar mass of the dissolved species as entered: for a salt that dissociates, the molar mass of the formula unit, not of one ion.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 35 g/L of sodium chloride (58.44 g/mol) in a solution of 1 025 kg/m³ is 34 146 ppm by mass, 3.415 % w/w and 0.599 mol/L. Checked by hand.
- Gas conversions reproduce the NIOSH Pocket Guide factors at 25 °C and 1 atm: 1 ppm of carbon monoxide is 1.15 mg/m³, of hydrogen sulfide 1.39 mg/m³ and of benzene 3.19 mg/m³.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above 1 % by weight the solution is usually denser than water; enter its actual density for mg/L and mol/L.
- Above about 10 bar real-gas behaviour makes mg/m³ from the ideal gas law less accurate; correct the molar volume with the compressibility factor.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Concentration: this is more than 100 % by weight of the solution; check the value, its unit and the density.
- Concentration: this is more than 100 % by volume at the stated temperature and pressure; check the value and its unit.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 35 g/L of NaCl in a 1 025 kg/m³ solution: 34 146 ppm, 3.415 % w/w, 0.5989 mol/L
  - Source: Hand calculation: w = c / ρ, molarity = c / M with M(NaCl) = 58.44 g/mol (IUPAC 2021)
- NIOSH factors at 25 °C and 1 atm: 1 ppm of CO is 1.15 mg/m³, of H₂S 1.39 mg/m³, of benzene 3.19 mg/m³ (M / 24.45)
  - Source: NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards (2005-149), conversion factors; NIOSH rounds the molar volume to 24.45 L (exact 24.465)
- Molar volume is 22.414 L/mol at 0 °C and 1 atm; 1 % by volume is 10 000 ppmv; mg/m³ round-trips to ppmv
  - Source: CODATA molar volume of an ideal gas (273.15 K, 101.325 kPa)
- 1 000 ppmv of CO₂ in air is 1 518.6 ppm by mass; in water 1 mg/L is 1 ppm; 100 mg/L of CaCO₃ is 0.999 mmol/L
  - Source: Hand calculation: w = x M / (x M + (1 − x) M_air) with M_air = 28.9644 g/mol (ISO 2533); M(CaCO₃) = 100.09 g/mol
- More than 100 % is rejected; strong solutions at the default density warn; a bad unit is rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 34 146, 3.415, 0.599 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards, DHHS (NIOSH) Publication 2005-149, Introduction: conversion of ppm to mg/m³ at 25 °C and 760 mmHg (mg/m³ = ppm × M / 24.45)
- IUPAC Compendium of Chemical Terminology (Gold Book): mass fraction, mass concentration, amount concentration
- CODATA 2018 recommended values: molar gas constant R = 8.314 462 618 J/(mol·K)

## Press tonnage calculator (punching and press brake)

<a id="press-tonnage"></a>

Folder `press-tonnage/` · Manufacturing · Punching and blanking force from perimeter, thickness and shear strength, with stripping force and press margin, and press brake air-bending tonnage.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Punching force is the sheared area (perimeter × thickness) times the ultimate shear strength, with flat-faced punches and normal clearance; shear angles on the punch or die lower the peak force, dull tools raise it.
- When only the tensile strength is known, shear strength is taken as a fraction of it: about 0.75 for wrought and alloy steels and 0.65 for aluminium alloys (Deutschman, Michels and Wilson, via Roymech); these are rough rules, so use measured shear strength where you can.
- Stripping force is entered as a share of the punching force; spring or urethane strippers load the press during the stroke, so it is added to the punching force.
- Press brake tonnage uses the makers' air-bending formula, 575 t² / V tons per foot for steel of 60 000 psi tensile strength, scaled by the tensile strength of the material; bottoming and coining need several times more.
- The margin sizes the press above the calculated load for tool wear, material variation and thickness tolerance.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 20 mm hole in 3 mm steel with 300 MPa shear strength needs π × 20 × 3 × 300 = 56.55 kN (5.77 tf, as in Durma's example); with 10 % stripping and a 20 % margin the press should have 74.64 kN. A 1/4 in plate on a 2 in V-die needs 575 × 0.0625 / 2 = 17.97 tons per foot. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The hole is smaller than the material thickness: the punch is very highly stressed and may buckle or break; check with the tooling maker.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- V-die opening V: it must be well over twice the thickness for air bending.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Durma: a 20 mm hole in 3 mm steel at τ = 300 MPa needs 56 549 N, 5.77 tonnes-force; +10 % stripping 62.20 kN; +20 % margin 74.64 kN
  - Source: Durma, How to calculate punching force (F = L t τ, worked example 56 547 N)
- US punching: 1 in hole in 1/4 in steel of 60 ksi UTS, τ = 0.75 × 60 = 45 ksi: π × 1 × 0.25 × 45 000 = 35 343 lbf = 17.67 US tons
  - Source: F = L t τ with τ ≈ 0.75 UTS for wrought steel (Deutschman et al.) (hand calculation)
- Bystronic air bending: 1/4 in mild steel (60 ksi) on a 2 in V-die needs 575 × 0.25² / 2 = 17.97 tons per foot, 179.7 tons for 10 ft; a 90 ksi material needs 1.5 times as much
  - Source: Bystronic, How to calculate press brake tonnage (575 constant, material factor UTS / 60 000 psi)
- Rectangle 1 × 2 in has a 6 in perimeter; four holes a stroke need four times the force; doubling the V-die opening halves the bending force
  - Source: F ∝ perimeter × number of holes; tonnage ∝ 1/V (formula structure)
- A hole smaller than the thickness warns; a V-die no wider than twice the thickness, zero holes and zero thickness are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 56.55 kN, 62.20 kN, 74.64 kN to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Durma (press maker), How to calculate punching force: F = L × t × τ, worked example 20 mm hole in 3 mm steel at 300 MPa = 56 547 N
- Bystronic (press brake maker), How to calculate press brake tonnage: [575 × t² / V / 12] per inch of bend, material factor = UTS / 60 000 psi, air bending factor 1.0
- Deutschman, A. D., Michels, W. A. and Wilson, C. E., Machine Design: Theory and Practice (Macmillan, 1975), ratio of ultimate shear to tensile strength (as tabulated by Roymech)

## Thin-wall pressure vessel

<a id="pressure-vessel"></a>

Folder `pressure-vessel/` · Mechanical · Hoop and longitudinal stress in cylinders and spheres, Lamé thick-wall check, ASME VIII-1 required thickness and MAWP with joint efficiency and corrosion.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Thin-wall membrane theory: stresses are uniform through the wall and the radial stress is neglected; accurate within about 5 % when the wall is at most one tenth of the radius. The Lamé maximum hoop stress at the inner surface is shown for comparison and the calculator warns when the thin-wall limit is exceeded.
- Internal gauge pressure only, on a cylinder far from its ends or on a complete sphere: stress concentrations at heads, nozzles, supports, welds and the head-to-shell junction are not evaluated; external pressure (vacuum, submergence) requires a buckling check (ASME UG-28) that is not included.
- The ASME formulas are those of Section VIII Division 1 UG-27 for the circumferential stress of cylindrical shells and for spherical shells, with R the inside radius in the corroded condition; they are valid for t ≤ R/2 and p ≤ 0.385 S E (cylinder) or p ≤ 0.665 S E (sphere), outside which Appendix 1 thick-wall formulas apply.
- The allowable stress S is the code value for the material at the design temperature (e.g. SA-516 Gr 70: 138 MPa up to about 340 °C in Division 1); the calculator does not look it up.
- Joint efficiency E reflects the weld radiography (1.0, 0.85, 0.7); the corrosion allowance is added to the required thickness and subtracted from the actual thickness for the MAWP.
- The end-cap force p π R² is the axial load carried by the heads and transferred through the shell; it sizes closures and bolted flanges but is not the flange design itself (ASME Appendix 2).
- Mill undertolerance, forming thinning, hydrotest and fatigue (ASME VIII-2 Part 5) are outside this calculator.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the 2 m × 10 mm cylinder at 10 bar gives 100 MPa hoop / 50 MPa longitudinal by thin-wall theory and 100.5 MPa by Lamé (0.5 % apart, as expected at t/R = 0.01); the ASME required thickness 7.28 mm at S = 138 MPa, E = 1 and MAWP 1.37 MPa for 10 mm were checked by hand.
- Design decision: both the textbook thin-wall stresses and the ASME code thickness are shown, because students learn the first and engineers are asked for the second.
- Design decision: the ASME validity limits (t ≤ R/2, p ≤ 0.385 S E) are checked and warned rather than silently switching to the thick-wall appendix formulas.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- t/R = … exceeds 0.1: thin-wall theory understates the inner-surface stress; use the Lamé value (… MPa).
- Outside the UG-27 validity limits (t ≤ R/2 and p ≤ 0.385 S E for cylinders, 0.665 S E for spheres): use the ASME Appendix 1 thick-wall formulas.
- As-built thickness is below the ASME required thickness for this pressure, allowable stress, joint efficiency and corrosion allowance.
- Thin-wall hoop stress exceeds S × E.
- Membrane stress only: heads, nozzles, supports, external pressure and fatigue need their own code checks.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Corrosion allowance must be less than the wall thickness

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Thin-wall cylinder 2 m × 10 mm at 10 bar: hoop σ = p R / t = 100 MPa, longitudinal 50 MPa; sphere σ = p R / 2t = 50 MPa
  - Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, 10th ed., §8-1 eqs 8-1 to 8-3
- Lamé thick-wall check: for t/R = 0.01 the inner-surface hoop stress is 100.5 MPa (0.5 % above thin-wall); for t/R = 0.5 it is 1.67 p vs 2 p thin-wall
  - Source: Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain, 8th ed., Table 13.5 case 1a: σ_hoop,max = p (b² + a²)/(b² − a²)
- ASME VIII-1 UG-27(c)(1): required t = p R / (S E − 0.6 p) = 7.28 mm at E = 1; 8.57 mm at E = 0.85; sphere UG-27(d) 3.63 mm
  - Source: ASME BPVC Section VIII Division 1, UG-27 (c)(1) and (d)
- ASME MAWP for 10 mm: S E t / (R + 0.6 t) = 13.72 bar; with 2 mm corrosion allowance the corroded 8 mm wall gives 10.98 bar and the required thickness becomes 9.28 mm
  - Source: ASME BPVC Section VIII Division 1, UG-27 (c)(1) rearranged for P; UG-25 corrosion allowance
- End-cap force p π R² = 3.142 MN at 10 bar on a 2 m vessel; stress utilisation 72.5 % of S E
  - Source: Axial equilibrium of the closed cylinder (Hibbeler §8-1 derivation of the longitudinal stress)
- Under-thickness and over-pressure are flagged: 6 mm wall at 10 bar is below the required 7.28 mm; 60 bar on 10 mm exceeds S E and the UG-27 pressure limit for E = 0.7
  - Source: ASME UG-27 limits p ≤ 0.385 S E; behaviour specification
- Unit layer: 10 bar = 145.04 psi = 1 MPa; 138 MPa = 20.0 ksi (SA-516 Gr 70 allowable)
  - Source: NIST SP 811: 1 psi = 6.894757 kPa; ASME II-D allowable 20.0 ksi
- Invalid inputs fail fast: corrosion allowance not less than the wall, zero diameter, unknown geometry
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 100 MPa, 50 MPa, 100.5 MPa, 7.28 mm, 2.7 mm, 1.37 MPa, 3.14 MN to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, 10th ed., ch. 8-1 "Thin-walled pressure vessels"
- ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section VIII Division 1 (2023), UG-27 Thickness of shells under internal pressure, UG-16 minimum thickness, UG-25 corrosion allowance, UW-12 joint efficiencies
- Young, Budynas & Sadegh, Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain, 8th ed., Table 13.5 (thick-walled cylinders, Lamé)
- ASME Section II Part D, allowable stresses (e.g. SA-516 Gr 70: 20.0 ksi = 138 MPa)

## Soil compaction calculator (Proctor relative compaction)

<a id="proctor-compaction"></a>

Folder `proctor-compaction/` · Civil · Field dry density from wet density and moisture, relative compaction against the Proctor maximum, saturation, air voids and the zero-air-voids density.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The wet density and moisture content come from a field test such as the sand cone (ASTM D1556) or the nuclear gauge (ASTM D6938), and the oven moisture content is preferred to a gauge reading.
- The maximum dry density and optimum moisture come from a laboratory compaction test on the same soil: standard Proctor (ASTM D698, 600 kN·m/m³) or modified Proctor (ASTM D1557, 2 700 kN·m/m³).
- The density of water is 1 000 kg/m³ (62.43 lb/ft³). The specific gravity of solids should be measured (ASTM D854); 2.65 to 2.75 is typical of most soils.
- Oversize particles removed from the laboratory sample need the rock correction of ASTM D4718 before the relative compaction is meaningful.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a wet density of 124.0 lb/ft³ at 12.0 % moisture gives a dry density of 110.7 lb/ft³, 96.3 % of a 115.0 lb/ft³ maximum; with G_s = 2.70 the void ratio is 0.522, saturation 62.0 % and the zero-air-voids density 127.3 lb/ft³. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The degree of saturation is above 100 %: the density, the moisture content or G_s is wrong, because a soil cannot lie above the zero-air-voids curve.
- Relative compaction above 105 %: check that the Proctor test is for the same soil and effort, or apply the oversize correction.
- The Proctor maximum lies above the zero-air-voids curve for this G_s: G_s is probably too low.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Field dry density: it is at or above the density of the solid grains (G_s × 1 000 kg/m³), which is impossible; check the density and G_s.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Wet 124.0 lb/ft³ at 12 %: dry 124/1.12 = 110.71 lb/ft³, 96.3 % of 115.0; e = 2.70 × 62.43/110.71 − 1 = 0.522; S = 0.12 × 2.70/0.522 = 62.0 %
  - Source: Hand calculation: ρ_d = ρ/(1 + w), e = G_s ρ_w/ρ_d − 1, S e = w G_s (Das & Sobhan, Principles of Geotechnical Engineering, ch. 3)
- Zero-air-voids density: G_s 2.68 at w 20 % is 2 680/1.536 = 1 744.8 kg/m³ (17.12 kN/m³); G_s 2.72 at 10 % is 133.5 lb/ft³
  - Source: Das & Sobhan, ch. 6: γ_zav = G_s γ_w / (1 + w G_s); hand calculation
- A soil compacted to the zero-air-voids density is 100 % saturated with no air voids; air voids equal n (1 − S) in general
  - Source: Definition of the zero-air-voids curve; V_a = n (1 − S)
- Dry-density input gives the same results as the wet density ρ_d (1 + w); saturation at the Proctor optimum 115.0 lb/ft³ and 11.5 % is 66.7 %
  - Source: Consistency; hand calculation S = w G_s / (G_s ρ_w/ρ_d,max − 1)
- Low compaction fails; a dry density above G_s ρ_w is refused; a point above the zero-air-voids curve warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 110.7 lb/ft³, 96.3 %, 0.522, 62.0 %, 127.3 lb/ft³ to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASTM D698-12(2021), Standard Test Methods for Laboratory Compaction Characteristics of Soil Using Standard Effort (12 400 ft-lbf/ft³ (600 kN-m/m³)), and ASTM D1557-12(2021) for modified effort (56 000 ft-lbf/ft³ (2 700 kN-m/m³))
- Das, B.M. and Sobhan, K., Principles of Geotechnical Engineering, 9th ed., Cengage, ch. 3 Weight–Volume Relationships and ch. 6 Soil Compaction (zero-air-void unit weight)
- ASTM D1556/D1556M Density and Unit Weight of Soil in Place by Sand-Cone Method; ASTM D6938 In-Place Density and Water Content by Nuclear Methods

## Propeller pitch and boat speed calculator

<a id="prop-pitch-speed"></a>

Folder `prop-pitch-speed/` · Maritime · Boat speed from propeller pitch, engine rpm, gear ratio and slip; the pitch for a target speed; or the propeller slip from your GPS speed.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Pitch is the nominal pitch stamped on the propeller (the second number of 14 × 19 is 19 in of pitch). Cupped and progressive-pitch propellers behave as if their pitch were somewhat larger.
- The gear ratio is engine turns per propeller turn (2.0:1 means the propeller turns at half the engine rpm). Use the lower-unit or gearbox ratio from the engine manual.
- Slip here is apparent slip: the shortfall of the measured speed against pitch × propeller rpm. It mixes propeller slip with wake, current and the error of the speed reading, so measure with GPS on runs both ways in calm water.
- The required pitch keeps the engine at the chosen rpm only if the propeller can absorb the engine power there; a larger pitch loads the engine and pulls the rpm down. Aim for the top of the rated rpm range at wide-open throttle.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 19 in pitch, 5 500 engine rpm through 2.0:1 gives 2 750 propeller rpm and 43.0 kn theoretical; at 12 % slip 37.8 kn; 37 kn on GPS means 13.9 % slip. Checked by hand (V = pitch[in] × rpm / 1 215.2).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Negative slip: the boat is faster than pitch × rpm allows. Check the gear ratio, the pitch, the rpm reading and any following current.
- Slip above 50 %: check the gear ratio and the rpm, or look for a damaged or ventilating propeller.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 19 in pitch at 5 500 engine rpm through 2.0:1: 2 750 propeller rpm, 43.0 kn theoretical, 37.8 kn at 12 % slip
  - Source: Gerr, The Propeller Handbook: V = pitch × rpm; US rule V[kn] = pitch[in] × rpm / 1 215.2; hand calculation
- Ship check: 6 m pitch at 100 rpm direct drive is 36 000 m/h = 19.438 kn (the propeller-slip calculator's example)
  - Source: MAN, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion (apparent slip); 1 nmi = 1 852 m
- Slip from GPS: 37 kn against 43.0 kn theoretical is 13.9 % apparent slip
  - Source: Slip = 1 − V / (pitch × rpm); hand calculation
- Pitch for 40 kn at 2 750 propeller rpm and 12 % slip is 20.1 in; feeding it back gives 40 kn
  - Source: P = V / ((1 − s) n); consistency check
- Negative slip warns; zero rpm and a gear ratio of 0.2 are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2 750 rpm, 43.0 kn, 37.8 kn to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- D. Gerr, The Propeller Handbook (International Marine, 1989): pitch, apparent slip and the theoretical speed pitch × rpm
- MAN Energy Solutions, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion (2018): apparent and real slip ratio

## Wageningen B-series propeller

<a id="propeller-bseries"></a>

Folder `propeller-bseries/` · Maritime · Wageningen B-series KT, KQ and efficiency from the 1975 polynomials at a given J, or the optimum pitch ratio and rpm for a thrust and diameter; Keller check.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The polynomials (39 KT and 47 KQ terms in J, P/D, A_E/A_0 and Z) are the Oosterveld & van Oossanen (1975) regression of the 120 B-series models at Rn = 2·10⁶; validity Z 2–7, A_E/A_0 0.30–1.05, P/D 0.5–1.4, J ≥ 0; Helma (2019) shows unphysical behaviour at high P/D with few blades, so results near the edges deserve a check against the published diagrams.
- Full-scale correction by the ITTC-1978 section-drag method as used in Holtrop & Mennen (1982): ΔC_D = (2 + 4 t/c)[0.003605 − (1.89 + 1.62 log10(c/k_p))^−2.5] with chord c_0.75 = 2.073 (A_E/A_0) D/Z, t/c = (0.0185 − 0.00125 Z) D/c, blade roughness k_p = 30 µm; ΔKT = +0.3 ΔC_D (P/D) cZ/D, ΔKQ = −0.25 ΔC_D cZ/D. The model values are also reported.
- Open water only: the propeller works behind the hull in a wake, so the speed of advance V_A = V (1 − w) must be entered and the relative-rotative efficiency and thrust deduction come from the hull (Holtrop–Mennen calculator).
- Design mode maximises open-water efficiency for the given diameter: for each P/D the operating J solves KT(J) = (T/(ρ V_A² D²)) J², and the P/D with the highest η_O is taken; the diameter is not optimised (a larger diameter at lower rpm is usually better until clearance limits).
- Cavitation is only screened with Keller's formula A_E/A_0 ≥ K + (1.3 + 0.3 Z) T/(D² (p_0 − p_v + ρ g h)) with p_0 − p_v = 99 047 Pa (15 °C sea water); K = 0.2 single screw, 0–0.1 twin screw. A proper check needs a cavitation diagram (Burrill) or lifting-line analysis.
- Standard B-series geometry: 15° rake, blade outlines and thickness of the series; skewed or tip-modified modern propellers differ by a few per cent in KQ.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: coefficient table checked term by term against two independent copies of the 1975 table (Fossen's Marine Systems Simulator WageningData.txt and the UMich Lie-MPC-AMVs copy); the Holtrop & Mennen (1982) example propeller (Z 4, A_E/A_0 0.7393 from Keller, D 8 m, V_A 9.538 m/s, T 2172.75 kN) is reproduced to about 1 %: ΔC_D 0.000956, c_0.75 3.065 m and t/c 0.03524 exactly; at the paper's operating point (n 1.6594 Hz, KT 0.18802) the polynomials give KQ 0.03296 (paper 0.033275, −0.95 %) and η_O 0.6523 (paper 0.6461); because the efficiency curve is flat (0.648–0.652 for P/D 0.90–1.10) the design optimum lands at P/D 1.017 and 1.683 Hz instead of the paper's ≈ 1.037 and 1.659 Hz — a 1.4 % rpm difference with the same thrust.
- Design decision: the ITTC-1978 ΔC_D route is used for scale effects instead of the 1975 paper's Reynolds-number correction polynomials, because it is what the Holtrop example uses and it needs only the blade roughness.
- Design decision: the P/D search is a coarse 0.01 sweep refined to 0.001 around the best value; J is solved by bisection on a function that is monotone in J.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- KT ≤ 0: the propeller is windmilling (J beyond the zero-thrust advance ratio).
- Blade area below the Keller minimum for this thrust and immersion: cavitation likely; increase A_E/A_0 and recompute (efficiency falls slightly).
- Optimum at the upper P/D limit of the series (1.4): the propeller is lightly loaded — a smaller diameter or higher rpm may be intended.
- Optimum at the lower P/D limit (0.5): heavily loaded — a larger diameter would help.
- High P/D with few blades: Helma (2019) shows the 1975 polynomials misbehave here; check against the open-water diagrams.
- Full-scale correction applied: ΔC_D = … (ITTC-1978, k_p … µm); model values shown separately.
- Open-water values: behind the hull multiply by η_R and use V_A = V (1 − w); cavitation is only screened by Keller\'s formula.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- No B-series propeller of this diameter produces the thrust at V_A … m/s (thrust loading K = … too high): increase the diameter or blade area

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Coefficient table: 39 KT and 47 KQ terms with the published first and last entries (0.00880496 … −0.00146564; 0.00379368 … 0.0000554194) and exponents within s ≤ 3, t ≤ 6, u ≤ 2, v ≤ 2
  - Source: Oosterveld & van Oossanen (1975) Table; reproduced in Fossen MSS WageningData.txt and Carlton Table 6.6
- ITTC-1978 correction for the example propeller: c_0.75 = 3.065 m, t/c = 0.03524, ΔC_D = 0.000956
  - Source: Holtrop & Mennen (1982) example (c_0.75 3.065 m, t/c 0.03524, ΔC_D 0.000956)
- Holtrop & Mennen example propeller (T 2172.75 kN, V_A 9.538 m/s, D 8 m): at the paper's point n = 1.6594 Hz, KT = 0.18802 the polynomials give P/D ≈ 1.037, KQ within 1.2 % of 0.033275 and η_O within 1.2 % of 0.6461; the design optimum (flat η curve) is within 2.5 % in rpm and 1.5 % in η_O
  - Source: Holtrop & Mennen (1982) example, "From the B-series polynomials" block (KT 0.18802, n 1.6594 Hz, KQ 0.033275, η_O 0.6461)
- Keller: K 0.2, Z 4, T 2172.75 kN, D 8 m, h 5.8 m, p0 − pv 99 047 Pa → A_E/A_0 = 0.7393 (the paper's value)
  - Source: Keller formula as given in Holtrop & Mennen (1982) §4
- Point mode at the design optimum returns the same KT, KQ and η_O; model-scale values have lower KT and higher KQ than full scale
  - Source: Consistency between modes; ITTC-1978 sign convention (ΔKT > 0, ΔKQ < 0 for a smoother full-scale blade)
- B4-70 at P/D 1.0 (model scale): KT falls monotonically from J 0 to 0.9, KT(0) between 0.35 and 0.50, zero thrust near J ≈ 1.0–1.15, peak η_O between 0.60 and 0.72
  - Source: Shape of the published B4-70 open-water diagram (van Lammeren et al. 1969; Bernitsas et al. 1981)
- Optimum search: a lighter loading (half the thrust) gives a higher optimum P/D and efficiency; a 2 m propeller for the same thrust is heavily loaded (η_O below 0.35, rpm far higher)
  - Source: B-series behaviour: efficiency rises and the optimum pitch increases as thrust loading falls
- Invalid inputs fail fast: fractional blade count, blade area outside 0.30–1.05, P/D outside 0.5–1.4
  - Source: Validity ranges of the 1975 polynomials (Z 2–7, A_E/A_0 0.30–1.05, P/D 0.5–1.4)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 3.065 m, 0.0352, 0.000956, 0.739 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- M. M. Bernitsas, D. Ray & P. Kinley, "KT, KQ and efficiency curves for the Wageningen B-series propellers", Univ. of Michigan report 237 (1981); T. I. Fossen, Marine Systems Simulator (github.com/cybergalactic/MSS, WageningData.txt) — reproductions of the table

## Propeller curve and light running margin

<a id="propeller-curve"></a>

Folder `propeller-curve/` · Maritime · Engine SMCR from the propeller design point with sea, engine and light running margins, the propeller curves, and the heavy running of a measured point.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Fixed pitch propeller on the propeller law P = c n³: at a constant advance ratio the torque coefficient is constant and power varies with the cube of the rpm (Everllence project guide 2.03).
- The propeller design point PD (design speed, clean hull, calm weather, design draft) lies on the light propeller curve (line 6); the specified MCR follows Everllence eqs 2.01.01 and 2.01.02: SMCR power = PD power × (100 + SM)/(100 − EM), SMCR rpm = PD rpm × (SMCR power/PD power)^(1/3) × (1 − LRM/100). The engine layout curve (lines 1 and 2, heavy running) passes through the SMCR.
- Light running margin as in eq. 2.01.02: at a given power the layout curve rpm is (1 − LRM) times the light curve rpm. Everllence recommends 4–7 %, up to 10 % in special cases (adverse weather, blunt bows, shaft generators, ice class); sea margin traditionally about 15 % of the PD power; engine margin 10–15 % (service at 90 or 85 % load).
- Heavy running of a measured point = 1 − n/n_light(P): the rpm deficit against the light curve at the same power, from fouling, weather or a deeper draft; the margin left to the layout curve = n/n_layout(P) − 1, negative when the point is heavier than the engine layout allows for.
- Sea-trial check: the light curve rpm at SMCR power should not exceed 110 % of the SMCR rpm (line 9; also at most 107 % of the L1 rpm, which needs the engine rating table). Torsional vibration, barred speed ranges and the torque/speed limit (line 4) need the engine data.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: PD 7000 kW at 80 rpm with 15 % sea margin, 10 % engine margin and 5 % LRM gives SMCR 8944.4 kW at 82.47 rpm, a service point of 8050 kW at 79.62 rpm and a light curve rpm of 86.81 (105.3 % of SMCR rpm) at full power.
- Design decision: the exponent is fixed at 3 (the propeller law); the steeper P ∝ V⁴ relation at elevated speeds concerns ship speed, not rpm, and is not used here.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A light running margin of … % is outside the Everllence recommendation of 4–7 %, up to 10 % in special cases.
- The light curve reaches … % of the SMCR speed at full power, above the 110 % sea-trial limit of the standard load diagram (line 9): a lower light running margin, or an extended load diagram on a speed-derated engine, is needed.
- The measured point is heavier than the engine layout curve: the light running margin is used up by fouling, weather or draft; check the torque/speed limit (line 4) and plan a hull and propeller cleaning.
- The measured point has used … % of the light running margin.
- The measured point is lighter than the design light curve: likely a lighter draft than the design point (ballast) or a measurement error.
- Below 50 % load the light running margin recommendation no longer applies; compare heavy running between 50 and 100 % load.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- SMCR from PD 7000 kW at 80 rpm with 15 % sea margin, 10 % engine margin and 5 % LRM: 8944.4 kW at 82.47 rpm
  - Source: Everllence project guide 2.01, eqs 2.01.01 and 2.01.02
- Service propulsion point at 90 % SMCR power on the layout curve: 8050 kW (PD + 15 %) at 79.62 rpm
  - Source: Everllence project guide 2.01: SP = PD with sea margin, placed on the engine layout curve
- At the same rpm the layout curve needs 1/(1 − LRM)³ times the light curve power: at 100 % SMCR rpm the light curve gives 0.95³ = 85.74 % of SMCR power
  - Source: Propeller law P = c n³ with the light running margin of eq. 2.01.02
- Sea trial: the clean ship reaches 1/(1 − LRM) of the SMCR speed at full power, 105.26 % for 5 %; 10 % LRM gives 111.1 %, above the 110 % limit of line 9
  - Source: Everllence project guide 2.03, line 9 (110 % of SMCR rpm at sea trial)
- A measured point on the light curve runs 0 % heavy with LRM/(1 − LRM) = 5.26 % margin left; on the layout curve it runs 5 % heavy with no margin left
  - Source: Heavy running = 1 − n/n_light(P); margin = n/n_layout(P) − 1
- A point heavier than the layout curve (8000 kW at 76 rpm) has a negative margin of 4.35 % and is flagged
  - Source: Everllence project guide 2.03: heavy running moves the propeller curve towards line 2 and beyond
- Invalid inputs are rejected: zero design power, an engine margin above 50 %, negative speed
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 8944 kW, 82.47 rpm, 8050 kW, 79.62 rpm, 86.81 rpm, 105.3 %, 2.3 %, 2.9 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

## Propeller slip and speed through water

<a id="propeller-slip"></a>

Folder `propeller-slip/` · Maritime · Theoretical propeller speed, apparent and real slip, speed through water and speed of advance from pitch, RPM and observed speed.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Pitch is the mean face pitch of a fixed-pitch propeller; for a controllable-pitch propeller use the pitch at the current setting and compare like with like.
- Apparent slip mixes propeller behaviour with current, wind, waves and the accuracy of the speed input; it is a trend indicator, not a measure of propeller efficiency.
- Speed through water is speed over ground minus a single along-track current; cross currents are ignored. A calibrated speed log reading can be entered as the observed speed with zero current.
- The wake fraction is an input, not a prediction (single-screw 0.20–0.35, twin-screw 0.10–0.20); with w = 0 the real slip equals the slip through water.
- Negative apparent slip is physically possible (following current or sea) and is reported with a warning rather than rejected.
- Revolutions per mile are referred to speed over ground, as kept in most engine logs.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: theoretical speed uses the exact nautical mile (6 m pitch × 100 rpm = 36 000 m/h = 19.4384 kn); slip definitions follow MAN "Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion".
- Design decision: three slips are reported (apparent vs speed over ground, through water, real vs speed of advance) because noon reports and model-test reports mean different things by "slip".
- Design decision: negative slip is allowed with a warning rather than rejected, since following seas and currents produce it legitimately.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Negative apparent slip: the ship is moving faster than pitch × rpm. Typical of a following current or sea, or a wrong pitch/rpm.
- Speed through water is negative — the current exceeds the speed over ground. Check the sign of the current.
- Apparent slip above 40 % is unusual in service — check pitch, rpm and speed.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Observed speed must not be negative

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Pitch 6 m at 100 rpm gives 36 000 m/h = 19.438 kn theoretical speed
  - Source: Vt = P × N × 60 / 1852 — D.A. Taylor, Introduction to Marine Engineering, 2nd ed. (1996), ch. "Propellers"; 1 nmi = 1852 m
- Pitch 6 m, 90 rpm, observed 14 kn → Vt 17.495 kn, apparent slip 19.98 %
  - Source: Apparent slip S_A = (p·n − V) / (p·n) — MAN Energy Solutions, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion (2018), "Slip ratio"
- Speed mode: 10 % apparent slip on Vt 17.495 kn gives 15.745 kn
  - Source: V = Vt × (1 − S_A), rearranged from the slip definition
- A 2 kn following current: STW 12 kn, slip through water 31.41 %
  - Source: STW = SOG − current (Bowditch, American Practical Navigator, 2019 ed., ch. "Dead Reckoning"); slip definition as above
- Wake fraction 0.25 on STW 12 kn: speed of advance 9.0 kn, real slip 48.56 %
  - Source: Va = V (1 − w); real slip S_R = (p·n − Va) / (p·n) — Carlton, Marine Propellers and Propulsion, 4th ed., ch. 5; MAN Basic Principles (2018)
- Observed 18 kn against Vt 17.495 kn gives negative slip −2.89 % and a warning
  - Source: Negative slip case — Taylor, Introduction to Marine Engineering (1996), "Propeller slip"
- 90 rpm at 14 kn over ground = 385.7 propeller revolutions per nautical mile
  - Source: Revolutions per mile = N × 60 / V — standard engine-log check (Reeds Vol. 12, Motor Engineering Knowledge, "Engine performance")
- Unit layer: a 20 ft pitch is 6.096 m; 100 rpm = 10.472 rad/s
  - Source: 1 ft = 0.3048 m exactly (1959 international yard and pound agreement)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero rpm, negative pitch, unknown mode
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 17.49 kn, 419.9 nmi, 19.98 %, 19.98 %, 19.98 %, 336 nmi, 385.7 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

## Pump and fan affinity laws

<a id="pump-affinity"></a>

Folder `pump-affinity/` · Mechanical · Flow, head or pressure and power at a new speed or impeller diameter from one known operating point, with efficiency and specific speed.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Efficiency is assumed unchanged at the scaled point; this holds within about ±25 % speed change and for trims above 80–85 % of the full impeller diameter.
- The laws move the pump or fan curve, not the duty point: with static head in the system the new operating point must be found from the intersection with the system curve.
- Impeller trimming uses the industry approximation Q ∝ D, H ∝ D², P ∝ D³ (same casing); geometric scaling of a similar machine uses Q ∝ D³, H ∝ D², P ∝ D⁵. Trims below 75 % are flagged as unreliable.
- NPSH required rises roughly with the square of speed; cavitation margin must be rechecked after a speed increase.
- Fan laws assume incompressible flow (pressure rise below about 10 kPa); density affects only the hydraulic power and efficiency outputs here.
- Specific speed n_q uses the European convention (rpm, m³/s, m); the US Ns in gpm and ft is 51.6 × n_q.
- Not applicable to positive-displacement pumps, whose flow follows speed but whose pressure is set by the system.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Design decision: two diameter laws are offered because impeller trimming (Q ∝ D) and geometric scaling (Q ∝ D³) are routinely confused; trimming is the default since that is what happens to an existing pump.
- Verification 2026-10-30: the 1 450 → 1 750 rpm case was checked by hand (×1.2069, ×1.4566, ×1.7580) and the specific speed against the radial-flow range in Gülich.
- Design decision: efficiency at the known point is reported so an inconsistent input set (hydraulic power above shaft power) is flagged before the laws are applied.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Hydraulic power exceeds shaft power — the known point is inconsistent (check units of flow, head and power).
- Efficiency below 20 % is very low for a centrifugal machine — check the known point.
- Trim below 75 % of the full impeller: the Q ∝ D approximation is unreliable and efficiency drops several points. Consult the pump curve.
- Diameter larger than the known impeller: trimming laws only apply to reducing a diameter within the same casing.
- Large speed change: efficiency is not constant far from the design point, and NPSH required rises with the square of speed.
- Pressure rise above 10 kPa: gas compressibility starts to matter and the simple fan laws lose accuracy.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Flow and power must not be negative
- Head must not be negative
- Pressure rise must not be negative

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Speed 1 450 → 1 750 rpm: Q × 1.2069, H × 1.4566, P × 1.7580 (200 m³/h, 50 m, 35 kW → 241.4 m³/h, 72.8 m, 61.5 kW)
  - Source: Affinity laws Q ∝ N, H ∝ N², P ∝ N³ — ANSI/HI 14.3 Rotodynamic Pumps for Design and Application; Karassik et al., Pump Handbook, 4th ed., §2.3
- Impeller trim 250 → 225 mm (ratio 0.9) at constant speed: Q × 0.9, H × 0.81, P × 0.729
  - Source: Trimming approximation Q ∝ D, H ∝ D², P ∝ D³ — Karassik, Pump Handbook, 4th ed., §2.3 "Impeller diameter change"; Gülich, Centrifugal Pumps, 3rd ed., §4.5.1
- Geometrically similar machine, diameter × 2 at the same speed: Q × 8, H × 4, P × 32
  - Source: Similarity laws Q ∝ N D³, H ∝ N² D², P ∝ N³ D⁵ — Gülich, Centrifugal Pumps, 3rd ed., §3.4; White, Fluid Mechanics, §11.3 (pump similarity rules)
- Hydraulic power ρ g Q H = 27.24 kW for 200 m³/h at 50 m; efficiency 77.8 % with 35 kW shaft power
  - Source: P_hyd = ρ g Q H — Karassik, Pump Handbook, 4th ed., §2.1; g = 9.80665 m/s²
- Fan: 10 m³/s at 1 000 Pa with 12 kW, speed × 1.2 → 12 m³/s, 1 440 Pa, 20.74 kW; efficiency 83.3 %
  - Source: Fan laws (same as pump affinity laws, pressure in place of head) — ASHRAE Handbook, HVAC Systems and Equipment, ch. 21 "Fans"
- Specific speed n_q = 1 450 × √0.0556 / 50^0.75 = 18.2 (radial-flow range 10–30)
  - Source: n_q definition (rpm, m³/s, m) — Gülich, Centrifugal Pumps, 3rd ed., eq. 3.4; radial impellers n_q ≈ 10–30
- Warnings: trim below 75 % and hydraulic power above shaft power are flagged
  - Source: Trim limit guidance — Karassik, Pump Handbook, 4th ed., §2.3 (trims beyond 20–25 % not recommended)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero speed, zero diameter, unknown law
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.207, 241.4 m³/h, 72.8 m, 61.5 kW, 27.2 kW, 77.8 %, 18.2 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

## Pump NPSH and suction lift

<a id="pump-npsh"></a>

Folder `pump-npsh/` · Mechanical · NPSH available from suction conditions, vapour pressure and losses, margin against NPSH required and the maximum suction lift.

### Assumptions and caveats

- NPSH available is computed by the Hydraulic Institute definition NPSHa = (p_abs − p_v)/(ρ g) + z_s − h_f with p_abs the absolute pressure on the liquid surface (atmospheric plus any vessel gauge pressure), p_v the vapour pressure at the pumping temperature, z_s the liquid level above the pump impeller centreline (negative for a suction lift) and h_f the friction and fitting losses of the suction line at the duty flow (from the pipe-flow calculator); the velocity head is not added because NPSHr is defined on the same basis.
- Vapour pressure of water from the IAPWS-IF97 region-4 saturation equation (the steam-table formulation, 0.01–100 °C used here, accurate to 0.01 %); for other liquids or seawater (vapour pressure about 2 % lower than fresh water) enter the vapour pressure directly.
- NPSH required is the pump maker's 3 % head-drop value (NPSH3) at the duty flow; the recommended margin follows ANSI/HI 9.6.1 — at least 0.6–1 m or a ratio of 1.1–1.3 depending on the energy level of the pump — and the user sets it. A margin met on paper can still cavitate with air entrainment, pre-rotation or hot liquid.
- Maximum suction lift is the static lift at which NPSHa just equals NPSHr plus the chosen margin; it falls with temperature, altitude and friction, and the practical limit for cold water is 6–7 m even though the theoretical limit at sea level is about 10 m.
- Suction specific speed (US customary, rpm · √gpm / ft^0.75) is a design-quality index of the pump: values above about 11 000 indicate a pump prone to recirculation at part load (HI historic guidance 8 500–11 000); it needs the duty flow and speed.
- Thoma cavitation number σ = NPSHr/H compares the required NPSH with the pump head; it is informative only.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: IF97 gives 2.339 kPa at 20 °C, 19.95 kPa at 60 °C, 70.18 kPa at 90 °C and 101.42 kPa at 100 °C (steam tables); the theoretical suction lift of 20 °C water at sea level is (101.325 − 2.339)/(998 × 9.81) = 10.1 m, the textbook figure; a 3 m lift with 1 m of friction gives NPSHa 6.1 m, and that layout reaches NPSHa = NPSHr at about 71 °C.
- Design decision: the vapour pressure can be taken from IF97 (water) or entered, because marine pumps handle seawater, fuel and lubricating oil as well.
- Design decision: NPSHr margin is entered both as an absolute value and a ratio and the stricter one is applied, following the two forms used in HI 9.6.1.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Hot water: the vapour pressure rises steeply (19.9 kPa at 60 °C, 70 kPa at 90 °C) — small temperature changes move NPSHa by metres; consider a flooded suction or a booster pump.
- Suction lift above 6 m: rarely workable in practice even when the arithmetic allows it (priming, air leakage, transients).
- Suction specific speed … above 11 000: the pump may suffer suction recirculation at part load (HI guidance).
- Closed vessel: the surface pressure includes the gauge pressure entered — for a liquid at its boiling point in the vessel (deaerator, condenser) the pressure head term vanishes and only the static head remains.
- Friction loss must be the suction-line loss at the duty flow (pipe-flow calculator), including strainer, foot valve and entrance losses.
- NPSHr is the maker\'s 3 % head-drop value; incipient cavitation starts at 2–5 times NPSH3, so margins per ANSI/HI 9.6.1 are advisable.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Surface pressure … kPa does not exceed the vapour pressure … kPa: the liquid is boiling at the surface

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- IAPWS-IF97 saturation pressure of water: 0.6117 kPa at 0.01 °C, 2.3393 at 20 °C, 7.3849 at 40 °C, 19.947 at 60 °C, 70.182 at 90 °C, 101.42 at 100 °C (steam tables)
  - Source: IAPWS-IF97 region 4 eq. 30; IAPWS steam tables (triple point 611.657 Pa; 100 °C → 101.42 kPa on ITS-90)
- Theoretical lift of 20 °C water at sea level: (101.325 − 2.339)/(998 × 9.81) = 10.1 m; with a 3 m lift and 1 m friction NPSHa = 6.1 m, margin 3.1 m, ratio 2.0 → OK
  - Source: Karassik Pump Handbook ch. 2 (NPSHa definition, ≈ 10 m theoretical lift); ANSI/HI 9.6.1 margin forms
- Maximum lift: NPSHr 3 m with margin max(1 m, ×1.2 = 0.6 m) → required 4 m; z_max = −(4 + 1 − 10.11) = 5.1 m lift; at 90 °C the pressure head is only 3.3 m so a flooded suction of 1.7 m is needed
  - Source: Rearranged NPSHa definition; vapour pressure of water at 90 °C 70.1 kPa (ρ 965 kg/m³)
- Closed vessel: 50 kPa gauge adds 5.1 m of head; a vessel under 50 kPa vacuum removes it; surface pressure below the vapour pressure is rejected (boiling)
  - Source: Absolute surface pressure = atmospheric + gauge (HI 9.6.1)
- Temperature at which NPSHa falls to NPSHr for the cold-water layout: pressure head must drop to 7 m, i.e. p_v ≈ 32.8 kPa, about 71 °C; the solver finds the root where NPSHa = NPSHr
  - Source: Bisection on the IF97 vapour pressure; steam tables 70 °C 31.2 kPa, 72 °C 34.0 kPa
- Suction specific speed and Thoma: 1450 rpm, 100 m³/h (440.3 gpm), NPSHr 3 m (9.84 ft) → N_ss = 1450 × √440.3 / 9.84^0.75 = 5 480; σ = 3/40 = 0.075; both null when the flow or head is zero
  - Source: Karassik ch. 2: N_ss = n √Q / NPSHr^0.75 in rpm, US gpm, ft; Thoma σ = NPSHr/H
- Custom liquid: entering 2.34 kPa directly reproduces the water case; invalid inputs fail fast (zero NPSHr, temperature outside 1–100 °C, unknown liquid)
  - Source: Consistency and validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2.34 kPa, 10.1 m, 6.1 m, 3.1 m, 5.1 m, 10.1 m, 5 480 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ANSI/HI 9.6.1-2017, Rotodynamic Pumps — Guideline for NPSH Margin; ANSI/HI 14.6 performance acceptance tests (NPSH3 definition)
- I. J. Karassik et al., Pump Handbook, 4th ed. (McGraw-Hill 2008), ch. 2 and 11 — NPSH, suction lift, suction specific speed

## Pump power calculator

<a id="pump-power"></a>

Folder `pump-power/` · Mechanical · Hydraulic, shaft and electrical power of a pump from flow and head or pressure, with efficiencies, the next standard motor size and the energy cost.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Head is the total dynamic head the pump adds (static lift plus friction and minor losses plus any pressure difference), in metres of the pumped liquid; a pressure rise converts with H = Δp / (ρ g).
- Pump efficiency comes from the pump curve at the duty point: roughly 40–60 % for small centrifugal pumps, 70–85 % for large ones. Motor efficiency follows the IEC 60034-30-1 class: about 85–96 % from 1 to 100 kW (IE3).
- The motor is the next IEC 60072 rated output at or above the shaft power plus the chosen margin; a margin of 10–20 % covers operation away from the duty point and viscosity changes.
- Viscous liquids lower the pump efficiency below its water rating (ANSI/HI 9.6.7); correct the efficiency for oils.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 50 m³/h of water against 30 m at 70 % pump and 90 % motor efficiency: at 998 kg/m³ hydraulic 4.08 kW, shaft 5.83 kW, input 6.47 kW, motor 7.5 kW with 10 % margin. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Pump efficiency below 40 %: check the duty point on the pump curve; a better-matched pump may save a lot of energy.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 50 m³/h of water (998 kg/m³) against 30 m: hydraulic 4.08 kW, shaft 5.83 kW at 70 %, input 6.47 kW at 90 %, 7.5 kW motor
  - Source: P_h = ρ g Q H; IEC 60072-1 rated outputs (5.5, 7.5 kW)
- US: 100 gpm against 100 ft at 60 % needs Q H SG / (3 960 η) = 4.20 hp brake horsepower
  - Source: Hydraulic Institute BHP formula, SG 0.998
- Pressure duty: 3 bar at 10 L/s is 3 kW of hydraulic power (Q Δp); head 30.6 m of water
  - Source: P_h = Q Δp; H = Δp / (ρ g)
- Energy: 6.47 kW for 4 000 h is 25.9 MWh; at 0.15 per kWh, 3 884 a year
  - Source: E = P t
- A low pump efficiency warns; zero flow and an efficiency above 95 % are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 4.08 kW, 5.83 kW, 6.47 kW to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ANSI/HI 14.6 and Europump/Hydraulic Institute, Pump Life Cycle Costs (P = ρ g Q H / η)
