## Quarter-mile ET and trap speed calculator

<a id="quarter-mile"></a>

Folder `quarter-mile/` · Automotive · Estimated quarter-mile elapsed time and trap speed from weight and horsepower, with eighth-mile time and speed and the weight-to-power ratio.

### Assumptions and caveats

- ET = K_t (W / hp)^(1/3) and mph = K_v (hp / W)^(1/3) are empirical fits to drag-strip results, with W the race weight in lb (car, driver and fuel) and hp the flywheel horsepower; they assume good traction, a prepared track and a competent launch.
- Real results scatter around the estimate: launch, tyres, gearing, aerodynamics, altitude and weather can move the ET by several tenths.
- Eighth-mile figures follow from the constant-power model behind the cube-root formulas: distance grows with t^1.5, so ET_1/8 = ET_1/4 / 1.587 and the eighth-mile speed is the quarter-mile speed / 1.260; real ratios differ slightly with traction and drag.
- Wheel horsepower is converted to flywheel horsepower with hp_crank = hp_wheel / (1 − loss) before the formulas are applied.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 3 500 lb and 400 hp with the Hale constants: 8.75 lb/hp, ET 12.00 s, 113.6 mph; eighth mile 7.56 s and 90.1 mph. Checked by hand.
- The ideal constant-power quarter mile (no drag, no wheelspin) has K_t = 4.803 (McCaul 2014, from 1 320 ft, g and 550 ft·lbf/s); the empirical constants are higher because real cars lose time at the launch.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Below 1.5 lb per hp the car is in pro drag-racing territory, where traction limits the run and the empirical formulas were not fitted.
- Above 40 lb per hp the estimate is rough; the formulas were fitted to performance cars.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 3 500 lb and 400 hp (Hale): ET = 5.825 × 8.75^(1/3) = 12.00 s, trap 234 / 8.75^(1/3) = 113.6 mph
  - Source: McCaul 2014, Table 2 (Patrick Hale / Quarter Jr. K_t = 5.825, K_v = 234.0); hand calculation
- ET × mph is the constant of each formula, whatever the car: 1 363 for Hale, 1 409 for Huntington
  - Source: McCaul 2014, Table 2, column CONSTANT (1 363 Hale, 1 409 Huntington)
- 2005 Mustang GT, 300 hp and 3 673 lb, ran 13.7 s at 103 mph; Hale predicts 13.43 s and 101.5 mph, within 2.1 %
  - Source: McCaul 2014, Table 3 (road-test figures of 2005–2006 cars)
- Eighth mile at constant power: ET_1/4 / ET_1/8 = 2^(2/3) = 1.587 and mph_1/4 / mph_1/8 = 2^(1/3) = 1.260
  - Source: Constant power from rest: x = (2/3) √(2P/m) t^1.5, v = √(2P t / m) (McCaul 2014, paragraph 4)
- 340 hp at the wheels with a 15 % loss is 400 hp at the flywheel and the same 12.00 s
  - Source: hp_crank = hp_wheel / (1 − loss)
- A weight of 10 kg, zero power and an unknown formula are rejected; under 1.5 lb/hp warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 8.75, 12.00 s, 113.6 mph, 7.56 s, 90.1 mph to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- E.L. McCaul, The ET & MPH Equations, June 2014, Table 2 Some published empirical ET and MPH equations (Hale 5.825/234.0; G. Fox 6.050/225.0; Huntington 6.290/224.0), and paragraph 4 (K_T = 4.803 from constant power)
- Wallace Racing, ET-MPH-HP calculator (wallaceracing.com/et-hp-mph.php): weight as the car sits on the line with driver and fuel, horsepower at the flywheel

## Quick statistics of a series

<a id="quick-stats"></a>

Folder `quick-stats/` · General · Mean, standard deviation, confidence interval, quartiles, trend with significance and outliers (Tukey, Chauvenet, Grubbs) of a pasted series.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The values are a random sample from one population; the confidence interval of the mean x̄ ± t(1 − α/2, n − 1) s/√n assumes approximately normal data or a sample large enough for the central limit theorem (n ≳ 30 for moderately skewed data); serially correlated data (time series of noon reports, sensor logs) make the interval too narrow, because the effective number of independent values is smaller than n.
- Sample standard deviation with n − 1; skewness G1 and excess kurtosis G2 with the small-sample corrections used by Excel SKEW/KURT; quartiles by linear interpolation between order statistics (type 7, the Excel PERCENTILE.INC / NumPy default — other software may differ slightly for small n).
- Trend: ordinary least-squares line against the observation number (one series) or against x (pairs), with the slope's two-sided p-value from the t distribution on n − 2 degrees of freedom; "significant" means p below 1 − confidence level; a linear trend through data with a step change or seasonality is a poor description of it.
- Outlier screening flags values for investigation; it does not justify deleting them (ISO 5725-2: remove only with a technical explanation). Tukey's fences (1.5 × IQR beyond the quartiles) need no distribution; Chauvenet's criterion (reject if n · P(|Z| > z) < 0.5) and Grubbs' test (G = max|x − x̄|/s against the critical value at the chosen level, ISO 5725-2) assume normal data and test one value at a time; the "without outlier" statistics drop only the single Grubbs outlier.
- Input: numbers separated by new lines, spaces, commas, semicolons or tabs with a decimal point (comma-decimal locales must be converted); lines starting with # are ignored; at most 100 000 values.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 gives mean 5, sample SD 2.138 (population 2), skewness 0.8185 and kurtosis 0.9406 (Excel), 95 % CI 3.21–6.79 with t 2.3646; the trend example 1, 3, 2, 5, 4 gives slope 0.8, R² 0.64, p 0.104; in the default fuel-consumption series 34.2 is flagged by all three tests (Grubbs G 2.75 > 2.290 for n = 10 at 5 %, Tukey fence 32.05).
- Design decision: the three outlier tests are shown side by side because practice differs between fields; none of them removes data automatically.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Fewer than 10 values: the interval is wide and outlier tests have little power.
- Strong skewness (G1 = …): the normal-theory interval and the Chauvenet/Grubbs tests are unreliable; the median and quartiles describe the data better.
- Flagged values should be investigated for a physical cause (sensor fault, transcription error, different condition) — do not delete data without one.
- A significant trend means the values are not one stationary population: the mean and its interval describe the period, not a stable level.
- Serial correlation (consecutive readings, noon reports) narrows the interval artificially; the values are treated as independent.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Line …: expected two numbers (x y), found …
- Enter at least two values
- At most … values

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Textbook series 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9: mean 5, median 4.5, sample SD 2.1381, population SD 2, skewness 0.8185, excess kurtosis 0.9406 (Excel SKEW/KURT)
  - Source: Standard-deviation textbook example (population SD 2); Joanes & Gill (1998) estimators
- Confidence interval: n 8, t(0.975, 7) = 2.364624 → 5 ± 2.364624 × 2.13809/√8 = 3.2125 … 6.7875; at 99 % t(0.995, 7) = 3.499483 → ± 2.6454
  - Source: Student t table (NIST/SEMATECH 1.3.6.7.2)
- Trend: pairs (1,1) (2,3) (3,2) (4,5) (5,4) give slope 0.8, intercept 0.6, R² 0.64, p 0.104 → not significant at 95 %; the same values as one series give the same line against the observation number
  - Source: OLS regression inference (Montgomery & Runger)
- Outliers in the default fuel series: mean 31.41, s 1.0137; 34.2 has G = 2.752 > 2.290 (Grubbs, n 10, α 5 %), Chauvenet n·P = 0.059 < 0.5 and lies above the Tukey fence 32.05 → flagged by all three; without it mean 31.10
  - Source: ISO 5725-2:2019 Table 5 (Grubbs n = 10: 2.290); Taylor (Chauvenet); Tukey fences
- Quartiles (type 7) of the fuel series: Q1 = 30.925, Q3 = 31.375, IQR 0.45, fences 30.25 / 32.05; a clean series flags nothing
  - Source: Hyndman & Fan (1996) type 7 (Excel PERCENTILE.INC)
- Parsing and validation: comment lines, commas, semicolons and tabs are accepted; text, a single value and a pair line with three numbers are rejected
  - Source: Input contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 31.41, 31.15, 1.014, 0.321, 30.7, 2.262, 30.7, 34.2 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5 (quantitative techniques: confidence limits, Grubbs' test, Tukey) and 1.3.6.7.2 (t table)
- ISO 5725-2:2019 Accuracy (trueness and precision) of measurement methods and results — Part 2, 7.3.4 Grubbs' test and Table 5
- J. R. Taylor, An Introduction to Error Analysis, 2nd ed., University Science Books 1997 — ch. 6 Chauvenet's criterion
- J. W. Tukey, Exploratory Data Analysis, Addison-Wesley 1977 (fences); D. C. Montgomery, G. C. Runger, Applied Statistics and Probability for Engineers, 7th ed. — regression inference

## Rational-method runoff

<a id="rational-runoff"></a>

Folder `rational-runoff/` · Civil · Design peak runoff from catchment area, runoff coefficient and rainfall intensity, with time of concentration (Kirpich).

### Assumptions and caveats

- Rational method Q = C i A: the peak discharge of a small catchment (under about 80 ha / 200 acres) when rainfall of uniform intensity i, lasting at least the time of concentration, falls on the whole area; C is the fraction of rainfall that runs off, composite over sub-areas by area weighting; the SI form Q [m³/s] = C i [mm/h] A [ha]/360.
- Time of concentration by Kirpich (1940): t_c [min] = 0.0195 L^0.77 S^−0.385 with the flow-path length L in metres and the average slope S in m/m (the US form 0.0078 L_ft^0.77 S^−0.385 is the same equation); it was derived for small agricultural catchments with defined channels and underestimates t_c on flat paved areas (a minimum of 5–10 minutes is usual); other methods (FAA, NRCS velocity, Bransby-Williams) give different values.
- Rainfall intensity: entered directly from the local IDF curve at duration = t_c, or from a fitted IDF relation i = a/(t_c + b)^n whose coefficients the user supplies for the chosen return period; the frequency factor C_f (1.0 up to 10 years, 1.1 for 25, 1.2 for 50, 1.25 for 100 years, C C_f ≤ 1) follows common US drainage manuals.
- Runoff coefficients are typical values for 2–10 year storms (roofs 0.90, pavement 0.85, gravel 0.50, lawns 0.10–0.30, industrial 0.75, woodland 0.15); they rise with slope, soil saturation and storm rarity, and local manuals govern.
- The method gives a peak, not a hydrograph: storage, routing, infiltration during the storm, snowmelt and tidal backwater at outfalls are outside it; the runoff volume reported assumes the design intensity over the duration t_c (a triangular hydrograph of base 2 t_c would hold the same volume).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: the published Houston case (C 0.57, i 4.2 in/h, A 15 acres → 35.9 cfs in US units) converts to 106.7 mm/h and 6.07 ha → 1.025 m³/s = 36.2 cfs, the 1.008 unit-factor difference the US form ignores; Kirpich 500 m at 2 % gives 10.5 min; the two Kirpich constants agree (0.0078 × 3.2808^0.77 = 0.0195).
- Design decision: composite C over three sub-areas because real sites mix roofs, pavement and grass; the IDF fit is optional so users with a tabulated curve enter the intensity directly.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Kirpich t_c … min below the … min minimum: the minimum is used (Kirpich underestimates on short paved paths).
- C × C_f capped at 1.0: runoff cannot exceed rainfall.
- Intensity … mm/h must be read from the local IDF curve at a duration equal to t_c = … min and the chosen return period.
- Very flat flow path: Kirpich gives long t_c and low intensity; ponding and backwater may govern instead.
- Peak flow only (no hydrograph): detention storage, routing, infiltration and outfall tide levels need a separate analysis.
- Runoff coefficients are typical 2–10 year values; local drainage manuals and soil conditions govern.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Enter at least one sub-area

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Published case (Houston): C 0.57, i 4.2 in/h (106.68 mm/h), A 15 acres (6.070 ha) → Q = 0.57 × 106.68 × 6.070/360 = 1.025 m³/s = 36.2 cfs (US form 35.9 cfs; the 1.008 factor explains the difference)
  - Source: Guilford County / HEC-22 rational method example (Q = C i A = 35.9 cfs); SI form Q = C i A/360 (CPHEEO)
- Composite C: 2 ha asphalt (0.85) + 1 ha roofs (0.90) + 3 ha lawn (0.10) → C = (1.7 + 0.9 + 0.3)/6 = 0.483; impervious share 50 %; 100 mm/h → Q = 0.483 × 100 × 6/360 = 0.806 m³/s = 134 L/s/ha
  - Source: Area-weighted runoff coefficient (ASCE MOP 77); SI rational formula
- Kirpich: 500 m at 2 % → t_c = 0.0195 × 500^0.77 × 0.02^−0.385 = 10.5 min; the US constant 0.0078 with feet gives the same (0.0078 × 3.2808^0.77 = 0.0195); 100 m at 0.5 % → 5.2 min
  - Source: Kirpich (1940); Iowa DOT 4A-5 (SI constant 0.0195, L in m) and Guilford County manual (0.0078, L in ft)
- Minimum t_c: a 50 m path at 5 % gives Kirpich 1.6 min, floored to 5 min with a warning; IDF mode i = 2000/(t_c + 10)^0.8 at t_c 10.5 min → 177 mm/h
  - Source: Common 5–10 min minimum (HEC-22); IDF fit form i = a/(t + b)^n
- Frequency factor: 100-year storm multiplies C by 1.25 (0.483 → 0.604); a fully paved site at C 0.85 × 1.25 is capped at 1.0 with a warning; runoff depth and volume follow C i t_c
  - Source: ASCE MOP 77 / state drainage manuals (C_f 1.0 / 1.1 / 1.2 / 1.25, C C_f ≤ 1)
- Applicability: 6 ha within range; 30 ha "acceptable with care"; 100 ha flagged (> 80 ha); invalid inputs fail fast (no area, zero slope, unknown surface)
  - Source: HEC-22 / ASCE MOP 77 area limits for the rational method; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.483, 0.483, 10.5 min, 10.5 min, 0.81 m³/s, 134, 50 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Z. P. Kirpich, "Time of concentration of small agricultural watersheds", Civil Engineering 10(6), 1940; Iowa DOT Design Manual 4A-5 and Guilford County stormwater manual (Kirpich forms)
- ASCE Manual of Practice 77 / WEF MOP FD-20, Design and Construction of Urban Stormwater Management Systems (rational method, runoff coefficients, frequency factors)
- CPHEEO Manual on Storm Water Drainage Systems (2019) — SI rational method Q = C i A/360
- FHWA HEC-22 Urban Drainage Design Manual, 4th ed. (2024) — rational method limits and composite C

## RC time constant and filter

<a id="rc-time-constant"></a>

Folder `rc-time-constant/` · Electrical · Time constant τ = RC, capacitor voltage while charging or discharging, time to 99 %, and the −3 dB cutoff frequency of an RC filter.

### Assumptions and caveats

- A single resistor in series with a single capacitor, driven by an ideal step from 0 to V_s (charging) or released from V_s (discharging); the source has no internal resistance of its own unless it is added to R.
- The capacitor is ideal: no leakage and no equivalent series resistance; electrolytic capacitors leak, which matters for long timing periods.
- The cutoff frequency is the −3 dB point of a first-order RC low-pass or high-pass filter feeding a high-impedance load; a load in parallel with the output lowers the effective resistance.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 10 kΩ and 100 µF give τ = 1.00 s and f_c = 0.159 Hz; at t = τ a 5 V charge reaches 3.16 V (63.2 %), and at 5 τ 99.3 %. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A time constant above a minute with a large capacitor: electrolytic leakage makes long RC timing inaccurate; use a timer IC or a microcontroller.
- Under 100 Ω the first-instant current is large; the source and the capacitor\'s ripple-current rating may limit it.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 10 kΩ and 100 µF: τ = 1 s, f_c = 1/(2π) = 0.159 Hz; at t = τ a 5 V charge reaches 63.2 % = 3.16 V
  - Source: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §1.4.2: τ = RC, V = V_f (1 − e^(−t/RC))
- Audio low-pass with 1 kΩ and 100 nF: f_c = 1.592 kHz and τ = 100 µs
  - Source: Horowitz and Hill, §1.7.1: f_3dB = 1 / (2π R C)
- Milestones: 99 % at 4.605 τ, 99.33 % at 5 τ; charging and discharging voltages always add up to V_s
  - Source: Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, ch. 10 (RC transients); 1 − e^(−5) = 0.99326
- At t = 0 the capacitor is empty and the current is V_s / R; the full capacitor stores ½ C V²
  - Source: Initial condition of the RC step response; W = ½ C V²
- A long timing period with an electrolytic warns; zero resistance or capacitance is rejected
  - Source: Validation contract; electrolytic leakage (Horowitz and Hill, §1.4.2)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.00 s, 0.159 Hz, 3.16 V, 5.00 s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., §1.4.2 (RC circuits: V = V_f (1 − e^(−t/RC))) and §1.7.1 (RC filters, f_3dB = 1/(2π R C))
- Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, 12th ed., ch. 10 (transients in RC circuits)

## Rebar weight and quantity calculator

<a id="rebar-weight"></a>

Folder `rebar-weight/` · Structural · Rebar weight per foot or metre for US #3–#18 and metric bars, and the number, length and weight of bars in a slab grid at any spacing.

### Assumptions and caveats

- US bars use the nominal areas and unit weights of ASTM A615/A615M Table 1; metric bars use 7 850 kg/m³ on the nominal diameter (0.006165 d² kg/m). Deformations do not change the nominal weight.
- In a grid, bars run the full length less the cover at both ends, and the first and last bars sit at the cover from the edges; N = floor((span − 2 × cover)/spacing) + 1 in each direction.
- Laps, hooks, bends, chairs and waste are added as one percentage; splice lengths depend on the bar size, concrete strength and code (ACI 318 Chapter 25, EN 1992-1-1 §8.7).
- The spacing and bar size come from the structural design; this page estimates quantities only.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 20 × 20 ft slab with #4 at 12 in each way and 3 in cover takes 20 + 20 bars of 19.5 ft, 780 ft and 521 lb; 12 mm bars weigh 0.888 kg/m. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The clear gap between bars is very small for the concrete to pass; check the minimum spacing of ACI 318 §25.2 or EN 1992-1-1 §8.2.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Bar size: unknown size "…".
- Number of pieces: enter 1 or more.
- Edge cover: twice the cover must be less than the slab length and width.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 20 × 20 ft slab, #4 at 12 in each way, 3 in cover: 20 + 20 bars of 19.5 ft = 780 ft, 521.0 lb, 0.20 in² per ft
  - Source: N = floor((240 − 6)/12) + 1 = 20 each way; ASTM A615 #4: 0.668 lb/ft, 0.20 in²
- ASTM A615 unit weights equal 490 lb/ft³ steel on the nominal diameter within 0.3 % for every bar #3 to #18
  - Source: ASTM A615/A615M-22 Table 1
- Metric: 12 mm weighs 0.888 kg/m (d²/162), 16 mm 1.578, 25 mm 3.853 kg/m; a 6 × 4 m slab, 12 mm at 200 mm, 40 mm cover: 50 bars, 236 m, 209.5 kg, 565 mm²/m
  - Source: EN 10080 nominal mass 0.006165 d²; hand count 20 + 30 bars
- Pieces: 25 bars of #5 at 20 ft with 10 % laps = 550 ft and 573.7 lb; two layers double a grid
  - Source: #5: 1.043 lb/ft; 25 × 20 × 1.1 = 550 ft
- Tight spacing warns; cover larger than the slab and unknown sizes are rejected
  - Source: ACI 318 §25.2 minimum spacing; validation contract

## Reliability and redundancy

<a id="reliability"></a>

Folder `reliability/` · General · Availability and mission reliability of series, parallel and k-out-of-n systems, and a Weibull fit of failure times by median-rank regression.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Reliability block diagram of independent blocks in series, each with n identical units of which k must work (k = n series, k = 1 parallel redundancy); unit failures and repairs are independent, every unit has its own repair (no queue), and switching to a standby unit is perfect (IEC 61078).
- Steady-state availability of a unit A = MTBF/(MTBF + MTTR); mission reliability without repair R(t) = e^(−t/MTBF) for a constant failure rate. A block works with probability Σ_{j=k..n} C(n, j) p^j (1 − p)^(n−j); the system is the product of its blocks.
- Weibull analysis (IEC 61649): complete (uncensored) failure times are ranked, given Bernard's median ranks F = (i − 0.3)/(n + 0.4) and fitted by least squares of ln t on ln(−ln(1 − F)); β is the shape and η the characteristic life. Suspended items, three-parameter fits and confidence bounds are not included.
- B10 life is the time by which 10 % of units fail, η (−ln 0.9)^(1/β); the mean life is η Γ(1 + 1/β).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: a 2-out-of-3 block of units with A = 4000/4012 has A = 3A² − 2A³ = 0.999973; failure times generated exactly at the median ranks of a Weibull with β = 2, η = 3000 h return those parameters to 10⁻¹² by the regression.
- Design decision: the year for downtime is 8766 h (365.25 days); the fit regresses ln t on the ranks (rank regression on X), which the literature recommends because the times, not the ranks, carry the scatter.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- R² = …: the failure times do not follow one Weibull line well; look for mixed failure modes or a failure-free period.
- β = … < 1: early failures dominate (infant mortality); preventive replacement would not help.
- β = …: wear-out; planned replacement before the B10 life can reduce failures.
- At least three failure times are needed for the Weibull fit.
- Fewer than six failures: the Weibull parameters are very uncertain.
- The weakest block is "…" (availability … %).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- …: expected name; units installed; units needed; MTBF h; MTTR h
- …: units installed and needed must be whole numbers with 1 ≤ needed ≤ installed
- …: MTBF must be greater than zero and MTTR not negative
- Enter at least one block
- Failure times must be greater than zero
- The failure times must not all be equal

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- k-out-of-n: 1 of 1 is the unit itself, 1 of 2 is 1 − (1 − p)², 2 of 3 is 3p² − 2p³
  - Source: IEC 61078 series, parallel and k-out-of-n structures (binomial)
- Default system: unit availability MTBF/(MTBF + MTTR), system = product of blocks = 99.5195 %, 42.1 h of downtime in an 8766 h year
  - Source: Steady-state availability of independent blocks in series
- Mission reliability without repair: the main engine over 720 h is e^(−720/5000) = 86.59 %
  - Source: Constant failure rate, R(t) = e^(−t/MTBF)
- Failure times placed exactly at the Bernard median ranks of a Weibull with β = 2 and η = 3000 h are fitted back exactly
  - Source: IEC 61649 median ranks F = (i − 0.3)/(n + 0.4); regression of ln t on ln(−ln(1 − F))
- With β = 1 (exponential) the mean life equals η and the B10 life is η (−ln 0.9) = 0.1054 η
  - Source: Weibull B life and mean η Γ(1 + 1/β) (Abernethy 2006)
- Invalid inputs are rejected: more units needed than installed, equal failure times, a block line with four fields
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 99.5195 %, 42 h, 2.17, 3464 h, 1230 h to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IEC 61078:2016 Reliability block diagrams — series, parallel and k-out-of-n structures
- IEC 61649:2008 Weibull analysis — median ranks and rank regression
- R. B. Abernethy, The New Weibull Handbook, 5th ed., 2006 — median rank regression, regression of X on Y, B lives

## Relief valve sizing (API 520)

<a id="relief-valve-api520"></a>

Folder `relief-valve-api520/` · Mechanical · API 520 required relief area for gas/vapour (critical and sub-critical) and liquid service, with the API 526 orifice letter and margin.

### Assumptions and caveats

- API Standard 520 Part I sizing equations in SI units (A in mm², W in kg/h, P in kPa absolute for gas, T in K, Q in L/min): gas or vapour in critical flow A = W/(C K_d P₁ K_b K_c) √(T Z/M) with C = 0.03948 √(k (2/(k+1))^((k+1)/(k−1))); sub-critical flow (back pressure above the critical pressure ratio (2/(k+1))^(k/(k−1)) × P₁) A = 17.9 W/(F₂ K_d K_c) √(T Z/(M P₁ (P₁ − P₂))); liquid A = 11.78 Q/(K_d K_w K_c K_v) √(G/(p₁ − p₂)) for valves certified for liquid service.
- Relieving pressure P₁ = set pressure + allowable overpressure + atmospheric pressure, the overpressure being 10 % of set (minimum 20.7 kPa) for a single valve, 16 % (minimum 27.6 kPa) for multiple valves and 21 % for the fire case (ASME VIII UG-125); inlet pressure losses and superimposed back pressure effects on the set pressure are the user's inputs, and the 3 % inlet-loss rule (API 520 Part II) is a separate check.
- Coefficients: effective discharge coefficient K_d = 0.975 for gas and 0.65 for liquid for preliminary sizing with the API 526 effective areas (0.62 with a rupture disk in place of a valve); K_b back-pressure correction 1.0 for conventional valves with built-up back pressure below 10 % (balanced-bellows values from the manufacturer or API 520 Figure 30/31); K_w = 1.0 for conventional valves in liquid service (bellows: Figure 32); K_c = 0.9 for a rupture disk upstream of the valve; K_v = 1.0 for low-viscosity liquids — viscous liquids need the Reynolds-number correction of API 520 5.9, entered here as K_v.
- Gas properties: ideal-gas specific heat ratio k and molecular weight from the preset list (API 520 Part I Table 7 values) or entered; the compressibility factor Z at relieving conditions must be entered (1.0 for an ideal gas); the critical-flow equation is the ideal-gas nozzle formula, and two-phase or flashing flow (API 520 Annex C) and steam (Napier) are outside this page.
- API 526 effective orifice areas (D 0.110 in² … T 26.0 in², converted at 645.16 mm²/in²) are used for selection: the smallest orifice with an area not below the required one; above T, several valves are needed (and the multiple-valve overpressure applies). The effective areas are valid only together with the API 520 equations and K_d values; certified manufacturer areas and coefficients govern the final selection.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: API 520 Part I example 1 (24 270 kg/h, T 348 K, Z 0.90, M 51, k 1.11, P₁ 670 kPa, K_d 0.975) gives C 0.02489 and A 3 699 mm², and example 2 (same, P₂ 532 kPa, sub-critical) gives F₂ 0.8548 and A 4 248 mm², as reproduced by the open-source fluids library (fluids.safety_valve, doctests "matches"); liquid example 5 (6 814 L/min, G 0.90, Δp 1 551.6 kPa, K_d 0.65, K_w 0.97) gives 3 066 mm². API 526 table from the same library (API526_A_sq_inch).
- Design decision: steam (Napier) and two-phase sizing are left out because the current API 520 edition changed the steam method; the page states what it covers.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Sub-critical flow with K_b < 1: the sub-critical equation is for conventional valves; for balanced-bellows valves API 520 uses the critical-flow equation with the manufacturer\'s K_b.
- Back pressure above 10 % of set pressure: a conventional valve\'s capacity and stability are affected — use a balanced-bellows or pilot valve with its K_b.
- K_v = 1 assumes a low-viscosity liquid; for viscous liquids compute the valve Reynolds number and apply the API 520 viscosity correction.
- Required area exceeds the largest API 526 orifice (T): … valves are needed, and the multiple-valve overpressure (16 %) applies.
- Fire case with a liquid-full system: the relief load is usually vapour generated by the fire — check whether vapour or liquid sizing governs.
- Preliminary sizing with API 526 effective areas and K_d; the certified area and coefficient of the selected valve govern, together with inlet pressure loss (≤ 3 % of set, API 520 Part II) and outlet back-pressure checks.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Relieving temperature must be above absolute zero
- Back pressure is at or above the relieving pressure: no flow through the valve

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- API 520 example 1 (critical gas flow): 24 270 kg/h, T 348 K, Z 0.90, M 51, k 1.11, P₁ 670 kPa, K_d 0.975 → C 0.02489, A = 3 699 mm² → API 526 "P" orifice (4 116 mm²), 90 % used
  - Source: API 520 Part I example 1 as reproduced by fluids.safety_valve.API520_A_g (0.0036990 m²)
- API 520 example 2 (sub-critical): same gas with P₂ = 532 kPa abs → r 0.794 > critical ratio 0.583, F₂ 0.8548, A = 4 248 mm²
  - Source: API 520 Part I example 2 as reproduced by fluids.safety_valve.API520_A_g (0.0042484 m²)
- Coefficient C: k 1.35 → 0.026694 (library doctest); k 1.40 → 0.027034, i.e. 356 in the US-unit form (C_US = 520/0.03948 × C_SI); k → 1 limit 0.03948/√e
  - Source: API 520 C formula; fluids.safety_valve.API520_C(1.35) = 0.0266942
- API 520 example 5 (liquid, balanced bellows): 6 814 L/min, G 0.90, set 1 724 kPag + 10 % = 1 896.4, back pressure 344.8 kPag → Δp 1 551.6 kPa, K_d 0.65, K_w 0.97 → A = 3 066 mm² → "P" orifice
  - Source: API 520 Part I example 5 (10th ed.) as reproduced by fluids.safety_valve.API520_A_l ("matches the 3066 mm² shown")
- API 526 table and selection: 14 orifices D 0.110 in² (70.97 mm²) … T 26.0 in² (16 774 mm²); an area equal to a table value selects that letter; 40 000 mm² needs 3 × T
  - Source: API 526 effective orifice areas (fluids.safety_valve.API526_A_sq_inch)
- Overpressure, rupture disk and validation: multiple valves 16 % and fire 21 % raise P₁; a 100 kPag set pressure takes the 20.7 kPa minimum; K_c 0.9 raises the area by 1/0.9; back pressure above relieving pressure is rejected
  - Source: ASME VIII UG-125; API 520 K_c = 0.9 with a rupture disk
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 670 kPa, 0.583, 0.02489, 3 699 mm², 4 116 mm², 90 %, 27 000 kg/h to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- API Standard 520 Part I, Sizing, Selection, and Installation of Pressure-relieving Devices — Sizing and Selection (9th ed. 2014 / 10th ed. 2020), sections 5.6 (gas/vapour) and 5.8 (liquid), examples 1, 2 and 5
- API Standard 526, Flanged Steel Pressure-relief Valves — effective orifice areas D–T
- ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section VIII Division 1, UG-125 (allowable overpressure 10/16/21 %)
- C. Bell, fluids (Python library), safety_valve module — API520_C, API520_A_g, API520_A_l and API526_A_sq_inch with the API example doctests

## Resistor colour code

<a id="resistor-color-code"></a>

Folder `resistor-color-code/` · Electrical · Resistance, tolerance and temperature coefficient from the colour bands of a 4, 5 or 6-band resistor, and the colour bands for any value.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Colours follow IEC 60062:2016: ten digit colours from black (0) to white (9), multipliers from silver (× 0.01) to white (× 10⁹), and the tolerance and temperature-coefficient colours that the standard and the major makers agree on.
- Four-band resistors carry two significant digits, five- and six-band resistors three; a value with more significant digits than the bands allow is rounded and flagged.
- The band order is read from the end with the bands grouped closer together; the tolerance band is usually set apart, and gold or silver never appears as the first band.
- The tolerance is the manufacturing tolerance at 25 °C; the temperature coefficient adds a drift of its value in ppm per kelvin away from that.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: yellow, violet, red, gold reads 4.7 kΩ ± 5 % (4.465 to 4.935 kΩ); brown, black, black, brown, brown reads 1 kΩ ± 1 %; encoding 4.7 kΩ in four bands returns yellow, violet, red. All checked against IEC 60062 tables.
- Design decision: tolerance colours with conflicting meanings between editions of the standard (orange, yellow, grey) are not offered, so a reading is never silently wrong.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- This value needs more significant digits than … bands carry; the bands mark … instead.
- This is not a standard E6 to E96 value; check the reading, or the part may be special.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Resistance cannot be marked with … digits and a standard multiplier (got … Ω)
- Tolerance band: only 4-band resistors may have no tolerance band (± 20 %)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Yellow, violet, red, gold = 47 × 10² Ω = 4.7 kΩ ± 5 %: 4.465 to 4.935 kΩ, an E6 value
  - Source: IEC 60062:2016 clause 4, Tables 1 and 2 (digits, multiplier, tolerance)
- Five bands brown, black, black, brown, brown = 100 × 10 Ω = 1 kΩ ± 1 %; six bands with a red sixth band add 50 ppm/K
  - Source: IEC 60062:2016, Tables 1–3 (three significant digits; temperature coefficient band)
- Fractional and large values: green, blue, gold, gold = 0.56 Ω ± 5 %; brown, black, green, silver = 1 MΩ ± 10 %
  - Source: IEC 60062:2016 multipliers gold × 0.1 and green × 10⁵
- Encoding: 4.7 kΩ in 4 bands is yellow, violet, red; 10 kΩ in 5 bands is brown, black, black, red; 4.75 kΩ in 4 bands is rounded with a warning
  - Source: IEC 60062:2016 (inverse of the colour code)
- Round trip: every E24 value from 1 Ω to 9.1 MΩ encodes and decodes back to itself in 4 bands
  - Source: IEC 60063 E24 values; IEC 60062 code
- Black as the first band, no tolerance band on a 5-band resistor and a value beyond the white multiplier are rejected
  - Source: IEC 60062:2016 (first band is never black; "no band" ± 20 % applies to 4-band parts)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 4.7 kΩ, 4.465 kΩ, 4.935 kΩ to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IEC 60062:2016 Marking codes for resistors and capacitors, clause 4 (colour code) and Tables 1–3
- IEC 60063:2015 Preferred number series for resistors and capacitors (to name the series a value belongs to)
- Vishay and Yageo through-hole resistor data sheets (colour coding, temperature coefficient bands)

## Series and parallel resistors

<a id="resistors-series-parallel"></a>

Folder `resistors-series-parallel/` · Electrical · Equivalent resistance of any number of resistors in series and in parallel, how the voltage or current divides, and the totals at a given voltage.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The resistors are ideal and linear, at their nominal values; tolerances add up in series and average out only statistically.
- Series means every resistor carries the same current; parallel means every resistor sees the same voltage. Mixed networks are reduced step by step: work out each parallel group, then add the groups in series.
- With a voltage entered, it is applied across the whole series chain or across the parallel group.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 100, 220 and 470 Ω give 790 Ω in series and 59.98 Ω in parallel; two equal resistors in parallel give half their value. Checked by hand.
- Design decision: values are typed the way parts are marked (4k7, 2R2, 1M) so a list can be copied from a bill of materials.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Only one resistor: series and parallel are both its own value.
- The values differ by more than a factor of 1000: in series the smallest hardly counts, in parallel the largest hardly counts.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Values: enter at least one resistor
- Values: resistor … must be greater than zero (got …)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 100, 220 and 470 Ω: 790 Ω in series and 59.98 Ω in parallel
  - Source: Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, ch. 2: R_s = ΣR, 1/R_p = Σ1/R
- Two equal resistors in parallel give half: 2 × 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ; n equal resistors give R/n
  - Source: Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, ch. 6 (equal parallel resistors)
- Marked values: 4k7, 2R2 and 1M read as 4.7 kΩ, 2.2 Ω and 1 MΩ; the series total is 1 004 702.2 Ω
  - Source: IEC 60062:2016 clause 5 letter and digit code
- At 12 V: 100 Ω + 200 Ω in series carry 40 mA and share the voltage 33.3 % / 66.7 %; in parallel they take 180 mA, 2.16 W, current shared 66.7 % / 33.3 %
  - Source: Voltage division V_i = V R_i / ΣR; current division I_i = I G_i / ΣG (Hughes, ch. 2)
- A wide spread warns; an empty list, a zero value and an unreadable value are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract; parallel total is below the smallest resistor, series total above the largest
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 790 Ω, 60.0 Ω to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, 12th ed., ch. 2 (series and parallel resistors, current and voltage division)
- Boylestad, Introductory Circuit Analysis, 13th ed., ch. 5 and 6 (series and parallel circuits)
- IEC 60062:2016 clause 5, letter and digit code for resistance values (4K7, 2R2)

## Retaining wall earth pressure calculator (Rankine)

<a id="retaining-wall"></a>

Folder `retaining-wall/` · Civil · Active, at-rest and passive earth pressure on a retaining wall by Rankine, with surcharge and sloping backfill, the thrust, and sliding and overturning checks.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Rankine theory: a vertical, smooth back face and a cohesionless, drained backfill; wall friction (Coulomb) would lower the active thrust slightly. With sloping backfill the thrust acts parallel to the slope; the stability checks use its horizontal component and ignore the small vertical one.
- Active pressure needs the wall to move or rotate slightly away from the soil (about 0.1–0.2 % of its height for sand); walls that cannot move (basement walls, braced walls) carry the higher at-rest pressure K_0 = 1 − sin φ (Jaky).
- The backfill is drained: water pressure behind an undrained wall can double the load and is not included. Compaction and traffic loads beyond the uniform surcharge are not included.
- The gravity-wall check treats the wall as a rectangular block founded on soil, with no passive resistance at the toe; cantilever walls with a heel and toe need the full design. Typical minimum factors of safety are 1.5 for sliding and 2.0 for overturning.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 3 m wall retaining sand with φ = 30°, γ = 18 kN/m³ and 10 kPa surcharge has K_a = 1/3, thrust 27 + 10 = 37 kN/m acting 1.135 m above the base; a 1.8 m wide concrete block gives FS 1.75 on sliding (μ = 0.5) and 2.78 on overturning. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Sliding factor of safety … is below the usual 1.5: widen the base, add a key or rely on passive resistance with care.
- Overturning factor of safety … is below the usual 2.0: widen the wall or add a heel.
- At-rest pressure with sloping backfill uses the approximation K_0 (1 + sin β).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Backfill slope: it must be flatter than the friction angle, or the slope itself is unstable.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 3 m wall, φ 30°, γ 18, 10 kPa surcharge: K_a = 1/3, thrust 27 + 10 = 37 kN/m at 1.135 m; 1.8 m concrete block: FS 1.75 sliding, 2.78 overturning
  - Source: Rankine active thrust P = ½ K_a γ H² + K_a q H; W = 24 × 1.8 × 3 = 129.6 kN/m; FS_s = 0.5 W / P; FS_o = W × 0.9 / (P ȳ)
- Coefficients: K_a 0.271 and K_p 3.690 at φ 35°; K_0 = 1 − sin 30° = 0.5; sloping backfill β 10°, φ 30°: K_a 0.350
  - Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, ch. 7 (Rankine tables); Jaky (1944)
- At-rest pressure on a rigid wall is 1.5 times the active at φ 30°; base pressure K γ H + K q
  - Source: K_0 / K_a = 0.5 / 0.333
- A narrow 1.2 m block warns on sliding and overturning; zero width skips the check
  - Source: Typical minimum factors of safety 1.5 and 2.0
- A backfill slope at or above the friction angle and out-of-range inputs are rejected
  - Source: Rankine K_a is undefined for β ≥ φ; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 37.00, 1.135 m, 1.75, 2.78 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Rankine, W.J.M. (1857), On the stability of loose earth; Das, B.M., Principles of Foundation Engineering, ch. 7 (Rankine coefficients, sloping backfill)
- Jaky, J. (1944), The coefficient of earth pressure at rest (K_0 = 1 − sin φ)
- EN 1997-1:2004 §9 (retaining structures) and Annex C (earth pressures; wall movement for active and passive states)

## Reynolds number and flow regime

<a id="reynolds-number"></a>

Folder `reynolds-number/` · Thermal and fluids · Reynolds number for a pipe, a non-circular duct, a flat plate or any length, from velocity or flow, with the regime: laminar, transitional or turbulent.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The fluid is Newtonian and its density and viscosity are uniform over the length considered; for a heated or cooled flow use the properties at the mean bulk temperature.
- Pipe and duct flow is fully developed internal flow running full; the limits 2300 and 4000 are the usual engineering bounds of the transitional range, and a very smooth, vibration-free pipe can stay laminar to much higher Reynolds numbers.
- A non-circular duct is represented by its hydraulic diameter D_h = 4 A / P; this is accurate for turbulent flow and only approximate for laminar flow in shapes far from a circle.
- The flat-plate regime uses a transition at Re_x ≈ 5 × 10⁵ for a smooth plate in a low-turbulence stream; roughness or free-stream turbulence can trip the boundary layer far earlier.
- Built-in fluid properties are reference values at the stated temperature; oils and fuels vary widely between grades, so use the custom fluid with the data sheet values when it matters.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: water at 20 °C, 1.5 m/s in a 50 mm bore gives Re = 74 701 by hand; a 300 × 200 mm duct has D_h = 0.24 m; the fluid table (shared/fluids.js) is identical to pipe-flow so the two calculators agree.
- Design decision: the regime text names the geometry's own limits, because the same Reynolds number is turbulent in a pipe and laminar on a plate.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Transitional flow: the friction factor can jump between the laminar and turbulent values, so pressure-drop and heat-transfer results are uncertain by a factor of two or more.
- Laminar flow in a non-circular duct: the hydraulic diameter is only approximate, and the friction factor depends on the shape.
- Air above about 100 m/s (Mach 0.3) is compressible; density and viscosity change along the flow.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Water at 20 °C, 1.5 m/s in a 50 mm bore: Re = 1.5 × 0.05 / 1.004e-6 = 74 701, turbulent
  - Source: White, Fluid Mechanics, ch. 6: Re = V D / ν; ITTC 7.5-02-01-03 fresh water ν(20 °C) = 1.004e-6 m²/s
- Heavy fuel oil of 380 cSt at 1 m/s in a 100 mm pipe: Re = 263, laminar
  - Source: Moody (1944), laminar zone below Re ≈ 2300; ISO 8217 RMG 380 viscosity 380 mm²/s at 50 °C
- A 300 × 200 mm duct has D_h = 4 × 0.06 / 1.0 = 0.24 m; air at 5 m/s gives Re = 79 156, turbulent
  - Source: White, ch. 6.6, hydraulic diameter D_h = 4 A / P; ASHRAE Handbook Fundamentals, ch. 21 duct design
- Flow rate and velocity agree: 0.01 m³/s in a 100 mm pipe is 1.273 m/s and gives the same Re as entering that velocity
  - Source: Continuity: V = Q / A, A = π D² / 4
- Flat plate in sea water at 2 m/s: Re_x = 841 526 at 0.5 m (turbulent), 168 305 at 0.1 m (laminar); transition velocity 5 × 10⁵ ν / x
  - Source: White, ch. 7: flat-plate boundary layer, transition near Re_x = 5 × 10⁵; ITTC 7.5-02-01-03 sea water ν(15 °C)
- Water at 0.05 m/s in a 50 mm pipe: Re = 2490, transitional, with a warning; the same Re in "any length" mode names no regime
  - Source: Transitional range 2300–4000 (White, ch. 6; Moody 1944)
- Custom fluid: glycerine-like ρ 1260 kg/m³, ν 1.18e-3 m²/s gives μ = 1.487 Pa·s and Re = 8.47 at 0.2 m/s in 50 mm
  - Source: μ = ρ ν (White, ch. 1); Re = V D / ν
- Zero diameter, zero velocity and an unknown fluid are rejected
  - Source: Input validation contract (shared/validate.js)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 74 700, 0.046 m/s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Reynolds, O. (1883) An experimental investigation of the circumstances which determine whether the motion of water shall be direct or sinuous, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. 174, 935–982
- White, F. M., Fluid Mechanics, 7th ed., ch. 6 (pipe flow, Re = ρVD/μ, transition near 2300, hydraulic diameter) and ch. 7 (flat-plate boundary layer, transition near 5 × 10⁵)
- Moody, L. F. (1944) Friction factors for pipe flow, Trans. ASME 66, 671–684 (laminar, critical and turbulent zones)
- ITTC Recommended Procedure 7.5-02-01-03 (2011), fresh water and sea water density and viscosity

## Rocket equation calculator (delta-v)

<a id="rocket-equation"></a>

Folder `rocket-equation/` · Automotive · Tsiolkovsky rocket equation: delta-v from Isp or exhaust velocity and the mass ratio, the propellant for a delta-v, and staging for up to three stages.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The ideal rocket equation Δv = v_e ln(m0/mf) holds with no gravity, drag or steering losses; a launch from Earth to low orbit needs well over the 7.8 km/s orbital speed to cover them.
- Specific impulse converts to effective exhaust velocity with standard gravity: v_e = Isp × 9.806 65 m/s², whatever planet the rocket flies from.
- Isp and exhaust velocity are taken as constant through the burn; for a first stage, a value between the sea-level and vacuum figures is a fair average.
- In staging, each stage drops its empty (dry) mass at burnout and the next stage starts with everything above it plus the payload; interstage hardware belongs in the dry mass of the stage it leaves with.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: Isp 300 s (v_e 2 942.0 m/s), 1 000 kg initial and 400 kg final mass: mass ratio 2.5, Δv 2 695.7 m/s, propellant 600 kg (60 %); 3 000 m/s from 400 kg final mass needs 709.0 kg of propellant. Two stages (payload 1 000 kg; 20 000 + 2 000 kg at 280 s; 4 000 + 500 kg at 320 s): 3 567.7 + 4 077.3 = 7 645.0 m/s. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A stage with zero dry mass is not physical: tanks and engines always weigh something.
- A mass ratio above 20 is beyond a single stage with real tanks and engines; split the delta-v over stages.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Stage …: dry mass: the stage burns out with no mass left; give the dry mass or a payload.
- Initial mass: it must be at least the final mass (the rocket cannot gain mass by burning).
- Delta-v required: it needs a mass ratio above one million with this exhaust velocity; use more stages or a better engine.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Isp 300 s, 1 000 kg to 400 kg: v_e = 2 942.0 m/s, Δv = 2 942.0 × ln 2.5 = 2 695.7 m/s, 60 % propellant
  - Source: Sutton and Biblarz, Rocket Propulsion Elements, Ch. 4 (ideal Δv) and Ch. 2 (v_e = Isp g0, g0 = 9.806 65 m/s²)
- A mass ratio of e gives a delta-v equal to the exhaust velocity (4 400 m/s); no burn gives zero
  - Source: Δv = v_e ln(m0/mf), limiting cases
- Propellant for 3 000 m/s at Isp 300 s with 400 kg final mass: 400 × (e^(3 000/2 942.0) − 1) = 709.0 kg, and back to 3 000 m/s
  - Source: Inverse of the rocket equation, m_p = mf (e^(Δv/v_e) − 1); consistency with the forward calculation
- Two stages (payload 1 000 kg; 20 000 + 2 000 kg at 280 s; 4 000 + 500 kg at 320 s): 3 567.7 + 4 077.3 = 7 645.0 m/s
  - Source: Staged rocket equation, each stage’s m0 carries the stages above and the payload (Curtis, Ch. 11)
- Staging pays: the same 24 000 kg of propellant and 2 500 kg of structure at 300 s in one stage gives only 6 065 m/s
  - Source: Rocket equation, single stage 27 500 → 3 500 kg
- An initial mass below the final mass, zero final mass and an empty stage with no payload are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2 942.0 m/s, 2.5, 2 695.7 m/s, 600 kg, 60 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- G.P. Sutton and O. Biblarz, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th ed., Wiley 2017, Chapter 4 Flight performance (ideal Δv = v_e ln(m0/mf), multistage vehicles) and Chapter 2 (Isp = v_e / g0)
- H.D. Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students, 4th ed., Butterworth-Heinemann 2020, Chapter 11 Rocket vehicle dynamics (rocket equation, staging, gravity and drag losses)

## Roll period and synchronous rolling

<a id="roll-period"></a>

Folder `roll-period/` · Maritime · Natural roll period from GM and beam (IS Code) or GM from an observed period, encounter period for speed and heading, synchronous and parametric roll checks.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The roll period uses the 2008 IS Code approximation T_R = 2 C B/√GM with C = 0.373 + 0.023 (B/d) − 0.043 (L_WL/100), which the Code offers "in the absence of sufficient information"; it represents a radius of gyration of about 0.35–0.40 B and can be 10–15 % off for ships with unusual mass distribution (containers on deck, heavy double bottom). An observed period from a rolling test is better and the GM mode inverts the same formula.
- GM is the metacentric height corrected for free surfaces (fluid GM); at large angles the roll period lengthens because GZ is not linear.
- The encounter period is the MSC.1/Circ.1228 formula T_E = 3 T_W²/(3 T_W + V cos α) with V in knots and α the angle between keel and wave direction (0° head seas, 90° beam, 180° following), valid for deep water with λ = 1.56 T_W²; when V cos α ≤ −3 T_W the ship overtakes the waves and the encounter period is reported as the magnitude.
- Resonance bands are a judgement: synchronous rolling is flagged as dangerous within ±10 % of T_E = T_R and as caution within ±20 %; parametric rolling is flagged when T_E is within ±10 % of T_R or of 0.5 T_R and the wavelength is 0.6–2.3 L (the range in which the Code says the stability variation on a crest is significant).
- Surf-riding and broaching: dangerous when 135° < α < 225° and V > 1.8 √L/cos(180° − α) knots, marginal above 1.4 √L/cos(180° − α) (Circ.1228 §4.2.1 and figure 2); successive high-wave attack: λ > 0.8 L, H_s > 0.04 L and T_E/T_W between 1.8 and 3.0 (§4.2.2).
- Irregular seas are represented by a single period and height; real spectra spread the energy, so the danger bands should be read as zones, not lines.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: B 32 m, d 10 m, L_WL 205 m gives C = 0.3585 and T_R = 18.7 s at GM 1.5 m; head seas at 15 kn in 10 s waves give T_E = 6.67 s, following seas 20 s, beam seas 10 s (Circ.1228 §1.6); formulas transcribed from the circular text and the IS Code §2.3.4.
- Design decision: the roll period approximation is the IS Code one rather than T = 0.8 B/√GM or a user radius of gyration, because it is the formula masters and surveyors recognise; an observed period can be entered instead.
- Design decision: the dangerous-zone bands (±10 % / ±20 %) are not in the circular, which only says "nearly equal"; they are stated as judgement in the register.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Roll period from the IS Code approximation (radius of gyration ≈ 0.35–0.40 B): an observed period from a rolling test is more reliable.
- Ship faster than the waves on this heading: the encounter period shown is the magnitude of the (negative) formula value.
- Beam seas near resonance: the roll amplitude is limited only by damping — bilge keels, speed and heading changes matter most here.
- Wave steepness above 1/10: near breaking; the linear deep-water relations are approximate.
- Single wave period and height stand for a spectrum: treat the danger bands as zones, not lines (Circ.1228 §2.1).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- IS Code coefficient C = … is not positive: the approximation does not apply to these proportions

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- IS Code roll period: B 32 m, d 10 m, L_WL 205 m → C = 0.373 + 0.023·3.2 − 0.043·2.05 = 0.3585; GM 1.5 m → T_R = 2·0.3585·32/√1.5 = 18.73 s
  - Source: IMO 2008 IS Code (MSC.267(85)) Part A §2.3.4
- Observed period 18.73 s returns GM 1.5 m (inverse of the same formula); a stiffer ship (GM 3 m) rolls in 13.2 s
  - Source: Rolling-period test inversion GM = (2 C B / T_R)²
- Encounter period (Circ.1228 §1.6): T_W 10 s, V 15 kn → head seas 6.67 s, beam seas 10 s, following seas 20 s; λ = 156 m (§1.5); wave celerity 30.3 kn
  - Source: MSC.1/Circ.1228 §1.5–1.6: λ = 1.56 T_W², T_E = 3 T_W²/(3 T_W + V cos α)
- Synchronous rolling: stern-quartering seas (α 135°) at 15 kn in 14 s waves give T_E = 18.7 s = T_R → DANGER; beam seas of 18.73 s period also; 10 s head seas are clear
  - Source: MSC.1/Circ.1228 §3.2 and §4.2.3.1 (T_E nearly equal to T_R)
- Parametric rolling 1:0.5: head seas at 15 kn with T_W = 12.98 s give T_E = 9.37 s = T_R/2 and λ/L = 1.31 → DANGER; the same ratio with a 400 m ship (λ/L 0.66) is still in band, with a 100 m ship (λ/L 2.6) only caution
  - Source: MSC.1/Circ.1228 §3.3 and §4.2.3.2 (T_E ≈ 0.5 T_R), §3.1.2 (stability variation for λ 0.6–2.3 L)
- Surf-riding (§4.2.1): L 200 m following seas → limit 1.8 √200 = 25.5 kn, marginal from 19.8 kn; 26 kn DANGER, 22 kn marginal, 15 kn clear; at α = 150° the limit is 29.4 kn; head seas and exactly 135° not applicable (strict 135° < α < 225°)
  - Source: MSC.1/Circ.1228 §4.2.1 and figure 2
- Successive high-wave attack (§4.2.2): λ 180 m (> 0.8 L), H_s 9 m (> 0.04 L), following seas 15 kn → T_W 10.74 s, T_E 20.1 s, T_E/T_W 1.87 in 1.8–3.0 → DANGER; with H_s 4 m not critical
  - Source: MSC.1/Circ.1228 §4.2.2.1–4.2.2.2
- Overtaking waves and riding with them: 25 kn in 6 s following seas gives a negative formula value reported as 15.4 s with a warning; V cos α = −3 T_W gives T_E → ∞
  - Source: Behaviour of the §1.6 formula when the denominator is zero or negative
- Critical speed: on a 135° heading in 14 s waves T_E = T_R at 15 kn (the synchronous case above); invalid inputs fail fast (GM ≤ 0, heading > 360)
  - Source: Inversion of the encounter formula; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.358, 18.7 s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IMO Resolution MSC.267(85), International Code on Intact Stability 2008, Part A §2.3.4 (severe wind and rolling criterion — rolling period formula)
- IMO MSC.1/Circ.1228 (2007), Revised guidance to the master for avoiding dangerous situations in adverse weather and sea conditions, §1.5–1.6, §3.2–3.3, §4.2
- IMO MSC.1/Circ.1200 (2006), interim guidelines for alternative assessment of the weather criterion (roll period from radius of gyration)
- Lewis (ed.), Principles of Naval Architecture vol. III, Motions in Waves (SNAME 1989) — roll resonance and encounter frequency

## Roof pitch calculator: rafters, area and shingles

<a id="roof-pitch"></a>

Folder `roof-pitch/` · Civil · Roof pitch in x/12, degrees and percent, gable rafter length, ridge height, roof area from the footprint, and shingle squares and bundles.

### Assumptions and caveats

- A simple gable roof: two equal planes meeting at a central ridge over a rectangular footprint. Hips, valleys, dormers and unequal pitches need their planes added separately.
- Pitch is the rise in inches per 12 in of horizontal run. The pitch multiplier √(1 + (pitch/12)²) converts any horizontal length or area to the length or area along the slope.
- The rafter length is measured along the slope from the ridge centre line to the end of the eave overhang; deduct half the ridge board thickness, measured horizontally, when cutting.
- A square is 100 ft² of roof surface; standard three-tab and most laminated shingles come 3 bundles to the square, but check the wrapper of your product. The waste allowance covers starter strips, ridge caps and cutting.
- Asphalt shingles are allowed on slopes of 2/12 and steeper; from 2/12 to below 4/12 the IRC requires two layers of underlayment.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 24 × 40 ft house with a 6/12 pitch and 1 ft overhangs: multiplier 1.118, rafter 14.53 ft, ridge 6 ft above the wall plate, roof area 1 221 ft², 13.43 squares and 41 bundles with 10 % waste. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Pitch steeper than 21/12 (about 60°): special fastening is needed for shingles; check the manufacturer\'s steep-slope instructions.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Bundles per square must be a whole number (got …)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Pitch multipliers √(1 + (p/12)²): 4/12 1.0541, 6/12 1.1180, 8/12 1.2019, 12/12 1.4142 (45°)
  - Source: Right-triangle geometry; the same values appear in rafter tables of a carpenter's framing square
- 24 × 40 ft gable, 6/12, 1 ft overhangs: rafter 14.53 ft, ridge 6 ft, area 1 221 ft², 13.43 squares, 41 bundles with 10 % waste
  - Source: Hand calculation: (12 + 1) × 1.1180 = 14.534; 26 × 42 × 1.1180 = 1 220.9 ft²; × 1.1 / 100 = 13.43; × 3 = 40.3 → 41
- Input forms agree: 30° is 6.93/12 and 57.7 %; a 50 % grade is 6/12
  - Source: tan 30° = 0.57735; 12 × 0.57735 = 6.928
- IRC R905.2.2 and R905.1.1: 1.5/12 is too flat for shingles, 3/12 needs double underlayment, 4/12 is standard
  - Source: IRC 2021 R905.2.2 (asphalt shingles only on slopes of 2/12 or greater) and R905.1.1 (underlayment for slopes from 2/12 to below 4/12)
- No overhang and no waste: a flat 10 × 10 m plan at 12/12 has 141.4 m² of roof; a zero span and 2.5 bundles per square are rejected
  - Source: Hand calculation: 100 m² × √2 = 141.42 m²; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.118, 14.53 ft, 6 ft, 1 221 ft², 13.43, 41 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- International Residential Code 2021, R905.1.1 (underlayment for slopes 2/12 to 4/12) and R905.2.2 (asphalt shingles on slopes of 2/12 or greater)
- NRCA Roofing Manual: Steep-Slope Roof Systems (2021), slope expressed as rise in inches per 12 in of run; roofing square of 100 ft²
- Trigonometry of the right triangle: tan θ = rise / run, slope length = run × √(1 + (rise/run)²)

## Rotor sail (Flettner rotor) thrust and saving

<a id="rotor-sail"></a>

Folder `rotor-sail/` · Maritime · Thrust, side force, spin power and net power saving of Flettner rotors from the true wind and ship speed, at the best spin, and averaged over a wind table.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Lift, drag and spin power coefficients of Tillig & Ringsberg (2020), eqs (7)–(9): fifth-order polynomials in the spin ratio SR = ωR/AWS, fitted to full-scale measurements on a 4 m × 24 m rotor, for a rotor of aspect ratio 6 with an end disc of twice its diameter; forces on the projected area A = D H with c_i = F_i / (½ ρ A AWS²) and c_P = P / (½ ρ A AWS³). The coefficients agree best between sources for SR 1.5–2.5, the usual operating range; they are held at their SR = 4 values beyond 4.
- Thrust and side force from lift (normal to the apparent wind) and drag (along it), eqs (2) and (3), with the apparent wind angle measured from the bow: T = L sin AWA − D cos AWA, S = L cos AWA + D sin AWA; the rotor turns in the direction that gives forward lift, so wind from either side gives the same result.
- Wind profile TWS(z) = TWS10 (z/10)^α above the sea surface, exponent 1/9 by default as in ISO 15016:2025 (C.9) (Tillig & Ringsberg used 0.27); the rotor is divided into 10 height strips, each with its own apparent wind and spin ratio at the common rpm (eq. 10).
- Net power P_net = T V_s − P_rotor (eq. 10) at the ship speed through water; the main engine power saved is taken as T V_s / η_D. The best spin maximises P_net up to the rpm limit and SR = 4 on every strip; a stopped rotor still has drag.
- Not included: the leeway and rudder drag caused by the side force, heel, interaction between rotors and with the superstructure or deck, gusts, the efficiency of the generators that power the rotor, and any reefing for stability or manoeuvring; the saving is therefore an upper estimate.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: the polynomials give c_L(3) = 9.52, the full-scale value of about 9.5 at SR = 3 reported by Tillig & Ringsberg (2020, Section 3.4), c_D(1) = 0.323 and c_P(3) = 0.297.
- Design decision: SR is defined with the local apparent wind speed, as the paper states in its text (its eq. (6) writes it as u), and the thrust power uses the ship speed through water.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The coefficients are for an aspect ratio of 6 with an end disc of twice the diameter; this rotor has ….
- The spin ratio exceeds 4 on part of the rotor at the conditions entered: the coefficients are held at their SR = 4 values there.
- The spin ratio exceeds 4 on part of the rotor in … wind table row…: the coefficients are held at their SR = 4 values there.
- In this wind the rotor costs power even at its best spin; a stopped rotor still adds drag.
- The side force is … times the thrust: leeway and rudder drag, not included, take part of the saving.
- Several rotors are added without interaction between them or with the superstructure, which changes their thrust and side force.
- The wind table shares add up to … %; they are normalised.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Wind table line …: expected "speed; angle; share" as three numbers
- Wind table line …: the wind speed must not be negative
- Wind table line …: the angle must be between 0 and 180°
- Wind table line …: the share must not be negative
- The rotor must stand above the waterline

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Coefficients: c_L(3) = 9.52 against the full-scale value of about 9.5, c_D(0) = 0.6375 with its minimum of 0.184 at SR 0.61, c_P(0) = 0 and c_P(3) = 0.297
  - Source: Tillig & Ringsberg (2020), eqs (7)–(9) and Section 3.4
- Apparent wind: 20 kn true wind on the beam at 12 kn gives 23.32 kn from 59.04° off the bow
  - Source: Vector sum of the true wind and the wind of the ship's own motion
- Apparent wind on the beam with the ship stopped: the thrust is the lift and the side force the drag, at ½ ρ D H AWS² × c_L and c_D
  - Source: Tillig & Ringsberg (2020), eqs (2)–(4) with AWA = 90°
- The best spin maximises the net power: at 6 kn in 30 kn of beam wind (best SR 3.22) rotor speeds 1 % and 5 % off, and a fixed 150 rpm, give less
  - Source: Tillig & Ringsberg (2020), eq. (10): initial rpm at the maximum net power of the rotor
- Head wind: the rotor gives negative thrust, the best spin sits near the drag minimum (SR about 0.6) and the loss is flagged
  - Source: Tillig & Ringsberg (2020): minimum drag at a low spin ratio, about 0.5 after Li et al. (2012)
- Two rotors without interaction give twice the thrust, side force and spin power of one
  - Source: Linear sum of identical rotors (interaction not modelled)
- Wind table: a single line at the conditions entered reproduces them, and the mean is the share-weighted mean of the rows
  - Source: Time-weighted average over the wind distribution
- Invalid inputs are rejected: a wind angle above 180°, a wind table line with two numbers, a fractional number of rotors
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 25.9 kn, 189 rpm, 3.70, 134.3 kN, 130.7 kN, 829 kW, 126 kW, 703 kW to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- F. Tillig, J. W. Ringsberg, Design, operation and analysis of wind-assisted cargo ships, Ocean Engineering 211 (2020) 107603 — eqs (2)–(10), Section 3.4 (CC BY 4.0)
- ISO 15016:2025, Annex C, formula (C.9) — wind velocity profile with the 1/9 power law
- D. Li, M. Leer-Andersen, B. Allenström, Performance and vortex formation of Flettner rotors at high Reynolds numbers, 29th Symposium on Naval Hydrodynamics, Gothenburg 2012 — the basis of the Tillig & Ringsberg coefficients

## Sea state statistics

<a id="sea-state-statistics"></a>

Folder `sea-state-statistics/` · Maritime · Wave spectrum moments and periods, the 1/10 and 1/100 highest waves, the expected maximum wave in a storm and exceedance probabilities from Hs and Tp.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Short-term stationary sea state described by a single-peaked spectrum: Pierson–Moskowitz for a fully developed sea or JONSWAP for a developing sea, in the form of DNV-RP-C205 §3.5.5 with σ = 0.07 below and 0.09 above the peak and the normalising factor A_γ = 1 − 0.287 ln γ (accurate to about 1–2 % in Hs).
- When no peak-enhancement factor is given, γ follows the DNV rule: 5 for Tp/√Hs ≤ 3.6, exp(5.75 − 1.15 Tp/√Hs) up to 5, and 1 (Pierson–Moskowitz) above; the rule is for Hs in metres and Tp in seconds and applies to wind seas, not to swell.
- Spectral moments are integrated numerically between 0.25 and 12 times the peak frequency with Simpson's rule and the ω⁻⁵ tail added analytically, so Tz, T1 and Te are those of the spectrum shape, not empirical ratios.
- Wave heights follow the Rayleigh distribution of a narrow-band Gaussian sea with H_rms = √(8 m0) = Hs/√2, where Hs = 4√m0 (Longuet-Higgins 1952); real seas are slightly broad-banded and their largest waves somewhat smaller (Forristall), so the Rayleigh values are on the safe side. The number of waves in the duration is the duration divided by Tz.
- Deep water and no current; in shallow water waves steepen and break, and the Rayleigh distribution overestimates the largest waves.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: for γ = 1 the integral reproduces m0 = Hs²/16, Tz = 0.711 Tp and T1 = 0.772 Tp; for γ = 3.3 Tz/Tp and T1/Tp agree with the DNV-RP-C205 regressions (0.778 and 0.835) within 1 %; the mean of the highest third, tenth and hundredth waves are 1.416, 1.800 and 2.360 H_rms; Hs 4 m with Tz 8 s over 3 hours gives 1350 waves and a most probable maximum of 7.59 m.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Peak steepness 1/… is steeper than 1/15: such a sea is breaking-limited and unlikely in deep water (DNV-RP-C205 §3.5.5.4).
- Tp/√Hs above 5: swell-dominated sea; the DNV rule gives γ = 1, but a swell spectrum may be narrower than Pierson–Moskowitz.
- Fewer than 50 waves in the duration: the maximum-wave estimates are very uncertain.
- Rayleigh statistics of a narrow-band sea; measured storm maxima are typically 5–10 % lower (Forristall), and shallow water changes both distribution and breaking.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Pierson–Moskowitz (γ = 1): the integral returns m0 = Hs²/16 exactly, Tz = 0.710 Tp and T1 = 0.772 Tp
  - Source: DNV-RP-C205 (2021) §3.5.5, Pierson–Moskowitz period relations Tz = 0.710 Tp and T1 = 0.772 Tp
- JONSWAP γ = 3.3: Tz/Tp = 0.6673 + 0.05037γ − 0.006230γ² + 0.0003341γ³ = 0.778 and T1/Tp = 0.835 from the DNV regressions agree with the integrated spectrum within 1 %; m0 is within 1 % of Hs²/16
  - Source: DNV-RP-C205 (2021) §3.5.5.6 regressions for Tz/Tp and T1/Tp (1 ≤ γ < 7)
- DNV γ rule: Hs 4 m with Tp 6 s (Tp/√Hs = 3) gives 5, with Tp 8 s (4.0) gives exp(5.75 − 4.6) = 3.158, with Tp 10 s (5.0) gives 1
  - Source: DNV-RP-C205 (2021) §3.5.5.5
- Rayleigh heights: the highest third, tenth and hundredth average 1.416, 1.800 and 2.360 H_rms; one wave in e² = 7.4 exceeds Hs; the mean height is 0.886 H_rms
  - Source: Longuet-Higgins (1952), Rayleigh distribution of wave heights
- Storm maximum: Hs 4 m and Tz 8 s for 3 hours give 1350 waves, a most probable maximum of 2.83 × √(ln 1350) = 7.59 m and an expected maximum about 0.3 m higher; Tz input finds Tp
  - Source: Longuet-Higgins (1952): H_max,mp = H_rms √(ln N), E[H_max] ≈ H_rms (√ln N + 0.5772/(2√ln N))
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero Hs, zero period, γ outside 1–7, an unknown spectrum
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 6.66 s, 7.20 s, 7.91 s, 1.78, 2.83 m, 5.09 m, 6.67 m, 1622 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- DNV-RP-C205 Environmental conditions and environmental loads (2021), §3.5 Wave spectra (JONSWAP, γ rule, period relations) and §3.3 short-term wave statistics
- M. S. Longuet-Higgins, "On the statistical distribution of the heights of sea waves", Journal of Marine Research 11 (1952) 245–266
- K. Hasselmann et al., Measurements of wind-wave growth and swell decay during the Joint North Sea Wave Project (JONSWAP), Deutsche Hydrographische Zeitschrift A8 (1973)
- ITTC Recommended Procedure 7.5-02-07-02.1 Seakeeping Experiments — wave spectra definitions

## Engine power and SFOC to ISO 3046 conditions

<a id="sfoc-iso3046-correction"></a>

Folder `sfoc-iso3046-correction/` · Mechanical · ISO 3046-1 power adjustment factor α and fuel consumption factor β between reference and site ambient conditions, with the fuel LCV correction.

### Assumptions and caveats

- ISO 3046-1:2002 clause 10 power adjustment: the ratio of indicated power k = [(p_x − a φ_x p_sx)/(p_r − a φ_r p_sr)]^m (T_r/T_x)^n (T_cr/T_cx)^s with the factor a and exponents m, n, s of Table 2 for the formula reference the manufacturer states (A–D diesel, F/G dual fuel, I/J spark ignition; E and H, low-speed two-stroke engines, have no recommended values and are not offered — the manufacturer's own factors apply); the power adjustment factor α = k − 0.7 (1 − k)(1/η_m − 1) accounts for the friction power that does not scale with the indicated power, and P_x = α P_r.
- Specific fuel consumption is recalculated with β = k/α (clause 10.4): the fuel per indicated kWh is unchanged while the brake power falls by α, so b_x = β b_r; the standard allows the manufacturer to declare other methods, and modern engines with electronic control may hold SFOC differently — the result is the ISO default, not a guarantee.
- Standard reference conditions of ISO 15550 / ISO 3046-1 clause 5: total barometric pressure 100 kPa, air temperature 298 K (25 °C), relative humidity 30 %, charge air coolant temperature 298 K (25 °C); manufacturers may declare substitute reference conditions (clause 10.3.2), which can be entered in the reference fields. Temperatures are absolute (K) in the ratios.
- The humidity term applies only where a = 1 (references A and I): the dry-air pressure p − φ p_s uses the saturation vapour pressure of water from the Magnus formula (Alduchov & Eskridge, ±0.1 % below 50 °C); where a = 0 the total barometric pressure is used.
- Mechanical efficiency η_m is the manufacturer's value at the declared power; 0.8 is the figure commonly used when none is declared (friction ≈ 20 % of indicated power); the exponent s is taken as zero where the charge air is cooled by engine jacket water at constant temperature (Table 2 note 3).
- Fuel heating value: ISO consumption figures refer to a fuel of 42 700 kJ/kg net; with another fuel the mass consumption scales with 42 700/LCV at the same energy per kWh (ISO 3046-1 clause 13 / ISO 15550 fuel specification; ISO 19030 uses the same reference), so b_fuel = β b_r × 42 700/LCV.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: reference D engine at site 45 °C air, 36 °C charge-air coolant, 100 kPa, η_m 0.8 → k = (298.15/318.15)^1.2 × (298.15/309.15) = 0.8921, α = 0.8733 (−12.7 % power), β = 1.0216 (+2.2 % SFOC): the derating magnitude manufacturers quote for tropical conditions on medium-speed engines (≈ 1 % per 1.5–2 K of air temperature).
- Design decision: Table 2 is reproduced from the ISO 3046-1:2002 preview (iTeh sample pages 5–6, 2026-10-31); references E and H are excluded on purpose because the standard gives no values (nr). β = k/α is the clause 10.4 relation as cited by CIMAC and engine makers; the preview did not include the clause text itself.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Site conditions are more favourable than the reference: ISO 3046-1 note 2 allows the manufacturer to limit the power to the declared value — do not uprate without agreement.
- Indicated-power ratio differs from 1 by more than 25 %: the CIMAC exponents were established for moderate deviations; consult the manufacturer.
- Humidity has no effect for formula reference … (a = 0) by the standard, although it does change the charge density slightly.
- Fuel LCV … kJ/kg: mass consumption scaled by 42 700/LCV at equal energy; density and injection effects on efficiency are not modelled.
- Table 2 factors are guideline values (note 2): the manufacturer may declare its own, and modern electronically controlled engines may limit power differently.
- β = k/α is the ISO default recalculation; engines held at constant brake power by the governor see the fuel consumption change through turbocharger and air-excess effects instead.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Dry air pressure is not positive: check pressure, temperature and humidity
- Power adjustment factor is not positive: conditions far outside the method

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Reference D at 45 °C air / 36 °C coolant / 100 kPa: k = (298.15/318.15)^1.2 × (298.15/309.15)^1 = 0.8921, α = k − 0.7 (1 − k)(1/0.8 − 1) = 0.8733 → 8 733 kW (−12.7 %), β = k/α = 1.0216 → 178.8 g/kWh
  - Source: ISO 3046-1:2002 formulae (1)–(3) with Table 2 reference D (a 0, m 0.7, n 1.2, s 1)
- At reference conditions every factor is 1: k = α = β = 1, power and SFOC unchanged, for all eight formula references
  - Source: Identity of the method at the reference point
- Humidity term for a = 1 (reference A): dry-air pressures p − φ p_s with Magnus p_s(25 °C) = 3.17 kPa and p_s(45 °C) = 9.59 kPa; k = [(100 − 0.6 × 9.59)/(100 − 0.3 × 3.17)]^1 × (298.15/318.15)^0.75; reference D ignores humidity
  - Source: ISO 3046-1 formula (3); Alduchov & Eskridge (1996) Magnus coefficients
- Table 2 transcription: A (1, 1, 0.75, 0), B (0, 1, 1, 0), C (0, 0.7, 2, 0), D (0, 0.7, 1.2, 1), F and J (0, 0.57, 0.55, 1.75), G (0, 0.7, 1.2, 1), I (1, 0.86, 0.55, 0); jacket cooling sets s = 0 so the coolant term becomes 1
  - Source: ISO 3046-1:2002 Table 2 (preview pages 5–6) and note 3
- Altitude and cold: 90 kPa at 10 °C for reference C gives k = 0.9^0.7 × (298.15/283.15)^2 = 1.034 → α > 1 with the "do not uprate" warning; fuel of 40 500 kJ/kg raises the mass SFOC by 42 700/40 500 = 5.4 %; fuel flow = SFOC × P/1e6 kg/h
  - Source: ISO 3046-1 note 2 (power limited to the declared value); LCV scaling at equal energy
- Validation: unknown formula reference, η_m above 1 and a zero declared power are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.9250, 0.9644, 0.8921, 0.8733, 8 733 kW, 1.0216, 178.8 g/kWh, 178.8 g/kWh to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)
