## Shaft critical speed calculator (Rayleigh and Dunkerley)

<a id="shaft-critical-speed"></a>

Folder `shaft-critical-speed/` · Mechanical · First critical speed of a simply supported shaft with up to three masses by Rayleigh's method, with the shaft's own mass by Dunkerley's rule.

### Assumptions and caveats

- A uniform round shaft, solid or hollow, on two simple supports (short or self-aligning bearings) at its ends; the masses are rigid discs treated as points, and their gyroscopic effect and rotary inertia are neglected.
- Rayleigh's method uses the static deflection curve under the weights as the mode shape (Shigley eq. 7-23); it slightly overestimates the true first critical speed. Dunkerley's rule underestimates it, so the two bracket the answer.
- The shaft's own mass enters through its uniform-shaft critical speed (Shigley eq. 7-22) combined with the masses by Dunkerley's rule, 1/ω² = 1/ω_R² + 1/ω_s², the modification Shigley suggests in Example 7-5; the result is conservative.
- Stepped shafts, overhung masses, flexible bearings and supports, and fixed ends change the critical speed and are not covered. Bearing and housing flexibility lowers it.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: Shigley Example 7-5 data (1 in steel shaft, 31 in span, E 30 Mpsi, γ 0.282 lbf/in³, 35 lbf at 7 in and 55 lbf at 23 in): influence coefficients 2.061, 1.734 and 2.472 × 10⁻⁴ in/lbf; Σ W y = 1.668 lbf·in, Σ W y² = 0.03109 lbf·in²; Rayleigh 143.9 rad/s (1 374 rpm); Dunkerley 136.2 rad/s (1 301 rpm); shaft alone 520.4 rad/s (4 969 rpm); combined 138.7 rad/s (1 325 rpm). Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The operating speed is within 30 % of the first critical speed: resonant whirling is likely. Stiffen the shaft, shorten the span or move the masses.
- The shaft\'s own mass is ignored: the critical speed shown is higher than the real one.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Bore diameter: it must be smaller than the outside diameter.
- Position of mass …: it must lie between the bearings, more than 0 and less than the span.
- Mass 1: enter at least one mass, or include the shaft\'s own mass.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Shigley Example 7-5 influence coefficients (1 in shaft, 31 in span, 30 Mpsi): a11 = 2.061, a12 = 1.734, a22 = 2.472 × 10⁻⁴ in/lbf
  - Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., Example 7-5 (Table A-9 deflection formulas)
- Example 7-5: Rayleigh 143.9 rad/s (1 374 rpm), Dunkerley 136.2 rad/s (1 301 rpm), shaft alone 520.4 rad/s (4 969 rpm), combined 1 325 rpm
  - Source: Shigley 10th ed., Example 7-5 data with eqs. 7-22, 7-23 and 7-32 (hand calculation)
- Single central mass: Rayleigh and Dunkerley both give the exact ω = √(48 E I / (m L³))
  - Source: Simply supported beam, central load: δ = W L³ / (48 E I) (Roark Table 8.1)
- Uniform shaft alone: ω_s = (π/L)² √(EI/(ρA)); a hollow shaft of the same outside diameter runs faster
  - Source: Shigley 10th ed., eq. 7-22
- Operating speed near critical warns (1 300 rpm against 1 325 rpm); ratio is reported
  - Source: Validation contract
- A mass outside the span, a bore larger than the shaft and no mass at all are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1 374 rpm, 1 301 rpm, 4 969 rpm, 1 325 rpm to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §7-6 Critical speeds for shafts: eqs. 7-22 (uniform shaft), 7-23 (Rayleigh), 7-32 (Dunkerley), Table A-9 (beam deflections) and Example 7-5
- Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain, 8th ed., Table 8.1 case 1e (simply supported beam with a point load, deflection equations)

## Shaft torque, power and diameter

<a id="shaft-torque"></a>

Folder `shaft-torque/` · Mechanical · Torque from power and speed, shear stress and twist of solid or hollow shafts, required diameter, combined bending, and the IACS UR M68 rule diameter.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Torque follows from power and rotational speed with no transmission loss: T = P/ω; enter shaft power for shaft torque and brake power for the engine output flange.
- Elastic torsion of a straight circular shaft (solid or hollow): τ = T r / J with the maximum at the outer surface; stress concentrations at keyways, fillets, holes and shrink fits are not included in the stress outputs (they are in the rule k factors).
- The angle of twist uses a uniform shaft of length L and shear modulus G (steel 79–81 GPa); stepped shafts need to be summed section by section.
- The required diameter for an allowable shear stress is the simple strength sizing at the same hollowness ratio; fatigue, vibration (torsional and whirling), deflection and alignment usually govern long shafts and are not covered.
- Combined bending and torsion uses the maximum-shear-stress (Tresca) equivalent torque T_e = √(M² + T²) and the maximum-principal-stress equivalent moment M_e = (M + T_e)/2 for a steady bending moment; alternating bending on a rotating shaft is a fatigue problem.
- The IACS UR M68 rule diameter d = F k [P / (n (1 − Q⁴)) × 560 / (σ_B + 160)]^(1/3) mm is reproduced with the standard F and k factors; the rule limits the tensile strength σ_B that may be used (600 N/mm² for carbon/carbon-manganese steel and for propeller shafts, 800 N/mm² for alloy-steel intermediate shafts) — enter the capped value — and the rule is a minimum, not a design.
- Rule check applies to propulsion shafting of conventional ships; thrusters, gearbox shafts and non-marine machinery follow other codes.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: T = 9 549.3 P/n reproduces the Shigley relation (eq. 3-42); the 8 000 kW / 90 rpm case (848.8 kN·m, 47.4 MPa on a 450 mm solid shaft, 1.51° twist over 10 m) was checked by hand, and the rule diameter 403 mm for σ_B = 600 is in the range of real intermediate shafts of that power.
- Design decision: the polar moment comes from shared/sections.js so shafts, beams and columns share one geometry module.
- Design decision: combined loading is reported with both classical equivalents (T_e and M_e) because marine engineering textbooks (Reeds) use them side by side.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Torsional shear stress exceeds the allowable value: increase the diameter or the material grade.
- Outer diameter is below the IACS UR M68 minimum for this power, speed and material.
- Twist exceeds 0.25° per metre, a common stiffness limit for machine shafting; check torsional vibration and alignment.
- Bore ratio above 0.7: a thin-walled tube — check local buckling and the rule limits for hollow shafts.
- Combined loading uses static equivalents; a rotating shaft sees the bending stress as fully reversed and needs a fatigue check (Shigley ch. 7).
- Stress concentrations (keyways, fillets, holes) and torsional vibration stresses are not included in the stress outputs.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Bore diameter must be less than the outer diameter

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Torque from power: 8 000 kW at 90 rpm = 9 549.3 × 8 000 / 90 = 848.8 kN·m; 1 kW at 1 rpm = 9 549.3 N·m
  - Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., eq. 3-42: T = 9.55 P/n (P in W, n in rpm)
- Solid 450 mm shaft: J = π d⁴/32 = 402 590 cm⁴, τ = 16 T/(π d³) = 47.4 MPa, twist 1.51° over 10 m at G = 80 GPa
  - Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, ch. 5: τ_max = T c / J, φ = T L / (J G)
- Hollow shaft 450/150 mm: J reduced by (1 − (1/3)⁴) = 98.8 %, stress up 1.25 %; a 450/315 mm tube (ratio 0.7) has 76 % of the solid J
  - Source: J = π (d_o⁴ − d_i⁴)/32 (Hibbeler ch. 5)
- Required diameter for 55 MPa allowable: solid d = (16 T / π τ)^(1/3) = 428 mm; with bore ratio 0.5 the outer diameter is 438 mm
  - Source: Inversion of τ = 16 T / (π d³ (1 − q⁴)) (Reeds Vol. 2, Applied Mechanics, "Torsion")
- Combined loading with M = 200 kN·m: T_e = √(200² + 848.8²) = 872.1 kN·m, M_e = 536.0 kN·m, τ_max 48.7 MPa, σ_max 59.9 MPa
  - Source: Reeds Vol. 2, Applied Mechanics, equivalent torque (Tresca) and equivalent bending moment (Rankine); Shigley §5-4
- IACS UR M68: 8 000 kW, 90 rpm, solid, σ_B 600, F 100, k 1.0 → d = 100 × (88.89 × 560/760)^(1/3) = 403 mm; k 1.26 propeller shaft → 508 mm
  - Source: IACS UR M68 Rev. 2 (2015), §2.1: d = F k [P/(n(1 − Q⁴)) × 560/(σ_B + 160)]^(1/3)
- Warnings: undersized shaft (300 mm) exceeds both the allowable stress and the rule minimum; excessive twist is flagged
  - Source: Behaviour specification; 0.25°/m stiffness rule of thumb for machine shafting
- Unit layer: 848.8 kN·m = 626 100 lbf·ft; 8 000 kW = 10 728 hp; 90 rpm = 9.425 rad/s
  - Source: NIST SP 811: 1 lbf·ft = 1.355818 N·m, 1 hp = 745.6999 W
- Invalid inputs fail fast: bore not smaller than the outer diameter, zero speed, tensile strength outside the rule range
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 848 800 N·m, 402 600 cm⁴, 47.4 MPa, 0.0264 rad, 0.428 m, 86 %, 403 mm, 12 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Budynas & Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §3-12 torsion (eqs 3-36 to 3-42), §4 angle of twist
- Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, 10th ed., ch. 5 "Torsion" (τ = T c / J, φ = T L / J G, power transmission)
- Reeds Marine Engineering Series Vol. 2, Applied Mechanics for Marine Engineers, ch. "Torsion" (equivalent torque and moment)

## Shaft torsion calculator (shear stress, twist, diameter)

<a id="shaft-torsion"></a>

Folder `shaft-torsion/` · Mechanical · Shear stress and angle of twist of solid and hollow round shafts, the torque they can carry, the diameter for an allowable stress or twist, and power to torque.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Elastic torsion of a straight, uniform, circular shaft (solid or hollow) under a constant torque: plane sections stay plane and the shear stress grows linearly from the centre to its maximum at the surface.
- Keyways, splines, shoulders and cross holes raise the local stress; apply a stress-concentration factor, or use the allowable stress of a code that already includes one.
- Only torsion is checked. Shafts usually also carry bending, which needs a combined (von Mises or Tresca) check, and fluctuating loads need a fatigue check.
- Torque from power assumes steady running, T = P/ω; starting, shock and torsional vibration can raise the peak torque well above it.
- The twist limit is the allowable angle over the length entered, so a limit per metre is entered with a length of 1 m.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: data of Gere and Goodno Example 3-1 (solid steel bar d = 40 mm, L = 1.3 m, G = 80 GPa): T = 340 N·m gives τmax = 27.1 MPa and θ = 0.0220 rad (1.26°); with τ_allow = 42 MPa and θ_allow = 2.5° the permissible torque is 528 N·m, set by the stress (675 N·m by twist). 15 kW at 1 450 rpm is 98.8 N·m and needs 23.3 mm at 40 MPa. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The shear stress exceeds the allowable stress.
- The angle of twist exceeds the allowable twist.
- Very thin-walled tube (k > 0.9): local buckling of the wall may govern before the shear stress limit.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Inside diameter: it must be smaller than the outside diameter.
- Allowable shear stress: enter an allowable stress, an allowable twist, or both, to size the shaft.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Solid bar d 40 mm, L 1.3 m, G 80 GPa, T 340 N·m: τmax = 16T/(πd³) = 27.06 MPa, θ = TL/(GJ) = 0.02198 rad = 1.26°
  - Source: Gere and Goodno, Mechanics of Materials, Example 3-1 data (eqs. 3-14 and 3-17; hand calculation)
- Same bar with τ_allow 42 MPa and θ_allow 2.5°: torque 527.8 N·m by stress, 674.8 N·m by twist, so 528 N·m governs
  - Source: Gere and Goodno, Example 3-1 (b) data: T = τ π d³/16 and T = G J θ / L (hand calculation)
- Power to torque: 15 kW at 1 450 rpm = 98.79 N·m; solid steel shaft at 40 MPa needs d = (16T/(πτ))^(1/3) = 23.26 mm
  - Source: T = P/ω (Shigley eq. 3-42); Gere eq. 3-14 solved for d (hand calculation)
- Hollow shaft k 0.6 needs (1 − 0.6⁴)^(−1/3) = 1.047 times the solid diameter for the same stress; twist sizing hits the twist limit exactly
  - Source: J = π d⁴ (1 − k⁴)/32 (hand calculation)
- Material moduli: steel twists 81/27 = 3 times less than aluminium for the same shaft and torque
  - Source: EN 1993-1-1 §3.2.6 (G 81 GPa) and EN 1999-1-1 §3.2.5 (G 27 GPa); θ ∝ 1/G
- Over-stress warns; a bore not smaller than the outside diameter and sizing with no limit are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 27.1 MPa, 0.0220 rad, 528 N·m, 675 N·m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

## Shallow water correction (Raven / Lackenby)

<a id="shallow-water-speed"></a>

Folder `shallow-water-speed/` · Maritime · ISO 15016:2025 Annex G (Raven) shallow-water power correction — viscous increase and sinkage — plus the legacy Lackenby speed correction.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Raven method as normative in ISO 15016:2025 Annex G: the shallow-water power increase P_SH is the sum of (a) a viscous resistance increase R_SHV = R_Vdeep × 0.57 (T_M/h)^1.79, with the deep-water viscous resistance from C_V' = 1.06 C_F (1+k) + ΔC_F (ITTC-57 line, roughness allowance G.8, form factor from G.9: (1+k) = 1.017 + 20 C_B (B/L_PP)² (T_M/B)^0.5), and (b) a sinkage displacement effect r_sink = (1 + δ)^(2/3) with δ = d A_W/∇ (max 0.05) and the additional dynamic sinkage d = 1.46 ∇/L_PP² [Fr_h²/√(1−Fr_h²) − Fr_hd²/√(1−Fr_hd²)] ≥ 0, where Fr_hd is the depth Froude number at the reference depth 0.3 L_PP; the deep-water power is P_Ddeep = (P_Dmsc − R_SHV V_S/η_Did)/r_sink and P_SH = P_Dmsc − P_Ddeep.
- The method corrects a measured trial power (already corrected for wind, waves and temperature) to deep water; it is valid where the trial itself is valid, i.e. for water depths above the ISO limit h ≥ max(2.5 T_M, 2.4 V_S²/g) (Formula 7), and for sub-critical depth Froude numbers (Fr_h < 1; the sinkage term diverges towards Fr_h → 1). Below the limit the trial is not acceptable and the correction is not meaningful.
- Lackenby (1963) is the legacy ISO 15016:2015 speed correction: ΔV/V = 0.1242 (A_M/h² − 0.05) + 1 − √tanh(g h/V²) with A_M the midship section area (C_M B T_M), applicable for A_M/h² ≥ 0.05; it gives the deep-water speed at the same power, V_deep = V(1 + ΔV/V), and is reported for comparison and for analyses still following the 2015 edition.
- The displacement volume is taken as C_B L_PP B T_M and the waterplane area as C_WP L_PP B unless the hydrostatics give better values; the propulsive efficiency in ideal condition η_Did is assumed unchanged in shallow water (ISO notes that wake and efficiency do change — a known limitation of the standard).
- Sea water density and viscosity from the ITTC 7.5-02-01-03 table at the trial temperature and salinity (shared/seawater.js).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 180 × 32 × 11 m, C_B 0.80, C_WP 0.88, S 7 000 m², 12 kn in 30 m of 15 °C water, 5 000 kW delivered, η_D 0.70 → Fr_h 0.360, (1+k) 1.313, d 0.146 m, δ 0.0146, r_sink 1.0097, R_Vdeep 306 kN, R_SHV 29.0 kN → P_Ddeep 4 699 kW, P_SH 301 kW (6.0 %); Lackenby gives a 4.1 % speed loss (12.50 kn deep-water speed), the same order (6 % power ≈ 2 % speed by the cubic law, the remainder being the different physics of the two methods).
- Transcription check: the G.12 bracket uses Fr²/√(1 − Fr²) (Tuck's shallow-water sinkage form), and the ≥ 0 clamp means deep water (h ≥ 0.3 L_PP) gives no sinkage correction by construction; the 0.3 L_PP reference depth is why the correction vanishes at h = 54 m for this ship.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Water depth … m is below the ISO 15016 trial limit … m (Formula 7): the run is not acceptable as a speed trial and the correction is outside its validity.
- Additional displacement fraction capped at 0.05 (G.11): very shallow water for this ship.
- Depth Froude number above 0.7: approaching the critical speed, where squat and wave pattern change rapidly and the method loses accuracy.
- Lackenby A_M/h² below 0.05: outside the range of the 1963 correction (effectively deep water for Lackenby).
- No sinkage correction: the depth is at or beyond the 0.3 L_PP reference depth, so only the viscous term remains.
- η_Did assumed unchanged in shallow water (ISO 15016 notes wake and efficiency do change); the trial power must already be corrected for wind, waves and water temperature.
- Displacement ∇ = C_B L_PP B T_M and A_W = C_WP L_PP B are approximations: use the hydrostatic tables at the trial draught when available.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Water depth must exceed the draught
- Depth Froude number at or above 1 (supercritical): the Raven sinkage formula does not apply

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Depth Froude numbers and trial limit: Fr_h = 6.173/√(9.80665 × 30) = 0.3599, Fr_hd at 0.3 L_PP = 54 m → 0.2683; minimum depth max(2.5 × 11, 2.4 V²/g) = 27.5 m → 30 m is acceptable, 25 m is not
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 Formula (7) and G.13
- Sinkage term: ∇ = 50 688 m³, d = 1.46 ∇/L² [Fr_h²/√(1−Fr_h²) − Fr_hd²/√(1−Fr_hd²)] = 0.1465 m; δ = d A_W/∇ = 0.01465 with A_W 5 069 m²; r_sink = 1.00974; deep water (h = 54 m) gives d = 0
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 G.10–G.12 (Tuck sinkage form)
- Viscous term: Re 9.351e8, C_F 1.5434e-3, ΔC_F 8.91e-5, (1+k) = 1.017 + 20 × 0.8 × (32/180)² × √(11/32) = 1.3135, C_V' 2.238e-3 → R_Vdeep 306.2 kN, R_SHV = R_Vdeep × 0.57 × (11/30)^1.79 = 29.0 kN
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 G.3–G.9; ITTC water properties
- Power correction: P_Ddeep = (5 000 kW − 29.0 kN × 6.173/0.70)/1.00974 = 4 699 kW, P_SH = 301 kW = 6.0 %; P_SH falls with depth (60 m < 30 m) and is only the viscous term at 54 m and beyond
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 G.1–G.2
- Lackenby: A_M = 0.98 × 32 × 11 = 345.0 m², A_M/h² = 0.3833, ΔV/V = 0.1242 (0.3833 − 0.05) + 1 − √tanh(gh/V²) = 4.14 %, deep-water speed 12.50 kn; at 200 m depth A_M/h² < 0.05 is flagged
  - Source: Lackenby (1963); ISO 15016:2015 shallow-water correction
- Validation: depth not exceeding the draught, supercritical depth Froude number (30 kn in 12 m) and zero wetted surface are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract; G.12 validity (Fr_h < 1)
- A short fast ship in water deeper than 0.3 L_PP gets no sinkage, even when the reference depth Froude number exceeds 1
  - Source: Range fuzzing (fuzz.js): G.12 is evaluated only below the reference depth, where Fr_hd < Fr_h < 1
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 27.5 m, 0.360, 0.268, 0.146 m, 0.0146, 1.0097, 1.313, 306 kN to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 15016:2025 Ships and marine technology — speed and power trials, 8.5 Formula (7) and Annex G (normative) Effect of shallow water, Formulae G.1–G.13
- H. C. Raven, "A new correction procedure for shallow-water effects in ship speed trials", Proceedings PRADS 2016, Copenhagen; Raven, "Shallow-water effects in ship model testing and at full scale", Ocean Engineering 189, 2019
- H. Lackenby, "The effect of shallow water on ship speed", The Shipbuilder and Marine Engine-Builder 70, 1963; ISO 15016:2015 Annex (shallow water correction)
- E. O. Tuck, "Shallow-water flows past slender bodies", Journal of Fluid Mechanics 26, 1966 (sinkage ∝ Fr_h²/√(1 − Fr_h²))

## Ship squat and under-keel clearance

<a id="ship-squat"></a>

Folder `ship-squat/` · Maritime · Barrass squat in open water and confined channels, Froude depth number, net under-keel clearance against a required margin and the maximum safe speed.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Squat follows Barrass's empirical formula S_max = C_B S^0.81 V^2.08 / 20, derived from model and full-scale data for 1.1 ≤ h/T ≤ 1.4; outside that range (and especially for h/T > 1.5) it is an extrapolation and tends to overestimate.
- In open water the blockage factor uses the Barrass "width of influence" F_B = 7.7 + 20 (1 − C_B)² times the beam, so S = T / (F_B h); in a confined channel S = B T / (W h) with the channel treated as rectangular (bank slopes and midship-section coefficient ignored).
- Speed is speed through the water; with a following current the speed over ground is higher than the squat speed, and with a head current lower.
- The static draft entered is the deepest draft at rest (even keel assumed); squat is reported as the maximum sinkage, at the bow for C_B above 0.7 and at the stern below 0.7, and trim changes are not resolved separately.
- Froude depth number F_nh = V/√(g h) is reported because squat rises steeply above about 0.7 and the formula is not valid near the critical speed (F_nh ≈ 1).
- The allowances input lumps swell and wave response, heel, density/fresh-water effects, chart-datum and sounding uncertainty; the calculator does not compute wave-induced motions.
- The required under-keel clearance is a user policy (typically 10 % of draft in open water, more in channels per PIANC or port rules); the maximum speed output is the speed at which net UKC equals that requirement.
- Ship-to-ship and ship-to-bank interaction, bow and stern wave effects at very low h/T, and squat of trimmed ships are not covered.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the general Barrass formula and the C_B V²/100 rule differ by 8 % at h/T = 1.2 (0.733 vs 0.80 m), consistent with Barrass's own comparisons; the maximum-speed inversion was checked by substitution (squat at V_max equals the available clearance to 10⁻⁹ m).
- Design decision: both the general formula and the simplified rule are shown so masters can see the spread between the two methods they are usually taught.
- Design decision: the required clearance is a percentage of draft set by the user (policy), and the calculator never silently chooses a margin.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- h/T = … is outside the 1.1–1.4 range the Barrass formulas were derived for; treat the squat as indicative (over-estimated for deep water).
- Froude depth number above 0.7: squat grows faster than the formula predicts as the critical speed is approached. Reduce speed.
- Blockage factor above 0.3: very restricted channel; the formula is at the edge of its data and bank effects become significant.
- The channel is wider than the Barrass width of influence — the open-water setting gives the same or a larger squat.
- Net under-keel clearance is … m short of the requirement at this speed; the maximum speed for the required clearance is … kn.
- No allowance for swell, heel or sounding uncertainty: the net clearance is the best case.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Water depth (… m) must exceed the static draft (… m) — the ship would be aground

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Barrass open-water rule of thumb: C_B 0.80 at 10 kn squats about C_B V²/100 = 0.80 m
  - Source: Barrass & Derrett, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed., ch. 43: open water S_max ≈ C_B × V² / 100 for h/T 1.1–1.4
- Barrass general formula in open water: F_B = 7.7 + 20 (1 − 0.8)² = 8.5, S = T / (F_B h) = 0.0980, S_max = 0.8 × S^0.81 × 10^2.08 / 20 = 0.733 m (within 10 % of the rule of thumb)
  - Source: Barrass, Ship Squat and Interaction (2004): width of influence and S_max = C_B S^0.81 V^2.08 / 20; value computed by hand
- Confined channel 150 m wide: S = 32 × 10 / (150 × 12) = 0.178; general formula 1.187 m, simplified confined rule C_B S^(2/3) V^2.08 / 20 = 1.520 m
  - Source: Barrass & Derrett ch. 43 confined-channel formula; Barrass (2004) general formula; values computed by hand
- Under-keel clearance: static 2.00 m, net 2.00 − 0.733 − 0.5 = 0.767 m, required 10 % × 10 m = 1.00 m → short by 0.233 m; maximum speed 8.32 kn
  - Source: UKC bookkeeping per PIANC (1997/2014); speed from inverting the Barrass formula for the available squat (0.5 m)
- Slowing to 8 kn makes the same case compliant (squat 0.464 m, net 1.036 m); zero available clearance gives zero speed
  - Source: Squat scales with V^2.08: (8/10)^2.08 = 0.629 (Barrass)
- Froude depth number: 10 kn in 12 m = 5.144 / √(9.80665 × 12) = 0.474; 16 kn in 12 m exceeds 0.7 and triggers the warning
  - Source: F_nh = V / √(g h); PIANC guidance that squat rises steeply above F_nh ≈ 0.7
- Squat location by block coefficient: C_B 0.80 at the bow, 0.60 at the stern, 0.70 even keel; h/T outside 1.1–1.4 is flagged
  - Source: Barrass & Derrett ch. 43: full-form ships (C_B > 0.7) squat by the head, fine-form by the stern
- Invalid inputs fail fast: depth not exceeding draft (aground), zero beam, unknown waterway
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.20, 272 m, 0.098, 0.73 m, 0.80 m, 0.47, 2.00 m, 0.77 m, 1.00 m, 8.3 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- C.B. Barrass, Ship Squat and Interaction (Witherby, 2004) and Ship Design and Performance for Masters and Mates (2004), ch. "Ship squat"
- Barrass & Derrett, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed. (2012), ch. 43 "Ship squat in open water and in confined channels"
- PIANC, Approach Channels — A Guide for Design (PTC II-30, 1997) and Harbour Approach Channels Design Guidelines (Report 121, 2014): squat methods and under-keel clearance components
- Froude depth number definition: F_nh = V / √(g h)

## Gross and net tonnage calculator (ITC 1969)

<a id="ship-tonnage"></a>

Folder `ship-tonnage/` · Maritime · Gross tonnage GT = K1 V and net tonnage NT by the 1969 Tonnage Convention (Annex I, regulations 3 and 4), with the convention's limits applied.

### Assumptions and caveats

- V is the total moulded volume of all enclosed spaces (hull and superstructures) and Vc the volume of the cargo spaces, both in cubic metres and measured as regulation 6 requires. Their measurement is the work of the Administration or a recognised organisation; this page applies the formulas only.
- K1 and K2 use the formula 0.2 + 0.02 log10 V. Appendix 2 of the convention tabulates the same function and permits linear interpolation between its rows, which can differ from the formula in the fourth decimal.
- D is the moulded depth amidships (regulation 2(2)) and d the moulded draught of regulation 4(2): the summer load line draught for cargo ships, the deepest subdivision load line for passenger ships, and 75 % of D for ships without either.
- The limits of regulation 4(1) are applied: (4d/3D)² not more than 1, the cargo term not less than 0.25 GT, NT not less than 0.30 GT, and passengers counted only when there are 13 or more.
- Results are shown to the nearest whole number; the tonnage certificate states whole numbers as the Administration determines them.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: V = 30 000 m³ gives K1 = 0.28954 and GT = 8 686.3; Vc = 16 000 m³ with d = 8.5 m and D = 12 m gives K2 = 0.28408, (4d/3D)² = 0.8920 and NT = 4 054.3. Appendix 2 values K1 = 0.22 at 10 m³ and 0.32 at 1 000 000 m³ are reproduced. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The draught is greater than the moulded depth: check d and D.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Cargo space volume Vc: it cannot exceed the total enclosed volume V.
- Total volume V: the convention\'s coefficient table starts at 10 m³; a space this small has no meaningful tonnage.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Appendix 2 table: K1 = 0.2200 at 10 m³, 0.2600 at 1 000 m³, 0.2800 at 10 000 m³ and 0.3200 at 1 000 000 m³
  - Source: ITC 1969, Annex I, Appendix 2 (coefficients K1 and K2)
- Cargo ship: V 30 000 m³ → GT 8 686; Vc 16 000 m³, d 8.5 m, D 12 m → NT 4 054
  - Source: ITC 1969, Annex I, regulations 3 and 4; hand calculation
- Passenger ship: V 60 000 m³, no cargo, 1 500 + 200 passengers: cargo term raised to 0.25 GT, K3 = 3.467, NT = 9 703
  - Source: ITC 1969, Annex I, regulation 4(1)(b) and K3 = 1.25 (GT + 10 000)/10 000; hand calculation
- Limits: (4d/3D)² capped at 1; fewer than 13 passengers ignored; NT not below 0.30 GT
  - Source: ITC 1969, Annex I, regulation 4(1)(a), (c) and the N1 + N2 < 13 rule
- A cargo volume above the total and a fractional passenger count are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.28954, 8 686, 0.28408, 0.8920, 4 054 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- International Convention on Tonnage Measurement of Ships, 1969 (IMO), Annex I, regulation 3 (gross tonnage) and regulation 4 (net tonnage)
- ITC 1969, Annex I, regulation 2 (moulded depth) and Appendix 2 (coefficients K1 and K2, linear interpolation)
- UK Merchant Shipping (Tonnage) Regulations 1997 (SI 1997/1510), Part II: the convention formulas as enacted in national law

## Short-circuit current (IEC 60909)

<a id="short-circuit-current"></a>

Folder `short-circuit-current/` · Electrical · Three-phase short-circuit current at a switchboard from source, transformer and cable impedances; peak current and breaker check.

### Assumptions and caveats

- IEC 60909-0 equivalent voltage source at the fault: I_k'' = c U_n/(√3 Z_k) with the voltage factor c (Table 1: low voltage c_max 1.05 for +6 % systems or 1.10 for +10 %, c_min 0.95; medium/high voltage 1.10/1.00), balanced three-phase fault far from generators (I_b = I_k = I_k''), no motor contribution, no fault impedance.
- Upstream network as an impedance Z_Q = c U_nQ²/S_kQ'' referred to the low-voltage side by the transformer ratio, with R_Q/X_Q = 0.1 (X_Q = 0.995 Z_Q) as IEC 60909-0 §6.2.2 allows when nothing better is known; the MV voltage factor 1.10 is used for the network impedance.
- Two-winding transformer: Z_T = u_kr U_rT²/S_rT, R_T = P_krT U_rT²/S_rT², X_T = √(Z_T² − R_T²), corrected by K_T = 0.95 c_max/(1 + 0.6 x_T) (IEC 60909-0 eq. 12a, c_max of the LV side) when enabled; tap position and no-load losses are ignored.
- Feeder cable: resistance and reactance per unit length at 20 °C for the maximum current; for the minimum current the conductor resistance is taken at the end-of-fault temperature θ_e with the factor 1 + 0.004 (θ_e − 20) (IEC 60909-0 §2.3.2.4, 160 °C for PVC-insulated copper), parallel cables divide the impedance.
- Peak current i_p = κ √2 I_k'' with κ = 1.02 + 0.98 e^(−3R/X) from the resulting R/X at the fault (method A/C of IEC 60909-0 §4.3.1.1 for radial networks); the thermal equivalent current I_th = I_k'' √(m + n) uses the DC-decay factor m from eq. 103 and n = 1 for far-from-generator faults.
- Protective device check compares the rated ultimate breaking capacity I_cu with I_k'' and the rated short-circuit making capacity with i_p; the let-through energy, cable withstand (k² S² ≥ I² t) and selectivity are separate checks.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 1 000 kVA, 6 %, 10.5 kW, 400 V transformer on an infinite source gives Z_T 9.60 mΩ, R_T 1.68 mΩ, K_T 0.963, I_k'' 26.2 kA (the textbook I_r/u_k = 24.1 kA times c_max and K_T), R/X 0.178, κ 1.595, i_p 59 kA; voltage factors, κ and K_T formulas checked against secondary reproductions of IEC 60909-0 (DIgSILENT FAQ, eng-tips thread, myCableEngineering).
- Design decision: the LV default voltage factor is 1.05 (+6 % systems, IEC 60909-0:2001 Table 1); the 1.10 option covers +10 % systems as the 2016 edition allows. Note that with K_T = 0.95 c_max/(1 + 0.6 x_T) applied, c_max cancels out of the transformer-only current (I_k″ ∝ c_max/K_T); the choice of c only matters through the network and cable impedances.
- Design decision: the minimum current is evaluated at the cable end with c_min and the heated conductor, which is what protection coordination needs; the maximum at the switchboard with cold cable.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Infinite source: the real network impedance lowers I_k″ by a few per cent for strong grids and much more for weak ones.
- Fault at the transformer terminals: the minimum current equals the maximum scaled by c_min/c_max (no heated cable).
- Minimum fault current at the cable end is below half the maximum: check that the protective device trips within the required time at I_k,min (IEC 60364-4-41).
- R/X above 1 (long cable): κ is close to 1.02 and the DC component negligible; the thermal factor m is ≈ 0.
- Far-from-generator fault without motor contribution: large motor loads (> 1 % of I_k″ each, IEC 60909-0 §6.6) add to the initial and peak currents.
- Single-phase and phase-to-earth faults, arc impedance, selectivity and cable withstand (k² S² ≥ I² t) are separate checks.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Transformer load losses … W imply R_T ≥ Z_T: check P_krT and u_kr

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Transformer impedances: 1 000 kVA, 6 %, 10.5 kW at 400 V → Z_T = 0.06 × 400²/10⁶ = 9.60 mΩ, R_T = 10 500 × 400²/10¹² = 1.68 mΩ, X_T = 9.452 mΩ, x_T 0.0591, K_T = 0.95 × 1.05/(1 + 0.6 × 0.0591) = 0.963
  - Source: IEC 60909-0 §6.3.2 eqs. 7–9 and eq. 12a (K_T)
- Infinite source, fault at the terminals: I_k″ = 1.05 × 400/(√3 × 0.963 × 9.6 mΩ) = 26.2 kA (the classic I_r/u_k = 24.1 kA scaled by c_max and K_T); I_rT = 1 443 A; I_k″/I_rT = 18.2
  - Source: IEC 60909-0 eq. 29 I_k″ = c U_n/(√3 Z_k); Schneider CT 158 transformer-only estimate I_r/u_k
- Peak factor: R/X = 0.178 → κ = 1.02 + 0.98 e^(−0.533) = 1.595, i_p = 1.595 × √2 × 26.2 = 59 kA; κ → 2.0 for R/X → 0 and → 1.02 for R/X → ∞
  - Source: IEC 60909-0 §4.3.1.1 eq. 55
- Thermal equivalent: m = (1/(2 f T_k ln(κ−1)))(e^(4 f T_k ln(κ−1)) − 1) = 0.0193 for κ 1.595, 50 Hz, 1 s → I_th = I_k″ √1.0193; m is larger for short durations (0.1 s → 0.19)
  - Source: IEC 60909-0 §4.8 eq. 103 (m) with n = 1 for far-from-generator faults
- Network feeder: 250 MVA at the HV side → Z_Qt = 1.10 × 400²/250 MVA = 0.704 mΩ (X 0.700, R 0.070) in series, lowering I_k″ at the terminals to about 24.4 kA; an infinite source is the upper bound
  - Source: IEC 60909-0 §6.2.2 eq. 5 with R_Q/X_Q = 0.1
- Cable: 50 m of 0.1 + j0.08 Ω/km adds 5 + j4 mΩ → Z_k = 6.62 + j13.10 = 14.68 mΩ, I_k″ at the fault 16.5 kA (vs 26.2 at the terminals); two parallel cables halve the cable impedance; minimum current with c_min 0.95 and copper at 160 °C (R × 1.56) is 13.6 kA
  - Source: IEC 60909-0 §2.3.2.4 conductor temperature factor 1 + 0.004 (θ_e − 20); series impedance
- Voltage factors (Table 1): LV +6 % 1.05/0.95, LV +10 % 1.10/0.95, MV 1.10/1.00; breaker check passes for a 36 kA / 75.6 kA breaker at 26.2 / 59.1 kA and fails for 25 kA; with K_T applied c_max cancels out of the transformer-only I_k″ (K_T ∝ c_max), without K_T c 1.10 gives 4.8 % more
  - Source: IEC 60909-0 Table 1 and eq. 12a; IEC 60947-2 I_cu and I_cm
- Invalid inputs fail fast: load losses implying R_T ≥ Z_T, fractional parallel cables, unknown voltage-factor class
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.05, 0.704 mΩ, 9.60 mΩ, 1.68 mΩ, 0.963, 15.3 mΩ, 24.4 kA, 15.8 kA to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IEC 60909-0:2016 Short-circuit currents in three-phase a.c. systems — Part 0: Calculation of currents (Table 1 voltage factor, §6.2 network feeder, §6.3 transformers with eq. 12a, §4.3 peak factor κ, eq. 103 factor m)
- IEC TR 60909-1:2002 Factors for the calculation of short-circuit currents; IEC TR 60909-4:2021 Examples for the calculation of short-circuit currents
- Schneider Electric Cahier Technique 158, "Calculation of short-circuit currents" (worked examples of the impedance method)
- IEC 60947-2 low-voltage circuit-breakers (I_cu, I_cm definitions); IEC 60364-4-43 overcurrent protection

## Sight reduction (intercept method)

<a id="sight-reduction"></a>

Folder `sight-reduction/` · Maritime · Observed altitude from the sextant reading, then the intercept, azimuth and intercept terminal point from the assumed position.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Altitude corrections as in the Nautical Almanac: index error (on the arc subtracted), dip of the sea horizon 1.76′ √h for a height of eye h in metres, refraction from Bennett's formula scaled by (P/1010)·(283/(273 + T)) for non-standard pressure and temperature, parallax HP·cos Ha (0.15′ for the sun, the almanac HP for the moon, nil for stars), and the semi-diameter added for a lower limb and subtracted for an upper limb.
- Planets are observed at their centre; the almanac's small additional correction for Venus and Mars (phase and parallax) is entered by hand. The moon's semi-diameter is taken as entered; its small augmentation with altitude (up to 0.3′) is neglected.
- Computed altitude and azimuth from the navigational triangle at the assumed or dead-reckoning position with the GHA and declination for the time of the sight (UT); LHA = GHA + longitude with east longitude positive.
- Marcq St Hilaire intercept: one minute of altitude is one nautical mile; the position line is the straight tangent to the circle of equal altitude at the intercept terminal point, perpendicular to the azimuth. The tangent approximation is good while the intercept is under about 30 nmi and the altitude below about 85°.
- Sights below about 10° carry refraction errors of a few tenths of a minute that grow quickly towards the horizon; non-standard dip from abnormal refraction is not corrected.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: refraction 9.9′, 5.3′ and 1.7′ at 5°, 10° and 30° (Nautical Almanac standard values); dip 7.0′ for 16 m; at latitude 40° N, declination 20° N and LHA 30° the computed altitude is 57.485° (57° 29.1′) and the azimuth 240.9°; an observed altitude 5′ above Hc puts the intercept terminal point 5 nmi towards the body.
- Design decision: the sextant altitude is entered as degrees plus minutes, as it is read; latitude, longitude, GHA and declination are decimal degrees (32° 15.4′ = 32.2567°).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Apparent altitude …°: refraction near the horizon is uncertain; prefer sights above 10° (avoid below 5°).
- Altitude above 85°: the circle of equal altitude is small and the straight position line is a poor approximation; plot the circle or use a better assumed position.
- Intercept of … nmi: the assumed position is far from the true one; rework the sight from the intercept terminal point.
- Computed altitude below the horizon: check the GHA, the longitude sign (east +) and the time of the sight.
- For Venus and Mars add the almanac\'s additional correction (phase and parallax), up to about 0.5′.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Sextant altitude degrees must be a whole number; enter the rest as minutes
- Apparent altitude …° is not above the horizon: check the sextant reading, the index error and the height of eye

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Refraction in the standard atmosphere (10 °C, 1010 hPa): 9.9′ at 5°, 5.3′ at 10°, 1.7′ at 30°; at −10 °C and 1030 hPa it is (1030/1010)(283/263) = 1.097 times larger
  - Source: Nautical Almanac refraction (standard conditions and the additional correction table); Bennett (1982)
- Sun lower limb at Hs 30°, no index error, eye 16 m, SD 16.0′: dip 7.04′, refraction about 1.7′, parallax 0.13′, total correction ≈ −7.04 − 1.72 + 0.13 + 16.0 = +7.4′
  - Source: Nautical Almanac altitude corrections: dip 1.76′√h(m), sun HP 0.15′, lower limb + SD
- Navigational triangle: latitude 40° N, declination 20° N, LHA 30° gives Hc = 57.485° (57° 29.1′) and Zn = 240.9°; LHA = GHA + longitude (east positive)
  - Source: Bowditch, "Sight Reduction": sin Hc = sin L sin d + cos L cos d cos LHA, azimuth formula
- Intercept: a star observed 5′ above the computed altitude gives an intercept of +5 nmi towards the body, and the intercept terminal point lies 5 nmi from the assumed position along the azimuth
  - Source: Marcq St Hilaire method: intercept = Ho − Hc, 1′ = 1 nmi
- Moon lower limb at Ha about 40° with HP 57.0′: parallax 57.0 cos Ha ≈ 43.7′ dominates the correction; index error on the arc is subtracted
  - Source: Nautical Almanac moon correction (parallax in altitude = HP cos Ha)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: 60 minutes, fractional degrees, a negative height of eye and a sight below the horizon
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces −1.5′, 7.0′, 0.6′, 0.1′, +16.0′, 30°, 240.9°, −0.2 nmi to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- The Nautical Almanac (HM Nautical Almanac Office / US Naval Observatory) — altitude correction tables, dip 1.76′ √h(m), standard atmosphere 10 °C and 1010 hPa
- G. G. Bennett, "The calculation of astronomical refraction in marine navigation", Journal of Navigation 35 (1982) 255–259
- The American Practical Navigator (Bowditch), NGA Pub. 9 — "Sight Reduction" (navigational triangle, intercept method, position lines)
- A. Frost, The Principles and Practice of Navigation; R. Hughes / Nicholls's Concise Guide to Navigation — Marcq St Hilaire method

## Slope calculator: percent, degrees, ratio and pitch

<a id="slope"></a>

Folder `slope/` · Civil · Convert slope between percent grade, degrees, ratio 1 in n and roof pitch, or find it from rise and run, with the slope length and height change.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Slope is rise over horizontal run. Percent grade is that ratio × 100, so 100 % is 45°, not vertical.
- Roof pitch is the rise in inches per 12 in of run; a ratio "1 : n" is one unit of rise per n units of run (road and drainage practice). Embankment batters written "n H : 1 V" use the same n.
- The slope length is measured along the surface, the length of material for a ramp, roof or pipe.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a rise of 1 m over a 12 m run is 8.33 %, 4.76°, 1 : 12 and 1 in 12 pitch; the ADA ramp limit of 1 : 12 is 8.33 %.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- (none — all conditions are hard errors or silent)

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 1 m rise over 12 m: 8.33 %, 4.76°, 1 : 12, 1 in 12 pitch, 12.04 m along the slope; at the ADA ramp limit
  - Source: 2010 ADA Standards §405.2 (1 : 12); tan θ = 1/12
- A 6 in 12 roof is 50 %, 26.57°, 1 : 2; 45° is 100 % grade and 12 in 12
  - Source: Roof pitch = 12 × rise/run; tan 45° = 1
- A 2 % fall is 1 : 50 and drops 0.2 m over 10 m; a 1 : 20 ratio is 5 %
  - Source: grade = 1/n; rise = grade × run
- Every input mode gives the same answer for the same slope
  - Source: Consistency of the conversions
- Zero run, 90° and an unknown mode are rejected; level ground is shown as 1 : ∞
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 8.33 %, 12.04 m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- US Access Board, 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, §405.2 (maximum ramp running slope 1 : 12)
- Trigonometry of the right triangle: tan θ = rise / run

## Snow load calculator (Eurocode and ASCE 7)

<a id="snow-load"></a>

Folder `snow-load/` · Structural · Roof snow load from the ground snow load for flat and pitched roofs by EN 1991-1-3 or ASCE 7-16, with exposure, thermal and slope factors.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The ground snow load s_k or p_g is the characteristic value for the site from the national annex map (Eurocode) or the ASCE 7 map and local amendments; the calculator does not look it up.
- Balanced (undrifted) load on a monopitch or each side of a duopitch roof. Drifts at parapets, steps and valleys, sliding snow, unbalanced loads and rain-on-snow can be much larger and must be added for design.
- Eurocode: C_e = 0.8 windswept, 1.0 normal, 1.2 sheltered (Table 5.1); C_t = 1.0 unless the roof is highly glazed and heated. The slope coefficient assumes snow can slide off; with snow guards μ stays 0.8.
- ASCE 7-16: C_e from Table 7.3-1 (simplified to fully exposed 0.9, partially exposed 1.0, sheltered 1.2 for surface roughness B and C); C_t from Table 7.3-2; I_s from Table 1.5-2. ASCE 7-22 changed the ground snow maps and removed I_s; use the edition your building code adopts.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: EN with s_k = 1.0 kPa, normal exposure and a 35° roof gives μ1 = 0.667 and 0.667 kPa; ASCE 7-16 with p_g = 30 psf, partially exposed, heated, risk category II, flat roof: p_f = 21 psf, minimum 20 psf, so 21 psf. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Balanced load only: add drifts at parapets, higher roofs and valleys, and unbalanced load on pitched roofs, as the code requires.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

## Soil bearing capacity calculator (Terzaghi and Eurocode 7)

<a id="soil-bearing"></a>

Folder `soil-bearing/` · Civil · Ultimate and allowable bearing capacity of strip, square, rectangular and circular footings by Terzaghi or Eurocode 7, drained or undrained.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The footing is shallow (depth no more than about its width), level, and loaded vertically through its centre; inclined or eccentric loads, sloping ground and layered soils need the full factors of EN 1997-1 Annex D or a geotechnical engineer.
- Soil parameters are characteristic values from a site investigation. Below the water table use the submerged unit weight (about γ − 9.81 kN/m³).
- Eurocode 7 Annex D gives the resistance without depth factors; Terzaghi's equation applies to general shear failure in dense or stiff soils. Loose or soft soils fail in local or punching shear at lower loads.
- Terzaghi's N_γ has no closed form; the Coduto (2001) fit used here is 5–6 % above the Kumbhojkar (1993) tabulation from 25° to 40° and up to about 20 % above it at 20°, where N_γ contributes little.
- The allowable pressure is the ultimate divided by the factor of safety (2.5 to 3 is traditional). Eurocode design uses partial factors instead, and settlement often governs before bearing failure.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: at φ = 30° Eurocode 7 gives N_q = 18.40, N_c = 30.14, N_γ = 20.09 and Terzaghi N_q = 22.46, N_c = 37.16 (Das, Table 3.1). A 2 m square footing 1 m deep in sand (φ 30°, γ 18 kN/m³) has q_ult = 750 kPa by EC7.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The footing is deeper than twice its width: shallow-foundation theory underestimates the capacity; treat it as a pier.
- A friction angle below about 28° in a cohesionless soil suggests loose sand, where local shear failure governs at lower loads.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Length L: enter the longer side as L and the shorter as B.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Eurocode 7 factors: φ 20° N_c 14.83, N_q 6.40, N_γ 3.93; φ 30° 30.14, 18.40, 20.09; φ 40° 75.31, 64.20, 106.05
  - Source: EN 1997-1 Annex D.4: N_q = e^{π tan φ} tan²(45 + φ/2), N_c = (N_q − 1) cot φ, N_γ = 2 (N_q − 1) tan φ
- Terzaghi factors match Das Table 3.1: φ 20° N_c 17.69, N_q 7.44; φ 30° 37.16, 22.46; φ 40° 95.66, 81.27; N_γ within 6 % at 30–40°
  - Source: Das, Principles of Foundation Engineering, Table 3.1 (N_γ after Kumbhojkar 1993: 19.13 at 30°, 115.31 at 40°)
- EC7 drained, 2 m square, 1 m deep, φ 30°, γ 18: q_ult = 18 × 18.40 × 1.5 + 0.5 × 18 × 2 × 20.09 × 0.7 = 750 kPa; 250 kPa at FS 3; 1 000 kN
  - Source: EN 1997-1 Annex D.4 with s_q = 1 + sin φ, s_γ = 0.7 for a square
- EC7 undrained strip, c_u 50 kPa, 1 m deep: (π + 2) × 50 + 18 = 275.1 kPa; a square adds 20 % to the c_u term
  - Source: EN 1997-1 Annex D.3: R/A′ = (π + 2) c_u b_c s_c i_c + q, s_c = 1.2 for a square
- Terzaghi strip, B 1.5 m, D_f 1 m, φ 25°, c 10 kPa, γ 17: q_ult = 10 × 25.13 + 17 × 12.72 + 0.5 × 17 × 1.5 × N_γ; L < B, deep footings and bad inputs handled
  - Source: Terzaghi (1943) strip footing: q_ult = c N_c + q N_q + ½ γ B N_γ
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 18.40, 20.09, 750 kPa, 250 kPa to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- EN 1997-1:2004 Eurocode 7, Annex D (informative): sample analytical method for bearing resistance calculation, D.3 and D.4
- Terzaghi, K. (1943), Theoretical Soil Mechanics, Wiley; Das, B.M., Principles of Foundation Engineering, Table 3.1 (Terzaghi factors)
- Coduto, D.P. (2001), Foundation Design: Principles and Practices, 2nd ed., eq. 6.8 (approximation of Terzaghi N_γ)

## Solar battery bank calculator

<a id="solar-battery-bank"></a>

Folder `solar-battery-bank/` · Electrical · Battery bank for solar or backup power from daily energy, autonomy, depth of discharge and temperature: Ah needed, batteries in series and parallel.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The bank must deliver the daily energy for the chosen days of autonomy without recharge; the energy drawn from the bank is the load energy divided by the inverter efficiency (enter 100 % for DC loads).
- Depth of discharge defaults are for a long cycle life: 50 % for flooded, AGM and gel lead-acid and 80 % for LiFePO4, in line with manufacturer cycle-life data (AGM about 600 cycles at 50 %, LiFePO4 about 2 500 cycles at 80 %).
- Temperature derating uses the IEEE 485 cell size correction factors for vented lead-acid cells (1.215 specific gravity), applied to AGM and gel as an approximation; above 25 °C no credit is taken for the higher capacity. For LiFePO4 enter the capacity factor from the data sheet.
- The margin covers ageing and load growth: IEEE 485 sizes stationary lead-acid batteries with an ageing factor of 1.25 so they still carry the load at 80 % of rated capacity, plus a 10 to 15 % design margin.
- Capacity is the battery rating at its standard discharge rate (often C/20 for lead-acid); high discharge currents give less (Peukert effect), which the battery runtime calculator handles.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 3 kWh a day for 3 days through a 90 % inverter is 10.0 kWh from the bank; flooded lead-acid at 50 % and 10 °C (50 °F, factor 1.19) needs 23.8 kWh, 992 Ah at 24 V, so 2 × 5 = 10 batteries of 12 V 200 Ah, 1 000 Ah and 24.0 kWh, of which 10.1 kWh is usable at 10 °C. Checked by hand.
- The IEEE 485 table was checked row by row against its reproduction in TSEWG TP-4 (2008); values between rows are interpolated linearly in °F.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Many strings in parallel share the current unevenly and are hard to balance; consider larger batteries or a higher system voltage.
- A depth of discharge above 90 % shortens the life of most batteries; check the cycle-life curve on the data sheet.
- Below 0 °C a partly discharged lead-acid battery can freeze; keep it charged or insulated.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Temperature derating: the IEEE 485 table applies to lead-acid batteries; for this battery choose "Capacity factor from the data sheet".
- Lowest battery temperature: outside the IEEE 485 table, −3.9 to 51.7 °C (25 to 125 °F).
- System voltage: it must be a whole multiple of the voltage of one battery (for example 24 V from two 12 V batteries).

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 3 kWh/day, 3 days, 90 % inverter, flooded 50 %, 50 °F: 10 kWh, factor 1.19, 23.8 kWh, 991.7 Ah at 24 V, 2 × 5 of 12 V 200 Ah
  - Source: Hand calculation from E = E_day × days / η, C = E k_T / DoD; IEEE 485 Table 1 (50 °F → 1.19)
- IEEE 485 Table 1 rows: 60 °F 1.11 (the TSEWG TP-4 example), 40 °F 1.30, 77 °F 1.000, 25 °F 1.52; 32 °F interpolates to 1.398
  - Source: IEEE 485 Table 1 as reproduced in TSEWG TP-4 (2008), Table 1
- LiFePO4 at 80 %, 10 kWh for one day through a 95 % inverter at 51.2 V: 13.16 kWh, 257.0 Ah, 4 × 3 of 12.8 V 100 Ah
  - Source: Hand calculation: 10 000 / 0.95 / 0.8 = 13 158 Wh; / 51.2 V = 257.0 Ah
- The IEEE 485 ageing factor 1.25 raises the capacity by 25 %; a warm battery (35 °C) takes no credit, factor 1
  - Source: IEEE 485 ageing factor 1/0.8 = 1.25; design decision (no credit above 25 °C)
- Days of autonomy of the bank as built are at least the days asked for; the bank Ah is a whole number of strings
  - Source: Consistency of the sizing
- A system voltage that is not a multiple of the battery voltage, the lead-acid table for LiFePO4 and a temperature off the table are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 10.0 kWh, 1.19, 23.8 kWh, 992 Ah, 10, 24.0 kWh, 10.1 kWh to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IEEE Std 485, Recommended Practice for Sizing Lead-Acid Batteries for Stationary Applications, Table 1 (temperature correction factors) and the ageing factor 1.25, as reproduced in Tri-Service Electrical Working Group TSEWG TP-4, Stationary Battery and Charger Sizing (2008), Table 1
- IEEE Std 1013, Recommended Practice for Sizing Lead-Acid Batteries for Stand-Alone Photovoltaic (PV) Systems (days of autonomy, depth of discharge)
- Victron Energy data sheets: Gel and AGM batteries (cycle life 400 at 80 %, 600 at 50 %, 1 500 at 30 % depth of discharge) and Lithium Battery Smart (2 500 cycles at 80 % depth of discharge)

## Solar panel calculator: how many panels do I need?

<a id="solar-panel"></a>

Folder `solar-panel/` · Electrical · Solar system size in kW and the number of panels to cover your yearly electricity use, from peak sun hours and losses, with roof area, output and cost.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The system is grid-tied: the panels cover a share of the yearly use on average, and the grid supplies the rest and takes the surplus. For off-grid systems with batteries use the solar PV array and storage calculator.
- Peak sun hours are the yearly average of the daily solar energy on the panels in kWh/m², which equals hours of 1 000 W/m² sun; look them up for your location and tilt in NREL PVWatts or the EU PVGIS tool.
- System losses cover temperature, soiling, wiring, inverter and mismatch; 14 % is the PVWatts default. Shading and a poor orientation lower production further.
- Panel size is the rated (STC) power; the area per panel is the module's outline, so the roof needs extra room for edges, walkways and fire setbacks.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 10 000 kWh a year at 4.5 peak sun hours and 14 % losses needs 7.08 kW, so 18 panels of 400 W (7.2 kW), producing 10 170 kWh a year on 34.2 m². Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Covering more than 100 % of the use only pays where the utility buys the surplus at a fair rate; check your net-metering or export tariff.
- More than 260 W per m² is above the efficiency of today\'s commercial panels; check the panel rating and area.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 10 000 kWh/yr, 4.5 sun hours, 14 % losses: 1 412.6 kWh per kW, 7.08 kW, 18 × 400 W = 7.2 kW, 10 170 kWh/yr, 34.2 m²
  - Source: E = P × PSH × 365 × (1 − losses), NREL PVWatts v8 default losses 14 %
- Covering half the use halves the system: 3.54 kW, 9 panels
  - Source: P ∝ E × offset
- Southern Europe flat, 4 000 kWh/yr at 4.8 sun hours with 450 W panels: 2.65 kW, 6 panels, 2.7 kW, 3 240 at 1.20 per watt
  - Source: 4 000 / (4.8 × 365 × 0.86) = 2.655 kW
- An exact fit needs no extra panel; more sun hours mean fewer panels; no losses gives P = E / (PSH × 365)
  - Source: Energy balance
- Offset above 100 % and an impossible panel efficiency warn; zero use and out-of-range sun hours are rejected
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 7.08 kW, 18, 7.2 kW, 34.2 m² to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- NREL PVWatts Calculator, version 8, technical reference (default system losses 14 %; production from solar resource and losses)
- European Commission JRC, Photovoltaic Geographical Information System (PVGIS) (peak sun hours and system loss for Europe and Africa)
- IEC 61215-1:2021 (module rating at standard test conditions, 1 000 W/m² and 25 °C)

## Solar panel payback calculator

<a id="solar-payback"></a>

Folder `solar-payback/` · Electrical · Payback year, 25-year savings, ROI, NPV and IRR of a solar PV system from cost, incentives, production, self-consumption, tariffs, price rises and degradation.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The saving in each year is the energy you use yourself valued at the import price plus the energy you export valued at the export price, less any yearly running cost; both prices rise by the escalation rate each year and the running cost stays flat.
- Production falls by the degradation rate each year; 0.5 % a year is the median rate Jordan and Kurtz found in their review of about 2 000 field measurements (NREL, 2013).
- The self-consumption share is the part of the production used on site at the moment it is produced; it depends on when the home uses electricity, and a battery, an EV or a heat pump raises it.
- Simple payback is the net cost divided by the first-year saving; the payback year adds price escalation and degradation; the discounted figures and the NPV use the discount rate, following the NREL manual of Short, Packey and Holt (1995).
- Inverter replacement (often once in 25 years), insurance, financing costs and taxes on the saving are not included unless entered as the yearly running cost.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 15 000 system of 6 kW at 1 300 kWh/kW makes 7 800 kWh in year 1; half used at 0.25 and half exported at 0.08 saves 1 287, simple payback 11.66 years; with 3 % price rises and 0.5 % degradation it pays back after 10.4 years and saves 43 876 over 25 years; NPV at 4 % 11 088, IRR 9.4 %. Checked by hand with the geometric series of the cash flows.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The first-year saving is zero or negative: the running cost is larger than the value of the energy.
- The system does not pay back within the period of the analysis.
- A specific yield above 2 000 kWh per kW is found only in the sunniest deserts or with trackers; check the site with PVWatts or PVGIS.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Grant or rebate amount: the incentives cover the whole cost, so there is nothing to pay back.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 6 kW × 1 300 kWh/kW, half self-used at 0.25, half exported at 0.08: 7 800 kWh, 1 287 in year 1, simple payback 11.66 years
  - Source: Hand calculation: S_1 = E_1 [s p_imp + (1 − s) p_exp]
- 3 % price rises and 0.5 % degradation: 25-year savings 1 287 × (g²⁵ − 1)/(g − 1) = 43 876 with g = 0.995 × 1.03; NPV at 4 % 11 088; payback 10.36 years
  - Source: Closed-form geometric series of the yearly savings (Short, Packey and Holt, NREL TP-462-5173, present value of a geometric gradient)
- No price rise and no degradation: the payback equals the simple payback, NPV at 0 % equals the net gain, LCOE = cost / lifetime kWh
  - Source: Limiting cases of the definitions
- The IRR makes the NPV zero: at a discount rate equal to the IRR the NPV vanishes
  - Source: Definition of the internal rate of return
- A 30 % tax credit and a 1 000 grant on 15 000 leave 9 500; entered production of 7 800 kWh matches 6 kW × 1 300
  - Source: Hand calculation: 15 000 × 0.7 − 1 000
- A system that never pays back gives no payback year and warns; incentives above the cost and a fractional period are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 7 800 kWh, 1 287, 11.66, 10.4, 43 876, 11 088 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Short, W., Packey, D. J. and Holt, T., A Manual for the Economic Evaluation of Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy Technologies, NREL/TP-462-5173, 1995 (payback, NPV, IRR, levelised cost of energy)
- Jordan, D. C. and Kurtz, S. R., Photovoltaic Degradation Rates — An Analytical Review, Progress in Photovoltaics 21 (2013) 12–29 (median degradation 0.5 % per year)
- NREL PVWatts Calculator technical manual (specific yield, kWh per kW per year, for a site)

## Solar PV array and storage sizing

<a id="solar-pv-sizing"></a>

Folder `solar-pv-sizing/` · Electrical · Array size from daily load, peak sun hours and system losses; battery storage for days of autonomy; charge controller current.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Energy-balance sizing for a stand-alone system: the array must deliver the daily load energy at the design month's peak sun hours (PSH, kWh/m²/day of irradiation on the array plane = equivalent hours at 1 000 W/m²) after the system losses — module temperature, soiling, mismatch, wiring, controller and inverter efficiency, battery round-trip — combined into one derating factor (0.70–0.80 typical; NREL PVWatts default 0.86 for grid-tied without batteries, 0.77 historic).
- Design month = the month with the lowest PSH for the load profile (winter for a constant load), with an optional design margin; the array is not oversized for cloudy-day recovery beyond that margin — cloudy spells are covered by the battery autonomy.
- Battery bank capacity from the daily load × days of autonomy ÷ (depth of discharge × inverter efficiency), at the nominal bank voltage in Ah; lead-acid 50 % DoD (cycle life) and lithium iron phosphate 80 %; the battery round-trip loss is already inside the system efficiency and is not applied again; the Peukert rate effect, temperature derating (lead-acid loses capacity in the cold) and ageing are covered only by the user's margin.
- Recharge time: the design-month surplus (daily yield minus daily load, both as energy delivered to the loads) is what refills the bank, so recharge days = usable capacity / surplus; at a 100 % energy balance the bank never recovers, which is why an array margin or a backup generator is needed.
- Charge controller: PWM controllers pass the array current, so the rating is the parallel-string short-circuit current × 1.25 (NEC 690.8 continuous-duty factor); MPPT controllers are rated by output current P_array/V_bat × 1.25 and by the maximum array open-circuit voltage at the coldest temperature (V_oc × (1 + β_Voc ΔT)), which the page estimates with a −0.3 %/K coefficient.
- Inverter: continuous rating from the peak AC load with a 25 % margin; surge (motor starting) and power factor are not modelled beyond the user's peak load entry.
- Module data at STC (1 000 W/m², 25 °C); series/parallel arrangement chosen to approach the array power with the given module, the string voltage limited by the controller's maximum input voltage entered.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: the published calculator case 8.5 kWh/day, 4.8 PSH, 75 % efficiency → 2.36 kW_p is reproduced (2.361 kW); 10 kWh/day, 2 days, 80 % DoD → 25 kWh of storage (per the Vatrer example, before inverter losses); 1 kW of 400 W modules → 3 modules.
- Design decision: losses are a single system efficiency because stand-alone sizing guides (IEEE 1562, Sandia) work that way; the register lists the components it covers.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Cold-weather open-circuit voltage exceeds the controller limit: reduce the series count or choose a higher-voltage controller.
- The array cannot recharge the bank while carrying the load (design-month yield at or below the daily load): increase the array or the margin.
- Recharging the bank from … % DoD takes … days of design-month sun with the load running: consider a larger array or a generator.
- Charge rate below C/20 for lead-acid: sulphation risk from chronic undercharging; add array or reduce the bank.
- System efficiency above 85 % is optimistic for a battery system (temperature, soiling, wiring, controller, battery and inverter losses).
- Less than one day of autonomy: a single cloudy day will empty the bank.
- Design-month energy balance: use the month with the lowest peak sun hours for the load; summer surplus is curtailed.
- Battery temperature derating, ageing and the Peukert effect are inside your margin; the battery-runtime calculator covers Peukert for the discharge side.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Array: 8.5 kWh/day at 4.8 PSH and 75 % efficiency → 2.36 kW_p (published example); with a 15 % margin 2.72 kW_p; 400 W modules in strings of 2 → 3 strings, 6 modules, 2.4 kW installed
  - Source: Firgelli off-grid sizing example (8.5 kWh, 4.8 h, 75 % → 2.36 kW; +15 % margin); IEEE 1562 energy-balance method
- Yield and balance: 2.4 kW × 4.8 h × 0.75 = 8.64 kWh/day = 102 % of the load; a 2 kW array would give 7.2 kWh (85 %)
  - Source: Energy balance E_yield = P × PSH × η
- Battery: 10 kWh/day, 2 days, 80 % DoD, inverter 100 % → 25 kWh (published example); at 48 V = 521 Ah; usable 20 kWh; lead-acid at 50 % DoD needs 40 kWh
  - Source: Vatrer off-grid battery example (10 kWh × 2 / 0.8 = 25 kWh); IEEE 1013 autonomy and DoD method
- Charge controller: MPPT 2.4 kW at 48 V × 1.25 = 62.5 A; PWM 3 strings × 10.5 A × 1.25 = 39.4 A; string V_oc at −5 °C = 2 × 49 × (1 + 0.003 × 30) = 106.8 V ≤ 150 V OK; 4 in series exceeds
  - Source: NEC 690.8 125 % continuous factor; V_oc temperature coefficient −0.3 %/K
- Inverter and charging: 3 kW peak × 1.25 = 3.75 kW inverter, DC input 3000/(0.92 × 48) = 67.9 A; average charge current 8 640/4.8/48 = 37.5 A (0.078 C); at the 102 % balance only 140 Wh/day is left over, so recharging 18.5 kWh usable takes 132 days — flagged; a 15 % margin (3.2 kW) brings it to 6.1 days
  - Source: Sizing rules of thumb (IEEE 1562; Sandia handbook); recharge = usable / (yield − load)
- Zero-surplus case: an 8.64 kWh/day load needs exactly 2.4 kW, so the yield equals the load and the bank can never recharge → recharge days null with a warning; invalid inputs fail fast (zero PSH, fractional series count, unknown battery)
  - Source: Behaviour specification (surplus ≤ 0 → null); validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 2 361 W, 3.2 kW, 107 V, 23.1 kWh, 481, 18.5 kWh, 3.75 kW, 68 A to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)
