## Specific gravity calculator (SG, API gravity, Baumé)

<a id="specific-gravity"></a>

Folder `specific-gravity/` · Process · Specific gravity of liquids from density, API gravity or Baumé degrees, and of gases from the molar mass, with density in kg/m³, lb/ft³ and lb/gal.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Liquid specific gravity is the density divided by that of water at the reference chosen: 999.016 kg/m³ at 60 °F (the petroleum convention, API MPMS Ch. 11.1) or 999.972 kg/m³ at 4 °C (the scientific convention); the two differ by 0.1 %.
- API gravity and both Baumé scales are defined on the specific gravity at 60/60 °F, so a density entered for them must be the density at 60 °F (15.56 °C); correct a density measured at another temperature with the ASTM D1250 (API MPMS 11.1) tables first.
- Baumé heavy (145 − 145/SG) applies to liquids denser than water and Baumé light (140/SG − 130) to lighter liquids, the US scales used in North American industry.
- Gas specific gravity is the ratio of molar masses to dry air (28.964 g/mol), which equals the density ratio for ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure; the gas density uses the ideal gas law.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 35 °API crude has SG 60/60 °F of 141.5 / 166.5 = 0.8498, density 849.0 kg/m³ at 60 °F, 7.09 lb/US gal and 34.7 °Bé on the light scale. Checked by hand.
- Published checks: water is 10 °API and 0 °Bé heavy; 66 °Bé sulphuric acid has SG 1.835; methane has a gas SG of 0.554.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above about 10 bar the ideal-gas density is less accurate; apply the compressibility factor Z (the gas compressibility calculator).
- Specific gravity outside 0.5 to 2.3, beyond the usual API and Baumé hydrometer scales: check the entry and its units.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 35 °API: SG 60/60 °F = 141.5 / 166.5 = 0.84985, 849.01 kg/m³, 7.085 lb/US gal, 34.7 °Bé light
  - Source: API MPMS Ch. 11.1 definition of API gravity; Baumé light 140/SG − 130 (ASTM E100); hand calculation
- Water at 60 °F is 10 °API, 0 °Bé heavy and 10 °Bé light; 10 °API round-trips to SG 1
  - Source: Definitions of the API and Baumé scales (the scales are anchored on water)
- 66 °Bé sulphuric acid has a specific gravity of 1.835 at 60/60 °F
  - Source: US Baumé heavy scale SG = 145 / (145 − °Bé); 66 °Bé is the commercial grade of concentrated sulphuric acid, sold as SG 1.835
- Reference choice: 850 kg/m³ is SG 0.85084 against water at 60 °F and 0.85002 against water at 4 °C
  - Source: SG = ρ / ρ_water with ρ_water 999.016 (API MPMS 11.1) and 999.972 kg/m³ (CIPM 2001)
- Gases: air is 1, methane 0.554, propane 1.522; methane at 15 °C and 1 atm is 0.6785 kg/m³ (ideal gas)
  - Source: Gas SG = M / 28.964 (ISO 2533 air); IUPAC 2021 molar masses; ρ = P M / (R T) by hand
- Out-of-range entries are rejected and an implausible gravity warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.8498, 849.0 kg/m³, 7.09, 34.7 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- API Manual of Petroleum Measurement Standards Ch. 11.1 (ASTM D1250), and ASTM D287 / D1298: API gravity = 141.5 / SG(60/60 °F) − 131.5
- ASTM E100, Standard Specification for ASTM Hydrometers (specific gravity, API and Baumé heavy and light scales at 60/60 °F)
- Tanaka, M. et al. (2001), Recommended table for the density of water, Metrologia 38, 301–309 (CIPM water density)

## Specific heat calculator (Q = mcΔT)

<a id="specific-heat"></a>

Folder `specific-heat/` · Thermal and fluids · Heat to warm or cool a material, Q = m c ΔT, or the temperature change, mass or specific heat, with the heating time at a given power.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Sensible heat only: no melting, boiling or other phase change between the two temperatures. Melting ice needs 334 kJ/kg more and boiling water 2 257 kJ/kg more.
- The specific heat is constant over the temperature range. For water it varies by less than 1 % from 10 to 90 °C; for gases over large ranges use the mean value.
- The heating time assumes all the power, reduced by the efficiency, goes into the material, with no losses to the surroundings during heating.
- Values for materials are typical room-temperature figures; alloys and composites vary.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 1.5 kg of water from 20 to 100 °C takes 501.7 kJ (0.139 kWh), 4.6 minutes in a 2 kW kettle at 90 % efficiency. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Water freezes at 0 °C and boils at 100 °C at sea level: the range crosses a phase change, which needs latent heat as well.
- Ice melts at 0 °C: above it, the heat to melt (334 kJ/kg) and the heat of the water must be added.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- End temperature: it must differ from the start temperature.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 1.5 kg of water from 20 to 100 °C: 1.5 × 4 181 × 80 = 501.7 kJ = 0.139 kWh = 475.5 Btu; 4.65 min in a 2 kW kettle at 90 %
  - Source: Q = m c ΔT, c_water = 4 181 J/(kg·K) at 25 °C (CRC Handbook)
- Final temperature: 89.7 kJ into 2 kg of aluminium (897 J/kg·K) from 20 °C reaches 70 °C
  - Source: ΔT = Q / (m c)
- Mass and specific heat: 418.1 kJ warms 10 kg of water by 10 K; 1 925 J warming 0.5 kg by 10 K means c = 385 J/(kg·K), copper
  - Source: m = Q / (c ΔT); c = Q / (m ΔT)
- Cooling gives a negative heat (heat removed); the heating time uses its size; no power gives no time
  - Source: Sign convention Q = m c (T2 − T1)
- Water heated past 100 °C warns about boiling; equal temperatures and zero mass are rejected
  - Source: Phase change not included; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 501.7 kJ, 0.139 kWh, 4.65 min to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics, 97th ed., "Heat capacity of the elements at 25 °C" and "Properties of water"
- Incropera, F.P. et al., Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, 7th ed., Appendix A, Tables A.1, A.3, A.4, A.5 (300 K)

## Speed–power curve fit

<a id="speed-power-fit"></a>

Folder `speed-power-fit/` · Maritime · Fit P = aVⁿ to speed and power data and compare it with a reference curve: power increase, speed loss and the ISO 19030 performance value.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The power law P = a·Vⁿ is fitted by ordinary least squares on ln P against ln V, which weights relative (percentage) errors equally across the speed range; R² is that of the log fit. The exponent is typically 3 to 4.5 for displacement ships in their service range and rises towards hull speed.
- The data must be at one draft and trim and already corrected for wind, waves, current, water temperature and depth (ISO 15016, ISO 19030-2); otherwise the fitted curve mixes hull and propeller condition with weather.
- Speed is speed through the water (log speed or corrected GPS speed), power the shaft power at the propeller shaft, consistently for data and reference.
- Performance value as in ISO 19030-2: the percentage difference between the measured speed and the speed the reference curve gives for the measured power; negative values are a speed loss. The power increase at constant speed is the alternative indicator, (P_fit − P_ref)/P_ref at the evaluation speed.
- Extrapolating the fit or the reference beyond the speed range of its data is flagged: the exponent changes with speed and a power law is a local description.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: data generated exactly on P = 0.95 V^3.4 are fitted with a = 0.95 and n = 3.4; data 6 % above that reference at every speed give a power increase of 6.0 % and a performance value of 1.06^(−1/3.4) − 1 = −1.70 % at every point.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Evaluation speed … kn is outside the data (…–… kn): the fitted power is an extrapolation.
- Evaluation speed outside the reference points: the reference power is extrapolated.
- Fitted exponent n = … is unusual for a displacement ship (2–5): check the data for mixed drafts, weather or units.
- R² = …: scattered data — filter for steady conditions and one draft before trusting the curve.
- The data span less than 10 % in speed: the exponent is poorly determined.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- … line …: expected "speed; power" as two numbers
- … line …: speed and power must be greater than zero
- At least two points are needed for a fit
- All points have the same speed: the exponent cannot be fitted
- Enter at least three data points
- Enter at least two reference points

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Exact data on P = 0.95 V^3.4 are fitted with a = 0.95, n = 3.4 and R² = 1
  - Source: Least squares on ln P = ln a + n ln V (ITTC 7.5-04-01-01.2 power curve)
- Fouled hull: data 6 % above the reference give a 6.0 % power increase at any speed and a performance value of 1.06^(−1/3.4) − 1 = −1.70 % at every point
  - Source: ISO 19030-2:2016 performance value PV = (V_meas − V_expected)/V_expected
- Speed loss at constant power equals the performance value: (V_fit(P) − V_ref(P))/V_ref(P) = 1.06^(−1/3.4) − 1 for a 6 % power increase
  - Source: Inverse power law V = (P/a)^(1/n)
- Reference given as points on the same curve gives the same result as the coefficients
  - Source: Same least-squares fit applied to the reference points
- Default data, 7 % above the reference with ±1 % scatter: the fit finds n ≈ 3.4, R² above 0.99 and a performance value of about −2 %
  - Source: Synthetic data from P = 1.07 × 0.95 V^3.4 with fixed scatter
- Invalid inputs fail fast: two data points, a zero power, a malformed line, all points at one speed
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.058, 3.385, 0.9995, 8013 kW, 14 kn, 7491 kW, 7.0 %, 14 kn to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 19030-2:2016 Ships and marine technology — Measurement of changes in hull and propeller performance, Part 2: Default method (performance value, reference curve)
- ISO 15016:2025 / ITTC Recommended Procedure 7.5-04-01-01.2 Analysis of speed/power trial data — power curve fitting
- MAN Energy Solutions, Basic Principles of Ship Propulsion (2018) — power and speed relationship P = c·Vⁿ

## Speeds and feeds calculator (milling, turning, drilling)

<a id="speeds-feeds"></a>

Folder `speeds-feeds/` · Manufacturing · Spindle rpm, feed rate and metal removal rate for milling, turning and drilling, with starting cutting speeds for common materials in HSS and carbide.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Spindle speed is n = v_c / (π D), with D the cutter diameter for milling and drilling and the work diameter for turning.
- The table speeds are starting values for sharp tools, rigid set-ups and coolant: HSS speeds are the traditional turning speeds of Machinery's Handbook (31st ed.), carbide speeds are the middle of Harvey Tool's ranges for solid carbide end mills. Indexable carbide inserts are rated by their maker.
- Milling feed is chip load × teeth × rpm at full chip thickness; at a radial engagement below half the diameter the chip thins, which the chip load calculator corrects.
- Turning removal rate is v_c × f × a_p at the starting diameter; drilling removal rate is the drill area × feed rate.
- A machine speed limit caps the spindle speed and lowers the actual cutting speed; the feed per tooth or per revolution is kept.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 1/2 in four-flute carbide end mill in 1018 steel at 200 sfm runs 1 528 rpm; at 0.003 in per tooth it feeds 18.33 in/min, and a 0.25 in by 0.25 in cut removes 1.146 in³/min. Checked by hand.
- Table provenance: HSS speeds read from Machinery's Handbook 31st ed. Table 1 (1117 at 100–150 HB 130 fpm; 1018 at 125–175 HB 110 fpm; 1045 at 175–225 HB 85 fpm), Table 3 (304 75 fpm, 316 70 fpm at 135–185 HB), Table 4a (Class 30–40 80 fpm), Table 6 (copper alloys group 1, cold drawn, 350 fpm) and Table 8 (wrought aluminium, solution treated and aged, 500 fpm); carbide ranges from harveytool.com General Machining Guidelines (aluminium 2024/6061/7075 800–1500, yellow and high-lead brass 800–1500, 10XX/11XX 100–300, austenitic 304/316 100–250, grey cast iron 100–400 sfm).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The spindle limit caps the speed: the tool runs below the chosen cutting speed, so feed rate and removal rate drop with it.
- Radial engagement below half the diameter thins the chip: raise the feed per tooth with the chip load calculator to keep the chip thickness.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Work material: unknown material "…"
- Width of cut a_e: it cannot exceed the cutter diameter.
- Depth of cut a_p: on a lathe it cannot exceed the work radius D/2.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Milling: 1/2 in 4-flute end mill at 200 sfm runs 3.82 × 200 / 0.5 = 1 528 rpm; 0.003 in/tooth gives 18.33 ipm; 0.25 × 0.25 in cut removes 1.146 in³/min
  - Source: Harvey Tool: RPM = 3.82 SFM / D, IPM = RPM × IPT × T; MRR = a_p a_e v_f (hand calculation)
- Turning: 2 in bar of 1018 at 110 fpm (HSS table value) runs 210.1 rpm; 0.010 in/rev and 0.100 in depth remove 12 × 110 × 0.010 × 0.100 = 1.32 in³/min
  - Source: Machinery's Handbook 31st ed.: N = 12 V / (π D), Q = 12 V f d; Table 1 (1018, 125–175 HB, HSS 110 fpm)
- Metric drilling: 10 mm drill at 25 m/min runs 795.8 rpm; 0.15 mm/rev feeds 119.4 mm/min and removes 9.375 cm³/min
  - Source: n = 1000 v_c / (π D); v_f = f n; MRR = (π D²/4) v_f (hand calculation)
- Table: 304 HSS 75 fpm, aluminium HSS 500 fpm, carbide 1018 = middle of 100–300 = 200 sfm; a spindle limit of 1 000 rpm lowers the cutting speed to 130.9 sfm
  - Source: Machinery's Handbook 31st ed. Tables 3 and 8; Harvey Tool carbide end mill table
- Light radial engagement warns about chip thinning; a cut wider than the cutter, a turning depth beyond the radius and zero diameter are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1 528 rpm, 18.33, 1.146 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Machinery's Handbook, 31st ed. (Industrial Press, 2020), Speeds and Feeds for Turning, Tables 1, 3, 4a, 6 and 8 (HSS speeds); N = 12 V / (π D) and Q = 12 V f d
- Harvey Tool, General Machining Guidelines: carbide end mill SFM and chip load tables, RPM = 3.82 × SFM / D, IPM = RPM × IPT × T

## Stair calculator: risers, treads and stringer

<a id="stair-stringer"></a>

Folder `stair-stringer/` · Civil · Number of risers and treads, riser height, total run, stringer length and stair angle from the total rise, checked against IRC or IBC stair limits.

### Assumptions and caveats

- A straight flight from floor to floor: the top riser lands on the upper floor, so there is one tread fewer than risers. Winders, spiral stairs and intermediate landings are not covered.
- All risers are equal: the total rise is divided by the smallest whole number of risers that keeps each riser at or below the maximum you enter. Measure the rise between finished floor surfaces.
- The tread depth is measured horizontally from nosing to nosing; the nosing projection is extra and is not part of the run.
- The stringer length is the length along the nosing line, √(rise² + run²); the board must be longer to allow for the cuts at the top and bottom.
- Code checks cover riser height, tread depth, headroom and the rise of a flight; width, handrails, guards and nosing rules also apply, and local amendments may differ.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a total rise of 108 in with risers of at most 7.5 in gives 15 risers of 7.2 in and 14 treads of 10 in; total run 140 in, stringer 176.8 in, angle 35.8°, 2R + T = 24.4 in. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- 2R + T is outside 24 to 25 in (610 to 635 mm): the stair will feel steep or long-striding; adjust the riser or tread.
- The total rise exceeds the code limit for one flight; split the stair with a landing.
- Headroom not checked: the code needs 6 ft 8 in (2 032 mm) clear, measured vertically from the nosing line.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 108 in rise, risers ≤ 7.5 in, 10 in treads: 15 risers of 7.2 in, 14 treads, run 140 in, stringer 176.8 in, 2R + T = 24.4 in
  - Source: Hand calculation: 108 / 7.5 = 14.4 → 15; 108 / 15 = 7.2; √(108² + 140²) = 176.82; atan(7.2/10) = 35.75°
- IRC limit exactly: risers of 7¾ in and treads of 10 in pass (R311.7.5.1 and R311.7.5.2); a 9¾ in tread fails
  - Source: IRC 2021 R311.7.5.1 (maximum riser 7¾ in) and R311.7.5.2 (minimum tread 10 in)
- IBC: a 7¾ in riser fails the 7 in maximum; 11 in treads are required; 78 in of headroom fails the 80 in minimum
  - Source: IBC 2021 §1011.5.2 (risers 4 to 7 in, treads 11 in minimum) and §1011.3 (headroom 80 in)
- A rise of 160 in exceeds the IRC 151 in limit for one flight and calls for a landing
  - Source: IRC 2021 R311.7.3: the vertical rise of a flight is limited to 151 in between floor levels or landings
- Comfort rule: 7.714 in risers on 10 in treads give 2R + T = 25.43 in and warn; rise 0 and an unknown code are rejected
  - Source: Blondel stride rule 2R + T = 24 to 25 in; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 15, 7.2 in, 14, 140 in, 176.8 in, 24.4 in to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- International Residential Code 2021, R311.7.2 headroom 6 ft 8 in, R311.7.3 rise of a flight 151 in, R311.7.5.1 riser 7¾ in maximum, R311.7.5.2 tread 10 in minimum
- International Building Code 2021, §1011.3 headroom 80 in, §1011.5.2 risers 4 to 7 in and treads 11 in minimum, §1011.8 rise of a flight 12 ft
- F. Blondel, Cours d'architecture (Paris, 1675): the stride rule, two risers plus one tread equal one pace of 24 pouces; US practice keeps 2R + T between 24 and 25 in

## Starting air receivers and compressors

<a id="starting-air"></a>

Folder `starting-air/` · Maritime · Receiver capacity for the consecutive engine starts of IACS UR M61 and the compressor capacity to charge the receivers from atmospheric pressure in one hour.

### Assumptions and caveats

- IACS UR M61 (Rev.3, 2024): the receivers must give, without replenishment, at least 12 consecutive starts alternately ahead and astern of each reversible main engine and 6 starts of each non-reversible main engine driving a controllable pitch propeller or other device that allows a start without opposite torque, plus the air of other consumers connected to them; for multi-engine plants the Society may agree to fewer starts per engine.
- At least two receivers of about equal capacity (M61.1.4) and two or more compressors, at least one driven independently of the main engine with not less than 50 % of the total required capacity (M61.1.2); the total compressor capacity must supply within one hour the air needed for the starts by charging the receivers from atmospheric pressure, divided about equally between the compressors (M61.1.3).
- Usable free air between the maximum and the minimum starting pressure for expansion with exponent n: u = p1 (1 − (p2/p1)^(1/n)) / p_atm per m³ of receiver, absolute pressures; n = 1 assumes the air regains the ambient temperature between starts (isothermal), n = 1.4 a rapid adiabatic sequence. Charging is taken as isothermal.
- The air per start and the minimum starting pressure come from the engine maker; free air is measured at atmospheric pressure and the receiver temperature.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 12 starts of 3 m³ between 30 and 12 bar gauge need 36 m³ of free air and 2.027 m³ of receivers (two of 1.013 m³) isothermally; 2.5 m³ installed give 14.8 starts and must be charged to 26.59 bar for the 12 starts, 65.6 m³ of free air from atmospheric pressure, i.e. 65.6 m³/h in one hour.
- Design decision: the compressor capacity is given both to the pressure that holds the required starts (the UR M61.1.3 minimum) and to the maximum working pressure, which the compressors usually also have to reach.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The installed receivers give only … of the … starts required: … m³ are needed.
- UR M61.1.4 requires at least two receivers of about equal capacity.
- UR M61.1.2 requires two or more compressors, at least one driven independently of the main engine.
- Fewer starts per engine than 12 or 6 need the agreement of the Classification Society (UR M61.1.5).
- Isothermal expansion assumes the air regains the ambient temperature between starts; a rapid sequence of starts yields less air (try n = 1.4).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The minimum starting pressure must be below the maximum receiver pressure

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Starts: 12 per reversible main engine, 6 per non-reversible engine with a CPP, so two CPP engines also need 12
  - Source: IACS UR M61.1.5 (Rev.3, 2024)
- Isothermal sizing: 12 starts of 3 m³ between 30 and 12 bar gauge need 36 × 1.01325/18 = 2.0265 m³ of receivers, two of 1.013 m³
  - Source: Free air between two pressures, V (p1 − p2)/p_atm; two receivers of about equal capacity (UR M61.1.4)
- Adiabatic expansion (n = 1.4) yields 79.6 % of the isothermal air between 31.0 and 13.0 bar absolute, so 25.6 % more volume
  - Source: Polytropic expansion of the receiver contents, m2/m1 = (p2/p1)^(1/n)
- The installed 2.5 m³ hold the 12 starts at 12 + 36 × 1.01325/2.5 = 26.59 bar; charging them from atmospheric pressure in one hour needs 65.6 m³/h, 74.0 m³/h to 30 bar
  - Source: IACS UR M61.1.3: total compressor capacity to supply the air for M61.1.5 within one hour from atmospheric pressure
- Receivers that are too small are flagged: 1.5 m³ give 8.9 of the 12 starts
  - Source: IACS UR M61.1.5
- The free air of the receivers at 30 bar, 2.5 × 31.01/1.013 = 76.5 m³, is what the CO₂ calculator adds to the engine room volume
  - Source: FSS Code ch. 5, 2.1.1.2 (receivers converted to free air volume)
- Invalid inputs are rejected: a minimum pressure at the maximum, a fractional number of engines, zero air per start
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 36 m³, 2.03 m³, 1.01 m³, 14.8, 26.6 bar, 65.6 m³/h, 32.8 m³/h to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IACS, Unified Requirement M61 Starting arrangements of internal combustion engines, Rev.3 (Feb 2024) — M61.1.2 to M61.1.5
- IMO, FSS Code chapter 5, 2.1.1.2 — free air of the starting air receivers added to the machinery space volume for the CO₂ quantity

## Added resistance in waves (STAwave-1)

<a id="stawave-added-resistance"></a>

Folder `stawave-added-resistance/` · Maritime · ISO 15016 STAwave-1 added resistance in head waves from beam, bow length and significant wave height, with the power increase at speed.

### Assumptions and caveats

- STAwave-1 estimates the mean resistance increase in irregular head waves for speed-trial conditions: short waves relative to the ship, small heave and pitch, where the added resistance is dominated by wave reflection at the bow; R_AW = (1/16) ρ_act g H_{1/3}² B √(B/L_BWL) (ISO 15016:2025 Formula D.31), with B the moulded breadth and L_BWL the distance from the bow to the point where the waterline reaches 95 % of the maximum breadth.
- The method applies only to waves within ±45° of the bow; for other directions ISO applies no wave correction, and this page returns zero with a warning. It carries no speed, wave-period or spectrum dependence: the result is the same at 5 and 15 kn and for any wave period, which is adequate only where the wave length is short compared with the ship (speed-trial sea states).
- For long waves, large motions, following seas or ocean conditions the SNNM method (ISO 15016:2025 D.4, spectral) or model tests are required; STAwave-1 then underestimates (ship motions add resistance) or misattributes the effect.
- Power equivalent ΔP = R_AW V_S/η_D at constant speed with the propulsive efficiency unchanged (ISO uses η_Did from the tank tests); the percentage is relative to the delivered power entered.
- Water density from the ITTC 7.5-02-01-03 table at the temperature and salinity entered (shared/seawater.js).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: B 32 m, L_BWL 40 m, H_{1/3} 2.0 m in 15 °C sea water → R_AW = 1/16 × 1025.9 × 9.80665 × 4 × 32 × √0.8 = 71.99 kN; at 12 kn with η_D 0.70 that is 635 kW, 12.7 % of 5 000 kW — the order of magnitude of a trial-condition wave correction for a Panamax hull.
- Design decision: the direction gate is implemented as ISO states it (zero outside ±45°) rather than a cosine taper, so the page reproduces the standard; L_BWL is an input because it must be read from the lines plan (typically 0.10–0.25 L_PP for full and fine hulls respectively).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Wave direction …° is outside the bow sector (≤ 45°): ISO 15016 applies no STAwave-1 correction — R_AW = 0. Use the SNNM method for beam and following seas.
- Significant wave height above 3 m: outside speed-trial sea states; heave and pitch are no longer small and STAwave-1 underestimates the added resistance.
- Bow length looks long for the breadth: check that L_BWL is measured to 95 % of the maximum breadth, not to midships.
- Bow length shorter than half the breadth: a very blunt bow; check the value from the lines plan.
- No dependence on speed, wave period or spectrum: valid for short waves relative to the ship (speed-trial conditions); ocean conditions need the SNNM spectral method or model tests.
- Propulsive efficiency assumed unchanged by the added load (ISO uses the tank-test η_Did).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Formula D.31: B 32 m, L_BWL 40 m, H_1/3 2 m, ρ 1025.9 → R_AW = 1/16 × 1025.9 × 9.80665 × 4 × 32 × √0.8 = 71.99 kN
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 D.5 Formula (D.31); ITTC water density at 15 °C
- Scaling: R_AW ∝ H² (3 m gives 2.25 × the 2 m value) and ∝ B^1.5 at fixed L_BWL; a longer bow (L_BWL 80 m) lowers it by 1/√2; R_AW/H² = 18.0 kN/m²
  - Source: Structure of Formula D.31
- Power equivalent: 71.99 kN × 6.173 m/s / 0.70 = 634.9 kW = 12.7 % of 5 000 kW
  - Source: ΔP = R_AW V_S/η_D at constant speed
- Direction gate: 45° is still inside the bow sector; 46° and following seas (180°) give zero with a warning
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 D.5 — bow sector ±45°, no correction outside
- Water properties and limits: 25 °C gives ρ 1023.2 and 0.26 % less resistance; H_1/3 4 m is flagged as beyond trial sea states; zero breadth and a 200° direction are rejected
  - Source: ITTC 7.5-02-01-03; ISO 15016 trial limits; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1025.9 kg/m³, 0.894, 72.0 kN, 635 kW, 12.7 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 15016:2025 Ships and marine technology — Guidelines for the assessment of speed and power performance by analysis of speed trial data, D.5 STAWAVE-1 (Formula D.31, Figure D.2)
- STA-JIP (Sea Trial Analysis Joint Industry Project), Boom, H. van den, Huisman, H., Mennen, F., "New Guidelines for Speed/Power Trials", SWZ Maritime, 2013
- ITTC Recommended Procedure 7.5-04-01-01.1, Preparation, Conduct and Analysis of Speed/Power Trials (2017) — STAwave-1 validation 2014
- ITTC 7.5-02-01-03 Fresh Water and Seawater Properties (density)

## Steam table calculator (IAPWS-IF97)

<a id="steam-table"></a>

Folder `steam-table/` · Thermal and fluids · Saturated and superheated steam and compressed water properties by IAPWS-IF97: temperature, pressure, enthalpy, entropy, specific volume and density.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Properties follow the IAPWS Industrial Formulation 1997 (IAPWS-IF97), the international standard for steam tables in industry; regions 1, 2 and 4 are implemented and reproduce the release's verification values to nine digits.
- Saturation properties are covered from 0 °C to 350 °C (0.6 kPa to 16.5 MPa). The near-critical region 3 (above 350 °C and above about 16.5 MPa) and temperatures above 800 °C are not included and give an error rather than an extrapolated value.
- Enthalpy, entropy and internal energy are measured from the IF97 reference: liquid water at the triple point has u = 0 and s = 0, the same as most published steam tables.
- A wet mixture is defined by its dryness fraction (quality) x, the mass fraction of vapour; x = 0 is saturated liquid and x = 1 dry saturated steam.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: at 10 bar (1 MPa) the calculator gives T_s = 179.89 °C, h_f = 762.68, h_fg = 2014.4, h_g = 2777.1 kJ/kg and v_g = 0.19435 m³/kg; superheated steam at 1 MPa and 300 °C has h = 3051.7 kJ/kg and s = 7.1247 kJ/(kg·K), matching published IF97 steam tables.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The temperature equals the saturation temperature: the state could be liquid, vapour or a mixture; use a saturation look-up with a dryness fraction.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Pressure and temperature: this state is in the near-critical region 3 of IAPWS-IF97, which this calculator does not cover.
- Pressure: saturation properties are covered up to 165.29 bar (350 °C); above it the near-critical region 3 applies.
- Pressure: below the triple-point pressure (611.2 Pa) water cannot be liquid.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Saturated at 10 bar: 179.89 °C, h_f 762.68, h_fg 2014.4, h_g 2777.1 kJ/kg, s_f 2.1384, s_g 6.5850, v_f 0.0011272, v_g 0.19435
  - Source: IAPWS-IF97 saturation table (Wagner and Kretzschmar, International Steam Tables, 1 MPa)
- Saturated at 100 °C: 101.42 kPa, h_f 419.10, h_fg 2256.5 kJ/kg, v_g 1.6719 m³/kg
  - Source: IAPWS-IF97 saturation table (100 °C)
- Superheated steam at 10 bar and 300 °C: h 3051.7 kJ/kg, s 7.1247 kJ/(kg·K), v 0.25798 m³/kg, 120.1 K of superheat
  - Source: IAPWS-IF97 superheated steam table (1 MPa, 300 °C)
- Wet steam at 1.01325 bar, 90 % dry: h = h_f + 0.9 h_fg = 2449.9 kJ/kg; compressed water at 50 bar and 100 °C is region 1
  - Source: Mixture rule y = y_f + x (y_g − y_f); IF97 region boundaries
- The near-critical region and saturation above 350 °C are refused rather than extrapolated
  - Source: IAPWS-IF97 region 3 not implemented
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 179.89 °C, 762.68 kJ/kg, 2777.1 kJ/kg, 0.19435 m³/kg to the digits printed

## Steel beam size calculator

<a id="steel-beam-size"></a>

Folder `steel-beam-size/` · Structural · Lightest W-shape (AISC 360, ASD or LRFD) or IPE beam (Eurocode 3) for a simply supported span: bending, shear and live-load deflection with self-weight.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The beam is simply supported, carries a uniform load over the whole span plus an optional point load at midspan, and its compression flange is braced continuously (for example by a floor deck), so lateral-torsional buckling is not checked.
- Sections whose flange or web is not compact (AISC 360 Table B4.1b) or not class 1 or 2 (EN 1993-1-1 Table 5.2) at the chosen grade are skipped, so local buckling of non-compact sections is never checked or relied on; web shear buckling follows AISC G2.1, and IPE webs satisfy hw/tw ≤ 72ε.
- W-shapes use AISC 360-22 with F_y of A992 (50 ksi) or A36 (36 ksi), E = 29 000 ksi and the ASCE 7 combinations 1.2D + 1.6L or 1.4D (LRFD) and D + L (ASD); IPE beams use EN 1993-1-1 with γ_M0 = 1.0, E = 210 GPa and 1.35 G + 1.5 Q (EN 1990 eq. 6.10).
- Deflection is checked for the live load alone against span / limit; total deflection is reported but not checked. Web bearing and crippling at the supports, vibration, fire, fatigue and connections are not checked.
- The beam self-weight is added to the dead load unless switched off. The table holds the common light and medium W6 to W24 shapes and IPE 80 to IPE 600 only; heavier or deeper sections are not considered.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: AISC Design Examples F.1-1A (35 ft span, 0.45 kip/ft dead including the beam, 0.75 kip/ft live, nominal depth ≤ 18 in, L/360) selects W18x50 with φM_n = 378.8 kip·ft and M_n/Ω = 252.0 kip·ft, as published. Worked example: 20 ft span, 400 lb/ft dead and 800 lb/ft live, LRFD, A992, gives W14x22 with M_u = 89 320 lbf·ft against φM_n = 124 500 lbf·ft (72 %), φV_n = 94.5 kip, live-load deflection 0.50 in against 0.67 in (75 %, governs). Checked by hand.
- Table provenance: W-shape values from the AISC Shapes Database v16.0, read from two independent copies that agree in every value used; A, d, t_w, b_f, t_f, I_x and S_x of W8x13, W8x21, W10x19, W10x30, W12x22, W12x26, W14x22, W14x34, W16x31, W16x40, W18x40, W21x68 and W24x84 agree with the AISC table reprinted in LibreTexts Strength of Materials (Table A.1), and Z_x of W8x10, W18x35 and W24x55 with a second web table.
- Table provenance: IPE values from the ArcelorMittal Sections and Merchant Bars table as published by STAD; G, A, I_y, W_el,y and W_pl,y of all 18 sizes agree within 0.6 % with a second copy of the ArcelorMittal table, and A_vz from the EN 1993-1-1 formula matches its A_vz within 0.05 cm² (IPE 300: 25.68 cm², IPE 600: 83.8 cm²).
- Design decision: ties in weight go to the section with the larger plastic modulus. E = 210 GPa follows EN 1993-1-1 3.2.6 for the IPE series rather than a rounded 200 GPa.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- … not considered although lighter: the flange is not compact at this grade (AISC 360 Table B4.1b), and flange local buckling is outside this calculator.
- Span over 30 times the beam depth: a floor this slender may be lively underfoot; check vibration separately.
- Total deflection exceeds L/240: consider a stiffer beam or a precamber.
- The shear from the point load exceeds half the shear resistance at midspan, so the moment resistance is reduced (EN 1993-1-1 6.2.8).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Loads: enter at least one dead or live load.
- Maximum nominal depth: no … in the table is that shallow; the shallowest is ….
- Loads: no … in the table works; the strongest one allowed, …, is at … in bending, … in shear and … in deflection. Shorten the span or use a deeper or heavier section.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- AISC Example F.1-1A: 35 ft, 0.45 + 0.75 kip/ft, depth ≤ 18 in, L/360 selects W18x50; M_u 266.4 kip·ft, φM_n 378.8, M_a 183.8, M_n/Ω 252.0, I_req 748 in⁴
  - Source: AISC Design Examples (v15.0/16.0), F.1-1A and F.1-1B; STAAD.Pro verification problem of the same example
- Worked example: 20 ft, 400 + 800 lb/ft plus self-weight, LRFD, A992: W14x22, M_u 89 320 lbf·ft, φM_n 124 500, φV_n 94.5 kip, δ_L 0.50 in ≤ 0.67 in
  - Source: Hand calculation: w_u = 1.2 × 422 + 1.6 × 800 = 1 786.4 lb/ft, M_u = w_u L²/8; φM_n = 0.9 × 50 × 33.2 / 12; φV_n = 0.6 × 50 × 13.7 × 0.23 (AISC G2.1(a))
- AISC G2.1: W12x14 (h/t_w 54.3 > 2.24√(E/F_y) = 53.9) takes φ_v = 0.90, φV_n = 64.3 kip; W14x22 (53.3) takes φ_v = 1.00; A36 makes W8x10 compact (b_f/2t_f 9.61 ≤ 10.8) but A992 does not (> 9.15)
  - Source: ANSI/AISC 360-22 G2.1(a) and (b), Table B4.1b case 10: λ_p = 0.38√(E/F_y); hand calculation 0.9 × 0.6 × 50 × 11.9 × 0.20
- EN 1993-1-1: IPE 300 in S275 has M_c,Rd = 628.4 cm³ × 275 = 172.8 kN·m and V_pl,Rd = 25.68 cm² × 275/√3 = 407.7 kN; 6 m span, 5 + 10 kN/m picks IPE 270 (M_Ed 100.0 ≤ 133.1 kN·m)
  - Source: EN 1993-1-1 6.2.5 and 6.2.6 with γ_M0 = 1.0; EN 1990 eq. 6.10; ArcelorMittal W_pl,y and A_vz
- A central point load alone deflects P L³/(48 E I); a large point load on a short IPE span triggers the 6.2.8 bending–shear reduction
  - Source: AISC Manual Table 3-23, simple beam with a concentrated load at the centre; EN 1993-1-1 6.2.8: ρ = (2V_Ed/V_pl,Rd − 1)², M_V,Rd = (W_pl − ρ h_w² t_w/4) f_y
- Invalid inputs: span outside 0.5–30 m, a depth limit below the shallowest section, and loads no section can carry are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 22 lb/ft, 89 320 lbf·ft, 124 500 lbf·ft, 0.50 in, 0.67 in, 149 in⁴ to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources
