- ArcelorMittal, Sections and Merchant Bars catalogue, IPE table (EN 10365 dimensions and properties)

## Stiffener with attached plating

<a id="stiffener-section"></a>

Folder `stiffener-section/` · Structural · Neutral axis, moment of inertia and section moduli at the plate and the flange of a stiffener with its effective plate flange.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Composite section of rectangles (or a tabulated profile) by the parallel-axis theorem; bending about the axis parallel to the plate, with heights measured from the outer surface of the plate.
- The effective breadth of the attached plating is an input: classification rules set it, for example as the stiffener spacing for local strength or a reduced breadth for shear lag and plate buckling.
- A flange on one side (angle) gives the same properties about this axis as a symmetric tee; the unsymmetric angle also bends sideways and twists, which this check does not cover.
- Tabulated profiles (bulb flats and rolled sections) are entered by their area, the height of their centroid above the plate surface, their own moment of inertia about that centroid and their height, from the maker's table.
- Corrosion additions, net thickness rules, fillet radii of built-up sections and weld material are not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: a 600 × 12 mm plate with a 300 × 10 mm web and a 100 × 15 mm flange gives A = 117 cm², a neutral axis 86.19 mm above the plate surface, I = 16 781 cm⁴ and Z = 1947 cm³ at the plate and 697 cm³ at the flange, the same as a separate hand calculation with the parallel-axis theorem.
- Design decision: the profile alone (without the plate) is also reported, because rules often state the required section modulus of the stiffener with or without its plating.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The neutral axis lies within the plate: the plate flange dominates and the stress at the free flange governs.
- A flat bar with a height/thickness ratio of … may trip or buckle locally; check the rule slenderness limit.
- A slender web: check the rule limit on web height to thickness.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The profile centroid must lie within the profile height

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Tee 300 × 10 + 100 × 15 on a 600 × 12 plate: A = 117 cm², z̄ = 1 008 450/11 700 = 86.19 mm, I = 16 781 cm⁴, Z = 1947 cm³ at the plate and 697 cm³ at the flange
  - Source: Parallel-axis theorem (Roark, Appendix A); hand calculation
- A 150 × 12 flat bar alone has I = t h³/12 = 337.5 cm⁴ and Z = 45 cm³
  - Source: Rectangle about its centroid (Roark, Appendix A)
- Equal plate and flat bar areas (100 × 10 each): neutral axis at 32.5 mm and I = 235.42 cm⁴
  - Source: Hand calculation: (5 + 60)/2 and 8333 + 833 333 + 2 × 1000 × 27.5² mm⁴
- The same tee entered from a profile table (45 cm², centroid 202.5 mm, own I) gives the same section properties
  - Source: Consistency of the tabulated-profile input
- The parts table adds up: total inertia = Σ own inertia + Σ A (z − z̄)²
  - Source: Parallel-axis theorem
- Invalid inputs are rejected: a table centroid above the profile height, zero plate thickness
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 117 cm², 86.2 mm, 16 781 cm⁴, 1947 cm³, 697 cm³ to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- W. C. Young, R. G. Budynas, A. M. Sadegh, Roark's Formulas for Stress and Strain, 8th ed., McGraw-Hill 2012, Appendix A — properties of plane areas, parallel-axis theorem
- O. F. Hughes, J. K. Paik, Ship Structural Analysis and Design, SNAME 2010 — stiffened panels and the effective breadth of plating

## Stopping distance calculator

<a id="stopping-distance"></a>

Folder `stopping-distance/` · Automotive · Car stopping distance from speed as reaction plus braking distance, with AASHTO design values, road friction for dry, wet, snow or ice, and grade.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Stopping distance is the distance travelled during the perception-reaction time at constant speed plus the braking distance at a constant deceleration: d = v t + v² / (2 (a + g G)).
- AASHTO design values: a perception-reaction time of 2.5 s, which covers most drivers including older ones in surprise situations, and a deceleration of 3.4 m/s² (11.2 ft/s²), which most drivers can achieve on wet pavement while keeping control (Green Book, Section 3.2.2).
- Friction values are Wong’s average sliding (locked-wheel) coefficients; with ABS and good tires the peak coefficient (0.8 to 0.9 on dry asphalt) can be used, while worn tires and standing water give less.
- The grade G is positive uphill and negative downhill, as a decimal of the rise over the run; the term g G is the small-angle form AASHTO uses.
- The calculation ignores brake response and pressure build-up beyond the reaction time, aerodynamic drag and load transfer; it is a single-vehicle estimate, not an accident reconstruction.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 60 mph, 2.5 s, 3.4 m/s² on the level: reaction 220.0 ft, braking 347.1 ft, total 567.1 ft (172.9 m); at 45 mph with 11.2 ft/s² it gives 165.0 + 194.5 = 359.5 ft against the Green Book Table 3-1 values 165.4 + 194.4 ≈ 360 ft (the table uses the rounded factor 1.47). Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A reaction time under 1 s assumes a driver already braking or expecting to; AASHTO designs for 2.5 s.
- A deceleration above 0.9 g is near the limit of road tires on dry pavement; check the value.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Road grade: the downhill grade is steeper than the friction allows; the vehicle cannot stop on it by braking.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- AASHTO Table 3-1, 45 mph: brake reaction 165.4 ft, braking 194.4 ft, stopping sight distance 360 ft (2.5 s, 11.2 ft/s²)
  - Source: AASHTO Green Book Table 3-1 (level roadways), as reproduced by Iowa DOT; table uses 1.47 V t + 1.075 V² / a
- AASHTO Table 3-1, 50 mph: calculated stopping sight distance about 423 ft (design 425 ft)
  - Source: AASHTO Green Book Table 3-1, 50 mph row
- 60 mph, 2.5 s, 3.4 m/s² on the level: 220.0 + 347.1 = 567.1 ft (172.9 m), 10.39 s
  - Source: Hand calculation, d = v t + v² / (2a), v = 26.822 m/s
- A 5 % downgrade lengthens braking to v² / (2 (3.4 − 0.49)) = 405.6 ft; a 5 % upgrade shortens it
  - Source: AASHTO braking distance on grades, d = V² / (30 (a/32.2 ± G)) in SI form
- Wet asphalt (sliding μ 0.45, Wong) at 60 mph: braking 26.82² / (2 × 0.45 g) = 267.4 ft; ice μ 0.07 needs 1 719 ft
  - Source: Wong, Theory of Ground Vehicles, 2nd ed., p. 26 (sliding coefficients); d = v² / (2 μ g)
- A downgrade steeper than the friction, zero speed and an unknown surface are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 220.0 ft, 347.1 ft, 567.1 ft, 172.9 m, 10.39 s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- AASHTO, A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets (Green Book), 7th ed. 2018, Section 3.2.2 Stopping sight distance, Table 3-1 (level roadways) and the braking distance on grades
- J.Y. Wong, Theory of Ground Vehicles, 2nd ed., Wiley 1993, p. 26: average values of coefficient of road adhesion (peak and sliding)

## Stress and strain calculator (Young's modulus)

<a id="stress-strain"></a>

Folder `stress-strain/` · Mechanical · Axial stress, strain and elongation of a bar from force, area, length and Young's modulus, or solve for the force, modulus, area or length.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The bar is straight and prismatic and the load acts along its axis, so the stress is uniform over the section: σ = F/A. Near holes, notches, threads and the load points the local stress is higher.
- The material is linear elastic (Hooke's law σ = E ε) up to its yield or proportional limit; the calculator warns when the stress exceeds the yield or proof strength held for the material, beyond which the elongation is wrong.
- Strain is engineering strain, ΔL divided by the original length; the change in area with Poisson's ratio is neglected (true stress exceeds engineering stress by the strain itself, under 1 % in the elastic range of metals).
- Compression uses the same formulas, but a slender bar buckles before it reaches these stresses; check buckling separately.
- Moduli are the values of the cited standards and data sheets (steel 210 GPa in Eurocode, 200 GPa in AISC); real values scatter by a few per cent.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 20 mm steel rod 2 m long carrying 50 kN (E = 210 GPa): A = 314.16 mm², σ = 159.2 MPa, ε = 7.58 × 10⁻⁴ (0.0758 %), ΔL = 1.516 mm, axial stiffness 32.99 kN/mm. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The stress exceeds the yield or proof strength held for this material: the bar yields and Hooke\'s law no longer gives the elongation.
- Strain above 1 %: far beyond the elastic range of metals; check the inputs and units.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 20 mm steel rod, 2 m, 50 kN, E 210 GPa: A 314.16 mm², σ 159.15 MPa, ε 7.579e-4, ΔL 1.5158 mm, k 32.99 kN/mm
  - Source: Gere and Goodno §2.2: δ = PL/(EA), k = EA/L (hand calculation)
- US units: 1 in² bar, 10 ft, 10 kip, E 29 000 ksi: δ = PL/(AE) = 10 × 120 / 29 000 = 0.04138 in; σ = 10 ksi
  - Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, eq. 4-2 (hand calculation)
- Inversion: the force, modulus and length modes recover 50 kN, 210 GPa and 2 m from ΔL = 1.51576 mm
  - Source: Consistency of σ = F/A, ε = ΔL/L, σ = Eε
- Area for an allowable stress: 50 kN at 150 MPa needs 333.3 mm², a 20.60 mm round bar
  - Source: A = F / σ_allow (hand calculation)
- Aluminium deflects three times as much as steel (E 70 against 210 GPa) under the same load
  - Source: EN 1999-1-1 §3.2.5 and EN 1993-1-1 §3.2.6 moduli; δ ∝ 1/E
- Yield warning above fy (S235 at 300 MPa); zero area, zero force and an unknown mode are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 314.16 mm², 159.2 MPa, 0.0758 %, 1.516 mm to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, 10th ed., ch. 1–4 (normal stress σ = P/A, Hooke's law, axial deformation δ = PL/(AE), eq. 4-2)
- Gere and Goodno, Mechanics of Materials, 9th ed., §1.4 and §2.2 (stress, strain, δ = PL/EA, axial stiffness k = EA/L)
- EN 1993-1-1:2005 §3.2.6 (E = 210 GPa for steel) and EN 1999-1-1:2007 §3.2.5 (E = 70 GPa for aluminium)

## Surface finish converter (Ra, RMS, Rz, N grades)

<a id="surface-finish"></a>

Folder `surface-finish/` · Manufacturing · Convert surface roughness between Ra in µm and µin, RMS, Rz and ISO N grades, and the theoretical turning finish from feed and nose radius.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Ra and Rq (RMS) are not equal: Rq = 1.11 Ra holds exactly only for a sine-wave profile; other profiles give other ratios, so the RMS value here is an estimate.
- Rz is estimated as 4 × Ra, the ratio of a regular triangular profile; an ideal turned profile gives 3.9 and a sine 3.14. Measure Rz when the drawing specifies it.
- Grade numbers N1 to N12 are the previous ISO 1302 roughness grades: N1 = 0.025 µm and each grade roughly doubles Ra up to N12 = 50 µm; the nearest grade is chosen on the logarithmic scale.
- The turning finish is the ideal geometric value of a round-nosed tool, R_t = f²/(8 r) and Ra = 0.0321 f²/r; tool wear, built-up edge, vibration and material tearing make real finishes rougher.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: turning at 0.2 mm/rev with a 0.8 mm nose radius gives R_t = 0.04 / 6.4 = 6.25 µm and Ra = 0.04 / (31.18 × 0.8) = 1.60 µm (63.1 µin, N7), Rq about 1.78 µm. Checked by hand.
- N grade table checked against Machinery's Handbook 31st ed., Surface Texture, Table 4 (preferred roughness values and previous ISO 1302 grade numbers N12 50 µm / 2 000 µin to N1 0.025 µm / 1 µin).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- N grades are whole numbers, so the value was rounded to N' + g + '.
- Ra was derived from Rz or RMS with a fixed profile ratio; the true ratio depends on the surface, so treat the other values as estimates.
- The feed is larger than the nose radius: the cutting edges beside the nose shape part of the profile and the finish is rougher than shown.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Value: N grades run from N1 to N12.
- Feed per revolution: it must be smaller than twice the nose radius for the nose to form the whole surface.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Grade table: N7 = 1.6 µm (63 µin), N9 = 6.3 µm, N12 = 50 µm (2 000 µin), N1 = 0.025 µm (1 µin)
  - Source: Machinery's Handbook 31st ed., Surface Texture, Table 4 (previous ISO 1302 grade numbers)
- Units: 63 µin Ra is 1.6002 µm (1 µin = 0.0254 µm) and grade N7; 3.2 µm is 126 µin and N8
  - Source: Definition 1 in = 25.4 mm
- RMS: a sine profile has Rq / Ra = π / (2√2) = 1.1107, so 63 µin Ra is 70.0 µin RMS; the conversion inverts exactly
  - Source: Sine profile: Ra = 2A/π, Rq = A/√2 (ISO 4287 definitions)
- Turning: f = 0.2 mm, r = 0.8 mm gives R_t = 6.25 µm and Ra = 0.0321 f²/r = 1.60 µm; halving the feed quarters both
  - Source: Boothroyd and Knight, Fundamentals of Machining and Machine Tools: R_t = f²/(8 r), Ra = 0.0321 f²/r
- A grade outside 1–12, a feed of twice the nose radius and a negative value are rejected; a fractional grade is rounded with a warning; a feed above the radius and an Rz input warn
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 6.25 µm, 1.60 µm, 63.1, 1.78 µm to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 1302:2002 Indication of surface texture in technical product documentation; grade numbers N1–N12 as in Machinery's Handbook, 31st ed., Surface Texture, Table 4
- ISO 4287:1997 Geometrical product specifications — Surface texture: Profile method — Terms, definitions and surface texture parameters (Ra, Rq, Rz)
- Boothroyd, G. and Knight, W. A., Fundamentals of Machining and Machine Tools, 3rd ed., CRC Press, 2006: ideal roughness of turning Ra = 0.0321 f² / r

## Tank sounding trim and heel correction

<a id="tank-sounding-correction"></a>

Folder `tank-sounding-correction/` · Maritime · Corrected sounding or ullage of a rectangular tank for trim and heel at an off-centre sounding pipe, with volume, mass and the wedge check.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Rectangular (box-shaped) tank of length L along the ship, breadth B and height H; the liquid surface is horizontal while the tank is inclined with the ship by the trim (positive by the stern, as a difference of draughts over L_BP) and the heel angle (positive to starboard); the sounding pipe is vertical in the ship and reads the local liquid depth at its position x_p from the aft bulkhead and y_p from the tank centreline (positive to starboard).
- Trim correction: the depth at the pipe differs from the mean depth at the tank centre by (L/2 − x_p) × trim/L_BP — a pipe aft of the centre reads more than the mean when trimmed by the stern; heel correction y_p × tan(heel) likewise — a pipe on the low side reads more; the mean depth is the reading minus both corrections, and the volume is L B × mean depth as long as the surface meets neither the bottom nor the top of the tank (checked), in which case the wedge formulas of the tank's calibration tables must be used instead.
- Ullage readings are converted with the tank height at the pipe (reading = H − ullage); the datum of the pipe (striking plate height, ullage reference above the tank top) is assumed included in the height entered.
- This is the correction the ship's sounding tables tabulate per tank for round trims and heels; it is exact for box tanks and a good approximation for prismatic tanks whose plan area does not change with depth, but not for hopper, wing or irregular tanks, where the calibration tables govern.
- Mass = volume × density at the liquid temperature (for fuels use the bunker-quantity calculator for the VCF); thermal expansion of the tank, list-induced free-surface effects and sediment are not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: a 20 × 15 × 12 m tank with the pipe 1 m from the aft bulkhead and 6 m to starboard, 1.0 m trim by the stern on L_BP 180 m and 1° heel to starboard, sounding 6.00 m → trim correction 9 × 1/180 = 0.050 m, heel correction 6 tan 1° = 0.105 m, mean depth 5.845 m, 1 754 m³ (2.6 % less than the uncorrected 1 800 m³) — the order of the corrections printed in sounding tables.
- Design decision: signs follow the sounding-table convention (corrections subtracted from the reading when the pipe is on the low side); the page prints both corrections so a hand check against the ship's tables is one line.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The liquid surface meets the tank bottom (shallowest depth … m < 0): the box formula over-estimates — use the wedge correction of the calibration tables.
- The liquid surface meets the tank top (deepest depth … m > … m): the tank is pressed up on one side — use the calibration tables.
- Corrections above 0.5 m: large trim or heel for a sounding — re-check the ship\'s condition or wait for an even keel.
- Mean depth below 0.3 m: soundings near the bottom are dominated by the striking plate, sediment and structure; low-level accuracy is poor.
- Exact for box-shaped tanks and good for prismatic tanks; hopper, wing and irregular tanks need their calibration tables.
- Mass uses the density entered at tank temperature: apply the volume correction factor for fuels (bunker-quantity calculator).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Ullage exceeds the tank height at the pipe

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Worked case: pipe 1 m from the aft bulkhead of a 20 m tank, 1.0 m trim by the stern on 180 m → trim correction (10 − 1) × 1/180 = 0.050 m; pipe 6 m to starboard, 1° heel → 6 tan 1° = 0.1047 m; mean depth 5.845 m
  - Source: Sounding-table trim/heel correction (Derrett & Barrass; Reed's)
- Volume and mass: 300 m² × 5.845 = 1 753.6 m³ against 1 800 m³ uncorrected (−2.58 %), 1 718.5 t at 0.98 t/m³, 48.7 % full; surface between 5.66 and 6.03 m — fully inside the tank
  - Source: Box-tank volume; arithmetic
- Sign conventions: even keel and upright give zero corrections; a pipe at the tank centre has no trim correction; trim by the head (−1 m) reverses the sign; heel to port (−1°) with a starboard pipe adds to the depth
  - Source: Geometry of the inclined box tank
- Ullage mode: an ullage of 6.0 m in a 12 m tank is a 6.0 m sounding and gives the same result; an ullage above the tank height is rejected
  - Source: reading = H − ullage
- Wedge check: a 0.4 m sounding with 5 m trim gives a surface that meets the bottom (WEDGE, warning); a 12.0 m sounding (full at the pipe) with 2° heel meets the top; large corrections (> 0.5 m) are flagged
  - Source: Validity of the box formula; sounding-table wedge corrections
- Validation: pipe outside the tank (x_p > L or |y_p| > B/2), zero tank height and an unknown reading mode are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.050 m, 0.105 m, 5.845 m, 6.03 m, 1 754 m³, 1 800 m³, −2.6 %, 49 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- E. A. Stokoe, Reed's Naval Architecture for Marine Engineers, ch. on tank soundings and the effect of trim and heel
- D. R. Derrett, C. B. Barrass, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed., Elsevier 2012 — tank calibration, sounding/ullage corrections for trim and list
- ISO 7507-1 / API MPMS Ch. 2 — tank calibration principles (datum, reference height)
- UK P&I Club, Bunker and cargo measurement guidance — trim and list corrections of soundings

## Tank volume and partial fill

<a id="tank-volume"></a>

Folder `tank-volume/` · Mechanical · Total and partial volume of cylinders, spheres and rectangular tanks at a liquid level, level for a target volume, mass from density and free-surface moment.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Ideal geometric shells with no internal structure: stiffeners, frames, pipes, suction wells, heating coils and manholes are not deducted, so a ship tank-table volume is typically 1–3 % smaller than the geometric value.
- Horizontal cylinders have flat ends or two hemispherical heads; torispherical, ellipsoidal and dished ends (the common pressure-vessel heads) lie between the two and need the manufacturer's head volume.
- The tank is level (no trim or heel); the liquid level is measured vertically from the lowest point of the shell. A trimmed or heeled tank needs the ship's tank tables with trim and heel corrections.
- Mass = volume × the density entered at the liquid temperature; for bunkers convert with the Table 54B method in the bunker-quantity calculator.
- The free-surface moment of inertia is taken about the longitudinal (fore-and-aft) centreline of the free surface: i = L c³/12 for a rectangular surface of length L and athwartships breadth c, π r⁴/4 for a circular surface; multiply by the liquid density to obtain the free-surface moment in t·m for the stability calculation. The horizontal cylinder is assumed to lie fore-and-aft.
- The level for a target volume is found by bisection to 0.01 mm; it is reported as the geometric level, not a sounding or ullage corrected for the tape position.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the horizontal-cylinder segment at a quarter of the diameter holds 19.55 % of the full volume, matching the standard partial-volume tables; the spherical cap formula gives exactly half the sphere at the centre, and the inverse level search reproduces the input level to 10⁻⁶ m.
- Design decision: the free-surface inertia is output alongside the volume because the two are needed together in stability work, and the horizontal cylinder's chord width is reported for the same reason.
- Design decision: hemispherical heads are the only curved-head option; other head shapes vary by manufacturer and are left to the tank tables.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Slack tank: the free surface moment of … m⁴ × ρ reduces the ship's GM by i ρ / Δ (see the initial-stability calculator).
- Tank above 98 % full: no expansion space for temperature rise — the usual filling limit for fuel tanks is 95–98 %.
- Geometric volume: internal structure, coils and wells are not deducted (tank tables are typically 1–3 % lower).

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Unknown tank shape "…"
- Liquid level … m exceeds the tank height … m
- Target volume … m³ exceeds the tank volume … m³

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Horizontal cylinder Ø2 × 10 m: full 31.416 m³, half full at 1.0 m, and 6.142 m³ (19.55 %) at 0.5 m — the standard quarter-depth fraction
  - Source: Circular segment A = R² acos((R−h)/R) − (R−h)√(2Rh−h²) (CRC Standard Mathematical Tables); partial-volume tables give 19.6 % at h/D = 0.25
- Sphere Ø2: full 4.189 m³, half at the centre 2.094 m³, cap at 0.5 m = π h² (3R − h)/3 = 0.6545 m³
  - Source: Spherical cap volume (CRC Standard Mathematical Tables)
- Hemispherical heads add a full sphere: Ø2 × 10 m cylinder with heads holds 35.605 m³ and is exactly half full at the centreline
  - Source: Segment × length plus spherical cap (CRC tables)
- Rectangular tank 10 × 5 × 4 m at 2 m: 100 m³ (50 %), free-surface inertia L b³/12 = 104.17 m⁴, free surface moment 103.1 t·m at 0.99 t/m³; vertical cylinder Ø2 × 4 m at 1 m: 3.14 m³
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass ch. 21: i = l b³/12 for a rectangular free surface; circular surface π r⁴/4
- Free surface of the horizontal cylinder at 0.5 m: chord 1.732 m, area 17.32 m², i = L c³/12 = 4.330 m⁴
  - Source: Chord c = 2√(2Rh − h²); rectangular free surface L × c (Derrett ch. 21)
- Level for a target volume: 6.1418 m³ in the Ø2 × 10 m cylinder is at 0.500 m; 15.708 m³ at 1.000 m; round trip for a sphere
  - Source: Bisection inverse of the segment volume (internal consistency)
- Warnings: a slack tank reports the free-surface effect; 99 % fill warns about expansion space; geometric-volume note always present
  - Source: Behaviour specification; fuel-tank filling limits 95–98 % (common practice)
- Unit layer: 31.416 m³ = 31 416 L = 197.6 bbl = 8 300 US gal
  - Source: NIST SP 811: 1 bbl = 158.987 L, 1 US gal = 3.785 L
- Invalid inputs fail fast: level above the tank, target volume above capacity, zero diameter
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 31.42 m³, 1.50 m, 6.14 m³, 19.55 %, 6.08 t, 1.73 m, 17.3 m², 4.33 m⁴ to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- CRC Standard Mathematical Tables and Formulae, 33rd ed., mensuration of the circular segment and spherical cap
- API MPMS Chapter 2 (tank calibration) for the context of real tank tables versus geometric volumes
- Derrett & Barrass, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed., ch. 21 (free surface moment i = l b³/12)

## Tap drill size calculator (metric and UNC/UNF)

<a id="tap-drill"></a>

Folder `tap-drill/` · Manufacturing · Tap drill for metric coarse and fine and UNC/UNF threads at any percentage of thread, with the nearest standard drill and the basic pitch and minor diameters.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Percentage of thread follows the tap makers' and Machinery's Handbook convention: drill = D − 0.01299 × % / TPI = D − % × P / 76.98, so 100 % is a double thread depth of 1.299 P and the basic minor diameter D1 corresponds to 83.3 %.
- Pitch and minor diameters are the basic values of ISO 724 and ASME B1.1 (d2 = D − 0.649519 P, D1 = D − 1.082532 P); the tolerance class (6H, 2B) adds a small band above D1 that the drilled hole should fall into.
- The standard drill is the nearest size in metric jobber drills (0.05 mm steps to 3 mm, 0.1 mm to 13 mm, 0.5 mm to 25 mm) or in fractional, number and letter drills; a drill cuts slightly oversize, so the real thread percentage is a little lower. Published charts sometimes take the next smaller drill (10.2 mm for M12, 12 mm for M14).
- About 75 % thread is the usual choice for cut taps in steel: it keeps most of the strength and eases tapping. Form (roll) taps need a larger hole; use the tap maker's chart for them.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 1/4-20 UNC at 75 % thread needs 0.25 − 0.01299 × 75 / 20 = 0.2013 in; the #7 drill (0.2010 in) gives 75.4 %. Basic pitch diameter 0.2175 in and minor diameter 0.1959 in (ASME B1.1). Checked by hand.
- Drill sizes checked against the number and letter tables of ASME B94.11M (via the Wikipedia drill size tables); ISO 724 values reproduced for M6, M10 and M24.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above 83 % the drill is smaller than the basic minor diameter: tapping torque and tap breakage rise sharply for little extra strength.
- Below about 55 % thread the strip strength drops noticeably; check the engagement length.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- ISO 724: M6 d2 5.350 / D1 4.917, M10 9.026 / 8.376, M24 × 3 22.051 / 20.752 mm
  - Source: ISO 724:1993 basic dimensions table
- ASME B1.1: 1/4-20 UNC E 0.2175 / D1 0.1959 in, 1/2-13 UNC 0.4500 / 0.4167 in, 1-8 UNC 0.9188 / 0.8647 in
  - Source: ASME B1.1, Table 2 basic pitch and minor diameters
- OSG: a 2"-12 tap with a 1.9242" drill gives 70 % thread; 70 % needs 2 − 0.01299 × 70 / 12 = 1.9242 in
  - Source: OSG Tap Drill Size and Pitch Diameter Limit chart, Vol. 3 (2024)
- At 75 %: 1/4-20 → #7 (75.4 %), 10-32 → #21, 3/8-16 → 5/16 in, 1/2-13 → 27/64 in, M6 → 5.0 mm, M10 → 8.5 mm (77 %), as on tap drill charts
  - Source: Standard tap drill charts (OSG, Machinery's Handbook); D − P rule for metric coarse threads
- Limiting case: 83.3 % thread drills exactly the basic minor diameter D1; nearest drill to 0.2013 in is #7 not #8
  - Source: D1 = D − 1.082532 P and 100 % = 1.299038 P (ratio 5/6)
- High and low percentages warn; an unknown thread and a percentage outside 40–100 % are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.2013 in, 75.4 %, 0.2175 in, 0.1959 in to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 724:1993 ISO general-purpose metric screw threads — Basic dimensions (d2 = d − 0.6495 P, D1 = d − 1.0825 P); ISO 261 and ISO 262 (pitches)
- ASME B1.1-2019 Unified Inch Screw Threads, Table 2 (basic pitch and minor diameters, UNC and UNF series)
- OSG USA, Tap Drill Size and Pitch Diameter Limit chart, Vol. 3 (2024): percentage-of-thread formulas (2"-12 with a 1.9242" drill = 70 %)
- ASME B94.11M Twist drills (number and letter drill sizes)

## Thermal expansion and restraint stress

<a id="thermal-expansion"></a>

Folder `thermal-expansion/` · Mechanical · Length change of solids with temperature, stress and force when restrained, and the volume change and pressure rise of a liquid trapped in a pipe or tank.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Linear expansion uses a mean coefficient α over the temperature range; α itself rises with temperature (carbon steel 11.5 at 20 °C to about 13.5 µm/m·K at 300 °C), so for large ranges use the mean value from the piping code tables (ASME B31.3 Appendix C) as a custom α.
- Material presets are typical handbook values for the alloy family, not certified properties; the yield strength used for the utilisation is a common grade (S235 for carbon steel, 304 annealed, etc.).
- Restraint stress σ = E (α ΔT − δ/L) assumes a straight, uniformly heated member held between rigid anchors with no bowing; real anchors and supports deflect, which lowers the force, and a slender restrained member buckles before it reaches the yield stress in compression.
- The thermal force σ A is the anchor load for full restraint and is independent of the member length; the allowed movement δ (expansion joint, loop, sliding support) is subtracted from the free expansion before the stress is formed.
- Volumetric expansion ΔV = β V ΔT uses a constant β near 20 °C; β of water varies strongly with temperature (near zero at 4 °C) and β of oils is given at 15–20 °C. For custody-transfer accuracy use the bunker-quantity calculator (Table 54B) rather than a constant β.
- The trapped-liquid pressure rise Δp = K (β − 3 α_pipe) ΔT assumes a completely filled, closed, rigid-walled system with no vapour space; the pipe or tank wall expansion (3 α_pipe) is credited but wall stretch under pressure and any air pocket are not, both of which reduce the real rise substantially.
- Temperature difference inputs are differences (K); the same number of Celsius degrees applies.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: 100 m of carbon steel over 100 K expands 120 mm and, fully restrained, develops E α ΔT = 240 MPa (2.4 MPa per kelvin), the classic textbook figure that exceeds S235 yield; a trapped column of water in steel pipe rises about 3.8 bar per kelvin, matching the engineering rule of thumb of 3–5 bar/°C for blocked-in water lines.
- Design decision: liquids are included alongside solids because the blocked-in thermal expansion of fuel, oil and water in ship piping is the practical question that follows the linear case.
- Design decision: the 3 α_pipe credit for wall expansion is applied and stated, since omitting it overstates the pressure rise by 15–20 % for water in steel.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Thermal stress exceeds the yield strength: a fully restrained member yields (or buckles in compression) — provide expansion joints, loops or sliding supports.
- Temperature change above 200 K: the mean expansion coefficient varies with temperature; use the code value for the actual range.
- Compressive thermal stress: a long slender member (pipe between anchors) buckles at a stress far below yield — check Euler buckling with the column calculator.
- The allowed movement exceeds the free expansion: no thermal stress develops.
- Blocked-in pressure rise above 10 bar: fit a thermal relief valve (API 521 §4.4.12) or ensure a vapour space — the rise assumes rigid walls and no air, so it is an upper bound.
- β of water varies strongly with temperature (zero at 4 °C, 0.21 ×10⁻³/K at 20 °C, 0.59 ×10⁻³/K at 80 °C): use a custom value for other ranges.
- Constant β near 20 °C; for bunker custody transfer use the Table 54B method in the bunker-quantity calculator.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 100 m of carbon steel heated 100 K expands 12.0 × 10⁻⁶ × 100 × 100 = 120 mm (1.2 mm per metre per 100 K)
  - Source: Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, §4-6, δ_T = α ΔT L; α steel 12 ×10⁻⁶/°C (Hibbeler back cover table)
- Fully restrained steel heated 100 K: σ = E α ΔT = 200 GPa × 12 ×10⁻⁶ × 100 = 240 MPa (2.4 MPa per K), above S235 yield; force on a 100 cm² section 2.4 MN
  - Source: Hibbeler §4-6 Example 4-10 type problem: thermal stress E α ΔT independent of length
- Partial restraint: allowing 60 mm of the 120 mm free expansion halves the stress to 120 MPa; allowing 150 mm gives zero
  - Source: σ = E (α ΔT − δ/L), Hibbeler §4-6 (gap problems)
- Cooling produces tension: steel cooled 50 K fully restrained gives −120 MPa (tensile); aluminium expands 23.1/12.0 = 1.93 × steel
  - Source: Sign convention of this calculator (compression positive when heated); α aluminium 23.1 ×10⁻⁶/K (Callister Table 19.1)
- Custom material: α 17.3 ppm/K and E 193 GPa (304 stainless) heated 100 K → 334 MPa, matching the preset
  - Source: Stainless 304 α 17.3 ×10⁻⁶/K, E 193 GPa (ASME B31.3 Appendix C / Callister)
- Volumetric: 500 m³ of heavy fuel oil warmed 10 K expands by 0.68 ×10⁻³ × 500 × 10 = 3.4 m³ (0.68 %), consistent with the Table 54B density slope
  - Source: ΔV = β V ΔT; β residual fuel ≈ 0.68 ×10⁻³/K ≈ α of Table 54B for 991 kg/m³ (0.681 ×10⁻³/°C)
- Blocked-in water in steel pipe: Δp = K (β − 3 α) ΔT = 2.2 GPa × (0.21 − 0.036) ×10⁻³ × 10 K = 38 bar (≈ 3.8 bar per kelvin, the 3–5 bar/°C rule of thumb)
  - Source: API Std 521 §4.4.12 hydraulic expansion; K water 2.2 GPa, β 0.21 ×10⁻³/K (CRC Handbook); pipe wall credit 3 α
- Unit layer: 12 µm/(m·K) = 6.67 µin/(in·°F) = 1.2 ×10⁻⁵/K; 100 K = 180 °F difference
  - Source: α per °F = α per K / 1.8 (temperature interval conversion)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero length, unknown material, zero liquid volume
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.120 m, 240 MPa, 2.4 MN, 102 %, 0.120 m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Hibbeler, Mechanics of Materials, 10th ed., §4-6 "Thermal stress" (δ_T = α ΔT L, σ = E α ΔT)
- ASME B31.3 Process Piping, Appendix C Table C-1 (thermal expansion coefficients of piping materials) and Table C-6 (moduli)
- Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering, 10th ed., Table 19.1 (linear coefficients of thermal expansion)
- CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics (volumetric expansion and compressibility of liquids); API Std 521 §4.4.12 (hydraulic expansion of trapped liquids)
- ISO 91 / ASTM D1250 Table 54B (thermal expansion of petroleum products, consistent with β ≈ 0.68 ×10⁻³/K for residual fuel)

## Three-phase power and motor current

<a id="three-phase-power"></a>

Folder `three-phase-power/` · Electrical · kW, kVA, kvar and line current for three-phase, single-phase and DC circuits; motor full-load and starting current from the nameplate; power-factor correction.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Balanced sinusoidal three-phase system with the line-to-line voltage entered; the formulas hold for star and delta connections alike because they use line quantities. Unbalanced loads and harmonics (drives, rectifiers) change the current and the real apparent power and are not modelled.
- Power factor is the displacement power factor cos φ between voltage and fundamental current, lagging for motors and transformers; the sign of Q is not tracked (leading loads enter the same magnitude).
- Motor mode: the rated output is mechanical shaft power (IEC 60034-1 nameplate kW); the electrical input is output ÷ efficiency, and the current uses the nameplate power factor. Efficiency and power factor fall at part load, so part-load currents are higher than a proportional scaling suggests.
- Starting current is the direct-on-line locked-rotor current as a multiple of full-load current (IEC 60034-12 design N motors typically 6–8 ×); star-delta reduces it to one third, soft starters and drives to 1.5–4 ×. Starting power factor is assumed 0.3 for the starting kVA.
- Power-factor correction capacitors are sized for the entered active power to reach the target cos φ at the fundamental; resonance with harmonics and over-correction at light load are not checked.
- Generator capacity is the apparent power the load draws; sizing a generator for motor starting needs the transient voltage-dip limit (typically 15–20 %) and the generator sub-transient reactance, not just the starting kVA.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the 30 kW, 400 V, η 0.92, cos φ 0.85 motor gives 55.4 A, matching typical IE3 4-pole nameplates (55–57 A); 400 V × 50 A × 0.85 gives 34.6 kVA / 29.4 kW / 18.3 kvar and the correction to 0.95 needs 8.6 kvar, all checked by hand.
- Design decision: three modes (from current, from load power, motor nameplate) share one output set so the same page serves generator-load estimates and motor-feeder sizing.
- Design decision: apparent and reactive power have their own unit groups (VA, var) rather than being mislabelled as watts.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Power factor below 0.8: the current is 25 % or more above the minimum for this active power; utilities and ship generators penalise this — consider correction.
- Target power factor is not above the actual one: no correction needed.
- Correcting above 0.98 risks over-correction (leading power factor) at part load and resonance with harmonics; 0.92–0.95 is the usual target.
- Direct-on-line starting: check the generator or supply can hold the voltage dip (typically limited to 15–20 %) at the starting kVA; star-delta or a soft starter reduces it.
- Nameplate efficiency and power factor apply at rated load; at 50 % load the power factor of an induction motor drops noticeably and the current falls less than proportionally.
- Single-phase load above about 7.5 kW is unusual; large loads are normally three-phase.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Three-phase 400 V, 50 A, cos φ 0.85: S = √3 × 400 × 50 = 34.64 kVA, P = 29.44 kW, Q = 18.25 kvar, φ = 31.8°
  - Source: Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, ch. "Three-phase systems": S = √3 V_L I_L, P = S cos φ, Q = S sin φ
- Current from load: 30 kW at 400 V, cos φ 0.85 → 50.9 A; at unity power factor 43.3 A; single-phase 230 V 2.3 kW → 10 A; DC 24 V 240 W → 10 A
  - Source: I = P / (√3 V cos φ), P / (V cos φ), P / V (Wildi ch. 8)
- Motor nameplate: 30 kW shaft, η 0.92, cos φ 0.85, 400 V → input 32.6 kW, 55.4 A full-load current, losses 2.6 kW (typical IE3 4-pole 30 kW motors: 55–57 A)
  - Source: IEC 60034-1 nameplate convention (rated output = shaft power); manufacturer catalogues for 30 kW IE3 400 V 4-pole motors (I_N ≈ 55–57 A)
- Starting: 7 × full-load current = 387.6 A and 268.5 kVA for the 30 kW motor; star-delta (2.33 ×) gives one third
  - Source: IEC 60034-12 locked-rotor current (design N 6–8 × I_N); star-delta reduces line current to 1/3 (Wildi ch. 14)
- Power-factor correction: 29.44 kW from 0.85 to 0.95 needs Q_c = P (tan 31.8° − tan 18.2°) = 8.57 kvar and cuts the current from 50 A to 44.7 A
  - Source: Schneider Electrical Installation Guide / IEEE Std 141: Q_c = P (tan φ₁ − tan φ₂)
- Generator kVA equals the apparent power drawn (34.6 kVA at 0.85 for 29.4 kW); unity power factor minimises it
  - Source: Generator rating in kVA at the load power factor (Wildi ch. 16)
- Warnings: low power factor 0.7 and DOL starting are flagged; over-correction target 0.99 is flagged
  - Source: Behaviour specification; common practice targets 0.92–0.95
- Unit layer: 34.64 kVA = 0.03464 MVA, 18.25 kvar = 18 250 var, 30 kW = 40.2 hp
  - Source: SI prefixes; 1 hp = 745.7 W
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero voltage, power factor above 1, unknown system
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 55.4 A, 32.6 kW, 38.4 kVA, 20.2 kvar, 2.6 kW, 388 A, 269 kVA, 9.5 kvar to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

## Thrust-to-weight, wing loading and stall speed calculator

<a id="thrust-weight"></a>

Folder `thrust-weight/` · Automotive · Thrust-to-weight ratio, wing loading, power loading and stall speed for aircraft, drones and rockets, with the vertical acceleration at full thrust.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Weight is mass × standard gravity 9.806 65 m/s²; 1 lb of mass weighs 1 lbf, so lb/ft² and lbf/ft² are the same number for wing loading.
- The thrust-to-weight ratio uses the static thrust given (sea-level static for jets and rockets, measured for a drone); above 1 the vehicle can accelerate straight up, and the net vertical acceleration is g (T/W − 1) before drag.
- The stall speed is the speed at which lift at CL_max equals the weight in level, unaccelerated flight: V_s = √(2 W / (ρ S CL_max)). It is a true airspeed; the equivalent (and roughly indicated) stall speed is the same at every altitude.
- CL_max comes from the aircraft or wing-section data and rises with flaps; a load factor n, as in a banked turn, raises the stall speed by √n.
- Air density is the ICAO standard atmosphere value at the altitude entered; use the density altitude for a hot or high day.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 2 550 lb, 174 ft² of wing, 180 hp, CL_max 1.5 at sea level: wing loading 14.66 lb/ft² (71.6 kg/m²), power loading 14.17 lb/hp, stall 53.7 kn; at 5 000 ft 57.9 kn true. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- T/W between 1 and 1.3 leaves little margin to climb vertically or to control a hovering drone.
- CL_max above 3 is unusual even with flaps; check the value.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 2 550 lb, 174 ft², 180 hp: wing loading 14.66 lb/ft² (71.6 kg/m²), power loading 14.17 lb/hp; CL_max 1.5 stalls at 53.7 kn

  - Source: V_s ∝ 1/√ρ; equivalent stall speed unchanged
- Rocket of 1 000 kg with 14 710 N of thrust: T/W 1.5, net acceleration 0.5 g straight up
  - Source: a = g0 (T/W − 1)
- A 1.5 kg drone with 2.2 kgf of thrust can climb; a jet trainer at T/W 0.4 needs its wing
  - Source: T/W > 1 condition for vertical flight

## Tidal height (rule of twelfths)

<a id="tidal-height"></a>

Folder `tidal-height/` · Maritime · Height of tide and depth at any time between high and low water by the rule of twelfths or the cosine curve, and the time a required depth becomes available.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The tide is treated as a regular semidiurnal curve between two consecutive turning points: symmetric, with the rule of twelfths (1-2-3-3-2-1 twelfths per sixth of the duration) or its continuous equivalent, the cosine curve h = h₁ ± R(1 − cos πt/D)/2.
- Both methods are approximations for places with a near-sinusoidal tide and a duration close to 6 hours; they are not valid for ports with double high waters, long stands or strongly distorted shallow-water tides (e.g. Southampton, parts of the Channel, estuaries), where the Admiralty tidal curve for the standard port must be used.
- Heights are above chart datum as given in the tide tables; depth available = charted depth + height of tide. Negative predicted heights (below datum) are allowed.
- Times are clock times in decimal hours in a single time zone; an interval that passes midnight is handled by adding 24 h to the second time; the query time must lie between the two turning points.
- No meteorological corrections: barometric pressure, wind set-up and seiches can change the real height by several decimetres and are not included.
- The rule of twelfths and the cosine curve differ by at most about 1/24 of the range (6.5 % of the range, near the first and fifth hours); the calculator shows both so the difference is visible.
- The time at which a required height is reached is interpolated on the chosen curve; it is the earliest time on a rising tide or the latest time on a falling tide within the interval.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: the rule-of-twelfths cumulative fractions (1/12, 3/12, 6/12, 9/12, 11/12, 1) were checked against the Admiralty Manual of Navigation / Bowditch rule; the cosine form gives exactly half the range at half the duration and the two curves agree at 0, 3 and 6 hours.
- Design decision: both methods are computed every time (one chosen, the other shown for comparison), and the required-height time is inverted analytically on each curve rather than searched.
- Design decision: clock times are decimal hours (no Date objects) so the pure function stays deterministic and testable; a midnight crossing is handled by adding 24 h.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Duration outside 5–7.5 h: not a standard semidiurnal interval; the rule of twelfths and the cosine curve assume about 6 h between turning points — use the port tidal curve.
- The two methods differ by … cm at this time; the real curve for the port may differ from both.
- No allowance for weather: pressure and wind can shift the actual height by several decimetres.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Time of interest … is outside the interval …–… between the two turning points
- The two turning points have the same height — the range is zero

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Rule of twelfths: 1, 3, 6, 9, 11 and 12 twelfths of a 4 m range after 1–6 h (heights 1.33, 2.00, 3.00, 4.00, 4.67, 5.00 m above a 1.0 m low water)
  - Source: Admiralty Manual of Navigation Vol. 1, rule of twelfths; Bowditch ch. 9
- Cosine curve: half the range at half the duration; 0.268 m after the first hour vs 0.333 m by twelfths (the largest disagreement, ≈ 1/60 of the range)
  - Source: Semidiurnal tide as a cosine curve (Bowditch ch. 9): h = h₁ + R (1 − cos πt/D)/2
- Inverse: a 2.5 m rise (⅝ of 4 m, i.e. 3.5 m height) is reached 3.5 h after LW by twelfths (05:30) and 3.47 h by cosine (05:28)
  - Source: Piecewise inverse of the twelfths; cosine inverse f = acos(1 − 2 p)/π
- Default case: 1.0 m LW 02:00 → 5.0 m HW 08:18; at 04:30 (2.5 h of 6.3 h) the twelfths height is 2.38 m, depth 10.38 m, 0.12 m short of 10.5 m; required depth from 04:38
  - Source: Hand calculation with the rule of twelfths (f = 0.3968 → third sixth, 0.3452 of the range)
- Falling tide HW 5.0 m 08:18 → LW 1.0 m 14:36: 3.0 m at mid-tide (11:27), depth 10.5 m available until 11:59 by twelfths (11.975 h)
  - Source: Symmetry of the curve; required height 2.5 m = fraction 0.625 of the fall → 3.5/6 of 6.3 h = 3.675 h after HW = 11.975 h, rounded to 11:59
- Interval across midnight: LW 22:00 → HW 04:18, query 01:09 is 3.15 h in (half the duration) → half the range
  - Source: Time wrapping by adding 24 h to the second turning point and to a query earlier than the first
- Rate of rise: cosine peak rate at mid-tide = π R / (2 D) = 1.047 m/h for 4 m in 6 h; twelfths third-hour rate = 3/12 × 4 m per hour = 1.0 m/h
  - Source: Derivative of the cosine curve; slope of the third twelfths segment (3 twelfths of the range in one sixth of the duration)
- Window edge cases: depth sufficient throughout, and never reached; non-standard duration raises a warning
  - Source: Behaviour specification of this calculator
- Invalid inputs fail fast: query outside the interval, zero range, clock time above 24
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 4.0 m, 6.3 h, 2.5 h, 2.38 m, 2.36 m, 10.38 m, 2.5 m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Admiralty Manual of Navigation, Vol. 1 (BR 45), ch. "Tides and tidal streams" — rule of twelfths and the tidal curve method
- Bowditch, The American Practical Navigator (2019), ch. 9 "Tides and tidal currents" (semidiurnal tide approximated by a cosine curve)
- UKHO Admiralty Tide Tables (NP 201–204), standard-port tidal curves and secondary-port corrections (the authoritative method)

## 555 timer calculator

<a id="timer-555"></a>

Folder `timer-555/` · Electrical · 555 timer astable frequency, high and low times and duty cycle, monostable pulse width, or R1 and R2 for a target frequency and duty cycle.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The timing follows the ideal 555 thresholds: the capacitor charges and discharges between 1/3 and 2/3 of the supply in astable mode, and charges from 0 to 2/3 in monostable mode, so the results do not depend on the supply voltage.
- The exact factors ln 2 = 0.6931 and ln 3 = 1.0986 are used; the datasheet rounds them to 0.693, 1.44 and 1.1, which changes the results by less than 0.2 %.
- Component tolerances, capacitor leakage, the internal propagation delays and the discharge transistor's saturation voltage are ignored; they matter at very high frequencies and with large electrolytic capacitors.
- In the basic astable circuit the capacitor charges through R1 and R2 but discharges through R2 only, so the duty cycle is always above 50 %; a diode across R2 or a different circuit is needed for 50 % or less.
- Resistors are typed in ohms or with a prefix (470, 4k7, 1M); capacitors are typed with a prefix (100p, 10n, 4u7), and a plain number is microfarads.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: R1 = 4.7 kΩ, R2 = 10 kΩ and C = 10 nF give t_H = 101.9 µs, t_L = 69.3 µs, f = 5.84 kHz and a duty cycle of 59.5 %; the datasheet form 1.44 / ((R1 + 2 R2) C) gives 5.83 kHz. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Below about 1 nF the stray capacitance of the board and the pins adds noticeably to C, and the real frequency comes out lower.
- A resistor comes out below 1 kΩ: a smaller capacitor brings both resistors into the kilohm range and keeps the discharge current low.
- The resistors come out in the tens of megohms: a larger capacitor gives values where leakage and the threshold input current matter less.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- …: …
- …: enter exactly one value (got …)
- …: the value must be greater than zero

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Astable 4k7, 10k, 10n: f = 5.84 kHz (datasheet 1.44/((R_A + 2R_B)C) = 5.83 kHz), t_H 101.9 µs, t_L 69.3 µs, duty 59.5 %
  - Source: TI NE555 datasheet SLFS022, astable equations; hand calculation with ln 2
- Monostable 100 kΩ and 10 µF: t = 1.1 R C = 1.10 s (ln 3 R C = 1.0986 s)
  - Source: TI NE555 datasheet SLFS022, monostable t_w = 1.1 R_A C
- Design 1 kHz, 60 % with 100 nF: exact R1 2.885 kΩ, R2 5.771 kΩ; E24 3 kΩ and 5.6 kΩ give 1.016 kHz and 60.6 %
  - Source: Inverting f = 1/(ln2 (R1 + 2R2) C) and D = (R1 + R2)/(R1 + 2R2); IEC 60063 E24 values
- Limiting case: R1 much smaller than R2 gives a duty cycle just above 50 %; marking notation and plain microfarads read correctly
  - Source: D = (R1 + R2)/(R1 + 2R2) → 1/2 as R1 → 0; IEC 60062 letter-digit code
- Invalid entries are rejected: text, two values, zero, and a duty cycle of 50 %
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 5.84 kHz, 59.5 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Texas Instruments, NE555, SA555, SE555 Precision Timers datasheet (SLFS022), Detailed Description, monostable and astable operation: t_w = 1.1 R_A C, t_H = 0.693 (R_A + R_B) C, t_L = 0.693 R_B C, f ≈ 1.44 / ((R_A + 2 R_B) C)
- Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., §7.2 (the 555 timer and its timing equations)
- IEC 60063:2015 preferred number series for resistors and capacitors (E24 values for the design mode)

## Tire size calculator and comparison

<a id="tire-size"></a>

Folder `tire-size/` · Automotive · Tire diameter, sidewall, circumference and revs per mile from size codes like 225/45R17, comparing two sizes for speedometer error and true speed.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Dimensions are the nominal design values from the size code: sidewall = section width × aspect ratio, overall diameter = rim diameter + 2 × sidewall (ISO 4000-1, ETRTO); a real tire differs by up to a few percent by brand, tread depth and inflation.
- Revolutions per mile and per km are geometric (π × unloaded diameter); tire makers measure them rolling under load, so their published figures are a little higher.
- Flotation sizes such as 33x12.50R15 give the overall diameter and section width in inches directly; the sidewall is half the difference between the diameter and the rim.
- The speedometer is assumed correct with tire A; with tire B fitted the true speed is the reading × D_B / D_A and the odometer is off by the same percentage.
- The section width is the nominal width on the measuring rim; a wider or narrower rim changes the actual width slightly.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 225/45R17 is 101.25 mm of sidewall and 634.3 mm (24.97 in) overall; 245/40R18 is 98.0 mm and 653.2 mm (25.72 in): 2.98 % taller, so a speedometer reading 60 mph means 61.8 mph true. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The diameters differ by more than 3 %: the speedometer, odometer, gearing and ABS and stability control may need recalibration, and the tire may not clear the body.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- …: enter a size code; ….
- …: the section width … mm is outside 100 to 500 mm; ….
- …: the aspect ratio … is outside 20 to 100; ….
- …: the rim diameter … in is outside 8 to 30 in; ….
- …: the overall diameter … in is outside 20 to 60 in; ….
- …: the section width … in is outside 5 to 25 in; ….
- …: the rim diameter … in is outside 12 to 30 in; ….
- …: the overall diameter … in leaves less than 2 in of sidewall on a … in rim; check the code.
- …: "…" has no aspect ratio; enter the full metric size with the ratio, such as 195/80R14.
- …: "…" is not a tire size code; ….

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 225/45R17: sidewall 225 × 0.45 = 101.25 mm, diameter 17 × 25.4 + 2 × 101.25 = 634.3 mm (24.97 in), 807.6 revs per mile
  - Source: ISO 4000-1 design overall diameter D = d + 2 S × aspect / 100; hand calculation
- 225/45R17 to 245/40R18: 653.2 mm against 634.3 mm is 2.98 % taller; 60 mph on the speedometer is 61.8 mph true
  - Source: Hand calculation, true speed = reading × D_B / D_A
- Flotation 33x12.50R15: 33 in tall, 12.5 in wide, 9 in sidewall; LT265/75R16 is 31.65 in
  - Source: Tire and Rim Association flotation designation (diameter x width R rim, inches); ISO 4000-1 for LT-metric
- The parser accepts P and ZR codes, lower case, spaces, dashes and load and speed indexes
  - Source: Size designation formats of ISO 4000-1 and the Tire and Rim Association
- Unreadable codes, a missing aspect ratio and impossible sizes are rejected with a plain message; over 3 % warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 3.99 in, 24.97 in, 25.72 in, 807.6, 784.2, 2.98 %, 61.8 mph to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 4000-1:2021 Passenger car tyres and rims — Part 1: Tyres (metric series): size designation and design overall diameter D = d + 2 H, H = S × nominal aspect ratio / 100
- ETRTO Standards Manual (European Tyre and Rim Technical Organisation), passenger car tyres, and The Tire and Rim Association Year Book (P-metric, LT-metric and flotation designations)

## Tolerance stack-up

<a id="tolerance-stack"></a>

Folder `tolerance-stack/` · Mechanical · Worst-case, root-sum-square and Monte Carlo results of a dimension chain, with the share of each dimension and the yield against limits.

### Assumptions and caveats

- One-dimensional chain: the resulting dimension (gap) is the signed sum of the dimensions; an unequal tolerance is replaced by its mid-tolerance value with a symmetric half-width h = (plus + minus)/2.
- Worst case adds the half-widths, Σ h_i, and holds for every combination of parts; the root sum of squares, √(Σ h_i²), assumes independent dimensions centred in their tolerances, each spread over the same multiple of its standard deviation.
- Monte Carlo: each dimension is drawn independently, normal with σ = h/z (z = 3 makes the tolerance ±3σ) or uniform over ±h, with a fixed seed so that a rerun repeats; the yield is the share of simulated assemblies within the limits. The tools that run the calculator many times (uncertainty band, long sweeps) repeat the simulation each time, so switch it off for them.
- Process mean shifts, correlated dimensions, geometric tolerances (form, position) and two- or three-dimensional chains are not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: the default chain 120 − 25 − 70 − 24.5 gives a 0.50 mm gap, ±0.29 mm worst case and ±√(0.0225) = ±0.15 mm by RSS; with normal parts at ±3σ the Monte Carlo SD converges on 0.05 mm.
- Design decision: the normal-approximation yield uses σ_gap from the chosen distribution; with uniform parts and few dimensions the true distribution is flatter than normal, and the Monte Carlo yield is the better estimate.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The worst case (… to …) goes outside the limits; about … % of assemblies would.
- Even the mid-tolerance gap is outside the limits: change a nominal dimension.
- With few uniform dimensions the gap is far from normal; rely on the Monte Carlo yield.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- …: expected name; + or −; nominal; plus tolerance[; minus tolerance]
- …: the direction must be + or −
- …: nominal and tolerances must be numbers
- …: tolerances are entered as positive amounts
- Enter at least one dimension
- The upper limit must be above the lower limit

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Default chain 120 − 25 − 70 − 24.5: gap 0.50 mm, worst case ±(0.10 + 0.05 + 0.08 + 0.06) = ±0.29 mm, RSS ±√0.0225 = ±0.15 mm
  - Source: Worst-case and root-sum-square stack-up (Drake 1999, ch. 9)
- An unequal tolerance 10 +0.2/−0 enters at its mid-value 10.1 with a half-width of 0.1
  - Source: Mean-shift conversion of bilateral unequal tolerances
- Monte Carlo with normal parts at ±3σ: SD within 2 % of RSS/3 = 0.05; uniform parts: within 2 % of √(Σh²/3) = 0.0866
  - Source: Variance of a sum of independent variables; seeded mulberry32 sampling
- Limits at ±3σ around the gap: normal yield 99.73 % and Cpk 1.00; the worst case exceeds them and is flagged
  - Source: Normal distribution; process capability Cpk = min(USL − μ, μ − LSL)/3σ
- The simulation repeats exactly for the same inputs, can be switched off, and the variance shares add up to 100 %
  - Source: Fixed seed; variance shares σ_i²/Σσ²
- Invalid inputs are rejected: a direction other than + or −, an upper limit below the lower one, a negative tolerance
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.50 mm, 0.79 mm, 0.15 mm, 0.65 mm, 99.73 %, 99.73 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- P. J. Drake (ed.), Dimensioning and Tolerancing Handbook, McGraw-Hill 1999, ch. 9 — worst-case and statistical tolerance analysis
- A. Fortini, Dimensioning for Interchangeable Manufacture, Industrial Press 1967 — root-sum-square stack-up

## Torque, power and speed

<a id="torque-power-rpm"></a>

Folder `torque-power-rpm/` · Mechanical · Shaft power from torque and rpm, torque from power and rpm, or speed from power and torque, in kW, hp, N·m and lbf·ft.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Power, torque and speed refer to the same shaft at the same instant; for an engine or motor the rated values come from its data sheet at the rated point.
- The relation P = T ω is exact for steady rotation; for a fluctuating torque (a piston engine) use the mean torque.
- Horsepower is mechanical horsepower (745.7 W); metric horsepower (PS, 735.5 W) is offered in the unit lists.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 15 kW motor at 1460 rpm gives 98.1 N·m; 300 lbf·ft at 5252 rpm gives exactly 300 hp, the crossover where torque in lbf·ft equals horsepower. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above 30 000 rpm only special high-speed machines run; check the inputs.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- A 15 kW motor at 1460 rpm: ω = 152.89 rad/s, T = 98.11 N·m = 72.36 lbf·ft
  - Source: Shigley, Mechanical Engineering Design, ch. 3: H = T ω, ω = 2π n / 60
- 300 lbf·ft at 5252 rpm is 300 hp: torque in lbf·ft equals horsepower at 5252 rpm
  - Source: Machinery's Handbook, "Horsepower and torque": hp = T n / 5252 (33 000 / 2π = 5252.1)
- Speed from power and torque: 100 kW and 500 N·m give 1909.9 rpm; feeding it back gives 100 kW
  - Source: n = 60 P / (2π T)
- A two-stroke main engine of 10 MW at 80 rpm turns 1.194 MN·m on its shaft
  - Source: T = P / ω for a low-speed engine (Shigley, ch. 7)
- Halving the speed at the same power doubles the torque
  - Source: T ∝ 1/n at constant P
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 98.1 N·m, 152.9 rad/s, 72.4 lbf·ft to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 11th ed., ch. 3 and ch. 7 (power transmitted by a shaft, H = T ω)
- Oberg et al., Machinery's Handbook, 31st ed., "Horsepower and torque" (hp = T n / 5252 in lbf·ft and rpm)

## Total dynamic head (TDH) calculator

<a id="total-dynamic-head"></a>

Folder `total-dynamic-head/` · Mechanical · Total dynamic head for pump selection from static lift, tank pressures, pipe friction and fitting losses, with the system curve and hydraulic power.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Steady flow of a liquid between two open or closed vessels; the head is referenced to the liquid surfaces, so the velocity heads in the tanks are zero and the exit loss is one of the fitting K values.
- Pipe friction by Darcy–Weisbach with the Colebrook friction factor (64/Re in laminar flow); one pipe size throughout. For several sizes add their losses separately.
- Fitting losses enter as a total K; the minor losses calculator adds up K from the fittings by the Crane method.
- The system curve H(Q) ≈ H_static + C Q² assumes the friction factor stays near its value at the design flow, which holds well in fully turbulent flow.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 20 m³/h of water at 20 °C in 100 m of 77.9 mm pipe with 15 m lift and ΣK = 8: v = 1.166 m/s, Re = 90 400, f = 0.0210 (Haaland 0.0207), friction 1.86 m, fittings 0.55 m, TDH 17.42 m. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Reynolds number in the transition zone (2 300–4 000): the friction factor is uncertain.
- Velocity above 3 m/s: friction losses and wear are high; consider a larger pipe.
- The total head is zero or negative: the liquid flows by gravity or pressure without a pump at this rate.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 20 m³/h, 100 m of 77.9 mm steel pipe, 15 m lift, ΣK 8: v 1.166 m/s, Re 90 440, f 0.0210, friction 1.86 m, fittings 0.55 m, TDH 17.42 m
  - Source: Darcy–Weisbach h_f = f L/D v²/2g with Colebrook (Crane TP-410 ch. 2)
- The Colebrook factor lies within 2 % of the explicit Haaland formula at this Reynolds number and roughness
  - Source: Haaland (1983): 1/√f = −1.8 log10[(ε/D/3.7)^1.11 + 6.9/Re]
- A closed discharge vessel at 2 bar adds 2e5 / (998.2 × 9.81) = 20.431 m of head
  - Source: h_p = Δp / (ρ g)
- Laminar oil flow uses f = 64/Re: 2 m³/h of oil (100 mm²/s) in 50 mm pipe gives Re 141 and f 0.453
  - Source: Hagen–Poiseuille, f = 64/Re
- Gravity flow (outlet 10 m below the inlet at low flow) gives a negative head and a warning; zero flow is rejected
  - Source: Behaviour specification
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.86 m, 0.55 m, 17.42 m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Crane Co., Technical Paper No. 410 (2018), ch. 2 (Darcy–Weisbach, Colebrook) and ch. 3 (pump head)
- ANSI/HI 1.3 Rotodynamic centrifugal pumps for design and application (total head, system curve)

## Transformer size calculator (kVA)

<a id="transformer-sizing"></a>

Folder `transformer-sizing/` · Electrical · Transformer kVA size from the load, power factor and growth, the next IEC or ANSI standard rating, rated currents, voltage regulation and losses.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Required rating S_req = P/pf × (1 + growth)/(maximum loading): the active load at the design power factor, a growth allowance and the permitted steady loading (0.8–1.0; IEC 60076-7 allows cyclic overloads, not applied); the preferred rating is the next IEC 60076-1 R10 value (… 630, 800, 1 000, 1 250, 1 600, 2 000, 2 500 kVA). Diversity between loads must already be in the active load.
- Impedance components from the nameplate: u_r = P_k/S_r (load losses at rated current), u_x = √(u_k² − u_r²), both in per unit of the rating; voltage regulation at a load fraction x and power factor cos φ by the standard approximation ε = x(u_r cos φ + u_x sin φ) + x²(u_x cos φ − u_r sin φ)²/200 (IEC 60076-8 / Say), lagging power factor positive; the no-load secondary voltage is the rated value.
- Losses: no-load (iron) losses constant, load (copper) losses P_k x²; efficiency η = P_out/(P_out + P_0 + x² P_k) with P_out = x S_r cos φ; maximum efficiency at the load fraction √(P_0/P_k). Annual energy loss uses the entered operating hours at the given load (a load-duration curve is not modelled).
- Secondary short-circuit current I_k ≈ I_r/u_k is the transformer-only, infinite-source value without the IEC 60909 voltage factor and K_T correction (the short-circuit calculator refines it); inrush current (8–12 × I_r for 0.1 s) is noted, not computed.
- Three-phase, two-winding, ONAN at nominal tap; harmonics (K-factor derating), altitude and ambient derating, parallel operation and tap-changer range are not covered.
- EU Ecodesign (Regulation 548/2014, Tier 2 2021) loss limits are given as a reference in the help texts for common ratings; the entered losses are the nameplate values.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 1 000 kVA, 6 %, P_0 1.1 kW, P_k 10.5 kW at full load and pf 0.8 lagging: u_r 1.05 %, u_x 5.91 %, regulation 4.47 %, secondary voltage 382.9 V, efficiency 98.57 %, maximum efficiency at 32.4 % load; 800 kW at pf 0.8 with 20 % growth and 80 % loading needs 1 500 kVA → 1 600 kVA preferred.
- Design decision: the regulation formula includes the second-order term so leading power factors (negative regulation) are handled; the rating list stops at 5 000 kVA, beyond which transformers are specified individually.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Voltage regulation above 5 %: consider a tap setting or a lower-impedance unit; downstream voltage drop adds to it.
- Power factor below 0.85: correction capacitors would reduce the required kVA and the regulation.
- Leading power factor: the secondary voltage can rise above the no-load value (negative regulation).
- …; the required … kVA includes … % growth at … % maximum loading.
- Nameplate losses assumed; EU Ecodesign Tier 2 (2021) limits for new units are often well below older designs — check the datasheet.
- Short-circuit current is the transformer-only estimate I_r/u_k; inrush can reach 8–12 × I_r (…–… kA) for the first cycles.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Required rating … kVA exceeds the preferred list (… kVA): specify the transformer individually
- Load losses … W give u_r = … % ≥ u_k … %: check the nameplate values

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Rating selection: 800 kW at pf 0.8 = 1 000 kVA; with 20 % growth and 80 % loading the requirement is 1 500 kVA → preferred 1 600 kVA; the R10 list runs 25 … 5 000 kVA
  - Source: IEC 60076-1 preferred ratings (R10 series); S_req = P/pf (1 + g)/k
- Per-unit impedance: 1 000 kVA, u_k 6 %, P_k 10.5 kW → u_r = 1.05 %, u_x = √(36 − 1.1025) = 5.907 %
  - Source: u_r = P_k/S_r, u_x = √(u_k² − u_r²) (IEC 60076-8; Say, Alternating Current Machines)
- Regulation at full load, pf 0.8 lagging: ε = 1.05 × 0.8 + 5.907 × 0.6 + (5.907 × 0.8 − 1.05 × 0.6)²/200 = 4.47 %; secondary voltage 400 × (1 − 0.0447) = 382.1 V; leading pf 0.8 gives −2.9 % (voltage rise)
  - Source: Standard regulation approximation ε = u_r cos φ + u_x sin φ + (u_x cos φ − u_r sin φ)²/200 (Say §; IEC 60076-8)
- Losses and efficiency at full load: 1.1 + 10.5 = 11.6 kW → η = 800/(800 + 11.6) = 98.57 %; maximum efficiency at √(1.1/10.5) = 32.4 % load; at half load losses 1.1 + 2.625 = 3.725 kW and η = 99.08 %; annual loss 69.6 MWh at 6 000 h
  - Source: P_loss = P_0 + x² P_k; η = P/(P + P_loss); x_max,η = √(P_0/P_k) (Theraja vol. II)
- Currents: 1 000 kVA at 11 kV / 400 V → 52.5 A HV, 1 443 A LV; 800 kW at pf 0.8 draws 1 443 A; secondary short-circuit I_r/u_k = 24.1 kA; inrush note 11.5–17.3 kA
  - Source: I = S/(√3 U); Schneider Electrical Installation Guide (I_sc ≈ I_r/u_k)
- Remarks: an existing 1 000 kVA unit with 20 % growth at 80 % maximum loading is flagged (150 % after growth → 1 250 kVA next); a 200 kW load on 1 000 kVA is "lightly loaded"; regulation > 5 % warned for u_k 10 %
  - Source: Behaviour specification
- Invalid inputs fail fast: load losses giving u_r ≥ u_k, requirement above the preferred list, unknown power factor type
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1 500 kVA, 120 %, 1.05 %, 5.91 %, 4.47 %, 382 V, 11.6 kW, 98.6 %, 32 %, 52.5 A, 1 443 A to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- IEEE C57.12.00-2021 General requirements for liquid-immersed distribution, power and regulating transformers (preferred continuous kVA ratings)
- IEC 60076-1:2011 Power transformers — General (rated quantities, preferred ratings R10 series), IEC 60076-7 loading guide, IEC 60076-8 application guide (voltage drop and regulation)
- M. G. Say, Alternating Current Machines, 5th ed. (Pitman 1983) — per-unit regulation approximation; B. L. Theraja, Electrical Technology vol. II
- Commission Regulation (EU) No 548/2014 (Ecodesign, Tier 2 2021) — maximum load and no-load losses for distribution transformers
- Schneider Electric Electrical Installation Guide, ch. B/N (transformer selection, inrush, short-circuit current I_r/u_k)

## Closed traverse calculator (compass rule)

<a id="traverse"></a>

Folder `traverse/` · Civil · Latitudes and departures of a closed traverse from bearings and distances, misclosure, precision ratio, Bowditch adjustment and adjusted coordinates.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The traverse is a closed loop that returns to its starting point, and the directions are already balanced so the angular misclosure has been distributed.
- The compass (Bowditch) rule spreads the misclosure in proportion to leg length. It suits traverses where angles and distances are measured with similar precision; least squares is the rigorous alternative.
- Distances are horizontal and in one unit, and every output length and coordinate is in that unit. Slope distances must be reduced to horizontal first.
- Azimuths are measured clockwise from north. Grid, true or magnetic north may be used, but all legs must share the same reference.
- The area is that of the adjusted polygon by the coordinate method, in the square of the distance unit. It assumes the legs do not cross.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: the default four-leg traverse (285.43, 582.10, 442.05 and 591.62 ft, total 1 901.20 ft) has latitude misclosure 0.028, departure misclosure 0.078, linear misclosure 0.083 ft, precision 1 : 22 818 and adjusted area 211 322 ft². The compass rule sums of corrections equal the misclosures exactly. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The precision 1 : … is worse than the required 1 : …; check the field work before adjusting.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Legs, line …: write "bearing; distance", for example N45°30'E; 120.50 or 135.5; 120.50.
- Legs, line …: "…" is not a bearing (N 0–90° E) or an azimuth (0 to under 360°).
- Legs, line …: the distance "…" must be a number above zero.
- Legs: a closed traverse needs at least three legs.
- Legs: the traverse misses closing by …, more than 1 % of its length; a leg is probably missing, reversed or mistyped.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Bearings to azimuths: N45°30′E = 45.5°, S45°30′E = 134.5°, S 12 15 30 W = 192.2583°, N10W = 350°, 135°30′ = 135.5°; N95E and 45°70′ are rejected
  - Source: Ghilani & Wolf, Elementary Surveying, ch. 7: bearing quadrants and azimuths from north
- Square 100 × 100 with the west leg 100.04: misclosure 0.04, precision 1 : 10 001; compass correction of departure 0.04 × 100/400.04 per 100 leg; point 3 at E 100.019998
  - Source: Hand calculation by the compass rule, C_dep = −ΣDep × L / ΣL (Ghilani & Wolf, ch. 10)
- Compass rule on the default traverse: corrections sum to −ΣLat and −ΣDep and the adjusted traverse closes; 1 901.20 ft, misclosure 0.083 ft, 1 : 22 818
  - Source: Ghilani & Wolf, ch. 10: the corrections equal the misclosure with opposite sign; hand calculation
- A 3-4-5 right triangle 400 north, 300 east, closing leg 500 at azimuth 216.8699° closes exactly; area 60 000 by coordinates
  - Source: Geometry: area = ½ × 400 × 300; azimuth 180° + atan(300/400)
- Fewer than three legs, an unreadable bearing, a zero distance and a gross misclosure (a reversed leg) are refused; a poor closure warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1 901.20, 0.083, 22 818, 211 322 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Ghilani, C.D. and Wolf, P.R., Elementary Surveying: An Introduction to Geomatics, 13th ed., Pearson, ch. 10 Traverse Computations (latitudes and departures, compass rule, coordinates)
- Ghilani, C.D., Adjustment Computations: Spatial Data Analysis, 6th ed., Wiley, 2017 (least squares adjustment of traverses, the rigorous alternative)

## Trench and excavation volume calculator

<a id="trench-volume"></a>

Folder `trench-volume/` · Civil · Volume of a trench or excavation with vertical or OSHA sloped sides, the loose volume and truck loads after swell, and backfill around a pipe.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The trench has a flat bottom of constant width and uniform depth; for a varying depth, split it into lengths of similar depth. Sloped sides are symmetric at n horizontal to 1 vertical.
- OSHA slopes are the maximum allowable slopes of 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P Appendix B for excavations up to 20 ft (6 m) deep; a competent person classifies the soil, and deeper or wetter excavations need an engineered protective system.
- Swell (bulking) converts bank volume to loose volume for hauling: typically 10–20 % for sand and gravel, 25–35 % for common earth and clay, 50 % or more for blasted rock.
- Backfill is the trench volume less the pipe's outside volume; compaction may need 10–25 % more loose material than the bank volume it fills.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 100 ft trench 2 ft wide and 4 ft deep is 800 ft³ = 29.63 yd³; with 25 % swell 37.04 yd³, four 10 yd³ loads. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Vertical sides at 5 ft (1.5 m) or deeper need shoring, a trench box or sloping under OSHA 1926.652, unless the trench is in stable rock.
- Deeper than 20 ft (6 m): OSHA requires a protective system designed by a registered professional engineer.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Pipe outside diameter: the pipe does not fit in the trench.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 100 ft × 2 ft × 4 ft with vertical sides: 800 ft³ = 29.63 yd³; 25 % swell gives 37.04 yd³, four 10 yd³ loads
  - Source: V = L b d; V_loose = V (1 + swell)
- OSHA Type B (1 : 1), 2 ft bottom, 6 ft deep, 50 ft long: top 14 ft, section (2 + 6) × 6 = 48 ft², 2 400 ft³
  - Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, Table B-1 (Type B 1 H : 1 V)
- Type A is ¾ : 1 and Type C 1½ : 1: at 3 m deep and 1 m bottom the sections are 9.75 and 16.5 m²
  - Source: OSHA Appendix B Table B-1
- Backfill around a 300 mm pipe in a 30 m × 0.6 m × 1.2 m trench: 21.6 − 2.121 = 19.48 m³
