  - Source: V_backfill = V_trench − π D² L / 4
- Vertical sides at 6 ft warn (OSHA 1926.652); a pipe wider than the trench and zero depth are rejected
  - Source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1); validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 29.63 yd³, 37.04 yd³, 4 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B, Table B-1 (maximum allowable slopes) and 1926.652(a)(1) (excavations under 5 ft)
- Caterpillar Performance Handbook, edition 49, section "Tables" (swell factors of materials)

## Change of trim and new drafts calculator

<a id="trim-change"></a>

Folder `trim-change/` · Maritime · New forward and aft drafts after shifting, loading or discharging a weight, from MCTC, TPC and LCF: bodily sinkage, change of trim and draft changes.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The weight is small compared with the displacement (up to about 10 %), so TPC, MCTC and the LCF read at the initial mean draught stay valid. For larger weights take them at the mean of the initial and final draughts, or use a full loading calculation.
- Positions are measured from the aft perpendicular, positive forward, and trim is positive by the stern, as in the hydrostatics calculator. LCF given from midships must be converted: LCF from AP = L/2 + LCF forward of midships.
- A loaded weight first sinks the ship bodily by w / TPC at the LCF, then trims it about the LCF by w × lever / MCTC. A shifted weight only trims the ship.
- Drafts are at the perpendiculars. Draught marks away from the perpendiculars need the usual correction for their position, as in a draft survey.
- Only the longitudinal effect is calculated; a weight off the centreline also lists the ship, and a weight moved vertically changes GM (see the initial stability calculator).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: L = 150 m, drafts F 7.20 m and A 8.00 m, LCF 72 m from AP, TPC 25 t/cm, MCTC 180 t·m/cm; loading 300 t at 110 m from AP sinks 12.0 cm, trims 63.3 cm by the head and gives A 7.816 m and F 7.649 m; a weight loaded 87 m from AP leaves the aft draft unchanged. Checked by hand.
- Verification 2026-11-08: shifting 120 t forward 45 m on a 126 m ship with MCTC 240 t·m/cm and LCF 60 m from AP trims 22.5 cm by the head: aft −10.7 cm, forward +11.8 cm. Checked by hand (method of Derrett & Barrass, ch. 15).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The weight is large compared with the ship: TPC, MCTC and LCF change with draught, so take them at the mean of the initial and final draughts or use a full loading calculation.
- A new end draft is negative: the operation is not possible as entered (check the units and the sign of the position).
- The trim exceeds 1 % of the length: the small-trim formulas lose accuracy. Recheck with the hydrostatic tables at the new draught.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- LCF from AP: the centre of flotation must lie between the perpendiculars.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Shift 120 t forward 45 m, MCTC 240, L 126 m, LCF 60 m from AP: trim 22.5 cm by the head, aft −10.7 cm, forward +11.8 cm
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass, Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, ch. 15 (change of trim = w d / MCTC, shared in the ratio of the LCF position); hand calculation
- Load 300 t at 110 m from AP (LCF 72 m, TPC 25, MCTC 180, L 150): sinkage 12 cm, trim 63.3 cm by the head, A 7.816 m, F 7.649 m
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass ch. 9 and 15 (bodily sinkage then trim about the LCF); hand calculation
- Loading at MCTC L / (TPC LCF) = 15 m forward of the LCF (87 m from AP) leaves the aft draft unchanged
  - Source: Derrett & Barrass ch. 15 (loading to keep the aft draft constant); consistency check
- Loading then discharging the same weight at the same place restores the drafts; loading at the LCF only sinks the ship
  - Source: Consistency checks
- LCF outside the length, zero MCTC and an unknown operation are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 12.0 cm, −63.3 cm, 7.816 m, 7.649 m, 87.00 m to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Derrett, D.R. and Barrass, C.B., Ship Stability for Masters and Mates, 7th ed. (Butterworth-Heinemann, 2012), ch. 9 (TPC), ch. 15 (trim: change of trim and the effect of loading, discharging and shifting weights)
- Lewis, E.V. (ed.), Principles of Naval Architecture, 2nd rev. (SNAME, 1988), Vol. I: hydrostatics, moment to change trim and the centre of flotation

## True airspeed calculator (TAS and Mach)

<a id="true-airspeed"></a>

Folder `true-airspeed/` · Automotive · True airspeed and Mach number from indicated or calibrated airspeed, pressure altitude and temperature, with equivalent airspeed and ground speed.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Calibrated airspeed is converted with the compressible (isentropic) pitot-static relations for subsonic flow, the same relations the airspeed indicator is calibrated to at sea-level standard conditions (a0 = 661.48 kn, p0 = 29.92 inHg).
- Indicated airspeed becomes calibrated airspeed by adding the position and instrument correction from the airspeed calibration table of the POH or AFM; with no correction entered, IAS is taken as CAS.
- The outside air temperature is the static air temperature; at jet speeds a probe reads a higher total temperature, which must be corrected first (the Mach number output gives T_total = T (1 + 0.2 M²) for that check).
- The static pressure comes from the pressure altitude through the ICAO standard atmosphere, valid to 65 617 ft (20 km).
- Ground speed is the true airspeed minus the head-wind component along the track (a tail wind is negative); the wind correction angle of a crosswind is not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: CAS 150 kn at 8 000 ft pressure altitude and 0 °C: Mach 0.2625, TAS 169.1 kn, EAS 149.7 kn; with a 20 kn head wind ground speed 149.1 kn; the 2 % per 1 000 ft rule gives 174.0 kn. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The head wind is at least the true airspeed: the aircraft makes no progress over the ground.
- Above Mach 0.3 compressibility matters: use CAS from the airspeed calibration, and correct a probe temperature reading for ram rise before entering it.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- IAS to CAS correction: the calibrated airspeed must be greater than zero.
- Airspeed: a calibrated airspeed at or above 661.5 kn needs the supersonic pitot relation, which this calculator does not cover.
- Airspeed: the flight Mach number would be 1 or more; the subsonic pitot relations no longer apply.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Sea-level standard day: TAS = EAS = CAS (150 kn), speed of sound 661.48 kn (340.294 m/s)
  - Source: Definition of calibrated airspeed; ICAO Doc 7488/3 a0 = 340.294 m/s
- ISA tables: 11 000 m is 22 632 Pa and 216.65 K (speed of sound 573.6 kn); 8 000 ft is 752.6 hPa
  - Source: ICAO Doc 7488/3 standard atmosphere tables
- CAS 150 kn at 8 000 ft and 0 °C: Mach 0.2625, TAS 169.1 kn, EAS 149.7 kn, ground speed 149.1 kn into 20 kn
  - Source: Hand calculation with q_c = p0[(1 + 0.2(Vc/a0)²)^3.5 − 1], M = √(5[(q_c/p + 1)^(2/7) − 1]) (Anderson, Ch. 3)
- Airliner: 280 kn CAS at FL350 on a standard day is Mach 0.821, TAS 473 kn; EAS is below CAS
  - Source: Same relations at ISA 35 000 ft (−54.34 °C); compressibility makes EAS < CAS
- IAS with a +2 kn correction equals CAS 2 kn higher; a 25 kn tail wind adds to the ground speed
  - Source: CAS = IAS + correction (POH calibration table); GS = TAS − head wind
- A supersonic CAS and a pressure altitude above 20 km are rejected; a head wind above TAS gives no ground speed
  - Source: Validation contract (subsonic relations, ISA to 20 km)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.2625, 169.1 kn, 149.7 kn, 149.1 kn, 174.0 kn to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ICAO Doc 7488/3, Manual of the ICAO Standard Atmosphere, 3rd ed. 1993 (p0 = 101 325 Pa, T0 = 288.15 K, a0 = 340.294 m/s, γ = 1.4, R = 287.05287 J/(kg·K))
- FAA-H-8083-25C, Pilot’s Handbook of Aeronautical Knowledge (2023), Chapter 8 Flight Instruments: indicated, calibrated, equivalent and true airspeed
- J.D. Anderson, Introduction to Flight, 8th ed., McGraw-Hill 2016, Chapter 3 (measurement of airspeed: compressible subsonic flow, calibrated airspeed)

## True wind from apparent wind

<a id="true-wind"></a>

Folder `true-wind/` · Maritime · True and relative wind conversion per ISO 15016 with the anemometer height correction to the 10 m reference height of wind data.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Vector triangle of ISO 15016:2025 Annex C.2 (formulas C.3, C.4, C.10 and C.11): the relative wind measured on board is the true wind minus the wind of the ship's own motion, which comes from ahead at the ship's speed over ground along the heading. Speed over ground is used because the true wind of meteorology is relative to the earth; with speed through the water the result is the wind relative to the water, which differs by the current.
- Directions are those the wind comes FROM: true wind in degrees true, relative wind in degrees off the bow, 0° on the bow and positive from starboard (ISO 15016 convention); a relative angle of 330° is entered as 330 or −30.
- Height correction by the power-law boundary-layer profile V(Z_ref) = V(Z_a)·(Z_ref/Z_a)^p with p = 1/9 (ISO 15016:2025 formula C.9) or 1/7 (earlier ISO 15016 editions and ITTC 7.5-04-01-01.1); the reference height of wind resistance coefficients and of the Beaufort scale is 10 m above the sea. The real exponent varies with atmospheric stability (about 0.10–0.20), and the profile does not hold in the airflow disturbed by the superstructure around the anemometer.
- In "true to relative" mode the true wind is taken as given at the reference height (a weather report or forecast is a 10 m wind); the relative wind at the anemometer is then found by moving the true wind up the same profile and recombining it with the ship's motion.
- Steady wind: the inputs are means over the same period (ISO 15016 uses 10-minute means); gusts and the ship's rolling and pitching are not modelled.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: a 20 kn relative wind on the bow at 10 kn over the ground is a 10 kn true wind from ahead; a 25 kn relative wind on the starboard beam at 15 kn on 090° is 29.15 kn true from 211.0°; from 40 m to 10 m the 1/9 profile multiplies the speed by 0.8572 and the 1/7 profile by 0.8203; true to relative and back returns the input to 1e-9.
- The 1/9 exponent was cross-checked against ISO 15016:2025 C.2.3 and the atlas-back wind resistance documentation, which records the edition change from 1/7.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- True wind is calm: the relative wind is the ship\'s own motion, and the true direction is undefined.
- Following relative wind: the anemometer sits in the wake of the funnel and superstructure, and small direction errors give large true-wind errors.
- True wind much weaker than the ship\'s own wind: the true direction is very sensitive to errors in the measured relative direction.
- Anemometer below the reference height: the profile extrapolates upwards; check the sensor height above the actual waterline.
- The anemometer reading is disturbed by the superstructure; ISO 15016 checks the true wind for consistency between the runs of a double run before use.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Wind on the bow: 20 kn relative from ahead at 10 kn over the ground is a 10 kn true wind from the heading; 10 kn relative from ahead at 10 kn is calm
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 formulas C.3 and C.4
- Beam relative wind: 25 kn from the starboard beam on heading 090° at 15 kn is √(25² + 15²) = 29.15 kn true from 211.0°; 330° and −30° are the same relative direction
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 C.3–C.4 worked by hand (relative wind = true wind − ship motion)
- Round trip: a true wind from 060° at 20 kn on heading 000° at 15 kn gives the relative wind of C.10–C.11, and converting it back returns 20 kn from 060°
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 C.10–C.11 are the inverse of C.3–C.4
- Height profile: from a 40 m anemometer to 10 m the 1/9 profile gives 20 × 0.25^(1/9) = 17.14 kn and the 1/7 profile 16.41 kn; the reference wind is what goes to the Beaufort scale
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 formula C.9 (exponent 1/9); ITTC 7.5-04-01-01.1 (2017) exponent 1/7
- Following wind at the ship's speed: a true wind from astern at 12 kn on a ship making 12 kn feels calm on board, and a relative calm means a 12 kn true wind from astern
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 C.3 and C.10 with α = 180°
- Invalid inputs fail fast: negative speed over ground, a zero anemometer height, an unknown profile and a relative direction outside −180…360
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 29.15 kn, 211.0°, 0.870, 25.4 kn, 21.8 kn, 85° to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 15016:2025 Ships and marine technology — Guidelines for the assessment of speed and power performance by analysis of speed trial data, Annex C.2 (formulas C.3, C.4, C.9, C.10, C.11)
- ITTC Recommended Procedure 7.5-04-01-01.1 Preparation, Conduct and Analysis of Speed/Power Trials (2017) — wind profile exponent 1/7
- The American Practical Navigator (Bowditch), NGA Pub. 9 — true and apparent wind
- WMO-No. 8 Guide to Instruments and Methods of Observation, Volume I, chapter 5 (surface wind at 10 m) and Volume III (marine observations)

## Truss calculator (Pratt, Howe, Warren)

<a id="truss"></a>

Folder `truss/` · Structural · Member forces, reactions and the largest tension and compression in a Pratt, Howe or Warren truss under a uniform roof or bridge load, by the method of joints.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The truss is planar and simply supported (pin at the left, roller at the right), with pinned joints and loads only at the top-chord joints, so members carry axial force only.
- A uniform load W over the span is lumped at the top joints: W/n at each interior joint and half that at the two end joints of a Pratt or Howe truss; a Warren truss has n top joints, each taking W/n.
- Self-weight of the members, secondary bending from continuous chords and eccentric connections are not included. Compression members must also be checked for buckling over their length.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a Pratt truss of 18 m span, 3 m deep, 6 panels, carrying 60 kN: reactions 30 kN; top chord at midspan 45 kN compression (M/H = 135/3 about the bottom middle joint); bottom chord in the middle panels 40 kN tension (M/H = 120/3 about the top joint 6 m in); end diagonal 35.36 kN tension; end post 30 kN compression. Checked by hand by the method of sections.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Span-to-depth ratio …: trusses are usually 1/8 to 1/12 of the span deep; a shallower truss has large chord forces and deflects more.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- The truss is unstable or not determinate.
- The truss is not statically determinate.
- Number of panels: enter an even number from 2 to 40.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Pratt, 18 m × 3 m, 6 panels, 60 kN: reactions 30 kN; top chord at midspan −45 kN (M/H = 135/3); bottom chord in panel 3 +40 kN (120/3)
  - Source: Method of sections, Hibbeler, Structural Analysis, ch. 3: chord force = moment about the opposite joint / depth
- Pratt end diagonal +35.36 kN (shear 25 kN × 4.243/3), end post −30 kN, midspan vertical −10 kN (the joint load)
  - Source: Method of joints at B0, T0 and B3
- Howe mirrors Pratt: diagonals in compression, bottom chord at midspan +45 kN, end diagonal −35.36 kN
  - Source: Howe truss: diagonals slope the other way
- Warren and every type are in equilibrium: reactions add up to W, and the reactions are equal for a symmetric load
  - Source: Global equilibrium ΣF_y = 0
- Odd panel counts and zero depth are rejected; a very shallow truss warns
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 30.0 kN, 40.0 kN, 45.0 kN to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Hibbeler, R.C., Structural Analysis, 10th ed., ch. 3 (method of joints, determinacy m + r = 2j, common truss forms)
- Megson, T.H.G., Structural and Stress Analysis, 4th ed., ch. 4 (statically determinate pin-jointed frameworks)

## Engineering unit converter

<a id="unit-converter"></a>

Folder `unit-converter/` · General · Convert pressure, torque, power, flow, length, mass, speed, temperature, energy and marine units (knots, nautical miles, long tons) from one table.

### Assumptions and caveats

- All factors come from shared/units.js, the single conversion table used by every calculator; exact definitions are used where they exist (1 nmi = 1852 m, 1 in = 25.4 mm, 1 lb = 0.45359237 kg, 1 hp = 550 ft·lbf/s = 745.69987 W, 1 PS = 75 kgf·m/s = 735.49875 W, 1 Btu(IT) = 1055.05585 J, 1 kcal = 4184 J thermochemical).
- Temperature converts with offsets (°C, °F, K); the separate "temperature difference" group converts intervals, where 1 K = 1 °C = 1.8 °F without offset.
- Currency units are placeholders with factor 1 and are not offered for conversion; no exchange rates.
- Horsepower means mechanical horsepower (550 ft·lbf/s); metric horsepower is listed separately as PS. Calories are thermochemical (4.184 J); Btu is the International Table Btu.
- Results are shown to seven significant digits; intermediate conversions through the base unit can introduce rounding in the last digit for chained non-exact factors.
- Gallons must be chosen explicitly as US or imperial; "ton" exists as tonne (1000 kg), long ton (2240 lb) and short ton (2000 lb).

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: a round-trip identity test covers every unit pair of every convertible group, and spot values are checked against NIST SP 811 Appendix B.
- Design decision: the unit lists are generated from shared/units.js at load time, so a unit added there appears here without any change to this calculator; single-unit groups (dimensionless, money, carbon intensity) are excluded.
- Design decision: the renderer gained dependent selects (optionsBy) for this calculator — the quantity choice drives the unit lists.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Below absolute zero — check the input.
- This converts temperature levels with offsets; for a temperature difference or tolerance use the "Temperature difference" quantity.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Marine units: 1 kn = 0.5144444 m/s = 1.852 km/h; 1 nmi = 1.150779 mi = 6 076.12 ft; 1 long ton = 1.016047 t; 1 fathom = 6 ft
  - Source: NIST SP 811 Appendix B.8 (knot, nautical mile, long ton); 1 nmi = 1852 m exactly
- Pressure: 1 bar = 14.50377 psi = 0.9869233 atm = 750.0617 mmHg; 1 psi = 6.894757 kPa; 1 mH₂O = 9.80665 kPa
  - Source: NIST SP 811 Appendix B.8 (psi 6.894757 kPa, atm 101.325 kPa, mmHg 133.3224 Pa)
- Power and energy: 1 hp = 745.6999 W, 1 PS = 735.4988 W, 1 Btu = 1 055.056 J, 1 kWh = 3 412.14 Btu, 1 toe = 41.868 GJ, 1 kcal = 4 184 J
  - Source: NIST SP 811 Appendix B.8/B.9 (horsepower 550 ft·lbf/s, metric horsepower, Btu_IT, calorie_th); IEA (toe = 41.868 GJ)
- Torque, force, volume, flow: 1 kgf·m = 9.80665 N·m, 1 lbf·ft = 1.355818 N·m, 1 kip = 4.448222 kN, 1 US gal = 3.785412 L, 1 bbl = 158.9873 L, 1 cfm = 1.699011 m³/h
  - Source: NIST SP 811 Appendix B.8 (kilogram-force, pound-force foot, gallon US, barrel petroleum, cubic foot per minute)
- Temperature with offsets: 100 °C = 212 °F = 373.15 K, −40 °C = −40 °F, 0 K = −459.67 °F; difference 10 K = 18 °F
  - Source: BIPM SI Brochure 9th ed. (kelvin/Celsius); NIST SP 811 §B.9 (Fahrenheit)
- Round trip is the identity for every unit of every convertible group (to base and back, and between every pair)
  - Source: Internal consistency of shared/units.js
- Default conversion 1 kn → m/s and the all-units listing contains every speed unit
  - Source: Schema defaults; 1 kn = 0.5144444 m/s
- Invalid inputs fail fast: unknown quantity, unit from another group, non-numeric value
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 99.9 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- NIST Special Publication 811 (2008), Guide for the Use of the SI, Appendix B (conversion factors)
- BIPM, The International System of Units (SI Brochure), 9th ed. (2019), Table 8 (non-SI units accepted for use)
- IEEE/ASTM SI 10-2016, American National Standard for Metric Practice
- International Hydrographic Conference 1929 (nautical mile = 1852 m); 1959 international yard and pound agreement

## V-belt length and centre distance calculator

<a id="v-belt-length"></a>

Folder `v-belt-length/` · Mechanical · V-belt pitch length from sheave pitch diameters and centre distance, or the centre distance for a standard belt, with the exact formula as a check.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Diameters are sheave pitch diameters and the length is the belt pitch length, the convention of belt catalogues and of Shigley §17-3. Outside or inside lengths differ from the pitch length by an amount that depends on the belt section; take it from the belt maker.
- The approximate formula replaces the exact arc geometry by the first terms of a series in (D − d)/C; its error grows with the diameter difference and is shown next to the exact value.
- The centre distance for a standard belt is the nominal value with the belt fitted; drives need adjustment for installation (shorter) and take-up (longer), usually given by the belt maker.
- Two-sheave open drive with no idler; the wrap angle on the small sheave is shown, and below about 120° the belt rating must be reduced.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: sheaves of 100 and 250 mm on 600 mm centres: approximate L_p = 1 200 + 549.78 + 9.38 = 1 759.15 mm, exact 1 759.17 mm; for an 1 800 mm belt the approximate inverse gives C = 620.58 mm and the exact inverse 620.57 mm. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Wrap angle on the small sheave below 120°: V-belt power ratings must be reduced for the short arc of contact; increase the centre distance if possible.
- Centre distance less than the large sheave diameter: below the usual minimum for V-belt drives; check the belt maker\'s recommendation.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Large sheave pitch diameter: enter the larger sheave as D and the smaller as d.
- Centre distance: it must be more than the sum of the two sheave radii, or the sheaves overlap.
- Belt pitch length: the belt is too short to pass round both sheaves without them touching; choose a longer belt.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Sheaves 100 and 250 mm on 600 mm centres: L_p = 1 200 + 549.779 + 9.375 = 1 759.154 mm; exact 1 759.166 mm
  - Source: Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., eq. 17-16a and eq. 17-1 (hand calculation)
- Centre distance for an 1 800 mm belt: ¼ {1 250.221 + √(1 250.221² − 2 × 150²)} = 620.579 mm; exact 620.573 mm
  - Source: Shigley eq. 17-16b; exact inverse of eq. 17-1 by bisection (hand calculation)
- Equal sheaves: approximate and exact formulas agree exactly, L = 2C + π d
  - Source: Limiting case D = d of eqs. 17-16a and 17-1
- The approximation error grows with the diameter difference: 100/500 mm on 400 mm centres differs by more than 1 mm
  - Source: Series truncation of eq. 17-16a against eq. 17-1
- Approximate inverse is the exact inverse of the approximate length (eq. 17-16b solves 17-16a)
  - Source: Algebra of eqs. 17-16a and 17-16b
- Too short a belt, overlapping sheaves and D smaller than d are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 620.58 mm, 620.57 mm to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Budynas and Nisbett, Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design, 10th ed., §17-3 V belts, eqs. 17-16a and 17-16b (pitch length and centre distance), and eq. 17-1 (exact open-belt geometry)
- ISO 4184:1992, Belt drives — Classical and narrow V-belts — Lengths in datum system (standard datum lengths)

## Vapour pressure calculator (Antoine equation)

<a id="vapour-pressure"></a>

Folder `vapour-pressure/` · Process · Vapour pressure at a temperature, or boiling point at a pressure, of water, alcohols, acetone, aromatics, alkanes, ammonia and more by the Antoine equation.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The Antoine equation log10 P = A − B / (T + C) is a fit to measured vapour pressures; each set of constants is used only inside the temperature range it was fitted to, and the calculator refuses temperatures and pressures outside the tabulated ranges rather than extrapolate.
- Constants are those of the NIST Chemistry WebBook (P in bar, T in K); water above 100 °C uses the Dortmund Data Bank set. Where a fluid has more than one range, the calculator switches at the range limits, so the curve can step by up to 3 % there.
- Checked against the NIST reference equations of state: most ranges agree within 0.3 %; water above 100 °C within 1.3 % (IAPWS-IF97), n-butane within 2.6 %, propane between 231 and 278 K within 3 % and ammonia within 5 %.
- The liquid is pure. Dissolved salts lower the vapour pressure, and a mixture follows Raoult's law only roughly; this page does not treat mixtures.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: ethanol at 50 °C: log10 P = 5.24677 − 1598.673 / (323.15 − 46.424) = −0.5303, P = 29.49 kPa; the same constants give a normal boiling point of 351.45 K (78.3 °C), against 351.44 K in the NIST WebBook. Checked by hand.
- Water against IAPWS-IF97: within 0.11 % from 0 to 100 °C (Bridgeman and Aldrich ranges) and 1.3 % from 100 to 374 °C (DDB). Ethanol and methanol ranges above their normal boiling points on the NIST page (Ambrose et al. 1975) are 6 to 8 % below the NIST equation of state and are not used; nor is the low-temperature n-heptane range (up to 5 % off).

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above 100 °C the water constants are within about 1.3 % of IAPWS-IF97; the steam table calculator gives the exact saturation pressure.
- These constants are within 2 to 5 % of the NIST reference equation of state; use refrigerant or hydrocarbon property tables for design.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Temperature: the Antoine constants for … cover … to …; the calculator does not extrapolate.
- Pressure: the Antoine constants for … cover … to … kPa; the calculator does not extrapolate.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Ethanol at 50 °C: log10 P = 5.24677 − 1598.673 / 276.726 → 29.49 kPa; normal boiling point 351.45 K (NIST 351.44 K)
  - Source: NIST WebBook Antoine parameters (Ambrose and Sprake 1970), hand calculation; NIST Tboil of ethanol
- Water from 0 to 100 °C is within 0.12 % of IAPWS-IF97, and from 120 to 370 °C within 1.3 %
  - Source: IAPWS R7-97(2012) eq. 30 (shared/iapws97.js psat)
- Water boils at 100.00 °C at 101.325 kPa and within 0.3 K of IAPWS-IF97 at 50 kPa and 5 bar
  - Source: IAPWS-IF97 saturation temperature (eq. 31, shared/iapws97.js tsat)
- At 25 °C benzene 12.70, toluene 3.799, n-hexane 20.16, n-pentane 68.35, cyclohexane 13.02, methanol 16.98 kPa within 0.3 %
  - Source: NIST WebBook fluid properties (reference equations of state), saturation pressures interpolated at 298.15 K
- At 20 °C ammonia 857 kPa (within 1 %), propane 836 kPa and n-butane 208 kPa (within 0.3 %)
  - Source: NIST WebBook fluid properties (reference equations of state)
- Boiling point inverts the vapour pressure in every fluid; ammonia warns
  - Source: Consistency of T = B / (A − log10 P) − C with the forward equation
- Temperatures and pressures outside the tabulated range are refused, not extrapolated
  - Source: Validation contract (Antoine constants are valid only in their fitted range)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 29.49 kPa to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- NIST Chemistry WebBook, NIST Standard Reference Database 69 (Linstrom and Mallard, eds.), phase-change data: Antoine equation parameters for each fluid
- Dortmund Data Bank (DDBST GmbH), Antoine constants of water, 99–374 °C: A = 8.14019, B = 1810.94, C = 244.485 (mmHg, °C)
- IAPWS R7-97(2012), Revised Release on the IAPWS Industrial Formulation 1997, eq. 30 (saturation pressure of water, used for the comparison)

## Vertical curve calculator (crest and sag)

<a id="vertical-curve"></a>

Folder `vertical-curve/` · Civil · Parabolic vertical curve: PVC, PVI and PVT stations and elevations, elevation at any station, high or low point, K value and AASHTO sight distance.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The curve is a symmetrical parabola, half its length on each side of the PVI, with stations measured horizontally. Unsymmetrical curves need two parabolas and are not covered.
- Grades are in percent, positive uphill in the direction of increasing stations.
- Sight distance uses the AASHTO Green Book formulas: on crests a 3.5 ft (1.08 m) eye height and a 2.0 ft (0.60 m) object; on sags the headlight criterion with a 2.0 ft (0.60 m) headlight and a 1° upward beam.
- The stopping sight distance needed for a design speed uses a 2.5 s reaction time and 11.2 ft/s² (3.4 m/s²) deceleration on level ground; grade corrections and comfort or appearance criteria for sags are not included.
- Stations before the PVC or after the PVT take the elevation of the tangent. On sag curves the AASHTO comfort length A V²/46.5 (A V²/395 in metric) is checked as a warning.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: g1 = +3 %, g2 = −2 %, L = 600 ft, PVI at 25+00 and 500.00 ft gives PVC 22+00 at 491.00 ft, PVT 28+00 at 494.00 ft, 495.33 ft at 24+00, high point at 25+60 and 496.40 ft, K = 120 ft and a sight distance of 508.9 ft against 423.7 ft needed at 50 mph. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The chosen station is outside the curve; its elevation is on the tangent.
- The sag curve is shorter than the AASHTO comfort length A V²/46.5 (A V²/395 in metric), … ….

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Grade out g2: it equals the grade in, so no vertical curve is needed.
- PVI station: it must be at least half the curve length, so that the PVC station is not negative.
- Station interval for the table: it gives more than 400 rows; choose a larger interval.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Crest +3 % / −2 %, L 600 ft, PVI 25+00 at 500.00 ft: PVC 22+00 at 491.00, PVT 28+00 at 494.00, 495.33 ft at 24+00, high point 25+60 at 496.40 ft
  - Source: Hand calculation: y = y_PVC + g1 x + (g2 − g1) x²/(2L); x_high = −g1 L/(g2 − g1) = 360 ft (Ghilani & Wolf, Vertical Curves)
- Middle ordinate at the PVI is A L / 800 = 5 × 600 / 800 = 3.75 ft; outside the curve the tangent applies; the grade is zero at the high point
  - Source: Property of the equal-tangent parabola: e = (g2 − g1) L / 8
- AASHTO stopping sight distance: 423.7 ft at 50 mph (design 425), 566.0 ft at 60 mph (570), 129.0 m at 80 km/h (130)
  - Source: AASHTO Green Book 2018, section 3.2.2 and Table 3-1: SSD = 1.47 V t + 1.075 V²/a, t = 2.5 s, a = 11.2 ft/s²
- AASHTO design K: crest 84 (50 mph, S 425 ft), 151 (60 mph, 570 ft), 26 (80 km/h, 130 m); sag 96 (50 mph) and 30 (80 km/h)
  - Source: AASHTO Green Book 2018, section 3.4.6 design controls for crest and sag vertical curves (K = L/A rounded up, from L = A S²/2158 or A S²/(400 + 3.5 S))
- Stations print as 25+60.00 and 1+250.000; equal grades, a negative PVC station and too fine a table interval are refused
  - Source: Validation contract; US 100 ft and metric kilometre station notation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 491.00 ft, 494.00 ft, 495.33 ft, 496.40 ft, 120.0 ft, 508.9 ft, 423.7 ft to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- AASHTO, A Policy on Geometric Design of Highways and Streets, 7th ed. (2018), section 3.2.2 Stopping Sight Distance and section 3.4.6 Vertical Curves (crest and sag length formulas, K = L/A)
- Ghilani, C.D. and Wolf, P.R., Elementary Surveying: An Introduction to Geomatics, 13th ed., ch. 25 Vertical Curves (equal-tangent parabolic curves, high and low points)

## Vibration isolation and severity

<a id="vibration-isolation"></a>

Folder `vibration-isolation/` · Mechanical · Isolator natural frequency and transmissibility of a machine on resilient mounts, and the ISO 10816-3 evaluation zone of a measured vibration velocity.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The machine is a rigid mass on mounts acting in parallel in one direction (single degree of freedom) with viscous damping ratio ζ; rocking modes, the flexibility of the foundation and the frequency dependence of rubber stiffness are not included.
- Force transmissibility T = √((1 + (2ζr)²)/((1 − r²)² + (2ζr)²)) with r = f/f_n; isolation starts above r = √2, and the isolation efficiency is 1 − T (Harris' Shock and Vibration Handbook, ch. 30).
- Evaluation zones of ISO 10816-3:2009 Annex A for machines above 15 kW at 120–15 000 r/min, broadband velocity r.m.s. measured on the bearing housings: group 1 (large machines, 300 kW to 50 MW) and group 2 (medium, 15 kW to 300 kW), each for rigid and flexible support. The same boundaries appear in ISO 20816-3:2022. The standards are not freely available, so the values were checked against several independent published reproductions.
- Support classification of ISO 10816-3: rigid if the lowest natural frequency of machine and support is at least 25 % above the main excitation frequency, otherwise flexible; with the automatic option the mount natural frequency decides.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: 2000 kg on four mounts of 1500 N/mm gives f_n = (1/2π)√(6 × 10^6/2000) = 8.72 Hz and 3.27 mm static deflection; at 25 Hz (1500 r/min) r = 2.87 and with ζ = 0.05 T = 0.144, 86 % isolation.
- Design decision: zone C/D and the other boundaries are taken as "at or above"; the zones are a first assessment and the machine maker's limits, where given, take precedence.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The disturbing frequency is only … times the natural frequency: below √2 the mounts amplify the force instead of isolating it.
- Near resonance: the machine will shake on its mounts; change the mount stiffness.
- Zero damping: the transmissibility at resonance is unbounded.
- Zone …: ….
- Starting and stopping pass through the natural frequency; check the run-up, rocking modes and the machine maker\'s vibration limits.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 2000 kg on four 1500 N/mm mounts: f_n = (1/2π)√(6 × 10⁶/2000) = 8.717 Hz and 3.27 mm static deflection, consistent with f_n = (1/2π)√(g/δ)
  - Source: Single-degree-of-freedom system (Harris, ch. 2)
- Transmissibility is 1 at r = √2 for any damping, 1/|1 − r²| = 0.125 at r = 3 without damping, and √(1 + 4ζ²)/(2ζ) = 10.05 at resonance with ζ = 0.05
  - Source: Force transmissibility of a damped isolator (Harris, ch. 30)
- Default machine at 1500 r/min: r = 25/8.717 = 2.868, T = 0.144, 86 % isolation
  - Source: Force transmissibility with ζ = 0.05
- ISO 10816-3 zones: 3.0 mm/s is zone C for a group 2 machine on a rigid support (1.4/2.8/4.5) and zone A for group 1 on a flexible support (3.5/7.1/11)
  - Source: ISO 10816-3:2009 Annex A, Tables A.1 and A.2
- Resilient mounts below 1.25 × the excitation frequency make the support flexible: the default 3.0 mm/s is then zone B (2.3/4.5/7.1)
  - Source: ISO 10816-3: rigid support when the lowest natural frequency is at least 25 % above the main excitation
- Invalid inputs are rejected: zero mass, a fractional number of mounts, damping above 1
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 8.72 Hz, 3.27 mm, 25 Hz, 2.87, 0.144, 86 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- C. M. Harris, A. G. Piersol (eds.), Harris' Shock and Vibration Handbook, 5th ed., McGraw-Hill 2002, ch. 2 and ch. 30 — transmissibility and vibration isolation
- ISO 10816-3:2009 Mechanical vibration — Evaluation of machine vibration by measurements on non-rotating parts — Part 3, Annex A zone boundaries; superseded by ISO 20816-3:2022 with the same zones

## cSt to SSU viscosity converter (Saybolt seconds)

<a id="viscosity-sus"></a>

Folder `viscosity-sus/` · Thermal and fluids · Convert kinematic viscosity between centistokes and Saybolt Universal Seconds (SUS, SSU) by ASTM D2161, with dynamic viscosity in centipoise.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The conversion is the ASTM D2161 equation for Saybolt Universal viscosity at 100 °F (37.8 °C), with its temperature correction for other test temperatures; it applies from 1.8 cSt (about 32 SUS) upward.
- Saybolt seconds are an obsolete empirical unit: the time 60 mL of oil takes to flow through a calibrated orifice. Modern specifications use mm²/s (cSt) measured to ASTM D445 or ISO 3104.
- Dynamic viscosity in centipoise is the kinematic viscosity times the density in g/cm³ at the same temperature.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 20.00 cSt gives 97.8 SUS at 100 °F and 98.5 SUS at 210 °F, and 50.0 cSt gives 233 and 234 SUS, as in ASTM D2161 Table 1; the equation coefficients were checked against the printed standard.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Above about 1 000 SUS, oils were usually measured in Saybolt Furol seconds (SFS), about one tenth of the SUS value.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Saybolt Universal Seconds: below about 32 SUS the Saybolt Universal scale does not apply.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 20.00 cSt is 97.8 SUS at 100 °F and 98.5 SUS at 210 °F
  - Source: ASTM D2161 Table 1 (row 20.00 mm²/s)
- 50.0 cSt is 233 SUS at 100 °F and 234 SUS at 210 °F
  - Source: ASTM D2161 Table 1 (row 50.0 mm²/s)
- Saybolt Furol at 122 °F: 103 cSt is 50.0 SFS and 203 cSt is 96.2 SFS
  - Source: ASTM D2161 eq. 7 and Table 3
- Above 75 cSt SUS approaches 4.632 × cSt (ASTM D2161 eq. 1, B = 4.632 at 100 °F); the inverse returns the input
  - Source: ASTM D2161 §5.2 and §5.4
- Dynamic viscosity 20 cSt × 0.870 g/cm³ = 17.4 cP; below 32 SUS and below 1.8 cSt are refused
  - Source: μ = ν ρ; ASTM D2161 §7.2 (32.0 s and above)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 97.82, 17.40 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASTM D2161-21, Standard Practice for Conversion of Kinematic Viscosity to Saybolt Universal Viscosity or to Saybolt Furol Viscosity, eqs. 1 and 2
- ASTM D445-24, Kinematic Viscosity of Transparent and Opaque Liquids (the modern measurement in mm²/s)

## Voltage divider

<a id="voltage-divider"></a>

Folder `voltage-divider/` · Electrical · Output voltage of a two-resistor divider, or the R2 for a target voltage with the nearest E24 or E96 value, plus current, power and the effect of a load.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The resistors are ideal and linear; their tolerance moves the real output by up to the sum of the two tolerances (about ±10 % of the ratio for 5 % parts in the worst case).
- With no load entered, nothing draws current from the output; a load in parallel with R2 lowers the output, which the loaded result shows.
- The input is an ideal voltage source with no internal resistance; for DC or for AC at frequencies where stray capacitance is negligible.
- A divider sets a voltage, not a supply: it cannot deliver power to a varying load without the output moving, so a regulator is the right part for powering a circuit.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 12 V to 3.3 V with R1 = 10 kΩ needs R2 = 3 793 Ω; the E24 value 3.9 kΩ gives 3.37 V and 0.863 mA, checked by hand.
- Design decision: the design mode picks the nearest standard value on a logarithmic scale and reports the output it actually gives, because the exact R2 is rarely a part you can buy.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The load is less than ten times R2, so it pulls the output down noticeably; buffer the output or lower both resistors.
- More than 10 mA flows through the divider: check the resistors\' power ratings, or use higher values.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Target output must be below the input voltage (… V is not below … V)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Equal resistors halve the input: 10 V across 10 kΩ + 10 kΩ gives 5 V, 0.5 mA and a 5 kΩ source resistance
  - Source: Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, §1.2.3: V_out = V_in R2 / (R1 + R2); §1.2.6: R_th = R1 ∥ R2
- Design 12 V to 3.3 V with R1 = 10 kΩ: exact R2 = 3 793 Ω; E24 gives 3.9 kΩ (3.37 V), E96 gives 3.83 kΩ (3.32 V)
  - Source: R2 = R1 V_out / (V_in − V_out); IEC 60063:2015 E24 and E96
- A 10 kΩ load on a 10 kΩ / 10 kΩ divider from 10 V drops the output from 5 V to 3.33 V, with a warning
  - Source: Loaded divider: R2 ∥ R_L = 5 kΩ, V_out = 10 × 5 / 15 (Hughes, ch. 3)
- Power: 24 V across 1 kΩ + 1 kΩ dissipates 144 mW in each resistor and warns at 12 mA
  - Source: P = I² R (Hughes, ch. 2)
- The ratio is independent of the input voltage, and a target at or above the input is rejected
  - Source: Divider ratio R2 / (R1 + R2); validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 3 793 Ω, 3.9 kΩ, 3.37 V, 0.863 mA to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Horowitz and Hill, The Art of Electronics, 3rd ed., §1.2.3 (voltage dividers), §1.2.6 (Thévenin equivalent)
- Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, 12th ed., ch. 3 (network theorems, potential divider)
- IEC 60063:2015 Preferred number series for resistors and capacitors (E24, E96)

## Water hammer (Joukowsky)

<a id="water-hammer"></a>

Folder `water-hammer/` · Thermal and fluids · Pressure surge from valve closure or pump trip: Korteweg wave speed with pipe elasticity, Joukowsky and Michaud surges, critical time, line pressure check.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Joukowsky (1898): an instantaneous change of velocity Δv in a liquid-filled pipe produces a pressure change Δp = ρ a Δv that travels at the wave speed a; "instantaneous" means the valve closes in less than the critical time 2L/a, the time for the wave to travel to the reservoir and back — any closure faster than that gives the full Joukowsky surge, however short.
- Wave speed by Korteweg: a = √(K/ρ) / √(1 + (K/E)(D/e) c₁) for a thin-walled pipe (D/e > 25), with the bulk modulus K of the liquid, Young's modulus E of the pipe wall and the restraint factor c₁ (1.0 with expansion joints, 1 − ν/2 anchored upstream, 1 − ν² anchored throughout, ν 0.3); entrained air lowers the wave speed drastically (1 % free air can halve it), which is not modelled.
- Slow closure (t_c > 2L/a): the surge is estimated by Michaud's formula Δp = 2 ρ L Δv/t_c, which assumes a linear velocity decay and is conservative for most valves; the real surge depends on the valve characteristic and needs a method-of-characteristics transient analysis for design.
- Line pressures: maximum = steady pressure + surge; minimum = steady pressure − surge; when the minimum falls below the vapour pressure the column separates and the subsequent collapse produces a second, often higher, surge not covered here; the pipe rating entered (e.g. PN class) is compared with the maximum pressure.
- Single straight pipe from a constant-head reservoir to the valve; friction, branches, surge vessels, air valves and pump inertia (for pump-trip events the velocity change equals the steady velocity and the check valve closure time governs) are outside the formula.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: fresh water in a 300 mm steel pipe with 8 mm wall → a = 1 481/√(1 + (2.19/207)(37.5)) = 1 254 m/s (the textbook 1 200–1 300 m/s for steel); stopping 2 m/s instantly gives 25.0 bar; a 200 m line has a critical time of 0.32 s, so a 1 s closure is "slow" and Michaud gives 8.0 bar — the upsurge (13 bar) is within PN16 at 5 bar steady, but the downsurge to −3 bar gauge separates the column, which the page flags; 5 s keeps the swing within 3.4–6.6 bar; an SDR 11 HDPE pipe of the same bore (27.3 mm wall) lowers the wave speed to 281 m/s and the Joukowsky surge to 5.6 bar (the same 8 mm wall in HDPE would give 154 m/s).
- Design decision: Michaud for slow closures because it is the standard first estimate and conservative; the page insists on a transient analysis for design where the result is close to the rating.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- D/e below 25: thick-walled pipe — the thin-wall Korteweg formula over-estimates the elasticity effect slightly (conservative on wave speed).
- Maximum pressure … bar exceeds the … bar rating: slow the closure, add a surge vessel or air valve, or re-rate the line.
- Minimum pressure below the vapour pressure: column separation — the cavity collapse can produce a surge above the Joukowsky value; a transient analysis is required.
- Minimum pressure below atmospheric (sub-atmospheric gauge): check for air ingress at vents and joints.
- Slow closure: the Michaud estimate assumes a linear velocity decay and is conservative for most valves; use a transient analysis for design where the margin is small.
- Rigid pipe: the wave speed is the liquid acoustic speed — the upper bound of the surge.
- Entrained air, friction, branches and pump inertia are not modelled: 1 % of free air can halve the wave speed; pump trips need the check-valve closure time as t_c.
- For design, confirm with a method-of-characteristics transient analysis (Wylie & Streeter), especially for long lines and column separation.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Wave speed: water √(2.19e9/998) = 1 481 m/s; 300 mm steel pipe with 8 mm wall → 1 481/√(1 + (2.19/207) × 37.5) = 1 254 m/s; rigid pipe gives the liquid value; HDPE (0.9 GPa) gives 154 m/s with the same 8 mm wall and 281 m/s as SDR 11 (27.3 mm wall)
  - Source: Korteweg formula (Wylie & Streeter eq. 1-24); textbook 1 200–1 300 m/s for water in steel
- Joukowsky: ρ a Δv = 998 × 1 254 × 2 = 25.0 bar; proportional to Δv (1 m/s → 12.5 bar); sea water (ρ 1 025, K 2.34) gives a slightly higher surge
  - Source: Joukowsky (1898) Δp = ρ a Δv
- Critical time and classification: 2L/a = 400/1 254 = 0.319 s; a 1 s closure is SLOW → Michaud 2 × 998 × 200 × 2/1 = 7.98 bar; a 0.2 s closure is RAPID → full 25.0 bar; period 4L/a = 0.638 s
  - Source: Critical time 2L/a (Chaudhry ch. 2); Michaud slow-closure estimate
- Line pressures and rating: 5 + 7.98 = 12.98 bar ≤ PN16 OK (81 %); rapid closure gives 30.0 bar → EXCEEDED and a negative minimum (−20 bar) → column separation warning; closure time for a 10 % surge = 2 ρ L Δv/(0.1 × 16 bar) = 4.99 s
  - Source: Pressure envelope; column separation criterion (Chaudhry ch. 9)
- Validation: zero closure time, zero diameter and an unknown material are rejected; thick-walled pipe (D/e < 25) is flagged
  - Source: Validation contract; thin-wall validity
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1 481 m/s, 0.32 s, 25.0 bar, 8.0 bar, 8.0 bar, 13.0 bar to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- N. Joukowsky, "Über den hydraulischen Stoss in Wasserleitungsröhren", 1898 (English: Simin, Proc. AWWA 1904)
- E. B. Wylie, V. L. Streeter, Fluid Transients in Systems, Prentice Hall 1993 — wave speed with pipe restraint (c₁), method of characteristics
- M. H. Chaudhry, Applied Hydraulic Transients, 3rd ed., Springer 2014 — Joukowsky, Michaud, column separation
- B. B. Sharp, D. B. Sharp, Water Hammer: Practical Solutions, Butterworth-Heinemann 1996 — closure times and surge protection

## Water heating time calculator (tank, element, gas or heat pump)

<a id="water-heating-time"></a>

Folder `water-heating-time/` · Thermal and fluids · Time to heat a water tank with an electric element, gas burner or heat pump, with standing loss, energy, cost and recovery rate in L/h or gal/h.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The tank is fully mixed: one water temperature throughout. A real tank stratifies, so hot water is available at the top well before the whole tank reaches the set point.
- Water has a density of 999 kg/m³ (8.34 lb per US gallon) and a specific heat of 4 186 J/(kg·K), i.e. 1 Btu/(lb·°F); both change by less than 2 % between 10 and 60 °C.
- Heat into the water is the input power times the efficiency (electric element 98 to 100 %, gas burner about 70 to 85 % recovery efficiency) or times the coefficient of performance for a heat pump. The COP is held constant, though it falls as the tank gets hotter.
- The standing loss is UA × (T − T_room) with a constant UA, so the temperature approaches T_room + P/UA exponentially. A tank losing S watts at 45 K above the room has UA = S / 45.
- The recovery rate is the volume heated through the given rise per hour with the full heater output, as manufacturers quote it; the standing loss is not deducted.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 50 US gal (189.1 kg) from 50 to 120 °F with a 4.5 kW element and UA = 2 W/K in a 68 °F room: 8.55 kWh into the water, 114.5 min, 8.59 kWh drawn, 1.29 at 0.15 per kWh; recovery 20.5 gal/h at 90 °F rise. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The target is at or above the highest temperature the heater can hold against the standing loss: it is never reached. Use a larger heater or insulate the tank.
- Heating takes more than two days: check the heater power and tank size.
- Above 65 °C most heat pumps cannot reach the temperature on their own and use a backup element; the COP also falls as the water gets hotter.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Target temperature: it must be above the starting temperature.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Recovery at 90 °F rise: 4.5 kW element 20.5 gal/h; 40 000 Btu/h gas at 76 % 40.5 gal/h
  - Source: Water heater recovery rule gph = Btu/h × η / (8.34 lb/gal × 1 Btu/(lb·°F) × ΔT) (ASHRAE HVAC Applications, Service Water Heating); hand calculation
- No standing loss: 50 US gal from 50 to 120 °F with 4.5 kW takes m c ΔT / P = 30.78 MJ / 4.5 kW = 114.0 min
  - Source: Q = m c ΔT; t = Q / P (hand calculation)
- With UA the exponential solution matches a step-by-step integration of m c dT/dt = P − UA (T − T_room)
  - Source: Lumped energy balance (Incropera Section 5.3) integrated numerically with 1 s steps
- A heat pump with COP 3 heats three times as fast and draws a third of the energy of the same electrical input as an element
  - Source: P_heat = COP × P_electric (hand calculation)
- A target above T_room + P/UA is never reached (null time and a warning); a target below the start is rejected
  - Source: Validation contract; equilibrium of the energy balance
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 8.55 kWh, 114.5 min, 8.59 kWh, 20.5, 77 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ASHRAE Handbook — HVAC Applications, chapter Service Water Heating (heater input, recovery efficiency and recovery rate)
- US DOE 10 CFR Part 430, Subpart B, Appendix E: uniform test method for water heaters (recovery efficiency, standby loss coefficient UA)
- F. P. Incropera et al., Fundamentals of Heat and Mass Transfer, 7th ed., Section 5.3 (energy balance of a lumped body with heat generation and convection)

## Water temperature and density correction

<a id="water-temperature-correction"></a>

Folder `water-temperature-correction/` · Maritime · ISO 15016 Annex E resistance and power correction for sea water temperature and density against the 15 °C / 1026 kg/m³ reference.

### Assumptions and caveats

- ISO 15016:2025 Annex E, transcribed term for term: R_AS = R_Tref (ρ_act/ρ_ref − 1) − R_Fact [(C_Fref + ΔC_Fref)/(C_Fact + ΔC_Fact) − 1], where the first term is the change of the whole resistance with density and the second the change of the frictional resistance with viscosity (through the Reynolds number in the ITTC-57 line and the roughness allowance E.7 with k_s default 150 µm); reference condition 15 °C and 1026.0 kg/m³ with ν_ref 1.1883e-6 m²/s.
- R_Tref is the total resistance at the reference condition: from the tank-predicted (or baseline) power and the propulsive efficiency as E.4, R_Tref = P η_D/V_S, or entered directly; ISO uses the tank-test power at the trial speed — in service analysis the baseline curve plays that role.
- Water density and viscosity come from the ITTC 7.5-02-01-03 table at the temperature and salinity entered (shared/seawater.js) rather than Annex E's own viscosity polynomial (E.8), which differs by 0.17 % at 15 °C and is second order inside the ratio; a measured density may be entered instead.
- Sign: R_AS is negative in water warmer (less dense, less viscous) than 15 °C — the ship had a hidden advantage — so the power correction ΔP_AS = R_AS V_S/η_D is negative and the corrected power P_ref = P_measured − ΔP_AS is HIGHER than measured in warm water; the opposite in cold water.
- The correction acts on speed through water (ISO clause 13) and assumes the propulsive efficiency is unaffected by the small resistance change; effect scale ±1 % of power over 5–30 °C for typical merchant ships.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: L_PP 180 m, S 5 500 m², 6.5 m/s, R_Tref 861.5 kN (8 000 kW, η_D 0.70) reproduces the atlas_physics production module to 1e-6: R_AS +2 683 N at 5 °C, −84 N at 15 °C (the harmless seam between the ITTC 15 °C density 1025.9 and the ISO reference 1026.0), −3 579 N at 25 °C and −5 413 N at 30 °C.
- Design decision: the ITTC table is used for both density and viscosity so that one consistent equation of state feeds both terms (E.8 gives viscosity only); a measured-density input is offered for trial reports that record it.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Temperature outside the 0–35 °C ITTC table: properties held at the table end.
- Frictional resistance exceeds the reference total resistance: check the wetted surface, the reference power or η_D.
- Correction above 3 % of the total resistance: unusual for sea water — check the temperature and density inputs.
- R_AS is negative in water warmer than 15 °C: the corrected (reference-condition) power is then higher than measured. Apply on speed through water.
- Propulsive efficiency assumed unaffected; the reference power should be the tank prediction (trials) or the performance baseline (service) at this speed.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Production pins (L_PP 180 m, S 5 500 m², 6.5 m/s, R_Tref 861.5 kN): R_AS = +2 683.0 N at 5 °C, −84.0 N at 15 °C, −3 578.9 N at 25 °C, −5 413.0 N at 30 °C
  - Source: atlas_physics.temperature_resistance.compute_ras_vectorized (ISO 15016:2025 Annex E), values computed 2026-10-31
- Term structure at 25 °C: density term R_Tref (1023.2/1026 − 1) = −2 351.1 N, friction term −1 227.8 N, sum = R_AS; R_AS = −0.415 % of R_Tref
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 E.1 decomposition
- Friction detail: ν 0.9425e-6 → Re_act 1.2414e9 against Re_ref 9.846e8; C_F + ΔC_F 1.6200e-3 actual vs 1.6303e-3 reference; R_Fact = ½ × 1023.2 × 5 500 × 6.5² × 1.6200e-3 = 192.6 kN
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 E.2, E.5–E.7; ITTC viscosity at 25 °C
- Power equivalent and sign: ΔP_AS = −3 578.9 × 6.5/0.7 = −33.2 kW at 25 °C (corrected power higher than measured); +24.9 kW at 5 °C; the sign note follows
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 clause 13 (corrections on speed through water); Annex E sign convention
- Resistance mode and measured density: entering R_Tref 861.538 kN reproduces the power mode; a measured density of 1023.2 at 25 °C equals the table result; salinity 38 makes the density term less negative
  - Source: E.4 equivalence; EOS haline slope
- Validation: zero wetted surface, η_D above 1 and an unknown reference mode are rejected; a 3 % correction is flagged
  - Source: Validation contract; plausibility warning
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces −3.58 kN, −33 kW to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

## Watts to amps

<a id="watts-to-amps"></a>

Folder `watts-to-amps/` · Electrical · Amps drawn by a load from its watts and the voltage, for DC, single-phase and three-phase circuits, with the power factor for AC loads.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The watts are the real power the load draws from the supply (its input power); for a motor the nameplate gives the shaft output, so divide by its efficiency first.
- For AC the current is the RMS value at the stated power factor; heaters, kettles and incandescent lamps are 1, motors 0.75 to 0.9, and electronic loads without power-factor correction can be 0.5 to 0.7.
- For three-phase the voltage is the line-to-line voltage and the load is balanced.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: a 1500 W kettle draws 6.52 A at 230 V and 12.5 A at 120 V; 3 kW three-phase at 400 V and unity power factor is 4.33 A per line. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- More than 1 kW at extra-low voltage draws a very large current; check the conductor size.
- More than 16 A single-phase is beyond an ordinary socket outlet in most countries; the load needs a dedicated circuit.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- A 1500 W kettle: 6.522 A at 230 V and 12.5 A at 120 V
  - Source: Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, ch. 2: I = P / V for a resistive load; IEC 60038 mains voltages
- DC: 60 W at 12 V is 5 A, and the power factor is ignored

## Wave properties and encounter period

<a id="wave-properties"></a>

Folder `wave-properties/` · Maritime · Linear wave theory: wavelength, celerity, group velocity, deep/shallow regime, orbital velocities and the encounter period for a ship speed and heading.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Linear (Airy) wave theory: small steepness, irrotational flow, flat impermeable bottom, no current; the dispersion relation ω² = g k tanh(kh) is solved numerically for the wavenumber, so no deep- or shallow-water approximation is made in the results — the regime labels follow the usual h/λ > 0.5 (deep) and h/λ < 0.05 (shallow) limits.
- A single regular wave of period T and height H represents the sea: for an irregular sea use the significant height and the peak or energy period, and read the orbital velocities as representative of the larger waves rather than extremes.
- Orbital velocities are the linear-theory amplitudes at the surface (z = 0) and at a chosen depth below the still-water level; near breaking and in very shallow water the crest velocities are larger than the linear value (Stokes/cnoidal effects).
- Breaking limit by the Miche criterion H_max/λ = 0.142 tanh(kh) (0.142 in deep water, approaching 0.88 h in shallow water); real breaking depends on bottom slope and wave irregularity.
- Energy flux per metre of crest P = ρ g H² c_g/8 for a regular wave; for an irregular sea with significant height H_s and energy period T_e in deep water the usual form is P ≈ ρ g² H_s² T_e/(64π) — half the regular-wave value for the same H and T.
- Encounter frequency from the linear kinematics ω_e = ω + k V cos α with α the angle between the ship's heading and the wave direction (0° head seas, 180° following); in deep water this is the exact form of the MSC.1/Circ.1228 approximation T_E = 3T²/(3T + V_kn cos α), and the two agree within about 1.5 %.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-30: T = 10 s deep water gives λ = 156.1 m, c = 15.6 m/s, c_g = 7.8 m/s (textbook λ = 1.56 T²); for h/λ₀ = 0.10 the solver gives h/λ = 0.1410 (kh 0.886) as in the Wiegel/CEM dispersion tables; the shallow limit c → √(gh) is reproduced within 1 %; head-sea encounter at 15 kn in 10 s waves is 6.69 s against 6.67 s from the circular's formula.
- Design decision: the dispersion relation is solved by Newton iteration from the Eckart/Fenton–McKee initial guess, so results are exact to machine precision in all depths.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Evaluation depth … m exceeds the water depth: velocity shown at the bottom (… m).
- Steepness above 1/20: second-order effects (sharper crests, flatter troughs) are noticeable; linear theory underestimates crest velocities.
- Shallow water: waves are non-dispersive and the linear profile is poor near breaking (cnoidal theory applies).
- Ship overtaking the waves (ω_e negative): the encounter period shown is the magnitude; the waves pass from ahead to astern relative to the ship.
- Ship running exactly with the waves: infinite encounter period (surf-riding regime).
- Deep-water assumption: for h/λ below 0.5 choose finite depth.
- Regular linear wave: for an irregular sea use H_s and the peak/energy period and treat the velocities as representative, not extreme.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Deep water, T = 10 s: λ₀ = g T²/2π = 156.1 m, c = 15.6 m/s, c_g = c/2 = 7.8 m/s, k = 0.0402 1/m; the 1.56 T² rule of thumb
  - Source: Dean & Dalrymple (1991) eq. 3.34; MSC.1/Circ.1228 λ = 1.56 T²
- Dispersion table: h/λ₀ = 0.10 (T 8 s, h 10.0 m) gives kh = 0.886, h/λ = 0.1410 and tanh(kh) = 0.709; wavelength 70.9 m instead of 99.9 m
  - Source: Wiegel (1964) Table A1 / USACE CEM Part II-1 Table II-1-1: d/L₀ 0.1000 → d/L 0.1410, tanh(kd) 0.7093 (kd tanh kd = 2π·0.1)
- Shallow limit: T 30 s in 1 m of water → c → √(gh) = 3.13 m/s within 1 %, c_g → c, regime shallow; Newton solver satisfies ω² = g k tanh(kh) to 1e-10
  - Source: Dean & Dalrymple (1991) §3.4 shallow-water asymptote; dispersion relation
- Wavelength input: λ = 156.13 m in deep water returns T = 10.00 s; in 30 m depth the same λ needs T = 10.63 s (shoaling lengthens the period for a given length)
  - Source: Inverse of the dispersion relation T = 2π/√(g k tanh kh)
- Orbital velocities (deep, H 3 m, T 10 s): surface amplitude π H/T = 0.942 m/s, at 10 m depth × e^(−k z) = 0.630 m/s, bottom 0; finite depth 30 m: bottom velocity a ω/sinh(kh) > 0
  - Source: Dean & Dalrymple (1991) eq. 4.14 horizontal velocity u = a ω cosh(k(h+z))/sinh(kh)
- Energy flux: H 3 m, T 10 s deep → ρ g H² c_g/8 = 1025·9.807·9·7.81/8 = 88.3 kW/m; equals ρ g² H² T/(32π) in deep water
  - Source: Holthuijsen (2007) §5.5; Dean & Dalrymple eq. 4.73 energy flux E c_g
- Breaking (Miche): deep water H_max = 0.142 λ = 22.2 m for λ 156 m (3 m wave stable); in 2 m depth with T 10 s the limit falls to ≈ 1.7 m so a 3 m wave is BREAKING
  - Source: Miche (1944) H/λ = 0.142 tanh(kh)
- Encounter period: 15 kn head seas in 10 s waves → T_e = 2π/(ω + k V) = 6.69 s vs 6.67 s by Circ.1228 (within 1.5 %); beam seas 10 s; following seas 19.8 s; overtaking waves flagged
  - Source: Linear kinematics ω_e = ω + k V cos α; MSC.1/Circ.1228 §1.6 approximation
- Invalid inputs fail fast: zero period, negative height, heading above 360°
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- In very deep finite water (kh far above 710) the orbital velocity equals the deep-water value instead of overflowing to NaN
  - Source: Range fuzzing (fuzz.js): cosh(k(h − z))/sinh(kh) evaluated as e^(−kz)(1 + e^(−2k(h−z)))/(1 − e^(−2kh))
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 156.1 m, 15.6 m/s, 7.8 m/s, 0.019, 22 m, 0.94 m/s, 0.63 m/s, 88 kW, 6.7 s, 6.67 s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources
