## Weir and flume flow calculator

<a id="weir-flow"></a>

Folder `weir-flow/` · Civil · Flow over rectangular (Francis), 90° V-notch and Cipolletti weirs and through Parshall flumes from the measured head, with USBR limits.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Free flow over a thin, sharp crest with an aerated nappe; the approach velocity is neglected, as in the Francis, Cone and Cipolletti equations. A submerged or clinging nappe gives more flow than calculated.
- The head is measured in still water at least four heads upstream of the crest; for a Parshall flume the upstream head H_a is read at the standard gauge point in the converging section.
- Contracted weirs and V-notches are fully contracted: crest height and side clearances of at least twice the maximum head. Suppressed weirs span the full channel width with ventilated nappes.
- Heads are limited to the ranges of the USBR Water Measurement Manual: at least 0.2 ft (61 mm) on weirs, at most L/3 on contracted and Cipolletti weirs, 1.25 ft on the V-notch, and the free-flow table range for each Parshall flume.
- Parshall flumes must be built to the standard dimensions; the free-flow equations apply while the submergence H_b/H_a stays below 0.5 (1 to 3 in), 0.6 (6 to 9 in) or 0.7 (1 to 8 ft). Accuracy is about ±5 % for weirs and ±3 to 5 % for flumes.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 2 ft contracted rectangular weir with 0.5 ft head carries 3.33 × 1.9 × 0.5^1.5 = 2.24 ft³/s (63.3 L/s); a 90° V-notch at 0.5 ft gives 0.446 ft³/s; a 1 ft Parshall flume at 1.00 ft gives 3.95 ft³/s, as in USBR Table A8-12. Checked by hand.
- Parshall coefficients and head ranges transcribed from USBR WMM Table 8-6 and the free-flow tables A8-7 to A8-12; the 2 to 8 ft flumes use the table formula Q = 4 W H_a^(1.522 W^0.026), which Table 8-6 rounds to two-decimal exponents.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Head more than half the crest height on a suppressed weir: the approach velocity is no longer negligible and the Francis formula underestimates the flow.
- Crest height less than twice the head: the weir is not fully contracted and the equation overestimates the contraction; raise the crest or use a calibrated rating.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Head: … ft is outside the free-flow range of the … Parshall flume, … to … ft (USBR tables)
- Downstream throat head: submergence H_b/H_a = … exceeds … for the … flume; the free-flow equation does not apply, use the USBR submerged-flow corrections
- Head: … ft is below the 0.2 ft (61 mm) minimum for sharp-crested weirs (USBR WMM chapter 7)
- Head: … ft exceeds the 1.25 ft (381 mm) limit of a fully contracted V-notch (USBR WMM chapter 7)
- Head: … ft exceeds one third of the crest length (… ft), the limit of the Cipolletti equation
- Head: … ft exceeds one third of the crest length (… ft), the limit for a contracted rectangular weir

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- USBR Parshall free-flow tables: 1 in at 0.50 ft 0.115, 3 in at 1.00 ft 0.992, 9 in at 1.50 ft 5.71, 1 ft at 1.00 ft 3.95, 4 ft at 0.50 ft 5.36, 8 ft at 2.50 ft 139 ft³/s
  - Source: USBR Water Measurement Manual, appendix tables A8-7, A8-9, A8-11 and A8-12 (free-flow discharge through Parshall flumes)
- Francis, 2 ft crest, 0.5 ft head: contracted 2.24 ft³/s (3.33 × 1.9 × 0.3536), suppressed 2.35 ft³/s
  - Source: Hand calculation of Q = 3.33 (L − 0.1 n H) H^1.5 (Brater and King, Handbook of Hydraulics)
- 90° V-notch: 0.2 ft gives 0.0460 ft³/s and 1.25 ft gives 4.33 ft³/s, the ends of the USBR range of about 0.05 to 4.25 ft³/s; 0.5 ft gives 0.446
  - Source: USBR WMM eq. 7-6 (Cone): Q = 2.49 H^2.48, used for 0.05 to 4.25 ft³/s
- Cipolletti, 3 ft crest at 0.6 ft head: Q = 3.367 × 3 × 0.6^1.5 = 4.69 ft³/s
  - Source: USBR WMM eq. 7-7: Q = 3.367 L H^1.5
- Limits: heads below 0.2 ft, above L/3 or above 1.25 ft on a V-notch, outside the flume table range, and a submerged flume are rejected; a low crest warns
  - Source: USBR WMM chapter 7 (weir limits) and chapter 8 (Parshall submergence 0.7 for 1 to 8 ft flumes)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.9 ft, 2.24 ft³/s, 63.3 L/s to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- US Bureau of Reclamation, Water Measurement Manual, 3rd ed. revised (2001), chapter 7: eq. 7-6 (90° V-notch, Cone) and eq. 7-7 (Cipolletti) with their limits
- US Bureau of Reclamation, Water Measurement Manual, chapter 8: eq. 8-3 and Table 8-6 (Parshall flume coefficients), submergence limits, and appendix tables A8-7 to A8-12
- E. F. Brater, H. W. King, J. E. Lindell and C. Y. Wei, Handbook of Hydraulics, 7th ed. (McGraw-Hill, 1996), sharp-crested weirs: Francis formula Q = 3.33 (L − 0.1 n H) H^1.5 for sharp-crested rectangular weirs

## Weld metal and filler consumption calculator

<a id="weld-deposition"></a>

Folder `weld-deposition/` · Manufacturing · Weld metal mass of fillet, single-V and double-V welds, filler needed for SMAW, GMAW, FCAW or SAW, electrodes or wire length and arc time.

### Assumptions and caveats

- Fillet welds have equal legs and a flat face (area z²/2); groove welds are symmetric, with the bevel measured as the included angle, a root gap and a root face; convexity and cap reinforcement are added as a percentage of the area.
- Deposition efficiency is the deposited weld metal divided by the filler consumed: 55 % for covered electrodes (stub ends, slag and spatter), 95 % for solid and metal-cored wire, 90 % for flux-cored wire and 100 % for SAW wire (Kobe Steel); the flux of SAW is extra.
- Wire length uses the density of the weld metal for a solid wire; flux-cored wire is lighter per metre, so it needs more length than shown.
- Arc time is the deposited mass divided by the deposition rate of the welding procedure; it excludes slag removal, positioning and other non-arc time.
- Steel weld metal is taken at 7 850 kg/m³; change the density for stainless steel or aluminium.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 10 mm single-V butt weld with a 60° included angle, 2 mm gap, 2 mm root face and 10 % reinforcement has 56.95 mm² of bevel and gap and 62.65 mm² in all; 1 m weighs 0.4918 kg, needs 0.5176 kg of GMAW wire (95 %), 58.3 m of 1.2 mm wire and 9.8 minutes of arc time at 3 kg/h. Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Flux-cored wire weighs less per metre than solid wire of the same diameter: order by mass, the length shown is a lower bound.
- A groove angle below 30° with a small gap is hard to fuse at the root; check the joint design.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Root face f: it cannot be larger than the plate thickness.
- Joint: the weld has no cross-section; give a gap, a bevel angle or a thinner root face.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Single V, 10 mm, 60°, gap 2, face 2: 20 + 64 tan 30° = 56.95 mm²; +10 % = 62.65 mm²; 0.4918 kg per metre; GMAW 95 % needs 0.5176 kg
  - Source: Kobe Steel ABC's of Arc Welding: C = (A1 + A2) × L × G / E / 10 (A in mm², L in m, G = 7.85 g/cm³, E in %)
- Wire and arc time: 0.5176 kg of 1.2 mm wire (8.878 g/m) is 58.3 m; 0.4918 kg at 3 kg/h is 9.84 min of arc
  - Source: Wire mass per length ρ π d²/4; arc time = deposit / deposition rate (hand calculation)
- Fillet: 1/4 in leg is 0.03125 in², 0.106 lb per foot of steel (0.2836 lb/in³); SMAW at 55 % with 0.03 kg rods needs 30 rods for 10 ft
  - Source: A = z²/2 (hand calculation); Kobe Steel E = 55 % for covered electrodes
- Double V needs half the bevel metal of a single V of the same plate; a square butt (0° angle) is gap × thickness; efficiencies 55/95/90/100 %
  - Source: Groove geometry (limiting cases); Kobe Steel efficiency list
- FCAW warns about wire length; a root face thicker than the plate and a joint with no cross-section are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 62.65 mm², 0.4918 kg, 0.5176 kg, 58.3 m, 9.8 min to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Kobe Steel, The ABC's of Arc Welding — How to calculate welding consumption: C = (A1 + A2) × L × G / E × 1/10, E = 55 % SMAW, 95 % GMAW, 90 % FCAW, 100 % SAW
- The Lincoln Electric Company, The Procedure Handbook of Arc Welding, 14th ed.: weld metal weight per foot from joint cross-sections

## Weld fatigue damage (DNV-RP-C203)

<a id="weld-fatigue"></a>

Folder `weld-fatigue/` · Structural · Miner damage and fatigue life of a welded detail from a stress-range histogram on the DNV-RP-C203 S-N curves, with thickness effect and DFF.

### Assumptions and caveats

- S-N curves of DNV-RP-C203 (October 2011), Tables 2-1 to 2-3: in air the curves are bilinear with the slope change at 10^7 cycles and m2 = 5 below it; in seawater with cathodic protection the slope changes at 10^6 cycles; for free corrosion the curves have one slope m = 3 for all cycles. Later editions of the RP revised some values (for example the reference thickness of tubular joints), so check the edition your project uses.
- Thickness effect, eq. (2.4.3): Δσ is multiplied by (t/t_ref)^k for t > t_ref, with t_ref = 25 mm for welded connections other than tubular joints and 32 mm for tubular joints in this edition; k from the tables, and for the T curve 0.25 when SCF ≤ 10 and 0.30 above. The SCF entered multiplies the stress ranges of the histogram.
- Linear damage accumulation (Palmgren–Miner, eq. 2.2.1): D = Σ n_i/N_i over the histogram period, scaled to the design life; the design criterion is D ≤ η = 1/DFF, with the design fatigue factor from DNV-OS-C101. The RP asks for at least 20 blocks when a long-term distribution is discretised.
- Screening (section 2.11): a detailed fatigue analysis may be omitted if the largest stress range is below the fatigue limit at 10^7 cycles (air and cathodic protection), reduced by DFF^−0.33.
- Mean stress, residual stress relief, post-weld improvement, low-cycle fatigue and the high-strength-steel base material curve are not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: the curve coefficients were read from the DNV-RP-C203 October 2011 PDF; the fatigue limits at 10^7 cycles follow from log a2 (D: 10^((15.606 − 7)/5) = 52.63 MPa, as tabulated) and the two segments meet at the slope change.
- Design decision: the equivalent stress range is defined on the same bilinear curve, as the constant range that gives the same damage in the same total number of cycles.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- The damage over the design life, …, exceeds the allowable 1/DFF = ….
- The largest stress range, … MPa, is below the reduced fatigue limit of … MPa: a detailed fatigue analysis may be omitted (DNV-RP-C203 2.11).
- The histogram has … blocks; DNV-RP-C203 asks for at least 20 when a long-term distribution is discretised.
- For the T curve the thickness exponent depends on the joint SCF: enter nominal stress ranges with the hot-spot SCF.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Histogram line …: expected "stress range; cycles" as two numbers
- Histogram line …: stress range and cycles must not be negative
- The histogram needs at least one block

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Curve D in air: 10^(12.164 − 3 log 100) = 1.459 × 10^6 cycles at 100 MPa; below the slope change 10^(15.606 − 5 log 40) = 3.94 × 10^7 at 40 MPa
  - Source: DNV-RP-C203 (2011) Table 2-1, eq. (2.4.1)
- Fatigue limits at 10^7 cycles from log a2 agree with Table 2-1: D 52.63, F 41.52, W3 21.05 MPa
  - Source: DNV-RP-C203 (2011) Table 2-1, fatigue limit column
- Seawater with cathodic protection: the slope changes at 10^6 cycles and D gives 2.51 times fewer cycles than in air at 100 MPa
  - Source: DNV-RP-C203 (2011) Table 2-2 (log a1 = 11.764 for D)
- Free corrosion: one slope m = 3 for all cycles; D at 40 MPa gives 10^(11.687 − 3 log 40) = 7.6 × 10^6 cycles
  - Source: DNV-RP-C203 (2011) Table 2-3
- Thickness effect: 50 mm with k = 0.20 multiplies the stress ranges by 2^0.2 = 1.149, thinner plates get no credit, and the T curve uses k = 0.30 when SCF > 10
  - Source: DNV-RP-C203 (2011) eq. (2.4.3), Tables 2-1 to 2-3
- Default one-year histogram on curve D in air: Miner sum 0.01666, fatigue life 60.0 years, utilisation 0.666 over 20 years with DFF 2
  - Source: Palmgren–Miner, DNV-RP-C203 (2011) eq. (2.2.1) with η = 1/DFF
- A single block is its own equivalent range, and ranges below 52.63 × 2^−0.33 = 41.87 MPa pass the screening of section 2.11
  - Source: DNV-RP-C203 (2011) 2.11; equivalent range on the same curve
- Invalid inputs are rejected: a histogram line with one number, a negative range, an unknown curve
  - Source: Input validation
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 0.0167, 0.333 to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- DNV, DNV-RP-C203 Fatigue design of offshore steel structures, October 2011 — 2.2, 2.4.1–2.4.9, Tables 2-1 to 2-3, 2.11
- DNV-OS-C101 Design of offshore steel structures, section 6 — design fatigue factors

## Wind load calculator (Eurocode and ASCE 7)

<a id="wind-load"></a>

Folder `wind-load/` · Structural · Wind pressure at any height by EN 1991-1-4 (peak velocity pressure) or ASCE 7-16 (velocity pressure q_z), and the wind force on an area.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The basic wind speed comes from the national annex map (EN, 10-minute mean at 10 m in open country) or the ASCE 7 map for the risk category (3-second gust at 33 ft, exposure C); the calculator does not look it up.
- EN: orography factor c_o = 1, turbulence factor k_I = 1, directional and seasonal factors 1, air density 1.25 kg/m³ (EN 1991-1-4 recommended values; national annexes may change them).
- ASCE: K_z from the power law of Table 26.10-1 notes with α and z_g of Table 26.11-1; K_d = 0.85 for buildings; K_e = 1 at sea level (Table 26.9-1 gives lower values at altitude). ASCE 7-22 revised α and z_g slightly.
- The force uses one coefficient for the whole area (a force coefficient c_f, or a net pressure coefficient); real design applies zone-by-zone external and internal pressure coefficients and, for ASCE, the gust-effect factor G (0.85 for rigid buildings) inside the coefficient.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: EN, v_b = 27 m/s, terrain II, z = 10 m: c_e = 2.35, q_p = 1.07 kPa; ASCE, V = 115 mph, exposure C, z = 30 ft: K_z = 0.98, q_z = 28.3 psf. Both match the code tables (EN Fig. 4.2; ASCE Table 26.10-1). Checked by hand.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- EN 1991-1-4 covers heights up to 200 m.
- Below z_min = … m the pressure is taken at z_min.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- EN: v_b 27 m/s, terrain II, z 10 m: c_r = 1.007, I_v = 0.189, c_e = 2.35, q_p = 1.07 kPa
  - Source: EN 1991-1-4 eqs. (4.4), (4.7), (4.8); Fig. 4.2 (c_e ≈ 2.35 at 10 m, category II)
- EN exposure factor at 10 m falls from about 3.0 (sea) to 1.2 (city), as on Fig. 4.2; below z_min the value at z_min is used
  - Source: EN 1991-1-4 Fig. 4.2 and Table 4.1
- ASCE 7-16 K_z: B 30 ft 0.70, C 15 ft 0.85, C 33 ft 1.00, D 30 ft 1.16, B 100 ft 0.99
  - Source: ASCE 7-16 Table 26.10-1
- ASCE: V 115 mph, exposure C, 30 ft, K_d 0.85: q_z = 0.00256 × 0.982 × 0.85 × 115² = 28.27 psf
  - Source: ASCE 7-16 eq. 26.10-1
- Force on a 20 m² sign with c_f 1.8 at 1.07 kPa is 38.6 kN; bad inputs are rejected
  - Source: F = q_p c_f A (EN 1991-1-4 eq. 5.3 with c_s c_d = 1)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.07 kPa, 2.35 to the digits printed

### Sources

- ASCE/SEI 7-16, Chapter 26: eq. 26.10-1, Tables 26.6-1 (K_d), 26.9-1 (K_e), 26.10-1 and 26.11-1 (K_z, α, z_g)

## Wind resistance (ISO 15016)

<a id="wind-resistance"></a>

Folder `wind-resistance/` · Maritime · Added wind resistance and power from the relative wind by ISO 15016:2025 Annex C with the Fujiwara coefficients or wind-tunnel data.

### Assumptions and caveats

- ISO 15016:2025 formula C.1: the resistance increase is the wind force at the relative wind minus the still-air resistance at the ship's own speed over ground, which is already contained in the calm-water baseline; both use the transverse projected area A_XV and the relative wind at the 10 m reference height (convert anemometer readings with the true-wind calculator, formulas C.3–C.11).
- C_AA from the Fujiwara et al. regression of ISO 15016:2025 C.3.5 (formulas C.12–C.18, Table C.19 constants) for the hull and superstructure geometry, with C.19 at exactly 90° (the mean of 80° and 100°, which makes the value at exactly 90° stand apart from its neighbours); positive C_AA is resistance, negative is assistance. When wind-tunnel or database coefficients for the ship type are available (Annex C.3.2–C.3.4) they take precedence and can be entered directly.
- Air density from formula C.2, ρ_A = p_A/(2.8705 (t_A + 273.15)) with p_A in hPa (1.225 kg/m³ at 1013.25 hPa and 15 °C).
- The added power uses the speed over ground and a quasi-propulsive efficiency, P = R_AA V_G/η_D, as the ISO 19030-2 Annex G wind correction does; directions are relative to the bow, 0° head wind and positive from starboard, and the coefficient is symmetric port–starboard.
- Steady wind only: gusts, the drift angle and rudder angle the wind induces, and the extra resistance of a yawed hull are not included.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-10-31: the coefficients reproduce the production atlas_physics.fujiwara_wind implementation to 1e-12 for two ship geometries at head, bow, beam, quartering and following angles (pinned values in the tests); the air density is 1.2250 kg/m³ at 1013.25 hPa and 15 °C.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- Exactly 90°: ISO 15016 formula C.19 replaces C_AA by the mean of 80° and 100°, which differs from the values just either side of 90°; check a few degrees off the beam too.
- Negative R_AA: the wind assists the ship (following wind stronger than the ship\'s own wind).
- Strong wind well off the bow: the drift and rudder angles it causes add resistance that this formula does not include.
- Use the relative wind at the 10 m reference height (ISO 15016 C.9–C.11); anemometer readings are disturbed by the superstructure.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- A_OD must not be negative

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- Pinned to production, ship A (200 m × 32 m): C_AA 0.76884 at 0°, 0.95105 at 30°, 0.62042 at 60°, 0.31477 at exactly 90°, 0.66351 at 120°, −0.20705 at 150°, −0.27906 at 180°; 330° equals 30°
  - Source: atlas_physics.fujiwara_wind.calculate_fujiwara_wind_coefficient (ISO 15016:2025 C.12–C.19, Table C.19), evaluated 2026-10-31
- Pinned to production, ship B (300 m × 48 m, centre of A_LV 20 m aft): C_AA 0.86568 at 0°, 0.67193 at 45°, −0.57883 at 135°; −45° equals 45°
  - Source: atlas_physics.fujiwara_wind.calculate_fujiwara_wind_coefficient, evaluated 2026-10-31
- Air density by formula C.2: 1013.25 hPa and 15 °C give 1.2250 kg/m³; 1030 hPa and −5 °C give 1.3374 kg/m³
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 formula C.2, ρ_A = p_A/(2.8705 (t_A + 273.15))
- Formula C.1 with given coefficients: C_AA(ψ) 0.9, C_AA(0) 0.8, A_XV 600 m², 30 kn relative wind, 14 kn over the ground: R_AA = ½ρA(0.9 V_WR² − 0.8 V_G²); power R_AA V_G/0.7
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 formula C.1; ISO 19030-2 Annex G power conversion
- No true wind: a relative wind equal to the speed over ground from dead ahead gives R_AA = 0 — the still-air resistance is already in the calm-water baseline
  - Source: ISO 15016:2025 formula C.1 (second term)
- Invalid inputs fail fast: negative wind speed, zero A_XV, an unknown coefficient source, η_D out of range
  - Source: Validation contract (README, "Conventions")
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 1.225 kg/m³, 0.943, 0.769, 82.6 kN, 14.7 kN, 67.9 kN, 699 kW to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- ISO 15016:2025 Ships and marine technology — Guidelines for the assessment of speed and power performance by analysis of speed trial data, Annex C (C.1, C.2, C.3.5 formulas C.12–C.19, Table C.19)
- T. Fujiwara, M. Ueno, Y. Ikeda, "Cruising performance of a large passenger ship in heavy sea", Proc. ISOPE 2006 — the wind load regression
- ISO 19030-2:2016 Ships and marine technology — Measurement of changes in hull and propeller performance, Annex G (wind resistance correction)
- atlas-back atlas_physics/fujiwara_wind.py — production implementation this calculator is pinned to

## Wind turbine power calculator

<a id="wind-turbine-power"></a>

Folder `wind-turbine-power/` · Electrical · Wind turbine power from rotor diameter, wind speed, air density and power coefficient (Betz limit), and yearly energy from the mean wind speed by Rayleigh.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The power is ½ ρ A v³ Cp: the kinetic energy flux through the swept area times the power coefficient. No turbine can exceed the Betz limit Cp = 16/27 = 0.593; small turbines reach about 0.25 to 0.35 from wind to electricity, large ones about 0.45 at their best.
- Air density comes from the ISO 2533 standard atmosphere at the hub altitude, optionally with the actual air temperature at the standard pressure of that altitude; humidity is neglected (it lowers the density by under 1 %).
- The yearly energy uses an idealised power curve: zero below the cut-in speed, P = ½ ρ A v³ Cp with a constant Cp up to the rated speed, the rated power up to the cut-out speed, and zero above it. A real power curve from the manufacturer gives a better estimate.
- Wind speeds follow a Rayleigh distribution (Weibull with k = 2) about the mean speed at hub height, as in the IEC 61400-12-1 annual energy estimate; sites with steadier or gustier winds have other shape factors. The mean speed must be at hub height: wind speed rises with height above the ground.
- Availability, wake and electrical losses beyond those in Cp are not deducted; the year has 8 760 hours.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: a 3 m rotor sweeps 7.07 m²; at 6 m/s, 1.225 kg/m³ and Cp 0.35 it gives 327 W, rated 2 017 W at 11 m/s; with a 5 m/s Rayleigh mean, cut-in 3 and cut-out 25 m/s the mean power is 338 W, 2 962 kWh a year, capacity factor 16.8 %. The Rayleigh integral was checked against (6/π) v̄³ and the ISA density against 1.1117 kg/m³ at 1 000 m.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A mean wind speed below about 4 m/s at hub height gives little energy; check the site with measurements before buying a turbine.
- Capacity factors above 50 % are rare even offshore; check the value.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Power coefficient: no turbine can exceed the Betz limit 16/27 = 0.593.
- Cut-in speed: it must be below the rated wind speed.
- Cut-out speed: it must be at or above the rated wind speed.

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 3 m rotor at 6 m/s, 1.225 kg/m³, Cp 0.35: A = 7.069 m², 327.3 W; rated 2 017 W at 11 m/s
  - Source: Hand calculation: P = ½ ρ A v³ Cp
- Wind power density at 10 m/s and 1.225 kg/m³ is 612.5 W/m²; the Betz limit is 16/27 of it, 363.0 W/m²
  - Source: Manwell, McGowan and Rogers, Wind Energy Explained, 2nd ed., ch. 2 (P/A = ½ ρ v³) and ch. 3 (Cp,max = 16/27)
- ISO 2533 standard atmosphere: 1.2250 kg/m³ at sea level, 1.1117 at 1 000 m, 1.0066 at 2 000 m
  - Source: ISO 2533:1975 Standard Atmosphere, tabulated density
- Rayleigh: the mean of v³ is (6/π) v̄³ (energy pattern factor 1.91); P(v > v̄) = exp(−π/4) = 0.456
  - Source: Manwell, McGowan and Rogers, Wind Energy Explained, 2nd ed., ch. 2 (Rayleigh distribution)
- Default turbine on a 5 m/s Rayleigh site: 338 W mean, 2 962 kWh a year, capacity factor 16.8 %, running 75.4 % of the year
  - Source: Numerical integration of the idealised power curve (Simpson, checked against the analytical moment above)
- Capacity factor mode: energy = rated power × CF × 8 760 h
  - Source: Definition of the capacity factor
- A power coefficient above the Betz limit, a cut-in at or above the rated speed and a cut-out below it are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract (Betz limit 16/27)
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 7.07 m², 327 W, 2 017 W, 338 W, 2 962 kWh, 16.8 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- Manwell, McGowan and Rogers, Wind Energy Explained: Theory, Design and Application, 2nd ed., Wiley 2009: ch. 2 (wind power density, Rayleigh distribution) and ch. 3 (Betz limit 16/27)
- IEC 61400-12-1:2017 Wind energy generation systems — Power performance measurements of electricity producing wind turbines (annual energy production from a power curve and a Rayleigh wind speed distribution)
- ISO 2533:1975 Standard Atmosphere (ρ0 = 1.225 kg/m³, lapse rate 6.5 K/km)

## Wire rope and chain safe working load calculator

<a id="wire-rope-swl"></a>

Folder `wire-rope-swl/` · Maritime · Wire rope breaking load (EN 12385-4) and safe working load with EN 13414 or ILO safety factors, and Grade 80 or 100 chain working load limits.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The minimum breaking force of stranded rope is K d² R_r / 1000 kN by EN 12385-4, with K = 0.330 for fibre core and 0.356 for steel core ropes of the 6×19 and 6×36 classes, d the nominal diameter in mm and R_r the rope grade in N/mm². A manufacturer's certificate overrides it.
- The termination efficiency covers the strength lost at the end fitting or over a sheave or pin: about 0.9 for a ferrule-secured eye (EN 13414-1) and lower for wedge sockets or bulldog grips. Bending a rope over a pin smaller than about 25 rope diameters cuts its strength further; use the maker's D/d curve.
- The ILO coefficients (ILO Convention 152, certificate form 4) are 10⁴ / (8.85 SWL + 1 910) with SWL in tonnes: about 5 for small loads, falling to 3 at 160 t. Slings use 5 up to 10 t. National rules and class may set other values.
- Chain working load limits are for a single leg in a straight pull at normal temperature, from the EN 818-4 table for metric Grade 8 and from the NACM tables for US Grade 80 and Grade 100 chain. Their minimum breaking force is at least four times the WLL.
- Sling angle, hitch type, dynamic loads and wear are not included: use the lifting sling calculator for multi-leg slings and reduce for worn, kinked or corroded rope or chain.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-08: 20 mm 6×36 IWRC rope of grade 1770 has MBL 0.356 × 20² × 1 770 / 1 000 = 252.0 kN (PFEIFER 6x36WS-WC table: 252 kN); with a ferrule-secured eye (0.9) and factor 5 the SWL is 45.4 kN or 4.63 t. Checked by hand.
- Verification 2026-11-08: the ILO coefficient is continuous: 10⁴ / (8.85 × 10 + 1 910) = 5.00 at 10 t and 10⁴ / (8.85 × 160 + 1 910) = 3.01 at 160 t.
- Design decision: the D/d bending reduction is left to an efficiency input because published efficiency curves differ between rope makers.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- A coefficient of utilisation below 3 is lower than any lifting standard allows for wire rope.
- The load exceeds the safe working load: do not lift.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- Chain size: … is not a size of ….

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- EN 12385-4 against PFEIFER tables: 6×36 IWRC 1770 at 8, 20 and 32 mm = 40.3, 252 and 645 kN; 1960 at 20 mm = 279 kN
  - Source: PFEIFER data sheet 6x36WS-WC (rev. 10/2020), according to EN 12385-4
- Fibre core K = 0.330: 6×36 FC 1770 at 20 mm = 234 kN and 1960 at 10 mm = 64.7 kN; 6×19 FC 1770 at 6 mm = 21 kN
  - Source: PFEIFER data sheets 6x36WS-FC (rev. 5/2019) and 6x19S-FC, according to EN 12385-4
- SWL of 20 mm 6×36 IWRC 1770 with a ferrule eye (0.9) and factor 5: 226.8 / 5 = 45.4 kN = 4.63 t
  - Source: EN 13414-1 (coefficient 5, ferrule-secured termination 0.9); hand calculation
- ILO C152: the coefficient is 10⁴/(8.85 SWL + 1910): 5.00 at 10 t, 3.01 at 160 t, 3 above; a sling uses 5 up to 10 t
  - Source: ILO C152 register form No. 4 instructions (OSHA 29 CFR 1918 Appendix I)
- Chain tables: Grade 8 13 mm 5.3 t; Grade 80 1/2 in 12 000 lb; Grade 100 3/8 in 8 800 lb; breaking force 4 × WLL
  - Source: EN 818-4 (Brindley LINX-8 table); OSHA 29 CFR 1918 App. II Table 4A (NACM Grade 80); NACM / ASTM A973 Grade 100 (1st Chain Supply data)
- Overload warns; a diameter of 1 mm and a size that the grade does not have are rejected
  - Source: Validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 252.0 kN, 226.8 kN, 45.4 kN, 4.63 t to the digits printed

- EN 12385-4:2002+A1:2008 Steel wire ropes — Safety — Part 4: Stranded ropes for general lifting applications, Table B.1 (minimum breaking force factors); PFEIFER data sheets 6x36WS-WC and 6x36WS-FC (2019–2020)

## Wire size calculator (AWG and mm²)

<a id="wire-size"></a>

Folder `wire-size/` · Electrical · Smallest AWG and metric wire size that keeps the voltage drop within your limit for a DC, single-phase or three-phase circuit, with the drop and the loss.

### Assumptions and caveats

- The wire is sized for voltage drop only. Its ampacity must also be checked against the wiring code for the insulation and installation (NEC Table 310.16 and 240.4(D), IEC 60364-5-52), and the larger of the two sizes used.
- Resistance is ρ/A at the conductor temperature with the ASTM B8 increment of 2 % for stranded wire; 75 °C matches the NEC Chapter 9 Table 8 basis. Reactance is neglected, which is conservative for conductors up to about 1/0 AWG (50 mm²); for large feeders use the cable sizing calculator.
- The length is the one-way route length from the supply to the load; the formula adds the return conductor (factor 2) or the three-phase factor √3.
- The percentage is referred to the supply voltage: DC voltage, phase-to-neutral or line-to-line for single-phase, line-to-line for three-phase.
- The drop limit is the designer's choice: the NEC informational notes suggest 3 % for a branch circuit and 5 % for feeder plus branch; IEC 60364-5-52 Annex G suggests 3 % for lighting and 5 % for other uses; 12 V DC systems often use 3 %.

### Notes (verification findings, design decisions, provenance)

- Verification 2026-11-07: 20 A at 120 V over 100 ft with a 3 % limit needs 7.24 mm², so 8 AWG copper (2.60 % drop) or 10 mm² metric; checked by hand from ρ = 2.0968 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 75 °C.

### Runtime warnings the calculator can raise

- No size up to 4/0 AWG meets the limit: use kcmil conductors, parallel runs or a higher voltage, and check reactance with the cable sizing calculator.
- No metric size up to 1000 mm² meets the limit: use parallel conductors.
- For conductors above about 25 mm² (4 AWG) the reactance adds to the AC drop at a power factor below 1; check with the cable sizing calculator.
- A drop above 5 % exceeds the usual NEC and IEC recommendations for AC circuits.

### Validation errors (in addition to the shared finite / positive / range checks)

- (only the shared validate.js checks)

### Checks (self-tests in tests.js, with the reference for each expected value)

- 20 A at 120 V over 100 ft with 3 %: 7.24 mm² needed, 8 AWG at 2.60 % (3.12 V), 10 mm² metric at 2.17 %
  - Source: ΔV = 2 I L R′ with R′ = ρ(75 °C) × 1.02 / A, ρ(75 °C) = 1.7241 × 10⁻⁸ × (1 + 0.00393 × 55) Ω·m (NEC Chapter 9 Table 8 basis)
- Cross-check with the NEC table: 12 AWG stranded copper (1.98 Ω/1000 ft) on 20 A over 50 ft drops 3.96 V
  - Source: NFPA 70 (2023) Chapter 9 Table 8: 12 AWG stranded uncoated copper 1.98 Ω/kft at 75 °C; ΔV = 2 × 20 × 50 × 1.98 / 1000
- Three-phase 100 A at 480 V over 200 ft with 3 %: 15.68 mm², 4 AWG from common sizes or 5 AWG from every gauge, 16 mm² metric
  - Source: ΔV = √3 I L R′ for a balanced three-phase circuit (line-to-line drop)
- DC needs the same area as single-phase; aluminium needs 1.639 times the copper area; solid wire 1/1.02 of stranded
  - Source: Factor 2 for DC and single-phase; resistivities 2.8264 and 1.7241 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m; ASTM B8 2 % increment
- 400 A at 400 V over 200 m needs more than 4/0: the AWG outputs are empty and a warning names the remedy; bad inputs are rejected
  - Source: Behaviour specification; validation contract
- Worked example of the article: the calculator reproduces 7.24 mm², 2.60 %, 3.12 V, 2.17 % to the digits printed
  - Source: content.md, Worked example (the numbers as printed there)

### Sources

- NFPA 70, National Electrical Code (2023): 210.19(A) Informational Note No. 4 and 215.2(A)(1) Informational Note No. 2 (3 % and 5 % drop); Chapter 9 Table 8 (resistance basis at 75 °C)
- IEC 60364-5-52:2009 Annex G (voltage drop in consumers' installations)
- ASTM B258-18 (AWG sizes) and ASTM B8-23 (stranding increment); IEC 60228:2004 (metric sizes)

## Shared modules

<a id="shared-modules"></a>

Modules under `shared/` used by several calculators: water properties, friction line and roughness allowance, statistics, formulas in number fields, and the tools panel below every calculator.

### Sea water properties and friction line (shared/seawater.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- Density and kinematic viscosity come from the ITTC Recommended Procedure 7.5-02-01-03 table for standard sea water of 35 g/kg salinity, interpolated linearly in temperature between 0 and 35 °C and held at the end values outside that range; a salinity other than 35 g/kg is applied as a linear slope (+0.77 kg/m³ and +0.13 % viscosity per g/kg, valid for oceanic salinities 30–41 g/kg).
- The ITTC-1957 friction line C_F = 0.075/(log₁₀Re − 2)² is the model-ship correlation line, not a physical flat-plate law; it is what ISO 15016, ISO 19030 and the ITTC-78 method prescribe.
- The hull roughness allowance is the Townsin form adopted by ISO 15016:2025 (E.7, G.8), ΔC_F = 0.044[(k_s/L)^(1/3) − 10 Re^(−1/3)] + 0.000125 clamped at zero, with the 1978 ITTC form [105 (k_s/L)^(1/3) − 0.64]·10⁻³ as the legacy option; k_s is the equivalent sand roughness (≈ the 50 mm-cut-off hull roughness Rt50), default 150 µm for a new coating.

#### Notes

- Verification 2026-10-31: the table and slopes reproduce the atlas_physics production module (ρ 1023.2 kg/m³ and ν 0.9425e-6 m²/s at 25 °C; ΔC_F 9.677e-5 for 150 µm, L 180 m, Re 9.846e8).
- ISO 15016:2025 Annex E also offers a viscosity polynomial (E.8); at 15 °C it differs from the ITTC table by 0.17 %, second order for every use here, so one table is kept for both density and viscosity.

#### Sources

- ITTC Recommended Procedures and Guidelines 7.5-02-01-03, Fresh Water and Seawater Properties (2011)
- ISO 15016:2025 Ships and marine technology — Guidelines for the assessment of speed and power performance by analysis of speed trial data, Annex E (E.5–E.8) and Annex G (G.6–G.8)
- ITTC 7.5-02-03-01.4, 1978 ITTC Performance Prediction Method (roughness allowance); Townsin R.L., "The ITTC line — its genesis and correlation allowance", The Naval Architect, 1985

### Statistics (shared/stats.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- Special functions: log-gamma by the Lanczos approximation (g = 7, 9 coefficients, relative error about 1e-15); regularised incomplete gamma by series / continued fraction and regularised incomplete beta by the modified Lentz continued fraction (Numerical Recipes 6.2–6.4), iterated to 1e-15.
- Standard normal CDF from the incomplete gamma function (accurate in both tails); quantile by Acklam's rational approximation refined with one Halley step (absolute error below 1e-9); Student t CDF from the incomplete beta function and its quantile by bracketing and bisection to 1e-14, falling back to the normal distribution above 1e7 degrees of freedom.
- Descriptive statistics: sample variance with n − 1, skewness G1 and excess kurtosis G2 with the small-sample corrections used by Excel SKEW/KURT (Joanes & Gill 1998), quantiles by linear interpolation between order statistics (Hyndman–Fan type 7, the Excel PERCENTILE.INC / NumPy default).
- Least-squares line with the slope's standard error, t statistic and two-sided p-value on n − 2 degrees of freedom; Grubbs' single-outlier critical value G = ((n − 1)/√n) √(t²/(n − 2 + t²)) with t at the two-sided level α/(2n) (ISO 5725-2).
- Monte Carlo sampling uses a seeded mulberry32 generator (reproducible runs, not cryptographic) with Box–Muller normal deviates.

#### Notes

- Verification 2026-10-31: Student t quantiles reproduce the table to 1e-8 (12.706 205, 3.182 446, 2.776 445, 2.364 624, 2.262 157, 2.045 230, 3.169 273, 6.313 752), GUM Table G.2 coverage factors to ±0.005 (13.97 … 2.025), Grubbs 2.290/2.482 for n = 10, and Excel SKEW 0.818 488 / KURT 0.940 625 for 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9.

#### Sources

- M. Abramowitz, I. A. Stegun, Handbook of Mathematical Functions, NBS 1964 — 6.1, 26.2, 26.5, 26.7
- W. H. Press et al., Numerical Recipes, 3rd ed., Cambridge 2007 — 6.1 (gamma), 6.2 (incomplete gamma), 6.4 (incomplete beta, Student t)
- P. J. Acklam, "An algorithm for computing the inverse normal cumulative distribution function" (2003)
- JCGM 100:2008 (GUM) Annex G Table G.2; ISO 5725-2:2019 Table 5 (Grubbs); D. N. Joanes, C. A. Gill, "Comparing measures of sample skewness and kurtosis", The Statistician 47, 1998; R. J. Hyndman, Y. Fan, "Sample quantiles in statistical packages", Am. Stat. 50, 1996

### Formulas in number fields (shared/expression.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- A number field accepts a formula: numbers (1.5, 1e-3), + − × ÷ and ^ (also * / ** and the Unicode signs), parentheses, the constant pi and the functions sqrt, abs, ln, log10, exp, min and max. A small recursive-descent parser evaluates it (never eval), and the result must be a finite number.
- Precedence is the mathematical one: ^ before × and ÷, × and ÷ before + and −, ^ right-associative (2^3^2 = 512), and a leading sign applies to the whole power (−2^2 = −4, as in Python; a spreadsheet gives +4). A decimal comma is rejected with a message rather than guessed.
- The calculator, the share link, scenarios, the batch template and the record receive the number, not the formula: a link or record restores the value (10 significant digits), and switching the unit of a field replaces the formula by the converted number.

#### Notes

- Number fields are text fields (inputmode decimal, or numeric for whole numbers) so that a formula can be typed; the arrow keys still step a plain number by 1 (Shift: 10). The tools read their own fields the same way, and a ± that is not a number or formula is reported instead of skipped.
- Verification 2026-10-31: 2 tests in shared/tests.js (precedence, signs, right-associative power, functions, Unicode operators; empty input, division by zero, unknown names, incomplete and unbalanced formulas, a decimal comma and stray characters rejected) and a browser check on shaft-torque: 1500/60 gives the same results as 25 with "= 25 rpm" under the field, an out-of-range formula shows its value next to the limit, the link carries 110 for 2*55, a unit switch turns 4*2000 kW into 8000000 W, and the sweep, goal-seek and ± fields accept formulas (goal seek for 1000/2 kN·m gives 4 712.4 kW = 500 kN·m × 2π × 1.5 s⁻¹).

#### Sources

- The Python Language Reference, 6.5 The power operator (binds more tightly than a unary operator on its left, less tightly than one on its right: the convention followed here)
- Microsoft Support, Calculation operators and precedence in Excel (negation before exponentiation, so =-2^2 gives 4: the difference users may expect)

### Article on the page (shared/markdown.js, build-manifest.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- The explanatory article of each calculator is its content.md, rendered at build time into its index.html between the article markers, so the page reads without JavaScript and search engines see the text; every build regenerates the block, so content.md is the only place to edit.
- Only the Markdown subset the articles use is rendered: "##" sections and "###" headings, paragraphs, bold, italic, code, links, "-" and "1." lists, pipe tables and formula blocks indented by four spaces. A list, table or formula block may follow a paragraph line directly (CommonMark would continue the paragraph). Raw HTML is shown as text, and only relative and http(s) addresses become links.
- In the FAQ section a bold first line is a question, and its answer is everything up to the next question, shown collapsed. The "#" title and the "**Summary:**" paragraph are left out because the page header shows them; the summary is also the meta description.
- The build fails when an article lacks one of the six sections (Introduction, Formulas, Assumptions and limitations, Worked example, FAQ, Related calculators, in this order) or links to a page that does not exist. The article is not printed: Print / PDF produces the calculation record.

#### Notes

- Verification 2026-10-31: all 115 articles render with their six sections, 5–8 FAQ questions each, 235 formula blocks, 8 tables and no unrendered markup; the 486 related-calculator lines became links (389 by exact name, 97 short names resolved through the related ids of the schema and checked one by one); 2 Node tests in shared/tests.js; browser check of beam-deflection in light and dark mode.

#### Sources

- CommonMark Spec 0.31.2 (emphasis, code spans, links, indented code blocks) and the GitHub Flavored Markdown table extension, for the subset used

### Worked example as data and "Load this example" (shared/example.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- Every calculator carries the worked example of its article as schema.example: the inputs, with the units the article uses, and the results quoted exactly as printed. Inputs not listed keep their defaults; for 102 of the 115 calculators the defaults are the worked example itself.
- "Load this example" resets the calculator, applies the example inputs and the units of the article (for the inputs given with a unit and for every quoted result), recalculates and scrolls to the calculator; the share link then carries the example.
- The check, a self-test of every calculator and a build gate, requires each quote to appear in the worked example as a whole (not inside a longer number such as −490.4 or a longer unit such as m³) and calculate() to round to it: within half a unit of the last printed decimal; a whole number to its last significant digit, trailing zeros not significant (848 800 means 848 800 ± 50); one unit of the last decimal when the quote is marked "≈" or "about"; or a tolerance stated with the quote. A quote shows the value only as precisely as the article prints it.

#### Notes

- Verification 2026-10-31: 115 examples, checked by run-tests.js and build-manifest.js. They were drafted by computing every output at the defaults and searching the article for it, then reviewed against each article; 13 were written by hand because the article uses other inputs or options (Holtrop–Mennen 1982 variant, Mercator on the sphere, beam deflection with the tabulated IPE 200, deep-water waves, a hydrostatics barge, among others), and a sweep over the select options flagged the articles whose main example differs from the defaults.
- The check found errors in five articles, each corrected with a note in its calculator: Holtrop–Mennen (the figures of the paper printed instead of the results of the calculator, R_F(1+k1), η_H and the 1984 increase), Mercator sailing (meridional parts), hull roughness penalty (speed rounded to 6.5 m/s), optimal charter speed (rounding) and pipe flow (friction factors). On the way, four calculators were found using a truncated knot (0.514444 m/s) instead of the exact 1852/3600 m/s of shared/units.js; they now take it from there.

#### Sources

- The worked example section of each content.md, with the references it cites

### Preferred number series for resistors and capacitors (shared/eseries.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- Standard values are the IEC 60063:2015 E6, E12, E24 and E96 series, repeated in every decade; the nearest value is taken on a logarithmic scale, because the series are spaced geometrically.
- The usual tolerances are E6 20 %, E12 10 %, E24 5 % and E96 1 %; a part from a series can be made to a tighter tolerance than its series implies.
- Component values are read as marked (IEC 60062 clause 5): a letter p, n, u or µ, m, R, k, M or G is the SI prefix and may stand in for the decimal point (4k7 = 4.7 kΩ, 2R2 = 2.2 Ω, 4n7 = 4.7 nF); a plain number takes the unit the calculator states.

#### Notes

- Verification 2026-11-07: the tables were checked value by value against IEC 60063:2015 Tables 1 and 2; E96 has 96 values and E24 contains every E12 and E6 value.

#### Sources

- IEC 60063:2015 Preferred number series for resistors and capacitors

### Reference fluid properties (shared/fluids.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- Fresh water at 20 °C (998.2 kg/m³, 1.004 cSt) and sea water at 15 °C and 35 g/kg (1025.87 kg/m³, 1.188 cSt) follow ITTC 7.5-02-01-03; air is taken at 20 °C and 101.325 kPa.
- Fuels and oils are typical values for the named ISO 8217 and SAE grades at the stated temperature; a real product can differ by several per cent in density and by a factor of two in viscosity, so the custom fluid takes data-sheet values.

#### Notes

- The table is identical to pipe-flow/calc.js FLUIDS, so pipe flow, Reynolds number, pipe volume, flow velocity, Bernoulli and hydrostatic pressure all agree for the same fluid (checked 2026-11-07).

#### Sources

- ITTC Recommended Procedures and Guidelines 7.5-02-01-03, Fresh Water and Seawater Properties (2011)
- ISO 8217:2017 Petroleum products — Fuels (class F) — Specifications of marine fuels (grade viscosity and density limits)

### Power, current and voltage conversions (shared/power.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- DC power is V × I; single-phase AC power is V × I × cos φ with RMS values; three-phase power is √3 × V_LL × I × cos φ for a balanced load, with the line-to-line voltage and the line current.
- Apparent power is real power divided by the power factor; harmonics are not included, so for drives and rectifiers the true RMS current is higher.

#### Notes

- The same relations as three-phase-power and kva-to-amps, gathered in one module for the conversion pages (checked 2026-11-07 against those calculators).

#### Sources

- Hughes, Electrical and Electronic Technology, 12th ed., ch. 2 (DC power) and ch. "Three-phase systems" (P = √3 V_L I_L cos φ)

### American Wire Gauge and conductor resistance (shared/awg.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- AWG diameters follow the ASTM B258 defining formula d = 0.005 in × 92^((36 − n) / 39), exact for the solid wire of each gauge; 0000 is 0.4600 in and 36 is 0.0050 in.
- Resistance is computed from the resistivity at 20 °C (copper 1.7241 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m per IEC 60028, aluminium 1350 2.8264 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m) scaled linearly with temperature, divided by the area; stranded conductors add the ASTM B8 increment of 2 %.
- Metric sizes are the IEC 60228 nominal cross-sections, 0.5 to 1000 mm²; real IEC conductors are made to a maximum resistance, not to a nominal area, so their resistance can differ from ρ/A by a few percent.

#### Notes

- Verification 2026-11-07: at 75 °C the module gives 3.07, 1.93 and 1.21 Ω/1000 ft for solid 14, 12 and 10 AWG copper, 1.24 Ω/1000 ft for stranded 10 AWG and 0.0608 Ω/1000 ft for stranded 4/0, as listed in NEC Chapter 9 Table 8.

#### Sources

- ASTM B258-18, Standard Specification for Standard Nominal Diameters and Cross-Sectional Areas of AWG Sizes of Solid Round Wires Used as Electrical Conductors
- ASTM B8-23, Concentric-Lay-Stranded Copper Conductors (standard increment of resistance 2 %)
- IEC 60028:1925, International standard of resistance for copper; IEC 60228:2004 Conductors of insulated cables (nominal sizes)
- NFPA 70, National Electrical Code (2023), Chapter 9 Table 8 (conductor properties; used only as a check)

### Premixed concrete bags and weight (shared/concrete.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- A bag of premixed concrete yields 0.60 ft³ per 80 lb of dry mix (0.45 ft³ per 60 lb, 0.30 ft³ per 40 lb), as printed on US premix bags; metric bags use the same yield per kilogram, 11.7 L per 25 kg. Mixes with a different aggregate yield a little more or less, so check the bag.
- The weight in place uses normal-weight concrete at 2 400 kg/m³ (about 150 lb/ft³, 4 050 lb per cubic yard).
- Bag counts are rounded up to whole bags after the waste allowance; ready-mix costs use the order volume including waste.

#### Notes

- Verification 2026-11-07: one cubic yard needs 45 bags of 80 lb, 60 of 60 lb and 90 of 40 lb, the figures in US premix yield charts.

#### Sources

- QUIKRETE Concrete Mix (No. 1101) product data: yield about 0.60 ft³ per 80 lb bag, 0.45 ft³ per 60 lb bag
- EN 1991-1-1:2002 Table A.1 (normal-weight concrete 24 kN/m³)

### Moist-air properties (shared/psychro.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- Saturation pressure from the Hyland–Wexler equations of ASHRAE Fundamentals Chapter 1 (eq. 5 over ice below 0 °C, eq. 6 over water), valid from −100 to 200 °C; below 0 °C the dew point is the frost point.
- Moist air is treated as a mixture of ideal gases (ASHRAE eqs. 20, 26, 30); the enhancement factor, below 0.5 % near atmospheric pressure, is neglected.
- Wet bulb is the thermodynamic wet-bulb temperature from eq. (33) above freezing and (35) below; a sling psychrometer reads close to it at normal air speeds.
- Standard atmospheric pressure at altitude follows ASHRAE eq. (3), the US Standard Atmosphere below 11 km.

#### Notes

- Verification 2026-11-07: saturation pressure 0.25990 kPa at −10 °C, 2.3388 kPa at 20 °C, 3.1692 kPa at 25 °C and 101.42 kPa at 100 °C (ASHRAE Table 3); dry air at 15 °C and 101.325 kPa is 1.2250 kg/m³; standard pressure at 1 500 m is 84.556 kPa (ASHRAE Table 1).

#### Sources

- ASHRAE Handbook — Fundamentals (SI), Chapter 1 Psychrometrics: eqs. (3), (5), (6), (20), (26), (30), (33), (35); Tables 1 and 3
- Hyland, R.W. and Wexler, A. (1983), Formulations for the thermodynamic properties of the saturated phases of H2O from 173.15 K to 473.15 K, ASHRAE Transactions 89(2A)

### Pipe friction and fitting losses (shared/pipes.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- Darcy friction factor from the Colebrook–White equation in turbulent flow and 64/Re in laminar flow (below Re 2 300); the transition zone 2 300–4 000 is uncertain in any method.
- Fitting losses by the Crane TP-410 method: K = f_T × L/D, with f_T the fully turbulent friction factor of clean commercial steel (ε = 0.046 mm) for the pipe bore; entrance K = 0.5 (sharp-edged) and exit K = 1.0.

#### Notes

- Verification 2026-11-07: f_T computed for 1, 2, 4 and 8 in Schedule 40 bores is 0.0225, 0.0190, 0.0163 and 0.0141, within 0.001 of the rounded values tabulated in Crane TP-410 (0.023, 0.019, 0.017, 0.014).

#### Sources

- Crane Co., Technical Paper No. 410, Flow of Fluids Through Valves, Fittings and Pipe (2018), Appendix A: friction factors for clean commercial steel and representative resistance coefficients (L/D)
- Colebrook, C.F. (1939), Turbulent flow in pipes, J. Inst. Civil Engineers 11

### Water and steam properties, IAPWS-IF97 (shared/iapws97.js)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- IAPWS Industrial Formulation 1997, Revised Release R7-97(2012): basic equations of region 1 (compressed liquid, 0–350 °C), region 2 (superheated vapour to 800 °C), region 4 (saturation) and the B23 boundary, up to 100 MPa.
- Region 3 (around the critical point, above 350 °C at pressures above the B23 line) and region 5 (800–2 000 °C) are not included; states there raise an error rather than an extrapolated value.

#### Notes

- Verification 2026-11-07: every value of verification Tables 5 (region 1), 15 (region 2), 35 and 36 (saturation) and the B23 test point is reproduced to all nine printed digits. Coefficients transcribed from the release PDF; exponents read from the superscript text spans.

#### Sources

- IAPWS R7-97(2012), Revised Release on the IAPWS Industrial Formulation 1997 for the Thermodynamic Properties of Water and Steam (Tables 1, 2, 10, 11, 34 and verification Tables 5, 15, 35, 36)

### Tools panel: share link, send to, sweep, heat map, goal seek, tornado, uncertainty, scenarios, batch, record (shared/features/)

#### Assumptions and caveats

- Share link: the address bar carries only the inputs and display units that differ from the defaults, in schema units and rounded to 10 significant digits (the precision of the number fields), under a version tag (v=1). Free-text inputs (data lists, budgets) travel in the link as well, so long data makes long links. Opening a link resets everything it does not name to the default; an entry that is not a valid input, option or unit is listed in the banner and never applied.
- Send to: a chain copies values into another calculator in that calculator's own schema units, converting only between units of the same quantity. A raw copy (same number, different quantity group, such as tonnes per day stored as a mass) is declared per link; select options travel only when the target has them or through a declared map. Inputs that are not sent keep the target's defaults, and the target page lists what it received.
- Send to checks: every chain is validated when the manifest is built (target fields exist, quantities match, options exist, conditional chains explain themselves) and run end to end at the source defaults (the target must accept every value and calculate); either failure stops the build.
- Sweep: one input runs over 2–200 linear or geometric points while the others keep their current values, and every point is a full calculate() call, so the curve is exactly what the page would show. Points the calculator rejects are left as gaps, never interpolated. The range follows the current value (½× to 1.5×) until it is edited; an edited range is converted when its unit changes.
- Heat map: two inputs run over a grid of 3–41 linear or geometric points each (whole-number inputs rounded, duplicates dropped) while the others keep their current values; every cell is a full calculate() call, and cells the calculator rejects are hatched, never interpolated. The colours are seven equal-interval classes of one blue ramp between the smallest and the largest result of that map (light to dark; the ramp flips in dark mode so low values recede into the surface), so a colour means different values on two maps; the legend, the per-cell tooltip, the table and the CSV give the numbers. The map is recalculated when the calculator inputs change unless a full map took more than 2 s, in which case it waits for the button.
- Goal seek: the range is scanned at 80 points (geometric when it spans 100× or more) for sign changes of result − target, and each bracket is refined by bisection to 1e-12 relative. Every root found is listed and the one nearest the current value is reported. A result that touches the target without crossing it between two scan points (a double root) can be missed; narrow the range to find it.
- Tornado: each input in turn is multiplied by 1 ∓ p/100 (default 10 %; whole numbers move by at least 1; clamped to the valid range) with the others held, and the inputs are ranked by the larger change of the chosen result. This one-at-a-time measure ignores interactions between inputs and, for a non-linear result, depends on p; inputs at zero cannot be scaled and are listed, as are inputs without effect and changed values the calculator rejects.
- Uncertainty band: inputs are treated as uncorrelated. The linear column is the law of propagation (GUM eq. 10) with central-difference sensitivity coefficients (step max(10⁻⁶|x|, 10⁻⁴u)), one-sided at the edge of an input's valid range. The ±95 % column is 1.96 u (normal, large degrees of freedom), not a Welch–Satterthwaite expanded uncertainty: use the GUM calculator for that. The Monte Carlo check (GUM Supplement 1) samples each input from a normal or rectangular distribution with a fixed seed, so a rerun repeats; draws the calculator rejects are dropped and counted.
- Probability of passing a limit: after a propagation, any result can be checked against a limit typed in its display unit. The Monte Carlo estimate is the fraction of valid draws above (or below) the limit, with a 95 % Wilson score interval that covers the sampling error only, not the choice of input distributions; a draw equal to the limit counts on neither side, and when no draw (or every draw) passes, only the 95 % bound is given. The normal approximation next to it reads the result as normal with the linear u, so it misjudges the tails when the result is non-linear in the inputs or an input is rectangular. Draws the calculator rejects are dropped (the count is reported), which biases the probability when they cluster beyond the limit. The results are cleared as soon as the calculator inputs change.
- Scenarios are stored per calculator in this browser's local storage: they are not shared with other browsers or devices and are lost when the site data is cleared. Values count as different above 1e-12 relative; free text is compared too and shown as a short preview with its line count.
- Batch: the header row holds input ids (a "(unit)" suffix is ignored) and the values are in schema units; columns left out keep the current values; decimal commas are accepted in semicolon-separated files only; at most 5 000 rows; each row runs the same calculate() as the page and a failing row reports its own error.
- Calculation record: the JSON file holds the inputs (schema units), the display units, every output, the warnings and three version stamps: the library version, a SHA-256 of the calculator's calc.js and one of the shared computational modules. Loading a record made with a different calc.js restores the inputs and warns that the results may differ. Print / PDF uses the browser's print engine with a print stylesheet: one column, tools hidden, notes opened, the version stamps in a header.

#### Notes

- Verification 2026-10-31: 17 Node tests in shared/features/tests.js (exact stand-in calculators: √2 by goal seek, u = √0.73 by the linear law, Monte Carlo within 3 %, the Wilson intervals of Newcombe 1998 and the normal tail for the probability of passing a limit, a tornado ranking with a rejected, a clamped, a whole-number and a zero input, a heat-map grid with a rejected cell and the class and cell-edge helpers, RFC 4180 quoting, record round trip, chain conversion and validation) and browser checks of every tool; the 39 chains of the library pass the build-time end-to-end check.
- A typed number that belongs to a unit (a sweep or search limit, a goal-seek target, an absolute ± tolerance) remembers its unit and is converted when that quantity's unit is switched on the calculator.
